I was looking through the Under $5 tag filtered by 'Lowest Price,' one of my favorite pastimes, and first on the list was a game called
. That was when I knew: somebody must have finally filled the gaping void in the Moscow subway system simulator genre! Without a second thought, I had the game in my queue.
really goes out of its way to get the little details right. Before I even made it to the main menu, my PC actually slowed to a grinding halt, like it was bogged down by a higher volume than it could handle. The information was presented in a way that was not readily apparent to somebody who did not already know what to do. Even the color inside the subway trains was accurate. It really brought back fond memories of my trip to Moscow!
After the first forty minutes or so, though, the game changed tone, and strayed away from the public transportation angle. You can walk down the rails, and you don't always get instantly hit and killed by a train with little or no warning. Also, there was a repair issue with the train I was started on. A fluorescent light was coming out of its fixture in the back car, creating a passenger hazard. The game didn't explain any of this, so maybe it was a bug they're patching, or maybe just a condition on my specific play-through?
I was worried I would get in trouble with Steam for trying to cheat, but I went exploring away from the rail to see if I could maybe catch another train. All I could find was a few thousand feet of empty hallways, some open sewage, and a couple ventilation shafts.
If there was one detail they could have improved, I would have to say it would be the people. The Moscow subway system is never this empty! There was just one girl who showed up from time to time. She didn't make a whole lot of noise and it was pretty obvious when I'd see her, so I didn't pay much attention to her. She was much less intimidating than the average Moscow subway rider, so I would say they can work on that in the next patch.
Overall, it was a pretty good sim, but I would have liked to see more than two trains, and only one of them could move! It was nice how the game ended with a train leaving, though, since it began with you on one, like the journey was coming full circle! Also, the mattresses weren't very bouncy. Maybe they could fix that too. 7/10; rent before buying.

It's crazy and quite challenging.  Even though I do recommend trying it out I have to say the game comes up short.  What I mean is that it has all the makings of a really amazing game but they just don't quite come through.
It has an awesome two-bladed brawling system with lots of options to mix up the combat, and a dashing system that allows you to move at incredible speeds, but there is no targeting system so it's easy to end up swinging or moving the wrong directions.
It has a third person shooter mode that allows you to break up the monotony of combat, but there is no cover system that allows you to take full advantage of this and switching between the combat modes is extremely frustrating.
The camera can be controlled, but if you are not actively controlling it then it wanders into the worst possible positions, and odds are that you don't have a free thumb to be manipulating it.
There's a decent story line that seems to be going on but it has no solid presentation to it, so we are stuck watching the conflicts between these various factions from one character's perspective and we hardly know what their motives even are.  All we really know is that Ayumi wants to get out of Dragonland (original) preferably with some treasure.  Everyone else just seems to want to kill you and that's all that seem relevant.
There is an upgrade system but it's largely unsatisfying.  Your basic skills remain largely the same you mostly just build on your magic.
The controls were not prioritized well and many functions just won't work at critical moments.  I almost think that the programmers thought that this should be the central idea for the final boss fight.  The game is challenging but some of the challenges feel like they went the whole wrong way.
There is some intense challenges in this game, but sometimes you'll just get stumped on what do, like when you encounter the Slasher on the Skydock.  You'll end up dead and then looking at the screen wondering where you went wrong.
In all, Blades of Time feels like a pretty good game with a REALLY AWESOME game trying to get out.  It mixes combat systems in a really cool way, but doesn't polish them to make them shine.  It gives us a story, but can't be bothered for good presentation.  It gives us controls that work except when it decides not to.  It give us puzzles and challenges with very little feedback on how things should be done.  In short, it needs a lot of work.
7/10.

Bastion should be counted among those few games that not only meet, buy even exceed all the promises we get in their early description. Being one of the most beautiful and climatic games of 2011 this action RPG shines brightly even now, still as fresh and original as during its release.
The game itself is not so complicated. You take up role of a Kid, waking up, all alone, surrounded by beautiful yet crumbling world falling apart into thousand pieces. What You need to do is get to the Bastion – safe heaven set up to shelter those who’d survive any crisis threatening Your homeland – city of Caelondia.
To Your aid, in a quest to find, and rebuild Bastion, You’ll get a vast arsenal of even the weirdest weapons, each coming with different mechanics and “special skills” which further enhance Your possible combat strategies. Further modifications to Your play-style can be achieved through quite original system of upgradable structures built inside the Bastion, which allow Kid to chose worshiped “gods” in a shrine, or special drinks in a distillery each differently affecting game environment, providing new opportunities or threats.
Despite game mechanics being pretty simple it’s not easy to get bored with ‘Bastion’ even after a few long hours, but what really makes this game stand out is its unique way of telling the story. Most of our actions are commented actively by omniscient narrator, who not only slowly reveals some details behind tragic events that left the whole world in ruins, but also perfectly portraits the Kid and his few friends, allowing us to immerse into the games plot on a level rarely seen in video games.
The last thing worth mentioning about ‘Bastion’ is it’s astonishing soundtrack. Composed by Darren Korb this game’s music fits its dreamy, hand-drawn canvas perfectly, strongly enhancing the impact of the narrative.
Overall, I consider this game to be one of the most amazing feats of storytelling in video games, and definitely one of my favorites. And don’t get scared that the game relying so heavy on its story will get boring after just one completion. NG+ and Score Attack modes, matched which some arena-styled levels will allow You to spend long hours in “Bastion's” captivating world !
- One of the most beautiful soundtracks out there.
- Light, yet interesting story with uniqe responsive narration.
- Vast amount of weapons, special skills and other modifications.
- High replayability with NG+ and Score Attack.
- To some, controls may feel a little unresponsive (I base on some friends opinions)

Nimble quest is an interesting game, but ultimately one I don't think is worth your time.
The game has a number of good points, it's well animated for what it is, the heros are varied and each one is distinct enough to be interesting, and the characters even gain new sprites when they level up.
But all of that is lost behind the appalling game design that stems from being made for mobiles.  You can spend 'tokens' to buy large boosts to damage, speed and health for runs through the game.  You can also spend them to continue your current run, but the cost doubles each time you do so, starting from one.  Tokens are rare drops, you get perhaps one every five levels.  So you're already stressed for tokens if you just use them as drops.  However, you can buy tokens for 'gems'.  Gems are your other ingame currency, which can be used to level up.
At a certain point in the game you simply need to level up and use the boosts to progress.  And that means grinding.  Lots and lots of grinding.
Now I'm not opposed to grinding in general.  After all, playing the game is why we're here, so being forced to play the game isn't bad, of itself.  The problem comes when you have to to a number of 'bad' runs without spending tokens on the boosts so that you can then do a good run in order to get to the next level and unlock the next character.
So it's a nice idea, it's a nice game, but you can smell the scent of addiction mechanics all over it.  And it just isn't a good thing.
Nimble quest.  Worth your money, but not your time.

This game is nice and short, and has a pretty good story. (Not a bedtime story though. No no no no -NO-. Don't make the mistake I made of playing it right before I had been intending to go to bed. Going to bed after playing this little gem wouldn't work out very well). I did notice that there are three phases and I'm pretty sure you have to get each and every little snippet out of each and every object to trigger the switches between phases. I did get kind of lost on occasion because I didn't create a set order to go through the objects in for myself, so sometimes I was left searching around for that one item I didn't examine during that phase. I'll give a small hint about how to handle the phases without spoiling anything.
Phase 1, you know you've got all the unique snippets you're gonna get from an object when you start getting said unique snippets repeated from that object, which is your cue to move on to the next object.
Phase 2, there's one common dialog set across all items once you've gotten all unique snippets from the particular object, so (after you figure out what the common set is) when a phrase from that common set is used, get moving to the next object. (There is one object that has a unique phrase -very- similar in nature to the common phrase set, however the wording is not 100% the same as the common set version so keep clicking if you think something's off).
Phase 3, once you've gotten all the unique phrases you're gonna get from an object, you won't be able to examine it anymore. Arguably makes this phase the easiest to navigate. Do be sure to avoid accidentally double-clicking or clicking again before he's finished speaking though- you won't get that dialog back without playing a second time through. (I guess that goes for phase 2 as well).
For the whole thing, I would try to go clockwise around the room (or whatever set pattern works for you). Try to really be sure there's nothing left to examine from your current standing point before switching to another standing point. Each new phase does open up some new things to examine, so you'll have to be sure again at every standing point every new phase. Don't just charge through the same things you examined in previous phases during new phases or you'll likely miss a lot of the (fairly good) story and possibly even get stuck.
I find the story's good point isn't so much the originality of the scenario, but the main character's reactions to his memories, realizations, and emotions. I'll admit the scenario itself is likely somewhat of a common one, however there are plenty of stories out there that are good more for their characters then their scenario. This is most definitely one of them, in spite of only having two characters (and only one that you ever actually 'see'). (Again though, for your own sake, please don't play this right before the time you're planning to go to bed. It's tagged as "dark" for a darn good reason. Any other time of day is 100% fine and even recommended). Short and sweet story.
Even if you don't end up enjoying it quite as much as I did, it only takes ~1 hour (maybe less) to play through, not a terrible amount of time, and it's free, so you've got absolutely nothing what-so-ever to lose from giving it whirl. Give it a try, you'll probably like it, and even if you don't then oh well- you didn't really lose anything.

Blades of Time is a second-tier game, but a good one.  The feel is similar to God of War, but somewhat less epic.  Combat is mostly straightforward - heavy on mashing the LMB, light on complex combo sequences - but the gradual addition of unlockable abilities adds enough tactical options to keep the fights engaging.
The big selling point to Blades of Time is the "Time Rewind" mechanic that allows you to stay in place while rewinding time by a few seconds, allowing you to team up with your past self to defeat difficult enemies or solve puzzles.  It's a minor innovation that pales after a few uses, and I quickly found myself eschewing the mechanic in favour of good old button-mashing mayhem, except when faced with bosses and puzzles that demanded it.
Gameplay is very linear; you're pretty-much marched down one continuous corridor from mob fight, to puzzle area, to boss arena and onwards.  That particular sin is typical of this genre, though, and when such games do give you the freedom to revisit past areas (as in Darksiders) it doesn't really add much to the gameplay, anyway.

A game in the vein of Game Dev Tycoon that aims to add some more depth with features like building & outfitting rooms.
While the added complexity is fun at first, the underlying mechanics don't work well. The success of games seems to depend entirely on the amount of "points" invested into them. That is, if you have a good and/or large enough Staff, producing a lot of graphics/sound/tech/gameplay points, EVERYTHING will get great reviews.
I just got a "Music FPS/Sports"-Game without graphics to get the Game of the Year award...
I prefer the Game Dev Tycoon model, where even if you sink extreme amounts of time and money into something, it might still flop because the initial concept just doesn't work. Just like in real life.
Another aspect is the economy.
Income & Development costs do not scale well. Now this might be due to the fact that due to the abovementioned problem, ALL my games were getting 90%+ reviews no matter what I did, but essentially I ended up with unlimited money at some point.
There is also not a really good progression system. Basically my first smash hit allowed me to go straight from a small studio to a huge office building, hire 40+ people and spam games with multiple production rooms/studios. Simultaneously, I could train a dozen code-monkeys in the training room which are now maxed out in most stats and producing the aforementioned >90% games en masse.
Now of course a lot of this might still be due to alpha status and might get finetuned down the road, but at its current state I would not recommend the game.
Overall, it does not handle its own complexity well and is fairly easy to exploit. A lot of refining in regards to the ingame economy is needed in order to make it more challenging & fun, so buying it now is really kind of a gamble.

It's been a while since I wanted to try a good Game development simulator. After reading the reviews and watching let's plays of Game Dev tycoon and Game Dev Story, I came to the conclusion that they both were lacking of deep gameplay and customization mechanics. On the contrary it seemed to be one of the strenght of Mad Games Tycoon which is exactly what convinced me to give it a try.
...and I do not regret it so far:  this game is already very good even on EA. There are flaws and annoying issues of course but also great gameplay mechanics and very good ideas in this game.
Pro's:
-Dozens of game genres (Rpg, RTS, FPS, TPS, Sim, MMO, Arcade, Sport, Fantasy, Strategy....) which can be mixed together with a subgenre AND one of the hundred of themes (SuperHeroes, WW2, Pirates, Mafia, Space, Wizards, Planes, Tanks...). This system allows you to make very unique and customized games following (or not) the public current expectations.
-Office configuration: You create the rooms where your developpers will work, allowing more space and more workforce to key sectors (Research, Development, Support, Server Rooms, Marketing...) This system reminds very much of Theme Hospital and Prison Architect.
-Characters levelling: Your developpers gain experience in different skills when making games or following courses on specific aspects. You can train a "Sound and music effect" expert team working specifically on music-based game for example, the possibilities are huge.
-Ability to create your own game engines: Another gameplay approach is the engine development. Bad at game development? You can create games dedicated engines (customizable with a lot of functionnalities) and sell them to the competitors that will send you royalties when they make games with your engines. This alternate gameplay is one of the examples of the game's depth.
Con's:
-The current major issue to me is balance: For my first game in normal difficulty, without knowing anything of the gameplay mechanics, I ended up with 360M$ in about 20 years, leader on the market, releasing only major hits (90%+, 3 MMO's and 50 games overall) with my own high end game engines, with nothing to fear from the competitors (top 20 games were mines).
-Lack of interaction between us and the competitors: we don't know much about them (stats, strength and weaknesses, no possibility to hire their developpers or see ours being recruted by them). I'd like to see major game companies leading the market with AAA titles like in real life, and struggling to get market shares on their lands. Currently this is simply not the case.
-Not enough building and rooms objects ATM, and more than half of them are useless (why buying cheap desks when you can have the best for almost nothing).
-Not enough control on the work force and the budget in general (you can't adjust the wages, no taxes, no charges...) I understand this would make the game a little more complicated but that's what economic simulations are for IMO.
-Other balance issues: Marketing is basically useless (the publishers do a great job at it and releasing the games on your own (game possibility) is not financially very interesting (you earn millions even without it). Fan mechanics is not developped at all (what do they want? ATM they are only a Score System, sort of...). Some game consoles or computers are not interesting, their market share is too low (why not make unique specificities for them to give them more attractivness: A company focused on casual gaming and movment recognition could target the wii or kinect for example and become one of the leader for these consoles or on this game trend. Or aim at a niche market on another one which would be the best at one type of game.... just toughts.
-Graphics and Music are poor at the moment, but that's not a major concern for me.
-No tutorial (I put it here because I saw a lot of negatives comments about that, but that will change for sure).
Overall this is a very good game but it seriously lacks balance at the moment. If the devs manage to balance all this and keep adding features to it, it will be one of the best economic simulator on the market.
6/10 for the current state of the game, but It has the potential to reach 8/10 easily.

This reminds me a lot of the good old Imperium Galactica, which was one of my big favorites.
You will research ship types and modules, and put together your own ship blueprints from these modules. This gives a lot of fun experimenting with different fighting styles.
Espionage is also very much like in Imperium Galactica, where you hire spies, train them in various missions, and they can get caught, killed, etc.
The tech tree is much like Civilization, it almost feels like some alternative version of Civilization. Same goes for diplomacy, where you have the well known table for exchanging maps, currencies, technologies, etc.
The exploration is more like Civ. There are barbarians attacking, independent planets to trade with, and some areas require you to research certain technologies first (almost like boats for the sea).
The game mostly feels polished, I've only met 1 bug so far - which I fixed by saving and reloading the game.
I also appreciate the possibility to make/apply mods to the game.

Long version:
Alright, so let's analyze how it started.
1. Devs released alpha version in 2012 as I remember well, and said full version will be ready in 2013. They created game with huge potential. Great music, Skyrim-like weapon mechanics, and planetary travelling. But despite that, worlds felt extremely lonely, and gameplay was♥♥♥♥♥♥ All monsters where copy-paste of some pokemons, that had same fighting mechanics. After playing Terraria, Starbound planets were really boring. It felt like in No Man's Sky - huge emptiness.
2. Devs lied. Game in 2013 was still in alpha stage, and devs suddenly stopped working on this game for some time. Players, including me felt betrayed. Starbound was flooded by negative reviews saying this game is just a unfinished promise, to get money from naive players. We were so♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off, and devs were ignoring our comments, so we felt it's over, game with huge potential ended right here.
3. Devs came back. It was 2014 or 2015, i don't remember very well, but they came back, and worked on game harder than ever before. They resurrected this game, and finally finished in 2016.
-----------------
Things they fixed since alpha/beta:
+ Game has lore. And you feel it, when you travel. That there is some great evil lurking far away.
+ Fighting mechanics. Weaponary has much higher variation, 2-handed weapons have special skills, and enemies are finally unique in way they're fighting. Plus they added 4 character skills, that you can use AT ONCE. Not like in Beta - only 1 at once. You start with 3 after first lore quest: Dash, Double jump, Transformation into a small ball (to sneak in small holes).
+ Planets are no longer empty. They have cities, and small villages. Sometimes 1, sometimes 2 or even 3. Populated by NPC, that have unique architecture depending on their race, bunch of shops and small quests, that are very nice to do. Deeper underground has some ruins populated with bad guys, and the deepest part is a lava and core fragments. I honestly was not expecting a great deal from this game, but in retrospect I think I gave the game too little credit on my first glance. This is actually a rather plesant slimed down Turn-Based Strat game, so for those who want a Sci-Fi version of Tottal War, but with a more basic aproach then this is an ideal game for you. If you want something intensely complicated and in-depth then this is a game to make a pass on and take a look at Stelaris instead.
I found myself drawn into the more minor characteristics of the game rather than the main mechanics. For one, I have to say the character visualizations in diplomacy is extremely well done, and the All-Star voice acting cast is much more of a draw for me than I anticipted. Combined, this made the diplomacy/narritive more engaging than typical games. With that said, this is the RARE strategy game that has a half-decent diplomacy system! Negociations are in general what one can expect, but I wish they would use my captured spies as bargining chips rather than just kill them. On that note, the spycraft for the game is somewhat basic, but still functional enough to make it a valid component of the game, but spycraft is a hard fit for this genra to balance out appropriately.
The combat system is one of the best parts of the game I find. I love the aspect that you can have a hybrid system where the AI takes over the multitasking functions while you can focus on a single task (or stack tasks via pause function). The combat visualizations are somewhat generic, but the gameplay itself is very solid. I find myself confident in my ability to command, but there is always still that edge of if I developed my fleet for the right task (where as some games its so imbalanced you can spam 1-2 units and call it a day).
Lastly, for those who are running a less than top-teir computers, this game is more lightweight (at least from my perspective) than other high-CPU demanding games.
All in all, this is a very good buy for the sci-fi gamer or the TBS type gamer. A must have for those who love both.

//N.P.P.D. RUSH// - The milk of Ultra Violet is friggin' weird, man. Set in a hellish cyberpunk future, you play the dying, limbless head-and-torso of a Nox junkie, freshly amputated and installed into a police-issue battlemech and sent forth to rescue 30 unfortunate women from the industrial dystopia that is Nauseous Pines before your life support systems fail or you simply get shot to pieces by drugged-up mutants and murderous nuclear snipers. The setting alone was more than enough to get me interested, and the gameplay certainly sounded compelling, but the final product is a whole lot more unpersonable than I'd hoped.
The game consists of five levels, each of which is filled with monsters, a number of women, and an exit that takes you to the next floor and offers you a chance to shop for upgrades. Killing opponents along the way earns you coins, which you can spend to delay the inevitable onset of time death, upgrade your weaponry, or rent a hooker for a health boost. More dubious services available include selling your "excess" organs for cash or getting a Nox hit, greatly healing you but causing your perception of time to get slippery. While there aren't too many enemies to encounter, the levels are randomly generated, so each game layout is at least a suprise. Unfortunately, that's exactly what you don't need in this game.
The visuals are heavily glitched out, resembling an NES game undergoing severe and likely fatal errors. Each foe you kill smears the screen with an opaque haze of red; each injury you sustain stains the screen blue. Every encounter leaves you semi-blind and hoping for the best. Even worse, your field of vision is intentionally so short that you'll be blazing along at high speeds, only to crash into an opponent and take heavy damage. The reaction time needed to not get mangled is inhumanly fast, and since the game has a timer, you're not exactly willing to go forward cautiously. The interlevel shops certainly help somewhat, but money's a scarce commodity, and spending time killing every opponent you come across is two kinds of suicide. In the end it winds up being a manic, stressful, anxiety-laden experience, and the lack of any sort of unlockables or achievements leaves you feeling that your 30 or 40 agonizing deaths served no purpose. Admittedly, you'll get better with time, but the game is still NES-title unfair and actively tries to aggravate you into quitting. It's a neat little art project with some gorgeous visuals and an enticing knack for authentic old-school agony, but if you're looking for a game you'll actually want to beat, look somewhere else.

Significantly better than Enemy Unknown, but still carries many of that game's problems such as graphics errors and some totally stupid hit percentages and thus, many a mission successful depends on hail maries and a save scum. As one review site described it, "XCOM 2 is a game where you can do everything right and still lose." — Which understandably can turn players off a STRATEGY game.
A 22% chance to hit a flanked Muton, from short range, from the high ground, is indeed absurd. Though overall, the hit chances have been improved and I suspect you can mod it if you really want to.
That being said, the strategic layer of the game has been improved immensely, the character customization is top notch, this game's version of "satellites" is better, the concealment and hacking are welcome additions, the sniper is much more useful, all the new classes are cool, melee is slightly OP but a welcome addition.
Despite some graphics glitches, if you can stomach or mod some of the numerical absurdities on the tactical level and suspend your disbelief regarding the need to establish comms towers to enable your flying fortress to traverse the globe and the fact that there are never any resistance fighters at resistance camps that are under attack — the game is a lot of fun and has tons of replay value.
As an aside, I bought this game on sale for $30 because I'm sorry, but 79.99 being the new Canadian-standard price for video games has no excuse and no, not "but muh Canadian dollar!" lie — this is digital distribution, come on — I heard a million times working game retail. They will continue to charge outlandish prices only if you continue to pay it, people!

Summary: Immersive, atmospheric game. It's like a visual novel, but much shorter. Visual short story, maybe.
PROS: The amount of interactions are just right for me: enough to be interesting, yet focused. Each interactive point reveals more about the story. I like how the game showed progression. Well-developed story overall. The graphics, layout and operation of the game were very intuitive. I am a heathen who plays games with a trackpad, so I promise you that it is easy to figure out.
CONS: DO NOT HIT THE ESCAPE BUTTON. It will destroy your progress. I was about 80% done when I got stuck and tried to look for a hint. When the game boots up, you're thrown right into the gameplay, similar to Dear Esther. I went with ESC to get out of full screen or to a menu, but that just quits the game. I have no idea if there is any actual way to save your progress.
I also don't know if there are any ways to change in-game settings, such as brightness and sound. There is a voice narrating the game, as well as subtitles for you to read. I did not like hearing the voice. That's not to say that it is bad voice acting; on the contrary, I think it was too well done. Listening to this guy for five minutes made me quickly understand why his relationship went the way it did. Unfortunately, I am not entirely sure that was the creators' intent. I just realized now I could have muted my speakers while playing... Learn from my mistakes.
NEUTRAL: [Slight spoilers] The story was fleshed out well, but I wouldn't say it was anything fresh. The idea of an unreliable narrator isn't really new or exciting, in my opinion, especially when it does not fundamentally alter the gameplay. The foreshadowing was a little heavy-handed in some places. There are moments in the game that are opportunities to elicit a reaction from the gamer, but unfortunately all but once, it just progressed as I expected. The one time I did have an actual reaction was right by the end, and that was to snap and cheer "YASSSSS SERENA!!"
TL;DR Serena is to games like Toyota Camrys are to cars. I recommend it because it is free, and the parts that bugged me may not apply to a wider audience.

Boy, I hope you like praise.
Bastion got it right. The visuals are gorgeous, the gameplay stays fresh all the way to the end of the final level, the soundtrack is my favorite of any game's I've heard in at least the last five years, the narrator could probably carry the game on his own without any of the rest of these elements, and the story is presented enticingly through the combination of all of the above. And it's all beautiful. Every last bit. The visuals, the soundtrack, the story, the narrator's gritty voice. Even the gameplay has a way about it.
The use of color alone is flawless. The world is drenched in vibrant color, without appearing tacky and garish. The locales you explore are always new and distinct in appearance. The art and design bring to life post-Calamity Caelondia and the surrounding regions so well, and there isn't a single dull moment for your eyes in any of it.
Bastion constantly introduces new weapons every level or two, and each weapon you wield brings with it a completely unique play style. The hammer is tough but not the quickest weapon, while the machete slices quickly and can be thrown at distant targets. The bow can shoot an accurate shot which pierces and gains power with proper timing, but the musket shoots a spread of weaker projectiles to blow through a crowd. My personal favorite combination is the pike and mortar. The pike has great distance and power but is a little slow between attacks, while the mortar fires an explosive round further the longer the attack button is held down.
Each weapon is introduced within a level, forcing you to use it until you can reach an Arsenal. This is a great design choice, forcing players to experience and understand the pros and cons of each weapon rather than tossing them aside without giving them a chance. I can say I probably never would have traded my musket in if it weren't for those mandatory stretches of seeing what the alternatives have to offer. They all come in handy, and they all come with their own tactics for use. And they can all be upgraded to improve various aspects from strength to distance, to number of blades thrown, to blast radius, and beyond.
That soundtrack. That *divine* soundtrack. "Build That Wall" would be enough to earn the commendation. It hits me right in the heartstrings, every time. The female vocals and guitar combine to reach some level of calming and touching I can't remember ever hearing in a video game before. The action tunes, the tense tunes, the chill tunes... after two playthroughs and many, many listens to the OST not one of them has lost its magic.
A good deal of the soundtrack has a western twang to it. It's very peculiar. The game is not a western. But the soundtrack, the narrator, bits of the visuals, and some of the weapons very much suggest one. And what can I say? It works.
The first anything you meet when you start Bastion is the disembodied voice of the narrator, whose tough and wise yet always calm demeanor evokes an old cowboy telling a story around a campfire. He's got something to say about everything, and there's no denying that you'll be hanging on each and every word. Even the less important stuff. Near the very beginning of the game, I spent some time destroying everything in an area for no particular reason, and the voice chimed in, "Kid just rages for awhile." Later on, I was racing along as the world fell away behind me, rolling for speed, and he made a note of all my somersaulting. Interacting with various things at the Bastion too many times, equipping a new combination of weapons or a new spirit, and any number of other actions can spark a comment from the narrator and a smile from your face.
The music, the narrator, the visuals, the gameplay - they all serve to present to you the story. And it's an impressively told story, at that. It's not overly long, or ridiculously complicated to that glorious Metal Gear Solid degree. But for a tale that starts immediately following a catastrophic event which left all but a few residents of a prosperous city as people-shaped ash, it doesn't spend as much time as you'd expect making you feel miserable. Which isn't to say that it can't. Bastion can do a lot with a little, making you feel empowered or sympathetic with but a musical drop or an ominous close to a thought by the narrator.
I loved Bastion. I loved everything about it. Well, not the Lunkheads, nor some of the Proving Grounds. But almost everything. To the point where I started a new game+ as soon as the credits finished on my first playthrough. I'm not saying that you will do this. But I am saying that if you are me then you already did.

Admittedly I could've worded my last review better.
Half-Life is a classic, but it's not one that holds up that much. It hasn't aged well, I'm trying to say. And I have plenty of reasons why.
Atmospherically, Half-Life 1 is amazing. Really. The idea of a scientific complex falling into chaos all around you as you desperately try to escape is executed really well, and it's one of the most atmospheric games of its time.
That's where my positive points end. In terms of level design itself, Half-Life 1 is bad. Really bad. There's no map system which is inexcusable in a game so labryinthine. On top of that, a lot of the levels can get cryptic and annoying, some are nearly impossible if you don't have enough health. Like the dam in Surface Tension, where you have to dodge both a fish monster and helicoptor fire while also standing in place opening a valve for just long enough to start drowning. I've hit roadblocks throughout the whole game, barely going 15 minutes without hitting a dead end and being stuck for twice that time. At least, that's my experience.
Black Mesa does everything so much better. It's really the best version of HL1. If you want a better experience with this game, go get that. Who cares about Xen?
Half-Life's actual gameplay is its strong point. It has lots of unique weapons, all of which are really fun to use. Like, really. There are a LOT of weapons. They're all really cool. Other than that, it's okay. I really don't think I have to describe HALF-LIFE'S gameplay to you.
But I do like the gameplay. However, as the levels went on, I started noticing a trend in my playstyle. I would just run past all the enemies, speedrunner-style. I don't really know why. Maybe it was the level design making fights unrewarding. Maybe I just wanted to beat the game to get it over with. But the most likely conclusion is that fighting enemies in HL1 is very unrewarding. In most cases you end up taking more damage by fighting than if you just dash through the area. And as mentioned, the level design doesn't help either. Nearly every enemy uses hitscan and sometimes you're pitted up against nearly 8 of them at once in a singe room.
The game uses music very sparingly. If there's a song, it'll only play once at a key point of the game. So most of the game is quite silent. That's okay, I guess. I don't like silent games, but It's just an excuse to use my own music. The songs it does play are pretty good, though.
Easily the best part of the game. I already mentioned how much I like the atmosphere, but the story is pretty good. That's all I'll say.
Kinda. Things go pretty well until you hit a killjoy roadblock. Something I really like about the game, though, is how small the hitboxes on projectiles are. You can hit someone through the tiniest crack in a wall with a crossbow without the bolt stopping in mid-air on the surrounding walls. If you can see the enemy, you can hit them. Can that be said for many other games? Refer to Level Design for my thoughts on the killjoys.
Look, I get it. Half-Life 1 is a decent game. But it's not a masterpiece. It has a lot of flaws, and I generally didn't enjoy playing this. I really want to like the game, because it's HALF-LIFE. But too much of the game design frustrated me to the point of never wanting to play it again. I did beat the game. But it felt like a chore more than anything. I didn't enjoy Xen at all. Who does? Really though, if you want to play through the best version of Half-Life, go get Black Mesa. It fixes EVERYTHING this game does wrong, and improves on it. If you want a better first-party Half-Life experience, get HL2. It's way more fun in every way and has its own unique set of weapons.
Overall, Half-Life 1: Good gameplay, ruined by awful level design. That being said though, it is quite moddable. Give the community creations a shot sometime, and you may like it better.

This game is the best of the game simulation titles that I have played and while comparable to Game Dev Tycoon it is more akin to Game Dev Story on Android devices. It has more variety, it allows you to build rooms yourself, it has a wider range of training parameters, and the story is considerably longer than other tycoon games. At six hours I just encountered the release of the PS2 where in other games we'd be finished the list of events.
That said the game can be much better. English is clearly not the first language of Eggcode (See event message for game release "3th World War 2") and there needs to be quite a few corrections. Secondly the animation and graphics of the people / employees is terrible. People barely look like people and females are only distinguishable by their names. The game allows you to succeed largely as a producer of engines if you don't have luck making games but I feel this could be expanded and improved to allow for engine marketing and support. Maybe even the design of periphreals to sell with the engine or game. Another issue is that the event messages are strictly limited to other game releases and profit reports. Eggcode should be looking at adding things like conventions, pirating issues, fan requests, and direct interaction with the publishers. The game tracks publisher relationship but that doesn't seem to extend in functionality any further than how likely they are to produce a marketing campaign for your game.

find common egg, raise to max level, raise another egg, fuse together to make uncommon egg. make another uncommon, fuse to make rare, make another rare, fuse to make legendary, make another legendary, fuse to divine.

How Creation Club has been implemented goes against the years of community support Bethesda may or may not have given. The biggest kick in the gut, however, is the fact that CC breaks the Script Extender. The f4se is the reason many mods exist. CC claims to add "mini-dlc", yet they've just pulled a Shadow of War on people, with no gambling, of course.
The single best thing for this game now, is to pull CC from Fallout 4.
Sadly, if they also bring this to Skyrim, then this review may stay negative until both games are fixed.
Yes, fixed. I'm in the firm belief that CC has 'broken' the game, as it can screw over people who play with mods. Basically, a large group of Bethesda's customers.
EDIT: According to many other people, CC mods break load-orders and conflict with normal mods.

Significantly better than Enemy Unknown, but still carries many of that game's problems such as graphics errors and some totally stupid hit percentages and thus, many a mission successful depends on hail maries and a save scum. As one review site described it, "XCOM 2 is a game where you can do everything right and still lose." — Which understandably can turn players off a STRATEGY game.
A 22% chance to hit a flanked Muton, from short range, from the high ground, is indeed absurd. Though overall, the hit chances have been improved and I suspect you can mod it if you really want to.
That being said, the strategic layer of the game has been improved immensely, the character customization is top notch, this game's version of "satellites" is better, the concealment and hacking are welcome additions, the sniper is much more useful, all the new classes are cool, melee is slightly OP but a welcome addition.
Despite some graphics glitches, if you can stomach or mod some of the numerical absurdities on the tactical level and suspend your disbelief regarding the need to establish comms towers to enable your flying fortress to traverse the globe and the fact that there are never any resistance fighters at resistance camps that are under attack — the game is a lot of fun and has tons of replay value.
As an aside, I bought this game on sale for $30 because I'm sorry, but 79.99 being the new Canadian-standard price for video games has no excuse and no, not "but muh Canadian dollar!" lie — this is digital distribution, come on — I heard a million times working game retail. They will continue to charge outlandish prices only if you continue to pay it, people!

Boy, I hope you like praise.
Bastion got it right. The visuals are gorgeous, the gameplay stays fresh all the way to the end of the final level, the soundtrack is my favorite of any game's I've heard in at least the last five years, the narrator could probably carry the game on his own without any of the rest of these elements, and the story is presented enticingly through the combination of all of the above. And it's all beautiful. Every last bit. The visuals, the soundtrack, the story, the narrator's gritty voice. Even the gameplay has a way about it.
The use of color alone is flawless. The world is drenched in vibrant color, without appearing tacky and garish. The locales you explore are always new and distinct in appearance. The art and design bring to life post-Calamity Caelondia and the surrounding regions so well, and there isn't a single dull moment for your eyes in any of it.
Bastion constantly introduces new weapons every level or two, and each weapon you wield brings with it a completely unique play style. The hammer is tough but not the quickest weapon, while the machete slices quickly and can be thrown at distant targets. The bow can shoot an accurate shot which pierces and gains power with proper timing, but the musket shoots a spread of weaker projectiles to blow through a crowd. My personal favorite combination is the pike and mortar. The pike has great distance and power but is a little slow between attacks, while the mortar fires an explosive round further the longer the attack button is held down.
Each weapon is introduced within a level, forcing you to use it until you can reach an Arsenal. This is a great design choice, forcing players to experience and understand the pros and cons of each weapon rather than tossing them aside without giving them a chance. I can say I probably never would have traded my musket in if it weren't for those mandatory stretches of seeing what the alternatives have to offer. They all come in handy, and they all come with their own tactics for use. And they can all be upgraded to improve various aspects from strength to distance, to number of blades thrown, to blast radius, and beyond.
That soundtrack. That *divine* soundtrack. "Build That Wall" would be enough to earn the commendation. It hits me right in the heartstrings, every time. The female vocals and guitar combine to reach some level of calming and touching I can't remember ever hearing in a video game before. The action tunes, the tense tunes, the chill tunes... after two playthroughs and many, many listens to the OST not one of them has lost its magic.
A good deal of the soundtrack has a western twang to it. It's very peculiar. The game is not a western. But the soundtrack, the narrator, bits of the visuals, and some of the weapons very much suggest one. And what can I say? It works.
The first anything you meet when you start Bastion is the disembodied voice of the narrator, whose tough and wise yet always calm demeanor evokes an old cowboy telling a story around a campfire. He's got something to say about everything, and there's no denying that you'll be hanging on each and every word. Even the less important stuff. Near the very beginning of the game, I spent some time destroying everything in an area for no particular reason, and the voice chimed in, "Kid just rages for awhile." Later on, I was racing along as the world fell away behind me, rolling for speed, and he made a note of all my somersaulting. Interacting with various things at the Bastion too many times, equipping a new combination of weapons or a new spirit, and any number of other actions can spark a comment from the narrator and a smile from your face.
The music, the narrator, the visuals, the gameplay - they all serve to present to you the story. And it's an impressively told story, at that. It's not overly long, or ridiculously complicated to that glorious Metal Gear Solid degree. But for a tale that starts immediately following a catastrophic event which left all but a few residents of a prosperous city as people-shaped ash, it doesn't spend as much time as you'd expect making you feel miserable. Which isn't to say that it can't. Bastion can do a lot with a little, making you feel empowered or sympathetic with but a musical drop or an ominous close to a thought by the narrator.
I loved Bastion. I loved everything about it. Well, not the Lunkheads, nor some of the Proving Grounds. But almost everything. To the point where I started a new game+ as soon as the credits finished on my first playthrough. I'm not saying that you will do this. But I am saying that if you are me then you already did.

BE WARNED: This game has NO SAVE FUNCTION and does not ask for confirmation upon quitting. So make sure you set aside at least an hour to play this game uninterrupted.
That said, Serena is well worth that small chunk of your time, especially at the price of a whopping zero dollars.
I'm the sort of gamer who loves to poke her nose into every corner of a game world and examine everything it is possible to examine. If you're like me, you'll get a lot of satisfaction out of exploring Serena's world, small though it is. The responses change as the game progresses, and that's how the truth is gradually revealed.
I found the dialogue to be a bit stilted in places; some of the lines sounded more like how a novel is written than how people actually talk. However, the emotion behind the words definitely feels genuine, making the slow shift in emotional tone that much more effective as you collect more and more tidbits of information.
All in all, Serena is a very well-crafted experience, and the hour or two you spend playing it will not be wasted.

Do I recommend this game? Absolutely. It's a great game. And yes, maybe it's graphics have aged a bit, but then so has System Shock's. Whether it's on sale or not, I would recommend it to just about anyone, so here are some pros and cons.
Pros
-Great music and sound effects. They might be aged like the graphics but they still got it.
-Takes the silent protagonist to a whole new level. You'll really feel like you are Gordon Freeman - even if you're a bit mute.
-The game has some choices that actually give you different endings for a little variety (not that they carry over to other games).
-Despite being a FPS/Survival type game, Half-Life has a godd story that is felt consistently throughout the game.
-Balanced gameplay and various difficulties for those of varying confidence.
-Unique enemies and weapons.
Cons
-The graphics and sound might not always age well, but this is easily countered by nostalgia.
-Though you can go about your journey in varying ways, it is, to an extent, very linear with little real choices. So if branching, choice-driven storylines are your thing, then this is a con. If not, ignore this.
So that's it from me. Not much I can say wrong about this game. And in my opinion, the cons were a bit of a stretch. So what are you waiting for? Get the game! Or wait for a sale...THEN get the game!
Just don't hold your breath for Half Life 3.

I'm a firm believer in that when it comes to Early Access, a review has to be about where the game is going, not where it's at.
Because it's early access, it's STILL in development.
But this is one of those games that I can review both sides of it
Where is it going:
This game is showing the potential to be an insanely great Tycoon game, with massive amounts of depth, intended more for a seasoned Tycoon player.
And if the developers listen to their community, it'll be a truly community shaped Tycoon game, with massive amounts of depth and features that the gamers want. (which is really what Early Access is all about, unfortunately, not every developer gets this)
Where it's at:
The game is rather stable, my computer can play it without crashing, or encountering many bugs at all (my computer is a 2013 high ender, it's due for an upgrade, but it's still really powerful) this is rare for a game so early in Alpha.
The game already has some really great things to play with, the core mechanics seem to all be present to my knowledge.
Where the game stands now, you can purchase it and have a lot of fun with it.
The game however has one downside that I personally hope gets addressed, progress on games, research, engines, general progression even progression relating to skills, is really slow, and this means that after finishing a game, you don't really get any real benefit from it in the skill department, your developers do get better at certain genres though, which is a separate system from the skill system.
And to add to that, you are often put in the situation of "I have nothing to do and I'm bored, because I'm just watching things happen" while you wait for a game to complete or an engine to be fully coded, or research to be completed, etc.
and there needs to be things implemented so you the player have something to do while you wait (maybe a mini game, or just general things to do, click this, this happens kinda thing, for example watering plants, collecting mail, something to keep you occupied)
The visuals are good enough, but I personally believe they should upgrade the graphics if the developers get the chance, and aren't bogged down with everything else. I'd also like to be able to zoom in further.
Where is it going scoreboard:
Has the potential to be:
Visuals 8/10
Gameplay: 10/10
Depth and scope: 10/10
replayability: 9/10
Where it's currently at scoreboard:

Gameplay 7.5/10 - (affected mostly by what I discussed above about there being nothing to do during certain parts)
Depth and Scope: 8.5/10
replayability: 8/10
Overall (currently): 8/10
Verdict:

Long version:
Alright, so let's analyze how it started.
1. Devs released alpha version in 2012 as I remember well, and said full version will be ready in 2013. They created game with huge potential. Great music, Skyrim-like weapon mechanics, and planetary travelling. But despite that, worlds felt extremely lonely, and gameplay was♥♥♥♥♥♥ All monsters where copy-paste of some pokemons, that had same fighting mechanics. After playing Terraria, Starbound planets were really boring. It felt like in No Man's Sky - huge emptiness.
2. Devs lied. Game in 2013 was still in alpha stage, and devs suddenly stopped working on this game for some time. Players, including me felt betrayed. Starbound was flooded by negative reviews saying this game is just a unfinished promise, to get money from naive players. We were so♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off, and devs were ignoring our comments, so we felt it's over, game with huge potential ended right here.
3. Devs came back. It was 2014 or 2015, i don't remember very well, but they came back, and worked on game harder than ever before. They resurrected this game, and finally finished in 2016.
-----------------
Things they fixed since alpha/beta:
+ Game has lore. And you feel it, when you travel. That there is some great evil lurking far away.
+ Fighting mechanics. Weaponary has much higher variation, 2-handed weapons have special skills, and enemies are finally unique in way they're fighting. Plus they added 4 character skills, that you can use AT ONCE. Not like in Beta - only 1 at once. You start with 3 after first lore quest: Dash, Double jump, Transformation into a small ball (to sneak in small holes).
+ Planets are no longer empty. They have cities, and small villages. Sometimes 1, sometimes 2 or even 3. Populated by NPC, that have unique architecture depending on their race, bunch of shops and small quests, that are very nice to do. Deeper underground has some ruins populated with bad guys, and the deepest part is a lava and core fragments. In high sky there are big flying birds through clouds, and above sky - asteroid belt with unique monsters and minerals.
+ No longer boring grinding. On alpha version you felt like this: |__| |__| |__| |__| You were in one of boxes, which means TIER. You couldn't go to the next "box" until you beat the boss of previous "box" that made you possible to progress. So next boxes had wall, that you couldn't pass, and previous boxes were useless, because you didn't need them anymore.
Now it changed. Progression is smooth, and even when you progress, you sometimes need come back for food. And what planets are best for hunting/farming? Those, where enemies are easier, because it's easier to hunt them down / defend yourself and your farm. You want to rush? You're desperated to get a lot of money (pixels) in a short time? Then take the risk, and check out very dangerous planets, that may be too hard for you right now. Nothing can stop you, and you decide how far in progress you are.
+ Tons of content, that is balanced so well, you enjoy doing every of them. Exploring world? You find new cities, and items. You want to dig underground? You gather tons of resources that helps you progress. You want to slow down and settle up on a peacefull planet? Farming will help you getting food for your further adventures. You want to do NPC quests? You recieve surprise reward, that will help you expand your character's skills.

9/10 Pretty damned good.
Forget Terraria, and Starbound. This is a game all its own. The only thing they really have in common is that they are in a 2D world, where you craft, and destroy things to tame the world.
The development team seems to be working hard to make this into a "AAA grade" title. (If you judge games like you judge eggs at the grocery store.)
The ambiance is great, the music is soothing, The planet seems alive, the wind is blowing vegitation.
Player animations are 9/10 so far. They need a little fine tuning, but that will probably come in later updates once the animator knows everything that is going to happen in the game. (Lets just hope the Developer is the animator, or they have not exhausted their animator funds yet.)
Pros:
* Nice graphics, A mix of 3D and 2.5D and 2D. Usually this is a bad mismatch, but this developer (or team) has meshed the 3 art styles together in a very stunning and nice looking way.
* Good animations, The animator has been hard at work it seems. The unarmed melee strike animations could use a little touching up, but in general the animator is doing a great job. (The animation needs to have more of a "snap" at the end of the swing, and a slight bounce if he/she hits an object.)
* Great monsters. They are well thought out, but the attack animations need a little touching up. The monsters fit the story, and the atmosphere very nicely.
* Tutorial system is fairly odd, but still good. You have the choice to click next to zoom through the tutorial. For first time players I recommend leaving the tutorial window open, and only clicking next after you have completed the desired task.
*No CRAFTING GRID!!! If you have researched the item , and you are near the right piece of crafting furniture, then you can create the item. You also can research new items, which unlock as you find things, and complete research of other things. Your little sub-quests are very aperient. It shows you exactly what you need , and gives you tool tips to help you find the components or materials needed.
Cons:
* Still in development, so sometimes odd things will happen like shadow spawning monsters spawning in your house, no matter how many torches you have lit. This only happens if you die with your enclosed structure in the screen it seems. This is early access, so you should expect some glitches and bugs, but all around it is a great game.
* No controller bindings that I see so far. Everything is mouse and keyboard only. You can make your own controller setup with Xpadder, or Pinnacle profiler. Just make sure you set the mouse controls to "mouse spring" so that the cursor stays on the player, and does not wander off when you are trying to aim at something. I just want the rumble effect when I shoot stuff, or fall, or get hit by something. Terrraria, and all of the other games of this class are really missing out on the potential of exporting the game to Xbox, or to playstation. All they are missing is control pad support, and they would definatly be marketable on console platforms.
TLDR: If you like 2D survival games, this is a must have. It is more advanced than any other early access game of this class. It is nearly a complete game now, and worth a play through.

Bastion was one of the gems that blessed Humble Indie Bundle 4, with its unusual gameplay mechanics and "almost constant" narrator through the game. In a world of games evermore gray and colorless, Bastion is really what it says on the tin: a bastion of excellent art and life, despite its introspective themes and overall gray-to-dark dialogues.
From the hand-painted sprites that constantly build the world you are exploring, to the subtle bloom and blur effects on the scenario (never though possible on the SNES days), to the spot-on and expansive soundtrack by Darren Korb, to the deep voice of Logan Cunningham as the Narrator, it's basically worth every penny.
Story-wise, it's dry narrative and inviting atmosphere make a good job of luring you into hours of gameplay fueled by the Narrator's insights into the characters's pasts, even his own.
Gameplay is better with mouse and keyboard, although I can say for myself that an Apple Trackpad works decently as well. It will run smoothly even on a GeForce 9400M, proving that a ridiculously beautiful 2D game, crafted with love and serious coding, does not need a monster of a PC to showcase its full glory. The controls are remappable to whathever suits you (big win), and don't require pixel precision to hit an enemy. They are not sloppy, either: the game rewards you for accuracy and timing.
Overall, it's just a bit short; perhaps, the game is too good that you just don't want it to end. Highly recommended.

Overall, BoT is a pretty decent game.
Combat is pretty good, but is made really interesting with this game's eponymous feature: time manipulation.  Essentially, you can do something, such as attack an enemy, and then rewind, and your previous actions will be enacted again by another (short-lived) you, while you can also do something, such as also attacking an enemy. This makes for interesting battles into which you're able to incorporate a good amount of strategy, which helps prevent the monotony of hacking and slashing so much.  However, this power is also poorly utilized, such as with annoying doors which you need to open, but since they then close nearly immediately, you must rewind time and wait for yourself (in the other timeline) to unlock it again and then quickly dash through.
If story/dialogue is something you focus on in games, this games' story is confusing and hard to follow, due to the very poor dialogue.  This is exacerbated by trying to make some characters talk in Old English-style (eg: "Thou dost...").  This is very poorly executed, and sounds extremely awkward.  Furthermore, some of the regular dialogue is just silly or sounds weird or unnatural.
On a brighter note, the game is relatively well optimized and runs quite well.  The scenery is quite imaginative and often is very beautiful.  I think I've taken more screenshots of this game than all the other games combined.

Serena is a neat-but-brief point & click thriller featuring a man, his memory-triggering cabin, and snippets of his wife (no pun intended).
Unreliable first-person narration drives the action, as interactions are largely limited to the man's verbal reactions to objects within the cabin. Fortunately, the tedium of this object-response structure is lessened by the setting's dynamism and
abundant easter eggs. Somber music and gradually-dimming lighting create an otherwise immersive atmosphere.
The voice acting –while not particularly compelling– brings credibility to Serena's character and accentuates the narrator's development. In the great tradition of the thriller, the plot twists and bends in unexpected ways. I'll let you decide whether it's convincing.
Ultimately, the game is a steal at $0.

Games in the Plaza Casino , the bowling, trivia, typing derby (you type words to get a metal horse to move along a track) are hosted by the devs servers. Do I recommend this game? Absolutely. It's a great game. And yes, maybe it's graphics have aged a bit, but then so has System Shock's. Whether it's on sale or not, I would recommend it to just about anyone, so here are some pros and cons.
Pros
-Great music and sound effects. They might be aged like the graphics but they still got it.
-Takes the silent protagonist to a whole new level. You'll really feel like you are Gordon Freeman - even if you're a bit mute.
-The game has some choices that actually give you different endings for a little variety (not that they carry over to other games).
-Despite being a FPS/Survival type game, Half-Life has a godd story that is felt consistently throughout the game.
-Balanced gameplay and various difficulties for those of varying confidence.
-Unique enemies and weapons.
Cons
-The graphics and sound might not always age well, but this is easily countered by nostalgia.
-Though you can go about your journey in varying ways, it is, to an extent, very linear with little real choices. So if branching, choice-driven storylines are your thing, then this is a con. If not, ignore this.
So that's it from me. Not much I can say wrong about this game. And in my opinion, the cons were a bit of a stretch. So what are you waiting for? Get the game! Or wait for a sale...THEN get the game!
Just don't hold your breath for Half Life 3.

Like Online Play, incredibly fun but pretty much dead since Blood Bowl 2 released. Chaos edition has something like 23 teams and it is worth picking up on sale. It's honestly very fun and actually got me into the tabletop version that Games Workshop released around a year ago. Give this a go, and give it some patience and like me you may find yourself sinking more than a few hours into it.
Or you know, you could just quit after one match and refund the game.
Oh and, Blood Bowl 2 exists (like I previously mentioned) and has a much higher polish, nicer graphics and some pretty cool added elements, though is essentialy the same game with less races and higher requirements.
Oh and for anyone who decides to get the game, treat every dice roll as if it will fail, prepare for it and you will generally do much better.

Ok so it's early access, a little rough around the edges, and player owned housing ranges from PG-13 to 'you are now on a register'.
But this is honestly one of my favourite things to just boot up for some quick carefree games on a lazy evening.
The attention to detail in the minigames like the golf, ball race, or virus, is a labour of love. The graphical fidelity is remarkably high considering this is an unfinished Source Engine project and the variety in levels and stage design shows the development team really cared about making your time spent in the minigames worth a damn.
As cheap as it is I'm not sure if I can outright recommend it at £11 (UK priced for me, consult your regional steam store equiivelant) as while the developers are very active and there are always patches and feature tweaks every month, there still remains a lot to come.
On the social aspect, there is a large hub 'plaza' that can be explored and items can be picked up for personalising the player-owned areas. This plaza is half stocked with shops and games, and the rest with incomplete buildings. It is hopeful of content to come, and I particularly appreciate that examining any of the 'coming soon' signs gives you a progress update on each individual attraction on the developers log.
But conversely, it does mean that each time I boot the game, and see content STILL not finished, I inevitably feel a little down and hope that everything is going alright with development.
Most prominently is the main menu. At time of writing there are 5 operational game worlds, with 4 more 'coming soon' and named on the main menu. This has been the case for several months however, and while lots of other features have been released in the mean time, for these games to be prominent on the main menu and perpetually 'coming soon' it can start to sow the seeds of concern.
I want to see a future for this game and hope that the developers are able to continue adding to and growing the project.
Whatever the future may hold, I know I have a lot more rounds of minigolf to get through.

The basic snake game meets an action-rpg with lots of characters to unlock. The gameplay is addictive. Graphics and sound serve their purpose. There's no gear, but in addition to character leveling, there are permanent over-all upgrades and per-game buffs that can be purchased with in-game currency. When you die you go back to the beginning, but character level and upgrades are permanent. (Continues and level skips can also be bought with coins.)
The original mobile version was free,, but had in-game purchases, whereas this version is $5 with no in-game purchases. Apparently, the game was not re-balanced because of this change, which makes the game a little grindy. But personally, I like it. Levelling and upgrading are very gratifyinig when it only comes with lots of gametime and good strategy. I think these changes make it much more what one would expect from a PC game, compared to the original model. Not having in-game purchases makes a game seem more legitimate to me, and I don't mind paying 5 dollars for that feeling of legitimacy.

This game.. looks a little shallow. It sort of is. It's casual- take Snake and put some light RPG elements in the mix, dress it up.. bam, Nimble Quest. Don't expect it to be anything else and you'll come out content.
Do you like getting upgrades? Seeing how far you can get, then trying to get a bit further? You'll enjoy this game. There's 16 different Heroes- you start with one. Beat level 1 and you unlock the second hero, beat level 2 and you unlock the third hero, etc.
I said it's like Snake, and it is. Instead of growing each time you get an apple (or whatever it was for that game), sometimes killing enemies will give you a hero that will join your conga line- only heroes you've unlocked can join you, so the more you unlock the longer your line can be and thus the more damage you can do and longer you can live.
Additionally, enemies will drop gems (currency) or pickups such as a bomb that will kill all the enemies in a certain radius when you pick it up or an ice crystal that will freeze all the enemies in the game area in place for a certain time which will allow you to murderize them with impunity.
Each hero has 3 upgrade levels: when you start a game you choose a leader. Getting kills will give the leader hero experience, and you'll level them that way, or you can spend the money you earn to level them faster. Each hero gets a specific buff at each level (they might shoot faster, hit harder, get more armor, root enemies with each attack, etc), and each one is noticeable. It's not like "oh I got this guy to the next level, cool..", you see them do more damage or live longer.
Additionally, you can spend the money on upgrading the pick-ups that enemies will drop- just a tip, do this first before you spend any money on levelling a hero. It's just much better to get that done first.
This is a fairly rambling review, but the game is absolutely wonderful especially at a $5 asking price. The only problem I have with it is that there are no achievements, but depending on your stance that may not matter in the slightest.

Please forgive me if this review is nothing but gushing, but this game deserves to be gushed about. It really, really does.
Never before have I played a game with such satisfying combat. It’s fluid and responsive, perfectly balanced with the story and all round great. In fact, that's something this game has over most video games ever. Somehow Supergiant Games have been able to perfectly balance story and combat in a way that neither disturbs or lessens the other. Both compliment each other wonderfully.
The art style as well is wonderful. A beautiful, watercolour artstyle, like pictures in a storybook, it suits the storybook style story that the game utilises. The game is told as if it was a bedtime story, with the narrator recalling the days after the calamity that has pretty much destroyed the world  in which our main character, “The Kid”, inhabits. Many parts of the world are now suspended in the air, and build themselves as you walk across them (it makes sense in context).
The story uses one of the most effective means of telling a video game story at this point: narration only. Other games such as Thomas Was Alone did the same,  and like TWA, Bastion doesn't let the fact that is doesn't have a full voice cast make it a lesser experience. Instead, it uses it to its advantage. Bastion only needs one voice actor, the rich-voiced narrator, who speaks his lines with such laid-back brilliance. The actor does an incredible job. And the narration responds to nearly everything you do. Every little action, every weapon choice, iof you break more boxes than normal, etc etc etc; whatever happens, the both humourous and compelling voice of the narrator will respond to it. It almost felt reasurring; that in this bizarre post-apocalyptic world there is still a constant companion for the Kid.
That’s not to say that the game is faultless, after all, what game really is? The bird enemies that appear at occasions are rather frustrating to deal with, and some of the checkpoints are poorly placed indeed.. But these are but nitpicks in the grand scheme of things, and after all, the rest of the game proves so enjoyable, fluid and engaging, both in story and game mechanics, that those quibbles matter not. Bastion is most certainly worth its price tag.

Not for everyone, but this is probably one of the only games I'd call "punk" - it knows what it wants to be and it's probably not made for you. A surreal, semi-8-bit top-down speed shooter with a heavy emphasis on your dodging and resource management skills. The only goal is to rescue 30 junkies in 5 minutes* and then take down club owning drug lord Ultra Violet, buuuuuuuut the game is... hectic. Surrealist overlays (the designers describe it as "glitchpunk") and overwhelming visuals turn it from a relatively simple game into an assault on the senses and I'll be honest? It adds to the charm.
It is a game you will probably have to play a few times to beat, and there likely won't be much replay value for you afterwards, but I'll be damned if it didn't accomplish its goal and tell a sick, fun story in the process. Good work from the team behind it.
* You can extend your lifespan but it involves some tradeoffs. Like selling your organs, for example, leading to constant HP drain.

I'd like to recommend this game. I really would. I'm not honestly a fan of these kinds of games, but this one is nice in a few ways, and honestly REALLY drew me into the world that had been set up. It creeped me the hell out, true, but it drew me in. The story is rich and really interesting, and truthfully can last you hours because it's all scattered and goes in no particular order; you're trying to work out a puzzle, not go on linear quests.
So you can imagine my dismay when I realized just how unfinished the game is. The crafting system is clunky and difficult to use, placing objects is often tedious/impossible, enemies scale in difficulty from a 2 to a 7 to a 10 in the span of about half a zone (Which can be very quickly crossed) which you really do need to eventually go to because a lot of ruins and crash sites are located there.
Then there are the falls.
The falls.
Sweet mother of Jesus the saviour, the falls.
Every ten feet or so is a dip, then another dip, then you see a cave and go explore and oop you just fell a thousand feet to your death. Or you're running down a cliffside when suddenly it drops out from under you and oop, half your life is gome and you landed on a wolf or a parasite.
I can understand some falling for a challenge while exploring, making it so you have to be careful - but this is ridiculous. I pretty much have to dig underneath caves in order to not die every couple seconds - which really gets tedious when you can only respawn at your home.
...That got a bit rambly. But that's my biggest complaint. Anyhoo, I can't, in good faith, recommend this game, even though I could honestly spend all day playing it and yelling at it. It's just got too many problems to really enjoy. If it's on sale for cheap (2-5 bucks) I'd say go for it - but otherwise, no. It isn't complete and likely never will be, despite its potential.

I have over 500 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews #25 - Blades of Time
I admit I didn't have very high hopes for this game going in.  Looking at the rather scantily clad heroine Ayumi, it struck me that this game was going to be some kind of lame Tomb Raider wannabe.  I definitely wouldn't have picked up this game on my own, but I got it as part of a Humble Bundle.
The story doesn't exactly get off on a strong start.  I start the game as Ayumi, the aforementioned scantily clad treasure hunter who gets teleported to some place called "Dragon Land".  Along the way Ayumi's partner is lost, so the game pretty much starts with 2 quests, one to find treasure, and one to find your partner.
I say quest lightly because this isn't really a role playing game where you have a quest journal and all that.  This is more of an action-adventure game that is fantasy based.  Rather than having a quest journal, Ayumi doubles as the narrator of the story, so you'll constantly hear Ayumi make comments about her situation and surroundings.  Unlike a lot of other reviewers, I actually liked the voice acting here.  Ayumi sounded really familar and I kept trying to figure out where I had heard her before.  I finally had to look it up on IMDB, and it turns out it's the same actress (Miranda Raison) who played Cassandra in Dragon Age: Inquisition.
Even though I liked the voice acting, the story isn't really that memorable.  It felt like the equivalent of watching a movie that just goes from set-piece to set-piece, with just enough story to stitch things together loosely.
What this game is really about is the combat, with some occasional puzzles mixed in.  The combat is fast paced with a lot of button mashing.  The fighting reminded me a lot of playing God of War.  Although the fights are fast paced, the enemies start out pretty simple to give you some time to warm up to combat.
As you progress, you'll run into altars which are part of the story, but gameplay wise is basically a way of handing out powers over time, so you gradually become more powerful and have time to acclimate to each new set of moves.  At first, your powers are basically just different ways of attacking, but then you start getting the ability to leap around.
Things got more interesting right as I was wrapping up my first hour of play, when the game gave me the ability to turn back time.  It's clear this is going to be used as a puzzle solving technique throughout the game.  The effect is pretty neat being able to rewind time to essentially create a clone of yourself who follows your original path while you can replay a section of time to do something different.
While I wasn't very invested in the story, the combat was fun and engaging, and the next thing I knew I had beaten my first boss fight, and wrapped up my first hour of play.  My expectations were low going in, but I admit I was pleasantly surprised at how much fun I had.
I definitely wouldn't recommend this game to everyone.  Combat is twitchy enough that I think casual players may become frustrated.  Also if you like your adventure games to have more of an emphasis on story, then this is probably not the game for you.  But if you are willing to set these concerns aside and embrace the combat, then your time in Blades of Time will be well spent.
