I already raged enough for one day on their forums, so I'll just add myself to the chorus of naysayers and give you the quick version.
This had the potential to be an incredibly cool game, but then it went unfinished because of ineptitude on the part of the devs. You can probably get about $5 worth of fun out of this game if you're really determined to do so, but I wouldn't recommend it.
Why?
Not because it isn't a thoroughly decent, half-finished game. It's because you'd be lending your support to a team that doesn't understand fair and ethical business practices. This game was billed as complete at launch, with extras on the way as a bonus... Those extras turned out to be essential parts of the game that were missing, and now the devs want to raise more revenue by charging EVERYONE for ALL of those additional portions of the game as DLC. Doesn't matter if you bought it at launch, doesn't matter if you were a beta tester--fork it over, cuz we're outta $$$.
To make matters even crazier, their OTHER plan to fund the completion of Darkout is to make another game, and use the profits from that. Sooo, we sold you an unfinished game, then lied about it... but trust us, this new one will be great! Yeah, OK. They don't seem to understand the damage that this has already done to their credibility as a studio.
They also asked for donations on their website. Because, when I think "charity", game development studios are at the top of my list for needy folks who could use some spare change or a simple cup of coffee.
Honestly, I don't know if it's desperation or sheer arrogance or both on their part, but I'd implore you to spend your money elsewhere, no matter how low the price of this game goes.

The game is a strange combination of frustrations. Despite the conveniently undisplayable evidence that the RNG is not biased (which many of the die-hard fans will insist exists anyway without any proof) the game routinely feels as though it is indeed very biased towards the AI dice rolls - even when you're winning and crushing the opposition! I can tell you that, in my experience, playing solo against the AI is a completely different experience compared to playing multiplayer vs a human opponent in terms of RNG fairness. This is why the developers refuse to show you the AI's dice rolls.
However, this is all balanced out by the fact that the AI is terrible - I mean so shockingly bad at the game that the developers had to give all the starting teams you face bonuses in order to make them even slightly challenging in solo play. Which they still aren't.
I have played it a fair bit largely due to nostalgia and my childhood memories of the table top game I used to love.
If you plan to play it solo then be prepared for what "seems" like a heavily biased RNG and the subsequent frustrations this causes and learn to live with it like I did. In this mode I don't really recommend the game unless you are a very laid back and patient person.
If you plan to play it multiplayer online then you'll probably have a lot more fun. The downside is that you'll have to deal with other internet users though - which is not my cup of tea.

There also is the freeware alternative called FUMBBL, that's 2d and java based. Both are a far better option than BB1 now for actual MP.
Ordinarily I would not go an remove and change the thumb to a down for a game simply because of the MP community drying up, but for Blood Bowl the entirety of the game is both MP, and has moved on to a nearly identical platform as well at that, and thus I feel obliged to steer people to those two alternatives, either the updated retail version, or the smaller, more hardcore community of the freeware game.

I lived with my decisions. I recovered several missions from the brink of complete failure. But it just wasn't fun.
My most recent foray into tactical games like this one was Steamworld Heist, a side-camera platform-strategy game that made me feel I should try the genre again and see how well I'd like a classic like X-COM. I also tried playing the game like it was meant to be played - no save-scumming, no fast mission restarts, just accepting consequences and making the most of bad situations. I only actually totally "failed" one mission, but there was a lot of death. I was playing on Normal difficulty.
This kind of lead to a pretty hard spiral. The game's difficulty curve is very sharp, more or less expecting you to constantly have your elite squad of heavy-hitters for the first N hours of the game to deal with enemies that get bigger health bars, and more abilities. I responded to these as much as I could, but with the game's meager supply income and long time to research new tools (both, in-game; committing the science center; and in-mind; learning the best tactical usage to mind) tactical options were limited aside from forcing squads into unsafe positions and ending up dead, or risk losing the objective. Worse, there was a moment near the beginning of the game where moving up to a civilian with my first action (being ready to retreat or move to cover) caused the introduction of a new "Shapeshifting civilian" mechanic, where it turned into a giant monster; and, my character's turn was inexplicably over, guaranteeing her death. "Gotcha, player! Shoulda thought ahead!"
I would say that this situation may appeal to the tactically hardcore who have been playing XCom a while and know the strategies much better than I do, but even beyond the difficulty there's plenty of issues. You spend a long accumulated time in this game waiting for the UI. Never more than 5 seconds at a time, but lots and LOTS of times in just 15 minutes of playing. This may involve staring at new enemies for 5 seconds when someone reveals them, or staring at the "ALIEN ACTIVITY" indicator wondering if the game's crashed, or watching the 3-second animation to open or close the Bridge Map again and again and again just because you wanted to exit and check whether your team has any armor available before flying back to HQ. 3 or 5 seconds may sound like a fickle complaint, but the frequency of it, and the number of times camera control is disabled to focus on something, practically makes the game feel like a bad Call of Duty clone in a way.
This even extends to the enemy abilit mechanics too. My soldiers got panicked, constricted, or mind controlled multiple times, and whether or not this is a balanced mechanic (I was able to pull off a recovery from it a few times, so it's not unbeatable) it just meant I was given less time making decisions for my soldiers. There were times out of a squad of 4 that I was only able to give one person an order during my turn - sometimes I never got to make any decisions at all. These tend to be unavoidable and 100%-chance, so even if you're good at surviving them, it means the game is playing itself even longer. Even if the status effects were equally harsh in some other way, I'd have felt much more interested in more dynamic effects that keep you in control of the game to some degree.
Going back to Steamworld Heist, I can't help but think that it's not just the fact that it's easier that makes it a more fun game. It's also more rewarding of experimentation - it doesn't require that you save scum once something doesn't work, and while things get harder, the game doesn't grind to a halt just because you're not able to keep pace with the difficult spikes. And most importantly, it barely uses any RNG. The game is still designed to let plenty of things go wrong, but it will usually feel like your fault; and you won't have to dampen a victory or narrow escape with "Well everyone's dead and I lost my best equipment, I'm either gonna lose now or save scum".

This game is very odd. But it is very beautiful. Exquisitely beautiful.

It's the stuff that happens in-between that's the real journey.
The game brings quirkiness and thoughtfulness in an unconventional way. You'll be desperately clicking around the screen hoping for something to help you move along, and next thing you know, there's a bunch of lil scribbly doods singing the most beautiful melody you've ever heard. Bizarre, but so beautiful.
The music in this game really is the standout for me. It's atmospheric, it's invigorating and it takes your breath away sometimes. You end up just sitting wherever you are for a bit and listening cause it's super nice. Even if you're stuck for an hour and a half on something, it's completely tolerable. Please play with the sound on. I promise you, it's a beautiful experience.
Botanicula has a good deal of replayability, as there's a lot of cool little achievements you can get. It'd be fun to like spend a day or so 100%ing this, as all achievements only require some particular clicking.
Overall, this game is one of those games that everyone needs to try when they feel like disappearing irl for a few hours and leaving an everyday mindset. It'll make you think, but it'll also make you smile, cause it's just one of those beautiful little indie gems that you come across once in a while (rhyming unintentional - but unapologetic).

Every once in a while the conversation will turn to "favorite games." I'll mention Klabi, and at least a couple people will snicker. I pay them no mind because I know that a year ago, these same people were moved to tears by that very game. And they're too embarrassed now to admit it.
I just replayed Klabi for the first time in a long time. Expecting to simply enjoy the story again, I was surprised to find that the game has lost none of its power over this year. I cried again.... in all the same places. It brought me back to 2016 when I can remember how a game that no one thought would break even became the most popular game of all time. A game that burst into the public consciousness like no other game I can recall (yes, even more than Bad Rats). And today, many people won't even admit they enjoyed it. Folks, let's get something straight -- you don't look cool when you badmouth this game. You look like an out of touch cynic.
No game is perfect and this one has a few faults. Some of the dialogue falls flat, and some of the plot surrounding the two lovers comes together a little too neatly. However, none of this is so distracting that it ruins the game.
Klabi and Birthday Cake are wonderful. Klabi is one of the finest rappers of his generation. Wait 'til you see him in Gangs of New York before you call him nothing more than a pretty boy. Birthday Cake was so strong in this game. The game really was hers, and she held it together beautifully.
This game is one memorable scene after another. Klabi opening a pink chest only to find one lollipop. Birthday Cake and Klabi enjoying a snickers. "Banana, right ahead!" The screws hanging unbelievably out of the ocean. Klabi drawing pyroblast twice on turn 7. And that ending that brought even the burliest man in the world to tears.
The music, which has also been a victim of the game's success, was a key ingredient. Mystic Games score was simply perfect. And the love theme was beautiful and tragic.
I confess, I am a Klabi buff. As such, I relished the opportunity to see the cake as we never got to see it -- in all its beauty. Perhaps watching it get eaten affected me more than some because I've had such an interest in the cake all my life. However, I doubt many of those I saw crying were Klabi buffs. I applaud Mystic Games for bringing this story to the masses in a way that never demeaned the tragedy. The game was made with such humanity.

The campaign can be annoying. Not necessarily the bosses, because they all have a certain weakness that you must figure and exploit, usually with your Rewind Spell (just recall the name of the game) - What is annoying is that certain actions can be unresponsive at times; I died a lot while platforming through the gauntlet after you meet Michelle and leave the crashed ship.
The worst part in this game (besides the ending –“Oh that (horrible thing) happened… END.”) was leaving that ship: the way in which you do it, and characters' responses to it... I've seriously never felt more bad-weird (or bad-wrong (badong)) because of something in a video game than I did in that moment.
The direction detection when, say, attempting to counter enemy attacks, and especially when having to use the Sphere of Order to move the energy through the conduits to activate a Portal (O.o) - when combined with the (at times) otherwise clunky/stiff controls… Platforming and fighting
become painful to go through (I shuddered at the thought of Hard mode, but your Powers carry over and by that time, you’ll have a much better feel for the mechanics).
USE.A.CON.TROLL.ER. Be precise in pushing the stick in the correct direction; it’s as simple as that.
Regarding that Sphere of Order comment: A lot of the puzzles in the game, though (theoretically at least) logical and very demanding mentally – I was reduced to spamming and ignorant trial-and-error until I passed them because I didn’t understand the logic, because the methods for manipulating the puzzles weren’t very, er, intuitive.
More often than not, the game recognizes its own shortcomings/bvllsh!t and has a generous auto-save function. There aren't even any load times to speak of when doing so; the worst part is when you auto-load into a segment that has characters talking (my buddy had all the voices muted, which is worth considering, though it’s the writing (I would guess the translation, actually) more than anything that is turrible).
So. For all the game's faults and lack of polish. I still recommend Blades of Time.
The universe in the game is too amazing to allow something like, er, mediocrity (incredibly good mediocrity) to discourage – comparable to Kingdoms of Amalur in artistic style. What I mean by “mediocrity” is, in terms of, er, game design/execution, it feels like an incredible indie title/a flop from a AAA studio; the combat is pretty good, the concepts and mechanics are interesting, the story is serviceable - the way it all comes together seems *meh*.
If someone has done/will do a Youtube series on it, you MIGHT be better off just checking that out...
- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
Multiplayer... “Outbreak” is amazing; the main reason for my recommendation.
Third-person hack 'n' slash moba.
The statements:
I cannot get into moba's.
Hack 'n' slash's: nothing special.
The bad:
The form of moba present in BoT is incredibly watered down, to the point that any who play such games would probably take offense at Blades' attempt to meld the genre with third-person hack 'n' slash, and to leave it so barebones (relatively).
The unintuitive control schemes are glaring when Bosses/Champions spawn (pumping a Skyguard full with your rifle and then being unable to dodge appropriately because your character didn't put their gun away in time sucks)(adapt and figure the nuances - it’s not actually
because of the game’s awkwardness).
Too few maps (even though one of the DLC’s added another map).
The good:
Incredibly fun and addicting - if I was to ever get into a moba, it would be because of the transition that BoT would have served. If you have a friend whom you’re trying to get into a moba, I would recommend both of y’all to play this game; to introduce them to the basic concepts of the genre while keeping the actual gameplay simple as a hack ‘n’ slash. You can even run the multiplayer solo and it's still incredible.
What's interesting is that any gear you acquire in the Campaign is carried over into Outbreak and vice versa (thus, there ARE duplicates and clearly superior gear, which could be seen as annoying). The maps look pretty big according to the minimap; at first you might be saddened at how little they are utilized. Treasure randomly spawns in the middle alleys - that is the reason for those alleys, totally neutral zones. Where the turrets spawn is random in the symmetrical maps; as the bigger maps, sometimes the turrets might spawn in the top-left quadrant, the next time in the bottom-right.
Linear Maps:
A desert in which the sun saps your health quickly, so you must fight in the shade.
A jungle that is very appropriately sized to accommodate the amount of turrets.
Symmetrical Maps:
A swamp in which the most difficult grunts reside.
A series of floating islands that allows you to “push” your opponent (in versus) off the map.
A mountain pass filled with lava that looks like something out of LotR.
You start the matches with your choice of three powers/passives (Fire or Frost, Heavy Strike and Rage Saving are the best). You gain experience (resets every match); whenever you die, you get to put those experience levels towards more powers.
I don't understand why you can't do so without dying; apparently, it's the game's way of consoling you upon your death.
Just as Treasure randomly spawns, Bosses do too; spawn rates for these *expletives* increases exponentially with each difficulty, as does their strength (playing as Michelle, I swear that I've been one-shotted several times because an Invisible Assassin touched me... wasn't even facing me, just touched me)(Ayumi is beast, Zero is a little too slow).

How the progression works:
You gain Runes from Treasure and from Match Bonuses. There are Challenges you complete to earn Medals.
Collections of Runes have passive effects (i.e. if you’re co-opping, whenever your partner opens a Chest, you also get a Rune); you complete Formulas with Medals – Formulas grant new gear (which, also, usually just grant passive effects, though more combat-oriented).

For example, 0-0 and in the second half, RNG going my way then the AI's, then back again, etc. With the ball two squares from the line, all of a sudden things take a turn for the worse! I lived with my decisions. I recovered several missions from the brink of complete failure. But it just wasn't fun.
My most recent foray into tactical games like this one was Steamworld Heist, a side-camera platform-strategy game that made me feel I should try the genre again and see how well I'd like a classic like X-COM. I also tried playing the game like it was meant to be played - no save-scumming, no fast mission restarts, just accepting consequences and making the most of bad situations. I only actually totally "failed" one mission, but there was a lot of death. I was playing on Normal difficulty.
This kind of lead to a pretty hard spiral. The game's difficulty curve is very sharp, more or less expecting you to constantly have your elite squad of heavy-hitters for the first N hours of the game to deal with enemies that get bigger health bars, and more abilities. I responded to these as much as I could, but with the game's meager supply income and long time to research new tools (both, in-game; committing the science center; and in-mind; learning the best tactical usage to mind) tactical options were limited aside from forcing squads into unsafe positions and ending up dead, or risk losing the objective. Worse, there was a moment near the beginning of the game where moving up to a civilian with my first action (being ready to retreat or move to cover) caused the introduction of a new "Shapeshifting civilian" mechanic, where it turned into a giant monster; and, my character's turn was inexplicably over, guaranteeing her death. "Gotcha, player! Shoulda thought ahead!"
I would say that this situation may appeal to the tactically hardcore who have been playing XCom a while and know the strategies much better than I do, but even beyond the difficulty there's plenty of issues. You spend a long accumulated time in this game waiting for the UI. Never more than 5 seconds at a time, but lots and LOTS of times in just 15 minutes of playing. This may involve staring at new enemies for 5 seconds when someone reveals them, or staring at the "ALIEN ACTIVITY" indicator wondering if the game's crashed, or watching the 3-second animation to open or close the Bridge Map again and again and again just because you wanted to exit and check whether your team has any armor available before flying back to HQ. 3 or 5 seconds may sound like a fickle complaint, but the frequency of it, and the number of times camera control is disabled to focus on something, practically makes the game feel like a bad Call of Duty clone in a way.
This even extends to the enemy abilit mechanics too. My soldiers got panicked, constricted, or mind controlled multiple times, and whether or not this is a balanced mechanic (I was able to pull off a recovery from it a few times, so it's not unbeatable) it just meant I was given less time making decisions for my soldiers. There were times out of a squad of 4 that I was only able to give one person an order during my turn - sometimes I never got to make any decisions at all. These tend to be unavoidable and 100%-chance, so even if you're good at surviving them, it means the game is playing itself even longer. Even if the status effects were equally harsh in some other way, I'd have felt much more interested in more dynamic effects that keep you in control of the game to some degree.
Going back to Steamworld Heist, I can't help but think that it's not just the fact that it's easier that makes it a more fun game. It's also more rewarding of experimentation - it doesn't require that you save scum once something doesn't work, and while things get harder, the game doesn't grind to a halt just because you're not able to keep pace with the difficult spikes. And most importantly, it barely uses any RNG. The game is still designed to let plenty of things go wrong, but it will usually feel like your fault; and you won't have to dampen a victory or narrow escape with "Well everyone's dead and I lost my best equipment, I'm either gonna lose now or save scum".

Trove is a good game, but it has it's draw backs. Many of which can be blamed on two things.
1. Some severe lag issues: For some people I hear the game doesn't even start. I haven't yet encountered that myself, and it runs fine for the most part for me, but there are moments where things just kinda break. Then again, try playing a game that doesn't have a glitch of some kind.
2. Pay2Win: Now this I can understand. I have seen the market place, and it is very restrictive on what you can get without pouring dollars into this game. HOWEVER: Like Warframe,(I know, of all games, why draw comparisons to that one. Hang with me, pls.) you can do just fine without spending a dime. Of course, it will take a helluva lot more time to do, but maybe it's worth it.
Despite that, I do reccomend this game, because of 3 things:
1. Friendly: It is a very nice game. In every way it is warm. All nearby players get the loot that drops, and there is no fierce competition over that Shadow lvl 3 staff; death isn't overly punishing, and the game gives you a pretty good start, and then encourages you to engage with the community.
2. Rewards cooperation: You get more together. When you're fighting with a team, all of you get XP, and all of you get loot. Even better, the punishment of death can be lessened when you have a team that can revive. Building becomes easier, and higher level characters can provide gear to lesser levels to help them gain rank.
3. Appeals to a very large audience: Everyone: young, old, builders, adventurers, people who like pretty places and people who like hell. Everyone will have a place in Trove. There are many different classes for people of many different playstyles, and each one can be tailored via the gear you get, and the gem system. Threre are clubs for the different types of people, those who like adventuring will be greeted very well by adventuring clubs, builders can show off there talents to eachother at building clubs, and so on. And the best part is that everyone progresses through their respective intrests in similar ways, resulting in a place where different interests collide and then are sewn together in a rather lovely way.
There is no way I could put this on the 1 to 10 scale and be accurate, so I'll give it a 89/100. Do the math, people!

Very enjoyable. It does have it's downsides though.
Pros:
-Runs very well(for me at least, not that my system is too old). Rarely had any issues with bugs or graphical issues. Only real bug that comes to mind is for some reson when I start flying (either in skyland or at the end) it would really mess up my keybindings with the only way to fix it is to quit and resume from the main menu. It would cause my LMB to use 2 every time I got a skull for it. It was quite fun to watch myself spamming fire everywhere. But at the last boss when having the right spell was important it became a problem. I had to beat him while avoiding using my wings even once.
- Looks nice. It overall looks like it could be real. But it does have a bit of cartoonish in it. Overall very well done and polished.
- Gameplay is very smooth. Aside from the flight bug I had. Animations for everything feels right.
- Characters are mostly interesting. Ayumi can get annoying. But this is mainly the script and not the character herself. As a few people have stated in relation to the voice acting. The script could use some improvements. I really think it wouldn't be so bad if we didn't have everything explained by her every time something new game along. Although outside of Ayumi there isn't much involvementwith other characters.
Cons:
- It feels like everything is handed to you. If there is some secret path to progress in the game it will show you the way. You're even given a compass to show hidden tresure. As long as you peek at it every once in a while you will have no trouble finding everything. Assuming I didn't forget to look at it a few times. Getting real annoying listoning to the main character explain everything to me. I would like to figure it out myself sometimes.
- Combo's are limited. Usually in these types of games you find you buy tons of attack combo's. In this game it's mostly about spells. And they're hardly challanging to use. I don't fully call this a bad thing. Since in most of these types of games with a bunch of attack combo's you find one you like and use it for 95% of the game. I prefer this game's approach. But there's nothing really crafty about using the spells. Enemies are not really weak or strong to the elements you use. You just used them based on the effects/items you want. Closest it gets is a boss that has a shield that can only be broken by the right element.
- Enemy(bosses make this the most annoying) attacks can easily rotate if you dash around them. You can be attacking a boss. Dash behind him as he attacks, and his next swing will instantly turn to you. The boss should have to turn or have an attack in that direction. Closest game I know of to seek improvement examples from would be Vindictus. Easily one of my favorite hack and slash games. Which I would still play if my account didn't get hacked and I lost everything with Nexon unwilling to fix it.
- I never felt I needed/wanted to use my time powers in fights unless it was required. Biggest problem to me is that you can push the enemies around so your close's attacks becomes messed up.
Overall 8.5/10

(updated March 2016) You might not want to believe it, but I still recommend this game.
Yes, Darkout is a bit unfinished storywise (not much though), also several targets of the roadmap (including regular patches/expansions) have not been reached. Since the developers have fallen silent after April/May 2015 and it seems like the main dev allegedly got a job elsewhere ,you can safely assume that this version of Darkout is most likely the final one with no further updates.
BUT this game is still very well worth its current price (12 Euro).
How many games (like adventures) are just "done" at one point without being patched any longer, and how many games have "open" ends like showing how the end-boss re-emerges indicating a continuation that often never is delivered? So what? Does this make games any less enjoyable?
If I hadn't played this game I definitely would have missed out on something inspiring :) So if you like games like Terraria, Starbound, Crea, Signs of Life and the like, and you have a little extra money to spend then give Darkout a try one day - it's a fresh take on the 2D-sandbox genre.
The pros:
The gameplay of Darkout is interesting nonetheless, the game looks and sounds beautiful, it has nice features, an atmospheric gameworld to explore and a lot of stuff that can be crafted & built. On my PC with Windows 7 prof. the game runs smoothly with nearly no bugs.
The speciality of Darkout is to light up the world while aiming for your goal (collect audio logs to find out what has happened and then defeat the boss-mobs). As dangerous creatures are all emerging from clouds of darkness you will have to protect yourself, your base and your paths by placing durable light sources all over the game-world. Torches will burn out though and lighting will be attacked by creatures, so placing durable lanterns or even setting up long electricity grids is highly recommended if you plan to play this game for a longer while.
You will have to create pathways between the many islands floating in the sky and you will also have to dig downwards to reach deeper layers of the world and caves full of crystals that you'll want for crafting more advanced equipment and useful stuff for your base and transportation. You can build teleporters later on (sadly the "sledges" do not really work so well, and the elevators are a bit uncomfortable to use because you can easily drop to your death if you miss your step and do not build a safety-ladder next to the elevator-shaft ).
If you are an "achiever"-type of player and/or a "builder"-type, you could set yourself the personal game-goal of unlocking all existing crafting-recipes and/or of building a giant (lit) base in whatever creative shape (there's a "builder"-mode too) and you will enjoy this game a lot. The surviving-, building- and crafting-features are well done with many things you can make and/or strive for, and these main features do not seem "unfinished" (or "clunky") in any way.
The cons:
- "story" and "quests"... this game DOES have a "story", but it's unrefined and unfinished. Unfortunately only the first "quests" within this storyline will ask you to build (rather "place") stuff. All the other "tasks" will just make you wait for data-logs to spawn in a specific biome (UPDATE: or go hunting for evil creatures in this biome) and then search for these logs - one after another, and again and again. Well, listening to them is not so bad because of the rather nice voice-acting
- many crafting-recipes also depend on receiving such data-containers purely by chance  (UPDATE: the chances that these will drop as a loot from creatures that you kill have seemingly been raised and you don't get "corrupted" ones any longer, but a message instead that no new data-logs are available currently until later on, so this is much better now)
- the starting "tutorial" consists of a bunch of tiring text-windows filled with small letters that you'll just want to click away, instead of being a quest-like "training" for your character
- the game does not feature an multiplayer-option even though this was originally in the pipeline
- more types of discoveries, creatures, biomes, drops and resources would have been nice, because the variety is lacking a bit and get a bit boring after playing for a while
- renewable ressources are lacking too - growing plants like trees yourself purposefully is not possible for example, and botanical materials are not used much anyways (plus your character does not need to eat nor sleep), and there's no mapping feature. However there are a lot of additional trees growing on the islands in the sky, and you can extract the most common ores from bits of stone and earth that you will collect when digging
- the development of Darkout has suffered from financial problems (like when Desura went bankrupt and did not pay developers or when Darkout was in highest demand during summer sales for very little money) for quite a while. However also some not-so-good decisions have been made along the way, like presenting the prospect of "upcoming" features like multiplayer and promising frequent updates time and again. It would have been better to just keep silent...
After this statement was published one year ago
a♥♥♥♥♥♥storm followed, and then Allgraf Studios
has seemingly gone into hiding.
Ever since then no news about the planned spin-off Darklings or anything else have ever been heard. It's very likely that this new game has been nipped in the bud because of the same lack of funds that Darkout and it's scheduled expansions/updates had suffered from, but perhaps also from all the badmouthing and even personal insults that people have thrown at the developer/s.
Like other players who enjoyed Darkout I still somehow harbour hopes that even though the developer most likely will never want to take up working on this nice game any longer, at least the game's source code might become open source - or perhaps might be handed over to someone who would like to fix some bugs and create a proper story-ending. Well, a complete overhaul of the quest-system starting with the tutorial and adding some substantial content to this quest-line as well as more creatures and - renewable, useful - flora to spice up the game would definitely be even better of course ;)

Gunjitsu is a fast paced shooter game which focuses on multiplayer. This game has power ups, 5 different weapons (+ side weapon) and grenade. As you shoot the platforms, the platforms will break which will create an unstable platform to walk on.
I don't really hear any bgm except a buzzing sound and i find it quite annoying. The only sfx i hear in the game is the gun firing sound.
This game has a UI feel similar to flash games and is using retro backgrounds with 3D characters in game. I find the menu wording to be quite confusing, especially the Profile menu where you can only see your weapon level.
The game is meant to be enjoyed in multiplayer. However, with multiplayer being dead, the dev started to add bots which is referred as experimental. I myself don't mind playing with the bots. It's working and i can select their difficulty (easy, normal, hard) which can reflect my skill. Although you will enjoy this game for a short while, it is not meant to be enjoyed in the long run, especially when it's still in early access and has been neglected by its own developer.
When you start the game, you'll be introduced to a tutorial which explains the control. I am quite surprised that this game gives a lot of freedom to my movement. You can walk, dash, double/triple/quadruple jump, wall jump, and use grappling hook to reach platform above you. However, i find it hard to master the controls. Some platform (especially the top right corner of the first map) has a small portion on its platform which can be skipped easily in one jump. Because it's hard for me to land there, i tend to have to jump from the platform near it to reach it. The grappling hook also has its own limit length so you have to make sure that you don't fall too far from the platform.
There are 5 different main weapons that you can use. All of them have their own advantages and disadvantages, although you can only change your weapon when you die. You also can kill yourself when you stuck somewhere and receive a penalty score of -1 for it. The weapon also has its own levels which will unlock different bullet skin when you reach certain level. Sadly, this information isn't explained clearly which might leave some confusion.
Although you'll usually use your weapons to kill the enemies, you also can destroy the platform with your weapons. You can either make a perfect defense spot to kill the enemies or even get stuck in the particular spot. As you kill more enemies, more platform will be destroyed which will make it hard to walk.
Besides the main weapon, there is a side weapon and grenade. Although the side weapon is weak and fires slowly, it can be used infinitely unlike the grenade which has a high damage and a limited ammo. However, the grenade "ammo" can be increased with power ups and will be restocked when you die. Speaking of power ups, there are also power up which can restore your health and give extra health to your maximum health and more.
There are 5 different maps with 3 different game modes. Although there are several different game modes, you'll mostly play one game mode, death match, as the others are just a speed run challenge.
When you are playing multiplayer, you can choose which server you want to go in. However, if you choose the server that's too far from you, you won't be able to move which is explained with just an exclamation mark in your character.
There is an in game chat. However, the chat is hard to close which might affect your performance.
Pros:
- 5 different maps
- 5 different main weapons
- side weapon + grenades
- powerups
- bots
- destroyable platforms
Cons:
- dead multiplayer
- it's hard to move when lots of platform are destroyed
- buggy chat

Bastion has an interesting story, and it's narrated perfectly. The graphics and art style are awesome, and the OST is truly incredible.
The gameplay is just mediocre, though. For one thing, the game is extremely easy. As you progress through the game, you unlock "Idols" which allow you to increase the difficulty for greater rewards, but even with all of them enabled, the game is still a breeze. There's a variety of weapons, and you can customize them to fit your play style. This helps to make your first run through of the game less tedious. But the combat is pretty simple, so should you play a "New Game+" and/or Score Attack mode (which is the same as the regular Story mode but with a score counter and the ability to replay levels at will), you will probably get bored like I did. And it's necessary to play those modes if you want to unlock all of the achievements.
Speaking of achievements, just like the game itself, they are very easy to 100%.
Bottom line, this game is worth playing one time through, but becomes tedious if you want to 100% it.

This would be a fine introduction to the 4X genre if you have a friend you'd like to get into the hobby.
That said,  some of my finest gaming memories are playing the original MOO and MOO2 back in my misspent youth, so I'm a bit more of a grizzled stellar emperor, and my standards are demanding.
We've had a bit of an abundance of riches after a decade long drought-- one thinks immediately of Stellaris-- which layers on substantially more complexity and depth.
There's also the absolutely amazing Endless Space series, which is crafted amazingly well.
So MOO has some rather stiff competition these days.
By those standards, is this title a success?
Well-- yes, and no.   The production values are absolutely first rate.   The game looks gorgerous.   The sound design and voice acting is also first rate.   Which is something you normally do not associate with a 4X title.
The no comes from the depth of gameplay-- I won a 10 hour campaign on Hard with basically one hand tied behind my back.   There were no surprises-- which was very disappointing-- the Klackon did not, for example-- seem to prefer smaller swarm strategies, as before-- and the Bulrathi did not lean towards larger, Battleship-type fleets.   Every race basically was super nice to me until I wiped the galactic floor with them.
The tech tree is almost unchanged from earlier games.
The antareans show up-- but their AI seems weird.   They sometimes start to bomb your colonies, but then change their mind and leave.   This makes them vastly less of a horrifying threat.
Taken holistically, this is a satisfying nostalgia purchase at its price point.  I'm happy another generation will get to enjoy some MOOOOOOOOO addiction.

I don't want to end up not mentioning Botanicula's art style and music. I found both of these to be excellent; the music above all else. It's not something I would normally sit and listen to, but it's the perfect soundtrack for this game. I love the music and how it's used here.
I played through the first four levels out of the game's entire six-level length, and while I could have played another hour or two and finished, I was not feeling any desire to keep going. The story is that you're trying to save a seed from some shadowy monsters that are pursuing you and sucking the life out of the tree and its inhabitants. The tree is big, compared to your characters, at least, who are a team of things like nuts and a mushroom, etc., who each occasionally use a unique talent to enable progress. Getting to the bottom of the tree to plant a seed seems to be the end goal, and honestly the plot doesn't seem like it's supposed to be the driving force here.
The gameplay mostly involves finding things on the screen to click and occasionally wiggle or pull the mouse around to obtain one of numerous objects you need to continue. I'm no stranger to point-and-click games. The Space Quest and Kings Quest series were some of my favorite games as a kid. However, though there are a few little changes in environment, one of the biggest problems with Botanicula is that all the environments feel at least a bit similar. In most adventure games, the environments tend to be widely varied, and I find it helps keep a game from getting boring. Many games benefit from this.
On the topic of the objects you have to obtain to progress, though...it's generally duplicate copies of the same item for an area. For instance, to complete level one, you need to find several bug-wing thingies. Then to beat level two, you need to find five keys. To beat level three, you need to find three missing children. Then to beat level four, you need to find
birds in a village on the tree consisting of a dozen or more little similar buildings. This became taxingly repetitious to me, and the puzzles became more and more obscure, with the 12+ buildings making it difficult to figure out if I was done or not with any given home.
I eventually had to resort to a walkthrough and found several solutions which I am certain I never would have figured out on my own, because I believed I was done in those particular buildings, having already obtained birds or seemingly having already completed everything in the buildings that there was to partake in. Navigating the walkthrough was even hell, thanks to how many of these buildings there were to check out. When an adventure game taking a long time to solve part of it while using a walkthrough, there's an issue.
When I saw/read that level 5 was labyrinthine, I called it quits. While the music and visuals are a treat, it's not enough of a treat for me to justify playing through more of this game. The 2 hours I played felt like 5 or more, which is not good. =/

Playing Serena may be a disturbing experience, but totally worth if you like psychological thrillers. My take on it (SPOILER ALERT):
What is love? How can love turn into obsession? What separates love from hate? Both are strong feelings that can absorb us completely. This game deals with this question with a simple mechanic: changing descriptions and character’s reaction to examining objects. All you do in the game is examining objects. There is no puzzle, except for a very simple one. Descriptions change (the photo, the poem) once you examine the objects around you, leading you to another psychological level. Nothing around you changes, but the comfortable cabin turns into an oppressive and scary limbo, because your mind changes. That’s the point I guess the game is trying to convey.
Games are the perfect platform to create this dramatic effect. In a movie, it is possible to show exactly the same scene and make it look like a completely different scene using a different soundtrack, for example. But in a game you can do it much better, because the character’s reactions complement the visible scene. The players feel attached to these reactions, taking them as their own, trying to see through the eyes of the character. In this case, not only we know that something changed, but the objects around you are “reframed”, even if they look exactly the same.
Serena also plays with the idea of slowly sliding into insanity. Games are also very good at this, because players can experience this transition on their own pace.
That’s all I have to say. If you played Serena, tell me what think about it. Let me show you that the value of a game is not related to how much time you spend (outside reality) playing it, but how much it can make you think about real things, things that matter. Thank you for reading.

Great game.
Can easily stand up to genre kings like Devil May Cry. Fast fighting fun in a very pure, uncompromised and likeable way. A solid selection and variety of moves, an interesting time-rewind feature to overwhelm enemies with multiple copies of oneself and solve basic button-press puzzles, nicely designed enemies, varied, beautifully designed and memoreable levels, a great soundtrack, a not necessarily revolutionary but nevertheless somewhat interesting story (it needs time to build up, but when it does it takes pretty epic shapes), increasingly likeable characters, a pretty good voice acting and big numbers of lines. It runs fast and smooth, the controls are easy (I played with an XBOX controller) and I picked it up very cheaply in a bundle. For which I feel like a thief now. I think I'm gonna buy one or another copy for the full price just because it seems that this game is a severly underrated gem.
There is even an online versus mode as well as a mildly strategic single- and multiplayer co-op arena tower defense mode with leveling and item mechanics and stuff. In other games I would usually see such a multiplayer mode sceptical, but as the singleplayer portion of this game is already great enough I think this is pretty awesome to have. I played the co-op mode once with a Japanese and it worked (which is not self-evident in such games). I didn't notice severe lags or synchronisation issues despite the distance to the host. We (well, I at least) had a blast. I didn't understand all he said over his mic because I don't speak Japanese, but we ran over tons of monsters and my screen was all slash and boom and peng and pow.
A few platforming sections I died in more often than I probably had to because the double-jump from the protagonist is not the most precise. There are some platforming and trap-evading parts where someone else might get a little frustrated, but I got through okay and the checkpoints in this game seem pretty fair.
Also, the story and character relationships can be a little confusing. Some good thoughts went into it, that's for sure, there are lore hinches that I liked. In the end everything gets resolved fairly well, but in the middle the game sometimes lost me a bit. I don't know if that is because I didn't play the prequel "X-Blades" (which I sure will too soon). But, as mentioned, it finds a satisfying and understandable end.

I looked up a few things on Bloodbowl, now that I've gotten the game, and people say the dice  are perfectly fair, they just seem not to be because we don't pay attention to the victories.
Bull.
On multiple occasions I've had the 'you hit the dirt face-first" roll four times in a row--a 1296-to-one chance.  On a normal randomization, this wouldn't happen once until you've played for months; I've only had it a few days.
There are very few things more stressful than putting together a good plan, thinking on my feet as circumstances change, accounting for my team's strengths and weaknesses--and my opponents'--preparing for setbacks, spending money for rerolls just in case...  and then watching the opponents plow through my defenses with disgustingly high rolls to undo all my work in a manner that's statistically impossible.
One of those few things is to have that happen, come up with a backup plan, set it in action--and watch the dice roller give it to me dry over and over and over again so that a team that should have  steamrolled up the field ends up tripping over its shoelaces.
Screw this game--if you haven't bought it yet; don't.

Starbound, in a word, is diverse. However, there is more, so I'll put it in a convinient list form.
Pros:
A very diverse amount of creatures and planets.
The planets are the same each session, so if one character needs something another one of your characters has, you could leave it in a chest on a planet and go get it with the other character. It also enables getting help online if you're looking for a certain type of planet.
Easy to use controls. If you're used to using the arrow keys, then they might need some getting used to, but all the menus are easy to access when you need them.
A customizable character. When you satrt out, you have a choice between different outfits, each specific to the species. As you get further, you can equip vanity items over your armour, and you could just decide to leave the awesome looking armour as your outfit. You can also change the colour of their outfit, and the colours of their hair, fins, foliage, etc., their main body, and other stuff, like underwear colour on humans and the symbol on Novakids.
Cool looking environments. A lot of times, background is put aside for other stuff, and sometimes that is right. But the background shouldn't hurt your eyes. Chucklefish did more than that. The backgrounds change depending where you are, and look extremely impressive, balancing High-Resolution and the pixelated style of the rest of the game perfectly.
Now, everything has it's sins, so I'll include a cons list:
Shared planets. Now, while I listed this as a pro just a couple seconds ago, it can also be a vice, considering that all characters start on the same planet with limited materials ON that planet. So, if you're like me and use multiple characters, good luck. This, however, can be fixed with a simple 'World reset' button or something.
Weapons. While I'm not saying that all of the weapons are bad, how fast they can get OP is. About 5 seconds into my first game, I had found at least 3 weapons that could almost or completely one-shot all of the creatures on that planet, taking away some of the fun.
And... That's all I could think of.

Very boring game. If you are a fan of in depth 4X strategy games I would skip this one. Everything is very simplified on one end and then overly tedious on the other. I tried to refund but I really gave this one a chance and spent 4 hours on it :(
Pros:
Graphics are nice
Voice acting is good(spent too much money here)
Cool ship design
Cons:
Boring gameplay. There just isn't much going on beyond the random super annoying pirate attacks and the random invasions from fleets that 2 shot your ships. Place the game on harder difficulties and your simply faced with more overwhelming fleets earlier.
Pollution is a silly mechanic that attempts to slow down planet development but is very tedious to deal with at random points in the game. All it does is force you to stop producing something useul to make these buildings to reduce pollution. Do that and you move on until the next "Tier" is hit where you have to research and/or produce more of these buildings.
So many other things could have been done for pollution.(I.E Pollution is something that all planets will have much like it is now based off population/type of buildings/type of planet. Pollution is a process that has different effects that a player can choose to reduce/increase/manipulate in different ways using research and buildings. The goal would then not to build X to reduce pollution level but rather X research combined with X building may take 25% of said pollution effect and apply it in a positive way to the planet. This way you have an interactive in depth element for the player to manage that isn't about making more buildings to make more buildings when this meter gets too high.
Fleet travel is overly tedious and has a very fake feel too it. You take space travel and have chunked it down into these tiny little movements. Huge spans of space are taken up with these knee jerk movements of your ships "traveling at warp". I would rather your ship have a wind up time at the one end of the space lane and then Warp all the way through to the other end then what you have now.
Fleet combat is just bad. The entire setting feels very fake and the look of the ship models as they glide across the map like it isn't even there gives your battle this weird "I'm playing a board game" thing which is just weird. The way ships turn during combat is very unnatural. I would rather have a simulated battle scene like Endless Space than what we have here.
Very much dislike how the galaxy is split up, again it gives the whole game that "board game" feel. This has a lot to do with the "choke point" feel that the universe has been given. So closed off and a poor simulation of the real thing. I know I've played a space strategy board game in my far past that this reminds me of so much. Wish I could remember the name.
Diplomacy is pointless? I don't really understand the point of it. There are a few diplomacy options that have any meaningful effect for the AI. Most of it they shrug off or horribly abuse.
Espionage also has little effect on the AI but can be very annoying when done to you. IF the AI even bothers to use it at all.
Leaders are a very expensive investment for not a huge return. This is especially true early on when you are constantly harrased by these leaders to hire them. If you don't know any better you will quickly find yourself in a positon where you have 3+ leaders and no income but they arn't really doing anything for you. Later in the game you come across leaders that can make you income. These are nice and useful.
Overall: 4/10 Buy this on sale for 10 bucks. Pass on the DLCs, they are a money grab that should have been released with the main game and don't add anything but new races.

This game just blows, man.
The main flaw with XCOM and the Firaxis handling of it is that it's just a glorified board game. And a greatly flawed one at that. This game has nothing going for it apart from the pretty exterior.
On the very top level you have the insult of a story which takes the bad ending to the first game and makes that the jump of point rendering all my struggles to get the good ending with that first ho completely meaningless.
The main flaw with the game however is the random coin toss you have to do to hit an enemy. Ignore all those stats and variables. They ultimately don't matter at all. It's a completely binary outcome every time and the game would be better off either admitting to it or altering that mechanic entirely. It's a videogame. Why are we going with board game rules instead of simulating projectiles and calculating shot spread with variables? Or make every shot a guaranteed hit like it seems to be handled in Phoenix Point. It would remove a lot of tedium from the game. All this current setup does is add unnecessary randomness to what is supposed to be a skillful strategy game.
Another thing is the half-baked stealth mechanics which just highlight how the game hates it's audience. Adding stealth to the game should in theory allow the player to create ambushes, getting enemies caught out in the open, trapping them in the players crossfire. This however is not possible unless the squad is set to overwatch and one of the team gets spotted and that just often isn't possible with the limitations that come with the 2 moves per turn and overwatch not always working as intended.
So if you've set your team to ambush the enemy and take a shot, what's even worse is that the enemy gets a free reaction to that shot. The whole point of an ambush is immediately made pointless when the enemy gets to take cover for free after just the first fire on a turn.
To add more frustration on top of this is that once you kill the troops that had spotted you, you don't then re-enter the stealth mode even if there are no other enemies in close range. This means that when you creep up on a squad of enemies that have not noticed you, they then become automatically aware of your position NOT because they saw you BUT because you saw them first.
Basically everything new in this sequel feels like it was designed to ♥♥♥♥ with the player and to spite them. There are even more timers forced upon you this time than in the previous game and all they really do in the squad command side of things is force you into a playstyle. The game being already as hard as it is asks that you just rush to meet a lot of the objectives it hands out where as in the map layer you often don't have time to do anything either. Many times the game would generate a more urgent mission for me to go to, just to laugh at me, right as I'm a day away from completing something else. With the whole Avatar project mechanic it's also a lot harder to discern if you've lost the game early or not. You could still have months of game time to go but who knows if you can do anything in that time. The whole experience just feels like work and most of that time is spent looking at loading screens. This game is not doable without heavy savescumming and anyone who boasts to have done this on ironman must just hate themselves.
The game also frequently soft locks, crashes or replays the same one-off cutscenes over and over again after loading.
I doubt the game will be fixed by the expansion.

Out of nowhere, one of my friends recommended we play this Poker Game during a Discord call, and I thought I'd give it a shot since it was free. Neither one of us expected to play all day and have a blast while doing so.
Perhaps the best quality about Prominence Poker is that it's easy to pick up, very accessible, and very enjoyable; there's an optional tutorial (that rewards you with a few free starter items if you do it), and you can very quickly go directly into singleplayer mode against CPU players, or join an online casual match. There are more serious ranked matches for more serious poker enthusiasts, as well as a casual mode for people who just want to pick up and play poker. For those who only want to play with friends and don't want to deal with random players joining the game, there is a friend-only private lobby you can invite them to and have your own private matches. Up to six people can play at once in each lobby.
I'd still recommend Prominence Poker even if you don't know how to play poker; the game offers helpful instructions in the "Help & Options" menu on both Poker Mechanics and the Game's Mechanics, and during play you can quickly view the list of possible Poker hands in ranked order from best to worst. There's even a Practice mode to allow any player as much time as they need to get the hang of how the game runs, as well as how to play poker.
To address what I would assume to be the Elephant in the Room (which is the in-game shop), the
thing I've noticed that costs real-world money are the poker chips used to play the game.
, the game is forgiving enough to provide you a "daily cut" which refreshes every 24 hours that provides you with enough poker chips to play casually. From my experiences,
Regarding the in-game shop itself, you can either purchase in-game poker chips with real money, or use in-game poker chips to purchase in-game cosmetics. If you don't want to purchase any in-game cosmetics for your character, the game rewards you with lootboxes that are
that provide you with various rewards such as poker chips or cosmetics.
The online mode seems rather active and it's very easy to just hop in and play whenever you feel like it. Prominence Poker provides an experience
better than I had expected to be, and I can definitely see my friends and I playing this together on a regular basis.

I'm not going to say that Cyanide's Blood Bowl is a fantastic videogame.  It is, however, arguably the best way to play the board game Blood Bowl over the internet.  Fumbbl, while a wonderful community, is built around an application that experiences server-wide glitches between patches that affect the meta of entire leagues.  I respect people who play on Fumbbl, and in many ways prefer the simple sprite-based interface.  However, Chaos Edition includes a tutorial and single player modes to ease new players into the game.
For a time, I refused to purchase any version of Cyanide's Blood Bowl after the barebones 2009 version.  Both 2009 Blood Bowl and Blood Bowl II force changes from the source material into the core game, whereas Legendary and Chaos Edition limit these changes to an alternate mode called "Blitz."
Something to always keep in mind is that Cyanide's Blood Bowl is not an original game, but an adaptation.  Chaos Edition is the most accurate and accessible verion of the board game.
Edit: It is worth noting that Legendary Edition is functionally the same, save for the new playable races, and I believe it can even play with Chaos Edition players.  So, if you main a race included in Legendary Edition, you might be able to get by with a cheaper purchase.  Additionally, the inclusion of Khorne Demons without something closer to base/accepted game like the Slann is a little disappointing.  However, that disappointment pales in comparison to the inclusion of Bretonnia in Blood Bowl II before the addition of staple teams like Undead and Nurgle.  Granted, both Bretonnia and Khorne Demons seem well balanced/tested and were adapted (with liberties) from a certain Fumbbl format.

Botanicula is a very entertaining short click and point game filled with tons of charm. This game kept a smile on my face throughout playing it, even getting a chuckle out of me at some points. The story is wordless and simple. That is appropriate, since a complex story would take away from the charm of the world. The sound effects given to each character combined with fun animation gives the creatures of Bontanicula their own voices and tiny story to tell. The creatures are fun to discover and click on, which the game encourages with a card collecting achievment system. As the game went on, I started to care less about the achievements and more about what cute animation would pop up when I clicked a leaf.
The puzzles are all based on these magical creatures, appropriatly starting simpler in the beginning and gradually progressing into more difficult tasks. With the fantastical nature of the game, some of the solutions are not always obvious, and took some clicking around the screen to figure out. I had to pull out a walkthrough during one point of the game, but that was after attempting the task multiple times. With a little thinking and lots of clicking, I was able to solve the rest of the puzzles.
If anyone is looking for a short puzzle game full of charming characters and creatures then Botanicula is a must have. While it's about a 3-4 hour play time, the $10 price tag is deserving due to the obvious time spent fleshing out the world and the creatures. There is a great ammount of polish and love put into this game. Please give it a shot!

As a standalone 4X-scifi game, MoO is quite pleasing. It's not unique or special, but it's generally a decent game that handles and looks good. Turns go by smoothly, the AI is mostly acceptable, and the patches has adressed a lot of the concerns from the negative reviews. Overall, I like the game.
The obvious comparison is to Master of Orion 2. And now I start to wonder WTF happened. Few of the gameplay elements feel like they are better or more polished than MoO2. Has nothing happened in 20 years of game development? Graphics and sound are definitely better, but you get the same buildings and races, a worse tech tree (copied from Civ?), duller exploration and it just feels like there's been no real improvements to the gameplay. The UI is a step back from the ease of MoO2, and ship designs have become static - instead of the total freedom from MoO2, you have a fixed amount of blueprints to alter, and all your ships are locked to that blueprint and it's upgrades.
So while I do recommend the game, I still rank MoO2 as a better game. And it was released in 1996.

My earlier review was about this game being bad. After playing it again this is what i came up with
=INFO ABOUT THE REVIEW=
1. This review might be a bit longer.
2. This review is about my point of view and opinion. [If you disagree on a certain point or want to correct me: Be reasonable or i will delete your comment]
=REVIEW=
So this game has changed since i last played it. My last review was about the long loading times and how confusing the game was.
The game is still a tad confusing since it is a game just like Terraria where you get thrown into a world and have to move on from that point but it is much easier then before. The little tutorial leads you through mining, building and construction fast and gets you your own shelter. From that point on you are on your own.
The game before was similar to what it is now. I did give it a thumbs down though due to the fact that the loading times for the game and the world were so big. I was sitting here at one point, the excact same PC, and waited for an hour until i decided to ALT+F4 the game and just delete it. Now even on a big world i am only waiting for about a minute and that is already a big plus. I wrote in my first review: "If you would be able to play it." Well you most certainly are able to play it now.
There are some problems with the game though. Ingame you start with a starterkit, what is totally fine. The tutorial leads you to your very own shelter, that you have to build, but what is also totally fine. From that point on though you are completly alone. Of course that is what the game is about but you dont know anything about your controls or how to deal with placed objects that you want to get rid of (BTW you hover over the object and hit Q).
Due to a lack of options the game has a few FPS issues and also graphical issues. The game is very beautiful but i noticed some graphical glitches. I dont know if that only occured to me but that is just what i saw so it will end up here. In total the game also isnt running as smooth as it should. And my PC can handle high definition games.
But overall the game is good. It is as hard as Terraria and in some points even harder but still enjoyable. The crafting is easy to manage and building, even though a bit tricky, is easy just as well.
So would i reccommend this game to a gamer that has not bought the game yet?
If you have spare money: Yes
But if you have a different game with the same price you also want i would reccommend for you to buy the other game first.

Generally I don’t write reviews, but this game has become a special kind of irritating.
On the positive side, the game is indeed very pretty and the soundtrack sets the mood well. The general sandbox activities of building and resource gathering are interesting, particularly wiring your base with power and lights.
Sadly that is where the upside stops. When I originally purchased this game in beta most all of the things you can now find in the “Future development plan & DLC” were to be included in the game by the time it was released. Especially the story and an ending for the game. An immersive story for a 2D sandbox was one of their main features at that time. However, now the designers have fallen on hard times and have decided to break those promises due to their need for funding. Additionally, work has effectively stopped on this game while they attempt to make a similar companion game to get more funding to finish this one. This information, along with a much longer explanation, can be found on a recent post of theirs on the official forums along with a passive suggestion that it is the purchasers fault for buying it on sale.
I realize beta is a fickle thing and you might not always get exactly what you expected. This goes well beyond that however in my opinion. To be realistic, this game by the standards of their original plan is still in beta and was simply rushed to release in an attempt to gain further funding. I whole heartedly recommend against this purchase. The DLC may never arrive at this rate and most of it was originally supposed to be in the actual release. It strikes of an unethical approach to development even if they had the best intentions to start with which is suspect at this point.
*UPDATE* It's been several months now since this change in the games direction with no recent news or updates from their main site. Given this was back on April 30th, it's probably fairly safe to assume the game is dead at this point with it being over 6 months.

At present, these are only my first impressions, but I have to say that from what I've seen so far, this game is really quite enjoyable. I'd describe it as a cross between Bayonetta and Tomb Raider - it's a hack-n-slash by nature but it also has a third-person shooter element, and you can switch between these modes on the fly, which I find to be a really interesting addition - it allows for a unique take on both genre's formulas, and contrary to what you might think, in the midst of a fight flicking between the modes feels rather natural - it almost feels as if the game encourages you to use both in tandem to achieve your goal.
In hack and slashes of this game's type, combos tend to be both essential and, for a gamer like me, rather hard to pull off. Blades of Time remedies this a little - whereas in a game like Bayonetta the combos would be a ridiculous string of button presses, Blades of Time has relatively simple button combos, press one button to ready, press another to attack. In that sense I found myself enjoyng the game a lot more, because I didn't really need to worry about all the ridiculous combos I'd have to pull off - While a more hardcore hack-n'-slash fan might not find this appealing, I personally think it's a nice touch, making the game easy to jump in and out of without needing pinpoint-precise button presses.
I have but two criticisms of this game: First, the english voice acting is pretty bad, though this is remedied by simply switching the voice language to Japanese, and second, the story makes absolutely no sense - the game goes straight from the title screen into the opening cutscene without a shred of explanation as to what is going on. However, when you're in the thick of it, hacking and slashing and shooting and magicking enemies like there's no tomorrow, you honestly forget about these errors, because you're just having too much fun to really care.
Overall, despite its shortcomings, Blades of Time is a lot of fun, and an interesting fusion of the hack & slash and third-person shooter genres, and I'd reccommend this game if you were a fan of either genre. An underrated gem, this game has enough action to keep you entertained for a long time.

I've been playing MOO games since the original and was stoked when I saw a new version available.  I have tried many of the newer 4X clones, and while they are enjoyable, none were as much fun as MOO2.  So far, I have enjoyed this new iteration of the game, though not quite as much as I hoped.
I would recomend this game to anyone who enjoys 4X games.  I know it's caught a lot of flak from some users (some of it deserved), it's still worth the money.  I like the new movement system even though many people seem to dislike it.  The graphics are very nice, the tech tree dynamics work OK, but it often doesn't seem to affect the game that much in regards to the order you research items.  Diplomacy seems to work well and the AI seems to act in its own best interest most of the time.  I have not experienced any of the bugs other players seem to have experienced, so maybe that would have changed my opinion.  The other thing I really enjoy is the fact that it supports mods through the Workshop.  Those community designed changes really help with certain aspects of the stock gameplay.
A couple of things I wish they had changed are the combat system and races.  Commanding the RTS combat system seems to make no difference in the outcome of the battles and is just boring.  I enjoyed the older turn based system where specialized ships really made a difference.  Now there is very little advantage in using anything but the stock designs.  Also, making the complete roster of races (including the Antarens) part of a paid DLC seems like a cheap decision.  They really should have been included in the original package to flesh out the game, not charged for to keep people playing.
Still, even with the negatives, it is a fun game and worth the money if you enjoy this type of game.

I'm an old fan of MoO2. This remake is one of the most decent turn-based 4X strategies. Yet, it does not fulfill MoO title contract to me. I definately hope that WG will keep tuning the game, but for now I have to vote a NO.
Problems:
1. The most glaring - lack of tactical combat. Half of MoO is the combat. I do not care for glamorous graphics if I can't properly control the combat. In it's current form only AI combat can be used. Fook the camera, fook the graphics. Make it 2D even, but make it a proper tactical combat.
2. Badly inefficient economics - always lacking income even with just the basic buildings built.
3. Lack of freighters and general food abundance makes all races feel the same. Rock-eating silicoids are not too  different from any other race. Just spam colony ships and get each and every planet you can get. Races just don't feel unique.
4. Minor, but annoying - combat evaluation vs monsters - it's just missing. I've built a fleet of 10 ships to attack amoeba - combat evaluation tells me I have 100% chances to win. Attack! Not a scratch on the amoeba, my fleet is annihilated. 100 turns later with quite significant tech updates - same fleet, same result. 100 more turns later - yet again. I'm voting for strong monsters, it makes it more interesting, but evaluator should be fixed, particularly to account for shield damage reduction.
5. Many additional modules is nearly impossible to evaluate (like modules, disrupting rockets) - they do not change stats of the ship, take up precious space, increase cost, and without tactical combat - I can't see their result. Either make a tactical combat, or make modules change ship stats, or remove them.
6. Same as #5 but towards point defense / antimissiles.
7. Overally, gameplay feels sluggish and slow. Like a simple thing - population management - it cannot be done from colonies overview (empire). Like too many notifications (dangerous fleet for every move of enemy factory, population rised for every colony of 100+ colonies empire, etc), like showing every move of a monster in nearby star system. It all takes precious seconds, that build up into wasted hours.
8. Tech tree feels soo civ-like that it's annoying.

Darkout version 1.3.1
I really wasn't quite sure to make of this game when I first laid eyes on it  a year ago. It looked interesting but something about it seemed off. Maybe it was just a hangover or I was coming down with the flu. Recently Darkout went on sale and all of a sudden I found myself saying :why was I not interested in this before?” It's like Terraria on a creepy planet. Needless to say I bought it and fell in love with it. Please keep in mind that the game is still very much a work in progress and by no means are any of my negative opinions to be taken into count for the final game.
The Good
The graphics are great and the lighting effects are really top notch. It's not difficult to imagine yourself on a dark lonely planet surface trying to survive against a swarm of shadow creatures. The story line has tons and tons of potential and definitely kept me interested with me wondering whats around the corner. Each time you research and get a new tool, weapon or device it feels rewarding, as if you really earned it. The creatures advance with you and the challenge of exploring, gathering and completing tasks progresses naturally. Worlds are randomly generated and available in 3 sizes so there is replay value for days and days.
The Bad
The sound design could use some real love. The music is kinda so so and rather unremarkable but the sound effects are really jarring at times and sometimes don't make any sense. Take for example when you hit a non shadow creature with a glow torch it makes bubble sounds like a water cooler. There are  several moments where the game simply stops you in your tracks and demands you to level up your tech or you simply run out of things to do and it can be frustrating to backtrack and try to find out what you missed or how to progress. While I'm against total hand holding, there needs to be better clues in place to help the player know what the next move is. There is a very limited assortment of creatures and it quickly escalates into tedium with some varieties.
The Ugly
Although very fun and easy to lose hours and hours in, there is a definite lack of content. I hate to bring this up only because the game is clearly not finished yet but after playing for awhile it's like you hit a wall, or a void as it were. There are lots of bugs yet to squash and some things don't function as intended. Development seems nearly glacial.
I feel horrible bringing up negatives about a game that is still in the works but I felt that they were worthy of a note. Bottom line: If you like Terraria, get this. It's a ton of fun and very engrossing. While the updartes may be slow coming, there is just a ton of potential here. If the devs continue along this line, by the time it's finished, patches and fixes not with standing, Darkout will be a completely epic game worthy of comparison to the mighty Terraria.
