So I’ve played this game for two hours so far, I’ve progressed about 30% of the way through the game.I think it’s good.
- I found it really challenging, I died frequently but it was still fun
- I thought that the visuals and sound effects were really well done
From the very beginning of the game I was dying over and over again. It was like this for me during every single section. You character is only able to take a few hits, healing is not easily obtained and there is not a large amount of room for error i.e. to make jumps, neutralize and avoid hazards. You have to patiently time your maneuvers really well and in the boss battle which I encountered you only have a split second to react to everything it does. I went through a LOT of trial and error to progress through the game. I found this frustrating sometimes, but it was challenging and good fun.
-----I found that I needed time to get the hang of the stance mechanic. For example when you attack an enemy,  you are switched automatically to the strength stance. But often I forgot to switch back to the green agility stance and would fall to my death because this meant that I could not make some jumps. Occasionally I sort of scratched my head and wondered why they felt it necessary to have this mechanic in some cases. But I don’t think it’s a bad thing overall, it’s just different. I did like being able to switch to a stance to run faster and jump higher.
-----You gain new abilities as you progress, by the time I finished playing I’d just acquired the ability to activate slow motion. I think that was kind of cool.
I think the game looks quite good. I like the sound effects. This game brought back fond memories of the old side scrolling Donkey Kong games.
I recommend checking this game out. At the rate I was progressing through it should provide five or six hours or so of gameplay. I feel that the time you can spend on this game is mainly because of the difficulty. Not because of the actual number and size of the levels. If it was easy I think the stages would actually be short. The way it is, is not necessarily a bad thing. I think it’s acceptable for a game is challenging rather having physically long levels. I’d rather play a game like that than something easy and unsatisfying.

I know no one reads these or cares what they say, but while I wait for Blades of Time to download I want to leave a short review;
This game tries to oversell itself as a stylish 3rd person action game in thhe vein of DmC, Bayonetta, or any of Platnium's work. This is false.
While there is some "style" to it, it doesn't have that tight heart beat that makes the combat flow like in those game. This game more is along the line sof Gauntlet or Dynasty Warriors - sans the strategy,
It's a "mash X to win" game (X for 360 pad users) with a few special moves you ccan activate via a single button press rather than a combo. You can map the skills to left bumper, right bumper, Y, and B. Though, they stupidly made dodge-roll double-tap-forward+jump which is awkward to execute, so I can guarentee once you have the ability to unlock the "teleport" skill, that will ALWAYS be mapped to one of your 4 slots.
The game is short, and the opening is rough - with the beginning mostly being "mash, mash, mash, earthquake....mash mash mash, earthquake." but after the first hour you begin unlocking more skills and eventually, this short game turns into a fun little romp.
Don't take the story seriously, it makes no sense. Play the game solely for it's mechanics, which aren't very deep, but I beat it and had a decent little time with it. I don't regret my purchase and it sold me on playing the (supposedly) superior spiritual successor. Give it a whirl - just don't expect something great. It's good and I think worth the $10 asking price even though the game has glaring flaws and seems like it was made on a very low budget.

I've put countless hours into this game on both the PS4 and Xbox One, only recently purchasing it for PC.
Short rant..... Yeah, the CC is pure horse ****, but that doesn't take away from the game. It's completely optional, and regular modding is still a thing, so I don't see why all of these people vote against this game just for that reason. I personally enjoy this game (even before mods), and modding just adds more to it
So, I obviously recommend this game. It is kinda light on the rpg elements, true, but that didn't really bother me that much. Visuals, while not the best, are still good enough to look like they came out in the current generation, unlike NV. Gameplay is very fluid and all around improved, so shooting without VATS is actually do-able. Story was good, not great but not bad. There are still choices to be made and consequences to suffer, even if they seem a bit underwhelming.
As for Dlc, I would only recommend Far Harbor and Automatron (I personally haven't used any of the settlement dlcs, but they seem fine if you enjoy that aspect of the game). FH has an interesting story, setting, characters, etc that I won't spoil. AM adds a fun mechanic of building your own robots with the addition of a minor quest line, plus it adds my favorite item in the game, being the Asaultron Helmet. It truly is bad***... Spoiler below, sorta
Nuka World was extremely underwhelming to me. It could be that I generally don't play as the "bad guy", but I just couldn't finish the main quest line. I got so far to the point where a slave informed me that I could potentially kill everyone to set NW free from the raiders, and I did exactly that. But if you do that, then there's really no point to having NW in the first place. Each area is themed, some more annoying to traverse than others. There are a few cool areas outside of the main park which I found more interesting, notably the Grandchester Mystery Mansion. It's a haunted attraction with clear tourist paths, but it's genuinely creepy, and there's even a little dead girl who runs and disappears around corners to go with it.
Anyway, I would give Fallout 4 a 7/10, 9/10 including mods.

I'm giving the game a positive review, though it doesn't mean it's perfect.  I'll get straight to the point via bullet-points.  Review is based on Dec 1, 2016 patch with latest DLC pack installed.
+ Oozes charisma and charm.  Some of the best voice work for aliens ever done for a game.
+ Animation and graphics for the aliens is superb.
+ Good tutorial to get you started (a bit too basic though).
+ Great game for new players to cut their teeth on a 4x game.
+ Interface for managing your empire is great.
+ Warp gates and choke points are a fun secondary 4x gameplay option that gives 4x space games some variety.  I'm glad we have this method for MOO, yet traditional hexes in Gal Civ 3.  Makes each game feel special.
+ Game plays quick.
+ I think I'm going to like the real-time combat aspect but I need to spend more time in it to formulate a better opinion.
+ Easy to manage your colonies.
+ Love GNN News!  I'd even pay DLC prices to have more GNN events added.  Same goes for more voice overs for more diplomatic options.
-  Music for some parts of the game are annoying.  The research screen in particular makes you want to gouge your ears out. It's disruptive and and loops too quickly.  Likewise in main game, the basic music that loops majes a huge mistake you should never put in a game.  It uses a *ding* that closely resembles one used for messaging in Apple devices and error messages in Windows.  It is distracting and annoying.  Rest of music feels uninspired.
-  Graphics for planets and stars on the main screen are bland and too small.   Can't zoom in much.  This make it hard to "immerse" yourself in the galaxy as you feel a bit distant from it all.  Galactic Civilizations 3 does this better.
- Ship Combat - I'm just not getting it yet.  I think it's because camera control and the options in the combat zone are not good yet.  Maybe I need to look at how some other people manage combat.

It's a turn based sports strategy game with a dark fantasy theme and an RPG leveling system. If you're still with me after that little description, then maybe Blood Bowl is for you.
You start the game by selecting a team of bloodthirsty monsters from the Warhammer universe. Each race plays a little differently. The Orcs want to bash their opponents into the dirt. The Elves want to dodge around and make big passing plays. The Goblins have a bunch of dirty tricks up their sleeves. You choose your name, logo and colour and then you begin.
The first time I played, I got completely thrashed by the computer. There is a learning curve present but there are plenty of guides online and a big community of players who can give you some pointers. Leveling up your guys in the right way is a big part of the game. Some skills like Block and Dodge are a must, other skills like Pass block are only used in specific circumstances and best saved for later.
The sound is satisfying. The commentators are hilarious. I though the graphics were fine. It's an older game from a smaller studio, so I wasn't expecting much. There is a nice variety of units in the game. The Chaos Edition comes with 23 teams and there is plenty of single player content here to play around with if you want to avoid the highly competitive online scene. Some guys have been playing the board game since the 80s and will mop the floor with newer players.
I'm loving Blood Bowl so far. Anyways, I've got to get back to trying to take my team "The New Ork Ragerz" to the Blood Bowl final.

Well, I've played this game extensively on Xbox, dablled some on PC, and to tell you the truth there isn't much difference between the two, apart from the amount of players.
You'll hear people complaining about "bots". I've played at a few tables on PC, and hundreds on xbox, and to be honest, I haven't come across one. To be perfectly honest, I don't see why someone would waste time to manage a bot on the pc  game, Theres just not enough people to actually reap rewards.
Yeah it's true, you get idiots who shove all in with 63 os, who end up getting raggy on the river and hitting a straight, sinking your pkt A's in the process. Though honestly, I'd like you to find me a poker game which isn't like that, because I'd be sorely interested in this unicorn. I play on poker sites for real cash, and there are idiots everywhere, whether you're in a free game, or a pay to play, you'll always get people "bullying" and getting "lucky", it's poker, you're never guarenteed a winning hand pre-flop.
This game is more interactive than most, you have voice chat, emotes and most of all you're not staring at a non-interactive table for hours from birds eye view. Theres character customisation which is pretty cool, and also different items and clothes you can wear to make your character a little more unique. You can either purchase them, or get them in brief cases (which you get from ranked rewards or by levelling up).
The single-player is a bit naff, the AI kind of forces you to "play big/stupidly". There are different factions too with boss matches which can net you some nice cash early-game and progress you with your current affiliation which are spades, clubs, diamonds or hearts. Once you've maxed out your current affiliation you can move on to the next.
The game seems fair in all honesty, I mean dont get me wrong I havent sat down just to record how people act vs win ratios, If you focus on the amount of times you get screwed over vs the times you win, I'd say it's pretty even. I played seriously on every table, and 9 times out of 10 I walked away from a table in profit. Yeah there were moments where I'd get done over on the river, but this happens in RL too, it's the luck of the draw. If you concentrate on the bad things, all you will see is bad things.
Now, for my recommendation, theres just not enough players to actually enjoy the game, unless you're dabbling on small casual ring games that is. Though, I'm here reviewing the game, not it's player base, so In that casem I DO recommend this product.. it's free, whats the harm in trying?

Aritana is a great little indie platformer. The visuals are fun and colourful, but do not let that deceive you cause the gameplay is pretty challenging (in a good way). I'd classify Aritana as a precision platformer with some action elements.
The visuals as you can see from the screenshots above are generally cheery (some levels are darker, like the ones in caves). The soundtrack is the same - cheery, happy-go-lucky music. The setting in the Amazon rainforest is a nice touch.
I wasn't too fond of the default controls, since movement is tied to WASD, but the good thing is that you can fully customize the controls. So I customized it to the way I like it - movement to the arrow keys, and use the left side for the action keys. As for the physics of the game, it feels good. The character is not floaty, and he doesn't feel heavy either.
The gameplay revolves around using your powers. You can switch the state you are in, and then activate a short burst of extra energy as well. The challenge comes from executing moves precisely to continue moving in a level. It gets pretty challenging, suffice to say, and for completionists, I am sure the challenge will be even greater.
It can get frustrating at times, but the checkpoint system here at least saves the day. You can lose 3 "leaves" (more earned later) and restart where you were, after which you go back to the last checkpoint. If you lose all your lives (1 live = 3 leaves, earn more as you play), you kinda get a game over screen. Shocked me the first time really, but actually you can go back and continue playing from the beginning of the current level.
Performance wise, it was decent, except for the parts where there was rain. Noticed a huge hit to my framerate there. I've played it for around 2.5 hours and am nearly halfway completed, so I assume there should be 5 hours of game time here (more if you want to 100% it of course).
Overall, I'd say Aritana is a pretty fun♥♥♥♥♥challenging platformer (and I never get enough of those!).  It's not particularly revolutionary, but it's well-made. Recommended to hardcore platformer fans especially!
PS: I got a key from the dev to test the game, so yeah, just wanna put it out there.
PSS: Steam, you're really censoring that? Come on! (No, it's not the A-word)

Master of Orion CTS is a strange beast.
On the one side, hey, it's not MOO3! THe game is certainly enjoyable, and you can have a lot of hours of fun with it. The campiness is back, all the races are there, fleshed out for everyone to see, graphics look good and there are no obvious setbacks.
On the other hand, IT seems like a missed oportunity at many junctures. While it's great to have MOO for our generation, it fails to be as memorable as the first two, because it's just not innovative. Everything you do here you probably already did in moo1 and moo2.
Also, some of the design choices are just odd. I mean, you can say yeah to starlanes or nay to starlantes, but once you decide to go with them, you have to own them, and i think they really missed the spot on this one.
Antarans are fun, but they fail to be a "Galactic scale" threat and just turn into the new pirates V2.0, And If starlanes and choke points are going to be that important, then why not make the star-system scale as engaging as the galaxy map fleet movement ? Having moving from one planet to the next be as time consuming as moving from one star to the next just doesn't feel all that right. I don't presume to know how to fix it, but i can certainly spot there's some parts of the magic that are not as shinny as they should.
I do enjoy the game a lot, and plan to get back to it tough. Hope you like the review!

This game is unbalanced and made so that you will eventually have to pay money for their chips.
I am a competent poker player. I found that the game favoured those players who would go all in before the flop with things like A5 os or 72os or 83 os. That sort of thing. I went all in against a guy on a dry rainbow flop while I held KK. He called to my delight with A,3 os. The turn paired the 9's on the board and the river was an ace to give him 2 pair AA,99.
This is just one of the many examples of this happening. I watched a player who raised pre-flop every single hand for over an hour win around 75% of the hands played. This wasn't to everyone else folding as much as you would think. I would say of the 75% he won, at least 35% of them went to showdown and he normally won on the river card with hand like J7 os or Q3 s.
I have played enough hours and play poker well enough to spot patterns and the patterns I spot are that the crazy all in players have the luck of the gods, Whilst the players who take the game seriously and are more likely to pay for chips to play are given hands like AA which will lose to 74os any day of the week.
As for the single player mode, it is short and worthless. The AI is there to further encourage this "all in with nothing attitude" in order to condition the players online to throw all their chips away.  There are five stages in total and 4 of those five stages have to parts to them. a 3-4 player game (you included) against idiots. Then a heads-up game against the apparent boss?!?! Who, while being slightly more intellegent, further pushes this idea that you should play every hand you are dealt and that folding is not an option.
In conclusion, if you want to play poker online with people who are competent enough to know what bet sizing and table position are at the very least, then go play at PokerStars. They have the same free chips they give you every day, however, because online poker for money is illegal in America, you get actual decent players on the play money part of the site.
Enjoy your poker future and please trash money grabbing games like this one that are programmed for you to lose. Like online roulette. :)

Actually playing the game proved that screenshots didn’t lie: Darkout is by far the most beautiful game in 2D sandbox exploration/building genre, and while I believe that graphics isn’t that important, great graphics like this certainly adds to enjoyment.
Graphics aside, Darkout has decent crafting and building system; there is a fair (but by no means spectacular) selection of decorative items to craft, and some interesting features, like research system or necessity to connect most advanced work stations to your base’s power grid.
Overall, Darkout has interesting early to mid-game. Finding resources and progressing can be quite challenging, as even early enemies can be deadly when you are poorly equipped, and environment itself can present hazards like long falls or deadly tar pits. As you progress through the game, however, the challenge diminishes, not increases: while you start encountering stronger enemies, their strength increase doesn’t match your stronger weapons and armor, and eventually even hardest areas become a walk in a park with late-tier sword and armor.
Aside from drastically diminishing challenge, as you keep playing you will eventually find Darkout rather lacking in variety: there are only 3 surface biomes, not counting very small and very empty coastline biome, and flying islands biome that looks the same as surface jungle biome (other than being composed of flying islands, naturally). There are several different underground layers, but only major difference between them is the music and what kinds of resources you can find there. Also, there is only one boss, and it can only be fought after a rather long questline.
In the end, despite its flaws, Darkout is a good enough game, and if you are a fan of 2D sandbox exploration/building genre, Darkout will likely give you many hours of enjoyment.

By far one of the most beautiful games I have ever played. Every environment looks like it was hand painted with the most vibrant array of colors I have ever seen used in a game to date. The story brings you in quick and keeps you invested with the deep, raspy voice of the narrator. The gameplay is fairly simplistic, staying in the style of an isometric fighter with a choice of two weapons and a skill, meaning there is no wrong way to play this game. The weapons are incredibly varied, both melee and ranged, ranging from a slow hammer to a ridiculously fast machete for the close range side of things. In the long range department, your options can range from a shotgun to a rifle to a cannon. Every weapon can be upgraded to change attributes, and the upgrades can be switched out at the main hub. Almost every level has a new weapon to introduce you to, and if you don't like the new weapon, a place to swap it back can be found shortly after. The new game + feature adds a lot of replay value, due to being able to take different approaches to levels. All in all, I highly suggest you pick this up if you love getting invested in stories.

As a developer I often see things that are obviously half-done and this, unfortunately, fits the bill.   The crafting is AMAZING and the world is absolutely beautiful, but story progression is a combination of tedium and luck with the Random Number Generator.   The devs are aware, but unfortnately, it leads to overcompensation and inventory bloat.
The premise of this game is that you are a member of a colony ship, unfrozen and jettisoned onto the world below.  No-one above is aware of the catastrophic events that led them to stasis in that ship, and it's on you to find out why.  I think.   The problems with the story quickly crack open when early quests have you fetch broken parts of a beacon.  Pulling these into your inventory doesn't trigger anything; you then have to kill an enemy and get it to drop a log file (which could also be a blueprint or minor side story item).  This log will look and sound like it was intended to play when you found the broken beacon piece (which happens to also be a random drop from chests and crates that spawn in the wild).
Once you've done this, the one voice acted character which isn't a computer but *is* interactive (sorta) grows ill in some way and bam, he's out of the story.  In fact, your entire beacon apparatus you spent tons of time building is also now just taking up space.  Hopefully by now you've been doing more things on your own and developing your base.  Enemies grow with your "Research Level" which is just your level, gained by mining and killing things and inventing.
The story gets harder to follow; the concepts are more abstract and the only indicator as to where to kill something to get it to drop a log or data cube (and yes, this is how all story elements progress) is to catch the one hint in the last log as to where it will be found.   While I appreciate making exploration necessary to progress, this is overdone; there are gates you encounter that need "purification" later which require a lot of searching for some hard to find items (such as big stacks of a certain color of Crystal).   Furthermore, if you start "purifying" a gate you can't work any other gate until that specific one is fixed.  When you finally face a boss, it drops a "leet loot" item but fails to progress the story in any way I can see.  All of the logs that are "above" your spot in the plot line refuse to unlock so you can read them, and I now have 5 metal chests full and am filling a Vault (which holds 100 items).
Some may say ripping on the acting in a game is nitpicky, but there is a limit to everything.   It's clear that someone from the sound studio must have quit their job during development; many of the audio clips have the actors rereading the line to deliver it how they want it to sound.  This normally doesn't make it past the sound studio; someone just grabbed the files and chucked them in.   You'll do a double-take the first time you read the line in the file, but hear the line spoken twice in a row with emphasis on different words.   Unfortunately, it does not have the endearing goof-up quality of the early days of TV like when Doctor Who had to be done in one take per scene.
Still, I recommend a buy ON SALE.   The gameplay itself is pretty solid, outside of some graphics-lag issues when too many items you can't pick up are on screen (i.e. when inventory is full).   You'll get stuck in the story, however; it's essentially an endurance test to see if you will keep playing until you get lucky enough to progress the tale, or if you get bored and stop playing before then.   I regret to say, I am probably in the latter, as will most people be.

Serena is a simple and free click-and-point adventure game, the adventure of size of log cabin and of lenght of hour at most. The game itself is supposed to be like a "tutorial" for upcoming developer's title "Asulym", mostly showing multiple character's reaction on objects. Each time that you click on the object, it will bring yet another character's thought, until it starts to loop in more generic lines. As the game progresses and overall mood of scene changes, each object will awake a different kind of thoughts in hero's mind with a different mood flavor.
It's also told that this game is "disturbing love letter" to adventure genre fans, that this game happened because of events that most of you didn't notice.
While the progression is not clear and is rather washed out, it does exist. There is no puzzle, you just have to explore log cabin and click-click-click it all. My hint would be to recheck photo on table from time to time. The story is not exactly clear, and most is told to be open for impretation. There is only one ending. The usual kind. For "art" games. The game is free and shouldn't waste too much of your free time, so you can easily check this out. If you like to immerse yourself. Other video gamers will find it to be an empty game.

Ive been playing Tower Unite since early access, and played Gmod tower since lobby one, the first iteration of this game, so let me give you the layout.
Due to how openended the game is, you will likely not find yourself bored for a long while. Its a house building game, not unlike the style Animal Crossing, but with way more content. You generate currency by playing minigames with friends (or strangers) which I will go through quickly here:
Once you've made some money (or as they call them, Units), you can head to the 5-6 stores, where you can do a number of things, such as buy accessories or pets for your character, instruments that you can actually play, or purchase a multitude of furniture and other decor for your condo.
The GUI for placing stuff is minimal and doesnt require any foreknowledge, its all very intuitive, though sometimes frustrating if you are trying to get something absolutely perfect. There is a huge amount of room for creativity, allowing you to place things on walls, ceilings, inside of other things, etc. as well as different ways to customize lighting, wallpaper and flooring, and even the time of day and weather inside your own little pocket dimension, and you can save and load your presets in case you want to turn your home from a recording studio into a home theatre. If you ever get bored of decorating the same area, they have ~6 different condos as of yet, all with unique looks and some even contain secret areas. After you've had a long day playing games with friends, you can also purchase a media player from the store and watch some Youtube videos or listen to some music off of soundcloud. The game is proud of its lack of microtransactions, with the only real thing you can buy with actual money after purchase of the game is a small donation which nets you a minimal amount of money and a cosmetic item for your condo.
While the 15 dollar fee is more than enough for the first 100 hours, you might soon find yourself exhausting the things you can do, often returning to the same game over and over again to grind those extra 100k units you need to get that one house you want. Soon after 200 hours, the updates feel like they take forever, as you often get bored of making money the same way all the time. what used to be a fun 18 holes of golf with a friend becomes the 37th playthrough of the same course tonight, whilst chatting about the fabled new update that will definitely entertain you for a good day or two, before it falls into the same catagory as the rest of the new minigames they release: Inefficient at making money, or so terribly expensive that you'll end up spending 2 days without sleeping playing one slot machine at the casino to gain money. (I actually did this once, its a story for another day but feel free to PM me about it)
The game runs on unreal engine, which means "'Anyone can run it'" even though that just means anyone running on anything below a breadbox sized computer from 2015 cant run it without making the resolution scale under 12 and have you play the entire game like you got bleach poured in your eyes and the recovery doctor gave you the wrong prescription glasses. If you have a good computer, something that can fallout 4 or Skyrim on low/med settings you should be fine. if not, its technically 'playable' if you can circumnavigate via echolocation.
Everything is really interesting for a pretty long time, until you do almost everything thats affordable and now you have to grind for 8 years to get money to do the rest of it. The updates, although coming out at a normal pace for a game, always seem to take forever in your mind and always look like they will rekindle your interest, till you either realize its too expensive for you to afford, or its a less efficient way of making money then just doing what you're already doing. I dont think this game will ever get enough content as it deserves, as there are only so many ways you can put a potato inside of a condo before it becomes unfunny, and the updates, although adding new stuff, always feel like the game didnt change. However, the first bits of the game are well worth the price tag, as its an excellent experience to share with friends, and there is never a better laughter as your friend accidently drinks 15 bottles of beer and proceeds to stumble around and puke on your tv halfway through a sentence.

I didn't mention the storyline above, because it's up to you to love it or hate it. I didn't find it amazing, but it's not bad either if you like the gameplay, you'll go along with the story too. Also, the storyline might last you around 8 hours depending on how many secrets you find and the difficulty you play on.
The puzzles are decent, and there are a few of them here and there. Not great, not bad, some are quick and some are frustrating.
The multiplayer looks interesting, but it's not working (or at least there isn't anyone playing). It's a shame truthfully, looks really fun and somewhat innovative imho.
If you happen to catch this game on sale or in a bundle, grab it if you can!
And that's it, if you like Hack'n'Slash games, you'll like this one, it's no Devil May Cry, but it's decent enough to give it a go. After all, you're playing this to kill everything around you, right?

A nice hack and slash game, that's fun in short bursts. The keyboard controls are sensible and reconfigurable, and it's also possible to play with a DirectInput gamepad combined with Joy2Key (unlike e.g. Darksiders, which goes crazy if it detects a DInput gamepad). I occasionally had a few graphical glitches with an AMD HD 3850 card, and some reviewers complained about a whole level (i.e. the environment) not loading in later parts of the game (the enemies loaded, so it might still be completable). I had no problems with an nVidia GTX-650.
The combat parts are fun, but using the gun with a gamepad was very frustrating (no aim assist), so I was constantly changing keyboard and gamepad depending on the situation.
Pros:
- configurable controls that don't go bonkers from DirectInput (XInput controls can't be remapped though)
- nice looking environments, hot protagonist
- voice acting is OK  (it's not ruining the atmosphere), but the story is all over the place
- lots of unlockable powers (you can choose from them, most of them seems viable)
- the time-reversal puzzles are nice, but not too hard
- no forced camera angles like in many 3rd person games
- check points are abundant
Cons:
- glitches with AMD videocards
The goes often on sales in various bundles, so if you're not sure about it, it might be good idea to wait for a sale.

This game is a ton of fun, though it's vast ruleset can be intimidating at first.  It's based on a somewhat high level table top board game and plays out like one in video game form.  Blood Bowl is a game of incredible depth and takes a serious amount of time to learn to do it well.  But if you do take that time and understand that this game is all about managing risk, you'll find it very rewarding in a reasonable amount of time.
While it might seem like a relaxing sit-back-and-click type take on the sports genre, it's rather tense.  Building your own teams, naming the players, and leveling them up has you second and third guessing each decision.  These players become extensions of you to a point, and risking them can be difficult!  The emotional and strategic depth in this game is unlike anything I've experienced.  I can't reccomend it enough for fans of table top board games or fans who might be into a sports/rpg hybrid.
I had played Blood Bowl 2 on the consoles first, which gives you a pretty good understanding of the rules and the risks involved.  This version is much more complete, with many more races to choose from than BB2. Like more than twice more.  The graphics aren't as good but this game runs well even on my old beatup laptop.  And it doesn't look bad.  The controls and interface is fantastic as I always feel like I'm making the move I want to make.
I know some of the negative reviews seem to be people who had frustrating dice rolls.  I promise that this game was never meant to be that hard.  It's supposed to be a deep table top board game at it's core, but it's not supposed require hours and hours of research before playing.  You will fail, but as long as you can understand why you fail in a rather short time you'll learn the rules pretty quickly.  I'm not the biggest fan of table top games in the world and I managed to learn the rules.
Pro tip: If you want additional resources theres a YouTuber named cKnoor who has excellent beginner and intermediate level strategy videos.  They helped my game immensely.

A game designed for tabletop and the odd evening with friends and beer that absolutely doesn't work online in an infinite open league; crippled by people powergaming and setting out to ruin your fun whilst a deliberately imbalanced skill system means that only a few teams can compete... combine that with a rule set that is set up to encourage "fun chaos" but instead ensures you fail constantly even with perfectly calculated dice odds, and that failure can mean your team ends up outright killed, and the game just isn't worth playing.
I tried to love it, I really did; I have fond memories of a few games of the tabletop with my brother long, long ago. But online every single game devolves into the same cycle of Chaos, Dwarves, Chaos, Chaos, or some other brute team which can simply cripple your players and eke out a win... or a few people abusing the Matchmaking by having 5 or so L6 players hidden amongst some throwaway L1s, and then use the overpowered skills stacked on the individuals to humiliate you.
Those masses of positive reviews? They're from people who really don't care about the community, but will do what ever they want online and damn what it feels like to you to try and play for fun; they're the people still here years down the line that didn't care the game never took off, because they're in it for the shallow ego boost that comes from using an easy team to win match after match. Seriously, the game designed teams as Easy and Hard difficulty and then suffocates under finding literal easy mode teams in match after match after match...
I'm told Blood Bowl 2 rebalanced the teams to make them a bit more equal? But after paying nearly £100 to make this one complete, I'm loathe to let the developers nickle and dime me to an equal level for a game they're already witholding teams for DLC from ...
And they never fixed the bugs in this either! Clicking on any player during kick off breaks your ability to swap substitutes out. Players can simply sit on the Intercept roll if you throw the ball and they have a chance to catch it, and force your entire timer to run down. And it's hard to escape the suspicion that people have individual RNG seeds, with some being much worse than others, when you run into bad luck game after game... someone even went as far as telling me my dice were cursed the other day. It's possibly not true, but in a game SO luck dependent, if you're the sort of person who isn't going to abuse the rules for quick overpower, and finds it frustrating to see your strategy fail because someone else did, or the dice went against you, this game will be absolute torture to you.
I've installed it twice now, and it kills me every time because of that. I end up seething at people being gits because the rules allow it, and you can't stop them, and I can't even have fun with my own team. If this sounds like you too, for goodness sake don't go near this game, not even with the lovely Warhammer Lore.

10/10 buy it, if you're ready to learn it.
Now a bit longer:
I used to play this game a lot back in a while, but stopped it, and now bought it on steam sale. It is a hardcore strategy: it's unforgiving, ugly, and you do need to learn quite a lot. Yes, the graphics aren't that great, yes, there is a big randomness factor for a hardcore turn based strategy, and yes, some races are extremly below the curve. But man, this game is rewarding as hell.
Once you get to the point, where you undestand basci tactics, and concepts, you can start playing the really interesting teams. The game itself has an incredible variety just from the tactics available. Add the 25 race, the leveling system, for each player individually, multi player, tournaments, single player campaign, and you can easily put in 100 hours into this game, if you ever get bored.
If you don't have any other Blood Bowl game, I recommend starting here. Buying the 2nd, is a waste of money, that game doesn't deserve to be called Blood Bowl. Buying the Legendary and saving 10 euros is something, but the three races are well worth it, believe me.
For learning, I recommend cKnoor's youtube channel, he made some tutorials for beginners, and has a lot of gameplay uploaded, you can learn a lot from him. He also streams on twitch, if I remember right.
If you need help with starting the game, I am more then happy to teach you the basics of the game, and some of the more beginner friendly races. So feel free to write me a p.m., but don't expect me up anytime soon, I have a social life to live after all, I can't spend every minute hitting people into the ground with a team of mummies and skeletons :DD

Amanita Design is one of those developers that I love to death, and in their case it's because all of their games are so unrelentingly joyful. From Samorost's kooky cosmic critters to the pleasant rustbuckets of Machinarium, their games exude pure happiness in the form of upbeat gibberish, uncomplicated puzzles, and positive themes no matter how dark individual moments may get. Botanicula is another notch in this merry belt, one that has no trouble juggling goofy vignettes with existential threats.
Once upon a time there was a very nice tree, full of little bugs and sprouts and assorted critters. Some spidery thing showed up and started devouring it all with a sort of creeping darkness, and a small band of the aforementioned critters escape with the tree's last seed. Struggling to stay one step ahead of their monstrous adversary, the critters journey through a colorful arboreal world in search of a new home and a fresh start.
What this actually means is you have five little dudes who roam around as a unit, following your clicks from screen to screen and interacting with the many living things of Botanicula's world. As an adventure game there's very little player input, relatively speaking. There's only left click (and on occasion mouse proximity has an effect) and only on specific points of interest like critters and items. You don't move your team directly, but rather click on arrows pointing to different areas.
These limitations actually serve to benefit the game, especially as the scope of the gameplay expands. Botanicula's world is strange and alien, and most of the puzzles wouldn't work at all if they required more exact input. Instead, you can just click on little creatures to make them fly or yell or burp, and as long as you do it at the right time or in the right order or at all, you can make progress. The scenes your clicks produce are so funny and heartwarming I doubt anyone will have a problem with relinquishing control for them. And then later in the game you'll get to pick specific critters on your team to do things, collect items to use in puzzles, and work through a few more nifty gimmicks.
The story is another strong point building on these basic mechanics, a remarkable feat given that it is told entirely without dialogue. The folks at Amanita have mastered the art of storytelling through action and expression and it does tremendous work here. All of the adorable denizens you meet speak in mumbly Sims-like chatter but get their points across through wild gesticulation and the occasional visual aid. This hands-off approach both heightens the impact of events (good and bad) when they occur, and also keeps the game feeling lighthearted and silly the rest of the time. You're also encouraged to experiment with everything you meet, because interacting with new critters earns you collectible cards that can score you extra scenes at the end of the game.
You'll experience the world of Botanicula through a mix of vector art and photoshopped works, a finely-blended style that gives everything just enough weight to seem real, without losing its fanciful, dreamlike energy. The peppy soundtrack follows suit with all sorts of cutely and folksy tunes to keep you engaged. The artistry on display here is rare and unique, and makes the game feel like a real treasure from its simple beginning to its unexpectedly epic conclusion. Botanicula makes another excellent entry in Amanita Design's lineup, and an unforgettable title for any fan of point-and-click adventures.

EDIT - it's been 7 months since the developers posted to explain a potential road to finishing Darkout... unfortunately that plan was to produce a totally new game (in the same world) and use income from selling that game to work on finishing this one. It's now been 7 months with no new news, and Allgraf's Facebook, Twitter, forums are all dead or spam-filled.
Switching my recommendation to a big fat NO.  If Adrian Banninga or Allgraf Studios are still around, they're certainly not focused on their customers.
-- ORIGINAL REVIEW --
I love this game and really hope the developers finish it and/or release more content some day.  If you want an incredibly beautiful sandbox mining, exploration, crafting, base building game in a very different SciFi atmosphere then Darkout is a great choice.  Environments, mobs, players and locations are all very well done.  Combat is decent but not ground-breaking.  Crafting is deep and can be a little confusing but the rewards for climbing the tech tree are consistent and fun.
There is a story, but it's more like background flavor at this point.  There is no ending or defined final objective, although there is a boss type creature you may encounter (but cannot fight).
The game was supposed to be survival-ey, but there's no food or exposure system, enemies cannot penetrate even the simplest of shelters, and no harvesting is required to run your power generators... so "survival" is reduced to not being killed by mobs when you leave home.
I still hope someday we see some things that were on the 'to do' list, including a real final objective to the game, enemy base attacks with mobs digging/breaking into bases, and multiplayer.
So yes... I recommend it for what it currently is - a beautiful exploring, crafting and base building game.
If you want a full story or a more survival-like experience then sadly you should look elsewhere.

At 450+ hours played and counting I have to say I am really enjoying this latest release of Master of Orion.  Now if you were looking for a clone of MOO II then you are going to be disappointed.  This is its own game but it does continue the tradition of the MOO series.
Most of the races you remember from MOO II return for this latest installment though some are not exactly as you might remember.  The same goes for technology.  A lot of it looks the same but don't assume any of it is an exact copy.  For me it is a nice blend of nostalgia and new features.
One feature that has some people irked is the inclusion of starlanes.  Personaly I don't see the problem but I also enjoyed Space Empires and they used starlanes too.  Once you get jump gates you will hardly notice starlanes anyway.
Another issue to keep in mind is that tatical combat is real time as opposed to turn based as it was in MOO II.  In smaller battles you still have a lot of control though in the larger fights there are just too many ships to effectively control in that environment.  The mouse controls are still a little clunky in that regard too.  There is a pause button so you can stop the battle as much as you like to give orders for movement and firing.
Finally I have to mention the UI.  This is one of the best designed UI's I've used in recent memory.

This game is in the same vein as God of War or Legacy of Kain. The blade combos are basic XXX or YYY style. This doesn't actually matter though since the real key here is the magic powers you gain throughout the game. It's not really the voice actors fault as most people say, but actually the script they were given to read.
You play Ayumi a treasure hunter so its natural you would be seeking treasure, but the games dialogue tends to beat you over the head with it so hard that it is really annoying. I mean your gaining magic powers and Ayumi remains conserned over treasure until the very end. With magic powers you don't need treasure would be a logical way of though along with why am I getting these powers?
The controls are pretty solid for the most part. The only real issue is the instances when you push the counter button and nothing happens. The enemies don't change a ton, but it wasn't bad either. The gunplay is actually very nicely done as well. This game reminded me Scratches in some way with it's grim atmosphere and permanent feel of light panic, as if you are waiting for some kind of a jumpscare to appear, however it never happens. But you can't actually call this game neither a quest, nor a horror. It is just a sad story of love between a writer and his wife, that has driven him mad. Although, some mysticism is present here too. Overall, this is how such story-driven short exploration games should be made. And it's simplistic love story is so much better than the piece of crap from another similar "game" called Gone Home, that is also hugely overpriced, compared to completely free Serena.
This game can be beaten in less than an hour. Give it a try and you won't regret.

As a big fan of the old “Point-And-Click” genre I was really happy to see the return of this style of game for PC. There are variants, some are puzzle and item hunting, some hidden object, and some are pretty much just a story with small bits of game play sprinkled in. The Walking Dead falls into the latter. Make no mistake; this is a story first; being a game is more or less incidental.
In this game you assume the role of a man named Lee, just as the world begins to collapse and the zombie apocalypse begins to spread. As Lee you will find yourself trying to lead a small band of ever-changing survivors through one desperate situation after another, whether it's the constant menace of zombie hordes, fending off marauders, trying to just find food and not starve. I'm being deliberately vague, as this is a story and I wouldn't want to spoil a thing. Needless to say in this short game, you will encounter some pretty big, pretty incredible situations. There is a desperation and intensity that make this experience pretty entertaining, and emotionally gripping.
Game play consists of some shooting segments where you will find yourself moving a cursor around to click and shoot a hostile. This isn't a first-person shooter by any stretch, the shooting in this more akin to whack-a-mole most of the time. There are also a lot of Quick Time Events, be prepared at any given moment to have to press the right button to dodge an attack, grab an item, or just ruin for your life. While I'm not a big fan of a lot of what was going on there was a solid variety of activity to at least give me the feeling I was still playing a game and not watching a show.
There are some frustrating control issues with this game that, while not a deal breaker, can make playing certain parts unnecessarily difficult. The lack of an
option during rare shooting portions threw me off a bit, making me have to retry a few times. While these were not specifically meant to operate as a shooting game, they were none the less presented as such and were made extra frustrating sheerly for the lack of what would have been a simple implementation of a common option. Minor oversights like this add up, and while they are not a serious problem, they are problems.
Visually the game is an odd duck for me. While I appreciate the artistic direction, I found the execution of this direction unappealing. The art style had a rough, very messy, very cheap look to it. The animations were stiff and robotic, and while I wasn't looking for total realism, something a bit more natural would have help out tremendously.
On the Other hand I found the characters themselves both engaging and endearing, thanks in no small part to the terrific use of facial expressions. The characters were visually emotive, and I found it difficult not to care about Lee's plight in trying to protect Clementine at the cost of his conscience, or her innocence.
There voice acting was really well done; I enjoyed the dialogue and character interactions. Though it had a dryness to its production quality that made them sound like actors on a stage, the delivery was great and truly helped foster the narrative in a compelling and meaningful way.
I was leery going in, but as a fan of The Walking Dead television series, I can say that I was very pleased with the content offered here, which both expanded upon and enhanced the world where walkers threaten at every turn.
Full of big moments, this is a heart-wrenching tale not to be missed by fans.
Soft recommended as an interactive story, but as a game this isn't going to thrill too much.

This is a tricksy game for me to recommend outright, but only because of the price. I picked it up in the Steam sale for £4.99 (iirc) and for that money I would say "don't miss it!". Turn based, simple concept, yet very complicated in the hands of skilled players, it's a rare game which has a long term draw. A cursory understanding of dice probability will be of huge help for those (like me) who might quit in a rage with the words "cheating computer!" when it seems like the AI teams are always passing their dice checks and I always fail mine! (it only seems that way!)
Long term players unanimously denounce the single player AI as useless although coming almost from fresh I'll say it's enough to give you the basic concepts and will punish mistakes. There are plenty of online leagues for you to cut your teeth on  and there is a healthy fan-base of regular players - the ideal place to learn not to get too attached to your players ;)
If you are looking at this and wondering whether to get it or Blood Bowl 2, I'll have to say I'm a little torn myself. There are plenty of threads for comparisons, but I think the key point is that those who have played these old editions are happy with where the balances are and the content (EVERY team). The new game (BB2) has changed a lot of things and in some areas this has actually broken some of the game blance, but someone completely new to Blood Bowl might not actually be affected by this. And the devs are finally listening to customer feedback and implementing some good positive changes.
For me it comes down to price though.  The game is like chess, in that while it's a simple concept, in the hands of good players it develops layers of intelligent enjoyment which the new version simply glosses up. if this turns up in the sale again grab it - and remember - those dice rolls really are random!  ;)

Intro:
Bastion is an isometric action-adventure game with an absolutely incredible visual style, fun and engaging combat, an engrossing narrative told by survivors of worlds that collided.  One of the core elements of Bastion is exploration and discovering the truth of the new world. You can uncover more through mementos, ash remains of old friends and folks long past, and the narration of a stranger.  The narration is remarkably well done and manages to convey so much without too much repetition.  They have tons of variations for even the small things like visiting a challenge area multiple times.
Gameplay:
Combat is very customizable and can suit pretty much any combat style if you invest enough shards of the old world into your weapons.  Each weapon has different strengths and benefits, as well as varying timings to excel with; this makes the combat extremely reactive and very skill oriented.  The only complaint I have regarding combat is the order with which you unlock certain weapons.  I think it could have had the player decide at least a few times what weapon to make/unlock and help them find their preferred play style more quickly. I tried pretty much every weapon and upgraded them all at least once, but I definitely found a few that I preferred over others.
I did have a little trouble distinguishing the actual level from the background at times due to perspective; some partially destroyed walls looked to be traversable and I would roll off into the oblivion as a result.
Story:
I won't go into much detail regarding the story as I think all players should experience it for themselves.  In my opinion, there are a few minor faults to the story, but they don't matter much and are just slightly inconsistent with the setting/world more than anything seriously problematic.  Thematically, Bastion's narrative has very clear and strong writing that the player can influence with how they approach the challenges set before them.  Some examples follow: If you choose to remove all the pests from an area, the narrator will remark on it; just keep running and ignore the enemies if you want, etc.
Audio:
Without a doubt, Supergiant Games created one of the very best sound designs and soundtrack I've ever heard for any artistic medium.  It blends so many different styles and musical instruments that it just feels completely different and fresh when you discover a new track.  I spent quite a lot of time just enjoying the music when I unlocked the gramophone, which lets you listen to any of the game's soundtracks.
Value & Time:
I spent around 10 hours to do most of the content available in the first playthrough, while unlocking 11 of the 24 achievements.  My plans are to play through some of New Game Plus to see the new content that is only playable in that mode, but I don’t think I’ll play through the whole game again right now.
Overall:
Bastion gets a Highly Recommended and is an extremely polished title that pretty much anyone will enjoy.  This is an incredible, memorable adventure that more people need to play through.

After 10 hours straight in one whole day, I would highly recommend this game. A large majority of the game feels polished, considering it's an early access game. The game devs are proactive and are willing to listen to the community and fix bugs quickly. In addition, the community so far has been fantastic, they are competitive, whilst being kind (unlike games such as League of Legends, Dota 2, CSGO and Overwatch). These are very rare qualities to find in such a game and I would recommend all friendly gamers to join.
However, there are still a few issues like any early access game, there are occasional bugs (however, they do not cripple the gameplay) and it can be frustrating if the captain doesn't have a mic or is unwilling to communicate. However,  this is easily fixed, as fittingly you can mutiny him (by pressing esc + mutiny captain)
Overall, the game devs hit gold. The whole premise is mesmerising and I find it peculiar that the idea hasn't been put into practice after all these years. I am also additionally looking forward to the game's future, as the game devs have promised very captivating ideas. This game is one of the must-haves of 2017 and is well worth the £14.

I want to thank Firaxis for giving me a chance to play a game i have long had on my wish-list. i played it on the free weekend.

All the old problems were there:
Of course there were the same wacky RNG issues but these were masterfully handled by making sure that you were constantly outnumbered and outgunned and generally also on a time-limit as well... so, no holding back and reloading for you!
More importantly you have to make sure your plan moves like clockwork on some of these missions and this was often interfered with by a miracle Overwatch shot by the Advent or by a crazy miss from one of your own guys. I dont think I need to write a lengthy post on Besthesda's buisness practices, but i will talk about one point i have not heard anyone make. everyone has probably figured out that Bethesda implemented creation club the way it did so that ps4 players can get mods, since these are considered official content, and are added via update to the game. while that is great for ps4 players (save for the ridiculous prices), it isnt so good for PC players, because now whenever they update the game to have more creation club content, the integral parts of pc modding like fallout 4 script extender, for low end pcs the very necessary shadowboost that has not been updated in awhile, or other framework mods need to be updated every time. this means that pc players will regularly lose access to their modded games and saves, until a new f4se patch comes around. then theyll have to wait for updates for the mods that use f4se like the mod configuration menu, and if a mod creator has decided they wont continue to support their mod, you can say goodbye to that one. they said this wouldnt harm or effect pc modding, but clearly it has. if you already own this game do whatever you can to avoid updating it. since creation club content will be released often, it could turn out that mods that require a lot of work to update will simply fall out of use, which is a shame because pc modding is built off of extensive quest and script mods. despite public condemnation they continue to embrace their new anti-consumer buisness strartegy, an the bethesda that was a hero of the people when they released skyrim and its mod tools, is mostly gone, replaced by a give me money enemy.
as for the actual game, if you liked fnv or fo3, it will disappoint you.

I got this game as part of a bundle for next to nothing, but having played it now, I would have paid full price if I'd known about it before! It's a trully awesome, smooth and gorgeous game, with a fair bit of challenge figuring out the Time Rewind skill!
The best way I can describe this title's gameplay  is Tomb Raider meets Heavenly Sword meets Max Payne meets Guild Wars 2. I would recommend playing this with a mouse and keyboard, though controller isn't too bad.
You have a bunch of usefull skills at your disposal (1-3 buttons), and a compass to guide you to treasure chests. You can grapple flying enemies and slash them into strips in mid air, and leap to the next one! And when some enemy has a shield that you alone are too weak to take down, you can keep rewinding time to spawn more and more clones that repeat your last actions...this can also be used to stand on 2 switches with clones, so you can safely get past the traps. It's a great concept and well executed!
The graphics are lovely, the voice acting though not perfect is nice enough, and the challenges presented are fun to figure out.
Grab it at Bundlestars in the Reboot 5.0 pack, which comes with the DLC free!! Also with some other games (those aren't so great xD).
Personal Rating: Lots of action! Cute Character! Good fun!
Score Rating: 80% - Not a masterpiece but good fun and worth playing

Although it's short, it has a ridiculous amount of style. Imaginative critters that are crosses between insects and plants essentially, but they're really hard to describe other than that, you just have to see them in action. You go through the game interacting with these critters, you play as a small team of 5 critters trying to save the "critter tree" from being drained of all life by black "Zlo" critters. Interacting with the area will introduce you to new critters who will help you progress. It's fun to see how creative the game designers got with the critters, all having their own signature sound effects that are sometimes quite humorous. The sound design is great in this respect, having hundreds of sounds between critters and many tunes that sound like the critters singing a ditty as a group. The area design is also quite varied, going from the canopy of the critter tree to a critter village to a branching cave of more gangled critters.
The game is short, but enjoyable all the way through. Puzzles aren't too obscure or confusing, it doesn't really have a hint system but it isn't too hard to figure out what to do. Very satisfying. This game has become one of my favorite point-and-click games, due to its style, music, and sound effects.

Intro:
Bastion is an isometric action-adventure game with an absolutely incredible visual style, fun and engaging combat, an engrossing narrative told by survivors of worlds that collided.  One of the core elements of Bastion is exploration and discovering the truth of the new world. You can uncover more through mementos, ash remains of old friends and folks long past, and the narration of a stranger.  The narration is remarkably well done and manages to convey so much without too much repetition.  They have tons of variations for even the small things like visiting a challenge area multiple times.
Gameplay:
Combat is very customizable and can suit pretty much any combat style if you invest enough shards of the old world into your weapons.  Each weapon has different strengths and benefits, as well as varying timings to excel with; this makes the combat extremely reactive and very skill oriented.  The only complaint I have regarding combat is the order with which you unlock certain weapons.  I think it could have had the player decide at least a few times what weapon to make/unlock and help them find their preferred play style more quickly. I tried pretty much every weapon and upgraded them all at least once, but I definitely found a few that I preferred over others.
I did have a little trouble distinguishing the actual level from the background at times due to perspective; some partially destroyed walls looked to be traversable and I would roll off into the oblivion as a result.
Story:
I won't go into much detail regarding the story as I think all players should experience it for themselves.  In my opinion, there are a few minor faults to the story, but they don't matter much and are just slightly inconsistent with the setting/world more than anything seriously problematic.  Thematically, Bastion's narrative has very clear and strong writing that the player can influence with how they approach the challenges set before them.  Some examples follow: If you choose to remove all the pests from an area, the narrator will remark on it; just keep running and ignore the enemies if you want, etc.
Audio:
Without a doubt, Supergiant Games created one of the very best sound designs and soundtrack I've ever heard for any artistic medium.  It blends so many different styles and musical instruments that it just feels completely different and fresh when you discover a new track.  I spent quite a lot of time just enjoying the music when I unlocked the gramophone, which lets you listen to any of the game's soundtracks.
Value & Time:
I spent around 10 hours to do most of the content available in the first playthrough, while unlocking 11 of the 24 achievements.  My plans are to play through some of New Game Plus to see the new content that is only playable in that mode, but I don’t think I’ll play through the whole game again right now.
Overall:
Bastion gets a Highly Recommended and is an extremely polished title that pretty much anyone will enjoy.  This is an incredible, memorable adventure that more people need to play through.

Blood Bowl is an adaptation of a tabletop game by the same name that was created by Games Workshop. It takes place in an alternate version of the Warhammer Fantasy universe where all of the races decide to settle their differences playing games of American Gridiron Football.
Much of the aesthetic of Blood Bowl was nailed perfectly. The look of the more general races like the Humans resemble 1950's caricatures of Football players. While the more fantastical races like the Undead look like mummified quarterbacks. There's a significant amount of content in this release, with a total of 23 races. Each with their own unique roster of players and distinctive gameplay balance.
My favorite aspect of Blood Bowl is it's extensive singleplayer experience that also appears in the multiplayer. If your players get injured this carries over into subsequent matches, and if they die you lose them forever. Your players also level up and gain Fallout style perks. It reminds me a great deal of strategy games like X-Com. The entire game is turn based and every action in the game is determined through rolling a 6 sided die. It is a surprisingly faithful recreation of the original tabletop game, which puts off a lot of players as a result.
Blood Bowl gets frequently referred to as an "RNG game with a mix of strategic elements". Which I personally disagree with. The random elements to the game make the game stand out to me compared to a lot of other strategy games. Where you can have a player void his entire turn because of a botched pass, forcing you to adapt. The meta of the game as a result revolves around minimizing the amount of rolls you might have to make, taking full advantage of your teams strengths. Because of these random elements, succeeding with a plan feels much more earned than it normally would be in any other strategy game. You feel that Ork score a touchdown, you feel your team win a tournament. It all feels really good when you win.
Which brings me to my criticisms of the game. While Cyanide did a hell of a job adapting the rules, the game doesn't really explain very core fundamentals. Things like the balance between the races, roster selection, and even what particular plays are more effective over others. Blood Bowl is a game that requires practice and most importantly patience. You won't fully learn the game without losing several matches and clocking in upwards of 10 hours into it even. It takes a lot of reading guides and practice to really understand how to play it.
But that's one of the most satisfying aspects of Blood Bowl. To me it's a turn based strategy game that's willing to anger you, that's willing to grind your teeth, that's willing to paint facepaint on your cheeks and dump Gatorade down your throat. This game is one of the finer examples of injecting variety into an otherwise bland sports game, and it really makes you feel like you're playing it in both body and mind.
One last thing to note is the "Chaos" edition to the game is the complete version, with more content than the Legendary edition. While you can play online with players from the Legendary edition, it comes highly recommended to get this version to recieve the full experience.

This game... ohhhh this game... It is actually with a very heavy heart that I can actually give it a thumbs down. I am torn and seriously torn at this. I have had a lot of great moments, but a lot of bad moments as well. The problem with this game is in its entire appeal to RNJesus. If you love dice rolling games with a twist of strategy, then this is for you. If you are a diehard strategy nerd, then this game will leave you bitter when the opposing team kills 2 of your star players and then procedes to dodge the rest of your team into a touch down after 3 turns of you rolling 2 attacker downs.
The temple of RNG is that of a 6 sided die where 1s are always failures and 6s are always successes. You can stack it in your favor where 2-6 is a success or a 6 is the only success, but you must realize that means there is always a possibility of 17% failure. To me, this is the deal breaker. This to me, breaks the game. This is akin to munchkin(a fine game in certain lights) which can be fun light-heartedly, but if I were to rank this game amongst other strategy games, it has to get the thumbs down.
This game does have many strategic aspects and so I thoroughly enjoy it for a Saturday sitdown, but the mental engagement is severally lacking. You can even tell since the AIs only ability to perform better is through just giving it more perks than you. This always leaves a fairly sour taste in my mouth, but I can usualy power through it if the game plays if engaging enough. This game play isn't.
So for the TLDR crowd, if you want an RNG game that mimicks strategy, get this game. If you actually like strategy games, then this game is a no for me.

A good free to play ARPG. However a little on easy side for experienced FPS players and ARPG players. Player customizatioon in terms of building a character is extremely lackluster compared to games like Diablo and more. But you can still put a thousand plus hours into this game and not unlock everything. You do a system for collecting some armor pieces and a weapon and some upgrading/customization abilities to keep getting stronger through this system, but there is no way of "building" a character, every player playing this game playing the same class has the exact same skills on their toolbar, so no customization in that expect, no skill trees to choose from etc. so this is by far not as in depth as other ARPG's. This game may lack dept of character customization but it makes up for it in the "collecting" game. There is thousands of costume like items to collect in the game and achievments to gather that level up your "mastery" level which also give you bonuses and more. This makes game somewhat enjoyable to play in long term. However quests and dungeon fighting does get repetitive. They do regularly add new lands, new thems, new dungeons, tons of new looks for weapons/clothing, etc on a rtegular bases. But the core gameplay is fairly shallow and competitive. At this point i feel like they will continue to add more content on a regular basis as far as new costumes, monsters, lands, dungeons to explore, etc. but core gameplay is as good as it's going to get at this point.
I'm assuming difficulty is low and complexity of game is disigned for younger audiences. This is kind of like a pokemon collection ARPG style game more then an in-dept character building game you would see in games like Diablo or Path of Exile. I would put this into a Casual-ARPG category.
Although i'm not super happy about lack of dept in this game i still recommend it for those looking for a more casual or collection based gameplay but still have some hack n' slash ARPG elements. I'd say this is like a casual Diablo mixed with minecraft mixed with pokemon only you collect item "skins" not creatures.

This is not a bad game. Don't get me wrong, for the industry standards of today it's rather trashy but this game wasn't made in 2015-16. It has a solid mechanic: Hack and slash through hoards of enemies. It has a fair ammount of skills and decent enemy variety so it's not at a lack of any redeeming qualites. No, I'm not going to recommend this game is because it's lackluster in terms of design.
The story suffers from high doses of cliche, awkward voice acting, and just being generally cheesy. While it's not the worst, it is certainly noticable. Cutscenes phase in and out rather abruptly. The combat gets repetitive VERY quickly, even in terms of hack and slash genres. Picking between your melee or ranged attacks have little to no impact and there's not much to discourage just spamming your spells untill everything is dead. However even these flaws are okay in my mind. It's the lack of world depth. This game is suppose to be an RPG, and yet it's almost as if they're trying to remind you it's just a video game.
Wanna use that ingame currency? Open up a menue that looks like it was designed with microsoft word art. The animation for picking up a rare treasure is a black screen suddenly popping up and having said rare treasure drunkenly take concentric swoops to the middle of the screen. The GUI is somewhat ornate but lacks a certain clarity, and I judge the man who's executive decision it was to make currency just a number in IMPACT font on the top right corner, with not even a simple icon to mark it.
It is such a beautiful solid concept of a game, but it needs another look. Some polish and redesign will do wonders for it.

DO NOT BUY THE DISMAL SWAMP DLC UNDER NO MEANS.... It is... Dismal. Really.
Got this in a bundle for a very good price. It's slightly worth it, but I recommend looking for the reboot bundle that comes with it and the useless dlc at the fraction of the cost. It runs like water and is smooth even on a meh laptop. Arrondale gma igpu.
As for the game... This feels like an apology for the last game than anything. Games like legacy of goku 2 and crimson gem saga come to mind because they are sequels to far lesser games. This is your run of the mill hack and slash game that properly adds platforming elements a bearable shooting element all under the usage of time. Appropriately you are more of a glass cannon than anything, and you have to use time and sometimes order to grab the advantage over enemies.
Essentially the game is still xblades. Cut things down with repetitive slashes interrupted by skills. But it's bearable now. The game is actually a game now and retains it's battle potential. Ayumi is pretty attractive, and her choice of attire gets better as the game progresses. But in a less revealing more fierce way. Which is a big improvement, as I think this game really sells the character, and not really the game.
Platformers... Beware. I have slipped off of ledges in early missions randomly, or fell off bridges quickly because when falling she has this weird offset bounce that is probably an error. It's extremely apparent in dismal swamp when the snail foe pretty much pinballs your character if you approach it quickly. She also falls like dark matter, it's really shocking how fast she falls after her usable trajectory ends.
Playing the game, you'll notice that if you fail a lot, the game will bend to making sure you still enjoy it. Sort of like how dying 10 times in crash bandicoot gave you a free witch doctor, and would boost it again if you kept dying. This game does the same by giving you maximum rage and later both the former and maximum health packs. In my opinion it is sometimes necessary as later in the game having less than half health will get you smashed if you are are selfish with healing. Or lengthy battles where you die shortly before winning and you would otherwise set the game down.
Biggest deal for this game? Playing it unlocks all equipment for use in outbreak mode, and I think a few items in outbreak mode went to the story too. Probably mistaken. If you do happen to have dismal swamp and beat it, I think it gives you a golden rifle. Anyhow, outbreak mode is like a tower defense outpost type game that you play a huge role in. Maya's legendary heroes for android is probably the closest comparison I can make to it  as the mechanics are almost exactly the same. It's online, and even off, and It's really cool to use as it had the same effect as those defense games but how you play in it makes a HUGE impact of how the battle goes. It's pretty much single player, but against others. Really well done and a good way to use their game assets.
The story is pretty decent, carefree treasure hunter getting caught up and experiencing things on the way to destiny. Pretty typical, but it came a far way from xblades. And their graphical detail is even furthered along, but the gravity and stability of the platform elements does throw you off from taking it seriously almost always. But the visuals and the clever time mechanics as well as the voice acting makes you wish they actually gave more than a visual quality test. Because everything else does well and does beg for more enemies to be had and combos to exist. And I can only hope the company continues learning how to make a good stable game... And not to release dlc that will make you want to swear the company off for stealing your money.
