I want to start this review by stating that although I may not have many hours on PC, I do have 200+ hours on the Xbox one version (which to my understanding is very much the same game).

Now, The first thing I have to say about Stardew Valley is that it does an excellent job at getting you lost in its world. The immersion, I found, is probably one of this games biggest strengths. It's very easy to dump an entire day into it and even easier to not regret all the time spent planting, mining, and fishing, etc. (which by the way, there is a massive amount of activities to do/plan for). The second (and most memorable) reason Stardew get a thumbs up is its soundtrack. The OST is a huge helper when it comes to the immersion and it makes for a relaxing and enjoyable experience. I remember how magical it felt the first time I started it up to be greeted by the friendly and soothing music. Has to be one of my favorite soundtracks to date.
It's pretty hard to find any problems with this game. I can see select people not enjoying this game if they don't like grinding or repetitive activities (Not to say that the entire game is repetitive, but it can get there if you're not good at creating your own goals in games). If you like Harvest Moon, grindy games, or are just looking for a relaxing and time consuming experience then please give this game a try.

I have had very bad experience with online poker games, or just gambling games in general.  I've given up on playing these type of games on my phone, and haven't played the older poker games or the popular casino game on steam in six months.
I downloaded Prominence Poker because I was looking to try out some new games on my newly built PC.  I didn't play it much at first, but after a while I started playing it again, and really started enjoying it.  The community is great and players play like they are supposed to.  People who go all in all the time will quickly be eliminated.  Unlike other online poker and casino games, this game doesn't seem to be rigged.  I win some and I lose some, sometimes I win big and sometimes I lose big.  I haven't seen unbelievable results like constant bad beats on the river or eight straights in a row as I've seen elsewhere.  I never feel like this game is rigged in such a way that you lose so often that you become some frustrated that you want to spend real money to buy chips to keep playing.
Speaking of chips, what I really like about this game, is that it is quite generous with your daily cut.  While other games only give you a few chips to play around with hoping you spend real money on chips, you can easily enjoy yourself and have enough chips to play with what they give you daily.  There are also frequent bonuses and achievements you can earn daily and weekly, to get even more chips.  Of course if you don't like grinding, you can always buy chips with real money.
In addition to playing poker with your chips, you can spend your chips on character items, clothing, and table items, this keeps the game fresh as there are pretty much unlimited customization, from the way your character looks to what he/she wears or uses.
If I had one complaint I wish there were more places you could play; maybe they'll add new places later?
I highly recommend this game, its the best online poker game I've ever played and not some rigged BS.

Stardew Valley is really something special.
You can lose yourself in this game. I fell into playing one day and completely lost track of time. Before I realized it, I had played for twelve hours.
Stardew Valley recaptures the magic of some of my favorite games from childhood; it reminds me of the way I felt playing A Link to the Past or Pokemon for the first time. At face value, Stardew Valley looks like a cute game, but there are some very adult and even dark themes to be explored if you look for them. The game exudes a sense of hope and optimism. You have to explore and really work towards developing anything in the game... be it your farm, relationships with other people, your money, your skills or tools. It feels like you are always working towards something and the amount of reward is directly proportional to the amount you work and prepare.
What I really appreciate about Stardew Valley is that it's a completely unadulterated gameplay experience. There are no microtransactions here. This is a game made by a person who very obviously loves video games. The game was made entirely by one person and it feels like he poured his heart into it.
Playing Stardew Valley is almost like a meditation. It's relaxing and therapeutic. It's always a positive experience. It just makes you feel happy.

This may be the best game I've ever played - it almost certainly has the best writing, and there's no doubt that it has the best sound. The narrator's voice is like wrapping yourself up in a warm blanket, and he's consistently backed up by an original score that's not only beautiful, but always perfectly aligned with the mood of the action and the story.
The emotional arc of the game is downright staggering; I ran into a theory some time ago that Bastion is actually about the aftermath of a bad breakup, and it really, really fits. Bastion has the same weight of emotional impact as Hotline Miami, Papers Please or Spec Ops: The Line - but the scope of those games is limited to the ugly and brutal, while Bastion is beautiful and uplifting.
I ran into a theory some time ago that Bastion is actually about a breakup - I strongly recommend looking at it through that lens as you play, as it really fits and adds an entire dimension to an already deep game.
The gameplay is probably the weakest component, in that it's just really good; combat flows nicely, the controls are clear and reactive, and while they haven't made any staggering revisions to the existing formula, it's a good formula and they implement it well.

If you're on the fence about whether you should add Stardew Valley to your library, just do it. It is well worth the $15.
The game starts with your customized character working a depressing, dead-end job at Joja Mart. In the opening cutscene, a letter from your deceased grandfather reveals that you have inherited his farm. You make the move to Stardew Valley, home to about 30 other residents each with their own memorable personality traits. Your goal now is simple, but vast: Begin your new life as a farmer.
First, if you don't want to read all my blabbering, my summary is below as well as at the end of my review.
(TL;DR:)
(All in all, the pros vastly outweigh the cons, and the cons aren't even really "cons" if you think about it, but instead ideas I think would enhance an already amazing game. Stardew Valley has a little something for everyone inside it, and even though you can finish the main quests within the first two in-game years, it still provides an excellent amount of gameplay (even more) for a $15 game. Stardew Valley does not limit itself to its original quests, as you can play with your own for long after you've completed them (my 300+ hours of gameplay is a testimony to that). It's cute, it's fun, it has a beautiful aesthetic and soundtrack, the townspeople are memorable, the opportunities are endless. If you're still thinking about it, stop. Just buy the game already.)
Now, on to the more detailed part:
There are many activities available to you, including:
*Planting/Watering/Harvesting crops
*Foraging the land for countless resources, minerals, crops, and hidden artifacts
*Designing your farm (layout, farm buildings, animals, interior of farm house)
*Fishing
*Mining
*Lots of social interaction with the townspeople (including gift-giving, cutscenes, special birthday presents, and building relationships with marriage candidates)
*Daily quests
*Collecting artificats for the museum
*Upgrading tools
*Using farm buildings/structures/tools to create artisan goods
*The satisfaction of earning money
And, perhaps the biggest quest in the game, completing the Community Center. In order to do so, the player must collect items (often seasonal) and offer them toward the completion of the Community Center, each "bundle" offering rewards for the players' hard work.
Another attraction of the game is the rotation of seasons. Each year is made up of four seasons, each season being one month (28 days) long. Each townsperson has a birthday, there are special events per season, and there are seasonal items such as fish and crops. The seasons do a good job of making the game feel fresh.
Overall Pros and Cons:
Pros:
*Stardew Valley offers a variety of "side quest"-like activities for the player. Even once the main quest of the game is completed, the Community Center, the player undoubtedly still has many other things to accomplish (such as leveling up skills, strengthening relationships with the townspeople, and unlocking achievements)
*Many aspects of the game can be customized. The player's appearance can be changed once a certain room is unlocked, and there are many design elements for the player's farmhouse (including furniture, wallpaper, and flooring) and farm (including craftable/placeable items and farm buildings)
*Stardew Valley is what I call a Replayable Game. I have several save files of different farm layouts (you have five to choose from when you start) in which I prioritize different goals
*There is no punishment for playing the game at your own pace or going against the grain. You can choose to disregard the Community Center, you can choose to solely focus on relationships, you can not give a damn about relationships and only focus on mining, you can do whatever you want.
*The game is STUNNING. I love the bright, simple, "feel good" aesthetic. In addition, the soundtrack is beautiful as well. Super relaxing and makes me feel happy. Sometimes I like to play with the soundtrack, other times I turn off the music and listen to podcasts or my own playlist.
*Once you complete the programmed quests, the open-endedness of the game allows you to create your own goals. Want 10-heart relationships with all townspeople? Do it. Want $1,000,000? Do it. Want to find all the museum artifacts? Do it. Want to see how deep into Skull Cavern you can get? Do it. And so on.
*There was a point when I got bored. I walked away from the game for a few months, and when I opened it up again, it was like I discovered it all over again. To me, that is an amazing quality in a game.
Cons:
*Stardew Valley is addictive. This could be also taken as a pro. Just be aware that it can suck you in.
*The game automatically saves the previous day once you wake up the next day. So, essentially, in order to save the game, you have to go to bed. There is no saving at 3:30pm (the days go from 6:00am to 2:00am) then carrying on to go to bed at 11:00pm and saving again. That being said, any progress you make during the day can be lost if you close the game before going to bed or if you lose power or something. Also, that means there is no saving before going into an area of monsters (however, the monsters aren't super challenging and there are many lengths you can go to to ensure survival). This is an aspect of the game that can get annoying, but after my 300+ hours of gameplay, I've gotten used to. It's just a part of the game.
*The nature of the game is very repetitive. Wake up every morning, every year repeats itself, birthdays on the same days, characters stay the same. For a game clearly designed to be played forever, the inital quests run out rather quick. That being said, I completed the game's original quests in my first 60ish hours of gameplay. That is GREAT for a $15 game, and I have over 300 hours logged, so clearly I've found other stuff to do. More programmed quests is just wishful thinking on my end.
*I am drawn to the social aspect of the game, so I wish there was a bit more dialogue with the marriage candidates (and even the others). I also wish there was a little something more to the married life once you chose a bride or groom. Sure, you can have kids, but the kids don't really do anything. Sometimes you get presents from your betrothed but, I don't know, I find myself wanting a stronger feature of Stardew Valley married life.
All in all, the pros vastly outweigh the cons, and the cons aren't even really "cons" if you think about it, but instead ideas I think would enhance an already amazing game. Stardew Valley has a little something for everyone inside it, and even though you can finish the main quests within the first two in-game years, it still provides an excellent amount of gameplay (even more) for a $15 game. Stardew Valley does not limit itself to its original quests, as you can play with your own for long after you've completed them (my 300+ hours of gameplay is a testimony to that). It's cute, it's fun, it has a beautiful aesthetic and soundtrack, the townspeople are memorable, the opportunities are endless. If you're still thinking about it, stop. Just buy the game already.

I recently purchased this on sale. I've also been a fan of MOO since the first, a fan of the 4x genre since forever.
I do enjoy this game but why did I not recommend this game you wonder?
Because for all the things they did to improve, the designers left out quite a bit that made this game unique and a loving title.
The new Master of Orion title is clearly built for a more "theatrical" experience. Plenty of cutscenes, camera angles in fighting (much like the much maligned MOO 3, but improved honestly), and a plentiful voice cast list.
However for all that multimedia spectacle, the game itself is rather shallow compared to earlier MOO titles and even 4x games that came after (i.e. Stellaris).
The Terran Khanate, a new faction, is only available if you purchase the Collectors Edition. Other races that were in the second title won't be in game until DLCs. These can be forgiven if they're recreating the first, but the game's ability to play should have been updated.
The games ability to keep track of ships is rather clunky, so is the ability to track colonies. Though you CAN rename systems that's pretty much it for customization.
Customizing races consists of picking a "gene" (one of the player template names) and picking your traits. So less creating your own race and more just tweaking an existing one.
Despite all of this I could see someone new to the 4x genre cutting their teeth on this, but then either putting it down later or picking up more polished games (i.e. Stellaris).
This game is no means a travesty like Master of Orion 3, but it clearly is built more for the cutscenes and presentation more than gameplay. Which is why, though I might enjoy it in small spurts, I cannot recommend for players.
Truth be told this revamp of the original title, complete with setbacks the original had, only highlight how things evolved after it (the original) was released. This title had the chance to take some of the original components and bring them into a design fit for the modern 4x experience, but rather adhered to both the old charm and limitations of the original. I cannot support fully such an ideal.

I have to give Master of Orion two scores.
As a single-player experience I'd rate it 4/5 stars. The graphics are gorgeous, it captures the spirit of the original game perfectly, and goes a long way to reclaimin the title of King of the Turn-Based Strat games. I do have to deduct a half star for not being able to set up custom-defined autobuild ques for extended planet development (beyond the 4 slots you're allowed). being able to set up a custom auto-build command for late game development would be invaluable. I also deducted a half point for the controls of the battle interface. Commanding your fleets hands-on can be tricky at best.
As a multi-player game though, I'd only rate it 2/5. There's no easy way for a disconnected player to jump back into a game, and the hands-on battle interface is just gone. you're only allowed the auto-resolve battle option. In my book, these are two huge hits to the quality of that side of the game. Overall though, I still reccomend this game and hope that these oversights can be rectified in the future.

I've really enjoyed this game. And here are 7 reasons why:
1) It's fast paced, dynamic and there is no time wasted backtracking or being lost. You are engaged form the first moment to the last.
2) The somewhat new concept of time rewinding in combat. Unlike Prince of Persia, here you watch everything go back in time while you remain unaffected. However a clone of yourself does backtrack all your actions. When you stop rewinding that same clone does everything you did until the moment when your started to rewind time. If you attacked an enemy before the time rewind now you get to attack it again, but now as duo with clone of yourself. You can repeat this process a few times until you have a small army of clones to swarm in on your enemy. How cool is that? Time rewind is also used a fair amount of time to solve puzzles and win special fights.
3) The combat is fast, energetic, although quite simple. You don't have a lot of combos, but you do have spells that freeze or burn your enemies. Not rarely you are required to use to time rewind to win a fight by solving a sort of combat puzzle.
4) This game does not have experience, however I really like they way you gain power. Basically when you get to a certain point you get to pick what skills to take from a small selection, and depending on your choice new skills open up next time, although you can't see the skill tree at any point. The here-and-now approach to level progression was a welcome change comparing to reading every skill upfront. The little surprises every time you are offered made the power progression much more enjoyable for me.
5) The level design is truly remarkable. The visuals are outstanding keeping in mind that this is a smaller studio and the environment feels vibrant and alive. There are a few memorable levels such as the one when you get to fly and the sand level in which you need to fight in shades because the sunlight can kill you if you are exposed to much to it.
6) The voice acting is not superb, but is far from atrocious like some reviews stated. Actually, it the scripted comments range from mundane to really fitting in with what you are doing (Once falling from a platform which holds the boss I thought to myself "dammit" which was the exactly same that my character said)
7) The story isn't spectacular but it is interesting and nicely woven into everything you are doing

I somehow magically had this game called Serena already purchased on Steam, and since it was an Indie game I decided to take it for a spin. You play the part of a man who has forgotten why he's in a rustic cabin, and whatever happened to his wife. In this point and click adventure game you will have to reassemble the pieces to discover what you do not know and what you forgot.
Graphically I have to say that this is a very good looking game. I felt like I was in a dusty old cabin, devoid of any true light, but showing that it was lived in, at least at some point, and that the clutter and the items found in the cabin make it all feel real. The only images that I didn't really like was the fact that there were two slightly different hand icons and sometimes made it hard to distinguish between cannot do anything and pick up this item to interact with it.
The sound was probably the hardest thing to pull off about this game, and I have to say that I was impressed. You could feel the emotion in the voices. To be a bit nitpicky I have to say that when the auditory memory flashes of the wife happened I couldn't really picture that voice coming out of the wife, but like I said, nitpicking.
This is not really that long of a game, and to be honest to tell this story it really didn't have to be. There were some very frustrating aspects to this game, most of them revolving around having to touch objects throughout the cabin over and over again trying to pull clues out after you found the last clue spot, but then again we are talking about a man who cannot remember a thing of why he is in the cabin, and where his wife is, so I can understand that as puzzle pieces fall into place, going back over something that meant nothing at first could make a hell of a difference later.
Now as far as I can tell, as of right now the game is free, I'm not sure if that will change, it was released at the end of January 2014, so take it as you would have. I do have to say that I was impressed by the fact that there seemed to be a lot of collaborators taking part in this, but at the same time I don't think it really shows, maybe with everyone adding their two cents and refining details it made it better, but it's hard to tell. Alright so lets give this game a grade shall we? Even though it was short, and there were some frustrating parts to it, once I started the game I literally did not stop until I got to the end, so for that this game gets an 8.9 out of 10.

What do you say to someone who’s played it all?
“Buy this game. Please.”
Bastion is one of the “big names” of the Indie scene. Although its reach has gone farther than most games made by small companies thanks to a partnership between Supergiant Games and Warner Brothers, Bastion still has the charm that only a small-time game can. From the graphics to the gameplay, the music to the narration, you know you’ve found something special from the moment the game begins.
The game follows the story of a boy known only as “the Kid” following a catastrophic event called the Calamity. With the world falling to pieces, it’s up to the Kid to collect cores to rebuild the bastion and restore life. An old man known as Rucks narrates the story as it plays out. Along the way, the Kid must fight off monsters, enemies, and even nature itself to retrieve the cores and save the bastion, with a few surprises along the way.
Artistically, Bastion is a gem. Jen Zee’s artwork gives the world an organic, colorful feeling that constantly evolves around the player’s actions. The soundtrack, composed by Darren Korb, is as beautiful as it is fitting for the game’s story. With a very down-to-earth feel and haunting lyrics on a number of tracks, the soundtrack makes for good listening both in and out of the game. Better yet, it’s also available for purchase on the Steam marketplace.
In respects to gameplay, Bastion is a generally easy game. I had little difficulty making my way through on my first play-through, and never encountered a game over. That being said, the “Shrine” portion of the game allows players to raise the difficulty in exchange for more fragments (currency used for upgrades and purchases) and XP. With that in mind, the game can be made as easy or as difficult as the player would like, with the best benefits reserved for those who play the hardest.
What Bastion is known for most of all is its narrator, Rucks, who narrates the game’s events as they play out. The old, weathered voice of the man gives a dimension to the game that few others can hold a flame to. His voice guides players through the plot at several key points, but is also free-flowing at other instances. Rucks might comment on the weapons the Kid uses, offer hints when needed, and even comment on little things such as falling off the stage. The story is framed as Zucks telling the story--to whom? That comes in time.
Bastion is a gem, and for good reasons. Its fascinating story is told through every medium--art, music, and plot--and culminates in one fantastic experience. If you have the opportunity to experience Bastion, do so.

With a very engrossing narration throughout the game, Bastion weaves the tale of a fallen society and its few survivors in a way that makes every subtle aspect of the story important and interesting, with the distinctive "acoustic frontier trip-hop" soundtrack complementing this tone perfectly. While it's not the longest game, Bastion offers replayability in a unique take on new-game+ modes. Overall, a must-play.

How do I even begin to describe this game…?
Botanicula’s visuals are soft and dreamy and really beautiful, and unlike anything I’ve seen before, surreal even! The many strange sounds all around you pull you right into this enchanted little world, and the wonderfully ambient music follows the mood of wherever you are, from sad to scary and all the way through to elatedly happy!  (“Yoohoo!” as the five little friends would shout Ü)

I must admit, I was slightly sceptical as to how much fun a point and click game could possibly be, but shame on me…  It brought me straight back to that childlike wonder you have when you come across something never discovered before; thinking hmmm, what might happen if I just…?
It is a think-outside-the-box puzzle game, where you have to trust your intuition and just try… anything goes, whether it’s in a little mini-game or a mini-quest, or one of the many, many puzzles; from the playfully simple ones, to the downright trying ones and finally the ones that are just extremely frustrating (yeah, talking about you caterpillar…)!
There is no tutorial, no instructions… you’re simply thrown in the deep end; so go explore, experiment and figure it out yourself… oh, and have tons of fun while you’re at it Ü!!!
Botanicula is imaginative and intuitive and to me it has been an absolutely delightful adventure! My only regret is that the journey through this magical world is way too short (the reason that I used such a long time is that I got completely, utterly, totally lost on several occasions throughout the game in the more maze-like levels; turns out I have no sense of direction in games either…) and also I suspect that much of its charm would be lost in a replay…
It may not be for everyone, but I loved every bit of it!

If you've never played this game and aren't familiar with the universe it takes place in, you may miss a bit of it's fun. Even if you're not a Warhammer geek however, this sports/combat game is well worth a look.
Blood Bowl takes many elements from Rugby and American football and combines them with the brutal and violent Warhammer universe. The rules are much simpler than football, but at the end of the day, the goals are essentially the same; getting the ball into the enemy's endzone, and outlasting (quite literally) the opponent. Death and performance impacting injuries can and will happen at any time, and can easily result in a turning of the tides.
You can play dirty and rely on injuries and special tactics to win, you can play passing and running games similar to traditional football, if you can consistently withstand the enemy, you can just run the clock out. Creativity is key in a game with so few rules! Not too much of a learning curve, well worth the reward.
The few cons are notable. There are definitely balance problems between the races, especially when starting a brand new campaign. It may be difficult to find opponents in multiplayer without joining a league, and you should be ready to get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked a lot. Blood Bowl is also notorious for random crashes, and Chaos Edition is no exception. It's worse for some than others, so make sure to save after each game.
All in all, if you're looking for a game that blends sports and hand to hand combat together, and can't afford/run Blood Bowl II, look no further. Highly recommended!

A beautiful little gem of a game, with an interesting twist to it. Not exactly Terraria to be quite honest. If only it had come out earlier instead, and gotten some love early on. As it stands now, the game is pretty damn polished and done as a base game. It needs more content though.
The crafting is very interesting and has a lot of depth to it. There's a real potential of making very interesting bases with electricity, generators, battery storage and the whole lot.. Only sad part is that it's not really that heavily focused upon. You can spend a lot of time progressing without even touching upon the tech that is available. Eventually and enevitably it will catch up to you though.
Interesting merge of self tought tech along with recipes you have to find out there. A story that could have gotten somewhere, if it wasn't for the unfortunate mechanic of how it progresses. There's a few tweaks and bugs in the story that needs to be ironed out, as it's terribly immersion breaking as it is right now.
There is a grind to the game (naturally), but nothing you can't handle or expect from a game of this genre. Like I pointed out earlier, there are some flaws to the way you progress in the story though.. Making it somewhat of a burden to have to soldier through..
But all in all I have to say I really like this game. A lot! I only wish it had more content to it. More story and a way to travel to other planets perhaps, or other planes. The maps are either small, medium or large, but even then.. they are only so big. Once you've explored it all, it's done. There's a saving grace in that you can use the same character with progression attached to it, on other worlds you create though. As a fresh start in a sense, but separated from your previous world.
I really recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of Terraria, Crea, Minecraft or any other game where you build, explore and and progress at your own pace. It's a beautiful and very underrated title that deserves much more attention than it's currently getting. Hopefully there's more content to come for this title!

Altitude at first: Obstacle course!
Altitude later on: Varied fights with constant maneuvering. The layout of the area and the speed, position and angle you have relative to your enemy when you encounter them all affect how the battle plays out.
Some beginners tips:
The most popular map, "Football", has no obstacles so is easy for beginners.
The bots who sometimes fill out teams on public servers are mostly on difficult settings with perfect aim, and can give even experienced players trouble. Their main weakness is that they will focus completely on whatever target or objective they have at the moment, ignoring other enemies unless you go straight in front of them.
When on a server, press TAB and look at the player's levels next to their badges. If there's no number, they're level 60. Sometimes a level 60 will start over from level 1, for prestige, but you can tell them apart by their more complex badges vs a beginners cartoony blue and yellow ones.
Anyway, level 60 people are usually pretty good. Sometimes I don't even fire at low level guys, just circle around them dodging their shots, and they often crash before managing to kill me :) The game has a high skill-ceiling. So you might want to find a server with beginners, the servers with just a few players on them often are.

This review must start out by being rude. There is no way around it. Darkout is a shameless attempt at replicating the success of other crafting games, no doubt. However, as tempting it is to mock and jeer at posers leaching off of other people’s good ideas, it is quite difficult to keep up the scorn if they do such a good job at it that it sometimes eclipses the original source of inspiration while bringing up new ideas and bouts of creativity.
Darkout can easily stand on it’s own rather than being a game people only turn to when they can’t get access to other crafting games. It has a steep learning curve, but otherwise it has everything a crafting game needs; resources, blueprints and places to build to your heart’s content. It also has an odd focus on lighting as a play mechanic and power consumption, which is different than almost all the other crafting focused games, but the game's ambition also has its minor hiccups.
The basic idea is that the player is a futuristic survivor that crash landed a spaceship on a planet that becomes more dangerous the darker it is. The survivor's goals boil down to savaging his/her way off the planet by exploring it, cultivating it, and finding out what happened to the other survivors through traces they left behind. The game is almost spooky in this way and playing tag in the dark while aliens are trying to eat you can be thrilling, but the same clash of elements that make the game interesting can also give way to long boring stretches.
For instance, the games’ learning curve and complete lack of direction more or less haunts the player the entire game if they are new. While using your own smarts is most of the fun, there are times where a bit of direction is needed. The best examples of this are usually when there are obvious solutions to problems the game won’t allow for; The player starts with a gun and ammo and then runs out the first night only to be forced to discover by accident that only torches, not obvious deadly sharp things like your axe, can be used to beat monsters to death until enough points and materials are earned to make a sword and arrows. Other oddities such as the player will invent things that run on a power source before they know how to build a power source also exist causing unexplained confusion.
In conclusion, the when player is on the roll inventing and discovering in the right order Darkout flows perfectly and really adds to that sense of thrilling survival, but when something is thrown out of whack and the randomly generated world gives out some secrets before others sometimes the pacing grinds to a frustrating crawl that leaves the player digging for long stretches searching for that next blueprint or that one unique material that doesn’t seem to be anywhere. Pacing disruptions are it’s only real fault however, and the rest of the games seems to function well enough so there is no reason not to try it anyway. There is some great fun to be had here and players are encouraged to see it for it's own unique qualities.

Master of Orion is a title that still gives me nostalgic shivers when I boot up one of the three previous editions (which I still do every year, even trying to get the original MoO to work on my Android tablet with some success). This reboot did so before I even had a copy however, happening when an old friend sent me an article about it before release.
MoO - the little acronym belies the epic galactic spanning game within, a game I spent many, many hours engrossed in as a young gamerling. And then came MoO2, and I was able to expand to conquering my friends - which brought many laughs and also a few almost Risk level arguments (and subsequent self imposed 'Geneva Conventions' on our sessions). MoO3 was a bit of a let down for most (and I can see why, it was by far the weakest of the three (now four)...however, I did see what they were trying to do and I did (unlike anyone I know) finish the game. I have conquered and colonized Orion in each and every title (doing so for this one just last night).
The new game draws on the strengths of each previous title, absorbing and melding each into a game that feels like the first one in flavour (especially with the races currently available, though the brand new Terran Khanate faction included as DLC hints at the possible inclusion of missing races from MoO2 and MoO3 - bring back my psychic Elerian babes! EDIT - Coming soon it seems!). However much of the colony mechanics, a good portion of the UI and the accessibility of the second is core to the gameplay. A few pieces of the UI - such as the galactic map, including the starlanes idea - and a much improved version of the combat style of the third have come along for the ride too...all in all, a solid choice on most aspects, and the game feels complete at launch unlike many other 'smaller' titles.
There are a few things that I would say warrant another go at (such as a better 'Empire Management' screen) and a few tweaks to the UI in places (moving multiple population from one job to another on the Colony/Planet Screen) but these aren't core gameplay issues, and could probably be fixed easily enough with a mod-patch ala 'SkyUI' for Skyrim, though hopefully the developer will follow them up in time. This would add another 0.5 to my score below.
8.5/10 - a strong game, lots of fun and great for the nostalgia reserves while still being something new. I am looking forward to some multiplayer with friends soon!

Imagine something for me, if you will. Imagine a game series based around pure, proper roleplaying. Open-ended dialogue with plenty of skills and attributes to design your own build that is unique to your specific playstyle. In later entries, a neat character customization system to allow you to be young, old, male, female, whatever you want to be, whoever you want to be. And all of this is wrapped up in a unique world with interesting characters, lore, and stories that can be bent and changed by the player's actions.
Now imagine it's 2015. Fallout 4, the latest entry in this series, comes out and screws all of this up. Roleplaying? Interesting characters? Engaging plot? Replaced with bland and stale, pre-determined backstories for the main character, voiced protagonists, roundabout and unengaging dialogue, and a story so poorly written and so full of holes it feels like I'm playing a fanfiction interpretation of the franchise. And the cherry on top is the blatant disregard and lack of care for existing lore and stories, thrown to the wayside for Bethesda's abysmal writing team to substitute with whatever they want. All this game wants you to do is "Shoot, Loot, n' Scoot." You go to a place. You kill some people. You steal their♥♥♥♥♥♥ You leave, and you do this again and again for a hundred hours.
This game design philosophy has infected every aspect of this series. The main plot is fetch quests and kill quests without so much as an attempt to mask that fact. All the side quests are God-awful "radiant quests" that are designed to never end so that you can have "infinite" bland and substance-less quests for playthroughs in a series where the whole point of each game is to reach the end and see the result of your actions. There are no Perks anymore, just skill-trees like Skyrim that CALL themselves Perks, which are also boring and uninspired. Almost all of them are just stand-ins for Skills that have been removed, increasing weapon damage, increasing healing item effectiveness, increasing defense... All it does is bog down the leveling system and make it feel boring. There's no flair, no style, and every single build ends up the exact same due to the merging of Perks and Skills.
Now, you'd think the plot I mentioned before may at least make up for this. Ha, no. No, not at all. The plot is, without any spoilers, an awful reversed-role rehashing of Fallout 3. Your child is missing, and you leave your Vault to go find them in the Wasteland. But instead of having compelling characters or intrigue to push you forward, you get cardboard cutout cliches and poorly-written schmucks that won't hold your attention at all, and the plot itself is just a string of awful contrivances that drag you along through the game. And to top THIS mess off, you don't even get any ending slides. There are zero moral choices in the game (asides from two at the beginning, robbing a caravan lady and helping some drug dealers) and no choices to make at all that effect the ending. Why?
The end slides are gone! No, instead you get the same cutscene for every single ending, asides from 5 extra seconds of footage if you choose the Institute. That's right, the iconic ending slides that made the story feel complete have been replaced with a boring, 2-3 minute cinematic that has no closure and does nothing but leave you frustrated and unsatisfied. That's just the main game. Far Harbor has the exact same problems, and has the extra issues of ripping off not only the main game (plot hook is a missing child that you have to go on an adventure to find, which results in a larger issue that you involve yourself in), outright stealing a quest from a popular New Vegas mod, AND ALSO ripping off Point Lookout with the setting and atmosphere. There isn't a creative bone left in the bodies of anyone at Bethesda game studios, and it very, very much shows with Fallout 4 and all of its DLC. Seriously, Workshops? That's worth $15? You know what else costs $15? Each DLC for New Vegas, which is leagues better and has the bonus of the good writing and engaging stories and characters given to us by Obsidian.
So, Fallout 4 is a spit in the face to all Fallout fans, is a disgustingly dumbed-down "RPG" (an insult to all RPGs) and is more shallow than any game I have ever played, with all the content being bland and uninteresting, but with enough of it to fill almost 200 hours spent desperately searching for anything enjoyable. Now with the Creation Club fiasco going on, it's the final nail in the coffin for the Bethesda of old. We'll never get another Morrowind. We'll never get another Fallout game like New Vegas. All we have now are shallow, poorly-written shooters with an XP bar thrown in to be an "RPG" that will be filled to the brim with microtransactions acting as glorified paid mods. It's time to bury Fallout as we know it, because it's dead, and The Elder Scrolls isn't too far behind.

It is a fantasy slasher consisting of connected arenas where you don't play typical levels but instead you fight boss-fights one after another.
Construction of game is weird because early it serves you most boring and unrewarding levels where it is only you and butt-crack of heroine [to wipe your tears away] and then gets better over time. Like it tries to scare away all but most patient ones instead of luring everyone with the best pieces at the beginning.
Levels: are monumental and well detailed, with great display of sunlight and shadows.
Enemies: are few but distinct and you will have to switch your attacks and spells/skills to defeat them. Later in the game enemies will appear in mixed groups so sometimes you will have to prioritize targets and apply different tools to different situations. Which is nice and i appreciate these moments a lot.
Even ingame bestiary is useful as you will learn from there about resistances of enemies.
Battles: with every level battles become more demanding, multiple stages of every boss fight, more resistances/vulnerabilities. Bad side is that there is too much repetition where you have to do the same action or series of actions over and over. But this is how boss fights were done over the years - i prefer to have endurance trial with bulletspoonge boss than QTE ;).
You can set your own difficulty level as game lets you heal during fight and it is only up to you if you use it - you have to pay for it with the same currency you buy upgrades, but it's some percent of your current wealth so you always can afford it.
pros:
+ gameplay [after early tutorial levels][yet during the game you will encounter another tutorial levels].
+ power-tripping - you are one-girl-army slashing through hundreds of enemies. Slaming ground to knock down enemies, fry tens of enemies with chainlightning, freeze everyone around you then shatter them with earthquake. Or enable transformation for speed boost and turn your pistols into machineguns. Just fave fun and enjoy the view.
+ great visual and audio effects.
+ cool soundtrack with vivid music for battles that calms down after last enemy falls so you can do sightseeing of beautiful levels with nice soundtrack in the background.
+ decent, but unfortunately scarce, platforming sections and bonus platforming for those who want to grab all collectibles.

cons:
- you can't play this game without being accused that you play it only to watch at the lower back of protagonist.
- poor early tutorial-levels. Probably were stuffed into the game day before release. Many people could become bored of it and fail to endure past it for the actual game.
- lack of some animations of enemies [like jumping or falling].
- anime characters doesn't suit the rest of the game artstyle [imo].
- no achievements for steam [not that i care but it's a steam release so lets play by the rules].
- story - dialogues, cutscenes, endings.

Starbound is big. Really big. You just won't believe how vastly, hugely, mind-bogglingly big it is. With a universe at your beck and call, where do you begin? Thankfully, Starbound starts off by tethering you to a single world as soon as you've named your character.
You're born into this 2D world with virtually nothing, bar a matter manipulator that lets you slowly chip away at pretty much anything, and in time this high-tech gadget is replaced by rustic farming equipment that allows you to chip faster. Fashioned out of the exploratory spirit of Minecraft and Terraria, Starbound's premise is to take you (be you boy, girl, robot, weird flower thing, or any of the other races) away from a single procedurally generated world and into an entire universe of planets whose earth you can swing your pickaxe into. There's a lot of opportunity and excitement here, even in the game's earliest days.
That's the beauty of Starbound, you come out of it with all sorts of anecdotes you'll want to share with people. This might be a bare-bones version of the game to come, but boy, check out those bones. The game's minutiae will be mapped out across various wikis for years to come, and many mechanics will be added and refined, but even now, Starbound is an enticing journey of discovery that reminds you just how exciting it can be to stare at a sky full of stars.

Blood Bowl is a fun, if frustrating, PC version of the classic table top game. If you enter it with the expectation that it will be funny and a catastrophy, then you'll probably have a good time. If you think it'll play like an actual ball game, then you'll probably hate it.
The Run Down: There are two types of teams: teams that smash and teams that play ball well. My recommendation is to start with a team that smashes well, such as The Undead, Necromantic, or one of the Chaos/Nurgal/Khorne teams. Everything is done by D6 rolls, so you will fail constantly at everything. You'll fail at picking up a ball that your players surround, you'll fail at throwing a ball to a player two inches away, and you'll fail at smashing a player 1/4 your size and strength. Luckily, the other team fails at an equal rate. Even on "Easy" this game is challenging. I picked this up in that massive developer pack with Styx, and this is one of the few games in that huge pack that's worth anything at all.
Try it out.

ARGH.  Darkout frustrates me.  So.  Much.
Is it frustrating to play?  OH YES.  But that isn't what frustrates me.  No, what makes me gnash my teeth is that in the grim and filthy world of Darkout, there's a little gem trying to shine its way into existence.    At the heart, Darkout is a Terraria-like crafting action game.   The platforming action is so-so.  It's not as polished as I would desire, but it's workable.
There's crafting, and that's well done.  Your crafting devices are even smart enough to pull materials from nearby chests, which something every damned Minecraft-y game should copy.  Right now.  (Really, why do I have to juggle around 20+ items in and out of my inventory just to build a few things?)
Crafting progression is..  Odd.  It's tied to tech level (which controls overall access to receipes), but tech level is independant for each class of item.  For example, I could have tech level 2 armor but tech level 4 tools.  It's not entirely obvious how these tech levels work together for progression, and it becomes even more complicated when some items or component receipes won't unlock until you either have their base materials available or their base components.  The game does not give you a list, but fills in the blanks as you figure things out.  Which means it can be frustrating unless you want to pour over the (sometimes incomplete/outdated) wiki to figure out how to build something.
Worse, some items are locked to quest progression.  You won't get the component or the receipe until you've triggered a certain quest.  And this is where the game basically makes me want to eat my keyboard.
The story quest is broken.  Simply BROKEN.  And horribly designed.  No other way to put it.  Items refuse to drop, or spawn.  Eventually, you can get the game to spawn the needed items by generating new worlds and exploring them, since like Terraria your character is easily transferred between worlds.  It's never clear exactly why you can't proceed in a quest either;  There are THREE different places to look in order to determine quest progression.  I kid you not.  Three different indicators across two different UI screens.  Even so, these hints are vague and often don't point to the real cause as to why you cannot progress.
I've given up trying to beat the story quests.  Maybe it's doable, with hours upon hours of careful combing and re-loading of games and generating new worlds in order to re-comb them for the necessary item drops, but screw that.
I had fun building my character so he could fly and have laser-guns and chop down trees with a plasma-cutter, but once I tried to actually beat the game, I realized it was totally not worth my time.
Do not recommend this game, even for $4 that I paid for it.
Pity, too, because the game looks rather nice and has an art style other than 8-bit retro, which seems like Every Damn Other crafting game has decided to copy.

I originally played X-Com - Terror from the Deep (back in the day) and loved it. When X-Com - Enemy Unknown came out I snapped it up purely on nostalgia. Later I got Enemy Within.  I wasn't dissapointed and both proved to be a great games. I still play them now. So when X-Com 2 came out I immediately purchased it as well. Having now played through the campaign 6 times and with another currently running, I can say it is perhaps my favourite game. I have found all the DLC to be useful, although I prefer my troops to have camouflaged military uniforms, so the more exotic options are not for me. However, its great they are there.
Game play wise, I enjoy the fact that real-time small team tactics work and the ability trees play to the arch types well.  These also serve to generate some memorable combat moments. After your squad has fired on five oncoming alien enemies, then your sniper using serial finishes them all off with five shots, you cheer!
The timed missions reflect the nature of guerrilla  warfare, where the raiders have got to hit hard and get out before reinforcements arrive. Some people have complained about this but I like it and think it adds to the flavour.
If you like small team tactical games, then this is one of the best I've found. I strongly recommend this game based on the many hours of enjoyment it has given me.

As someone that's sunk a large portion of their life into Natsume's Harvest Moon series, I was disappointed at the lack of diversity and quality the newer games provided. Stardew Valley, with its diverse cast, plentiful options and lovable characters, is the best Harvest Moon game that Natsume never made. I hardly have the proper words to describe what a wonderful, peaceful, and fullfilling experience this game brings. Everything about it from the sound design to the beautifully detailed sprites and the heartwarming interactions you have with each citizen of the darling Pelican Town brings about a sense of belonging. This is a game with true heart and one that I've found myself unable to quit. Concerned Ape has done a fantastic job of painting a world you want to live in and practically can for as long as you care to stay. For me, even at 170 hours of gameplay, I don't see myself quitting this game any time soon. If you like life simulators with slow burn romances wrapped in an adorable aethetic that glows with warmth and joy, than I'd recommend giving Stardew Valley a try. There's bound to be something for everyone in this game, be it making friends, working the land, hunting monsters in the deep caverns of the mines, fishing in Pelican Town's various streams and ponds, or foraging the lush woods for food and supplies. I imagine that when the multiplayer system releases, I'll be throwing even more time into building a new farm with my friend. I look forward to seeing updates to the game in time and, in the meantime, have been having fun with modding the game - something that is mercifully easy. Thank you to Concerned Ape for such creating such a beautiful game. I can never express just how much it has come to mean to me.

Honestly, this is one of the games I should have got when I first came on Steam, but sadly it wasn't released yet. By saying that, I'm just saying it's a really fun game to play, helps you find some new friends on Steam, and is definetely one of my favorites!
If you just want to see more specifically into what is in the game and what plans to be in the game, just check here:
otherwise continue reading...
There is not really any specific goal to the game, you basically choose if you want to have a goal in the game or just play and mess around without any goal. You can go after trying to create the best condo with your imagination, trying to save up a lot of in-game cash and become really rich, or really have the best parties or something. Those are just ideas.
The Plaza is the main area of the game with a few dedicated servers by the development team and a few unofficial servers from others. The Plaza is basically a hub and center for the whole game with stores to shop at, places to socialize with others, carnival-like games to play, bowling, Laser Tag, and more. Oh, there's also a theater if you want to blast your YouTube meme collection for people to watch. In summary, it's basically the main area of action in the community. If you're looking to find some new friends, that is a great place to go.
The mini games range from trying to not get infected by zombies to casual games like mini golf to Ball Race which seems to be a mini-game, multiplayer inspiration of the Super Monkey Ball series.
Overall, the mini games are more like party games and are fun to play with just random people over Steam or gather up some friends and play and chill.
The condo feature is really nice. It gives you the ability to make anything you can plan with your imagination or your heart's desire. So, if you want to make a waifu shrine with waifu body pillows and a picture of your waifu next to candles, go ahead. If you want to make a club, customize the lights with different patterns from a rainbow cycle to a candle lighting design pattern and more, add a bar for people to buy drinks, get some spotlights, bubble machines, and a dance floor and party until you fall asleep on the keyboard. If you just want to be a home designer, get some furniture, design a nice condo in paradise, take some screenshots and share it with the world, go ahead.
Overall, the condo customization is REALLY NICE and I love it!
The community is really nice and in my experience going onto some of the most populated servers on the game, there are friendly and funny people on there and it makes the experience much better from milk carton cults to in a video seeing a group of people walking together spreading their bee cult to people blasting memes in the theater and more, it's definetely a community I want to be a part of. There definetely seems to be a lot of chill, laid-back people here in my experience.
Just a warning and I know that not everyone really cares for it or really worries about encountering it, but some condos or some content played in the theater can be a bit explicit sometimes so if you really want to avoid explicit condos, just don't go to people's condos much and you're good and if you don't like whatever is being played in the theater, just leave that theater and go to a different theater.
So before you look into this some more, I suggest you take a look at my speculations for more of an idea on how yours may run compared to mine.
Manufacturer: CyberPowerPC

System Type: x64-based processor
Processor: AMD FX-4300 Quad-Core 3.80 GHz

Before playing, be sure you keep your drivers updated, makes a really huge difference for this.
I play the game at 1600x900, sometimes in maximized window mode on a 1920x1080 monitor resolution. For my internet, I have a ping of around 30-150 average on the official Plaza dedicated servers depending on how full it is.
The game runs very well giving me usually around 25-120 FPS with the range being that some areas in the game need graphics card optimizations for frame rate to be normal. For certain parts such as the Plaza, there is some frame rate dropping every few seconds just traveling a bit at a sprinting speed or jetpack speed and it does mess with the ping quite a bit. For the Snow map on Mini Golf, I experience a strange frame rate drop.
Although, this game's in Early Access so I expected some issues like this, overall, it's mostly stable, just needs some optimizations and some fixes for online, that's all.
The developers seem to take feedback seriously and seem to love to engage with their community, see what the community likes, and seem to take value into community feedback, more than most other game devs (in my perspective) seem to have.
They have a forum on their website for people to post and give feedback. They also release announcements there for new features in-game and reply to the community. To take a look at it, here's the link:
They have a Discord for the community to come together and to answer some questions from the community. I won't be posting a link for that because that's more for the community.
They also more importantly have a Trello board for their roadmap. It features ideas they talk about putting into the game, ideas they are working on, and features that are already in the game, so more importantly check that out!
It's a really good game and I love it and it's one of my favorites on Steam, I love all the features it has, it just needs some optimizations here and there, but overall it's a really good game and you should definetely buy it and it was worth my 15 bucks. :)

This game is great, it's a pity it's such underrated. Besides it's splendid visuals, that can still hold against the newest games, the time-rewinding\time cloning mechanic makes all the fights an extremely interesting mix of action and puzzle. The most common example of this is using yourself as bait, lure enemies, then port back in time, take another route, and attack them from behind while they follow your "time clone". Stronger enemies can be utterly destroyed the first time you land a strike because you can actually port back, and land another hit with your second clone, then go back and do the same with another and so on, this is very useful in boss fights as the boss have enormous health bars and aren't hittable most of the time.
Basically, this game is great. It uses the main game mechanic very well and it's setting is at least intereting and beautifully rendered even if story and dialogues aren't great. But who the hell plays this kind of games for the plot anyway?

An adventure game with many choices to be made. The game does a great job of putting the player into a Walking Dead experience. There are some great characters in this story and you will get attached to them, making for some difficult situations in terms of the choices you will make in order for you and your friends to survive. The game is best played by adults, and you will be able to complete the game no matter what choices you make. It's a point and click adventure focusing heavily on selecting responses during dialogue with the other characters.  Some choices are timed and there are also some quick-time events where they player needs to react in a timely manner, but you are able to redo these if it goes wrong. Overall this is the best game Telltale have done of this kind with very memorable characters and a great finish. It's a slow pace and you are going immerse yourself into a Walking Dead story, don't expect arcade-like zombie slaying action, that's not what this game is about. Highly, highly recommended.

When I first started this game, I hated every character and loved the combat. I thought the story was incredibly stupid and I was kind of surprised a game like this even had a story. It's the kind of game where every female character looks like they just came out of a 14 year old boy's wet dream. Ayumi isn't even the worst offender of this!
Shockingly enough, the characters evolved such that I actually *liked* them- each main character received enough characterization to become real, likeable, *people*, rather than the walking videogame cliches they look like (ridiculously musclebound man, ridiculously over sexualized women). This astounded me; I was not expecting to have anything but contempt for the game's seemingly pathetic attempt at story. The main plot, too, evolves into something worthwhile. The biggest problem this game has is probably the fact that the story and characters are overwhelmingly generic for the first half of the game.... but it does metamorphose into something unique towards the end. Well, the characters do; the story is largely generic still but there are several key plot points that separate it from the rest.
Unfortunately what did not evolve over time was the combat. As far as I know there are no combos to learn besides the very limited set you start out with. One of the combos brings you up into the air as you swing your sword about wildly, *but there are never ever any enemies that will be in the air with you*. What ends up happening is a lengthy animation of you swinging your sword in the air for 5 seconds while all the enemies wait for you to return to the ground. This happens automatically when you jump and attack- so if you need to jump over to an enemy *quickly* and attack him, unless you're very careful you might accidentally start that useless combo and it will prevent you from doing time sensitive things (there is no way to stop once started). I feel like I missed out on a mechanic or two though- you can lock onto enemies and dash at them, but 90% of the time the game bugs out and the dash is in slow motion and you never even reach the enemy. Then I read something about hanging from enemies in midair and hitting them with your sword. Huh. The most I was ever able to do was slide off them like they were covered in motor oil. You gain the ability to use fire, ice and generic projectiles very early on and then (with one exception) from there on out, all upgrades are minor and passive (for example, you might gain the ability to do more damage by using fire on someone who is frozen. No expanded gameplay, just ways to optimize damage). I started out really loving the combat, but it gets very old very fast. And it's very buggy. The entire game is buggy actually. Luckily you can usually fix everything by reloading the last checkpoint, but if your checkpoint is before a particularly challenging battle, that can be frustrating.
Another major problem with this game is there are too many different mechanics. It feels like I'm playing a very long demo of hundreds of different games. Yes, the combat is boring, but constantly changing the rules of the world is not the way to fix that. At one point you gain wings and can fly, and I don't even think it is explained... then you lose your wings shortly after, also unexplained. I found out by jumping off a cliff and falling to my death. At one point you are given a gun which you are required to use; if you kill the enemies without the gun, they keep regenerating indefinitely, and this is *not explained*. It was pretty obvious I had to use the gun to kill them, but I couldn't quite figure out how, and I couldn't proceed by killing them normally. The biggest problem was the stupid jump combo- you had to freeze the enemy with the gun, then drop the gun and hit them before they thawed, except I would always activate that useless combo and never get to them in time.
The time rewind itself is also problematic. For example, the ability is not explained at all. You are told that you have it, then you need to figure out how it works, which is a process that will take the rest of the game. But the game arbitrarily changes the way it works and often doesn't even let you use it! How can you learn to use it if it keeps alternating between different rule sets and often isn't even available to use? So far what I *think* happens with the standard set of rules is; any time clones of you will disappear if the main you alters enough variables in the past. So if you go back in time and get an enemy to follow the current you instead of the past you, the past you just disappears. Which is a problem because most of the time the point of time rewind is to distract enemies- but they mostly seem interested in *you*, not your past clones, which makes them all vanish, which makes the game frustrating. OK, so I understand that, I'll try to use it against this boss now that I'm a little better with it. Oh wait, you can't. Why? Because. Time rewind is not available to you for nearly *every single boss*. Then, some of the larger enemies require that you use it, but the way it works is completely different for those enemies. In one case- there's a quick time event which you need to do twice at the same time. Cool right? Not really. You do it once, you rewind time and if you don't press the button *immediately*, you lost your shot at it and you need to spend 5 more minutes weakening the enemy again. To reiterate- you can't just go back in time and wait for the opportunity to use the quick time event going forward in time, you have to hit the quick time event whilst going backwards in time.. because for some reason your clone disappears in this particular context (you can't make time rewind clones). Then, on the giant worm boss, you can make time rewind clones but the moment you do the boss just retreats, changing variables and erasing all your clones immediately. The logistics of this time rewind thing is complicated enough without all the arbitrary exceptions and changes.
I can't decide if I like this game or not. On the one hand, there are unique gameplay and story elements that are definitely worth experiencing; there is nothing else like it. On the other hand, the game doesn't respect itself enough to expand upon the more interesting elements and instead chooses to try 100 different things, which all collapse into one incoherent mess of a game. I suppose I recommend this game only because the length is short enough that you can actually complete it before being fed up with its many issues, and I think it is worth at least $10, so pick it up in the next sale.

Blades of Time is a joy of a game that relies heavily on its time-adjust ability.  Unfortunately, it comes to rely on this a bit too much. While there are plenty of puzzles to solve, great graphics and entertaining gameplay, the story (complete with full voice acting!) falls short about mid-way through the game.  Several encounters begin to feel forced and the gimmic of the game begins to really show.
Don't get me wrong, I really, really liked this game.  Until about 70% complete.  It's definitely worth playing through the first time and the gameplay is fun while the art pulls you in.  It feels like the love child of Kingdom Hearts and Prince of Persia: Sands of Time, but without the tremendous story to fall back on.  This game is a terrific find when on sale, but it just doesn't have enough hutzpah to keep me completely in love and justify a full price purchase.

It may not be very long (less than an hour) and the point and click style of the game can make it slightly confusing over what you need to do next, but it is an original game with a very good story. Highly recommend even for such a short game.

Alright, let me give you guys an in-depth review of this game.
My name is Jordan, and I played RotMG for many years and had multiple 8/8 characters (8 stats maxed out of 8), and had some of the best items you could own. Then, there was mass duping which let to UTs (Untier) items being Soulbound, meaning they cannot be traded. This was a long time ago, and the items are still soulbound. Did it affect the dupers? No. They can still dupe the items, and sell accounts with the items active on them. It hurt the regular community more than the people duping.
Then came pets, and I quite enjoy pets. People say they are P2W, and cause people to be immortal, and that is untrue. Before pets came along, some dungeons took longer, due to either not having a priest with you to heal, or you just got chuncked and had no potions so had to wait for basic regen. Pets just made most of the game more convienient, as you would have to wait less time to heal. The higher the pet level, the more it heals (if you have the heal stat ofcourse). Now, you can upgrade your pet by feeding it items, or buying pet food (which costs real money). Buying pet food can speed up the process, but is in no-way P2W, as a player who invest time can also achieve the same stats as the person buying pet food.
The game itself is fun, but gets VERY repetitive. You grind out dungeons, pot up your characters, die on characters and repeat. The fun diminishes over-time once you have done it all.
The worst part about the game, is the lack of communication from the developers. I was (and still have access to) a closed tester. Meaning I tested content before it was released. I stopped playing the game a while ago (I play on flash player no steam) due to the game finally taking its toll on me. Throughout my time of testing, there was decent communication from the devs to begin with, but as time went on, less and less communication was given. It has gotten to the point that the last time the devs communcated with the testers was 5 months ago. 5 MONTHS! That is appauling for a gaming company, especially for those who are TESTING their game. But then they just throw out another "Player appreciation month" which is a scheme to get players to spend more money on their game.
All in all, the game IS fun, but it will wear off pretty fast.

I couldn't help but compare it to Dear Esther while playing -- the music, aethetics, and general tone is similar in both games, although I would definitely say that Dear Esther is the more immersive, more cohesive, and overall superior game/experience. The voice acting in Serena, especially that of the female character's, was wooden, the story predictable, and the ending abrupt and not in keeping with the tone of the rest of the game. Neglecting to properly flesh out parts of a plot is not the same as tastefully leaving certain details up to the player's interpretation. The mechanics are clunky and buggy. Pros: If you're easy to spook, like me, this game will keep you in suspense purely due to atmosphere (and a bit due to anticipation of what you KNOW is coming, regardless of how clever the writing thinks it's being). The abundance of detail in this couple's shared life is pretty good, although some more practical background would have been nice to make the characters more believable (it bugged me that I never found out how they met or what they each did for a living). BUT I liked the way the main character starts twisting his own ideas and memories. There are some good physical details, too: the porn magazine (my personal favorite), the close-ups of interesting book titles, the poem on the wall that changes . . .
Despite these, I still wouldn't recommend this game except as an example of how NOT to write an adventure plot/hire voice actors. It's a good thing it was free.

I've never been a gambling person as far as casinos go.  Sure, I would hang out and play cards with a group of friends sometimes.  I never liked the whole "Texas Hold'em" fad that came up and really wasn't into it.  And to me, it was a fad, that seemed to be glorified on televisions and made celebrities of players, some players were just celebrities.  I don't know much about it.  I'm pretty sure there is a whole gambling world with professional poker players that spans back to way before I existed or many of us did.  This is just to show you my view on gambling and poker in general.  I'm not into it obviously and never have been.
I saw one of my streamer friends playing this one day, and I was like, "Meh, a poker game.", and really wasn't that interested.  However, I watched for a little bit, and I liked how interactive the characters were, and asked him questions about the game.  I also found out you could completely customize your character, it used your steamname as the character name, so I had no issue having to use a weird name, and you could join affiliations, and it seemed more immersive than loading up a Poker version of Solitaire for windows would be.
Anyways, my question was, what's the catch?  Am I gonna run out of poker chips so fast I gotta buy them?  Are there stuff locked behind a paywall?  Are only the cool stuff purchasable with real money? -  The answer was, no, no, and no.
If you do run out of poker chips, just go challenge some henchmen or a boss, in a solo match, that costs you no chips to do over and over, and grind up some chips.  None of the items are locked behind a pay wall, in fact, I don't recall a single item being over 150,000 poker chips, which is fairly easy to get.  The only thing I could even find to buy were in fact poker chips, and you get so many, I don't see why one would even need to, you get them from logging in daily, you can grind them in solo play, and nothing seemed locked behind a paywall.
So, what were the problems?  None that I could find.  For many, I would guess grinding reputation to be a problem, to gain ranks in affiliations, which unlocks specific items for that affiliation.  You can in fact swap to any affiliation whenever you want.  You begin as a Tourist, and upon reaching level 10, you can choose to join the Hearts or the Clubs.  A a higher level, you unlock the Spades, and at level 50, you unlock the Diamonds.  They all have different tables, and different styles of clothing.  (Hearts being Italian Mafia, Clubs being a Biker Gang, Spades being Russian Mafia, and Diamonds being Japanese Yakuza.)  It's a well done game.
There are many events that help you to gain reputation, like 50% more rep with certain table items during certain parts of the day, different days have different events, like one day, if you were your affiliation uniform, all your reputation is doubled.  Reputation is how you gain levels, and every level you gain, you gain loot crates, which have titles, reputation boosts, more chips, or vanity items for your character.  You can be some skinny dorky young ginger guy, or some fat ugly old lady.  You can rock a mohawk that is purple, or wear a nice tuxedo or gown that you'd see in a James Bond movie.
To me, this game is enjoyable.  There is absolutely no ingame chat, except a voice chat system that nobody seems to use.  You can play in public games with random people, or private games with just your steam friends, and choose the table you want, the buy in amount, if it's a tournament, or even head to head.  Then there is ranked play, which I have never played, however there seems to be a lot of complaints in the reviews about there not being enough people for ranked, again - Never touched it, probably won't.
The game is very fun, is very free, and very enjoyable.  I highly recommend it and if my review has persuaded you to install and play it and you like it, hit me up with a friends request, and I'd be happy to sit at a table with you, to chill and play some poker.

Nothing extraordinary, but overall a very solid Poker game for the PC market.
Normally Poker games tend to either come with the burden of using real money or having extremely intrusive microtransactions. Thankfully Prominence Poker doesn't have this hiderance. Only once does the game ever show an 'ad' for any sort of microtransaction, and it never requires real world money to play.
The visual style is solid, nothing inspired or really unique, but clean and simple. Each table you're randomly sent to is well designed and simple, with some nice background details, like a butcher chopping meat in the Meat Locker area. CUstomization spects are also pretty nice. You can spend chips for different hats, earrings, clothing, glasses, and even drinks or accessories to have at the table.
However, the biggest and best aspect is the frequency of earning chips. You get experience for doing almost anything, from dealing, to ending turns with a certain hand (not winning, just making it through to the end without folding), doing gestures, and winning hands. As you level up with said experience, you can earn more chips, loot cases, and accessories. Some of the goals, such as winning 5 times with two pair, even reward you with chips as well. The flow is steady, meaning you never feel pressured into buying more with real world money.
Prominence Poker is a solid PC poker game that thankfully is easy to play, alone of with friends. It solves the problem that plagues PC poker games by being both solidly made and good looking, as well as never pressuring the player into buying chips. For any fan of Poker, at least give it a spin.
