I did not understand why this game was so praised when I played it. People called Bastion a gorgeous game with a very unique narration, but I honestly didn't think this game brought anything truly new and innovative to gaming or storytelling. It's actually a typical, linear action/RPG-esque game with a slightly retro feel, some good but repetitive music and a story that hasn't really impressed me.
Bastion is a good game, but I didn't understand why it was hyped and, despite my numerous attempts, I was simply never able to finish it and got bored about halfway through. I just found the gameplay very repetitive : you basically click on everything that moves until it dies in a typical action-RPG fashion, except you don't have the loot, gold or rewards that make these games so addicting. Combat just wasn't satisfying and was often a matter of mashing Mouse1 and blocking once every five seconds before repeating until the monster/boss was down. Challenge levels are more frustrating than they are challenging and the special gear you find in these levels isn't very useful or fun to use because it often simply gives you more ways to kill enemies you could already easily kill with your hammer by left-clicking them to death.
It's unique in its visual presentation, but in my opinion, the game's originality ends there, and it does not compensate for its lackluster gameplay.

When the stars fell from the sky they ran into the moon and fell into the earth like seeds. From those seeds sprang beautiful trees with many creatures that lived inside. But one day strange, dark parasites began consuming the life from the trees without giving anything back. There's nothing really to be done but plant a new tree so life can begin anew!
The best I can describe this is a exploration, point and click. It's beautifully drawn, with strange and lively music. The sound effects from the things you click become part of the background music. There's no dialogue, and any directions are communicated through pictures or arrows, including the plot.
This is a game where you click around to figure out the next step, moving along through trial and error. The puzzles are generous, giving you infinite lives if you mess up. Not all the puzzles reset but most of them don't need to.
My biggest complaint is that the difficulty ascension is a little awkward, going from easy, easy, much harder, ahh, WHOA, and easy-ish again. Levels four and five are the hardest and longest by far, and I had to look at guide to figure out a lot of the smaller details.
Basically it went from having one step to take to get an item, to having a more Zelda-like approach with three or four steps. There wasn't much warning that this was going to happen.
I'm not sure it's a "humourous" game but it made me smile in many places. This is a delightful point and click to explore, with well designed puzzles. Absolutely add it to your library!

I would buy Botanicula just for the soundtrack. The music is beautiful and relaxing, and suits the ambience of the game perfectly. There are a range of moods, from dramatic to soothing to upbeat and lively and no matter what is happening on-screen the accompanying music serves to increase the atmosphere and immersion. There are also hundreds of unique sound effects associated with the different creatures in this game that serve to highlight the different personalities of each despite the fact they never actually talk (see my characters section for more). This clever use of sound effects draws you in and makes the game even better.
Game Play: 8/10
Overall the game mechanics are very simple and there is little that could go wrong other than the usual annoyance that comes with all point & click games. When you have clicked everything on the screen and nothing at all happens you have to vent your frustration by finding the nearest guide, at which point you face-palm at how “obvious” the solution is. But that didn’t happen that often in Botanicula so the pain was kept to a minimum.
The only other minor complaint I have is that I spent quite a lot of time getting lost despite the helpful little map leaf in the corner, although that might be due to my own incompetence more than anything else.
Characters: 10/10
Another characteristic of Amanita Design games is that their characters have a tendency not to speak, instead communicating via a series of incoherent sounds. This gets no complaints from me given most voice acting is horrendous and only decreases the player’s immersion. The burbling noises made by all the creatures in Botanicula suit the game perfectly and make them all so lovable! It really is incredible how quickly you grow attached to all the various nuts, mushrooms and tiny creatures you encounter and they all have so much character. And anyway, as a biologist I feel I should point out that these little guys don’t speak human language anyway and the idea of a grub with an American accent is just silly.
Bad points?
The game could do with more settings as the options menu is barely present, but apparently the game runs on almost anything so I guess it doesn’t really need a lot of options. Other than that I really can’t think of anything bad to say!

I remember watching the trailer for Darkout and getting excited by the atmosphere that was conveyed therein.  You crash-land on an alien planet to find it ravaged by long, pitch-black night cycles where a great number of light-sensitive monstrosities come out to hunt and feed, with the only real respite being the interspersed periods of daylight or the artificial light created by bonfires, large electrical networks and even creative usages of harvested bioluminescence.
Having picked the game up through a Humble Bundle, I only just now decided it was about time I finally give the title a try.
Terraria is, of course, the clear point of comparison here.  I don't think anyone can really argue that a considerable amount of "inspiration" is drawn from Terraria's gameplay mechanics (above and beyond what's required for a game in the "2D sidescrolling sandbox" genre).  Not that there's anything wrong with that, but I'm just going to try and justify why I'll be making comparisons between the two.
I'm first struck by the graphics.  The terrain, foliage and such are absolutely gorgeous.  Really, it's amazing stuff.  The lighting system is quite wonky, but when it works it's also quite pretty.  Unfortunately, the many times it *doesn't* work make things look a bit janky, particularly for a game with a core mechanic based solely around light...
And then we have the character model.  A 3D rendering in a 2D environment.  It seems to me that the designers, in attempting to make a compelling and interesting character model, wound up trying to put too much detail into it, and the end result is rather off-putting.  Not only does the 3D model look completely out of place to begin with, but the art style seems to be taken from somewhere else entirely as well.
The backgrounds also are...  Well, not the best.  It's like looking at a close-up of the horizon, if that makes any sense.  If it doesn't make any sense, then you're probably picturing a very accurate representation of Darkout's backgrounds.  In their defense, the colors are generally neutral enough that you can generally just ignore them entirely in favor of the much prettier foreground.
And then we get to the meat of it, the game...  It starts off with a short, poorly-written tutorial (though not nearly as plagued by spelling mistakes and grammatical butcherings as the rest of the ingame tooltips) that begins by saying that there's no time to lose.  And, indeed, there most certainly isn't.  By the time I had managed to decipher enough of the tutorial messages to progress to where you're supposed to build your first shelter against the darkness and its dangers, it was already nighttime and nasties had started spawning all around me.  So, uh, better hope you're a fast learner.
After that, and then suddenly shoving some entirely unwanted story and bored voice acting down my throat, we're left completely to our own devices.  I should make a note here that the game actually has some very good tools for getting what you want done, and I'd very much like to see more of that kind of thinking.  Namely, the "auto" tool, which will automatically use the necessary tool from your inventory on whatever object or terrain you have selected.  So, with "auto" selected, you can click on a tree to chop it down with your axe, mine some ore with your pick, and then shovel some dirt with your shovel without ever having to bother with switching over to a different tool slot and remembering where you put what.  Also, there's a mining feature that lets you dig three tiles at once instead of having to select them all individually.  The total time spent is the same as doing it one by one, so it's no shortcut in that sense, but it does make things considerably less tiresome.
Unfortunately, "auto" can sometimes be a bit confusing, as the cursor icon won't always be the tool you're actually going to use on what's actually selected, as the cursor uses a different targeting mechanic than the actual tool...  This is only made worse by the fact that the game indicates which doodad you're aiming at by fading it into near-invisibility.  It's basically the exact opposite of highlighting, and it's quite unhelpful at the best of times...
Block placement is a thing of crossing your fingers and hoping something winds up close to where you want it after clicking a few times, and hoping it doesn't spring any new rules on you.  Such as, you can place wooden platforms where there's an electrical wire, but you can't place an electrical wire where there are wooden platforms.  The electrical wiring itself, apparently intended as some core part of the game, is obscenely bad...  You cannot directly wire through walls, so the game requires you to place "sockets" over your wall tiles and then connect from one side to the other.  Unfortunately, this rarely works all that well as attempting to connect the gadget will frequently make it try and target the /wrong side of the socket/, at which point it will claim (correctly) that there's a wall in the way so it can't string the wire.
On the subject of electricity, I may as well mention that the "tech tree" is completely wonked.  You're granted a little doohicky at the start that generates enough energy to power one appliance, so that you can advance far enough to start making your own generators.  The problem with this is that in order to get to that point, you'll need to be regularly using *three* different electricity hogs, and wiring them all up at the same time will cause them to flicker in sequence like so many ugly christmas lights (note that while many things do have togglable on/off states, such as the furnace and the starting generator, which should never need to be off for any reason, it does not appear possible to actually turn these electrical appliances on or off in order to focus power to the one that needs it).  Not that this actually matters, mind, because you can still craft things on them if you just open the craft menu and hammer the button a few times.  Eventually you'll catch it during the split-second it's flashing "on", and the item will be made without a hitch.  Slight oversight, I feel.
But crafting and building aside, we still have high adventure and glorious combat, right?  Well...  Your character's movement is incredibly unpredictable, at times lunging forward into an abyss and at others getting caught on a pebble while attempting to run away.  This isn't at all helped by the fact that it's incredibly difficult to accurately determine where YOU are, as the model's graphics in no way correlate to your actual presence.  You'll get stopped by overhangs that look to be about a foot above your head, while falling down single-tile gaps that appear to be only a third of your width.  And as for combat, the game introduces its core mechanic by giving most enemies in the game an insane amount of damage reduction, which can be temporarily removed when they're in brightly lit situations.  The more light, the more of a reduction.
The problem with this is...   Actually, there are several problems, with probably the biggest one being a distinct disagreement between player and game as to where and what exactly is "light".  You'll frequently see enemies standing in a circle of torches while comfortably protected by their full-strength shadow armor.  Second, actually shining light on the damn things is harder than you might think, as you can't actually Alan Wake your way around with a flashlight in one hand and weapon in the other.  This generally leads to just spamming a bunch of torches onto a flat area and luring things over there to fight you.
I could rant on and on, but there's apparently a character limit...  Heh.  To summarize, there are a lot of good ideas here, layered on top of excellent potential...  And supported by about five rotten toothpicks.  It could've been so much more, but it isn't.  If you're looking for a thematic sandbox survival...  This isn't it.

I was spictive at first, buying a $20 farming sim. But as I slowly played it more and more I came to realize that Stardew Valley isn't just a farming sim game like a 2D pixelated version of farming simulator, but more of a story game.
The story starts off with you inheriting your father's old cottage and all the surrounding farmland, but on the first day there's not much to do there so I decided to explore the map and explore the town a little bit, when I came across a person just minding their business, so I talked to her and she said something back to me: “welcome to stardew valley Kash” she says, and from that moment I began to think to myself: “ that's interesting she actually talked said something to greet me”. I continue around town talking to people, and eventually it gets late and I have to go home. At this time in the game there is no way to fast travel back home making you remember the layout off map so you don't get lost and end up passing out, making the game that little bit more difficult.
The way the story was designed is brilliant being more realistic. Stuff come out of nowhere, like one day I might get a letter from my girlfriend, or from someone who want to meet meet somewhere to give me an item, Then there's events with the stardew valley fair, spirits eve, festival of ice, and so many more. Then you get to the mines, you having to go deeper and deeper to find quest items or too show your bravery to someone. There's so much more I could talk about this masterpiece of game but this review would never end.
Stardew valley is an amazing game, and I would strongly give it a 10/10.

'Blades of Time' packs a sexy heroine with lots of action and puzzles. The controls are a little weird at first but once you customize and get used to them there's a lot of exploring, fighting and gun play around the corner, the story unfolds pleasantly and the different landscapes are very beautiful to watch. Sounds confusing? Time travel always is, but despite it's complications it's definetly recommended for casual adventure gaming!
Multiplayer: It's a real shame you can't play with at least 4 players at the same time because the defense/attack principle with a base works really well.
Dismal Swamp DLC: Very short and not very challenging but still fun as it shifts the game's focus from puzzles and special abilities to simple hack and slash and shooting survival mode.
PS: The game is easy to find on certain bundles or on sale so don't pay more than 10 bucks! Manage your expectations! It's fun but it's no masterpiece!

This little title is far from perfect, but for what it is, I found it was solid.
It’s a point-and-click game that looks pretty good for a free title, barring a few lagging issues (especially around the cabinet near the bedroom area).
The story was interesting, and the ending was pretty good. I began to feel myself more and more immersed in the narrative as the story went on. That being said, there were still a few things that jarred me out of the experience.
The voice acting left a lot to be desired. It’s not terrible by any stretch of the word (I have heard much worse in my time), but it certainly was lack-luster at times, especially with Selena’s character. Both of the main voice actors’ voices occasionally sounded flat, and sometimes it sounded like they weren’t putting enough emotion in their performances. Again, it’s not abysmal, but there are definitely some issues.
It's not a long game; I finished it in little over an hour, and I sort of wish that it had been longer or that there had been more areas to explore. However, the game didn’t overstay it’s welcome either. Overall, for a free title, it was good.

I did not understand why this game was so praised when I played it. People called Bastion a gorgeous game with a very unique narration, but I honestly didn't think this game brought anything truly new and innovative to gaming or storytelling. It's actually a typical, linear action/RPG-esque game with a slightly retro feel, some good but repetitive music and a story that hasn't really impressed me.
Bastion is a good game, but I didn't understand why it was hyped and, despite my numerous attempts, I was simply never able to finish it and got bored about halfway through. I just found the gameplay very repetitive : you basically click on everything that moves until it dies in a typical action-RPG fashion, except you don't have the loot, gold or rewards that make these games so addicting. Combat just wasn't satisfying and was often a matter of mashing Mouse1 and blocking once every five seconds before repeating until the monster/boss was down. Challenge levels are more frustrating than they are challenging and the special gear you find in these levels isn't very useful or fun to use because it often simply gives you more ways to kill enemies you could already easily kill with your hammer by left-clicking them to death.
It's unique in its visual presentation, but in my opinion, the game's originality ends there, and it does not compensate for its lackluster gameplay.

I have enjoyed this game greatly, I feel it important to note that the majority of my time has been spent offline and thus I do not have a great amount of time logged, but I have spent hours and hours on this. As far as bugs I have only encountered a rash of broken worlds when I was transferring computers, but I was more than happy to start from a clean slate with my new, much improved computer. It does require a pretty strong system to run without constant lags and freezes, I imagine this is due to some lack of optimization that'll be cleared up in the future. But if you can run this at it's full potential then there is little that is more rewarding. It does, as most games that involve mining, take a little luck and A LOT of patience to really form a thriving base, but there is little that could rival the beauty of four whirring fusion reactors in a titanium fortress with colored lights throughout. Devs have not been  very active due to some serious roadblocks, but if enough people read this, and buy it then activity will pick up, so BUY IT!
Update: I am trepidatious. After a long time of absolutely nothing from the devs they release a statement that says that they will be releasing DLC's to finish the game. If they had been at least releasing small updates and micro patches to keep the game running and showing an effort to hold customer attention I would not mind A (1!!!) DLC to see to it that this would go to the end. However, the dev's fortitude is definitely admirable. I just question how viable DLC's and a second game are going to be. I had my fun with what is on this so if the DLC's fail then I cannot complain about the money I spent. However, it is a bit shady to come up this short after such a long time. I still recommend it because it is still good, but I am unsure of the future. Hold for future updates.
Update: I expect this to be my last. This game has a great atmosphere and an excellent system, but the developers are too busy to really make it work to its full potential. It has been 8 months since we last heard from the devs after 6 months or more with no word from them. These words feel weird to type, but this game is abandoned. It would be nice to have the developers at least affirm their existence once in a while, but we have no such affirmation. As such I am changing this review to negative and officially filing this game as one that almost transcended all others before failing.

It is hard to write a small review about a game that you are enjoying in some aspects but despising in others. I will keep it as short and simple as possible:
Pro:
-Gorgeous Environments, for the most part.
-An (also for the most part) decent voice acting in all available languages (japanese best tho.)
-Large Variety of Enemies with some fresh ideas
-Good Animations
-Nice Time Rewind Mechanic
-Actually fun puzzling
-A decent fighting system with awesome magic skills...
Con:
-...which sadly lacks ANY impact in normal swordfighting (not magic) due to horrible sound effects and just not really good audiovisual feedback. Seriously, for the most part it sounds like you would try to rub cardboard swords against a cardboard enemy. Often you can't tell if your attacks stagger an enemy or if he attacks back.
-The controls, while fluid for the most part, just infuriate sometimes. WHY does the character stop after a jump, so you have to wait a second to run on? That just doesn't fit the gameplay. Same with dashing.
-Some annoying glitches (rare though. I clipped through the ground twice, which is not gamebreaking but annoying.)
-Horrible, horrible...HORRIBLE cutscenes. The characters move and act like paper. The voice acting, like stated in pro, is alright though.
-While, like stated in pro, the environments and enemies are often enjoyable and lush, there are WAY too many muddy textures that should just not have been there. It really drags down the otherwise beautiful scenery.
In the end it is still recommendable if you can overlook the lacking impact of fighting and some of the above issues. It is still fun, and while you will often shake your head about issues, the game is still...just, fun. Simple fun that the issues won't take away - luckily.
Personal Score: 7,5/10

Minute 20 as an example, when he breaks a crate, then he hits a large enemy 10-15 seconds later).

even the old snes beat em ups got those things right. Fallout 4 was one of the most disappointing game releases I have personally experienced. The gutting of the RPG mechanics, the lackluster and predictable storyline and the shallow quests which amounted to, for the most part, kill everything in a specific location, return to quest giver, repeat made this game by far the worst Fallout game to date ( out of 1, 2, 3 and new vegas ). The only only saving graces for this game were the combat, which is a massive improvement over Fallout 3 and new vegas, although still not remarkable by modern standards, and the massive open world which is filled with cool details and areas to explore.
On release i'd probably give this game a 6.5/10 and would have probably pushed up to a 7/10 if it wasn't for downright awful performance in some areas of the game. Despite all of its very major flaws it was honestly a pretty fun game if you treated if for what it is, a post-apocalyptic sandbox with decent shooter mechanics and a fair amount of customization. It certainly wasn't good enough for me to recommend, especially for £40, but also wasn't bad enough for me to give a not recommended score for. The recent updates to the game by Bethesda are enough to change that.
The creation Club is the most anti-consumer thing Bethesda has done. Simple as that. It is a system which mixes paid mods, one extremely anti-consumer practice that Bethesda has already tried to implement in the past, and microtransactions in the form of of Creation Club credits. The Creation Club is not the main issue here though, if Bethesda had actually released some decent content for it, mods with the scope and quality of enderal for example, there would not have been anywhere near as much backlash, and a lot more people would have certainly been open to the idea of a Creation Club. Instead they release content such as pip-boy skins, power armour skins and backpacks. This alone is awful, but the way you have to pay for this content makes it even worse. For example a Pip-boy skin is 50 Creation Club Credits and each Credit is worth around 1.25 pence, bringing the price for the skin up to around 62p. Not too bad you might say, overpriced yes but not terrible. The problem is you cannot simply pay 62p for this specific skin you want, you have to pay £6 for 750 Credits.
If people support these sort of anti-comsumer practices Bethesda will continue them and other companies will follow. Do not buy this game and do not buy any Bethesda products until they shut down Creation Club and stop these anti-consumer practices.

Man... If only I was able to describe my feelings about this game more precisely I would. I don't exactly have a black and white opinion about this game, although I do feel that I don't exactly recommend this game. Knowing that this game WAS a budget title it did deliver its value... Sort of. The game is good over-all the combat is pretty fast-paced, the level design was great. Locations deliver that very "fantastical" sort of idea that, that kind of world would only exist in a dream. I haven't gotten that far into the game yet, considering the amound of time I've played before writing this review (about less than an hour). I feel though that I've gotten enough things to cringe about in Blades of Time.
One, the animations. Man... I don't exactly understand the whole dynamic as to why this is a problem in the first place but, considering I know just a tad bit about animation, is that every movement takes a TON of time. Walk cycles are the worst when trying to animate by hand, without a mocap device. Anyways, I noticed one big peeve of mine for BoT: Ayumi's running  cycle. If you don't pay much attention to it, it looks decent enough to make a big deal out of it. But, what I notice is that with every step, her head just turns with her body. 95% of the time she's looking left and right and rarely to the front. I see myself already in the future when I play the game and just have those long running sequences I'll just get constantly bothered by the fact that she can't look at one damn direction when she's running. I thought it sort of made sense at first since, she was in a completely new world and she wanted to just take as much of its beauty in as possible. But nope, just a damn animation problem. I don't think it would have taken much to lock her head relatively in the same position as she's moving: forward. It shouldn't take much precision either, as long as it's in approximately the same location the whole time, it should be flawless. Another problem that I have with her running is her arms and legs. She flails her legs outward while keeping her knees in so she sort of pushes her body in a diagonal direction (which may explain why she keeps turning her damn head, although probably not). It's hard to describe for me through text but just look up gameplay and I'm sure you"d understand. Also her arms are kept way too close to her body for her to even look like she's running comfortably. Her arms, instead of moving forward and back while she runs, they more rotate around her body in a sort of elbow-to-chest-then-to-shoulder-blade movement. Ridiculous I know, but I'm not known for being good at describing things.
Second, the narrative that Ayumi does. THE CONSTANT NARRATIVE. I swear after every minor part, she's going to speak her mind about either the world or what she thinks about the new enemies she'll encounter. It becomes a bit of an annoyance. Again, I'm still not that far into the game, maybe that'll change but, we'll see. Also the way the game gives you hints about how to progress the level is... I don't know. Compared to other games, the way the hint is either presented or shown, it sort-of makes me feel idiotic. Like, I could have figured that out all by myself? Yet, that's all based on opinion and I don't want to force you to believe me on that point. But let's look at the wider aspect, the voice acting itself. It's pretty good, to say the least. The only problem I'd have is with Ayumi's narration, sometimes it's very noticeable that she's reading off of a script rather than being immersive into the BoT world. I'll update my opinion once I've finished the game.
Last, the shooting mechanics. It's too locked for me. Like, I'm moving on an axes instead of fluid mouse motion. Also the way Ayumi moves when in "Gun Mode" is way too smooth. She's basically sliding on the ground rather than walking when she's aiming. I feel like there'd need to be some sort of bobbing motion while you move to at least make the game feel just a tad bit more, normal? I'd say? The movement is too mechanic rather than fluid. But I could also incorporate this with my first point but I'm too lazy to care (heheh..)
Overall I'd say this game is playable if you don't pay attention to much of the details in which I've pointed out thus far. It's got a pretty promising story line, fast-paced combat, awesome level, character, and monster design (no it's not because the main character looks attractive, although in my opinion it's sort of wierd to say she is, since... I don't know I guess you'll have to see it for yourself and establish your own decision), pretty good sountrack too! Well yeah, I'd say a 7 out of 10. I got the game off of a bundlestars bundle so if you want to pick the game up? I'd say you'd get your money's worth if you got it through that, and hey, you'll get 7 extra games that you most likely will not play along with it. But for $4.01? I'd say it's worth a shot.

Blood Bowl is a...How to put this? Turn based fantasy sport satire boardgame?
It's quite unique, and I have difficulty describing it in a simple way so I will explain the gameplay
You have a team of 11-16 pieces(Your players), and you face off against a team of similar size. Only up to 11 per team can be on the field at once. It is vaguely remniscent of American Football(Handegg for you Europeans out there), where you have a ball and you need to run it into your opposition's endzone to score. Different from the sport however is that you take turns moving your pieces.
This leads to a more strategic and tactical game, with the dice-based mechanics making it mainly a challenge of risk avoidance, while maximising the risk for your opponent.
Of course, being a Warhammer universe, there are races other than humans. And everything is much more violent. It is not unusual for a team to have players die on the field, or to have them permanently injured. And tactics are much less throwing balls and passing for the less dextrous races(Orks tend to not have a great catcher for one, and the passing game of a dwarf team is notorious for being poor), and more other things. Stalling, outmanouvering your opponent, or just plainly trying to beat them all to a pulp and walk right through them are options. There are plenty of tactical choices to be made, and several strategic ones as well - A team can last you a very long time, and knowing how to build the skills on your team is crucial to your success in the later matches.
In the end, it is a very interesting game. It has a little something for everyone, from amazing comebacks out of a long pass by an elf team to the pure carnage of a band of orks having themselves a good old brawl while there just happens to be a ball in the mix somewhere, to entirely other playstyles entirely.
While often I think of something to say that would let you know whether or not you'll like it, the only way to know for sure with Bloodbowl is to try.
It's very hit and miss.  If you end up enjoying it, you can get a long, long time out of your money. And if not, well. It was cheap(If you got it on sale), and you tried.
And even then, it's a great game to play with a friend while just talking or doing something else on the side.
Blood Bowl Chaos edition includes all content of Legendary edition.
New in Chaos edition are three new teams/races you can pick, none of them overpowered so you are not buying power here, while at the same time being 100% compatible with Legendary edition.
There are extra voice lines, a new stadium, and a new price tag!
Buying Chaos edition gets you all the content in Legendary as well, so you can consider it the 'full edition' at this point. (Before Bloodbowl 2 anyway)
Is it worth a whole 10 bucks more? Up to you. But do know that during sales it is often available for a much cheaper price, a total of 7,50 seems to be customary.
Worth it on sale? You bet it is. Worth it for everyone? As before, maybe. But I do recommend giving it a try just in case you like it. Because if you do, you'll wonder where the hours went, and why the sun is coming up already.

This game is another example of a great concept that is crippled by poor execution.
The concept was infinite player and developer generated worlds, dungeons, and monsters within a simplified Minecraft boxel world. That part they got right. For quite some time I was amazed at the neat biomes and surprisingly creative dungeons from a haunted crypt to an hourglass to a lighthouse to a pair of zepplins with tons in between. A Tron-inspired world sat next to Candyland sat next to Jurassic Park sat next to the Old West.
However, it didn't take long to see the flaws. Every class is unique and different, but only has two main moves and two special cooldown moves. Some of the bigger bosses do some interesting things, but eventually they just blend together into one big blah. And then you realize you have to do it hundreds if not thousands of times to get anywhere without paying cash. The dungeons are novel, but what you do in them is boring and has no real meaning. Then you see how much your XP bar moves, and it gets depressing.
I think the two big knocks against Trove is the utter lack of story and the short chunks of time. No story means there is no context, no inspiration, no reason to actually do anything. There is no call to action. No character development. No real victory or defeat or development. The incredibly short chunk of time required to do anything means most small dungeons have a dozen monsters or less and are cleared in a minute or two. Larger dungeons are a bit longer unless you run into trouble. This makes them feel incredibly small and unimportant. In other words, worthless. That lack of driving force only adds to the drudgery of grinding. It does mean you don't have to commit an entire afternoon to do something, but it also means when you're done, you don't feel like you've actually done anything.
So sad to see something with so much promise be so flat and repetitive. I'd say fire it up to look around, but then be done before the gloom of the grind overshadows everything.

Bastion is an epic action/adventure with a little bit of RPG elements involved like weapon and character stats. Overall your character will go through different floating islands in order to acquire new weapons and restore the Bastion to its full glory. During this the kid will acquire many different weapons including the Cael Hammer, Fang Repeater, Breaker’s Bow and many others. Also there are fragments in the world for killing various things including non creatures that allow you to upgrade your weapons with the corresponding pieces to the weapons.
The combat is fairly simple in that you have 3 main buttons to remember (this is for PC). The left mouse button is assigned to one weapons and the right mouse button to the other weapon. Q is your special skill that is equipped that can vary between special weapon skills or items like mirror shield and grenade. Along with those 3 buttons you have shift being used for block and locking on and space being used for roll/jump. WASD is your standard movement keys and looking around with your mouse allows the player to attack at different directions. The combat is quite simple to get used to while being a little harder to master but oh so satisfying when you do master it.

The story is a simple one but interesting and unique. The Kid (his actual name in game) wakes up to find his world being destroyed by the Calamity, a mysterious event that fractured the world into many floating pieces and turns people into ash. All while he is travelling around an older man named Rucks is narrating everything you do, something very unique to this game. Rucks tells him that in order to get the Bastion fully up and running “the kid” needs to get the cores and later shards so that he can either restore the world to the way it was before the Calamity or just escape. Along the way he meets two other characters Zia a Ura girl and Zulf the Ura ambassador. Eventually Zulf returns back to the Ura but not before destroying the Bastion’s central device after finding out about Zia’s father being the one that started the Calamity. “The kid” must work to get the shards in order to get Bastion up and working and prevent the Ura from doing anymore damage.

The Graphics are simple but the art is very impressive.  Each creature looks distinct and the worlds are all different. As “the kid” walks around the world pieces of it come together making it look like the islands are coming together as he walks around and destroys things. The sound/music is above and beyond some of the best of any indie game or any AAA game I’ve ever played. The music is amazing and even the vocal songs sound really nice. On top of that Rucks the old man narrates everything “the kid” does and I mean everything. If you jump off the island he talks about that, if he sits around just killing random items he mentions that. It isn’t perfect but it makes it feel like he is narrating the players story and nothing is scripted.

Overall the game is clearly a must play for anyone that is a fan of good story, art, sound and action adventure. It was an enjoyable experience even though it was on the shorter side of about 6-8 hours.

Darkout is already a surprisingly complete game, at least until the end game. The research mechanic, as well as the simple wiring that is mandatory to power most crafting stations, makes it fairly engaging without being overly difficult (you can almost always see what sorts of loot you want with a simple mouseover). Needing to find blueprints for all the top end items (for example, the top Mark 3 version of the basic leather armor can't be crafted until you find the blueprint) instead of just unlock them through research gives you an incentive to explore and fight tough monsters, while the frequency of drops for those sorts of recipies dont leave them feeling a grind.
The light/dark mechanics still need some work, as it is high light just massively increases the damage you do, but overall its fairly simple. Sadly, a highly illuminated base is just as likely to get swarms of monsters running through as one that's completely dark, but at least they are far easier to chase off.
The game has a narrative/quest line, which can be pretty engaging, but sadly it has a habit of bugging up and not advancing. For the most part this has no negative impact on gameplay - only the very first step is mandatory to be able to achieve anything, and all that requires is to use a piece of your characters starting gear so I doubt it will cause any real problems.
Some parts of the game are a little unclear (for example, to fight the City boss, you need to purify relics, but while the relic will tell you what you need to purify it, it doesn't tell you how to apply the items - you need to go back to the relic gate you got the relic from and activate it with all the items in your inventory). For the most part it's very easy to figure out what you are doing though.
One thing that bugged me to no end however, is that the order of items in your crafting list is determined by the order you unlocked them in your research list (NOT the order you research them). So you might have all the mark 3 metal armour above the mark 2 leather, or you might have an exo helm near the top of your armour list, the legs in the middle, and the bodyarmour at the very bottom. I'd much prefer if the crafting list had a pre-determined order for items to go in, to keep it nice and neat.

It's a game w/ a world that is so lovingly crafted, you get lost in it. You'll find yourself saying, "Just one more day." and before you know it, 3hrs have elapsed. The music is especially note worthy, as you won't find yourself getting sick of hearing familiar tracks; quite the contrary, you'll be looking forward to them. I also love finding new ways to challenge myself and I still have yet to find everything.
I didn't know going into this game whether or not I'd still want to keep playing once the main story was over. I can honestly say idk when I'll ever stop playing. Considering that not only is new content being added, but the developer also has plans to implement multiplayer this year as well.
TL;DR - An outstanding game that is one you just have to experience for yourself. Be prepared to get lost in Stardew Valley, and not caring about finding a way out for a long, long time.

I'm going to preface this with the fact that I'm only playing it not for the story.  Sandbox games are usually about exploration, building, and discovery.
Since this game emphasises light and dark as a gimmick you would imagine that there would be effort in making sure the light mechanics work.
They mostly do as long as you have the dynamic lighting option checked.  Otherwise mobile light sources are virtually useless as they do not brighten anything at all.
What I find nice for this game is that you don't need to have everything in your inventory to do crafting.  All you need to do is be close by the container and the game grabs it from there for you.  This is similar for researching as well, the only cost I've seen for them is the basic resource and the research point (My armor wasn't consumed when researching upgrades) so farming research points is a necessity in order to unlock new crafting items.
Stone seems to have been turned into a resource vein instead of becoming more and more common the further down you go.  In Terraria and Minecraft dirt becomes less common as stone becomes more common the further down you go.  I went down as best as possible with the resources I have but I only saw veins of stone.
I'm also under the assumption that trees are currently not replantable.  I've not seen a seed that allowed me to plant more trees or even plants for that matter.  The regular plants, though, do regrow on their own after some time.

Disclaimer: I'm only 2 hours into the game so far (3rd 'world').
Blades of Time was something I picked up on a lark while it was on sale. The fact that it was from the people who made X-Blades (never played, but it looks really fanservicey) and checking a few reviews made it seem mediocre.
I was wrong. This game is wonderful.
Don't get me wrong, it is flawed. Graphics aren't great and the controls aren't as tight as you'd want in a 3rd person platform/hack and slash game but the core mechanics: adding powers to your character, the combat combo system, ranged combat and melee combat all feel great. The real shining point, however, is the time manipulation.
In games like Prince of Persia, you rewind time to recover from mistakes. Here, you rewind time, which locks you in place and rewinds everything ELSE in the world. Then, there are two copies of you running around. Your former self just continues to do whatever it was that you did at that time, and enemies AI kicks back in.
An example of this is if you wanted, you could copy yourself a bunch and all have them aim rifles, shooting at a tree. Then make a final copy which kites the bad guy over to where the shots are happening. It's unlikely that you'd need to do this, but it's possible!
Anyway if you see this game on sale, grab it. It's not going to push the boundries of PC gaming, gaming or even your expectations of games, but it will provide you a solid amount of *fun*.

Holy smokes. I was wondering how poor games can get on Steam, and bought this.
First impression? Obviously QUALITY CONTROL - M.I.A! Seriously, if I had the choice, I would not have passed this game. The fact that the original asking price is 0,99€ for this sounds like a joke. I'd say this game has, at most, the standard of a mediocre Gamedev 101 course exercise, not beyond that.
The game is riddled with badly tested, ill-designed and/or nonfunctional mechanics. The character can fall through moving platforms with no reason whatsoever. Jump and movement mechanics, while not exhibiting the vertical direction lock as in Action 52, are not as fluid as they could be. Objects are misleading - a candy bar can lead to death when rotated to one side, but not when to an another? Store mechanics seem to work, but the GUI is hastily done as texts do not indicate their user interface behavior, either by mouseover color change or any other means. The store seems to work somewhat, but due to the problematic mechanics, I have not been able to test them to their full potential. The store, and dying also induces major lag, which has crashed the game several times when I tested it.
Music is.. eh, practically nonexistent - the only thing I heard is the same short piano clip as in the trailer - but only in the main menu.  I've been unable to turn music on for the main game, even though I've clicked the button for it. Sound effects do also exist, but are very repetitive. As of graphics, they seem to generally have some relation as to what they represent - however, the lack of graphics design is painfully obvious with cheesy, non-uniform environments and obviously stretched textures.
The idea does have potential, I give it that. But the frankly atrocious implementation renders the game unable to render any reasonable value to its player beyond being comic relief for its bad design.
The maker of this game needs major remedial education in programming, testing, game design.. perhaps music and arts classes could also do positive things for the possible future ventures of the author. If one is not interested in supporting the developer in their development with this kind of show for the work, or buying poor games for comic relief, they should ask for a refund.

Tower Unite, at the time of this review, is pretty shoddily made. Corners are very obviously cut, the graphics don't look that impressive compared to its predecessor in GMOD, and it is very severely unoptimized with some severe memory leaks and (at least for me) runs at incredibly high temps. That said, I ♥♥♥♥ing love this game and you should definetely buy it.
The minigames, despite a lot of flaws such as inconsistency, hitreg, and the ever present netcode issues that no game will ever be able to solve, are full of variety and...they're just fun as hell to play! Each of the minigames are a wonderfully executed, infinitely replayable romp that will last you about half an hour and then some. Hell, for being a side of the main game, they do better than most full games based entirely around the initial concept.
You've got Minigolf with some amazingly fun and frustrating level design, you've got Super Monkey Ball with levels that introduce some interesting concepts and are a hellalot more difficult, Virus which is tag with guns reminiscent of the older, fast paced iD titles, Little Crusaders which is an inconsistent but fun game about pushing buttons on a deadly dragon, Laser Tag which is exactly what it sounds like, some smaller games like Trivia and Typing Derby, and
, with so many more to come.
All fun as hell, and rewarding with units that you can gamble away at a casino that everyone seems to spend their time in,  or spend on items that you can use to customize yourself with or your condo. And holy hell, decorating condos is somehow one of the best times I've had in video games. Decorate it however the ♥♥♥♥ you want; a nice living room, a home theater you can watch videos with friends in, a replica of Hotline Miami, a museum, a porn museum, a scale replica of Lobby 1 from GMT, a
, whatever the ♥♥♥♥ you want! It sounds boring, but you can just mess around however the hell you want to in these condos.
And this community is just one of the greatest around. Yeah, it's dominated by weebs and furries and antisocial aholes, but they are just fun to ♥♥♥♥ around with. Maybe they'll go around as skeletons reading the Bee Movie script aloud, or maybe they'll invite you to their porn museum, or maybe they'll just chill with you in a gamemode and teach you something neat, maybe have a nice conversation or two (or 30) about how much better GMTower was. Or maybe they'll just sit in the casino gambling their lives away being incredibly self-deprecating. It's often that. Mostly that. Eh screw it, almost always that.
And just, god damn, I love this game. I'm horrendously biased because of the 500 hours I spent in GMTower, yeah, but for good reason. At the cost of sounding really, really generic, GMTower was one of the reasons I am who I am today. It's why I'm a self-deprecating♥♥♥♥♥♥that acts like Charlie from Always Sunny. But, it was a big thing for me, and Tower Unite continues to add to that. A great port of the popular and well-received turn-based strategy board game which uses the newest LRB 6 edition of the rules. Blood Bowl (BB) is the game of Fantasy Football, akin to real-life Rugby (play only halts when a point is scored) or American Football, only with excessive violence, death, secret weapons and even magic. Oh, and the ball has spikes on it. The players who form the 23 types of team to choose from come from a range of classic fantasy races: Elves, Dwarves, Undead, Orcs - they're all there. Each has its own play style, so I would advise you try a variety to find ones that suit you (for me, it's Wood Elves especially, with their incredible Wardancers). Races not for beginners: Chaos, Goblin, Halfling, Khemri, Nurgle, Ogre and Vampire.
Be aware: this game is based on dice-rolling, so luck plays a part. BUT there is also lots of strategy to it, from more basic ideas like risk management and positioning, to the more complex such as chainpushing and team builds/management/development (useful site -
. 90% of the few hundred games I've played have felt like the better player won. Sometimes bad luck really does strike yes, but if you analyse your game-play you usually could've made some better decisions, too. Don't be put off by what seems like bad luck in your first few games, but be warned that this game requires some patience to get good at.
Online leagues are where this game really comes to life. The AI seems hard at first, but can become too easy quite quickly. Online you get the challenge of real players, can choose options such turn length (I would highly recommend 2 minute turns) and even make your own league! 'Naggaroth Open' league is great for matchmaking, as it has a very good community, but it's probably a good idea to start off in Auld World (once you can regularly beat the AI on 'Medium'). There are a couple of rare, minor bugs in online play (the '12-player' and the infamous 'invisible player' bug), but these are not game-breaking, and most community-run leagues have agreements about ways to get around it.
Some of my best gaming experiences have been in Blood Bowl. The chaos, fun and replayablity is huge. It's just great.

Great game concept, good visuals and great gameplay. Sadly as any other game Trove has its setbacks. Many times have I found myself grinding dungeon after dungeon, biome after biome just grinding my way to the top, just to come across a new player who just opened his/her first box and got the rarest drop. Understanding the massive gap in this game's RNG system is quite lucrative... if you're in the end-game. This is because you need to stack massive amounts of caches in order to even have a chance at those "rarer" drops. This can be good, since it means that you have to work for the gear, but it divides the players from those who can afford the time and effort, and those who only have 2-5 hours a day, not counting the individual player's efficiency(how good a player can do the work in the fastest way possible). In the end, the game has good class/skill synergy and enough material to keep a player busy for a substantial amount of time, with even more content being added continuously. In my personal opinion, this game has a bright future with much more room for improvement.

Botanicula is an average point and click game that just barely makes up for it in a cute world of plants and creatures.
Pros:
- The game takes place in a lovely environment full of plants and life. The colors are nice too.
- You control a group of people? Objects? I don't know have to describe them. You control a group of nature heroes, and its funny to see them react to the environment.
- I don't normally like when games have no spoken words, but in this case I think it worked. Nothing in this game talks, and its charming.
- I enjoyed the music. There is just one part in the game where you control the instruments being played by two creatures, and its entertaining to hear the music develop.
Cons:
- The controls (can I even call them controls, all you do is click on things) were very unclear. It was at times difficult to figure out how and when to click on something, even when I knew exactly what to do in that situation. That was annoying especially toward the end. There is a section where you have to get a light orb from a pod, and you have to click on the white arrows in a VERY specific way to get the orb. I knew exactly what I had to do, but I had to resort to a youtube video to figure out how to pass this part.
- There is no way I found to make the game full screen, so I was playing with a black frame around the game. It was distracting.
- Steam overlay wouldn't work while I played, so I was unable to see achievements when they popped up. I also had to alt tab to get to a browser.
- When I completed the game, the main menu only gave me an option to play a new game, so I guess there is no way to go to specific chapters in the game. I hate when games do this.
Botanicula is very bizarre and trippy which was nice to see. The story was very basic and was satisfying in the end. I can't say I'd recommend this game at regular price. Definitely pick this one up on a sale.
There are no jump scares, but there are dark sections toward the end with cartoony-creepy creatures. I wouldn't describe it as scary either.

This game's story, atmosphere, style, and everything else is masterfully done. Except the RNG. I've been playing strategy games for years, both on screen and off, but I've never come across anything like it.
I get that they're trying to make the game feel like a desperate last stand, with the odds stacked against you, but at the end of the day it just comes off wrong. I love setting up neat little traps for my enemies to walk in to. I loathe it when my guys then miss every single shot and the enemies wipe out half my team to as a result. Do I think that I should wipe them out without paying for it at all (one-shot)? No, but nor do I think that the enemy should be allowed to do the same.
The RNG permeates through everything. Campaign progression, map generation, enemy unit composition. The worst thing is that the game doesn't even recognise some situations for their true difficulty. Some maps will say that they are easy and after an hour trying to work it out, I'm still sitting there believing the only win scenario is with 3 or more of my guys dead. Other maps say they are difficult and take me a teeny tiny number of turns to complete, without a single soldier wounded. What gives?
Oh yeah, RNG.
This isn't a game about strategy as it current plays, it's just about dice rolling. Steam-rolling a supposedly difficult mission feels great, but often feels cheap because you know you've just rolled lucky dice. Losing repeatedly on "easy" maps using when you've set up excellent firefights, hacked every turret and mech and sniped the most dangerous enemies, just because of dice rolls, is exhausting.
Edit: I should probably add that I am aware that some folks love the RNG style of this game, and that's okay. I don't meant to rail against it, its just that I prefer games where strategy is more a focus than luck. I don't feel that the RNG is biased against the player, its just frustrating that its part of every single interaction in the game.
UPDATE: So today I finished the game. I wanted to stick with it because as I've said there are many aspects of the game that are top notch. As for RNG, its actually pretty sad because later on in the game (after mid-game) the RNG aspect practically disappears. Your soldiers hit harder and much more accurately and the game then becomes focused on careful placement and meticulously weighing up which target is best to hit with which soldier each turn. You know, actual strategy stuff. Its about avoiding being overwhelmed, hunkering down in a choice position, and outpacing your enemies in gun fights. So for that, the game is forgiven.
I really, honestly, and deeply wished that they'd do away with the over focus on RNG in the early to mid game. Yes, soldiers still miss during the end-game but they have so many skills and buffs that it no longer means a total wipe. Plus, its rare for more than one to miss in a single turn.
I'm aware people have told me to choose an easier difficulty and while I'm not playing on the hardest difficulty, I'm easily outstripping the AI in game in terms of tactically sound decisions. Dumbing down the AI just because RNG screws me over at times isn't really a solution. It would just make the game more tedious.

So as I'm writeing this I've logged around 400 hours of Blackwake. As one of the kickstarters and very active alpha players one can consider this review as a bit biased but I'll try to adress some concerns other and myself have with the current game.
What is Blackwake?
It is basically a FPS game with a little twist to it. The twist is that most of the map can't be rached for the players and you have to fight on those moveing platforms called "ships". those ships have powerfull weapons called canons and can be directed, damaged and so on.
Is it accurate naval battle? Of course not that would be downright boring (Nelson's approach at Traffalgar took hours before the real fighting even started). But it has all the element fantasy pirate battles need. You have chainshot swivels to damage sails, roundshot to shoot holes into enemy ships and of course grape hot to slaughter the enemy crew.
What I personally love is the chaos that can happen when you plan only kind of works. Those are the moments of great comebacks (or of you going to take a unwelcome bath).
Also there are no classes the only player who is a bit different is the captain which is voted into office at the begining of each round and can be mutinied during the round! Being a captain and leading your crew to victory is one of the best things in gameing I have ever expirienced (when it is defeat blame the crew or the allied ships). It's not like the commander function in so many other games but bascially one of the crew and they can always leave the wheel to take part (i.e. repair something or help in a boarding).
What are current concerns?
1. The server issue. Joining nearly full servers is currently a major headache. But I'm very sure the devs will work on that. When we had server issues during the alphas they were always looked at ASAP.
2. Repeatetive nature of the current game modes. Well first of all 1v1 plays a good amount different to the 2v2 modes so try that. But also there will be new game modes. There just wasn't enough time to create and test them before release.
3. Some players seem to dislike the glitchy nature the game sometimes has. For me that is part of the charm. It also allows a lot of stuff. Because you are so free to explore the ship you actually can not only climb to the top of the mast but also walk to the tips of the sails. Good spots for stowaways ;).
Well that's it you dirty landlubbers. I see you on the high seas.

What makes A New Day so compelling is its attention to appearance, plot, and character development. To help with clarity, the art sheds the black-and-white style of the comics in favor of vibrant color, though it uses similar art to that drawn by Charlie Adlard in the current issues. Fans may yearn for an option to go into a black-and-white mode, but the game art builds nicely on its paper inspiration. The PC and console versions of the game look much the same, although the PC edition is best overall with the smoothest animations. Its 360 counterpart is extremely dark even with the in-game brightness turned up all the way, though the only serious issue is the camera, which is often too close to the action to get a good look at your surroundings. You get a good cinematic view of everything, at least, although this doesn't help much when you're scrounging through the drugstore for goodies or checking out nearby zombies.
The story has been crafted adroitly to weave in and out of the events told in the comics and on TV, blending the new with the familiar. So while you take on the role of the previously unseen Lee Everett, the adventure takes you through parts of rural Georgia also visited by Rick Grimes and the gang. Many of the events here fill out backstories from the comics. You visit Hershel's farm before he started that interesting collection in his barn, for instance, and rescue Glenn when he gets trapped during one of his scavenging runs.
All of the characters are very well written and voiced as individuals (none of the TV actors reprise their roles here, though), which makes you care about whether or not they get munched on by ravenous corpses. It's difficult to get up from the game, so expect to finish it in a two- or three-hour single sitting. Granted, there are some cliches. Lee is a stereotypical man of mystery, with a sinister past that may involve his killing the US senator messing around with his wife. His kid sidekick, Clementine, while lovable and tough in her own right, is obviously a plot device to help tragic Lee find his way again.
And Carley used to think that stray dogs and the odd crack in the road were hazardous during her morning jogs.
And Carley used to think that stray dogs and the odd crack in the road were hazardous during her morning jogs.
Actual gameplay is of a more so-so quality. Although this is a point-and-click adventure, the puzzles are few and far between. Exploration is a must in a couple of places, and there are a few spots where you need to gather items to push the plot forward. Controls are basic. On the PC, you use a mouse-and-WASD combo, occasionally resorting to the number keys to change between the standard looking, taking, talking, and using abilities. Consoles work in a similar fashion, with the left stick moving, the right stick taking care of the point of view, and the four face buttons handling character abilities. Other than the control scheme, there isn't much to figure out. Most of the game deals with interacting with fellow survivors through dialogue.

Serena is amazing. Playing it is like reading a short-story written by Edgar Allan Poe: it's dreary, haunting and the storytelling... ah, it is marvelous. The environment looks just like Poe's chamber in the poem "The Raven", or like the shack in Lars von Trier's "Antichrist" - so you can tell that things are going to get creepy at some point. Serena is an inviting point-and-click (or rather a point-and-read) adventure game with no puzzles for you to solve, so you'd better go with the flow. The plot is about longing, resentment and despair (or even hope, anger and guilt) and how memory and perception alter our judgments regarding the things that surround us. At the core of it all are also themes such as love, hatred and murder, so be prepared to deliver some thinking in order to make sense of this fantastic story. The voice acting, the graphics and the gameplay are decent, so, if you are into reading letters and listening to thoughtful remarks, then this is one of the finest games you're going to get nowadays.

Fallout 4 was one of the most disappointing game releases I have personally experienced. The gutting of the RPG mechanics, the lackluster and predictable storyline and the shallow quests which amounted to, for the most part, kill everything in a specific location, return to quest giver, repeat made this game by far the worst Fallout game to date ( out of 1, 2, 3 and new vegas ). The only only saving graces for this game were the combat, which is a massive improvement over Fallout 3 and new vegas, although still not remarkable by modern standards, and the massive open world which is filled with cool details and areas to explore.
On release i'd probably give this game a 6.5/10 and would have probably pushed up to a 7/10 if it wasn't for downright awful performance in some areas of the game. Despite all of its very major flaws it was honestly a pretty fun game if you treated if for what it is, a post-apocalyptic sandbox with decent shooter mechanics and a fair amount of customization. It certainly wasn't good enough for me to recommend, especially for £40, but also wasn't bad enough for me to give a not recommended score for. The recent updates to the game by Bethesda are enough to change that.
The creation Club is the most anti-consumer thing Bethesda has done. Simple as that. It is a system which mixes paid mods, one extremely anti-consumer practice that Bethesda has already tried to implement in the past, and microtransactions in the form of of Creation Club credits. The Creation Club is not the main issue here though, if Bethesda had actually released some decent content for it, mods with the scope and quality of enderal for example, there would not have been anywhere near as much backlash, and a lot more people would have certainly been open to the idea of a Creation Club. Instead they release content such as pip-boy skins, power armour skins and backpacks. This alone is awful, but the way you have to pay for this content makes it even worse. For example a Pip-boy skin is 50 Creation Club Credits and each Credit is worth around 1.25 pence, bringing the price for the skin up to around 62p. Not too bad you might say, overpriced yes but not terrible. The problem is you cannot simply pay 62p for this specific skin you want, you have to pay £6 for 750 Credits.
If people support these sort of anti-comsumer practices Bethesda will continue them and other companies will follow. Do not buy this game and do not buy any Bethesda products until they shut down Creation Club and stop these anti-consumer practices.

Firstly, I want to preface this review by saying that I've been a diehard Assassins Creed fan since the beginning up until a hiatus after AC4 where I became overly fatigued and embittered with the franchise. I'll confidently say that this title gave me the same wonderful feeling I got when jumping from AC1 to AC2, that feeling of wonderment after discovering how much better an IP could become.
Let's run through my personal list of pros and cons for this game:
PROS:
+ I really enjoyed the story and Arno as a character, I would honestly put him second on my list of all-time favourite asssasins after Ezio
+ The combat is really satisfying, fun and deliciously brutal in my opinion. The presence of finishers with real physicality, along with weapons that all feel different to handle, really adds up to crafting an enjoyable combat experience for me - the cherry on top, being the context-sensitive animations that trigger depending on the location or prior movements of the player.
+ The stealth is much improved with the implementation of a crouch button and (albeit clunky) cover system, and helps improve the general feeling of being an *assassin*  - which prior titles lacked with their assassins' inabilty to crouch ;(
+I loved the world design, Ubi really nailed the feeling of Paris in the midst of the revolution - and it harkened back to Brotherhood's focus on one large city as a map, which I personally adored.
+ The graphics are jaw-droppingly gorgeous, with Ubi's global illumination system conjuring up some absolutely stunning views both outdoors and in!
+ Performance is stable in its current state, I'm able to run it on my specs at ultra at 70-90fps.
+I like the RPG-lite levelling system that differentiates the city zones and enemies - I prefer this implementation to Origins because it doesn't make it too 'gamey' in the sense that a hidden blade through the gullet should kill a person regardless of their arbitrary level being higher than yours.
+ Customisation is vastly improved with a myriad of armor options available with different stat boosts and appearances - along with the option to add colour schemes to your customised armour sets. Finally, you also have the abilty to wear full outfits from prior games, or newer outfits you just unlock as you progress throughout the story.
+ I really enjoyed the parkour improvements, I think the inclusion of designated "up", "down" controls removed the often treacherous scenarios available in previous games, when trying to  get down from somewhere high up. The new animations are also a winner, helping sell the fluidity of an assassin's movements.
+ Interiors add a fair bit of choice to the gameplay loop in my humble opinion as they offer up new opportunities when free running around the city/escaping from enemies etc.
CONS:
- The lack of French accents can be a bit of an immersion breaker, but I suppose could be explained away in-universe as being the product of the animus's abilty to translate languages to suit the user.
- Pop-in is much reduced over its initial state at launch, but is still fairly noticeable.
Disclaimer: I play all AC game with an Xbox One controller so any complaints relating to controls in other reviews definitely don't apply to using a game pad - it's good as always.

It goes a little like that. It's a dice game. So if you can't understand the mechanics behind it then please don't play this.

So, I recommended this game way back in November of 2014, and with several major updates completed I decided it might be a good time for me to come back in look over the game again.
Gotta say, I love the game even more now. The new features make the game much more interesting, and now that the Novakids are in, oh boy, I am a happy ♥♥♥♥ing camper. The addition of teleporters and bookmarking planets makes it so you can essentially revisit old planets to grind or gather materials you missed earlier on. It also allows you to essentially build a permanent home on any planet you like, as you can just find a teleporter core, gather some pixels and boom, instant way to teleport back to home sweet home wherever you are in the universe.
The option of 7 playable races, with a hinted 8th possibly on the way, makes the game not only unique amongst its closest competitors, but also rich in lore, as all of the races have their own naming conventions, cultures, and histories. Take for example, the Apex. Inspired by a bizarre mix of "Planet of the Apes" and the 1949 George Orwell novel "1984", the Apex are a race of sentient apes who live in an oppressive culture of constant monitoring and suspicion, where the face of their great leader, "Big Ape", is plastered everywhere they look. They are also brilliant technical minds, and possess unrivaled intelligence.
There are also the Novakids I mentioned earlier, mysterious beings that resemble humanoid stars with a old western style culture, the Novakids are beings made of pure nuclear energy, powered by the fission reactions occuring within their bodies that are contained by the brands in their faces. They possess short attention spans, and as a result, any technological advances made are typically lost within a few decades. They are also a bit pretentious, and completely oblivious to social customs, as there is a recorded incident of a Novakid asking an Avian diplomat if his chosen god was real.
The lore isn't the only selling point though. The gameplay is utterly superb. It does share similarities with Terraria, but with a never ending galaxy filled with procedurally generated worlds to explore gives this game a massive edge over Terraria. Couple that with the fact that each world is completely unique and filled with cool monsters, awesome dungeons, and interesting items to kill, raid, and loot, respectively, and Terraria doesn't stand a chance.
Also, I have to take a minute and mention the soundtrack. OH GOD THE SOUNDTRACK. Its perfect for this game. It has a beautiful ambient tone with just the right amount of sci-fi elements to fit the games brilliant premise. This is one of the VERY few games I play where I actually keep the music volume UP. And trust me, I'm a musical snob, that is no small praise.
And if all this weren't enough, here's some really good news. The devs on this game ARE ACTIVE. Admittedly, they could handle criticism a bit, well, better, but they actively work on the game. New things are added relatively frequently, and big updates are always BIG. The game always has new stuff to do, and the devs address bugs and gameplay issues fairly quickly.
To sum it up, I've had this game for well over a year, and it is still absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing incredible. The gameplay is fantastic, the lore is brilliant, the premise is fun, and everything works absolutely beautifully together, and the game isn't even DONE YET. Most would take that as a bad sign, but in Starbound's case, it is most definitely a good one. I love this game. I love everything about this game. I'll still be playing this game 5 years from now. It is THAT GOOD.
Pros:
-Awesome gameplay, think Terraria with awesome sci-fi elements.
-Soundtrack is brilliant.
-Cool lore. Interesting races.
-Planets are incredibly varied and fun to explore.
-Runs very, VERY well, even on my old piece of crap 2010 iMac.
-Active Dev Team.
Cons:
-Gameplay can get a bit repetitive.
-Grinding for pixels (in-game currency) and materials is annoying, but never takes too long.
-Needs some slight balancing done. (Seriously, the Novakids start with guns. What the hell!?)
Overall, game is utterly fantastic. It is everything I could reasonably ask it to be and just a little bit more.

Blood bowl is the Nascar of football leagues, where the fast majority of fans come to see wrecks rather than good sportsmanship and stratigic play. Is your opponent scoring touch downs left and right? Kill them. Are they trash talking you? Kill them. Are you winning? Kill them. Are you being killed? Kill yourself?.... In this game the only thing that comes easy is brutally losing. It's about making the best out of the worst situations by being ready. You can see that turd slowly migrating over to that fan. Its quite a distance away, but you're certain that sneaky little crap nugget is inching towards it behind your back. So, when it isn't looking, you get yourself a jumbo tarp and pin it to every surface in your room. Suddenly, when it hits the fan, you're ready, and not everything goes as badly as once thought.
That all being said, this game is utterly rage enducing. You could have everything perfectly planned out, where your opponent has 1/1000 odds to score that touchdown. Suddenly, their star halfback dodges 4 players, dives into a crowd of players, grabs the ball, does a front flip over your towering ogre, hurls a hail mary, which a wide receiver catches in heavy traffic. They then proceed to dodge 2 more tackles, and score a touchdown.
Another instance. You kick off the ball, and the fans rush onto the pitch, brutally violating every orifice of your players bodies. While downed, the opponent gets an easy touch down setup, and proceeds to kill half your team in three turns.  with no nope of recovery, you lose everyone that you cared about, even your wife and child.
Yet another instance. Your star player with 35/36 odds of evading a tackle gets pimp slapped and breaks his neck, instantly dying. Your star players best friend rushes over to cradle his dying comrade, but trips on his own shoelaces, dying tragically by impaling himself with his own horns in a somersault. The apothecary rushes onto the field to try and save them, but ends up only able to get one into a wheel chair.
In some cases, you seemingly have a majestic dice rolling god on your side. Giving you the power to smite anything that even looks at your team with spite. The game does what it wants. You can either hate it or love it.
The game is great fun, and thanks to the ability to customize your players with a plethora of abilities, mutations, and stat upgrades, makes it feel like its truly your team.
Its american football, or rugby for the most part.... with legal murder tacked on! Just try to bare with the game and it'll grow on you like a sick and twisted cluster of tentacles.
