Well I picked this game up as part of a bundle, and truly did not expect to have as much fun with it as I have. I understand it is technically still being added to, although it is no longer in beta, but it feels far more complete to me than many other Early Access/Early games in the same genre that I have played. As the game stands now, it has furnished me with many hours of entertainment and I have still not maxed out all of the tech trees or fully explored the world I generated. In general, my rule for buying games that are not yet finished, is this: If, hypothetically, development on this game stopped tomorrow, would I still enjoy playing it? And I feel that with Darkout, the answer is probably yes.
If you are familiar with 2d sandbox-style sidescrollers like Terraria and Edge of Space, you will feel at home here. However, what Darkout does differently is adds light as a game mechanic, since the world you are building on is never fully illuminated, and enemies both spawn and gain health in darkness. There are several beautiful glowing plants that spawn and will keep you from dying before you set up your homebase, but you'll very quickly find that creating light sources will become your primary occupation. Once you've progressed further down the tech tree, your options for creating light sources become more elaborate, and you can create your own wonderland of lights just for the heck of it, if you like. I should probably also mention that this game does not have very many RPG elements, which is a big plus in my book. One of my gripes with other sandbox games is that they relied too much on random drops or big boss fights to get to the next level of crafting.
There is a storyline in the game, but finishing these quests is optional and shouldn't interfere with the rest of the game. As far as I know, you can completely ignore it if you wish, and still manage to find every ore, tool, machine, etc. while you build to your heart's content.
It is true that some of the building systems in the game are a little bit unintuitive, and if that's something that tends to get on your nerves, you will probably be unsatisfied, as I did find myself having to look a few things up here and there. However, having grown up with older games in which this was much more common, it's never particularly bothered me. The graphics in the game are quite lovely and allow for some really impressive building options. I suppose one of my gripes is about the music, which resembles the sort of track you'd find in a space-themed action movie these days. I guess it fits, but I get a little bit annoyed after a while, since it is tense, and I feel like the pace of the game is slower and a bit more peaceful.
Tl;dr version:
PROS
- Looks great
- Huge tech tree, lots of crafting options
- More based on crafting than roleplaying
- Multiple options for gathering ores
- Playing with light and colors is fun!
CONS
- Crafting is sometimes unintuitive
- Music gets annoying at times
- A few other small gripes which don't break the game: (Trees don't currently respawn, Game occasionally gets interrupted by autosave)

First things first, this is a beautiful game. It's set on a world of perpetual night, and it manages to make it look amazing with the different zones all looking spectacular.
The combat is pretty frantic, especially when you get into the game and start coming across the different enemy types, all of which have their own little set of abilites and attacks to deal with instead of the far too common 'just give it more HP and make it red' style of enemy progress. It can get a little bit too hectic towards endgame though, with enemy spawns becoming extremely rapid. By that point you can just ignore them though.
Building is fun and fairly satisfying, watching your wooden hovel evolve into a high tech fortress is never going to stop being enjoyable and the tech progression is both big and fairly straightforward too. There's a fair few different 'this looks like a wall from Star Trek' type backgrounds and walls you can build with, but they are all kinda the same so that's a downside for the people who have to build that perfect unique base. You do need to wait for different items to be researched once you have the components, and there are build times too, which some people find annoying. I never had a problem with them, I just queued a few things up and went and did some renovations.
The real problem with this game is that it is not better known. Hopefully there'll be a decent bit of word of mouth going on at some point because this really does deserve a much bigger audience.

Bought this game less than 2 weeks ago. Already put 53 hours into it, as of the writing of this review.
I am someone who grew up with Harvest Moon, but after getting into PC gaming and dropping my consoles during the early 2000s in favor of competitive shooters like Counter Strike and other first person shooters, I all but completely forgot about the series. Not too long ago I came across this game, and it was on my radar, but due to my desire for competitive games (nowadays, CSGO and Overwatch) I have passed on it until this winter sale.
I fell in love within the hour of purchase. It has basically all the same mechanics and paradigms of the Harvest Moon series... you start off with a farm overrun with wood, weeds and rocks. You have to incrementally clean it, and plant some crops. You eventually get a dog, upgrade your tools, buy a barn and coop to get animals, etc.
What this series does, though, is take this genre and push it to the extreme. More mechanics. More characters. More crops, products and items. In addition to adding combat and the mine, there is more to farm, more to collect, more contraptions to build (such as the beehive, keg, sprinklers, etc) and in general more to do than the old Harvest Moon games (I can't speak on behalf of any of them past HM: Save the Homeland from 2001). Additionally, there are good reasons to befriend the different characters, and with the museum, community center, and daily fetch quests, the collectathon feels worthwhile and engaging. Not to mention, replayability is actually possible in this game due to having different starting farms that cater to those that prefer fishing, mining, fighting, etc, and mods (MODS, IN THIS KIND OF GAME!?). All of this is compounded by the tighter and more accurate controls that being on PC provides, and being the only game I own that my laptop can run, it makes it quite a catch for those on the go that don't always have their hefty gaming rig on hand.
tl;dr: If you have ever played and enjoyed Harvest Moon, buy this ♥♥♥♥ing game. You won't regret it. Even if it isn't something you'd play in favor of your favorite shooter or MOBA or RPG, it's an absolute go-to for those that have off-time at work, on campus, or while traveling and only have a lowspec laptop or notebook on hand.

This game's story, atmosphere, style, and everything else is masterfully done. Except the RNG. I've been playing strategy games for years, both on screen and off, but I've never come across anything like it.
I get that they're trying to make the game feel like a desperate last stand, with the odds stacked against you, but at the end of the day it just comes off wrong. I love setting up neat little traps for my enemies to walk in to. I loathe it when my guys then miss every single shot and the enemies wipe out half my team to as a result. Do I think that I should wipe them out without paying for it at all (one-shot)? No, but nor do I think that the enemy should be allowed to do the same.
The RNG permeates through everything. Campaign progression, map generation, enemy unit composition. The worst thing is that the game doesn't even recognise some situations for their true difficulty. Some maps will say that they are easy and after an hour trying to work it out, I'm still sitting there believing the only win scenario is with 3 or more of my guys dead. Other maps say they are difficult and take me a teeny tiny number of turns to complete, without a single soldier wounded. What gives?
Oh yeah, RNG.
This isn't a game about strategy as it current plays, it's just about dice rolling. Steam-rolling a supposedly difficult mission feels great, but often feels cheap because you know you've just rolled lucky dice. Losing repeatedly on "easy" maps using when you've set up excellent firefights, hacked every turret and mech and sniped the most dangerous enemies, just because of dice rolls, is exhausting.
Edit: I should probably add that I am aware that some folks love the RNG style of this game, and that's okay. I don't meant to rail against it, its just that I prefer games where strategy is more a focus than luck. I don't feel that the RNG is biased against the player, its just frustrating that its part of every single interaction in the game.
UPDATE: So today I finished the game. I wanted to stick with it because as I've said there are many aspects of the game that are top notch. As for RNG, its actually pretty sad because later on in the game (after mid-game) the RNG aspect practically disappears. Your soldiers hit harder and much more accurately and the game then becomes focused on careful placement and meticulously weighing up which target is best to hit with which soldier each turn. You know, actual strategy stuff. Its about avoiding being overwhelmed, hunkering down in a choice position, and outpacing your enemies in gun fights. So for that, the game is forgiven.
I really, honestly, and deeply wished that they'd do away with the over focus on RNG in the early to mid game. Yes, soldiers still miss during the end-game but they have so many skills and buffs that it no longer means a total wipe. Plus, its rare for more than one to miss in a single turn.
I'm aware people have told me to choose an easier difficulty and while I'm not playing on the hardest difficulty, I'm easily outstripping the AI in game in terms of tactically sound decisions. Dumbing down the AI just because RNG screws me over at times isn't really a solution. It would just make the game more tedious.

There's no real learning curve either, you can't "do it wrong" there is no right or wrong way to do anything, if u want to fish for a whole in-game month then go ahead, if you want to explore the mines, gather ores, kill monsters or find rare items then go ahead, fancy some farming? go ahead. You don't have to worry about "getting it right" because you'll learn what you enjoy doing and do it some more, bored of fishing? fine, do something else.
I didn't even start building relationships with the other residents of stardew until the end of my first year because I spent so much time just exploring the mines and reshaping my farm. I didn't speak to a single soul as I was so engrossed in what stardew had to offer I never really felt the need to converse with the residents. Now after  almost half a year plugging away with a couple of characters, giving them gifts and chatting to people im now married to a character called Haley and she moved in! (i'd also like to point out that the game allows same sex marriage which is a beautiful idea too)
I feel like I havn't even scratched the surface as I havn't unlocked the new mining area or even finished half the quests I have in my list, i'm still plodding along at my own pace enjoying my farming, enjoying rebuilding the community centre, just enjoying the whole damn thing and that's the most important thing, enjoyment is key and that's exactly what i've got from this game, sheer enjoyment.
Is it a thumbs up from me? Absolutely, 10/10 and theyre also introducing multiplayer early this year that will just add a whole new dimension to the game, wanna farm with friends? go ahead, wanna do it alone? go ahead, that's stardew, do what u like when u like.

Cons:
1) Diplomacy = AI's proposals are ridiculous, and it almost never agrees to yours:
E.g,Neutral AI gives 10 gold + their map, and for that generous proposal I should start war against their enemy. If I refuse, AI gots massive relationship hit with me. Funny? Not at all.
Another example, AI asks to open borders, but refuses not to settle colonies near you, and then gets mad when you close your borders.
2) Ship Design = cool at first sight; but much worse when you get into it, resulting in "more guns = win".
Almost all modules are horribly worse compared to additional weapons.
3) Warfare = waiting game if you want to conquer:
just wait for midgame massive ships...
and wait again for AI to get into another war and then declare on it...
and then wait again to build your troop-ships who will sieze planets...
and then wait again and again to gather all them in one sector, so that you can destroy any enemy fleet...
and after that wait again to build your troop-ships who will sieze planets (they are disposable)...
and after that wait again some more time to gather all in one sector, so that troop-ships won't be destroyed...
and even after this and that wait some more time again...
4) Economy = two ways: rush to +5 population // +2 additional gold per population; OR conquer (not colonize!) more planets.
Otherwise, buildings, including defensive ones, will eat all your surplus.
5) Assistant voices = female voices are nice, but other squeezy 'alien' voices are a way to harsh for my ears.
6) Technology = you need to frequently choose one of two/three bonuses; although, you can still trade the other bonus with an AI, but it is dumb and dully stubborn in its considerations.
7) Polution = the more you have workers and the better is your planet, the more polution you produce.
This means that a dump with -150 polution is the only reasonable choice in technology tree.
8) Warfare 2 = loosing a massive battle is a disaster, especially for AI. They never have even a ghostly chance to get back on their feet, so they are eventually conquered.
9) Espionage = you can easily play without any of them.
Pros:
1) Graphics = A+ for 4x space game.
2) General gameplay = despite all the cons, this is still a good game to play for several days (it becomes too bo-o-oring early).

My take on Master of Orion... the new one.
As a space-based 4X, it's pretty cool.
As a Master of Orion... it falls short in a number of places.
Let's compare it first to Master of Orion 2.  The... after much debate... champion of MoO.  The one that everyone, for generations, continued to look back at as the "Legendary" game when it came to space 4X.
Master of Orion 2 not only made sense in what it did, but it had a tactical combat system that was unparralelled at the time, and often attempted, but never matched to.  When Master of Orion 3 came out, one of the major complaints was that the tactical combat was no longer available.
This tactical combat system is part of what made MoO and MoO2 so legendary, and what broke the series when MoO3 came out and disappointed people, (I know... I was there when it came out.  Installed it and tried it and went back to MoO2.)
The fact that the new MoO has decided to leave all tactical combat to real time strategy combat makes it no different than... say... Sins of a Solar Empire.  It has, instead of embracing Master of Orion's winning module, embraced today's game expectations.  Instead, the level of tactical combat that is available has put your combat control just a step above Endless Space, (I play a lot of these kinds of games,) but at about the level of Sword of the Stars.  Making it... just another space 4X game.
In MoO2, your planets grew at a believable rate.  To have adequite food meant that nobody was starving.  The planet thrived, and about every 5 turns you'd get another population.  To have less than adequite food, the growth would be lowered, and with enough negative, would become starvation.  In new MoO, it takes after games like Civilization, Endless Space, and such, where now the excess food suddenly means more people reproduce.  Does gluttany = sex?  It does not.  This makes sense, perhaps, in a single city setting, where on the level of food means that just enough people are adequitely fed, but still not everyone.  Yet, planetary?  This food format does not makes sense.  Yes, it is a game, and this is a game mechanic, but this is a space (sci-fi) game, and much of it should be based off of science.
In MoO2, (and even in games like Endless Space,) the more your ships fight, the more experience they gain, and they gain bonuses to attack and defense.  You can also recruit leaders for your planets and your ships.  NewMoO?  Not so much.  In fact, there is no such thing as ship experience, uniquely upgrading single ships, or, in fact, leaders.
In MoO2, and this is sort of a tactical combat thing, you could disable your enemy ships.  Take out their engines, their systems... and then raid them with your crew and capture the ships.  This happens all the time in sci-fi movies, and is probably one of my favorite features from MoO2 that just about every other game is missing out on... including every other Master of Orion.
I don't think I need to go on as to how NewMoO is not living up to the ideal of Master of Orion.
All that being said, it is a good game.  It's worth checking out.  It has upsides and downsides in comparison to the other 4Xs of todays generation.  I have played this, Endless Space, Sword of the Stars, Sins of a Solar Empire, and many other space 4X games.  Today's space 4Xs all feel very similar.  This and Endless Space are both currently at the top of my list for MoO2 replacements.
Oh, but I don't have to replace it anymore.  It's now playable through Steam!  So I no longer need any of them... do I?
Ah, but alas, MoO2's difficulty is at the high end of the bell curve.  So you'd all better be wary of it, if you intend to try it for the first time.  When I was a young teen, I would play it non-stop for weeks.  My own personal empire dominating the galaxy, or falling before those damn Psilons taking over the council.

Starbound is really fun but it has some serious flaws. My advice is that you play this game with friends and install some mods. You can play alone if you really want to but co-op is where this game truly shines. This game was built from the ground up to support modding and there's some amazing stuff on the workshop. You'd be silly to not take advantage of it. The multiplayer in combination with the huge modding scene is this game's saving grace.
Because Starbound is a sandbox game, by its very nature it's going to be a bit grindy. If spending lots of time collecting resources isn't your cup of tea then this game probably isn't for you. You'll be spending a lot of your time upgrading your gear and running around different planets scanning objects for clues with your matter manipulator.
The game does have a story but it's nothing to write home about. It's just your typical 'hero defeats the ultimate evil and saves the universe' cliche. The characters you meet along the way are all pretty bland for the most part. You'll find much more interesting lore through codices than you ever will from the story.
Don't jump in expecting intense, skill-based gameplay either. You'll encounter plenty of monsters and enemy NPCs throughout the game, but they all behave in predictable ways and almost always tend to be pushovers. The bosses are an absolute joke for anyone with even a modicum of competence at platformers.
Despite these downsides, Starbound is still an enjoyable game. The real enjoyment comes from exploration and building. The art style, soundtrack and varied environments will have you drowning in atmosphere and it's amazing. Discovering brand new biomes, dungeons, monsters and even races is very exciting and leaves you wanting more. NPCs in villages offer side quests with rewards and sometimes they have some pretty funny dialogue.
There are so many blocks and objects in the game that it's practically a builder's paradise. People have built some absolutely stunning structures, just go look at the BOTW (Build of the Week) entries on the Starbound subreddit. Big projects can be a massive time sink but it feels really rewarding to finally finish that base, farm or space station you were working on. The amount of freedom you have when it comes to building and colonizing planets is a huge plus for this game.
Another great thing about this game is how customizable it is. I already mentioned how good the modding scene is but it even goes beyond that. There's commands you can use to create entirely new weapons and gear that are completely vanilla friendly (no mods required). The character creator is very indepth for a 2D game like this, allowing you choose your species, gender, posture, colors, etc. There's even cosmetic armor slots that let you wear stuff over your regular armor so you can make your character look exactly how you want them to. Roleplayers really seem to like this game for these reasons.
Overall, I'd say Starbound is worth getting. There's plenty of mods that make the game more challenging on the survival/combat front if that's what you're looking for. This game is really chill and it's great if you've had a long day and just want to kick back and relax.

Imagine something for me, if you will. Imagine a game series based around pure, proper roleplaying. Open-ended dialogue with plenty of skills and attributes to design your own build that is unique to your specific playstyle. In later entries, a neat character customization system to allow you to be young, old, male, female, whatever you want to be, whoever you want to be. And all of this is wrapped up in a unique world with interesting characters, lore, and stories that can be bent and changed by the player's actions.
Now imagine it's 2015. Fallout 4, the latest entry in this series, comes out and screws all of this up. Roleplaying? Interesting characters? Engaging plot? Replaced with bland and stale, pre-determined backstories for the main character, voiced protagonists, roundabout and unengaging dialogue, and a story so poorly written and so full of holes it feels like I'm playing a fanfiction interpretation of the franchise. And the cherry on top is the blatant disregard and lack of care for existing lore and stories, thrown to the wayside for Bethesda's abysmal writing team to substitute with whatever they want. All this game wants you to do is "Shoot, Loot, n' Scoot." You go to a place. You kill some people. You steal their♥♥♥♥♥♥ You leave, and you do this again and again for a hundred hours.
This game design philosophy has infected every aspect of this series. The main plot is fetch quests and kill quests without so much as an attempt to mask that fact. All the side quests are God-awful "radiant quests" that are designed to never end so that you can have "infinite" bland and substance-less quests for playthroughs in a series where the whole point of each game is to reach the end and see the result of your actions. There are no Perks anymore, just skill-trees like Skyrim that CALL themselves Perks, which are also boring and uninspired. Almost all of them are just stand-ins for Skills that have been removed, increasing weapon damage, increasing healing item effectiveness, increasing defense... All it does is bog down the leveling system and make it feel boring. There's no flair, no style, and every single build ends up the exact same due to the merging of Perks and Skills.
Now, you'd think the plot I mentioned before may at least make up for this. Ha, no. No, not at all. The plot is, without any spoilers, an awful reversed-role rehashing of Fallout 3. Your child is missing, and you leave your Vault to go find them in the Wasteland. But instead of having compelling characters or intrigue to push you forward, you get cardboard cutout cliches and poorly-written schmucks that won't hold your attention at all, and the plot itself is just a string of awful contrivances that drag you along through the game. And to top THIS mess off, you don't even get any ending slides. There are zero moral choices in the game (asides from two at the beginning, robbing a caravan lady and helping some drug dealers) and no choices to make at all that effect the ending. Why?
The end slides are gone! No, instead you get the same cutscene for every single ending, asides from 5 extra seconds of footage if you choose the Institute. That's right, the iconic ending slides that made the story feel complete have been replaced with a boring, 2-3 minute cinematic that has no closure and does nothing but leave you frustrated and unsatisfied. That's just the main game. Far Harbor has the exact same problems, and has the extra issues of ripping off not only the main game (plot hook is a missing child that you have to go on an adventure to find, which results in a larger issue that you involve yourself in), outright stealing a quest from a popular New Vegas mod, AND ALSO ripping off Point Lookout with the setting and atmosphere. There isn't a creative bone left in the bodies of anyone at Bethesda game studios, and it very, very much shows with Fallout 4 and all of its DLC. Seriously, Workshops? That's worth $15? You know what else costs $15? Each DLC for New Vegas, which is leagues better and has the bonus of the good writing and engaging stories and characters given to us by Obsidian.
So, Fallout 4 is a spit in the face to all Fallout fans, is a disgustingly dumbed-down "RPG" (an insult to all RPGs) and is more shallow than any game I have ever played, with all the content being bland and uninteresting, but with enough of it to fill almost 200 hours spent desperately searching for anything enjoyable. Now with the Creation Club fiasco going on, it's the final nail in the coffin for the Bethesda of old. We'll never get another Morrowind. We'll never get another Fallout game like New Vegas. All we have now are shallow, poorly-written shooters with an XP bar thrown in to be an "RPG" that will be filled to the brim with microtransactions acting as glorified paid mods. It's time to bury Fallout as we know it, because it's dead, and The Elder Scrolls isn't too far behind.

If you like strategy and wargaming, you'll like this game.  But be warned:  it's hard, unforgiving, and frustrating as hell.
A lot of people buy this game without having a background in wargaming type games, and they start thinking the RNG is broken.  I can understand that, because it can be frustrating to play well then get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked down the field because of bad dice rolls.  But that's how wargames are - you're making strategy based on the odds of the rolls.
If you can get that in your head, then you can start to learn the strategies - like doubling up on blocks to improve your odds.  Making use of the special skills of the various players.  Changing tactics against teams based on if they pass, brawl, etc.
It took me a good 12 hours to get the hang of it, and I've been playing wargames a long time.  I'm finally starting to win against the AI.  I played one online game, and they other player mopped the pitch with me, so I need a lot more practice.
But if you have the patience to develop the skills, you'll find this a lot of fun (even though it's very frustrating).  I also recommend looking for various online strategy guides that will help you with concepts / tactics like "The Cage", etc.  It reduces the learning curve and makes the game enjoyable sooner.

After playing Terraria pretty much to death, Darkout seemed to catch my eye the most. I guess I wanted to switch to a more sci-fi setting after dealing with bows and arrows for so long. I like the crafting progression, e.g. you don't use the useless torch the entire game like in some cases but move up to better lights. Also the user interface improves usability a lot in some cases. I love the AUTO feature, where you just have all the tools (axe, shovel, etc.) in your inventory and then the game automatically selects the correct one. I never realized how much of a useless chore it is to change between different tools manually. Also there are other nifty features, like opening two containers and moving stuff between them without actually having to pick it up yourself, etc. I also like that you can extract more valuable resources (copper, iron, etc.) from sand and stone (albeit not very efficiently, which is good for balancing reasons). Instead for having chestfuls of useless dirt and stone (I don't like to throw stuff away), you can simply chuck it all into the machinery and convert some of it to better materials. The game is not perfect, but I am having a lot of fun playing it. The most important thing is that they are still improving it. And the essential thing is that it's not alpha or beta or whatever that smells like early access. The game is done and playable as it is, so you don't have to wait forever for them to develop it and wipe your world in the process. I'm going to stop talking now and go play the game some more. Cheers.

Botanicula is a point-and-click adventure but also a game of exploration. It doesn't take you by the hand, you have to experiment to find out what you are supposed to be doing. Everything moves, makes sounds, reacts in some way and you have to find the pattern that makes it all come together. Almost every location has it's own puzzle, 123 in total (you get in-game cards for completing them). It is a difficult game, sometimes a silly game, always an immensly satisfying game. The music and sound as well as the art style is simply amazing.
My only criticism is that I needed only 4 hours to complete it. I wanted more!
I recommend this game for everyone who loves point-and-click adventures and wants to experience a somewhat different take on the genre. And for everyone who loved this game I strongly recommend the other adventures from Amanita Design: Machinarium and Samorost 1-3. They are all fantastic.

I have held off on doing a review of this title to see how it would evolve. As a long time fan of the original MOO 1&2 and, with sufficient community patches/modifications even MOO 3(to a point), I find that this latest installment of the "franchise" sits squarely as MOO 1.5.
Overall colony management et al. is decent. Graphics are above average. Core races are present (though lacking relative to MOO 2 and MOO 3 in quantity and variation/backstory). Music and sound effects are typical of a strategy title. The UI is viable with most areas being reasonably intuitive for a 4x design.
I find the lack of backstory to be a great detriment to this iteration of MOO. Other titles, even MOO 3, had a greater atmosphere in terms of racial distinctiveness--there was a feel of something more vs. a generic 4x that's founded on an excellent series.
Though I have never been a hard set fan of leaders, certainly their absense from this product is clearly a detriment--as previous titles in the series and many modern competitors (Stellaris) have such implemented.
Space battles are a very curious beast. They lack the hands on control and tactics of MOO 1 & 2, but are more fluid than the system utilised in MOO 3. The bias towards long ranged weaponry, ala MOO 3, remains and the lack of tight hands on tactical control (to the degree of MOO 2) has me often gearing fleets for autoresolution rather than for any sort of finesse (which makes me think of combat in Spaceward Ho!).
Overall, however, development has continued. Additional content has been added and many bugs have been fixed. Though this title is far from complete/polished, continued improvements are clearly evident. This, with the nostalgia of the MOO universe/franchise, makes me optimistic as to the true "end product" that will be generated.
I recommend this title to anyone who is a fan of the MOO franchise--there is enough here, and the promise of more, to afford fans of the MOO series and enjoyable experience.
For others who are not veterans of the franchise I would advise waiting to see if the new DLC content is enough to flush out the core options to make this, functionally, more on par with Stellaris (which is curently a more complete 4x experience without MOO nostalgia).

I've just beaten this game and might beat it to 100% completion later. This game is damn good. Fun gameplay, nicely stylized graphics and beautiful map design. Not to menion an amazing soundtrack that makes the game quite atmospheric.
Let me start with the art. The art is very nicely stylized and adds to the feel of the game. Due to the style it feels like you are truly in an aerial land of magical properties. The enemy design varies rather nicely and are usually introduced nicely in an area that fits them.  There is however one problem with the art design, and that is that it can be quite unclear as to where you can or can not stand.
The Soundtrack too was amazing. During the entire game I felt like I was in a true mystic place. Calm, soothing but yet gives you an unexpecting feeling of wanting to save this land. And even while it is soothing, during combat it is still rather fitting, which is weird as the combat is rather fast-paced at times, yet the slow and soothing music fits it just perfectly.
The story is relatively simple. It's nothing to brag about but is rather good. The narrator told the story very well and this again added to the whole feel of the game.
Now to gameplay, the most important factor of the game. The Gameplay is fun and smooth, with a 2-weapon combat system, dodging, special skills and blocking. While blocking it also locks on targets so you can aim quite nicely, although sometimes it is better to just aim for yourself. There are many weapons with a nice variety for both close and ranged combat, although there are some balancing issues as some weapons are clearly better than others and some others will be left in the dust for the entire game. Every enemy you have to really attack in a different manner. The faster ones with low health you have to aim and shoot and the bigger, slower enemies are sometimes better to stun and hit. The issue, however, is that every enemy can be killed with ranged combat, but if you even try to get close to some you are going to find out that melee is quite a bit worse than ranged almost all the time.
Difficulty of the game is scaled quite nicely. The earlier areas are rather easy and it gets harder over time, as to where the last area was sometimes just a massive pain in the backdoor. Although, on a regular playthrough, it's not like you are going to have a super hard time. I have yet to try New Game+, so perhaps that boosts up the challenge quite a bit.
Do I recommend this game? Yes. Very much so. Fun gameplay, nice graphics and amazing sound design makes this game a must own.

I kept hoping, but feared I'd never see the day, where another 4x space sim would ever top the original Master Of Orion (MOO).  That day is finally here!  And wouldn't you know it, it's a reboot of the original!!!  If you love the original Master Of Orion, and have been waiting for years like me for a game that is just as great, and better, than the original, that wait is over!
Master Of Orion (reboot) is an amazing game in every aspect!  Graphics, Sound and Presentation are the cream of the crop and AAA!  But where this successor really shines is in the Gameplay!  The original game is unrivaled and the reboot doesn't disappoint.  It fixes the two small niggles that stunted the first game, slow start of each game, and some late game micromanagement.  The original Master Of Orion was the first of its kind (4x space sim) and of course there would be things to improve on.  After playing the original MOO, the only improvements I wished for was an up in graphics (of course) and to fix the two aforementioned items.  Well the reboot fixes just that!  The reboot flows amazingly from start to finish with no lag/grind time, and the management (sans micro) is so streamline that there is no problem controlling your empire as it grows.  Every aspect of the game fits neatly with every other aspect making the game perfectly seamless!  And with every turn showing everything you need to manage at the time you need to manage it at the bottom right hand corner of the screen every turn, you don't even have to go into any menus manually if you don't want to!  THIS IS GAME CHANGING!  This makes the game accessible to ANYONE AND EVERY TYPE OF PLAYER OUT THERE!!!  This is so major that if every other 4x space sim adopted this, every game could be this AMAZING!  And for those who still want to have more hands on and dig deep into management systems, IT'S ALL STILL THERE!  This game is extensive enough for veterans while also being simple enough for newbie's!  How many games get this right?  It's EXTREMELY RARE!  This kind of rarity should be, and is, appreciated!
So you may be wondering, many fans claim that the sequel, the original Master Of Orion 2 (MOO 2), is actually the best game in the series.  I never understood that, or comprehended why.  Yes, it expanded on the original Master Of Orion, and it looked like the original Master Of Orion, but it didn't feel like Master Of Orion.  This is when the series started going more down the "micromanagement rabbit hole" that most 4x space sims build themselves on today.  MOO 2 lost the "pick up and play" aspect that made the original Master Of Orion so great, and at its heart, what it was.  MOO 2 was prettier (and that's all that needed to be updated) but its predecessor was about giving players a choice of being as simple, or as complex as desired.  With MOO 2's unnecessary large amount of micromanaging, it pushed all simplicity aside.  It became a numbers game and sacrificed its simple fun making it feel more like a job rather than a game.  One only has to look at the horrible Master Of Orion 3 to see how they built upon micromanaging at its worst.  This is why the series lay dormant for so many years.
The original Master Of Orion spoiled me to the point that I expected better of any game that tried to do what it did.  I waited so many years for a true successor, and it brings a tear to my eye to finally have that.  The new Master of Orion is perfect in almost every way, but like its predecessor, it too has one minor niggle; not game breaking in anyway.  The game introduces a cinematic camera view during battles, that is great in concept, but doesn't work as well in practice, or as well as I'd like.  The camera doesn't show the best of the action most of the time and often you miss the best parts of a fight.  If they fix this (and this is the only thing they need to fix about the game in a patch or even a sequel) then this series will stay in the top spot of 4x space sim perfection!
Go buy this!  We need to show developers that we want more games like this.  Though I got it on sale, I believe it's well worth full price!

Updated 11/24/16 - Steam does it again!  They created an Award celebration where we get to nominate games we think are the best of the best!  I'm giving Master Of Orion what I think is Steam's most prestigious award, since they don't have a "Best of the Year" category, I'm giving it the “Just 5 More Minutes” Award!  You can't stop playing!
It's a shame to not see Master of Orion on any "best of" 2016 award lists this year.  This by far is now the best 4x Space Sim you can play!  I hope you decide to pick it up, sale or no, because it's an experience you simply can't miss!  This is my pick for game of the year 2016!
So now that Master Of Orion has rebooted so successfully, there is a HUGE opportunity to grow this franchise right, avoiding the pitfalls of the past.  So what do I want to see as an evolution to Master Of Orion, either as an extension to the existing game, or its possible sequel?  I would love to see random story missions/events.  The kind you find in the side stories of games like Elder Scrolls and Mass Effect.  And make many of them!  So many that you won't be able see all of them in a single play through.  This way, multiple play through's will be unique, and things you do will make you feel more connected to the experience like no other 4x Space Sim before!  Sure there have been other games that have made linear story lines in 4x Space Sims, like Galactic Civilizations, and although they can be quite good, they are still too constraint, and people end up skipping them and just jumping into what makes these games so desirable in the first place, the random sandbox experience.  But if someone could program story elements, that don't force you into a predetermined end, or handful of endings, that would be amazing!   And since this is Steam, why not workshop it!  Make a "Choose Your Own Adventure" interface and make it easy enough that people can come up with their own stories on the fly to share, and you could continually have more and more events all the time!  The possibilities are endless!
So yeah, Master Of Orion, Game of the Year 2016, and best 4x Space Sim of all time!

So, I recommended this game way back in November of 2014, and with several major updates completed I decided it might be a good time for me to come back in look over the game again.
Gotta say, I love the game even more now. The new features make the game much more interesting, and now that the Novakids are in, oh boy, I am a happy ♥♥♥♥ing camper. The addition of teleporters and bookmarking planets makes it so you can essentially revisit old planets to grind or gather materials you missed earlier on. It also allows you to essentially build a permanent home on any planet you like, as you can just find a teleporter core, gather some pixels and boom, instant way to teleport back to home sweet home wherever you are in the universe.
The option of 7 playable races, with a hinted 8th possibly on the way, makes the game not only unique amongst its closest competitors, but also rich in lore, as all of the races have their own naming conventions, cultures, and histories. Take for example, the Apex. Inspired by a bizarre mix of "Planet of the Apes" and the 1949 George Orwell novel "1984", the Apex are a race of sentient apes who live in an oppressive culture of constant monitoring and suspicion, where the face of their great leader, "Big Ape", is plastered everywhere they look. They are also brilliant technical minds, and possess unrivaled intelligence.
There are also the Novakids I mentioned earlier, mysterious beings that resemble humanoid stars with a old western style culture, the Novakids are beings made of pure nuclear energy, powered by the fission reactions occuring within their bodies that are contained by the brands in their faces. They possess short attention spans, and as a result, any technological advances made are typically lost within a few decades. They are also a bit pretentious, and completely oblivious to social customs, as there is a recorded incident of a Novakid asking an Avian diplomat if his chosen god was real.
The lore isn't the only selling point though. The gameplay is utterly superb. It does share similarities with Terraria, but with a never ending galaxy filled with procedurally generated worlds to explore gives this game a massive edge over Terraria. Couple that with the fact that each world is completely unique and filled with cool monsters, awesome dungeons, and interesting items to kill, raid, and loot, respectively, and Terraria doesn't stand a chance.
Also, I have to take a minute and mention the soundtrack. OH GOD THE SOUNDTRACK. Its perfect for this game. It has a beautiful ambient tone with just the right amount of sci-fi elements to fit the games brilliant premise. This is one of the VERY few games I play where I actually keep the music volume UP. And trust me, I'm a musical snob, that is no small praise.
And if all this weren't enough, here's some really good news. The devs on this game ARE ACTIVE. Admittedly, they could handle criticism a bit, well, better, but they actively work on the game. New things are added relatively frequently, and big updates are always BIG. The game always has new stuff to do, and the devs address bugs and gameplay issues fairly quickly.
To sum it up, I've had this game for well over a year, and it is still absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing incredible. The gameplay is fantastic, the lore is brilliant, the premise is fun, and everything works absolutely beautifully together, and the game isn't even DONE YET. Most would take that as a bad sign, but in Starbound's case, it is most definitely a good one. I love this game. I love everything about this game. I'll still be playing this game 5 years from now. It is THAT GOOD.
Pros:
-Awesome gameplay, think Terraria with awesome sci-fi elements.
-Soundtrack is brilliant.
-Cool lore. Interesting races.
-Planets are incredibly varied and fun to explore.
-Runs very, VERY well, even on my old piece of crap 2010 iMac.
-Active Dev Team.
Cons:
-Gameplay can get a bit repetitive.
-Grinding for pixels (in-game currency) and materials is annoying, but never takes too long.
-Needs some slight balancing done. (Seriously, the Novakids start with guns. What the hell!?)
Overall, game is utterly fantastic. It is everything I could reasonably ask it to be and just a little bit more.

There have been multiple times I wanted Arno to do an action and he does something different. For instance, I wanted to do a ledge assassination. So I directed my camera to the guy I wanted to ledge assassinate. But sadly, the game translated that in me wanting to assassinate some random ruffian on the ground. Or even better... I wanted to jump through an open window, but Arno decides to hop around from one side of the window to the other, taking me a good 10 seconds to get his backside inside.

Starbound is really fun but it has some serious flaws. My advice is that you play this game with friends and install some mods. You can play alone if you really want to but co-op is where this game truly shines. This game was built from the ground up to support modding and there's some amazing stuff on the workshop. You'd be silly to not take advantage of it. The multiplayer in combination with the huge modding scene is this game's saving grace.
Because Starbound is a sandbox game, by its very nature it's going to be a bit grindy. If spending lots of time collecting resources isn't your cup of tea then this game probably isn't for you. You'll be spending a lot of your time upgrading your gear and running around different planets scanning objects for clues with your matter manipulator.
The game does have a story but it's nothing to write home about. It's just your typical 'hero defeats the ultimate evil and saves the universe' cliche. The characters you meet along the way are all pretty bland for the most part. You'll find much more interesting lore through codices than you ever will from the story.
Don't jump in expecting intense, skill-based gameplay either. You'll encounter plenty of monsters and enemy NPCs throughout the game, but they all behave in predictable ways and almost always tend to be pushovers. The bosses are an absolute joke for anyone with even a modicum of competence at platformers.
Despite these downsides, Starbound is still an enjoyable game. The real enjoyment comes from exploration and building. The art style, soundtrack and varied environments will have you drowning in atmosphere and it's amazing. Discovering brand new biomes, dungeons, monsters and even races is very exciting and leaves you wanting more. NPCs in villages offer side quests with rewards and sometimes they have some pretty funny dialogue.
There are so many blocks and objects in the game that it's practically a builder's paradise. People have built some absolutely stunning structures, just go look at the BOTW (Build of the Week) entries on the Starbound subreddit. Big projects can be a massive time sink but it feels really rewarding to finally finish that base, farm or space station you were working on. The amount of freedom you have when it comes to building and colonizing planets is a huge plus for this game.
Another great thing about this game is how customizable it is. I already mentioned how good the modding scene is but it even goes beyond that. There's commands you can use to create entirely new weapons and gear that are completely vanilla friendly (no mods required). The character creator is very indepth for a 2D game like this, allowing you choose your species, gender, posture, colors, etc. There's even cosmetic armor slots that let you wear stuff over your regular armor so you can make your character look exactly how you want them to. Roleplayers really seem to like this game for these reasons.
Overall, I'd say Starbound is worth getting. There's plenty of mods that make the game more challenging on the survival/combat front if that's what you're looking for. This game is really chill and it's great if you've had a long day and just want to kick back and relax.

I got this game in a bundle not having heard anything about it. I decided to try it out since it seemed similar to Terraria which I quite enjoyed. I read up a bit ahead seeing people saying that it was just another "Terraria-clone" and even more saying that it could hold its own - I will join the ranks of people who think this is a great game that brings new things to the "Terraria"-idea.
There is no denying this game is very similar to Terraria, meaning a lot of what made that game fun is present in this game - advancing your knowledge through exploration, research and crafting . However, I definitely enjoy the building part a lot more in Darkout than I did in Terraria. In Terraria it only felt like a necessary evil to get further down the layers, whereas in this game the building is more intricate and detailed, giving more options and satisfaction as you discover new things.
Darkout also offers a story, which although I have not yet got far through seems really interesting and was something I missed in Terraria.
Everything isn't 100% intuitive and I struggle to figure out pretty much the same things I did when playing Terraria, how to interact with objects and how to make them interact with eachother, but it's never been anything that's annoyed me. The game is incredibly dark (hence the name I guess!) initially and I remember thinking that you need painfully many lights to see anything, but that's a hurdle quick overcome given some exploration and time.
Some have complained about buggyness which is something I have not encountered yet while playing.
Overall I really recommend this game if you had any fun with Terraria and/or similar explore+create adventure games. It offers just the same amount of "just a little bit more mining so that I can craft X" as the best of the genre.

At first when I purchased Botanicula, I wasn't too sure I would like it. Truth be told, I only bought it because the characters and art style looked super cute. I never really had any experience with point-and-click games - at least not in a long while - so this purchase was something of a risk for me. But, every risk has the possibility of becoming a sweetass reward, and, now that I've beaten the game, I can definitely consider my purchase of Botanicula to be just that.
As I've mentioned, the characters and art style are super cute, and they surely have enough charm to match its cuteness. I couldn't stop smiling and giggling throughout my 6 hour playthrough due to the oodles and oodles of OMGEVERYTHINGISSOCUTENESS. Like, if you wanna see what I'm talking about, watch this 27 second YouTube video I made of some singing frogs from the game:
So, yeah: The game's as cute as a bug, and considering I have, like, 87 mental disorders involving the symptom depression, that's pretty important to me. But, what's also important to me is for there to be some sort of meaning to the game. Like, why are these bugs just going around talking to singing frogs and solving puzzles (more on the puzzles in a moment)? Well, the game does a really good job of explaining its story in a way that provides empathy for the characters' plight without using words to do so. Like, the game doesn't use any words at all. Everything is expressed using imagery and emotional gibberish; it's adorable and heart-touching at the same time. By the end of the game, I was so determined to help the buggos, that I didn't mind failing at puzzles again and again and again - so long as I knew that eventually I'd perservere, and Mr. Twig and his buddies would eventually be happy again!
The puzzles themselves are, well, they're certainly satisfying to solve! Just about every time you solve a puzzle, the characters go all "YooHoo!" and it's THE CUTEST THING EVER OMG! I'm normally pretty terrible at puzzles (I blame those aforementioned mental disorders), so I eventually needed a guide to help me through the game. However, one thing I did notice was that it was also pretty difficult to identify where exactly puzzles were supposed to be. Like, not just what you were supposed to do in a puzzle, but what exactly was a puzzle? Where to start a puzzle? Sometimes it was tough to just get started, and I feel like this might be a problem for more people than just myself, especially near the end of the game. There's this awfully mazy-like area, and it practically forces you to use a guide for at least some of it. For me this wasn't a really big deal, since I didn't really buy this game for its puzzles anyway, but I could definitely see some people becoming upset by this.
So, there ya have it: my feelings about this game. I'm sure you're all very scared now by all of this, but you shouldn't be scared of purchasing this game, at least not if you like cute things and puzzles. Very, very, very nice game, and I'm looking forward to playing the other games done by Amanita Design.

If you are looking for a Terraria-like game, this may be for you. But be warned, it is much more difficult. Where Terraria has modes that cater to those who like building and adventure, Darkout does not. Darkout has two modes: Builder and Normal. In builder, you have unlimited resources and do not have to research anything to craft it. In Normal, you have to find and research for crafting. However, instead of creating a Hard or Hardcore mode, the developers screw over the casual audience by making you have to retrieve your gear on death. That's not all though, because instead of having monsters from coming from off-screen, it is made artifically difficult by having them spawn on top of you occasionally.
I know you are thinking "...you are whining because the game is too difficult!". That may be true, but the developer needs to realize that a large portion of the audience in games like Minecraft, Terraria, and Darkout ARE the causal player who wants a game with a bit of a challenge, but not too much. But let me say, it isn't a BAD game. It just needs a difficulty level somewhere between "Creative Sandbox" and "You fell 20 feet, and now you are dead. Go fetch your gear."

As much as I hate knocking gifts, I can't say I really enjoyed Serena, a short adventure game designed by several veterans of the adventure game industry and released free of charge. In Serena, you play a man idly exploring the cabin he and his wife shared in happier times, looking for her and trying to remember where she went. As you examine all the old souvenirs of happier times, the story unfolds and the sordid truth of the matter is revealed. Gameplay is limited to clicking on an area of the cabin to explore, then selecting objects in the environment to examine. It's a simple game, and I honestly love the idea of using interactive environments as a medium for telling a short story, but the execution here just failed critically on a few fronts.
Perhaps it was an intentional move, but I quickly resented the protagonist, finding him more whiny and irritating with each inane object he babbled on about. Examples include a salt shaker, a dried flower, and a piece of gum on a chair. His story did eventually pull me in, but I kept finding myself loathing the stereotypical bitter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ beta male he embodied. What was less intentional and much more harmful was the painfully phoned-in voice work for Serena; while the protagonist's voice acting wasn't half bad, Serena's voice actress sounded like she was just reading off cue cards she'd only just seen for the first time. This wouldn't be too killer an issue, but voice acting is how the entirety of the story is told.
The stranger issue I had with the game was how much the Kickstarter extras destroyed the atmosphere they were trying to create. Don't get me wrong; I love goofy extras in games. I just prefer when some effort is required to find them. Serena instead chooses to blast you with them right off the bat. Every aspect of the intended story is painfully sincere, and the environment they place you in is dark, decrepit, and tragic, but moments into the game you find a bookshelf full of novels about lesbian goat zombies and goofy retro video game references. Various Kickstarter donors were allowed to populate the bookshelf, and this is the outcome. At another point, you find an inexplicably non sequitor Lovecraftian comic book page in a dresser drawer. I have no idea what it's supposed to represent, but I assume it was another Kickstarter donor addition, since there's no other Lovecraftian elements in the entire cabin. In such a short game, with so little room to wall off the goofiness, these elements were just tossed in wherever they'd fit. They contributed little and seriously threw off my ability to get into the actual narrative.
Serena is free. If you own a Steam account, you already own Serena, so there's no point in me saying whether or not to buy it. On top of that, you can easily beat it in just under an hour, so there's no real commitment stopping you from playing it. If you enjoy adventure games, it's not without merits, but it also makes me feel grateful for games with bigger budgets and longer development times. If nothing else, consider it an excellent example of what not to do with Easter eggs.

Everything comes together in a gorgeous mesh of perfection. There should be a museum where you go to the art wing you will see this game in one of the portraits featured; then an LED TV at the side showing off how epic everything unfolds in the game. It's that kind of game that it would be a sin to miss.

I may not be a grizzled veteran with thousands of hours, but I've definitely been around. I can easily say this is one of my top 5 favorite games, but, it does come with ample warning -- it is most definitely not for everybody. Let me explain... (TL;DR version at the bottom of the post)
Currently, the largest issue is the lack of new players. Within a week, you can usually catch about 50 or so veterans at least once (many every day). However, it is becoming rarer each day to find new players. This means that unless you're playing with bots, you'll probably have a hard time.
I'd suggest getting a few friends and hosting a server of your own in order to get decent at the game before hopping onto, for instance, ball dojo (the "top tier" open server). Who knows, you might become good enough to join a permanent team or recieve an invite to ranked. The hardest part of this game is most definitely the initial push to be able to compete with the big dogs of Altitude, and after that, it's always extremely fun (and many times equally frustrating) to play.
I do not claim to be an extremely great player. Sometimes, I can get a goal. On a great day, sometimes 3. However, much of the veteran community is much better than I am and sometimes it
shows. I only bring this up to say that even when your team is losing and you're one of the last players on it (maybe because you accidentally passed to an enemy that zipped past you to score), it is still a very fun game.
Worst case scenario, you just wasted... 0.00 dollars/pounds/euros/colourful rocks. If not for anything but for the sake of the community, give the game a shot. It is very friendly and close, since most people know of eachother (and if not, somebody else that knows who they do not). Many people are willing to help teach you and give you pointers.
Oh yeah, and gameplay. The steering is tight (mouse+keyboard at least), there are literally controls if you use mouse+keyboard (3 on the mouse, up and down on the keyboard), you rank up in order to unlock new planes then new parts for said plane, there is a prestige system in order to get a better graphical rank, and there is
. That alone is extremely rare for a free-to-play multiplayer game, and for these many reasons, I cannot recommend this game enough.
It will be a very difficult game at first, but after getting used to it (no more than a week at most, really), you will wonder how you've never played this game before. Not a huge community, but it's hard to tell since there's always at least 2 viable servers. NO in-game real cash payments. Tight controls and gameplay that doesn't feel repetitive. And, it's completely free -- there's no reason it's not worth trying.

Serena is an interesting way to while away some time.
It's short, probably about 45 minutes long. I'd recommend playing it in one go as I quit out of it after half an hour hoping (but unsure) it would carry on where it left off. Much like the protaganist in the game, it's memory is somewhat fuzzy and it didn't which was a bit annoying.
Sadly this tainted the affair as I rushed to redo everything again which kind of ruined the build up second time around. My own fault I know, but an option to resume would have been nice. Patience is key with this one.
From a purely gameplay point of view, the mechanics of the game are ultimately dull and repetitve. It's a point and click adventure set solely in a small environment with a limited number of things to click on. You simply repeatedly point and click your way around the objects in the cabin over and over again. This isn't what matters though. It's about the story or mystery unfolding as you do so, and what it reveals. The atmosphere and mystery help make it what it is. As the tale plays out, you get lots of snippets of information - thoughts and recollections related to various items and objects.
Once the game is finished, things tend to linger which is a laudable acheivement in the rather throwaway culture of modern media these days. What makes it interesting is how the protagonist's memories, recollections and point of view change over time, giving the player an extended knowledge of the relationship that's being explored. A sad and melancholic reflection of souring releationships perhaps or maybe a realist view of personal (in)tollerance. I don't know but I like that it makes me think about such things.
The voice acting is probably the biggest let down for me. It feels a little unrealistic and fake at times which is a real shame as it represents your main connection to the game. It's by no means terrible, but I feel it broke the connection between player and protagonist when more natural approach would have helped.
Ultimately, I've enjoyed the game and have no real reason to grumble at a free title. I found it a melancholic and thought provoking piece. It's nice to see a game tackle interesting themes and issues without outstaying it's welcome or resorting to cheap scares or heavy handed moralising.

If a couple years ago you've ever logged onto Gmod and saw an immensely popular server called GM Tower, Tower Unite is the standalone successor to that digital playground among Gmod servers and Steam games in general. However, GM Tower no longer exists as a server on Gmod due to the release of Tower Unite. I've played a lot of GM Tower when it was around, perhaps not as much as a lot of Tower Veterans like to brag, but I can at least say that I've played enough to know that I always had the time of my life playing it with so much friendly and funny fellow players; Tower Unite on the other hand, does not live up to my expectations sadly and here is why:
When I got the news that Gmod Tower was being shut down to promote the sales and kickstarter funds for Tower Unite, I'll admit that I was pretty bummed out. Despite donating a bit of money towards the progress of Unite, GM Tower was the ONLY EVER reason I logged onto Gmod; Hell, even Steam in general. All the desperate amount of hours I have on Gmod was me playing GM Tower. Many of you might not care and you're always allowed to have your own opinion and reasons (no, that's not sarcasm) for things, but I never cared about playing TTT or Deathrun or Prophunt or DarkRP, etc... I always went straight to Tower because I was able to make friends so easily on there, nobody was ever mean and when they were, it was clear that they weren't being totally serious. It always felt as if you were encouraged into being a friend to someone in the game by pure self control, which is GREAT feeling. Not to forget that I always had a compelling sense of competition when playing any of the minigames. I was nervous about Tower Unite since I had no idea what the future had in place for the server and community, but I at least played it hopeful. Hence donating money towards the kickstarter campaign.
Tower Unite has it's flaws, but it's easy to overlook them when you first launch it and play. I will come out and say that the game looks beautiful in terms of graphics and scenery, and it really is a step up from the original server. A lot of the layout is still the same, making way for much familiarity given you've actually played on Gmod. There a lot of new attractions too such as Bowling, Trivia, Lazer Tag, new condos, which tells me that Pixeltail Games is trying to push beyond their limits to be innovative, and I can admire that. On the downside of things, it DOES lag a lot, which is to be expected from an early access game; but given the time that Pixeltail could've worked on these utmost neccessities is what confuses me. Ever since I've taken hiatus on this game since it first came out and coming back to it today, they've added so many things without tweaking out the basic flaws like gittery animation, insane lag spikes, horrid loading screen lengths (which crashed my entire PC by the way, my PC isn't THAT weak), and weird glitches that may sometimes be game-breaking. While it is technically true that GM Tower had a ground basis to work off of, it must've been easier to fix bugs and issues due to an existing engine to offer foundation for practically limitless possibilities. That's why it worked so well. When it didn't, all it needed was an easy fix. I'm not familiar with the engine that PixelTail made Unite with, but it seems to me they're having trouble since none of the things I've mentioned have barely been attempted, or at least that's what I think is probable. They've also ripped a plethora of flesh off of Gmod and the inner workings of the Gmod engine, minus the godly physics...
Seriously, the game style is practically ripped from Gmod with the character look, character animation, interactive qeues... Everything, and it really bothers me for some reason. I guess nobody else has an issue with this, but I feel like this was a huge chance for them to break off and to try something new completely, but it feels like PixelTail was too afraid to go any further than they did out of fear that, nobody would play their game if it 'didn't feel like Gmod.' And that's what really turns me off. EVEN Ultimate Chimera Hunt got ripped from Gmod with a different name and theme, called "Little Crusaders", which is about little knights trying to fight off a dragon while struggling to press the button on it's back. Sound familiar? I'm not saying it ever had to be completely different, but not a true mirror with the addition of an upgraded engine and different name. Maybe I'm not the only one who feels this and if so, maybe that's why Unite servers are so, so dead and assertive.
I usually join the the most populated server on Unite which, still isn't THAT many people, compared to the original server at least. The most I ever see is 45-50 players tops during the day, and around 25-30 at night. I guess it's not really worth complaining about because at least people are playing the game thus giving feedback, but whether or not that feedback is good or not, this new community that plays this game feels much more hostile and needlessly witty to be considered more favorable among my standards at a bare minimum. I'm nothing special, and I can take an insult without running to my room and crying, but it feels like you're walking on eggshells around these players. In GM Tower, I could always voice my opinion through mic or type my thoughts out on a given topic in chat without worring about some uptight prick getting offended about what I said regardless of what I was talking about being controversial or not. In Unite, it feels like nobody wants you to talk unless you're shouting out or spamming stupid memes, and you always need to be moderately careful about discussing general ideas, lest you want a troll to talk down to you simply because what you're saying 'isn't funny.' It takes a lot of the fun out of the game and is much less motivating to play any of the minigames, because you don't want to play games with these asshats. Other than the occasional friendly, kind-hearted player who likes to interact, the spirit from GM Tower is completely gone, and that's what I felt mattered the most. Probably sounds cheesy, but eh. I don't give a damn about this anymore.
To be fair, a lot of this isn't PixelTails fault because like I said, there was no way of telling what was going to happen at ALL with this games' release, these are MY expectations, and I'm simply writing this review for people who might feel the same way I do about this game. My fingers grow tired, so I shall conclude by saying that I am not impressed. I will continue to keep playing this in hopes of future development to be taken more seriously, and while praying for a good fanbase to flock towards this game's direction. However until PixelTail puts more important priorities dead ahead of them, and until I feel this game has as much as GM Tower had going for it, this is going to be a negative review. Hopefully PTG can remember what made GM Tower extraordinary.

Let me start off by saying, don't let the player count put you off. There may be a peak of 400 players per day, however that is plenty for you to have fun and play games with. 99% Of the community is welcoming and Nice to new players and will play minigames with you if you ask in the chat.
- The Plaza:
The plaza is awesome. It may be a little unoptimized at the moment, but it is bearable. In the plaza you have access to everything you need: Minigames, Stores and more. The plaza gives you access to areas such as: The Casino (Where most of the server is quite a lot of the time lol), Lasertag (Fun Team Based FPS minigame), Bowling (You know what that is, c'mon!), Trivia (Great fun, questions get thrown at you and a bunch of other players - awesome!), Typing Rally (Where you have to type as fast as you can to get to the end with your horse) and much much more.
- The Minigames (Virus, Little Crusaders, etc...)
The Minigames are amazing! Each minigame feels like its own unique game. Virus is an FPS game in which you start off as a survivor, 1 person out of all of the survivors is infected and has to infect all remaining survivors. The survivors have to survive for around 2 minutes. It is a really fun mode (One of the best in my opinion). Little Crusaders is a game in which you either play as a Knight or a dragon. 1 player plays as a Dragon, the others as Knights. The Knights have to Push a button on the Dragon's back while the Dragon has to eat all Knights. Simple, but really, really fun and addicting.
There are quite a few other minigames (Ball Race, Minigolf and another which is in a rough state right now (It is being fixed though)) and these are great too, I just don't have hours to write this review.
By playing these Minigames you earn Units, which you can use to Purchase:
- Buyable items
Using units you can buy many things. Units can be earned by playing Minigames, or by gambling at the Casino. With Units you can buy Clothes, Character Effects, Equipable items (Such as confetti guns), Furniture and electronics for your Condo (Your own House/ Apartment basically). There are many things to buy after playing a few mini-games.
- Your Condo
You Can Own A Condo (A Small Apartment or Large House of sorts). These Condo's can vary in size and what they look like, but they are ALL customizable. Most recently they have added an Underwater condo, it looks cool but is pretty expensive (400,000 Units!). You can design many things in your condo, you can decide what the walls, floor and ceiling looks like aswell as many other things. As I said earlier, you can also buy and place furniture. In Your Condo you can watch Youtube with your friends (If you own a TV), mess around and pretty much just have fun.
- Do You Need Friends To Play?
No. The simple answer is No. Friends may make it more enjoyable, but they are not needed. By playing Tower Unite you will 100% make friends. After my First 10 Hours Playing the game, I already had 3 new friends, we play together quite a lot. If you play on your own you will still have fun. The game is great with, or without friends.
- To Wrap Up
Tower Unite is an amazing game and is 100% worth your time, and your money. Even at full price this Early Access game is amazing and will provide you with Hours of Fun even at its current state. More stuff is also being added Constantly, so the fun will never really run out. Get bored? Wait a few months and have tons of new stuff to do!
- Warning
Do not, whatever you do go into the Casino. You will never escape, you will never ever get out. Legend even tells of one lonely soul who was stuck in that hellhole for decades. Beware.

I know a game moved me somewhere in my deeper emotions, when I dream of it. Now that I dreamed of this game after finishing it, I feel compelled to writing a recommendation.
Serena is a short exploration game with emphasis on narrative design. As opposed to Gone Home, which brought many haters due to its price tag, Serena is completely free, so nobody can complain here. You basically explore the same room over and over again, while your character undergoes several emotional changes, slowly understanding what actually happened.
The narration is cleverly integrated into the exploration and the emotional response can be quite intense. This is one of those "a game for an evening"-games and as it is free, you can't complain, you'd gone into the cinema for the same price. Free doesn't come without setback, though. While the graphically, the game might not look too bad and delives the dark atmosphere well, the sound design is dreadful and the voice acting could have been a -lot- better. Especially the recording quality of Serena's voice is horrible and always brutally kicked me out of my into the story immersed state.
Yet, as mentioned several times, the game is free, one can overlook these flaws. Yet I can't help but think, that some polishing here and there would intensify the atmosphere immensely.
Recommended nonetheless, because it delivers an strong emotional experience for the small price of free.

Tower Unite features 5+ games (with plenty more to come) that you can play in order to earn in-game currency which you can later use to play at a casino, purchase your own home, buy cosmetic items, and much more.
The game features no microtransactions, paid DLC or premium currency, the only way to obtain "Units" (The in-game currency) is simply to play the game, which you don't really see in a lot of games of similar nature these days.
The games available offers a good amount of variety, everything from Mini-Golf (The most popular game mode and my personal favorite) to Laser Tag, Trivia and much more in-between. I'm also really impressed with the amount of content the games hold, especially the min-golf. It currently has 8 maps with 18 holes each making it a total of 144 holes.
The developers also put out regular content updates which adds lots of improvement and new content for players to enjoy. And from what I've heard a lot of exciting things are in the works.
You can also purchase furniture and such to decorate your own home, everything from working basketball courts to TV's in which you can watch Youtube and such with your friends or other players in your home.
For $15 you definitely get what you pay for. This game offers a lot of great times especially if you play with friends. But the community also seems to be very friendly and I've been invited to participate in various games with people I don't know, so even if you decide to play by yourself you shouldn't have a hard time meeting new people or find someone to play with, even if the game doesn't have a HUGE playerbase.
Once again, huge respect to the developers for being commited to their game and regulary updating it and all this without adding any microtransactions, well done!
