This is probably the most flawed Assassin's Creed title I've played so far, but nostalgia might play a part in this. Still, I'm quite frustrated by this game. My main points of criticism:
The parkour system is really borked. Arno sticks to surfaces as if they were flypaper and often moves in entirely the wrong direction. Attempting to make the system more usable by having seperate commands for parkouring up, down or relatively straight ahead is a commendable attempt, but there were several times where Arno moved down when I wanted him to go up. It's also not always clear which walls are climbable, and as in other titles, Arno runs up a short distance any unclimbable wall, then drops down again, wasting several seconds which can be crucial in a chase. Climbing through windows also often takes way more effort than it's supposed to. Certain extremely long jumps feel like Arno's changing direction in mid air and look very unnatural.
Fighting is influenced a lot by small breaks in the terrain, making either Arno or his enemies lose their target mid swing or even leaving combat mode entirely because someone bumped against the edge of a carriage. Several times enemies did not telegraph their attacks at all. While fights are more dangerous than in previous titles, they can be cheesed quite easily with smoke bombs. They stun everyone for quite a while (enough to dispatch several enemies), the right equipment will give you ten of those, and there's a skill on a relatively short cooldown that refills them for free. You'll never need ten, though. Stun bombs, expressly designed for stunning enemies in fights, are inferior as targets you attack wake up from the stun after the first hit, and I don't think any equipment gives you quite as many, though they're refilled by the same skill.
The UI is a mess. The map feels more cluttered than earlier titles, especially because there are four kinds of chests. This probably wasn't as big a problem at release because some of those chests were made available through a mobile app, but since that's not working anymore, the chests are all unlocked from the start. Almost nothing appears on the map immediately, but just running around a bit will fill up that map very quickly. There are filters, but they only help so much. The biggest problem I have with the UI, though, is that certain messages overlap hints gained in murder mystery missions and riddles during their respective missions, meaning that often you have to wait for potentially several messages (new hint, new entry into the glossary, money in your chest...) to clear before you can read the hint you just picked up.
General bugs. I've had crashes, Arno once got stuck in mid air while jumping from one small gable to another, white lines sometimes shone through at the edges of floor and wall textures, that sort of thing.
I usually try to 100 % games like this, but this time it just wasn't that much fun.

At first when I purchased Botanicula, I wasn't too sure I would like it. Truth be told, I only bought it because the characters and art style looked super cute. I never really had any experience with point-and-click games - at least not in a long while - so this purchase was something of a risk for me. But, every risk has the possibility of becoming a sweetass reward, and, now that I've beaten the game, I can definitely consider my purchase of Botanicula to be just that.
As I've mentioned, the characters and art style are super cute, and they surely have enough charm to match its cuteness. I couldn't stop smiling and giggling throughout my 6 hour playthrough due to the oodles and oodles of OMGEVERYTHINGISSOCUTENESS. Like, if you wanna see what I'm talking about, watch this 27 second YouTube video I made of some singing frogs from the game:
So, yeah: The game's as cute as a bug, and considering I have, like, 87 mental disorders involving the symptom depression, that's pretty important to me. But, what's also important to me is for there to be some sort of meaning to the game. Like, why are these bugs just going around talking to singing frogs and solving puzzles (more on the puzzles in a moment)? Well, the game does a really good job of explaining its story in a way that provides empathy for the characters' plight without using words to do so. Like, the game doesn't use any words at all. Everything is expressed using imagery and emotional gibberish; it's adorable and heart-touching at the same time. By the end of the game, I was so determined to help the buggos, that I didn't mind failing at puzzles again and again and again - so long as I knew that eventually I'd perservere, and Mr. Twig and his buddies would eventually be happy again!
The puzzles themselves are, well, they're certainly satisfying to solve! Just about every time you solve a puzzle, the characters go all "YooHoo!" and it's THE CUTEST THING EVER OMG! I'm normally pretty terrible at puzzles (I blame those aforementioned mental disorders), so I eventually needed a guide to help me through the game. However, one thing I did notice was that it was also pretty difficult to identify where exactly puzzles were supposed to be. Like, not just what you were supposed to do in a puzzle, but what exactly was a puzzle? Where to start a puzzle? Sometimes it was tough to just get started, and I feel like this might be a problem for more people than just myself, especially near the end of the game. There's this awfully mazy-like area, and it practically forces you to use a guide for at least some of it. For me this wasn't a really big deal, since I didn't really buy this game for its puzzles anyway, but I could definitely see some people becoming upset by this.
So, there ya have it: my feelings about this game. I'm sure you're all very scared now by all of this, but you shouldn't be scared of purchasing this game, at least not if you like cute things and puzzles. Very, very, very nice game, and I'm looking forward to playing the other games done by Amanita Design.

This game is really addictive for about 20 hours. Then you realize there's not enough variety. There are probably billions of planets you can visit but there's only ~20 different types of planets that exist. Once you've explored an avian airship, glitch castle, floral village, etc., you don't need to visit another one because it'll be nearly identical.
At that point you're going to stop exploring every planet and, some time after that, you stop exploring new planets altogether. I've just been going to the same teleport points over and over to get crafting ingredients. I think the developers could have made exploration more exciting by decreasing the amount of planets you can explore but making them drastically different and have missions where you have to try and find extremely rare planets.
As for the crafting aspect of the game, it just doesn't seem as fun as Terraria's because you're building in peace (unlike Terraria where you're constantly under attack) and you can't affect the terrain for missions. So you end up with 2 distinct game plays: (1) building a base and (2) playing a platformer for the missions. Once you've built your base, you're done. There's no incentive to modify it with better material, weapons, or gizmos, to survive the next enemy like there is in Terraria.
Overall, it's a fun game, but it's variety could be improved a lot. Just off the top of my head, the devs could have made some ore only appear on planets covered with apex cities. You'd have to raid the cities to steal the ore. Apex ships would chase you as you flee. You'd be forced to stop at random planets to repair your ship and the planet might have extremely strong monsters forcing you to build a fortress to complete your repairs in safety. Basically, some challenges and goals that force you to try and give you a sense of accomplishment instead of the current "I'm just playing to see what I can unlock" style.

A surprisingly fun and atmospheric side scrolling crafting game. The obvious comparisons to the likes of Terraria and Starbound don't really do it justice. The various shadow creatures hit softer and take a lot more damage in a well-lit area. A particular brilliant bit to exploit this is that the various guns (once you have a power source for your armors and batteries to charge those power sources) have a tactical flashlight. This means your shotgun will weaken them before you even fire it.
All in all, there are worse games to buy. It's an interesting interpretation on a market that's quickly being saturated with unimaginative clones.

There is quite a bit to say about Darkout. I'll try to be as non-partisan as possible.
With the explosion of greenlight games and the large number of 'Metroidvania' sandbox style games on Steam, it's hard to make one stand out from the rest. Darkout, like Terraria, or Starbound, takes yet another approach at these sandbox style games, but, of course, is still very much the same.
Indeed, Darkout is much the same old grind. Spending hour upon relentless hour, mining through piles of the same dirt, and rock, only to fill your inventory and discard, rinse and repeat. Just enough to get you the resources to build an elevator to reach the depths of the shaft you just dug. With the same old spotty mouse targeting as others, a horrible grouping system for mining, a terribly inaccurate crafting system, and a slew of other annoying bugs, it is tedious at best during these hours, searching for resources, and can often be a real chore, during these times, to play.
It has more base in sci-fi than others in it's genre, even more so than Starbound, only short of having a spaceship and being able to explore a number of alien worlds. With crafting devices like the Combinator, the Molder, and the Chem-Lab, weapons such as the Laser gun, and fusion based power devices, it's a sci-fi sandbox geek's dream come true. Coupled with a fragmented, yet deeply frightening storyline, and some absolutely dazzling light effects and much better graphics and visuals, overall, Darkout is a step ahead of the rest. With a fairly extensive research/tech/crafting tree and some fun and interesting exploratory and combat scenarios, heavily focused on the use of light, Darkout is, again, in a class of it's own.
A key thing to remember is that being another 'early release' title, or beta, at this point, the small Independent Developers,
----
are slowly, but surely, diligently churning through bug fixes and adding new content for upcoming stages of the game, including more story, new monsters and biomes and of course, more craft items.
While I might not recommend it, at this time, for anyone who is easily frustrated, I am excited for the future of this great game, and can imagine recommending it to any player who enjoys this genre of game, and possibly even players who don't, upon the game's completion.
In short, after all of that, Darkout is an absolute GEM. Recommended? Definitely.

Master of Orion it is!
I'm not really a Review person, yet when I saw a remake of this fantastic gem made in the 90s, I thought I simply had to try my hand at writing a review. Not to mention that -honestly- I don't know why there are so many unfavourable reviews that I just have to write this one.
So is the modern version of Master of Orion any good and worth a try? In my opinion it is. It's a good game. It's a great game! It's Master of Orion at its best, so what else do you people want? :)
The new game has got the same planets colonization system as the original game from the 90s, the same good folks like Darlocks, Mrrshan, Sakkra, Alkari etc. (folks that we all love so much!), the same galaxies to conquer, the same GNN robot (well with a female-robot colleague this time) and so on. All of the good elements of MoO plus the amazing graphics, animations, music and visuals a modern game must have.
The major comment I hear is that the modern gaming can offer much more than just a neat-looking clone of an old game. I haven't really played the other space civ games these days, games like Stellaris, so I can't compare to them. Yet the concept of the old MoO is an immortal one and a well thought-out one. So why complicate it, add to it or change it?
The new game resembles the old Master of Orion quite colsely in my opinion. Game mechanics are similar. Just the graphics are of high quality.
Throughout several matches which I played, it became obvious that there were some minor bugs here and there, but nothing too serious. Nothing that would spoil a good match. Although I agree, the devs should take some time to fine-tune the game.
I found the difficulty levels to be a bit out-of-balance, something that was very well established in the DOS game. I started off with a "very easy" difficulty level and that occured to be quite difficult actually. The major problem was the 'upkeep' costs, which really made it impossible for one race to speed up the growth. That is because if you buy too many assets, you will run into a deficit and that's not good (your money supply will run out and then the game will auto-sell your goodies). As I watched the charts, my race grew in line with the others over time and only in the mid or even late game I was finally able to get a better hand.
The voiced-over advisor is really annoying and does not suit there at all. They should have provided a "fire the advisor" button. :)
I imagine that any new player will find the game confusing at first. Someone who doesn't know the old Master of Orion or doesn't know the civ games. The learning curve is rather steep and the game is not intuitive at all at the beginning. You need to delve into it and be patient, learn and you will get a hang of it after a while.
I found the music to be great as well as the graphics. The themes are exactly the same as in the DOS game, but of course improved in qulity. The sound when you have a new discovery, for instance, is just fantastic.
Population grows slowly and it takes a lot of time to fully populate a planet, but that was exactly like this in the old game as well.
The interface is made in such a way that you need to patiently move all of the single units and click on every single planet to adjust production. Sure, there are shortcuts and improvements, but it still takes time and it's a tedious routine. However in my opinion, that's what it is, it defines Master of Orion really. If moving patiently every single unit is not "your cup of tea" than don't bother.
Also what I really liked in the new game is the emphasise on the races. They are unique and presented in a great way. Let's say, when you first meet Sakkra, they are big, monstrous creatures and that is impressive. Darlocks are mysterious, dark and malicious. Every race is very well presented and introduced. That was also a big thing regarding the old game.
I hear that people complain that the battles are real-time rather than turn-based. I didn't find that to be a big problem, although yes... it's different compared to the old game.
Regarding Diplomacy I found out that in the new game, the races seem to be less sensitive to the changes, which is good. It was always too unpredictible in the DOS game.
Overall, I was plesently surprised to find out that Master of Orion got its 2016 remake. I was more surprised to find out that the remake is good actually. If you're a fan of Master of Orion, you will enjoy the matches with the good-old enemies, which the new remake offers.

Bastion is full to the brim with personality. It features a narrator that responds to what the player is doing in the world, making remarks that will make you smile, and allowing for some interesting story-telling moments. This feature does, at times, get a little close to sounding like a gimmick, but it never really strayed to the other side of the line and ultimately comes off as being an interesting unique aspect of Bastion. It helps that the writing is rather strong and the story is enjoyable.
While Bastion boasts a beautiful art style and soundtrack, it's more than just a pretty face. The gameplay mechanics are very enjoyable and tight, and the controls are very intuitive and responsive. There are nearly a dozen different weapons that can be unlocked and upgraded in different ways throughout the course of the game, as well as all kinds of special abilities and passive item bonuses. These allow you to custom how your character fights to a surprising degree.
One aspect of the game that really shines is its variable difficulty system. As you progress through the game, you will unlock new Shrine Idols, each of which makes the game more difficult in a specific way if enabled. These range from enemies doing more damage and being able to take more damage to enemies occasionally reflecting projectiles, dealing damage to the player when injured, or dropping explosives when they die. There are ten of these idols, and enabling each one increases the amount of currency and experience the player will receive. This allows you, as the player, to really tailor the game's difficulty towards your liking instead of just selecting Easy, Medium, or Hard, and it can be changed between every mission in the event you're running into problems. This, combined with the challenge levels that unlock throughout the game, makes for some very interesting, difficult, and satisfying challenges. I found myself having to radically change the weapon and passive load-out I was using in order to finish some of these.
Bastion is a game worth playing for both its artistic aspects, like its writing, visual appeal, and soundtrack, and for its tight and satisfying gameplay.

So far this game is absolutely great:
Graphics:
looks relatively good especially the weather effects the battles in stormy nights are stunning
controls:
relatively easy to learn the loading screen is pretty much enough of a tutorial
Gameplay:
There are currently 5 modes:
hoy vs hoy (two small one decked ships 8 cannons each)
galleon vs galleon (two larger ships with a good lot of cannons and severel decks)
2hoys vs 2hoys (explains itslef)
2galleons vs 2 galleons (also explains itself)
fleet (1 galleon and 2 hoys vs 1 galleon and 2 hoys)
The games are extremely fun and relying on teamplay you really have to work together and focus on the important parts (e.g. holes in the ship, fire, damaged sales).
Every ship has a captain that has been elected by the crew. He is steering the ship and giving the orders.
There are two ways to fight either you shoot the enemy till he isn`t able to repair all holes in time and sinks OR
you board him. For this you need a special command by the captain and you have to grapple the enemy with your cannons first.
community:
So far great community friendly and gets along with the game pretty well
verdict:
This game is in early acces so expect to experience some bugs though I haven`t had any really bad ones. Also keep in mind that not all of the content is in the game yet though everything that is in the game is extremely fun. If you are ok with the two other points and think that this game may appeal to you then I can only recommend it.

This game is actually alright.
The things you can get up to around the Plaza range from trivia quizes to bowling to lazer tag, and I've yet to find something there I don't like. The Casino is definitely where it's at though; poker, slots, blackjack and more, with all the bells, whistles and flashy lights that make real gambling so enthralling to a lot of people. It's surprisingly addictive, which would be quite worrying if this game had micro-transactions, which it luckily does not.
There's a few more competitive game types too, like minigolf and stuff like that. While they can be pretty chill when played alone, they can become very different with a group of friends. Running around inside a hamster ball while screaming "MELON!" can be more entertaining than one would think at first, and it does wonders to bring out the kid in you.
Once you've got some money (in the form of units), you can spend it on various customization items, both on your PC and your personal condo. The condos themselves can be outfitted with various items of furniture, TV screens and "canvas" objects, which can be personalized with your own custom textures. These objects include framed pictures, candlelit shrines, literal dakimakura body pillows and even the very walls and floors. And yeah, that means you can finally have that daki you can't afford IRL. Hell, buy one for each waifu. I know I'm going to.
Also, I forgot to mention the TVs will actually play YouTube videos. When it comes to media in this game, if you can link to it, you and your houseguests will see it. Sure, the video queue becomes unresponsive sometimes. Which brings me to my next topic...
Does this game run perfectly? Of course it doesn't; it's still in early access. Does it look pretty? ♥♥♥♥ no. I literally bought a bucket of chicken to wear over my head because seeing my own character's face gives me an aneurysm.  But... this game likes to put emphasis on what precisely you're looking at rather than how it looks. The whole condo thing is pretty much an exercise in individualism; it doesn't really matter if you only get 15 fps while looking at that painting if you like the painting you're looking at. Then again, I'm running this game from a USB with a potato laptop, so take that as you will. Just bear in mind that other people have had similar issues.
On the whole, this game advertises itself as a "virtual party throwing" game, and it backs that up to great effect. It lets me do everything I'm too anxious to do in real life; gamble, go to parties, and have people visit my house and look at my anime posters.  10/10 would play Healthy Social Life Simulator again.

Remember the grappling hook from "Worms"? You liked that mechanic? Then go and buy this game!
Gunjitsu makes a lot right. The whole game is built around the grappling hook and that is, how a game should be. Take the the mechanic that brings the most fun and add some features that support it. The swinging around works great and is really fun, once you figured out how to use it best. Generally, the movements in this game just work. Swinging, jumping, dashing, it all makes you feel like some sort of sci-fi ninja. Awesome!
The shooting part is a perfect addition to that. You quickly pick up all the controls you need and can start playing with bots or online with friends. While it's easy to learn the basics, it will take some time to master the controls and perfect your timing. I had not a single frustrating moment in this game, even when I died several times in a row, as it is very fun to watch. Getting shot with a pumpgun in the middle of a jump let's you skid away like ragdoll. Quite amusing.
So, buy this game, convince your friends to do so as well (the price is really fair I think) and have some fun!

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I wanted to like this game so much. There are so many good things about it-but unfortunately it all fell apart for me pretty quickly.
When the game opens, the cabin is perfect-its bleak, oppresive, and dark. The details are wonderful, as is the curiosity and anticipation that it brings. When your character starts narrating, I was able to overlook  the terrible voice acting at first. I was still in awe at the atmosphere, and hanging onto the reviews that some gaming sites gave the game. To clarify, I'm not sure that it is just because he did a terrible job, but his actual voice was not proper for this story. It just didn't sound believable-at all.
While this started to frustrate me, I became more frustrated with the idea of having to click the same items over and over and over and over again. I am not exaggerating either. There was so much different dialogue for the same damn item. After clicking it until he started to repeat himself, you would think you were done with that item-nope! Walk around the cabin a bit and what seems to be randomly, the same item elicits different dialogue, and then again, and again, and again. Are you getting the idea yet?
To ice the cake, there is no pause, and if you try to pause it via hitting the escape button (like every other game's menu/pause normally pops up) it will close the game, and you have to start all over again! Seriously? Now I understand this game was free and I really do appreicate developers that work their a$$ off to bring us cool free stuff. I can also tell that a lot of work went into this game. Sadly it fell flat with a jumbled story, that consisted of WAY too much dialogue, that was poorly narrated. I was so very disapointed, because this game could have been SO much more =(

Highly recommended. Gorgeous graphics & haunting sound effects make for an extremely atmospheric game. I have played pretty much all of the recent 'sandbox block builders' like Terraria, Starbound, Edge of Space, Windforge, Asteria, Signs of Life, etc and I find Darkout to be the most enjoyable Single Player experience yet. It has a great many sci fi items to craft and the building mechanic is very easy and fast to use, similar to Starbounds and superior to Terraria imo. Combat is fast paced and fun with the weapons responsive. I have been playing the game exstensibly now for about a week and have yet to see a single crash, it is very stable. The gfx are smooth with no performance issues whatsoever and the character is easily controllable. The spelunking is great fun and ive often found myself saying 'im off to bed' only to still be awake many caves later! A very enjoyable experience so far and Im looking forward to seeing the new content thats been promised by the devs.
If, like me, you have read some of the negative reviews and posts for this game and are 'umming and ahhing' about purchasing because of it then id really advise you to give Darkout a chance. I have yet to experience any of the so called game ending bugs or glitches and ive been playing it all day solid for the last few days. The only bug I have found is a very minor irritation at most, sometimes when dragging an item out of your inventory the item will be dropped from your cursor to the floor or placed in a storage device if you happen to be stood near one. Finding the next Story log can be a bit random but the devs have said there will be more story structure to come. On a final note the only thing lacking is a co op mode to play with your mates, once that is included, as the devs have said it will be, then I think Darkout will be a real gem of a game.
UPDATE :
After 100+hrs of play there are a couple of things I should add to the above. Firstly there could be alot more variety to the mobs, yes there are several types but they do all feel a bit samey. Whilst I stand by what I said previously that the audio is nice there is a distinct lack of ambient sounds. Whilst not immediately apparent it can make the world feel a bit more sterile than it would otherwise and as the gfx are so atmospheric the ambient audio can be conspicuous by its absence. Finally the main issue I had after so many hrs of play is the definite lack of endgame content. On Terraria I have over 300+ hrs mainly due to endgame content that I played with a friend but there really is nothing to do in Darkout endgame other than building projects once all research is done and you have explored all biomes.
I have still had a great time playing Darkout even with the negative aspects above and £10 for 100+ hours of entertainment is a great deal by anyones standards, so still very recommended just be aware of the longevity of it in its current form. According to the developers there is alot more content to come so hopefully that will address the issues mentioned here.

Bastion is full to the brim with personality. It features a narrator that responds to what the player is doing in the world, making remarks that will make you smile, and allowing for some interesting story-telling moments. This feature does, at times, get a little close to sounding like a gimmick, but it never really strayed to the other side of the line and ultimately comes off as being an interesting unique aspect of Bastion. It helps that the writing is rather strong and the story is enjoyable.
While Bastion boasts a beautiful art style and soundtrack, it's more than just a pretty face. The gameplay mechanics are very enjoyable and tight, and the controls are very intuitive and responsive. There are nearly a dozen different weapons that can be unlocked and upgraded in different ways throughout the course of the game, as well as all kinds of special abilities and passive item bonuses. These allow you to custom how your character fights to a surprising degree.
One aspect of the game that really shines is its variable difficulty system. As you progress through the game, you will unlock new Shrine Idols, each of which makes the game more difficult in a specific way if enabled. These range from enemies doing more damage and being able to take more damage to enemies occasionally reflecting projectiles, dealing damage to the player when injured, or dropping explosives when they die. There are ten of these idols, and enabling each one increases the amount of currency and experience the player will receive. This allows you, as the player, to really tailor the game's difficulty towards your liking instead of just selecting Easy, Medium, or Hard, and it can be changed between every mission in the event you're running into problems. This, combined with the challenge levels that unlock throughout the game, makes for some very interesting, difficult, and satisfying challenges. I found myself having to radically change the weapon and passive load-out I was using in order to finish some of these.
Bastion is a game worth playing for both its artistic aspects, like its writing, visual appeal, and soundtrack, and for its tight and satisfying gameplay.

In the age of builder games becoming a fad and a "me too" dev bandwagon. Darkout manages to maintain enough uniquness to still be found enjoyable and not another complete clone.
Darkout is set in the 2d perspective much like Terraria and Starbound, It appears to be directly influenced by terraria due to how some of its more basic features (foreground/background, block selection, etc) are handled. It lacks some of the more condensed easier features of Starbound but the game still manages to be interesting. The most noticable difference between Darkout and other games of the genre is its graphics level, a full head and shoulders above most other games in the genre it provides lush jungles, beautiful reflective crystal caves, and ominous ruins for the player to traverse that all look stunning.
Darkout's plot is fairly simplistic, you are crash landed on a planet that mankind in their ages of space travel not only avoid but have largely forgotten in a "we don't go there" fashion. Not long into your first nights you encounter shadow beings that inhabit the planet and from here a greater plot of what happened on this world forms which is also continually expanded upon by found audio logs and the like, the main story involves the distress beacon and it was either bugged for me or is as far as the devs currently have it as even with objectives completed I could not advance the story.
That brings us to the next thing to note about the game, dispite not being marked early access, many aspects of the game are still under construction and things change from patch to patch. Some of their concepts for how crafts are made make very little logical sense (copper + sulfuric acid = platinum??) and these to me feel like place holders till the real content can be developed. In all though as far as the game goes, this game manages to offer enough to be more than "just another builder" and I recommend it, though you might want to wait for a sale.

TL;DR - If you're looking for a free poker game that simulates an actual poker night, this is the best you can hope for. Just try to get used to the unorthodox visuals and input, as it serves the purpose of simulating an actual poker game and not the mobile app you're probably used to playing. I'm writing this because I'm bored and high on post-surgery painkillers, so get ready for an eyefull.
At the time of writing this, you'll be hard pressed to find a better poker game on PC or Mobile. The game puts a lot of personality into the hands played so it feels more like you're at an actual poker table with real people than with a bunch of avatars going all in on every hand. There are gestures, tells, emotes and other things that spice up the hands played. This also means it is a bit slower paced than a mobile game. In regards to UI, it also isn't very much like the normal mobile poker games, so prepare to take a few minutes to get used to it. The odd presentation chased me away the first time I tried it, but it works for what they're trying to do.
If all you're here for is to play cards for monopoly money against bots or real people, Prominence delivers. There is a single-player experience available were you rank up by clearing bots from tables in specific venues against specific "gangs", giving you goals, vanity unlocks and exp boosters. And in single player, your plays aren't timed so you can step away when you need to. The downside to this is most venues represent the gangs you're up against with table accessories to boot, and it feels a little wierd for my dude in a hoodie to be playing cards with a couple of russian gangsters in a butcher shop carrying knives and brass knuckles.
Visually the game is fairly good, particularly for a free poker game. But it is indeed a free game, and poker, so of course some corners are cut. I do have some complaints. First would be lack of camera options, such as not being able to zoom in on the table or get a good look at chip stacks. They also took the time to flesh out the venue you're playing cards in, but didn't add in many moving parts or activity in the background, to make the place feel more alive. You'll play in the quietest bar ever, where the one patron stands in place in front of the bar until the stars burn out. The character animations can be a bit wooden, like when the avatars take drinks, smokes or move chips. But bear in mind that they're actually here and visible, in a genre that tends to barely animate anything.
The audio is a mixed bag. The sounds of chips and cards are average, the music is mediocre, but the avatar voices are bad, bad, bad. Funnily, my favorite effects are from ranking up and turn signalling. There's a lot of good audio feedback from the game pointing things out to you.
Random notes: No in-game chat is an odd choice, especially with the limited number of provided emotes. By design, I'd imagine, since most people online are the poster children for eugenics. The game is kinda bad at revealing to you the hands of the losing players and a lot of informative text blurbs dissapear quickly with no input from the player. The game has a feature I've never seen where you can muck cards if you're still in the hand but not in a showdown(?) - very poor form in poker, IMO - if I'm seeing it right. The all-in and winning hand animations and jingles could be a little more snappy, it gets tiresome to hear the same 7-note flute chime every time someone wins with a pair. Play with real people when you can - for some reason it's waaay more enjoyable to play it this way than with Zynga movile clones, and since there's tells, there's more for you to pay attention to. You also get more time to make decisions. I could really go for creating custom games with venues, card backs, tables and lighting.
Pros: Excellent game feel, player tells, healthy progression, varied scenery. E-motes and caracter customization. Card and chip sounds are nice. Drink/smoke accesssories give exp boosts. A lot of personality and quality in what is normally a very flat genre. The best poker experience on PC.
Cons: Cards in the UI are small-ish and not in the center, which seems strange, but it does give room for animation across the table. Muisc and voice acting is pretty bad. The "underground" vibe of the game means a lot of available venues look like places that people get murdered, and not swanky places you'd personally rather play in. No in-game chat, only emotes.

I know they tried to make the combat less "I countered one guy and now I can slaughter 30 of them in a combo" as that was the case for the 4 previous games but this combat I found quite un-interesting. They finally let you crouch and take cover in these games but gave you no way to lure guards, making you sit behind cover in doorways for extended periods of time as the fat french pigs slowly waddle up and down their patrol routes. I've played every AC and this felt like the series' weakest game in my opinion, which is a shame because it was finally set in the French revolution, a highly anticipated setting for fans before the release of this game. With this much practice you'd think the AC games would keep getting better, but they always manage to screw something up. Initial performance issues have been fixed, but a new slew of new game play issues have appeared. Paris looks great, it's immersive, there's a little more control over parkour movement, and the historical aspect is interesting. That's the good stuff. On the bad side: combat has become clunky, they've removed whistling (ruining stealth), removed the ability to hide bodies and use human shields, then added gear levels, basic skill unlocks and micro transactions. Shameful.
It really feels like they're all over the place on this one. I knew it was going to be a downhill ride after seeing they'd added two new currencies to the game, and one of them is for real money. You can now buy all your new gear from the menu, gear now has 'levels', and indicates the power of your character. You can also buy a new currency for real money to 'hack' unlock gear, and gear can be upgraded (which you upgrade by paying in a currency that you earn over time, or with real money). Half of the gear can only be attained by playing in co-op.
On top of that, they’ve made combat a lot clunkier. I wouldn’t mind this if it were to deter getting in to combat, but at the same time they’ve also removed the ability to whistle, and the ability to hide bodies. The only way to get guards to investigate something now is to deliberately get seen then run away, or by using a cherry bomb (another consumable), except that guards almost never investigate the spot you’re cherry bombing - they just look over and go “Hey I wonder what’s happening over there!” and then go back to standing where they were without even getting close enough to kill from cover.
It's still worth playing if you like the AC games, but I feel bad giving money to Ubisoft for this microtransaction crap.

Look.... In all honesty trove is an amazing game, its fun, simple, relaxing and its quite the blast to play with some mates...
However! Its made by Trion Worlds... one of the worst Devs in my experience. If you are looking at playing trove, take it from someone who has been playing for about two years, DONT!
Hear me out:
Trove is a great game, however that is simple the Game itself! Everything within it though is a massive waste of your time. Trove is Free to play not Pay to play, nor is it Pay to Win, but it ise Pay to have a "Chance" at having a good time.
Look, Trion is killing this game, they really dont seem to understand that they are just driving it 6 feet under and its getting worse.
Trove is almost like Trion attempted to create a game that would never die, but they have failed HORRENDOUSLY! to do anything in this game you have to grind, want a new class? Grind, want to make your gear stronger? Grind, want to progress at all? Grind! This game is nothing but one huge grind that never ends, so yes Trion has made a never ending game, but the thing is.... ITS A WASTE OF YOUR TIME! The game is so horrificly unbalenced that you could spend HOURS even days making ONE of your classes stronger to progress, but once you finally become strong enough to enter a new area, BOOM its like all the work you just did was for nothing! you weak as hell once again! back to the grind!
Seriously, dont even bother, this game is the most unfriendly game towards new players, really the only plays above about Uber-4 or 5 (In game areas) Are people who have spent hours upon hours of time grinding and/or spending money to become stronger.
The worst thing about this game is the fact that everything is "Chance" based, prepare yourself, ill be saying the word "Chance" alot!
At first the game was simple, level your class collect gear, go to the next area then repeat! it was easy, just get higher tier gear and you would progress, however, the leveling was horrible, once you hit level 20 which can be done within a few hours, it takes DAYS to level ONCE... it only got worse after the release of Mantle Of Power,,,
So then we have the MoP update... this just added to the allready bad grind Trove had, now the gear you collected became completely useless other then giving some basic stat boosts, now you needed to grind Dungeon after Dungeon to collect Gem boxes to get gems... which had a CHANCE to give you one of three gem colours (Later you could go to worlds that gave one specific colour) and on top of that, you had a CHANCE to get stats for your class. The classes in trove are rounded up into two groups, Magic and Physical, however, trion being... well trion, decided it was a smart idea to make players not only have a CHANCE at getting the stats they wanted as well as a CHANCE of getting a higher tier gem, but they also had a CHANCE at getting a gem for their class! I can event begin to tell you how many times i have gotten bloody physical gems when the only classes i enjoyed were magic ones!
Now we go onto the "Chests" within trove.
There are many different kinds of chest in trove, adventure ones, chaos ones and gems ones are Three, and boy! are chests a waste of time! So remember the whole "Chance" thing? Yeah!... these are the peek of the pyramid when it comes to that! You want a good gem from your empowered gem boxes? CHANCE! You want somthing thats actually worth in game currency from chaos chests? CHANCE! The Rng in trove is so horrific, ever seen a trove youtuber do an unboxing? They unbox 1000 chests at times and they only get ONE rare item if they are EXTREMELY lucky, everything else is either trash or just mastery fodder... dont waste your money on them.
Look... yes i am simply stating alot of bad within trove, but the matter of the fact is, there isnt alot of good! Every update is just a bigger disapointment then the previous one! On the day i am writing this, my mate and I were going through the new Shadow Towers brought in the Eclipse update, and it took us 15 minutes to get the new Dreadnaught boss down to 1 third of its health then it just one shots us with a insta kill move that you have only a few seconds to avoid... i play alot of MMORPGS, World of Warcraft being one of them, so i know about dangerous moves like that but this one is complete crap! The new shadow towers have been scaled to the point where someone like me, who has a power rank of 6000 on his favorite class which could clear the final shadow tower within about 2 minutes with ease! takes 10 minutes on the new Hydra boss which is weaker then the final boss! My point here is, Trion has screwed over the towers scaleing so that Normal mode is just stupid, Hard Mode and Ultra Mode are so difficult you needed to be at End game do have a chance, and that was before the Eclipse update, now you dont stand a chance without a raid group basically.
Listen, Trove itself is a good game and it has alot of potential, but Trion Worlds is just digging its grave and it is just not worth your time in the end.
If you want to give it a try then go for it, just know that it has a horrific grind behind its cute design and if your looking to actually progress in the game then you will either have to sell your soul and devote months upon months worth of time to do so, or spend hundreads and hundreads of dollars for their stupid as hell patron system and over-priced cash shop items.

I wanted to post another review of this game after having actively played it for some months and in it I want to talk about all the game's aspects. If you are wondering why I'm still playing it, it's because of my club world project and fast progression so far.
Lets start with the good.
+ The game is free to play and you get at least 3 free classes. By default you get the Knight and after reaching mastery rank 3 and 25, you get 2 more classes of your choice (you can get 1 extra class if you are referred by someone).
+ The creative side of the game is nice. You can make a lot of things from blocks to your cornerstone or club world.
+ There are lots of things to do. Shadow Towers, crafting things, recipe collecting, fishing, merchanting, mining, expanding your club world,  leveling up and so on.
+ You can do all these things with your friends as well
+ Most of the things can be earned through gameplay or logging in daily and playing for some time.
+ Gameplay is fun overall and environments look great.
+ You can design your own dungeons or styles and send them to trion for review and chance of having them added to the game.
Then the bad.
- Everything takes long to get nowadays unless you have everything (obviously, but some people like to complain about instant gratification when they have bought everything long ago when prices were 5x lower and when they don't need to farm more than a couple of hours with high Magic Find to get everything from the next patch). In other words, you progress slowly unless you luckily find a ganda from Trove of Wonders chest and decide to sell it.
- The game has a economy where rich get richer with no effort while new players have to work hard for little benefit. If by some miracle a new player manages to understand the market and make some money all the while leveling up and collecting things, they can get a pricy Patron status to greatly help them level up. Patron also gives free daily rewards, thrice more cubits for logging in and playing, twice more drops, twice more gem karma bar per box opening and higher bonus multiplier to daily bonuses. The problem is that for this kind of benefit you have to wait for very long unless you are multi-logging in, because market slots require you to spend cubits and cubits are needed for things like emblems (which increase your damage by a lot). Oh and you also have to make use of those 30 days.
- As I said, market slots cost cubits to buy - up to 2500 cubits each (5 days of waiting just for one slot). You get up to 500 cubits a day without patron.
- if gems fail to upgrade they can "crack" and the crack has to be fixed with 1 or 2 re-gemerators costing 500/1000 cubits (1 to 2 days just to fix a crack). A character can equip 9 gems, so it's pretty absurd at first when you don't have crack-preventing booster items and might not be aware of them only coming from weekly contest rewards, daily chests (very low quantity), gem booster boxes (500 cubits each) or the jade clover tome (premium currency exclusive, but can be bought from other players). After some time, this is not as bad as it sounds, but when you try to remove an empowered gem with a lot of upgrades (to loot collect it for dust and empowered gem fragments), it costs 2 re-gemerators (1000 cubits). They say it's to prevent quickly increasing power rank for contests on other characters, but really a cooldown system or character-binding system could have been placed instead of encouraging players to buy credits or spend more hard-earned cubits.
- Gems that make most of your Power Rank have many factors of RNG: The base Power Rank, Star Rank, PR from upgrade, gem stat count
- Bought Store Pack-exclusive mastery point giving allies and mounts
- Promo-exclusive mastery point giving mounts and allies, including ones that require spending a lot of time on other players streams just to have a small chance (Streamer Dream codes, Dev stream codes).
- New content consists mostly of new player-created dragons (requiring hundreds of dragon coins each), player-created dungeons, player-created styles, "double events", slight UI improvements, ability description fixes and some bug fixes.
- No option to report players for anything else than spamming.
- Players are allowed to multibox "as long as no third-party software is included" according to Avarem and Trove TOS. This can make things very easy for such players. For example, a multiboxer gets multiple daily log-in rewards, can fish much faster (because fishing takes over 15 seconds on average), gets more event rewards and more slots to sell items on the market. All they need is a club world with a chest to share items in and soon each account is in patron status, getting 25+ chaos chests per day.
- There is a bot-driven economy
- Frequent disconnects
- Other players can host a Shadow Tower from your Club World after they grow impatient (after 1 minute) of waiting for you to gather a party and there is no way to remove that opened portal (and have your own) as long as there are players left in the club world.
- Again emphasis on no report options - some mean players kick you from Shadow Tower runs after your hard work just to get a laugh or to let their friends get rewards instead (usually in order to look better to them, but also because of being the same).
- Some rank-based contests still require insane amounts of time invested just to have a chance at rare rewards not obtainable elsewhere. Should be fully score-based IMO..
- A lot of content is only available through spending cubits and you get them very slowly.
- Shadow Tower power level requirements are poorly labeled, especially for ultra difficulty.
- Empowered Gems can't be reforged. You could go months without getting any useful empowered gem upgrade for any class (unless you want to make a tank out of every class) and the same could happen with the stellar empowered gem boxes you get from loot collecting useless radiant empowered gems.
- More monthly dragons keep coming - now we got another one within two weeks of the old one.. again for 300 dragon coins and a huge farm of pumpkins (limited time to grow). WOOT for more grind and spending everything on greater dragon caches.
- Shadow's Eve event is so grindy. You get about 0.5 candy corns per dungeon and then trade in 5 for box (which has a very low chance to give mounts - the mounts needing thousands of pumpkins).
The botting, multiboxing and moneymaking in general makes me feel less achieved when some players have it so much easier. I understand rewarding endgame players, but I don't see why players that have almost everything get so many rewards just from completing a few dungeons each day.
So I would only recommend it if you can spare a lot of time, if you like building things or if you want to see how each class works (you can play classes in trial up to level 4).

The jumping physics felt very imprecise to me.  Unfortunately, that killed my enjoyment of this otherwise interesting game.  I just couldn't stand the frustration of so many missed jumps.  For example, I built my base on a leveled piece of ground.  I put a floor in, so the base was 1 square higher than the plain on which it was built and the door was just tall enough for my character.  Jumping up that 1 square gap to get into the door was maddening; eventually I extended the floor out past the door.  If that were the only situation where the jumping precision bothered me, I'd be able to ignore it... but this is a side scroller, so you'll be digging and jumping and digging and jumping a *lot*.

As others mentioned, this is a Terraria clone. The graphics are prettier...but that's all it has going for it. I had a real hard time even doing simple tasks like placing blocks or a torch. Half the time you place the block, and the other half you sit there madly clicking the mouse while nothing happens. There also seems to be an issue with lighting. Personally, this is one of my all-time favorite games.
The two main selling points of this game are obviously the amazing art style, which you can see right off the bat is super unique and interesting, and secondly the narration. The narration of this game plays dynamically depending on what actions the player takes. The story is told from the all-seeing, all-hearing narrator telling someone the story of your tale as the Kid. His silky smooth voice is a pleasure to listen to as you're beating up bad guys and unfolds the story in a very natural yet immersive way. The fact that he comments on your actions in the game gives you a sense of place that you are actually in this world, exploring and fighting your way through this brilliant apocalypse. The ending is an emotional rollercoaster and it will leave you thinking for long after the game is finished.
Of course, the gameplay is solid too! It is an isometric brawler at heart, with some rpg elements thrown in for extra customization to your own unique play style. After you unlock the shrine, you get to choose how difficult the game will be. Activate more shrines and the game will be harder in different ways, but you will receive a greater payoff. This works really well and is a fun way to handle difficulty. That being said the combat IS probably the weakest part of the game, but it is more than enough to keep you playing through the (about) 12 hour long storyline.
I wholeheartedly recommend it.

A few things could certainly be improved on, and might affect your enjoyment of this game, so be aware:
* Although injuries, including death, are permanent for your team, they mean absolutely nothing to the computer teams, which return to their starting condition after every single match. That gets a little old after a while. There's no sense of permancy other than on your side of the pitch, and it makes it tempting to rely on "save-scumming" to get through tricky matches.
* I would vastly prefer a way to choose exactly which teams are 'legal' - even if it was just a way to pick which of the expansion teams were included rather than the current all-or-nothing approach. Be prepared for constant, tedious battles with Khemri...
* If playing a solo game, the computer continually spams pathetic 'smack talk' style messages at you in chat, which do nothing to aid immersion but reveal rather more about what the developers think of you as a person (or what kind of person they think plays their game).

While the dialogue is poorly executed (at least in English), the combat in Blades of Time offers enjoyable button mashing.  If you can keep track of which Prince of Persia or Devil May Cry entries may work on your computer then you'll probably want to purchase them instead, but this plays much better than Garshasp.  I'm curious to see how the previous telling, X-Blades, holds up.
Where Blades of Time seems to shine is in its Outbreak mode.  This is a MOBA variant which can be played either cooperatively or between teams.  There's a catalog of items/effects to earn and I appreciate having an entry in the genre with decent gamepad controls.  Unfortunately, there is little online competition despite some enthusiasm in the Steam forum.  There is, however, a single player mode where most of the same awards can be earned.  If my review sounds too vague, it's because I've been playing short sessions of this for so long I've forgotten the subtleties of the campaign.
Dumb story aside, Blades of Time's real cardinal sin is the placement of checkpoints before cutscenes instead of after.  There's a button to skip through them, but it's still annoying after a dozen deaths in a boss fight.
I wouldn't bother getting the Dismal Swamp DLC on its own.  The included mission removes character abilities in favor of allies to protect.  An Outbreak map might also be included, but if that's what you're after then you might as well get the Limited Edition for the Sky Islands one as well.

Você vê este jogo em promoção, barato, talvez deva comprar. Vê a expressão pensativa do Kid e gosta das letras de "Bastion", e o nome também não lhe parece nada mal. Você olha os reviews, a maioria positivos, vê as imagens e pensa "ahhhhh, é mais um daqueles joguinhos".
Minha situação é a do homem que está diante de uma obra de arte coberta, enquanto todos ao redor dele vêem apenas o pano vazio. Como explicar Bastion? Ele difere de vários outros jogos pelo simples fato de ser inteiramente narrado por um homem, mas não é "somente um narrador não-personagem". Ele não só está na história, como faz tudo parecer muito mais profundo sob a voz dele.
"Now here's a kid whole whole world got all twisted, leaving him stranding on a rock in the sky."
Ele acorda, descobre-se sozinho numa ilhota de chão, no meio do céu. Como se tivesse dormido e tudo tivesse desaparecido, menos o chãozinho e o colchão. Mas quando ele anda, as pedras surgem e formam um caminho! Bom, você nada pode fazer senão seguir. O garoto encontra seu fiel martelo, e também alguns seres que antes trabalhavam como operário, mas por algum motivo resolvem te atacar.
Para onde ele irá? Para o Bastion. Onde todos devem ir em caso de emergência. Mas ao chegar lá, esperando encontrar as pessoas, ele encontra primeiro um homem. "He finds me", diz o narrador. E então a verdadeira história começa.
Bom, tudo parece estar suspenso no céu, então tem claramente alguma coisa errada. Você precisa então juntar Cores espalhados pelos... bom, pelos lugares restantes de Caelondia, porque os Cores têm poder e os mantém no lugar. Ao mesmo tempo você encontra alguns fragmentos, que, primitivamente falando, seriam como a "moeda" do jogo.
A jogabilidade é bastante simples. Teclas para se mover, botão esquerdo do mouse pra usar uma arma, botão direito para usar a outra. Barra de espaço para rolar, shift para bloquear, botão do meio do mouse ou Q pra usar habilidade especial. A Calamidade aconteceu, mas você não sabe a causa, e ficará, durante o jogo inteiro, perguntando-se o que é isso. A cada Core reunido, você pode recriar um novo edifício em Bastion. E vamos dizer que reunir os Cores é... Bom, não quero estragar a surpresa.
Você tem algumas armas que vai ganhando ao longo do jogo, e pode escolher duas delas pra usar. Cada arma possui cinco upgrades, e cada upgrade possui dois melhoramentos. Você escolhe um melhoramento de cada upgrade, podendo alterar quando desejar. Há poções que conferem efeitos passivos, um Achados-e-Perdidos, um Memorial com missões... E criaturinhas que você encontra, lembrando-se de que nem todos são seus inimigos.
É um jogo fácil, pelo menos até você libertar os deuses do Santuário, que conferem mais dificuldade ao mesmo tempo que aumentam o ganho de Experiência. Há também os Proving Grounds, que são desafios específicos para cada arma(e um para o escudo). Alguns chegam a ser moleza, mas a maioria são mesmo desafios, e Bastion é um jogo completo, desafiador, profundo. Há também os "Who Knows Where", que são "desafios" onde o Kid dorme, e o narrador conta uma parte especial sobre determinada personagem.
E no final, tudo terminará com uma grande decisão sua.
Feito para ser completado duas vezes. Não digo isso porque "O jogo é tão bom que te dá vontade de completar de novo", de jeito nenhum - quando você completá-lo pela primeira vez, entenderá.
Usei muitas palavras para meu jogo inde favorito, mas se eu só pudesse usar poucas, elas seriam "Esse jogo possui uma alma".

The gameplay is exactly like other turn based 4Xs; expand, manage, bide your time and plot your enemies demise.
Pros:
- I've never found a space 4X that you can conveinently terraform gas giants into usable planets with worker units.

Suddenly the colony ships I had following my armada weren't even going to be used.... I made the Jedi weeep as I literally shattered the remaining planets my enemies held.
Cons:

Overall, I would recommmend you get this one if you like fantasty galactic geneocide as much as I do!

Note: I haven't played the multiplayer yet, so I'll only be talking only about the singleplayer.
I used to be an active poker player back in 2008 when competitive poker was all the rage, but I stopped then, and haven't picked it back up until now. The poker games available these days, I just don't like; not even Telltale's Poker Night at the Inventory or browser based games. So I decided to give this a shot because...why not? I discovered the singleplayer is good, the A.I. has a good variety of play-styles, and the game is very fair overall - it doesn't cheat. However, this game still leaves alot to be desired. The game lacks the option of limit games and cash games, as well as the diffrent variations of poker, like Horse and Omaha. It would be great if these options were available, but they aren't.
Being that I'm tying to re-learn Texas Hold em again, I find the pacing of the game very enjoyable. However, if you're totally new to poker, this game won't help you to learn the game in any way - you're on your own. It would be nice to have an "advice" button like the game Stacked did where you can get mentorship on how to play your hand based on the cards on the board.
As for the free-to-play model, it's your standard cosmetic micro-transaction deal. You can also buy extra chips for multiplayer if you go broke and don't want to grind it out in singleplayer. Speaking of grinding, you also get a couple thousand free chips granted to you daily as a login reward.
In summary, the game isn't the best it could be, but what's currently there is really enjoyable. Give it a shot!

Oh my god. Where do I even begin.
A brief explanation of the plot/overview of this game, I guess (might be inaccurate since I gave up less than an hour after playing):
This is a hack-and-slash game where a greedy lone wolf treasure hunter ignores the advice of an ancient temple guardian, touches a magic object (that she was directly informed by said guardian that the power within the object is completely fatal to humans; by the way, she is, in fact, a human, so she is no exclusion to this reality), and gets the♥♥♥♥♥♥cursed out of her.
Alright, onto the specifics.
This game tries to be fast-paced and cool with a sexy heroine main character to keep people interested (i.e. the half-dressed protagonist that has jello for breasts that will dramatically move around even if you are just walking, and whose♥♥♥♥♥is always hanging out in hopes that you stay focused on that as often as possible; I was able to ignore both things and focus on the absolute terror that was the gameplay since I have no interest in either of those subjects [laughs in aseuxal]), but in reality, this game is just a wildly unpleasant experience all around.
The movement controls are disorienting as♥♥♥♥♥♥ Your default movement speed is "a desperate sprint for your life." If you jump too close to a ledge, Ayumi will abruptly roll forward instead of doing the logical thing and jumping up. The double jumping is also commonly unresponsive.
The melee combat is standard at best. It controls like a hack-and-slash game. Run up to common enemies, and spam a button at everyone until they stop moving. That much is at least correct.
The gun combat is honestly funny as♥♥♥♥♥♥ If you are locked onto an enemy, Ayumi will not miss a
, even if they are all the way across the area from you. In the second level, I was practically in tears when I became a sentry gun and skipped enemies across the beach with my guns like a rock getting skipped over water. Ayumi being a sentient aimbot program is fairly useful, I guess.
The magic combat is okay. In order to use magic, you need to build up "rage" by either attacking enemies until you have enough rage to use a spell, or by holding down the key/button that your spell is bound to until her rage is charged up enough to use the attack. Since this game likes to fling large hordes of enemies in your direction at once, you typically have enough rage to last you the whole fight.
The combat interface as a whole is rather confusing. Nine times out of ten, I did not even know that I was getting hurt. Usually, in games with a health/damage feature, you know when you are getting attacked since your character will typically make a noise or flinch or something when harmed, or maybe the screen will flash red for a second or whatever. Ayumi does
if it is not a big enough attack to stagger her. I kept looking up at her health and getting surprised at how much I had lost without noticing anything.
Ayumi as a character made me want to stop playing before the opening cinematic for the first level even ended. She sounds like the "mean girl in high school," and she talks as if she is above everyone else. For example, in her
, she outright states that she is "the best treasure hunter ever." That opinion is open to a staggering amount of debate, have some ♥♥♥♥ing humility. Later on, when the aforementioned temple guardian warns her that the object that she is trying to steal will straight-up kill her and tells her to leave while she still can (without trying to harm her, by the way; he was literally going to just let her turn around and walk out of the temple unharmed and without a fight), her reaction was to flip her hair, roll her eyes, adamantly state "yeah right," try to steal the object anyway while the guardian was not looking at her, and then get cursed like a dumbass since she thought that grabbing an object that is "fatal to humans" was a bright idea. For the "best treasure hunter in the world," she sure does make some goddamn thoughtless decisions. I am almost completely certain that all of her previous heists up to that point were from children that were holding a coin that they found on the ground.
On a related note to Ayumi, the physics in this game are abysmal. I am not talking about her earthquake jello breasts again, either. I am talking about her three ponytails. I have never seen hair move that erratically in my whole life. In every cutscene or moment of gameplay where she was moving around too fast, her ponytails went ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. They looked like the tentacles of the Kraken emerging from the waters and searching for a ship full of sailors to pull into the depths of the sea. This was a game for the Xbox 360 and PS3, too. Those consoles had pretty good graphic capabilities for their time. I am not forgiving this one. If her hair was that unstable, they should have changed it to something more usable.
This game, at the time of writing this review, is on sale for $10. That is the normal retail price. But, from what I have experienced, this game certainly is not even remotely worth that much money. If you seriously want to buy the game that badly, please wait for the price to drop hard first.

Fallout 4 was one of the most anticipated games of 2015, the critics loved this game, however I could not help but feel disappointed. I found the game had the potential to be great, it improved upon the original looting system and shooting mechanics but the atmosphere didn't feel like a typical fallout game. The game is noticibally more colourful and doesn't have the green or orange tint feature in Fallout 3 and New Vegas, however the saying "you don't now what you have till its gone" becomes relevant here as the tint gave the idea that the world had ended and that life had become bland, relenting and difficult. The ligher and more colourful environment does not tie in well with the story or soundtrack. This story is noticibly darker and sadder than the other 3D fallouts and the soundtrack does a great job of further expressing the darkness and sadness, which is a good thing until you realise that the story is the same as Fallout 3's *spoiler's ahead*.
In fallout 3  your mother dies and you leave your vault to search for your father only to get dragged into a war because of them, In fallout 4 your wife/ or husband dies and you leave your vault to find your son only to get dragged into a war because of him. There the same plots just instead of finding your father your finding your son.
Like most Fallout and Elder Scrolls games the characters that inhabit the world don't show you any recognition even if you just saved them from a raider attack or rescued there daughter. For a world that supposed to be full of life there is no expression of that life, leaving you with forgetable characters and events.
The game offers no closure, humans naturally seek closure within their real lives, so when you complete this game you feel as though there should have been more. They could have ended the game with the funeral of your family, or showing the changes that the winning faction inspired within the common wealth or settling down alone or with your romance partner. All 3 of these endings would have added closure.
Also for an RPG game there are very little choices that are hard or morally questioning. The only easy to remember choice  is deciding what faction to choose. Choosing your faction doesn't change the way your character acts either, your choices don't impact upon the world or yourself to an effective measure.
The dlc which could have improved the game were also dissapointing.
Bethesda stated that there would be 6 major content dlc released after launch.
3 of those 6 dlc are stuff packs, and in no way are stuff packs major, adding conveyer belts is not an amazing thing its can be useful but it is also quite lame.
The Automatron dlc does have it's moments, but calling a 2 hour experience major is pushing it. Like the main story this dlc doesn't have great closure. *Spoiler* After you beat the villian, who is actually someone trying to do good, she becomes depressed but chooses to stay in her lair, instead of returning to the commonwealth to fix her mistakes, but don't wory she says that you can fix her mistakes for her by going on unlimited amounts of search and destroy quests.
Far Harbour is offers no hard choices, it's easy to get a peaceful ending and outside of that your given numerous search and destroy, and fetch quests. Definetly not worth the money there charging.
Nuka World completely ignors morals, the character is pitted against traps set by elite raiders and when you finaly talk to a raider your character sounds all chearful and willing to join them. This doesn't make sense if your character until that point has been nice, selfless and willing to help. But don't worry you can just kill all the raiders with no plan or struggle, no inspirational speech to cause the slaves to riot and no sense of achievement once you complete the dlc. Completely unimmersive.
I could not recommend vanilla fallout 4 even with the greatly improved ghouls.

Having played pretty much all of the Assassin's Creed games, I think I can say without the shadow of a doubt, this is by far ome of the best installments in the series. After being bashed on at its release due to the obnoxious amount of graphical bugs / crashes / faulty mechanics / frame rate drops, the game has seen major improvements, to the point where you can play it flawlessly at ultra, 120 FPS with no stutters or graphical glitches whatsoever.
The story is engaging, ang the main character, Arno, is in my opinion much more likable than Connor / Haytham / Edward ever were, bringing the sarcasm and irreverence lost since the end of AC Brotherhood with Ezio Auditore's character.
After some UPlay connection issues (to be honest, the biggest gripe with the game at this point is the UPlay DRM), I was able to run some Multiplayer and Co-op runs with my brother, and we were both blown away by how much content there is to be done in the free roam mode, as well as the complexity of the mechanics and level design shown in the coop missions (it's not a complete co-op campaign, but it's well worth the money if you want to have a good time with a friend or relative).
Also tried the Companion app that syncs with your game to give another depth to the map, and the content in both single and coop. Not my cup of tea, but worth giving a try if you're into those kind of things.
All in all, a pleasant surprise to have a game that received such flak, be redeemed through updates that improved the experience, even if all of that effort seems to end up being shadowed by its former errors.
A game worth your money, and a solid 9/10, not 10/10 due to the obnoxious UPlay connectivity issues.

XCOM 2 is the strongest game in my library of games. It's a game you can return to again and again because the enjoyment is from facing against a strong challenge and bringing home a well earned victory again and again.
A lot of people have complained about the turn timers for missions but ultimately the reason for the timers is to put the player on the back foot and force them not only to defeat the enemy but to take risks. These are the sort of risks that an underground resistance movement would have to take. Losing a mission isn't game over by any means - you can even lose an entire well trained team on a mission and still recover a campaign. The people who are really hurt are the people who think that only 100% victory on every single mission counts as success. You can complain that the timers are unfair but this is a game about succeeding against an unfair opponent.
In every way XCOM 2 improves on XCOM - it is an incredibly detailed puzzle game where balancing risk and reward is key. If you think you can achieve success without risk you will be punished ultimately. Your rookies might miss easy shots but if you are a good commander you will find a way to turn the sum total of all those shots into a success.

Personally, this is one of my all-time favorite games.
The two main selling points of this game are obviously the amazing art style, which you can see right off the bat is super unique and interesting, and secondly the narration. The narration of this game plays dynamically depending on what actions the player takes. The story is told from the all-seeing, all-hearing narrator telling someone the story of your tale as the Kid. His silky smooth voice is a pleasure to listen to as you're beating up bad guys and unfolds the story in a very natural yet immersive way. The fact that he comments on your actions in the game gives you a sense of place that you are actually in this world, exploring and fighting your way through this brilliant apocalypse. The ending is an emotional rollercoaster and it will leave you thinking for long after the game is finished.
Of course, the gameplay is solid too! It is an isometric brawler at heart, with some rpg elements thrown in for extra customization to your own unique play style. After you unlock the shrine, you get to choose how difficult the game will be. Activate more shrines and the game will be harder in different ways, but you will receive a greater payoff. This works really well and is a fun way to handle difficulty. That being said the combat IS probably the weakest part of the game, but it is more than enough to keep you playing through the (about) 12 hour long storyline.
I wholeheartedly recommend it.
