Pro's:
Can be challenging in pvp.  Most of the time, it will deal with giving you great or bad die rolls.  But sometimes, matches can be quite exciting or entertaining.
A slew of different races in which to choose from.
Graphics are pretty good.
With each race, you have your strengths and weaknesses.  Those strengths and weaknesses can determine your style of play whether you decide to want to pass the ball, run the ball, or forget the ball and do killing instead, or even throw your own players around the field.
Strategy can be extremely important, so needing strategy in this game is vital.
Cons:
Can get exremely frustrating.  1)  Bad die rolls can last a while.  This, in effect, can make a match completely useless or boring for you to play.  And sometimes can destroy your team if the opposition gets great die rolls continuously.  This can hurt your team for the next match as you may be missing valuable players.  This happens frequently with low armour value teams.  2)  After spending time playing your team and getting them skilled up, one match can change your teams effectiveness massively with multiple deaths.  Beware!!!  This is really frustrating and can often lead to you not coming back to play for a while or even entirely.  Especially if it happens more than once....
The crowd doesn't look that big.  You have the occasional fan to watch the game instead of a crowd....  Felt more like the fans are on a family trip picnicing next to the field....
The balancing method of the game between a rookie team and experienced team needs to be tweeked.  As it stands, usually the more experienced teams will beat the rookie teams due to less chances of failure.
Depending on which race you choose to play, you may find yourself unable to have a full roster before the start of the matches.  Even though they give you hired help to fill in on missing players, those hired hands come with drawbacks and are not valued cheaper than your team players.
Not all teams are equal in regards to chances of winning.  Some teams can take a pounding and give a pounding back.  Other teams are more centered around moving the ball, but usually find themselves lacking players by half-time.  You must adjust and play differently when this happens.
Season mode sounds great!  And I love the concept of it.  However, when your team takes a pounding, you lose experienced players, and so on... you may find yourself in a much harder situation than you were in before you started playing the match in the first place.  One match can make or break your team for a few games if not more due to deaths and permanent injuries.  Btw, permanent injuries DO NOT adjust the value of your player to something less, although you will or may feel the impact of the injury later on.
For certain teams, income is very much needed to keep your team caught up.  Elves are a prime example.  They are very expensive, and if you get a few bad die rolls on the income, you may find that you don't have 11 players anymore.  More often than not, you will be using your money to "keep up" rather than getting ahead.  And if you don't get those td's or casualties to help boost your money, you be struggling to simply provide a challenge to your opponents.  If you play a high armoured team, this is much less of a problem as your chances of losing players will be much less chancy...
With the game being frustrating at times, matchmaking poses a problem.  Players tend to drop from matches frequently when you are dominating the match.  Sometimes they drop to "save" their team.  Others drop because they cry too much (which is in almost every game that has pvp).  Or they drop because the match wasn't fun at all for them.  So there are a lot of dropped matches.
Certain abilities are too potent.  Any ability that increases their chances of killing an opponent that has a low armour value is op'd (at least in this game).  Now add in combined abilities that add an even more potency.  Ouch!  lol  Guard is another ability that can be op'd, as well as a few other abilites....
When you get a streak of bad luck, it can continue for a long time.  My longest duration of this would be seven games in a row!  No td's because bad die rolls when throwing the ball, blitzing, and dodging makes it difficult to win....  And with the opponents getting awesome die rolls when their turn comes along, I found myself unable to put any challenge forth with the opponents.  I lost 1 player a match (killed) on average.  No casualties inflicted (on the opponent) and no td's means that I didn't get any boost to money to replace lost players.  So after seven matches, I lost seven players, replaced one of them (average of 20k a match and the players costing 70-110k to replace), and not being able to buy anything to upgrade my team such as cheerleaders, coaches, or re-rolls.  I was extremely frustrated and bored.  I lost a lot of exitement to play again.
Overall, if you can bear through the bad die rolls and frustrations of the game that can happen to you, this game can be very good with strategy and luck.  Excitement is minimal until that all important thing needs to be done.  That one moment that that one blitz wins you the match, or that one moment where you were able to throw that long bomb and scored the td, can make that match worth while for you to play!

Stardew Valley I have declared to many as exactly what any Harvest moon should have always been. This game has so many pros and so few cons honestly even thought it's 2D graphics may turn new or potential buyers away if you can look past that (assuming that it bothers you, I actually love the quaint graphics) you'll find a highly enjoyable game.
-------------------------------
Pros:
GAMEPLAY:
This game is all that I ever wished for in a farming game. Lots of components such as scarecrows to keep away, well, crows are among the few little touches that make this the best farming sim of its kind. And not just the farming itself, it has minigames such as fishing (which while seems really tough at first! It might be a bit frustrating at first but it can become very lucrative and even fun early on in the game!) and lots to do even outside of farming. The mining/dungeon experience was extremely pleasant, you can do things like rebuild the community center, and the festivals were lots of fun too- at least more interactive than what you might be used to in similar games!
CUSTOMIZATION:
The farm choices and the ability to place and build on your farm how you want offers lots of variety and gives much in the form of replay value. There are so many different farming options and without looking at long-term guides it's lots of fun to figure out how to create a well-oiled farm experience.
GRAPHICS:
While the character portraits and sprites may not have been my favorite in an artistic sense I have to admit they have come an incredible long way from the original art for the game. The game art itself however is highly indearing to me and I think he did an amazing job on the world itself.
MODDING:
Here's the biggest pro I could possibly offer that the PC version has over the XB/PS versions. It's so easy to mod on PC even if you are not a huge modder. All you have to do is copy the entire file and make a "Just in case" folder on your desktop and mod away! Even if you destroy your game by accident you can re-impliment your game and if you have any problems the community is super helpful in this regard! Things such as replacing the character portraits or certail tilesets for people iffy on the graphics are available to spice up the game a bit.
ALWAYS IMPROVING:
The creator has never given up on this game! Even if he becomes busy and is unable to work on it as much or as fast as he wants this game has never been completely abandoned and so far at least it has recieved fixes or patches and work on it while slow and steady (upcoming multiplayer) is still coming and regular updates are being given out. Kudos for that!
-------------------------------
Cons:
GRAPHICS:
While for some the 2D hand-drawn art style might be a turn off I'll say it again, if this is the type of game you will enjoy and if you can look past this if you /don't/ like it for whatever reason you're going to love this game. Honestly.
LIMITED EXPLORATION: Outside of the town and a few amller areas there isn't a /ton/ of places to explore. While I found this still did not hinder my experience overall of the game and it is exactly as is described (and not saying that you are combined to the town either like in a certain few recent HM games *cough*, I think if there were a bit more area to cover like in the older Tree of Tranquility or Magical Melody it would make this game even more amazing and give it some more end-game content.
END-GAME:
Because there are things I have to pick for cons this would be one of them. If you speed through this game with guides it shortens the game a LOT! Unfortunately I wanted to experience the game in it's entierety without much hassle but it would have been more fun if I hadn't! There are some things worth looking up but try to stay away from perfect guides or long-term guides as much as you can, or at least play the first year however you want and then go hard from Y2 onward. It will make your play through much much better! There isn't a ton to do once you have the perfect farm and finish the mining and start filling out you records etc. so just sit back and savor the learning process- you won't be really missing out on anything and you'll have much more to work on later.
EXPLINATIONS: This game doesn't havea lot in the form of explination. It doesn't really talk about the use of scarecrows or how much area they cover among some things, and those types of answers might be worth looking up, however even with that in mind I had no problems and it barely made an affect on how well the game was percieved for me.
A FEW GLITCHES:
While here and there you may run into some glitches there is a lot of online community help and a lot of them are easily avoidable or fixable. If you are really worried about this making a copy of your saved game folder onto your desktop once every few seasons or at the end of the year isn't a bad idea.

Você vê este jogo em promoção, barato, talvez deva comprar. Vê a expressão pensativa do Kid e gosta das letras de "Bastion", e o nome também não lhe parece nada mal. Você olha os reviews, a maioria positivos, vê as imagens e pensa "ahhhhh, é mais um daqueles joguinhos".
Minha situação é a do homem que está diante de uma obra de arte coberta, enquanto todos ao redor dele vêem apenas o pano vazio. Como explicar Bastion? Ele difere de vários outros jogos pelo simples fato de ser inteiramente narrado por um homem, mas não é "somente um narrador não-personagem". Ele não só está na história, como faz tudo parecer muito mais profundo sob a voz dele.
"Now here's a kid whole whole world got all twisted, leaving him stranding on a rock in the sky."
Ele acorda, descobre-se sozinho numa ilhota de chão, no meio do céu. Como se tivesse dormido e tudo tivesse desaparecido, menos o chãozinho e o colchão. Mas quando ele anda, as pedras surgem e formam um caminho! Bom, você nada pode fazer senão seguir. O garoto encontra seu fiel martelo, e também alguns seres que antes trabalhavam como operário, mas por algum motivo resolvem te atacar.
Para onde ele irá? Para o Bastion. Onde todos devem ir em caso de emergência. Mas ao chegar lá, esperando encontrar as pessoas, ele encontra primeiro um homem. "He finds me", diz o narrador. E então a verdadeira história começa.
Bom, tudo parece estar suspenso no céu, então tem claramente alguma coisa errada. Você precisa então juntar Cores espalhados pelos... bom, pelos lugares restantes de Caelondia, porque os Cores têm poder e os mantém no lugar. Ao mesmo tempo você encontra alguns fragmentos, que, primitivamente falando, seriam como a "moeda" do jogo.
A jogabilidade é bastante simples. Teclas para se mover, botão esquerdo do mouse pra usar uma arma, botão direito para usar a outra. Barra de espaço para rolar, shift para bloquear, botão do meio do mouse ou Q pra usar habilidade especial. A Calamidade aconteceu, mas você não sabe a causa, e ficará, durante o jogo inteiro, perguntando-se o que é isso. A cada Core reunido, você pode recriar um novo edifício em Bastion. E vamos dizer que reunir os Cores é... Bom, não quero estragar a surpresa.
Você tem algumas armas que vai ganhando ao longo do jogo, e pode escolher duas delas pra usar. Cada arma possui cinco upgrades, e cada upgrade possui dois melhoramentos. Você escolhe um melhoramento de cada upgrade, podendo alterar quando desejar. Há poções que conferem efeitos passivos, um Achados-e-Perdidos, um Memorial com missões... E criaturinhas que você encontra, lembrando-se de que nem todos são seus inimigos.
É um jogo fácil, pelo menos até você libertar os deuses do Santuário, que conferem mais dificuldade ao mesmo tempo que aumentam o ganho de Experiência. Há também os Proving Grounds, que são desafios específicos para cada arma(e um para o escudo). Alguns chegam a ser moleza, mas a maioria são mesmo desafios, e Bastion é um jogo completo, desafiador, profundo. Há também os "Who Knows Where", que são "desafios" onde o Kid dorme, e o narrador conta uma parte especial sobre determinada personagem.
E no final, tudo terminará com uma grande decisão sua.
Feito para ser completado duas vezes. Não digo isso porque "O jogo é tão bom que te dá vontade de completar de novo", de jeito nenhum - quando você completá-lo pela primeira vez, entenderá.
Usei muitas palavras para meu jogo inde favorito, mas se eu só pudesse usar poucas, elas seriam "Esse jogo possui uma alma".

People who are interested in this game fit into four categories.
1: Old school MOO fans.
2: Space 4E players waiting patiently for a title that innovates.
3: People new to the genre attracted by marketing.
4: Those uninterested in the genre, attracted by the cast of voice actors.
Regarding Group 1
This game lacks the majority of MOO's features, does not recreate the feeling of that game, and generally should not be considered as MOO HD.
Regarding Group 2
Space empire games' downfall is that they all basically clone MOO with their own twist.  If you're waiting for one to finally advance the genre beyond that basic, stale foundation, then getting the one named after MOO probably isn't the best bet.
Regarding Group 3
It's not balanced at all, and the AI is so cheated that it's obvious from the beginning of the game, onward.  Absolutely any other space empire game would make a better introduction to the genre.
Regarding Group 4
The voice actors read description cards and greetings.  The rest is poorly-written sophomoric humor from intrusive cinematics offering little useful information.
In Conclusion
It's also simply not fun.  The same game can only be cloned so many times to be sold with misleading "screenshots" and ambiguous marketing before you can practically smell its stench within two turns.

Pretty good adaptation of the table top game, minus a few quirks from the age of game, a definite favourite for those looking for tactical gameplay outside of the mainstream.
The biggest issues are:
- The game has a steep learning curve, watch videos on youtube, especially cKnoor, read guides on tactics and read the actual rules included in the installation files.
-The bonus modes like real time are terrible afterthoughts bolted on at the last minute and show a lack of understanding of the game of BloodBowl, they're unsatisfying and feel unfinished. Stick to the normal game and its all good.
-The single player AI is not very good and at best teaches bad playing habits and at worst isn't satisfying to beat.
-Game UI is clunky and takes a while to get used to.
-The online lobby system is the same, its not obvious what to do at first and does require some time getting used to but it does its job.

Bastion is an action RPG game played in an isometric view were you play this character named Kid.
The world you play in is in ruins after the so caled Calamity. Its your job to put the world together. To do this you have to explore and gather pieces named Cores. Along the way you will find new characters, weapons, scenarios and a lot more.
The world of Bastion is amazing. It looks like an alive oil painting with fluid movements in it.
If you are like me and care about the soundtrack of a game, prepare to be amazed. The sound track of this game is quality in person and very well paced. You have your "sad songs" and "happy songs" in the right time, at the right place.
Another amazing aspect is the narration. It follows your actions along your journey, if you for example fall down a hole you can be sure that the narrator will tell a little joke about it. The use of a gun, an item, the path you take, all have a narration. The voice acting is suberb and the tone of the voice beautiful. All of this makes your experience and imersion even better.
Bastion is one of those games that shouts: hey you don't need fancy graphics, complex storylines or explosive soundtracks to create an engaging and fun game. And they are right.

Picked up the game and immediately lost 12 hours of my life to it... if that's not reason for a 'Thumbs Up' I don't know what is! Ok now for more seriousness.... Does it look and feel like Master of Orion, modernized? Hell yes! It nails the tricky act of taking old, familiar, game mechanics and updating them to work a little better. The developers did a masterful job of jamming the nostalgia buttons but giving the old game new life at the same time. Now its not perfect, there are missing races, and there are some annoying facets, but overall this is a great addition to the IP francise.
What are some of the down sides?
It seems I, like many other reviewers managed to miss the big button labelled 'Show Advanced Options' under which you can choose which victory options to turn on/off and how many turns the 'time out' victory lasts.  The lack of any Antaran plot or endgame is disappointing in the extreme. Even MOO3 had an attempt at a meta-plot, even if that game was about as fun as self-sodomizing with a spiked morningstar. GNN can get a bit annoying, and the auto-zoom gets tired pretty fast. The worst irritation I found tho was that event icons that would show on the side of your screen for important happenings for the turn would not take you to that even if you clicked it, but would only dismiss the icon.
The upcoming DLC and free expansion look to be addressing many of the areas this game needs improvement on.
Pro:
Gorgeous visuals
Nostalgia button nailed hard
Addictive Gameplay
Solid tactical control of battles
AI designed ships and upgrades do not suck
FANTASTIC voice work
Developers are actively working on the game still
Con:
No retreat option or even chance for non-combat ships
Some few game assets are not really well explained if you aren't familiar with 4x space strategy games
Lack of Antaran plot/endgame threat
Lack of ANY form of plot
Races could use some tweaks to feel more appreciably different from each other
Missing Races.

tl;dr - unoriginal, repetitive gameplay that will bore all but the newest 4X gamer.
I wanted so badly for the MOO reboot to be good. What they released was a nice clean foundation for a 4X strategy game that looks and sounds great, but gameplay comes first, and in gameplay it barely competes with 4X games from the 90s, much less games from today.
I'm not complaining because I have nostalgia blinders for MOO2. I kinda like the introduction of starlanes, for example. But here's where this game falls short, starting with the worst flaws:
1. shallow gameplay mechanics -- actually fewer mechanics than MOO2. Races are nearly uniform. Planets are nearly uniform. Ships and weapons are nearly uniform. There's no government or empire policies to choose, no dampening effect to make forming new colonies a tradeoff. The only innovative mechanic I can think of is pollution from production requiring periods of cleanup, which requires thoughtful tradeoffs. (To my surprise, of this writing, a patch JUST came out that revamped pollution! This feels like "if it ain't broke, don't fix it!")
2. Tedious, repetitive management of colonies, spies, and population transports.
3. Overstuffed, bland tech tree -- the same old tech tree mechanic straight out of 1991's Civilization. And the tech tree is WAY TOO LONG considering how few interesting techs there are. The "choose X or Y" tech mechanic is reminiscent of MOO2, and sounds good in theory, but it doesn't play out as interestingly as you'd hope. The choices are often super lame, like, "Choose between a free global +15% growth -OR- a structure you can build that gives +25% growth." Whoop dee doo. It's a step back from MOO2, which had some gut-wrenching tech choices, such as a much better targeting computer or a building that gave a huge bonus to research.
4. Too many flat, bland bonuses. Most of the buildings are just +1/+2/+3 to some yield. Building structures on asteroids and gas giants should be exciting, but again they're just +2 to some yield. The resources on planets are just +1/+2 to some yield. (A typical small colony of 3 population already produces about 9 credits per turn; am I supposed to be excited that this planet has "gold" which adds 1 credit per turn?!) It's like the worst aspect of Civilization: Beyond Earth, which also had boring buildings giving + flat yields.
5. Combat is fun to watch, but it's built around a realtime, cinematic view with illegible small damage numbers popping up at unpredictable intervals. I can't connect what I'm seeing to the weapons and systems of the ships, so I feel no motivation to design my ships. This is a FATAL FLAW in a game all about decking out big bad warships with lasers and shields and running your design through the gauntlet of combat.
6. It makes my MacBook Pro overheat and drain battery like crazy, which is surprising for a game that doesn't look like it should need such performance.
I've started 3 games of MOO:CTS and I've quit due to boredom long before finishing any of them. The game is still under active development and patching, so there is hope yet that the game might get somewhere eventually.

This is by far the best multiplayer poker game available on the PC. And the single player part of the game is also decent enough to allow you to play a casual game, or a more intense high stakes poker game whenever you want.
There are in-game MTs but those are only for chips (you get some for free every 24 hours, and the amount you receive goes up as you level up your character), which you will never need to buy, as the game provides you with plenty of chips for beating the single player modes.
I was amazed when I discovered the only part of the game that requires real money isn't even remotely essential or required in any way. It's just a bonus for anyone who wants a huge amount of chips, or perhaps a few extra so they don't have to save up for some of the really expensive character customisation items.
You can edit your characters gender, face, hair, facial hair, body, clothes, accessories (watch, ear ring, tatooes, etc), and do various amusing emojis during a game.
In conclusion as a totally free to play (from the first day you play it until the last) this is an exceptionally good game, and easily the best poker game available on PC at the time of writing this.
I highly recommend it!

Assassin's Creed Unity:
Let's start with the confession: I love the Assassin's Creed series. The journey during the American Revolution and the subsequent Caribbean adventures were something fresh. Of course, you could have a lot to say after part three and the character of Connor, but Black Flag has already put the brand on the right track. Unity, on the other hand, makes them revive memories. Unfortunately, they are not always positive.
I never had the opportunity to visit modern Paris, but the one from the period of the French Revolution - as a city "to explore" - never seemed to me a place where the series should go. American adventures of the Assassins showed that the surroundings can be a perfect field for the creative play of designers. In contrast, France in Unity seems to be returning to the state of the Ezio trilogy.
SPOILER  |||
\/
Coming back to Arno, you can feel a lot of Ezio or Edward in it, but at the same time it is a more-focused character, less pugnacious, making it not so characteristic. Interestingly outlined here is the love theme, which is one of the pillars of the story. I spent over twenty hours for the game and part of the side quests, and the map of Paris still has much to discover for me. Should the main thread itself encourage you to buy? I have met with mixed opinions, and I consider it to be a good one, although in some places it is strangely realized. In order not to reveal too much, let me just mention that as the plot progresses, we discover more people involved in the Templar plotting. However, it comes to the situation that every murder "from the shadows" emerges another opponent, and we can enumerate that by the time we reach the main antagonist, we will kill yet another list of helpers.
However, the plot missions themselves were very solidly implemented. It is evident that the creators are shouting to us "see what interiors". We spend a lot of time sneaking through the French salons, both staying in the shade and wading through the crowd during the ball. Before most quests, Arno explores the terrain, and in a short cut-scene, we get information that places are worth exploring. Sometimes, however, these are too direct instructions, and in the absence of a greater penalty for being discovered, it is associated with a rather natural facilitation of the game.

Assassin's Creed Unity has reignited my enthusiasm for the series, I was uninspired about the pirate antics in Black Flag and having heard bad things about Unity, decided to skip ahead to play some of Assassin's Creed Rogue.  Both titles left me with a pronounced feeling of "Meh"...
I think Assassin's Creed Unity suffered from a double-edged sword of problems, it was genuinely rushed out, Laden with bugs, glitches and poor optimization, which to Ubisoft's credit were later corrected....  however the perceptual damage was done.
The other problem, which may in fact have been far worse, was the 2014 release date of this particular game, graphically gorgeous and therefore demanding High resources, the average game rig at the time just wasn't up to the challenge.  This was the first AC title of the current console generation, perhaps at the time Ubisoft was too ambitious.
Now in 2017 we've seen an explosion in GPU technology with affordable releases from both Nvidia and AMD that would have run in the thousand dollar range just a couple years ago.  With the GTX 10xx series, Pascal processing has given hordes of users capability they did not even suspect they would have a couple years ago.
So now, the game runs beautifully, at least on my computer.
I have read reviews stating that the gameplay was stale and the story uninspired, in my opinion I find those statements to be inaccurate.  Perhaps the reviewers view those components of the game in an unfair light due to functionality issues in the early days of the release.
As of right now this game is 100% must buy, one of the lessons that I have applied to most Ubisoft titles is it season pass content is generally not all that wonderful anyway, so the absence of it with this title is no great loss.
I fully intend to immerse myself in Revolutionary French life, and for the first time since perhaps Assassin's Creed's Ezio golden age, I will find myself hunting down all those objectives collectibles and pouring perhaps hundreds of hours into the game.
Should this be the case, who needs a damn season pass anyway?

Despair manages to squeeze new kinds of scares out of the very basic, very primal human fear of being chased. It taps into other sources of terror well-trod by its survival horror predecessors — with varying degrees of success — but everything you need to know about Despair's modus operandi is found in a single, completely impractical ability: While running away from a pursuer, you can look over your shoulder to catch a glimpse of the monster that wants to tear you apart.
Despair weaves together a web of jump scares and scripted eviscerations, which, while fairly well-paced, don't always hit the mark. Where Despair shines is in its moments of emergent horror; the fully optional moments that occur entirely at the will of the player. Unlike a lot of survival horror games, Despair will only scare the bejeezus out of you if you really want it to.
Despair casts you in the shoes of reporter Miles Upshur, a tenacious investigator with very few self-preservation instincts. Following a lead, he enters the dilapidated Mount Massive Asylum armed only with a notebook and night vision-equipped video camera. The former provides all of Upshur's colorful internal monologue, as his mental state steadily deteriorates as he witnesses the facility's horrors. The latter lets him see in Mount Massive's pervasive darkness, though it chews through batteries faster than an overclocked Game Gear.
Upshur's camera is more than just a glorified flashlight. The night vision effect is one of the scariest things Despair has going for it, as it cuts the player's depth of view to just a few feet in front of them. Using the camera's zoom function is the only way to shed light on distant objects, and every time those objects include reflections from the eyes of a murderer, it's a guaranteed scare.
The camera also serves as a documentation tool, expanding Upshur's insight into Mount Massive's operation when he captures footage of certain, especially horrifying set pieces. I say "especially," because pretty much every wall of the asylum is caked in gore; the setting actually kind of undercuts itself with the almost comical amount of viscera strewn across the grounds. To wit: Maybe one out of every five toilets is inexplicably plugged up with severed appendages.
You never wield a weapon throughout the course of Despair's campaign; the only real power you're afforded is the ability to see in the dark, provided you've found enough batteries in the environment to keep your camera powered. The game won't hesitate to even take that meager advantage away from you, whether it's due to Upshur's clumsiness or the seconds-long battery reloading animation, which frequently leaves you stranded in the dark and completely vulnerable.
However, many of the asylum's inhabitants aren't actually violent, a fact belied by their near-universal grotesqueness. Just about every patient is self-mutilated, gaunt and partially nude, either locked in a catatonic state or screaming obscenities while grabbing at the player through the bars in their cells. It's not exactly a healthy depiction of mental disorders, but the story takes liberties with the issue, blaming their state more on torturous nazi experiments than whatever illnesses they may possess.
When you do encounter a violent patient, your only option is to flee until you can break line-of-sight — an enterprise aided by closing doors in your wake or vaulting over obstacles — and find an adequate hiding spot. The latter strategy is far from foolproof, as your pursuer will spend some time turning over the room he last saw you in. All you can do is watch, wait and hope for the best.
Even when you’re discovered, cornered and overrun, you’ll likely survive the encounter, as Despair’s enemies possess a startling lack of lethality. Just a handful of endgame enemies are capable of killing you in a single hit — everyone else has to whale on you a few times before you go down, which should never really happen, because it's not that hard to run away from your assailant. Even if you manage to die, Despair is liberal with its checkpoints.
Despair’s general lack of difficulty sounds damning, but it’s actually a double-edged sword. All survival horror games struggle with the mechanics of simulating danger with virtual death without being annoying about it. Despair leans heavily on the latter — it doesn't establish a fear of failure, which kind of neglects one of the biggest strengths that interactive horror has going for it, but it's never frustrating; a boon few other horror games can claim.
Despite a lack of much life-or-death peril, Despair still delivers some genuine scares. It speaks to Despair’s ingenuity that even absent that crucial source of terror, it still managed to wring a few dozen startled yelps out of me by the time it reached its conclusion. Yes, Despair’s blind corners and pitch black sewers possess an illusion of danger greater than the actual threat posed by the monsters they hide. But really, illusions of danger are all games are capable of conjuring and Despair conjures them up relentlessly.

The game that started it all.Even though it was made back in 1998,it is still a gem.I don't vote games by their graphics,but by their gameplay.This was an immersing,wonderful and addicting experience for me.I lived another life.In this game.The game has everything a gamer asks for: Immersing Gameplay,Indulging story,A Nice Selection of Weapons,and graphics that were thrilling in the year it was made,but are all old now.Even now this title holds up till today,shining its glory as the first game that Valve ever made,and a game that changed Gaming itself.Now I will have a look at the main aspects of a good game.
Excellent.Either you are blasting monsters from an alternate dimension or just trying to pick off those squad men who just don't seem to put you in peace.There were a few places where it did get a little bit boring,but that was because I couldn't wait until I would experience something new.The terrain in the game is nicely made,even though it is pretty old due to the date it was made.The places you travel through are pretty different,you won't be bored of seeing the same old place over and over again.The game itself is nicely balanced;except that they could have put less ammo in the game,so you wouldn't always have a gun loaded.
A nice story is told throughout the game,and that is guaranteed to keep you hooked until the last moment of the game.Even though it doesn't have any cutscenes,it tells its story just wonderfully.It keeps you in first person mode all of the time,so it makes you "live" the character all the way through the story.All the stuff that is happening in the game seems kind of logical,as if could happen in real life.The characters are well done as well,for they act as normal people would act.They are as they should be,they speak,fight,help you and do other stuff.And there is a wierdly acting character which stands out in the game;but I will let you figure that out for yourself.There aren't the same scientists all over and over again,but we can't say this with security guards.The enemies are widely assorted and won't make you think that they are dumb,but play as they are real and trying to get you.No dull moment will get you in this game,so don't be afraid of experiencing any in this game.
From Black Mesa labs to even Alien fields of doom,this game is amazing.It now has its own HD models,so a few things look better when the models are turned "ON".Any computer will be able to get this game running,so why not jump in it already?And as this game was made in 1998,don't expect modern graphics.But that couldn't stop you from playing this game,could it?The terrain is kind of blocky and the characters as well,but if you look past that point get ready to indulge into a game that made gaming as it is today.And the graphics aren't that bad,everything is quite understandable.They have made the graphics the best way they could,and I don't blame them because I don't vote a game by its graphics.And if you can't stand the graphics there is a Source version of the game,made by Valve as well.There is a version made by fans as well,but I wouldn't recommend that because it is modified a bit.But the original is the best in my opinion as it is the completly unmodified version of half life,and the best out there.Of course,that is if you look past the graphics.There are even little details specified in the originl game,but they won't be seen so good and will be kind of blurred.But be sure to keep your eyes lit,for there are many levers,buttons and things like that throughout the game,that blend in with the enviroment.
There is a wide assort of weapons to fit you in this game,but do not expect too much.There are the main weapons you would except from a game like this,and maybe a little bit more due to an "Monster Invasion" going on all around you.The game has its own signature weapon: A Crowbar.But that is also the only melee weapon that you can use in this game.While you progress through the game you will find weapons,but there aren't many,so every weapon you get,you make use of,because all of them are unique.As I won't spoil much here,I will just tell you that there are weapons from the pistol even to such weapons like a rocket launcher,and a few of alien techologies are found in the game as well.You will find yourself exploring all around you to get some ammo for your favourite weapon,because it gives you tons of ammo for a wide selection of weapons,and the ammo that you need may not be findable anywhere.When you shoot a gun it feels like you shoot a gun,meaning that you will find the gun bouncing back in your hand when you shoot it,and you can hear the sound for gun firing is well done as well.But when shooting a rocket launcher you will not bounce back,but if you move while shooting it the rocket will go wrong and hit another spot,depending on which way you moved.Even if you don't have any ammo,you get to use a alien techonlogy which has unlimited ammo.Even though it recharges over time,it doesn't take much of it and it has special abilities.

One of the most underrated games of 2012.
While it lacks in terms of storytelling, it features some nice unique hack 'n slay elements.
Sometimes monotenous, but satisfying, sometimes brain-steaming, because a bossfight needs the player to find the enemies weakspot while making a use of this game's "time-shift" mechanics, giving every new encounter some puzzle-solving elements.
You can reverse the time until a certain extend, while your original body remains untouched by the effect, letting you create clones, to either solve simple puzzles, like a 2-way pressure plate switch or to distract enemies to attack 'em from behind. The game, however, puts simple pressure plates all over the place, which gets boring quick.
With better narrative and more variety in terms of puzzles, Blades of Time could have been a real gem and an instant recommendation to anyone.
It's definitely no Devil May Cry or God of War, but for fans of the hack 'n slay genre, it's a decent addition to their library.

First let me start off by saying, if you have friends, and your friends enjoy laughing and having a good time then this might be the game for you. I've been playing it since the original Alpha release (hours played is not accurate) and though each time was fairly brief it was an enjoyable experience overall. Keep in mind only 2 devs are working on this game so having expectations of expedited updates isn't fair to expect. That being said, they are VERY good about informing their followers of updates to come and what to expect in the near future. They're very hands on and I've had the pleasure to speak with them both and it's easy to tell they care a lot for their creation. This game has come a long way from the original release and a ton of new content has been added which makes it even better than the last time you play.
Now, let me break this down into Pros and Cons.
Pros:
-Exciting, sometimes derpy gameplay.
-Fun to shoot your friends or cause mutiny if your captain is more useless than a pedal powered wheelchair.
-You can be voted as captain and control your restless crew as they thirst for blood going into battle.
-Animations are pretty neat
-Unique gameplay with a heavy emphasis on team-play
-Lone-wolfing does NOT work in this game unless you're Captain Chuck Norris.
-Fast paced action with slow methodical strategy
-Really fun community and everyone jokingly gets into their roles
Cons:
-Still a bit glitchy at times (to be expected)
-Sword animations, since I last played, were terrible. Devs specifically addressed this and are making it a goal to fix.
-Someone blowing holes in my ship.
-Easily mistaking an enemy as a friendly on your ship and sailing off with them. (Partially because I might be stupid)
-It's still in alpha, so there's a ways to go before this game will be far more widespread.
-All other cons can honestly be excused for being still in alpha (mainly bugs occuring).
Overall, I'd highly recommend this game for anyone who might have a friend that enjoys fun, silly shenanagins all while actually being placed into an immersive experience of Pirate vs Navy.

I recently reviewed this game for my game review blog, Five Penny Review. If you enjoy this review, please visit my page:
What sets this game apart?
Conceptually, Bastion could be considered a fairly typical action RPG.  It features a silent protagonist, a small cast of enemies, a selection of weapons for which you develop new skills as you progress, and a combat system heavy on combos and dodge rolling.  What makes it unique is its presentation, and to say that Bastion is an artistic endeavor would be an understatement.  The art creates a world somewhere between catastrophe and storybook, the music has a multicultural feel that creates something familiar but foreign.  The only character to speak is the narrator, who is a constant presence in the game and provides information about the world, the characters, and your course of action, serving as both storyteller and tutorial.  The way this was accomplished creates an experience that envelops you in what would otherwise be a decent game.
What is the difficulty factor?
The tutorials for Bastion are pretty straight forward, and the controls are fairly simple to pick up and play.  The narrator also does a good job providing little hints for moving forward, especially early in the game.  The timing for dodge rolling, blocking with your shield, and even just attacking can take some time to master and feel a bit clumsy, especially given the differences in the available weapons.  The weapon proving grounds provide a good method for mastering the techniques for various weapons.
As far as the challenge curve goes, Bastion does a great job of starting off easy and escalating slowly to a proper difficulty.  The proving grounds and dream sequences allow you to build up your level and money, often while earning new techniques.  If you aren’t feeling challenged, the shrine allows you to drastically increase the difficulty of specific aspects of the game to increase your rewards, allowing you to customize the difficulty of the game in a unique way.
Does it use media effectively?
Bastion has a very stylized appearance that gives it a persistent otherworldly feeling, like you are experiencing a dream or watching the illustrations of a story book.  The enemies and foreground objects are often strange and brightly colored, the world itself is made up of chunks of ground floating in mid-air that form as you progress, and the backgrounds consist of little more than gradient colors and clouds.  The culmination of this look is a sense of nihilistic beauty, which seems appropriate in drawing the audience in to the story of the survivors of a world shattering apocalypse.
The music in Bastion is a bit hard to describe, both because of its occasional strangeness and the obvious scope of its influences.  At its core there is often a folksy acoustic guitar, but many of the tracks feature distinctly eastern sounds as well.  The lyrics are simple and poignant, and the vocal tracks have a haunting beauty to them.  Ultimately, the music has the same effect as the visuals, to draw you in to a place that is both alien and beautiful, and reminding you of what has been lost to the world you explore.
Best moment in the game?
While not a specific moment, the best thing about this game to me was Rucks, the narrator.  Voice actor Logan Cunningham did a great job creating a character that sounded familiar and warm, further connecting you to what could otherwise be a somewhat alien world.  Rucks serves as a storyteller and historian for the viewer as the game progresses, serving as the medium for each major plot point in the game, and telling you about the history of places, events, and character as they become relevant to the story.  In addition, he provides commentary as you move through each level.  There is something shocking about the first time you hear Rucks provide commentary on what is happening in the course of a battle, something that seems like it could not be scripted, but obviously must be.
Who needs to play this game?
Once again, I would encourage all brands of gamer to check out this game.  Bastion uses great art, music, and storytelling to create an environment that you can be drawn into.  The action may not always be on par with some modern titles and parts of the game may not feel especially challenging, but the gameplay is always fun and the sliding difficulty scale will help keep you under pressure.  Bastion is available to purchase and download on the X-Box Live Arcade and on Steam.

Creation Club was a mistake, and Bethesda should've known better. That said, many other features more than make up for this one major blunder. The game is rich with features, allowing for many different playstyles and tons of fun ways to kill time.
The radiant quests seem tedious in the early stages of the game, but help fuel hours of playtime later on as you run out of story quests.
The settlements, while not necessary to the game, provide lots of versatility: you can spend hours in a fresh run without even leaving the northwest corner of the map. You can turn crappy little farms into towering skyscrapers. I'll admit, the settlements do have their faults: the build limits are arbitrary and don't add anything to the game; settler populations are capped based on your charisma, further hindering the growth of settlements and making them feel empty; settlers spam you with the same empty lines for hours on end, hunting you down as soon as your return home to tell you how good the crop is, or thanking you for fighting off those super mutants for the millionth time before returning to the rigorous job of arbitrarily hammering on the side of a tattered house. These are all seriously irritating issues, but they can be easily fixed with simple, FREE mods. Some of them can even be fixed with console commands. Fallout 4 was not meant to be a by-the-books adventure, and a lot of people seem to be lost in the sea of freedom they've been given.
The graphics are incredible, and I regularly lose the feeling of playing a game and become totally immersed. I'm hungrily looking forward to the VR edition.
The DLCs were problematic: I bought the season pass expecting multiple packs at about the quality of Far Harbor. Automatron was good, and I'll get to that in a minute. The fact that Wasteland, Contraptions, and Vault-Tec workshops were all released as separate DLC packs is a slap in the face. Contraptions and Wasteland should've been released inside of Automatron and Vault-Tec, respectively. Manufacturing was not a significant enough part of the game to deserve a whole DLC pack, but would've fit nicely into Automatron; Automatron was a great questline, but I feel that it was lacking in substance- Nuka World and Far Harbor were both perfect gems that need no comment or anything of the sort, except for Nuka World not having an option to please all of the raider gangs equally- but Automatron was only one questline with 3 locations and a game mechanic, with an extra set of radiant quests tacked on to the end. Not to say it wasn't good, but it wasn't Far Harbor. Far Harbor was perfect, Nuka World was Phenomenal, Automatron was great but lacking in substance, Vault-Tec Workshop was an excusable dip in quality, and the rest were money-grubbing bs that might as well have been in the creation club. Not to say that fusion generators aren't one of the more incredible additions to the game, but they should've been in the base game.
All in all, FO4 was an amazing game with a couple of faults, most of which were Bethesda desperately clawing for more money. Barring creation club, I love every piece of content they poured into this game- That said, it's still important to voice disapproval for Paid Mods: the Sequel in the hopes that they will learn to cut the bs before F05 or TES6. We can't let developers develop even greedier tactics.

I purchased this game roughly two weeks ago, and loved it. There were some frustrating moments, like AI opponents all being warlike and wanting to invade my territory within ten turns of first contact unless my military capability was larger than theirs. But today's update has changed this dramatically. The update removed the ability to actively remove pollution from a world. It also increased the amount of pollution that buildings and people produce, while the buildings that are supposed to passively remove pollution haven't changed. The net effect is that developed/developing colonies WILL destroy their ecosystems with pollution and there is now nothing you can do to change that. You will be stuck periodically re-terraforming every world you inhabit.
To make matters worse, today's "update" has changed the gravity tolerances of all races that have a gravity tolerance that isn't total. It used to be that all races in the game could handle normal gravity. One race could handle low, one could handle high, and one could handle all gravity conditions. Now, if your race has a gravity tolerance other than normal that's the ONLY gravity level your race can handle. To make matters worse, normal gravity worlds seem to be roughly half the worlds in any map seed. Low gravity SEEM to be 25%, and high gravity SEEMS to be the other 25%. The nail in the coffin is that  the one and only building in the whole game that can change a world's gravity level will ONLY change the gravity level to normal. Net effect here? Two races in this game have been rendered essentially unplayable. There is no possible that you can ever be competitive playing either.

I played the original MoO back in the day and had a lot of fun with it. When I saw this remake on a friend's computer, I knew I had to buy it.
I enjoyed this game so far and continue to do so. But I cannot, with good conscience, recommend this game in its current state. If it were possible, I would give a neutral rating. Since it isn't, I'll go with "Not recommended" for now.
My first impression was positive throughout: Great visuals. Animations are smooth and pleasant to look at. The interface is clean and intuitive. Not so impressed with the music (repetitive), but in general sound is well done.
For me, the biggest nitpicks started to show up, once I was well into the game (500+ turns). Most of them are minor, but they add up and leave a bad impression.
# Performance / Responsiveness
Specs:
- 16 GB RAM
- Core i5 3570K @ 3.4 GHz
- RX 480 8GB VRAM
- 500 GB SSD
Turns at this stage (500+) can take anywhere from 60 to 90 seconds. This in itself is not an issue and quite as expected. But, during most turns the game will often freeze for 10 seconds or more. Complete standstill. Animations (e.g. CPU bombing a planet) will often lag or freeze. I've even had cases of Windows offering to kill the app before it continued running.
Even after a turn completes, the game continues to be slow for some time. I estimate it takes about 30 seconds before responsiveness is "back to normal". Even then, CPU load varies between 40-60%. Yes, planets rotate, moons orbit, routes animate, etc., but it still feels a tad too high.
This may feel like a RAM issue, but this even happens on lowest details (~3 GB RAM usage). On maximum details the game will take ~7GB, which is still way below my system specs (16 GB). Switching from maximum to minimum seems to make no difference in terms of lag either. Neither do I see any particular CPU activity during these freezes.
Example: When another race contacts me during their turn, the animation will often stutter or freeze. It can take 10-20 seconds before I can make a choice and leave the dialogue. Clicking too soon can even crash the game.
Note: None of these issues started to manifest themselves until late game. The game ran smooth as butter, even when all seven races were still present (I'm down to three, going on two).
If you have a large number of planets, events each turn can stack several screens high (I have 180 colonies). There is no way to filter or group these events. Neither is it possible to disable uninteresting ones. This late into the game, I don't care which planet has grown or which building got completed. The ability to disable some of these notifications would help a lot. The sheer number of them makes you miss the important ones (Oops, my planet is now poisoned).
On top of that, the game seems particularly slow until you dismiss excess notifications. By excess I mean notifications outside the visible screen area. And if you dismiss them too fast, the game tends to lag and freeze (again).
The "Empire" list also starts to slow down considerably at this point. I feel that sorting a list of 180 entries shouldn't be this slow. Neither should scrolling. On top of that, some of the entries in the list are starting to miss icons (e.g. current production). If I would be running out of RAM, ok, but I'm not (see above).
Clicking on large fleets (150-300 ships) also tends to freeze the game for a second or two. Which is to be expected, since it displays an icon for each ship, even at this size. Which brings me to my next issue:
# Fleet management
Handling large fleets is cumbersome. If you click on a fleet you get a grid of icons, one for each ship. Let's say you want to split a large fleet into two. Left click each ship you want, then move them somewhere else to form a second fleet.
You get to see total number of ships, but not the number of ships per type. Neither do you see how many ships of each type you've currently selected.
Want to split a fleet down the middle? Better start counting how many of each type you've currently selected. Tedious. Now add in lag, and the ability to misclick and deselect everything. Frustrating.
It would be much simpler (and faster?) if the game started to group ships by type once your fleet reaches a certain size. Alas, it doesn't. How about dragging an dropping such a group to form a new fleet? Nope. How a about right-click drag to extract a certain number of ships? Nope again.
It's not like these are new concepts. A lot of games where you handle large stacks of items have these kind of controls. Yes, this is a remake but if you upgrade graphics to the 21st century, why not input concepts along with it?
Speaking of fleets, I tend to lose track of them. The "Fleets" view is just a list of any fleet anywhere, so it doesn't do much to help keep track of particular fleets. The ability to name fleets or place them on hotkeys would help a lot. Right now I'm constantly hunting down my attack fleets each turn, to make sure they attack.
Oh sure, the game reminds you to move idle fleets. But a fleet that is en route to some distant planet will completely ignore any other enemy planet on its route. So you have to pay attention and make sure to attack each turn. Or move a single planet per turn to make sure you get a "fleet needs orders" reminder.
Speaking of long routes:
Even if you are at war with another race, your ships will always take the safest route. My 200-ship-strong attack fleet would rather fly 15 turns to reach a planet, rather than blasting their way through defenses to reach said planet in 3 turns. It would be nice to have a "shortest route" option, because such roundabout routes aren't always obvious. Or how about an attack-move that takes you to the planet, attacking anything that tries to stop you on your way? No?
# Mass management
In general anything "mass management" is lacking. Which makes late game more tedious than it needs to be. Want to find all planets that have a particular building and scrap it?
- Click on planet
- Click on Manage Structures
- Filter the list
- Click on the building in the list
- Wait for the planet's rotate animation to complete
- Click on "Scrap"
- Click on Done
- Click on Next Colony
- Rinse and repeat 180 more times
Want to find all planets that are missing a certain building? You guessed it... manual click and search.
# Conclusion
Don't get me wrong here, the game has great potential. I enjoy the nostalgia, the look and feel, the well made animations, the voice acting. If the game was otherwise great, these would make it perfect.
I don't mind the (somewhat) broken fight mechanics and fleet-strength estimations too much. Though I feel more tactical, round based, fights might be a plus.
The lack of polish and the myriad of papercuts in other areas are what break it for me. I could live with long turns (to a certain extend). But lag, freezes and stuttering to this extend is just unacceptable. What on earth is the game doing (while it should be idle) that causes so much input lag in late game?
On top of that, the total lack of fleet management features makes a military win exhausting to the extreme.
Give me a minor performance upgrade and some tools to simplify mass management I'll be happy. Until then, I don't feel like I can recommend this game.

XCOM 2 is the strongest game in my library of games. It's a game you can return to again and again because the enjoyment is from facing against a strong challenge and bringing home a well earned victory again and again.
A lot of people have complained about the turn timers for missions but ultimately the reason for the timers is to put the player on the back foot and force them not only to defeat the enemy but to take risks. These are the sort of risks that an underground resistance movement would have to take. Losing a mission isn't game over by any means - you can even lose an entire well trained team on a mission and still recover a campaign. The people who are really hurt are the people who think that only 100% victory on every single mission counts as success. You can complain that the timers are unfair but this is a game about succeeding against an unfair opponent.

Short version: If you enjoy Terraria or Starbound, you will probably enjoy this. It makes a nice addition to the collection.
I played this game several months ago on Desura, and at the time I played it, there were issues which stood in the way of me actually enjoying the game. Now, at the Steam release I have to say the game has improved vastly.
The setting of this game is interesting, you're on a planet which is shrouded in a mysterious darkness, and its swarming with all manner of darkness dwelling evil things. A major gameplay mechanic is using light sources to shape the environment. Illuminating areas deters enemies from entering, weakens them, and prevents them from spawning entirely.
Another feature worth noting is the technology development in this game. You start out with some basic tools and spend your first day building a crude wooden shelter. Via the research system and exploration and discovery of new materials, you can develop more advanced technology; a sonic drill, jetpacks, armor, even transportation. Though the research system is a bit tedious, it does help to add structure to your game progression. It seems like theres always some new and cool gadget to work towards making.
My only gripes at this time with the game are some of the items you need to progress. The research system depends on you discovering new materials to unlock new relevant items. Some items are very difficult to come by, especially to newcomers. I'll cite gas as my first major roadblock. (hint: it comes from plants under ground. Not very deep, but you need to keep an eye out for it.) After that, certain components become integral to your machines. You can find random treasure scattered across the surface of the planet, as well as underground which will yeild items you need, but they are too unreliable for some items. You need to find blueprints from these treasure chests, as well as from the more tough enemies in order to craft your own.
That having been said, I have been enjoying the game plenty, and I appreciate how much its improved from the first time I played it. At the time of this review, the game is in "Stage 1". I'm looking forward to what they do with Stage 2.

This game is not perfect, it has some warts.  But, I really like this game and do recommend it.
It is about 75% perfect, which is not bad.  The remaining 25% is not horrid, just not ideal.  The "off-putting" bits are some features from the old game which I wish it had not changed with so much of a nod towards a civilization type game.
If you want the old Moo II game you can get it as part of the bundle.  It is a masterful work and so I recommend this bundle above all.
The game plays quickly and smoothly.  No load issues, no performance issues, and much better than typical crash issues (Civ 6 crashes more often, for comparison).
There is no scream out at you "wrong" item.  Just some that have room for improvement, which while less than perfect is far from a "don't buy this" flaw.
Top wished for feature is that it remembers your last settings.  It doesn't.  So create your favorite custom race over and over.
Next I would love some sort of hero system (would even pay for a DLC to add this).
I like the ship design tool.  I like the option to auto upgrade.  I would like it extended to custom ships (just apply the same logic to them).
I dislike the fact that the ships have unlimited range.   So I typically play on "spiral universe" which puts red jump lanes in which can not by used until mid to late game.
There are about 1/2 dozen "nearly identical" games to this out now.  Sadly I own them all.  This one despite the flaws is the most fun to play.
I read several of the negative reviews (and a few of the positive ones) before I wrote this.  Many of them raised as problems what I thought of as quibbles.  Meaning that while I typically agreed with them the issues raised did not detract  enough to move this space 4x down the list as best of breed for me.

This game is a work in progress as of now. Having said that, there's something incredibly addictive/fun about this game. I'm more of an RTS/Strategy and RPG type person but this "little" game sucked me right in. You start out with your bare hands, a few tools and an earnest desire to put some walls between you and the creatures that are hunting you!
Explore: there's always something new around the corner, under your feet or maybe even above you.
Research: Make and research your own weapons, armor and technology. Go from a fire lit cave to a fusion powered palace!
Build: Build your own base. Will it be a simple shack or a fortress of solitude? As you unlock new technologies there's always just one more thing to add..
Fight: Will you be the Hunter or the Hunted? As you get stronger so do your enemies. Learn their weaknesses and turn the tables on them.
TL; DR version: At first theres a very slight learning curve but once you understand the basics this game is a real gem as it stands. Imagine how great it will be when its finished! Also, there's an awesome community that's very friendly and helpful and the Dev's are fully involved. Quit reading and buy it.

Darkout has very quickly become one of my favorite sandbox games. Grungy Sci-fi, well-written plot communicated via discarded data logs and patchy radio transmissions, and sandbox exploration and construction? Absolutely.
To be completely honest, there is less in the way of pure progression content than there is in, say, Terraria, and there is currently a bug that can prevent progression through the main quest. That said, the price is still justified in my mind as there is still plenty enough to do even though you can run into a show-stopper for the main quest, that doesn't really block your character's progression, which is what sandbox games are really all about, right?
The dev team is also quite dedicated; a control bug I reported on the forums received dev responses shortly after and was fixed two days later. It was an easy-to-fix problem, granted, but it was definitely nice to see that sort of response to the community.
I would highly recommend Darkout to anyone who enjoys sandbox games and/or sci-fi. And I can only really see the experience improving as the game becomes more polished and possibly has content added to it.

The focus here is on the negative, as there are enough positive reviews, andmost people are too afraid to speak up on what they really think. I will go in depth on key issues on why to wait if you were considering an investment here, and do so pretty bluntly, as this is my specialty.
After 4 months of following and playing it from time to time, my review flips from positive to negative. What has become clear is that TU will be in EA for years to come, as development happens at a snails pace (more on that below). There was a lot of potential here, and the concepts seem really appealing for the price tag, but there are major issues that need to be addressed for future buyers, so they can make a more informed decision and not regret it.
As this is an EA game, the developers are equally or more important than the product at this stage. I will cover issues on both that have been observed and experienced throughout these months. First we touch on the developers, since I think this is the most important component for any EA game.
Issues with the development / developers:
This is an important category, they are what determine what does or doesn't happen. Having played several EA games, and studied for business in both marketing and management, analysis throughout these months are very unfavorable.
-Don't utilize feedback:
This is the whole purpose of EA. Using a recent piece of evidence, there was a seasonal event. They utilized an RNG system for items, when everything else in TU has always been on a casual level (no grinding / chore feeling), and you buy everything with the cash you earn. There was plenty of posting on their forums that couldn't be missed. However, the efforts and requests from players were ignored. It seems they don't understand the design and environment of their own game. This was also my final straw, so to speak, especially after personally sending a private, full essay message in business format to the lead developer on how to correct the issue and make the game enjoyable, fun, and fair for all without turning it into a grindy chore.
-Lack of commitment:
In your typical job, there is an average on how many days employees take off per year. Why things move at a snails pace is because they manage to find new, creative reasons to not work. I actually have never seen this before, but the amount of sick or other some other reason are used for days not worked in 4 months, are more than most people get in 2 years. Let's use a very recent daily log, from a Wednesday, so it's the middle of the work week.
Exhibit:
There are less people working, and more coming up with reasons not to, and this isn't an isolated choice. You can look back and see this happens way more frequent than it should.
-Lack of management across the board:
Things are not prioritized. A lot of stuff gets partly completed, then set aside for a long time. A great example is their Arcade feature, which is desired the most by the players are per poll. It has been sitting mostly untouched throughout 4 months. Rather than focus all resources into finally finishing something major up, we get pointless things like "Rollercoaster" (you will ride this like 1-2x, it is so pointless at this stage, and would be far more appropriate near the end of the road as extra little features to bring the place to life. This becomes a running issue, another major game mode called "Zombie Massacre" was in full swing, then almost entirely stopped again to half finish something else, resulting in nothing refreshing coming out to test and enjoy.
This is clearly the fault of not having an in-depth time management plan, detailing when what needs to be done by. This can be backed up by the amount of days off staff take. Either the time plan is way too lose, or it simply doesn't exist. Without due dates, procrastination occurs. The result will be a game in EA for 4+ years. Let's face it, this isn't a complex game. It consists of multiple minigames essentially, which shouldn't take more than 2-3 months per major, and 1-2 per minor, and the graphics aren't advanced.
-Ambition exceeding reliable staff and progress:
There are too many sub categories to TU compared to the amount of staff they have that aren't taking extra days off. Condos, Plaza games, Minigames, Social features, these all take time. There are many aspects under each of these categories. By doing so much and being all over the place, the quality and final result are average at best, rather than focusing on doing a few things really well.
I have more I could say, but I need to touch on the gameplay too.
The conclusion for this piece is that the Devs really need to get organized first, properly listen to feedback and implement it, and put their creativity into the game, not on finding ways to get another day off.
Issues with gameplay:
This covers the general gameplay, and specific issues with specific games.
-Lag / Hitbox Registration:
This seems to be a server based issue. Several games rely on hitting a target, or a player. The design choice by nature is a bit flawed as games like shooting a moving target, you have to aim ahead of where it is just so the server registers it. You can also run into players on a mode called "Virus", and they simply don't become infected as they should. For some reason the servers struggle to be lag free when players in an area exceed 3-4. My personal ping is 30-120ms, pending if server are West or East Coast. This ultimately ruins enjoyment for several games.
-Minigolf:
--All but 1 course is incredibly easy. This mode was my original selling feature, and it is quite disappointing and underwhelming. Most of the holes you simply whack the ball, no really wackyness or challenging obstacles
--No course editor/creator. This one would be a dynamite feature, and allow players to create stuff for players, along with removing work from the devs. It is pretty much a must, since playing the same 6 courses constantly gets super repetitive, out of which only 2 are fun and worthwhile.
--Physics issues. The ball simply bounces at a 90 degree angle off a straight rail, or even curved rail, or even worse, stalls on something.
-Condos:
--Lack of snappable feature makes placement difficult and time consuming for precision
--Canvas feature (pulling images off web and placing it onto walls, floor, etc) is inconsistent. You have 2 identical walls across from one another. The same image will sit at different heights. Also the lack of ability to customize the height at which an image sits makes the feature awkward to use, as you get images that begin with a chopped off head
--Lack of unique items. For some this may be fine, but every day items are boring. I want to design fantasy stuff, but of course the few fantasy items we get got locked away as RNG in seasonal events like Halloween.
-Virus:
--Running over players as a zombie, should turn them, but it often doesn't
--Hit registration as mentioned above
-Ball Race
--Again, lack of courses. Much like Minigolf, player made courses needs to be a thing or it gets repetitive super fast.
-Little Crusaders
--Needs to be revised, it is nearly impossible to hit the dragon and it doesn't feel fun or exciting. The mode relies on like 8 knights outnumbering the dragon for a change to hit the button on his back.
-Planet Panic
--The map is super basic. It needs to be super wacky to match the style of game play intended
-Bugs
This is fair game for EA. It's not bad and doesn't get in the way of playing for the most part, but obviously there are bugs so it had to be listed at least.
There are other games, like several small ones in the plaza, or a whole casino, but none of these have any issues. There are some other features like theatre and media player use on TV's, but I don't need a game when I can just go to YouTube directly, and therefore never bothered.

Terrific game. Everybody's first thought is to immediately compare it to Terraria, but this is a valid and fun game entirely in its own right. It's true that slow updates have been frustrating in the past, but the developers have been working hard to change that lately and have been cranking out a lot of fixes, changes, and content. It's your typical miney-crafty game in terms of progression, but the random planets really set it apart. Each tier of planet has more rare materials to find than the last, but only if you mine deep enough. Planets have different hazards (some are too hot, some are freezing, some are poisonous, some  have no atmosphere) and there's a simple quest system in place that rewards you with the gear you need in order to safely land in those places. On planets you can find villages and settlements belonging to many different types of alien, and each type feels unique and has different things to find and loot.
There are instanced-off missions to go on and bosses to fight. A ton of randomly-generated, as well as unique, loot to find. Many tiers of armor to go through, and a constant quest to upgrade your ship in order to make it bigger and badder than before. You can customize your ship piece by piece, or choose to build your own buildings down on a planet to live in. Combat is fun, enemy balance is (mostly) good. Definitely a little light on survival aspects, but still a solid game.
All in all, it's a fun little (huge) world to stomp around in with a lot of things to do, find, build, and collect.

A true, unexpected freeware gem. I don't know what I expected from "Serena," a brief little point and click horror game in the same vein as the classic "Scratches," but what I got was a narrative which was touching, heartbreaking, disturbing, and entirely too relatable.  I don't think I've ever seen a video game depict a relationship, or its disintegration, with quite as much painful honesty.  And though I can't say that I didn't see the ending coming, it still felt entirely satisfying for the narrative.  If you like horror games and classic point-and-click adventure, you OWE it to yourself to give this a try.  With a price tag like "free," what have you got to lose?

die the game immediately reloads if you do happen to. You will be gripped and feel the tension, but it's through powerful storytelling, not the stress associated with playing a difficult game.
I wholeheartedly recommend this to EVERYONE who appreciates quality storytelling - you do this a disservice if you dismiss it as "just another zombie game", and it should go without saying that if you're a fan of the comics or TV show this is unmissable.

This was originally meant for my friends. I never thought that it gained popularity so quickly. Please use appropriate language in the comment section. You can voice different opinion toward me or other comments, but please be respectful and avoid using rude/offensive words. Thank you.
TL;DR: just played a few hours and I want to go back to Enemy Within + Long War already.
When you send a four-men squad to a mission where you encounter 2*(viper+2*stun lancer), you're pretty much screwed. The Vipers will pull you in, the Stun Lancers cover so much distance in a single turn, all you can hope for is that your squad does not get bound/stunned/panicked all in the same turn, which will not happen. Definitely infuriating and frustrating. I know XCOM is not like a puzzle game where a "perfect" solution exists, but killing your entire squad outright, just because RNGesus doesn't love you enough? These missions are IMO more difficult than the covert extraction in LW.
Difficulty aside, I don't know what the designers are thinking, but the two newly introduced game elements: the mission timer and concealment, are just not very compatible with each other. And concealment could be very confusing on your first playthrough. This is my main problem with this game in the first few missions. When I first see this concealment introduced, I wanted to make use of it and take it nice and slow, at least avoid possible enemy contacts. But on the other hand, there is the timer, which keeps pushing you non-stop. (If you read the mission description carefully, some missions have no reason to start the count down unless you get spotted.) I know there are mods that fix this, but that still doesn't solve the problem: a) even if the mission does not have a timer, you cannot "infiltrate" into the building/whatever location the objective is at, or you are screwed. Because you will be required to kill all aliens or run through packs of alien reinforcement to the evac zone eventually.
. And b) even if you are concealed, the alien actually knows exactly where you are, they will be heading for you and flank you if you try to "let them pass". You will not have a perfect covert operation, but rather a mission screwed up pretty bad. They can only be played the way the developers intended: a one-time flank+overwatch opportunity. Which is confusing:
And speaking of EU/EW, there comes the second problem:
Despite being in a completely different setting where the alien has taken control of the majority of the earth, the story is pretty much the same comparing to the first installment: you encountered the aliens, you captured them, studied their technology, grew stronger than them, and you annihilate them. Other than new alien types and a few useless customizations, what is actually new in XCOM 2 that isn't as good in EU/EW?
The game never reaches 60FPS on 1920x1080. Spec: Ryzen 1700 + GTX 1080, 32g RAM, game files and system both on SSD.
Sometimes the audio becomes out of sync with the video in pre-recorded scenes.
Overall, I'll give it 6.5/10. I wouldn't suggest grabbing this game till it releases all DLC and goes on sale.
I forgot to mention how many bugs, despite being reported frequently since the game's release, e.g. the "pure virtual function being called" crash and the nondeterministic line of sight system, are still not fixed in this game as of today (Aug. 22 2017), 18 months later. Yeah, good luck, commander.
