The game is fun to play when you feel like a casual game of Texas Hold'em.
Good thingsa aside, there are some problems, and by "some", I mean A LOT!
It would be nice to see other forms of poker and be able to have the choice of selecting them. After all, the game is called "Prominence Poker", not "Texas Hold'em".
The game is extremely laggy, especially considering that what's being run shouldn't be very graphics heavy. I've played action games with little to no lag for hours without breaks, but if I play this game for more than 10 minutes, it starts to lag and eventually crashes.
I've also found that I have to open the task manager to close the game because if I close it from within the game, the music continues to play. This makes it hard to do other things without first loging off my computer and loging back in.
And two more things that bugged me were the affiliations and the "story". Currently, you can only join two of the four affiliations in the game, and that isn't much of an issue considering the developer(s) are working on making the other two joinable. What IS frustrating is not being told how to rank up in the affiliations when joining them and having to ask for help on the community. I googled how to rank up and found a post from another player who had asked the same question and was asked for his affiliation and how many gams he had played. After he had answered the question, the Dev who was "helping" him gave an unhelpful comment:
"We had a look at your account, and it looks like you *are* gaining ranks withing the Hearts affiliation. Currently, you're at level 10 with the Hearts. You can verify this yourself by either going to the store and looking for the Hearts-exclusive outfits (they'll be the red ones that are available at no cost), or by looking in the Affiliation screen. You should see that you're about 1/5 of the way toward the maximum Rank.
It appears that the issue is a glitch in how the game is displaying Ranks to players. That's why it seems like you aren't gaining Ranks properly. We'll look into that. Thanks for letting us know."
This was (obviously) not an answer to the question asked.
As for the "story", there really isn't one. The game starts with a tutorial that shows you playing a game with the mayor and winning. After you win, he asks you to beat the other affiliations in order to play him once again, this time for real. after half a day of playing against the other affiliations (which really should have different weaknesses rather than the same ones), I was excited for the final game and to hopefully get some new titles and goodies, only to be disappointed to find that there was no final round against the mayor.
Don't get me wrong, I love to get on and play a couple rounds before the game crashes, but these issues kind of ruin the game. if these were fixed, you could be looking at an award-winning game. But for the time being, try to fix these instead of releasing holiday themed items or patroling the comments for issues.
Hope this was helpful (even though the game is free).

So I just had to know why this game got so much bad publicity.
I get it now.
It's bad. It's because it's bad. That's why it got bad publicity.
I don't even know where to begin with this game... I feel like they get a lot of things right! It looks amazing and I just really loved the graphics, the sound, the design - I mean it's Paris during their revolution for crying out loud! This is a very exciting setting!
However, this game just fails on so many other levels. By the way, by the time I got this game, it was very bug free (compared to how it supposedly was when it first came out.)
So, I thought I'd let you know, the menus SUCK. Everything involving GUI just sucks. It's a rat's nest. The "pause" menu is full of online store content that no one cares about. Want to restart a mission? You have to scroll past a bunch of weird other menu items involving online stores or some crap. The relevant menu items are in the bottom - but if you want to jump into the ubisoft store in the middle of a mission, oh boy! It's like the second option in the list!
The HUD is also a circus. Sometimes the tips overlap really important elements of the HUD and you can't see what's going on and you're just waiting for the stupid tips to go away... tips that tell you things that it has already told you a hundred times. And no, there's no way to get rid of just the tips. (Heyo!) Also, the HUD has so many elements on screen at one moment that it's tough to quickly perceive the information you actually care about at the moment, AND makes it even harder for you to enjoy the best part of the game! The scenery! THE SCENERY! Why are there so many elements distracting me from the SCENERYHYYAHEIAFEAJFOEA
Where was I... ah yes, also, the story is boring. They kind of introduce surprise vilains out of nowhere and I don't even understand what's going on with the Creed or whatever and I just don't even know. Whatever. Story's bad. I miss Ezio. Moving on.
The controls suck! They try to keep making certain things better - and in theory they are better - but at the end of the day, all that matters is that I can maneuver Assassin's Creed where I want him and not have him just jump to his death or right in front of the baddie or whatever. Just like the first Assassin's Creed, controlling him is frustrating.
Now, the other thing that Assassin's Creed games do excepetionally well is getting to actually assassinate people with those little wrist knives! That's all I ever want to do! I just want to explore, learn about France during the revolution, and knife people in the neck with my wrists. It's really fun! There's nothing like scoping out a landmark building, planning your way in, and shanking your target!
However, most of the time you spend in the game, is not doing the fun things I mentioned above if you consider how frustrating exploration can be between the bad GUI and the bad controls. If you also consider the seldom amount of times you get to wrist-knife people and how stale the story is, this game just ends up being boring. I'd say you spend most of your time in the game doing boring things or being frustrated.
I don't even want to continue wasting my time to "finish" this game. It's just boring and it makes me very sad.
To say that this game is rough around the edges is an understatment. It needs way more than just polish, it needs entire sections either looked over again or completely removed. I really wanted to like this game, I love the setting, I love the graphics, and the knifey-knifing, but bad controls, a GUI designed by Jackson Pollock, and a stale story really drag this game into the Parisian Catacombs. (Ooooo relevant reference!)

The beauty of this game, aside from its graphics, lies in the research and crafting. In most resource-gathering games, basic tier materials are soon forgotten near end-game but not so here. The same copper, coal and tar u find initially are still useful and necessary many levels down the tech tree. For example, tar can be turned to sulphur which becomes sulphuric acid when mixed with water. Throw in copper with the acid and u get platinum. Every material is linked in more than 1 way to another and the constant combining/mixing of chemicals and compounds to get others really reinforces the sci-fi theme of this game.
The initial going can be tough but if ur willing to invest some time/effort the eventual sense of accomplishment is strong. U go from working with simple copper and stone to eventually anti-matter and motors. Ur wooden shack lit by basic torches and glow jars soon become high-tech labs with fluro lamps powered through an electrical sys u lay urself.
The main story is a little clunky and in some cases, broken right now but it doesn't impede the actual progression. That said, data logs are still abound which add backstory and flavor to the atmosphere. The devs seem to be quite active and hands-on with the forums so the game will hopefully improve over time.
Overall, if ur a fan of the sandbox/resource-gathering genre and crave a sci-fi take with increased graphical fidelity, give Darkout a shot.

Stardew Valley is an enigma to me.  I've put 300 hours into the game, and would comfortably and happily play it.  But if someone were to ask me if the game was fun... I'd have a really hard time saying yes.
I can't recommend this game to my friends because when I think about it and look back on it, it was really tedious and boring.  But at the same time I have 300 hours in it, and I don't remember being bored while I played it.  It's really confusing.
The game is adorable.  It's overflowing with charm and heart, and I think that counts for a lot.  But you don't actually DO a whole lot in the game, and what little you do, you do over, and over, and over, and over again.... for 300 hours.
I guess the best way to look at this game is the same way someone might look at Solitaire.  You play it because it's low stress, easy, doesn't take a lot of thought, and gives you a nice way to kill time while you just zone out and do nothing.  And for that purpose, Stardew Vallye is great.
But if you're looking for a game that's "fun"... I don't want to say you SHOULDN'T play this game... but I do have to say it really isn't all that fun.
And since steam makes me boil this down to a yes or no on the recommendation, I'm going to say yes -- because the game is charming and does a really good job of filling that weird time-killer role.

Stephen King's The Mist + science fiction + Terraria = Darkout.  I've been having a great time playing this game.  The graphics are beautiful, the atmosphere is creepy, and the music is one of the best soundtracks for a game in years.  Tons of weapons and armor to build, and all sorts of base accessories.  There are a couple of drawbacks.  The controls have a little bit of a learning curve, so don't expect to know how to play from the start, they are different enough from other 2D builder games that  you will have to take some time to learn them.  There are a few bugs, not too many, and nothing game breaking, but the patchs have been comming once or twice a week, so I'm sure they'll get squashed.  Also the game is a bit difficult at the start, but once you have a foothold, it becomes easy, yet still a joy to play.  I recommend this to anyone looking for something that plays kind of like Terraria or Starbound, but is serious and mature in its tone.

(Some stuff I say may spoil the experience for you if you've never played. Just saying.)
What can I say about this game? It's among my all time favorites.
When I first discovered this game, at first by merely seeing the cover art, I initially thought it was going to be some Japanese  RPG kind of game, but it piqued my interest nonetheless. The graphics were far and away much different than the AAA games I'd been seeing churned out, all without an immediate distinction to set them apart. After watching the first trailer, my prenotions were quickly blown out of the water: "no, this isn't a Japanese game, but whatever, you should probably play this." My curiosity got the better of me and I eventually sat down and installed the demo.
And then I finished the demo.
And then I bought it immediately.
It was a very impulsive buy, but I REALLY wanted to know where I was going next, to know what the rest of the beautiful worlds looked like. It sucked me right in! The first time I played, I was hooked for hours. And let me tell you, in a game where damn near everything is the result of a collective stroke of genius, it's easy to see why. This game is unlike any other game out there. (Also, one of the diamond-rare few where you are genuinely interested in the world history.
And now, the actual review.
I can't say enough about the graphics but I won't say too much. I love them so much. Courtesy of artist Jen Zee, arguably the most impressive self-taught artist today, Bastion's glorious worlds and remarkable character designs are vibrant, colorful, and entirely unique, married with spaghetti-western and oriental touches. It's hard to call the game cartoony, such as it is, because of the painterly and fully-fleshed aesthetic of the graphics. One way or another, they're a breath of fresh air.
Gameplay-wise, Bastion is not entirely new, although it still offers a very fun, and sometimes very hectic, beat-em-up bird's-eye-view experience. It offers you the choice of two weapons plus a special to go into battle with, and those are really all you need. The real fun is getting materials to upgrade said weapons at the armory, where you are given a two-way choice to improve your tools... and the differences show. Additionally, you can stack up to 10 drinks to give you extra buffs, some of which are decidedly unique. On top of all of that, I would say the most unique thing about the gameplay is the ability to invoke the gods, up to 10. The game becomes much, much harder, but the rewards become greater. You learn to fear them early on. There are other nice additions, such as the lost and found, the memorial, and other challenges to complete, but I won't go into those.
The narration is more or less the cornerstone of Bastion, in a way. Logan Cunningham, who I don't know why is not world famous yet, makes the game what many would remember it for: the rich, deep, near-serenading narration of Rucks, whose impossibly cool and sharp one-or-two liners really present an example of just how a game can end up being more badass than the majority of AAA, M-Rated, FPSes with huge guns and huge explosions being produced right now. (I suppose that's a very one-sided comparison, but you get the idea.) Oh, and it was recorded in musician Darren Korb's closet.
And finally, the music. Oh my heavenly days the music. This is one game I had to buy the soundtrack to. I don't know what musician Darren Korb's earlier material sound like but if sounded like this I would buy it in a heartbeat if it came to light. Darren mixes elements of electronic, trip-hop, American Frontier, orchestral, Middle-Eastern, and God knows what else to create the most unique soundtrack I've heard. Ever. And it works so brilliantly. Oh, and that was recorded in Darren's closet, too.
I won't spoil the story, but I will say this: it's surprisingly different and somewhat-multifaceted. It works very well with the game and helps to get the player interested in the history of the world and the conflict between two peoples. Bits and pieces of the story are told through each place visited, along with the place's history, though the biggest pieces are told through brief cutscenes. Finally, the characters backstories are presented in survival challenges in which the player must survive 20 waves to discover. Surprisingly, none of the characters ever really display much, if ANY, personality, and yet the way the are fleshed out in their backstories, the cutscenes, and bits of narration during gameplay, makes them believable, human.
To sum it up, Bastion is wholly impressive. In design, execution, and ultimately the final word. I would go so far as to call Bastion and immediate classic, one that will stand the test of time.
The elements of this game take SO many different routes--graphically, narratively, and musically--and yet, they all find common ground, seemingly impossibly yet somehow effortlessly, to mesh together to create a perfectly unique experience, a game that stands alone so well that no sequel is necessary. The only sequel I'd want is the complete history of the world of Bastion. I hope it exists eventually.
Buy this game. If you haven't yet, I'm very sorry.

Been a MoO fan forever. This is a nice addition to the series and LEAGUES better than that piece of garbage 3, but ultimately comes nowhere in comparison to MoO2 with regards to fluidity and content. Considering it's a reboot, they did some interesting design choices - namely I absolutely love the voice acting and the 3d graphics as well as revamps and consolidation in the lore of Master of Orion. Ultimately, I wasn't entirely satisfied with the finished product, but I do understand the love and detail added to this game. It's a MoO lite. It takes major themes and dummies down some of the more complex game mechanics and makes it easier for people to jump into the 4x titles. While I was disappointed at the overall lack of depth shared by such titles as Galactic Civilizations 2 and Stellaris, I also found myself smiling at certain points that I found charming and unique to this game. I wish there were several elements added to the game that harken back to MoO2 - system leaders, turn based combat, better events, better exploration (like stellaris or even Star Trek for that matter), better storytelling, and making war, diplomacy, economics, espionage, and science feel like a much greater achievement.
There are a lot of shortcomings, but as a reboot, it's a nice step in the right direction (considering the developer is exploring new territory for them, haha - so props for the love and detail they added). I hope expansions and dlc will add to this game and make it far more robust. If they come out with a new game in the next few years, I will be far more critical, but for now, I am just glad this genre defining series is back from the development graveyards. So, thanks for bringing it back and being really interested in what the fans had to say.
Tldr: MoO Lite - not MoO2 by any means, but a fun game with some unique aspects. I would recommend waiting for a sale, or if you want to support the developer, buy it full price. If you are new to 4x, I say give it a shot! If you want a deep 4x experience, you will find this game lacking compared to other 4x games currently out, but it's still a fun experience nonetheless.

This game is a work of art. Its environments are utterly stunning, with every piece of rubbish and every frame of animation drawn by talented hands. In a world stifled by "next-gen" grays and browns, Bastion's lush environments and unique oversaturated art style are a fantastic breath of fresh air. You are followed from stunning place to stunning place by the calming voice of an omnipresent narrator, who amazingly manages to never become grating or fall on tropes throughout the game's multiple-hour campaign.
Gameplay is classic twin-stick action which is heavily rooted in skill and timing. Your character begins with only a melee weapon, and over time you will accumulate several others, each with their own unique play style and a history rooted in the lore of Ceylondia. Finding a new weapon is always a joy, primarily because you're immediately able to try it out, but also because it means earning another segment of extremely well-voiced dialogue from the narrator. With the recently-added "No Sweat Mode," Bastion can appeal to audiences looking for any level of challenge--the hardest difficulty is crushing and requires extreme skill and a sharp eye, while the easiest will get out of your way and let you enjoy the story. Putting together an arsenal, upgrading your tools, and coming up with a set of weapons and skills that fits your talents are all part of the fun of Bastion.
Highly recommended.

I'm going to be honest, I'm not a fan of point-and-click games. I hate the feeling that I can't really control what the character is doing. Horror games are the worst, getting away with cheap jumpscares that you have no control of. Serena was an exception.
Serena is not a horror game. It is not scary...but it does give off an eerie, yet appropriate, feeling as you stumble around the cabin.
You walk around your decaying cabin, discovering items that spark memories back into you. Where is Serena? What did she look like? I can't quite remember...
The quiet that you face in the cabin (with the exception of a ticking clock) is unsettling. Our protagonist slowly makes connections that ultimately lead to our solution. However, if you're like me, you've probably figured out what's going on before the game ends.
The game doesn't take that long to play, so if you have half an hour, you should be able to complete it.
The only problem that I believe the game faces is, like most point-and-click adventure games, you may reach a point where you have no idea what to do. You've clicked on everything ten times over and are running around trying to find the next connection. (The game features different dialouge on the same items, so you could click a chair three times and get a different response from our protagonist) Other than that, this game is worth your time, especially since it is free.
One of the best games I have ever played. Also, definitely listen the soundtrack album.

This is actually the first Infinite Space game I really got into. There are three of them
- Strange Adventures in Infinite Space (2002)
- Weird Worlds: Return to Infinite Space (2005)
- This game (2015)
I played the second one first, I was probably on a roguelike binge. I played a little past the "this is awful, uninstall" timeframe to the "hey this is pretty good" timeframe, I'd say 2 hours. I didn't understand that it was released as a coffee break game at the time so I probably didn't appreciate it as much as I could have.
I then played the first one (which is free) and put about 2 hours into that as well. I then went back to the second one and racked up 5 hours total.
This game then came out about a year later after an extended Early Access period, it was not popular with it's Kickstarter backers, they took issue with it being bundled and re-bundled into not just Humbles, but also Indie Gala's, Bundle Stars etc. etc. during the Early Access period. This was done at a much lower price than they backed it for. From my point of view their criticisms were an even split of fair and unfair, the unfair was the usual assumption that Kickstarter is somehow a special underground market where you can get extra goodies/deals etc. before the product hits the "normals" which it isn't, you pay what you can afford to make sure something that currently can't happen, actually happens.
The fair criticism was also the usual, the developers were lousy communicators and on a couple of occasions said the absolute worst thing at the wrong time, I remember one time someone raised an issue with premature low-price bundling I mentioned in the last paragraph and the developers response was something like (heavily paraphrased) "Yeah the money from the Kickstarter's getting low so we had to do the bundle thing, you can help us by buying the game again through the bundle!!". If you were anyone other than the backers this was hilarious stuff at the time, but for them it understandably hurt some feelings, they lost a few fans by the looks of it. However I think it's really important to mention they did
do a Tim Schafer with the Kickstarter, they said "we will give you XYZ, here's the development screenshots and preview video", they then delivered XYZ, with nothing missing.
Anyway I bought the third one in one of those aforementioned desperation bundles.
It's a 3D version of the previous two games. The previous two games are a procedurally generated explore-em-up. You can travel X amount of light years from your starting planet, around a solar system before you have to return to base and say "look how much money I made/things I destroyed/good deeds done" etc. etc. your score get's tallied, added to the high score list, done. You can die and never make it back too, you'll get a (reduced) score for that though too.
You can trade with alien races to get more valuable items, your ship has weapons, you can get other ships (piloted by other people) so that you have a "flotilla" of ships. When you enter into battle you deploy your ships into a
grid and then tell them where to go, when they're in range of an enemy, their frequency and accuracy of weapons fire is actually determined by add-on systems, like guidance computers etc. it's one of the examples of the "hands-off" aspect of the fighting mechanism has its own special charm.
As you can see above I did say that the fights were 2D, the 3D aspect is the exploratory map in which you go from planet to planet. This has come in for the most criticism, a lot of reviewers insist that this should have been 2D because it's difficult to see nebulae (purple clouds that slow you down), it's not a problem though, if you hover over a planet it tells you how many light years it takes you to get there, if that number is followed by a + symbol, it means the nebula will get in the way at some point so you know you're going through one.
The game can still be coffee break in length but if you pick a large map style you'll definitely get close to an hour out of a single session. The trading and ship upgrade (i.e. the non-fighting aspects) are thoroughly streamlined, you drag the icon to your inventory to buy, you drag the icon to their inventory to sell.
Each playthrough also has a big mystery mission that usually involves saving the whole solar system or an entire race, it'll typically be triggered by you finding something and allows for a big bonus to your score.
They do a very good job with the sound effects and ambience, there's very little music but the background radio transmissions and ominous groans of space really sets the mood just right.
That just leaves battle, which takes place in real time. You deploy your ships to the 2D grid when the battle starts, the most important thing to know is that they can be pulled out again to safety and re-deployed during the battle. Once a ship lands on the grid you can tell it where to move and it will start firing at enemies within range (hover over a ship in battle and you'll see it's weapon range), weapons and systems can get damaged during battle and stop functioning. That's all you can do during battle which is unusual because it takes a lot out of your hands, it works though as it streamlines the game further.
Great game, you can tell how long it's going to last you after about 15 playthroughs because by then you've seen every item combination and how to formulate winning strategies, mastering combat is a necessity which will take you longer to figure out. At the time of this review I've put 10 hours in and I'll definitely get at least another 10 out of it. At that it's definitely worth the full £6.99 it's currently going for.

Master of Orion is a reboot of the serie that pretty much definied space 4x games with Master of Orion 2. Which ultimately is both a strength and a weakness for this title.

In essence this is a steamlined freshed up version of the legendary Master of Orion 2, it has superb production value, and what it does, it does extremly well making it a genuinely fun game.
And that is preciesly sort of the main problem of this title: yes it does everything beautifully, but it doesn't do that much as it's missing some key features the previous title had such as:
- Lack of heroes
- Lack of an end game attack on Antares
- Missing races which in turns offers less race customisations
- Lack of Goverrnments
- The battles are in real time, which for me is totally fine, bur can be seen as a negative for some people
This all contributes to the feeling that this master of orion is a good, fun game, hence the positive recomandation *especially at such a low price point*, but is just not as deep or as engaging as the 20 years old MoO 2. That being said, one good expansion and a couple of patches could do wonders to this already engaging game.

I struggled with whether to give this a positive or negative review.  I decided on positive because if you just take it on its own merits, and buy it during a Summer Sale or something, I think you will have plenty of fun for your money so long as you don't this to be a mainline 4X space game.  However, my guess is that many, like me, who play this game will have played Weird Worlds, its predecessor first.  When compared to WW I'd say WW was overall better, especially if you downloaded some of the great mods made for it.  When I think about playing this game, I often just go back to WW instead.  My comments below, then, compare this to WW.
- As others have mentioned, the transition to a 3D star map adds nothing to the game.  In fact, I think it is just more confusing.
- The new interface for adding upgrades to your ships is fine, but I liked WW better since it was more intutive that if I was putting a gun on the port side of the ship it would have a firing arc from the port side of the ship.  With the new UI for this I have to compare where I'm placing the gun in the UI with the picture of the ship to see which gun is changing.
- I do like the new mechanic for fighters since in WW getting a fighter generally means hiding it behind your capital ships to keep it from dying quickly and hoping maybe it will help out should an enemy fighter get past the point defense of your capital ships.
- I like how you move your ships in combat versus WW since this game allows you to easily set a path.  However, having to individually bring each of your ships into the combat can be cumbersome.  I'd at least like to still have the option of bring them all in at the same time in a set formation like in WW.
- I guess all the effort went into creating the new 3D environment because as others have noted much of the content is exactly the same as in WW.
- I actually like the WW art style better.  Again, I would have preferred that time have been devoted to new content versus new art.
- I definitely like the better capability comparison in this game between different upgrades.  In WW it was often difficult to determine what gun was better than another, for instance.  This game makes the trade-offs between damage, range, DPM, etc. much more clear.
- Both games have a variety of well-animated weapons that show some attention to detail and make combat, while still simple, pretty fun.
So, again, not a bad game and I think most people who want a relatively simple game will have fun.  However, I think WW along with the mods for it available for free on the Digital Eel website (including a Babylon 5 total conversion, yay!) is on net the better game.
I hope Digital Eel makes another game and takes feedback like this to bring the best of this game and WW together.  I would start with WW, add some of the features I mention above as definite improvements, and then just add a bunch of new content.  Part of the fun is replaying the game over and over and seeing which of the random events and items you happen to get in that play through, so just adding a lot more of those random possibilities would be fun (again, not to beat a dead horse, but that's basically what the mods do).  I love sci-fi but find that the bigger 4x games with their complicated enonomies just don't interest me.  A game that focuses on basic exploring to find cool stuff, combat, random events, and humor is just my speed.

Weird Worlds, the second game in this franchise, was amazing.  It was essentially "Star Control 2 in 30 minutes."
Strange Adventures In Infinite Space, the very first game, wasn't much to look at graphically but contained all the elements that define this franchise.
Sea of Stars.....  Has pros and cons.  It's not quite as polished as Weird Worlds.
There was a forum post I saw on the Weird Worlds forum way back when.  It mentioned something along the lines of having hostile fleets move around (instead of just the Kawangi and Ravians), different races preferring different trade goods and offering varied selections, and so forth.  I suspect the developers read that post because this game delivers on that front.
It's exciting to have maurading Tan-Ru and Garthan ships harassing worlds across the sector, with the heroic races also having numerous patrols and, thankfully, numerous ways to establish alliances.  Sure, this existed in the previous game too, but the additional elements finally give a sense of agency in it all.  Before it was just your ship exploring the worlds.  Now, now you'll find that the sector isn't all that quiet after all.
Yet even though the setting is more vibrant, and the flavor text is as amusing as ever, the 3D map is a definite downside.  Without the calibrator it can be extremely annoying getting from place to place, and unlike Weird Worlds it doesn't look like your ships can pool their FTL Drives.  The removal of the latter feature makes death far more frequent once you get the fabled Hyperdrive.  Sure, one might mention backups and the like, but with limited storage space, Esmerelda, and [insert extremely frustrating spawn here] that's not as foolproof a plan as one would believe.
I really enjoyed how they put a lot of effort into making every tech in a category seem different.  Every drive displays different exhaust, and weapons have differing glowy bits.  I think shields are somewhat different too but I haven't confirmed that. DayZ is a mod for Arma 2 that turns the base game into a zombie survival simulator. DayZ is one of the most detailed, if not the most detailed, and immersive zombie survival sims available. When you play DayZ, you create a character and spawn on a beach with nothing but your clothes and from there you have to make your way inland and try to find the tools you need to fend off the undead and to survive in this new world. Generally you are looking for things such as a melee weapon, medical supplies, light sources, food and you might even be lucky enough to find a gun or camping gear.
As you make your way through formerly populated areas like villages, farms and the three large cities, you will run into hordes of zombies that you will have to deal with. You can lose them by running into buildings or otherwise breaking line of sight with them. But the zombies are actually not the real threat in this game; the biggest potential threat comes from the other players who are attempting to survive just like you. Some of them will try to help you or trade with you, but usually in exchange for something of equal value, or if you are both being attacked by zombies or other players and you band together out of desperation. Most players though, are bandits, which you can tell by their clothes and covered faces. These players are out for your blood, and only want the stuff they can loot off your dead body.
You want to be very cautious in approaching other survivors that you do not know in DayZ because a lot of bandit groups will try to bait victims by having one of their number pose as a "friendly" and then when the victim runs over to trade or help, the rest of the bandits ambush him or her. Players in this game have gotten very paranoid in the last year and a half, and so a lot of times players will shoot each other on sight rather than risk losing their gear to a potential bandit.
So what do you actually do in DayZ once you have your basic weapons and tools needed to survive? Well you want to find a safe place that you can use as a home base. Generally you want to be far away from areas frequented by zombies, so somewhere in the woods usually. You want to be close enough to a town that you can raid it for supplies every few hours but far enough that zombies and players will have a difficult time tracking you home.
Once you have your things safely stashed, the best thing you can do is band together with your friends or any friendly people on the server you can find and get a vehicle. A bicycle is great for solo scout and loot missions to town, but a car, truck or SUV will provide cover from bullets, a large inventory and quick transport for multiple people. Focus on getting the necessary car parts you will need to fix up one of the junked cars you find laying around. After that, once you get enough loot and establish a territory, you can even build a house in some versions of DayZ and barricade it against zeds and meddlesome players.
At some point you will get into a fight with another player. Most of the time these fights aren't fair. Maybe a group of players rolled up on you while you were looting and shot you as you came out of a house. Other times you'll follow someone and not realize that they have friends with them and their friends flank and kill you, or you just get shot by someone while you are running from zombies that have aggroed you. All of these things will happen to you on a regular basis, and since everything stays on your corpse when you die, chances are they will loot and take your stuff. But other times you get lucky and you kill a guy with a huge gun that you need because you were lucky enough to catch him with his pants down. So now you have a big gun, and then when you go around the side of the house he was in, you find his giant military truck full of more guns and supplies. Now you are a zombie slaying god and you can bring all of that back to your base.
It is very easy to either get very, very mad at this game and ragequit or try to keep deaths in perspective, play smart and take all the opportunities you get. If you are observant and patient in every situation you will do well. If you run into a building without checking the surroundings for players watching or for zombies that will attract attention to you, you will die a lot. If you take your time and all necessary precautions you will catch somebody making a mistake and profit from it, and continue to survive the apocalypse.

If you've come to this game looking for your usual space 4x then look elsewhere! This is a rogue-like space trader game rather than a 4x! I only say this first as I too was expecting more of a 4x-type at first!
Infinite Space 3 also differs from many other space trader types by swapping the "months, even years long" careers typical of traders for small rogue-like random games that will last a few hours. Everything happens quickly here, there is NO grind whatsoever. In short, this game swaps long-term cerebal gameplay for short-term fun gameplay. I think this is a reason for quite a few negative reviews - the game is not what many people are expecting it to be!
The plot seems to be explore the game's galaxy to find stuff! You will jump from star to star, which all have one planet each, and each of those planets reveal random treasures, alien lifeforms, ship components that you can use, equip or sell as you see fit. You many also find new wingmen to join you in your journeys. You start off at a "human homeworld", being sponsored by some dodgy crimelord to "explore the galaxy, grab whatever you can, and make *me* a fortune". Though there is also at least one other plot going on, one game I played ended when some mysterious, powerful alien race appeared and destroyed this "human homeworld" whilst I was busy elsewhere! Bet that taught Mr Dodgy Crimelord a thing or two! I'm sure there will be a few plots running side-by-side in each game - I've not many hours into the game as I write this, I'm sure I will discover more.
There are alien homeworlds too, most are indifferent or downright hostile to start with. Some can be cajooled into being friendly if you find the right things/wingmen as you explore other worlds. Once friendly you can trade with them too..... but other races credits won't mean zip to them, you will have separate credit accounts with each friendly race! Others, forget it, they will simply *never* be friends!!!!!
So far, it seems a high difficulty level game too..... but as I mentioned earlier, I'm only just starting out here!

[As I write this with steady hand]
Okay granted on writing this review I only have 78.9 hours in the game so far. I'll share my experiences good and bad the pros and cons, and finish off with my conclusion on why my rating is how it is.
I got news of this F2P game not via steam itself, but because I mostly played Console games in my spare time. A friend I met through a community of like minded people such as myself, introdused me to this game while he was developing his club world and was livestreaming it. Being he was from the UK and I was from the US it was pretty late at night for me to see it.
After watching him go making his club world as it was I got the idea to try it for myself. I was doing this on my old potato of a pc till I could afford a better one. But nevertheless, I enjoyed my time playing it till I got my new pc.
Con: high-level players
Granted being a new player comes with its risks, and one being high level players could come at any time during the time you could be working on your mastery (collective) level and come swoop in bypass all the lesser enemies and take away a dungeon boss quicker than you could sneeze. All because a event could be in your biome to earn dragon coins/souls.
Pro: high-level players
I'm not one to nickpick on a sole detail here but that alone makes me want to stop playing because it takes the fun out of clearing the dungeon if at the end there's no climatic boss at the end of it. But I'll digress if your coy enough and haven't dove into these dungeons and a high level player goes in. You could just wait outside for them to clear it and just piggyback behind them to make an easy score for coins yourself. But still I consider this a con, because its not 'enjoyable' sitting there waiting for a high level to finish off one for you.
Resolution: high-level players
The biggest thing to combat this is a more secure limiter that stopped higher levels from accessing lower levels with their high class character so say you have a low level class and then swap to you most powerful class it voids your chances on getting coins because you went to a lower 'UBER' level to farm for coins. Disrupting other's enjoyment of the game. Hark me if you want but I'm pretty sure everyone who starts out agrees with me on this.
Pro: Mounts
But I'll be honest I didn't have the sligest clue on getting a mount, and it was nice to meet the other high level players who helped throw me a bone and pass me a basic dog and a cat mount to start out on. Which I honestly felt like I should've paid them in dragon coins, but being 'labeled' a currency I soon learned you couldn't trade them. Embarassed on how I realized this and being a new player I felt I had owed this player for handing me free mounts to use. But being as I had no structure on how the game should be played it only felt right to pay him for the effort of helping me at least.
Con: Mounts
In the least bit, even though I had this simple dog and cat mounts it was a difficult pill to swallow seeing how those other players had played even longer than I had they paid for the mounts they got through their access to 'Patron' and so forth. This game is a blast.
While the game starts off slow and a bit confusing due to a clunky tutorial, as you delve into it deeper you find an amazing adventure.
Darkout has an excellent atmosphere, and a very creepy feel to it throughout. Not just form the beautiful graphics and art style, but from the story that is told to you through various ways. Between the creepy text data modules you find while exploring, to the audio ones with some very creepy messages, to the beacon that you set up from the start. This game has a very sci-fi thriller theme.
On top of this it has a very detailed crafting system. A system that is backed by a very deep and rewarding reserch tree. You must explore and mine to collect resources that allow you to further your research and give you access to new crafting items and materials. The research trees are quite large and you will be finding new and great technologies for tens of hours while playing. It's not something you just can blow through quickly. There are double digit tiers of research that have dozens of new items, weapons, armors, devices, building material, etc. in every tier. The more you research the more crafting options unlock, as well as higher end research options.
You also have to deal with powering up many of your machines and finding ways to keep your bases powered up. Be it through fuel, or various generators having a good power setup will keep your base fully operational. This is a nice touch for this genre and isn't a micromanaging thing. Once you figure out how to use it and create enough power you will not have to worry about it. You just need to figure out how to wire things properly and make sure you have enough power generators to keep the lights on! IF devices and lights are blinking...you know you need more power sources.
While this game has a fascinating and creepy story it still is part of the whole sandbox genre that Terraria was a part of. You still must build a shelter, gain access to devices and crafting equipment, and can build a massive base if you choose to. The game even has a building mode that you are basically free to build with no distractions , or need to unlock anything. As you research you have things like elevators, jetpacks, an enormous amount of light sources, and tons of furniture to build as much as you like. There really is some amazing tech.
The game uses a darkness mechanic in which enemies can become stronger, or weaker when confronted by light. They thrive in darkness and can spawn from it. Even in your own shelter if you fail to provide enough light! You have dozens of weapons such as melee swords, guns, crossbows, grenades, and many more as well as things that allow you to emit light in some ingenious ways. The armors you can make are beautiful and have some very interesting functions. You can equip accessories as well to give you even more passive abilities as you explore.
You still do a lot of mining for resources of course so the game goes underground to darker caves and not just left and right. You can even go up into the sky once you figure out how to get there. :)
This is a game that just gets better the deeper you go into it. The world seems to slowly change as you get stronger. Gets darker and creepier as you go further and learn interesting stories throughout the main quest. If you are looking for a happy experience with fuzzy animals and sunshine you will not find it here. This is a sandbox game that is set in darkness.
There are a few small bugs early on, but the developers are very active in fixing them and have taken polls aobut what the best ways to implement new control options could be. The game is FULL release even if the store page suggests it is in Stage 1. The wording is a bit off, but the new stages are new features that are going to be added in the coming months for free, including Multiplayer.
I purchased this game when it was in kickstarter as well as Starbound at roughly the same time...back in 2012, and have been eagerly awaiting Starbound much more than I was Darkout. By some strange coincidence, BOTH games were released on Steam on the exact same day. The dilemma of which to play was there from the start, but after playing both I have found myself playing strictly Darkout since the first few days I had with Starbound. Since Starbound is extremely early in Beta, and we have had a character save wipe already, I have not even touched it since maybe a week ago, while I am playing Darkout constantly. The early beta of Starbound has actually been a bit of a positive since it allowed me to dedicate more time to Darkout.
I recommend you check this game out and don't even bother trying to compare it to games like Starbound or Terraria. This game is MUCH darker, and the art style is leaps and bounds above the others.

- UPDATED! I no longer recommend this game, don't waste your money on it's current state!
Updated Introduction and Summary sections! -
[ Introduction ]
My opinion about this game WAS very ambiguous: I couldn't say if it was worth buying or not. Now that I sinked in more hours to discover what the game's about, I must label it as DO NOT BUY.
The current major version of the game is 1.2 and there's too many bugs (including game breaking bugs), story progression is broken, and there are many unfinished features.
Hopefully the review below will shed light on people that haven't bought yet and are looking for an unbiased review (I'm not an early supporter nor an early hater).
[ Overview ] :
This game is a cross of Under the Ocean and Terraria.
It's graphical style is very cool, with nice looking objects, equipment, armor, bases and world.
Also, a non-blocky-pixel-sandbox is a great change.
You're dropped in a planet that is very dark and the days are very short. The darker it is, the more frequent are monster spawns and some can even get tougher if you fight them in the dark (no worries on that, though, since your armors have lights - once you get some energy storage equipment).
Note: I have no idea why a human ship is orbiting such planet and no idea why you crash land in a pod there.
You discover the backstory through datalogs you find during exploration.
[ Positive Points ] :
- Tutorial gets you through the basics, enough to move ahead.
- Non-blocky-sandbox.
- 3D characters on nice 2D environments.
- Tech-tree and rich crafting system comprised of resources and components. Your tools, equipment and armors aren't made only of metal ingots - sometimes you need to make secondary components like rubber and silicon, or more complex ones like a dynamo or motor. It is a fresh and interesting crafting and discovery scheme with great potential.
- Diverse lamps, technology, power and wiring makes base building look cool and planning ahead is necessary.
- Digging/mining spread of 3 blocks or 1 block, toggleable.
- When crafting or researching, the craft/research system takes resources from inside storage containers, like barrels and closets, so you don't have an inventory full of resources everytime you want to do something - you just have to be near your storage.
- Some itens takes time to crafting or research, which feels better than "instant crafting" in this case.
- Elevators, hover-platforms, switches, rifles..technology - nice features.
[ Negative points ] :
- ANOTHER game that puts "Survival" in it's description and features no survival at all. If "surviving" aggressive mobs is "survival", so all the games that feature aggresive AI is a survival game? There's no need for food, water or sleep, which made me wonder what's the fun in "surviving" an alien planet in this situation.
- Technical-wise, the game feels like a beta. It seems that every technical detail was made to annoy the player. If you keep autosave on, it will interrupt your game abruptly and prints a big "SAVING YOUR GAME" title every time it autosaves, it's terrible. Graphics can't be tuned at all (except toggling 5 or 6 options). This makes playing on older machines really hard or even impossible. Also, turning off dynamic shadows breaks the (bad) lighting system. Last but not least, the game can crash everytime you try to exit it - in my case, forcing me to CTRL-ALT-DEL my way out.
- Lighting system is weird (radius/spread/emanation) and annoying for a game that tries to be beautiful. It also doesn't look realistic - underground, you have to put way too many torches because of it.
- Performance can be bad for no reason in many situations, leaving me to believe the game isn't optimized at all.
- Movement system is annoying. Even if you tap a button, your character starts running, which looks bad and can give you many fall deaths (combine this with poor performance and autosave, guaranteed deaths).
- The music, initially "Okay", gets repetitive and annoying really quick, and the sound-effects sometimes are awkward or way too loud compared to other effects.
- Backgrounds look very ugly and out of place. Also, you can break very deep cave walls, and the background is usually a plain blue color that may or may not emanate light.
- Resource gathering and base-building takes a long time compared to other games.
- Research system feels weird: you waste the same resources to research a new item that you would use to craft it (also investing research points). It feels like a relabeled leveling system for crafting.
[ Summary ]:
Based on the points above, the game feels unfinished and lacking heart, which makes it, currently, a DO NOT BUY title. Plus, the devs had the boldness to launch it with no "Early Access" label.
It would show potential if it was a beta, but it seems the developers think it's safe to say it's an 1.0 (1.2 actually).
Even for 10$, it's not worth getting in this: no one should launch an unfinished, buggy and broken game with no warning about it.
If the devs leave it in it's current state, this will just be forgotten.
For your current sandbox needs, go for Starbound instead - even in BETA it's more finished, polished and stable.

...Of course, I suppose you want a far less concise review, so here you go.
Starbound is a 2D sidescrolling sandbox; you can think of it in a way as a spacefaring Terraria.
Many elements of the game are randomly generated. Most monsters are pre-made, but there are several variants with random body parts. Weapons are one of the most prominent random features; each possesses a different appearance and a special ability.
By far the most unique feature is the spacefaring. Starbound has you travelling around in your starship, discovering new and alien worlds on your quest to defeat the being which destroyed Earth.
Each planet and biome has exclusive loot, and occasionally you can find a settlement! The villagers can give you randomly generated quests, which you can complete for small rewards. Some may even wish to join you on your adventures! These new crewmembers become shipmates which can follow you around and give several passive buffs; some include the Soldier, Medic, Engineer, Tailor, and totally-not-useless Janitor.
Many unique premade weapons and other items can also be found on these planets, in addition to the random weapons; some are humorous, others creepy or downright strange.
Steam multiplayer and servers are also available for people who want to adventure together, or simply get together.
Modding is one of the game's finer aspects. Modding Starbound is nearly as easy as it gets; it simply requires a bit of knowledge of .json and .Lua code. There's even a mod folder directly in the game files! You can find many, many,
of these mods on the Workshop. Experiment a little and find what
like in your game!

The crafting element of this game is like solving one process which then reveals more crafting processes to solve. The rewards for creating something new is satisfying as it is something new you can place in you own designed shelter. I would not go as far to say that the designs of shelters in the game are endless but there are a lot of layout possibilities.

The sound effects are done well adding to the atmosphere of the alien world around you.
Controls are simple but can be a little annoying at times however you set them up.
This is a good game to get involved in. I definitely recommend this game. As it is a Greenlight game it is by far complete. But with a bit more work this game could potentially be fantastic. The creator's of this game appear to be listening to the players and are actively responding.

I am gonna have to be an ever so slightly dissenting voice. Yes, the digging and finding new stuff definately works on my Minecraft/OCD center. It's very addicting. However, the UI commits some unpardonable errors. Dragging stuff from your inventory to your hotbar will instead dump it on the ground 60% of the time. Trying to close a door can make you drink a health potion instead. Attacking a monster will sometimes open a cabinet, or stick a light on a wall. You shift-right click to pick up some stuff, but other stuff you can just walk over it to pick it up. It's breaking the first rule of UI design - if the player does something, it must be consistent throughout and work as the player expects it to.
I also have issues with the procedurally generated worlds not producing good worlds to game in. Something like tar should be available after a little searching. I had to abandon one world and start another because I was stuck without it. Another world, I literally had none of those squid things to kill until I quit and reloaded. Then suddenly they were there. The algorithm needs to put common stuff near you and rarer stuff farther away, and the player should be able to complete the first couple quests more easily, to give him incentive to continue. There is good potential here, and as I said, it's a very addicting game, but I think it needs another 6 months in the oven.

This film went from being just something I watched when I was browsing Netflix, to something I have bought several copies of. It is one of my favorite movies of all time, and here is why:
- Oddly enough, there is this "Disney/Pixar Magic" kinda thing going on. WAIT! DON'T GO! READ ON!
It has a very innocent feel. It has a very "Adventure is out there" feel. Something about it will just make you giddy inside...then someone gets thier eye socket jammed-in with a screwdriver, and suddenly all is right with the world again.
- Speaking of which, this movie is a literal bloody good time. There is a copious amount of gore, over the top on purpose. It is part of the charm!
- There is a lot of light hearted, tasteful humor that is woven into the actions and interactions of the characters, the entire premise, and the relationship of our main characters. On top of that, the movie doesn't really take itself seriously, even in some of the grimest of parts. This helps to keep the experience from being bogged down by a tear jerker.
- The relationship. It isn't some thick and hard to swallow pill like you might find in The Notebook or something. It too is very light hearted, charming, cute, and something that will just warm you up inside.
- 80's cheese is abundant here, from the bravado of a side character, the impossible action pieces (see the end), and the slightly off-acting of our actors. It is all there and it serves the movie quite well.
- The soundtrack is spectacular and fits very nicely! It is somewhat similar to Blood Dragon. Synth heavy. It sets the moods perfectly in ways I didn't think synth could do.

Probably, Botanicula - one of the cutest games that I had seen. This is one of those games whose charm lies in its simplicity and even a certain naivety, combined with excellent art-style.
Storyline is fully revealed in the first minute of the game. Our brave heroes must save last tree seed from voracious spider-like parasites and... that is it. Well, on the way from the top of tree to its roots, heroes will visit quite strange, unexpected and unpredictable places. Here I must say that sometimes Botanicula seemed for me, well... too eclectic. The first part of the game has a beautiful and clearly defined style, but in the middle of the game appeared... inappropriate elements; for my taste, they just do not fit in original style.
Last part of the game is excellent, it offers an impressive contrast with the beginning. Live intertwining branches, filled with sunlight and scurrying creatures, are replaced by dark and eerie domain of parasites. The tree is dying. I was deeply impressed by last scene... and inspired by hope. The idea is simple and clear: despite everything, do not despair.
As for the gameplay. It is very simple, puzzles are not difficult but well designed and interesting enough. There is almost no inventory management and, in my opinion, it is good, because I do not think that collecting weird stuff and guessing how all this junk should be used, is a necessary element of good game. There are some arcade mini-games, they are well designed and fits perfectly in the mood of the game.
World of Botanicula is inhabited by a variety of strange creatures and I humbly advise you to not hurry. Explore the game, click everywhere and see what happens then. In many cases, your curiosity will be rewarded with short funny scene. Botanicula is filled with humor, this game is truly created with love.
I really liked the soundtrack, this strange and charming melodies, filled with buzzing and other strange sounds, it creates a very special atmosphere. Great job!
Well. I sincerely recommend Botanicula. Odd, touching, optimistic... that is it. Not a masterpiece, maybe, but close enough.

Played a few online poker games, but I have to admit I'm loving this one. Dedicated to poker, no blackjack or other stuff so every feature and event is dedicated to people who want to play poker. Plenty of different table stakes, tournaments/ring/head-to-head options, both ranked and unranked for tournaments and head-to-head. Skill levels seem to vary from total scrubs to pretty solid players, and ranked play pairs you up against similar strengths (or at least similar records, YMMV). Free handouts are insufficient for big stakes, but plenty to play many hours on the low stakes tables which is about perfect, microtransations are basically "buy more chips", and it's the chips you spend on the cosmetics, so there's no real P2W anywhere. Playerbase is reasonable, never had any difficulty finding a low or mid-low stakes game at any time of the day, and some amusing mind-games to be had on the table. Because of the hand options, there's plenty of people reading as well as cards (Check-raising is legit, there's a sensible timer so you can gauge when someone's having a serious think, you can see when people are repeeking cards etc) -- anyone who says otherwise doesn't really understand poker.
For a F2P/PayToHaveCoolStuffButNotAnAdvantage game, I can't see a single down side to what is an excellent poker experience.

Summary: They tried to clone the extinct MoO species from Civilisation-DNA, sadly loosing some essential traits in the process. A good deal only for casual players, or to rekindle old MoO-memories without much available play time. The game looks good and starts very accessible.
If you're looking for a deep 4X experience, look elsewhere.
Explore (yawn) - scouts without range limits plod through a circular galaxy to map the stars. Rarely a reward beyond some credits or a vessel. Meeting races early to reap in trading boost.
Two other setup options separate sections of the galaxy until midgame. Prevents early diplomacy and stresses expansion and research.
Expand - planets operate separately. Their properties matter most in the beginning. Some good, close fertile planets boost growth excessively, while hostile environments cripple colonies.
Much later in midgame, solar systems may pool their production and planets specialise more.
Exploit - planet food and production slots are limited, with small spread and decreasing yield. Works only well at start, in the long run technology levels out differences. Planet size matters most.
This is far from the old system where the galaxy might look completely different according to your race.
Exterminate - Stationary defences add initiall resillience, invasion tech is delayed. Using star lanes feels more like combat along mountain passes than in space.
There's tactical decisions and challenges. Still battles failed to excite me. Went to just calculate combat in the end. Invasion looks unfinished. Conquered planets don't revolt.
In mid-game, portals may connect a side's systems, specialised shipyards churn out fleet. Travel in enemy territory stays slow; mopping up a war becomes a drag.
Science - Instead of independent fields of research, we get a Civi tech tree with crowded nodes. The frowned upon old choice system is consciously reduced to a few select applications.
This means that more than 85% of technology can never be traded, stolen or conquered but must be researched instead.
Money - main source is population tax, with trade second. This is probably the biggest design change, as the forerunner used industry for taxation. Money and production were interchangeable then. No more.
All ship upgrades can no longer be produced but must be bought, and there's no alternative to a large population base to fund your buildings or excess fleet.
My brand's canary chokes on several features, mechanisms and concepts that often match the forerunner just in name.
UI problems pop up in midgame and with huge positions. The game increasingly reacts sluggish and information is missing. MoO2's UI could handle 100-planet empires, MoO can't.
Zooming into a planet looses the strategic view. Event list can't be scrolled, when overflowing you must klick through the least important items first. Some events pop up first, ignoring your selection.
Planet list can't be sorted by production type, to e.g. check fleets in construction. Planet uniformity makes sorting by resource (food, science, production) way less usefull. And the list goes on...
All this is known and unadressed since EA 4
Diplomacy is listless. Incoming offers can't be put on hold and checked, no counter offers possible. Swap charts without knowing what you trade for is the most frequent offer.
Get an embassy. Trade and research deals have to be continually refreshed, with the AI later often too broke to accept. Cultivating AIs is possible to get access or alliances. Otherwise the AI is simplistic with no real grasp of reality, demanding when ready to strike, or crawling when currently involved in another war.
Espionage mostly consists of offensive spy micromanagent. Some Intelligence; stealing of the 'choice' techs is best done at lowly, undefended outposts, the rest is sabotage.
Sabotage works like a separate game, after succes the victim can't react, e.g. can't attack a revolting planet but must wait it out.
Defense is static by race traits or expensive buildings, or dispatched spies, without a good view to coordinate.
Races - Most predefined ones work, but use way more perk points though than a player gets for a custom race. Race differences are noticeable, but very timid.
Ship customisation has some wellcome improvements (like scout autoupgrades or the UI layout). On the other side a convoluted system obscures this.
Payload is consumed at rates differing by class by essentials. A 25% payload extension consumes part of this for itself. And so on. You can't just compare the numbers displayed.
This also hurls another wave of micromanagement at the player, e.g. each new drive is slightly bigger, often forcing a ship redesign.
The final result is a wasted opportunity - a good looking time waster, not without appeal - but too shallow and boring for me.

I'll be honest. I never heard of Gmod tower before I bought this game, nor was I interested in the game itself, but I wanted a new mini-golf game and Steam recommended this game.
So I bit the bullet and bought it, $15 USD sounded fair for a mini golf game, but I got much, much more for my moneys worth.
The easiest way to explain this game is to mention Virtual world games like the Playstation Home game/app (Which this game is more akin to) and Second Life (Which Tower Unite is not trying to be, but it has some similarities with).
The most basic point of the game is to enter a server (There is a good number of official servers running 24/7 and some 3rd party ones) and find something to do in the "Lobby" (Lobby here means the whole server world), this can be as mundane as going to the casino and mindlessly playing gambling games which may or may not reap big income rewards, going to the theater and watch and/or share videos from YouTube with other people that are in the theater, go to mini games that are around the lobby like Trivia, Bowling or Laser Tag, or you can go for one of the more fleshed out games like Mini Golf, Ball Race (A Super Monkey Ball inspired multiplayer game), Virus (My favorite of the bunch, inspired by the Halo Zombies user game) and a couple of others (With 4 more games planned for future updates).
While playing these games, you get in game money called units. With these units you can buy stuff in the Lobby, and these items can vary from things you can equip and use like the Jet-pack or the Confetti gun (A must for new players) to cosmetic items for your character, and also furniture and building materials for your condo.
Now, about the whole condo thing, I've never been much into the whole making a room/home type of games, but this one piqued my interest and I've been loving the amount of customization one can do to one's condo. You can make a nice mini theater to watch videos with friends, or put down instruments and jam (MIDI support so you can connect your MIDI keyboard is planned for the future), or make a museum dedicated to your art or them dank memes if you are into showing that.
All in all, this game offers a lot of things to do, buy and explore for the measly price of $15 USD, and from what I've seen, the devs are working non stop to finish this game properly and make it as fun as possible without modern day issues like microtransactions or subscription fees.
TL;DR Buy it for the mini-golf, stay for the socializing and different activities/games.

I regret not picking up this game when there was a deal on it. Turned off by the negative reviews, I decided instead to wait.
Then one day, after playing Long War on the original XCom, I decided to buy this on a whim, and by golly, I did not eat,♥♥♥♥♥♥or sleep for the next 30 hours.
I was instantly in love from the minute I saw the character pool. You can now create persistent characters that are recruitable through multiple campaigns. Before I jumped into the campaign I spent a lot of time playing around with it. While it isn't a feature that's particulary unique or innovative, it is in-depth (and further enhanced by potential mods). I definitely felt like the old aesthetic options were kinda bland, so I was pleasantly surprised to see the new ones. I spent a lot of time customizing my squad and making them look how I want; giving them backstories as I went along. An Irish mercenary with an affinity for explosives, a Japanese prodigy with a background in tech and robotics (sorry if it's a little racist lol). That feeling of loss when your favourite squaddie dies from sniper fire. If you've played the past games, you'll know what I mean :'(
Soon after, I found myself completely engrossed in the campaign. I absolutely love the concept of waging a guerilla war. The stakes feel much higher than the previous game, and you never, ever feel like you have the advantage over the aliens. You will be hounded at every turn by ADVENT. They will send UFOs to hunt your mobile base, they will drop in random reinforcements on your missions. The feeling that you are waging a war against a much stronger, well-supplied enemy is always there. You're trying to expel a foreign invader, but the odds are never in your favour. The game is about making hard choices, and that's what I like. Most of the time you will only be able to stop 1/3 of the ops they launch against you every month, which forces you to carefully evaluate your decisions moving forward. You will never have all the supplies you want/need, you will lose squad members you like (especially if you're playing on Ironman), and sometimes all you have before you are ♥♥♥♥♥♥ options and one slightly less ♥♥♥♥♥♥ option.
I also felt like the general ambiance was much darker as well. Earth did not fare well against the alien invaders. They won, and the resistance is beat up, bitter and hopelessly outgunned. The aliens are definitely more brutal this time around. Without giving away the plot, I'll just say the atrocities they commit against humankind are not pretty.
I was also pleasantly surprised to see some of the older characters show up in one way or another. Central is back, and much more badass than in the previous installment. Shen... You'll see.
It's been a year, and a lot of issues that people didn't like about the game during launch don't seem to be there anymore (zip mode alleviates the slow pace, and you can download mods to shorten cinematic sequences). I didn't really feel like there was any other major issues. Some people don't like that everything is timed (I love it. I love the pressure and the high stakes)
As for the RNG, I didn't feel like it was particularly unfair towards the player (though I did notice that going from Veteran to Commander is a fairly significant increase in difficulty). However, I'm also the kind of person who likes Mordeheim, and mod my FO4 to be a punishing and severe experience, so do consider the possibility that you and I may not agree on what 'fun' should be. That being said, you can always use mods, or play on casual. I don't see a shame in it. I think the real shame would be missing out on a good campaign and fun mechanics simply because you thought a game was too hard or too slow, so try it out.
There are some things I wish they did better. Would've been nice if there was more in the way of weapon choices (3 tiers like in the last one), or more squad choices (binary skill trees). I also would've liked to see more prominent Resistance characters (20 years of occupation would create a lot of animosity and a lot of angry people), but for the most part I felt like the characters were kinda shallow (Central and Shen I liked). In the end the game leaves you to create the backstories for your squad. In a way you largely determine how the world looks 20 years after the invasion .The plot is fairly linear (not like Witcher 3 with the multiple endings and challenging ethical decisions), but I absolutely fell in love with the story regardless. Price Tag...? A little steep considering it's a year old. I'm Canadian and shelled out 60+ for the game, so I was a little disappointed by it's price tag. Considering the new Metal Gear dropped significantly in price, and it's a FAR better received game, I do feel the high price is not fully justified, though personally, I did not mind paying it at all (I'm gonna hold off on the expansion though, and I'd advise you do too. See the ratings for the last one lol)
All in all. I'd still highly recommend the game despite the high price tag. Once you're sick of the vanilla campaign, you can download Long War 2 and start again
