Later in the game you become more cautious, consolidating your gains or taking advantage of your opponents' weaknesses to attack them. It's fun and exciting and I enjoy it thoroughly.
I don't prefer the combat system, as many have stated, so I just put it on cinematic unless it's a close battle that I think my human brain needs to participate in. Most of the time, though, it isn't.
The AI seems fine, nothing extraordinary. No complaints or accolades yet.
All in all, if you liked MoO2, you'll like this one. If you're a MoO2 purist, though, believing that any successful sequel must copy it exactly (except updated graphics or what have you)...then maybe not. Although it really DOES feel like that to me, honestly.

This is a really great game that offers you value for your money.
While it is still in early access, the game has hours of content already and ALL of it is available with an easily obtainable in-game currency. There are NO MICROTRANSACTIONS in this game. This was a selling point for me.
One of the big features of Tower Unite is the ability to purchase different homes and decorate them in any way you you see fit. You're able to import images from the internet to display on your walls, and you can play media from various sources, such as YouTube and Souncloud, and enjoy this content with your friends in the condo.
You get the currency to buy this stuff by playing various games. One of them in particular is definitely ripped from GMOD, but every other mode is really unique and interesting. At it may look like the games are shallow, but then you play them more and they grow in depth. In addition to these games, there is also a casino, and small other activities you can do around a main hubworld.
There is a great community of accepting and helpful people, and there is always something cool to look at in someone's condo. I have been in the same server as the developer who was politely answering people's questions. The developers are active and hotfix stuff very quickly, and we are looking at great content down the pipeline including possible custom workshop avatars.
Overall this game was definitely worth the $10.49 I got it for while it was on sale. I would easily pay $14.99 for the 25+ hours of entertainment I have gotten out of this.

Fans of FTP Hold 'Em games rejoice!
Loved Zynga's Hold 'Em but hated Facebook or the W10 app adaptation to it? No worries, Prominence Poker has arrived and the developer (Pipeworks) appears to really have nailed it! They included everything we've come to love about FTP Texas Hold 'Em games like the usual drop-in drop-out tables and Sit-N-Go style torneys which can be found in the ranked area of this game. There are some extras that other games did not have like the inclusion of a single player campaign / circuit that you can use to build up your initial bankroll.
The characters and animations are all really well done, far above what I expected from a FTP poker game. Overall I'm really impressed with Prominence Poker and I feel like I'm counting my lucky stars for it since leaving Facebook long ago has left a void when I had to leave behind Zynga's Hold 'Em. Say what you will about Facebook games but Zynga Hold 'Em was beast and its insane player count I think was testiment to that, at least back in the day since I haven't been back to it in a long time. I have really been enjoying my last two play sessions slowly building up my bankroll.
The production quality is also worth noting. I find it ironic that a game I so far haven't payed a cent into has run flawlessly for me yet the $40 retail game I recently got is having technical issues that those devs have acknowledged and is awaiting hotfixes.
There are a few things which would be nice to get a QOL pass but please note none of these are fun killers or gamebreaking. This game will fit your FTP poker needs, however these are the things that I hope get addressed:
-Ambient sounds in some of the play areas especially the butcher factory loop far too often and can be come a bit annoying.
-Placing 3rd in a full table Sit-N-Go torney nets you a loss of chips if I'm reading that correctly. At the lowest levels it's a $5000 buy in but 3rd only gets you $4500. Placing 3rd should at the very least be a break even point but as in other FTP poker games, it really should net you a small gain. In this game placing 3rd is still a losing position so placing only first or second is the only gains to be found in Sit-N-Go. First is making over 3x buy-in so I'd like to see them pull a few K off of first and put it in 3rd place winnings and first place would STILL be making 3x buy in.
^In other FTP poker games, Sit-N-Go style torneys you feel like you come out ahead if you "place" in that torney. In Prominence poker however, you still lose if you placed 3rd.
-The pacing, especially in ranked tables can be a bit slow. You can que up your actions but the problem is that there is like a five second delay when it goes to take that action in case you wish to cancel it. Much time can be saved if the system used a check box style que action system with a few more options and the system was instant (like Zynga). The que system usually is designed to save time but in this game I'm noticing people not even bothering with it because of that five second delay. It's faster if you just manually take your action which is instant so that you don't get that 5 second delay. Also some of the character animations, while nice at first start to also slow up the game. When you want to look at your whole cards, you have to wait for your characters animation to do so in some situations. Other animations like your character having to actually pick up the deck to deal out I wish were really sped up. It's a nice visual affect at first but after a while, those seconds it takes start to add up and affects pacing overall IMHO.
There are a few other minor things but again, nothing that is going to make you annoyed to the point of quiting. In any case, if your looking for a FTP Hold 'Em game without the hassle of social websites and the like, this is it! Well done Devs, really well done.

I do not normally review games, but given the incredible amount of work these two developers have done to create such an immersive game, I thought I would write a review to support them.
TLDR; A beautiful game designed around solid ship and crew mechanics. Teamplay and VOIP is a must if you and your crew is planning to win the day! While graphically beautifully, the game does need further optimization, as FPS can significantly vary between different PC specs. At this point in time, definitely worth the $17.00 I paid for this game at the time of writing this review. (25FEB17)
Pros:
(+) - Teamwork - This game fundamentally operates on the principle of teamwork. If you don’t have communication; down to Davy Jones’ locker, you’ll go.
(+) - Amazing Visuals & Animations - Reloading animation is one of the best I’ve seen. On par with WoR’s.
(+) - VOIP - Crew chat, Captain Chat (Ship to Ship,) Global Chat.
(+) - Ship Naming and Ship Customization - Once given Captainship, Captain can change the name and paint of ship.
(+) - Complexity of Ship Engagements - Many ways to destroy enemy ships. You can sink them through ramming, blowing holes in their ship, setting them on fire, or even through grappling and boarding.
(+) - Multiple Maps and Weather Effects - Game features multiple maps and amazing weather effects that vary from round to round.
(+) - Character Customization & Level Progression - While limited, the character customization and character progression is great. As your character gains levels, he/she is able to unlock additional clothing styles and traits.
(+) Price - At $20.00 this game was an immediate buy for me regardless if it’s in Early Access or not. The developers have worked hard over the past three years to deliver a robust and enjoyable game at a relatively small price and have succeeded in doing so.
Cons:
(-) - Optimization - While the game runs amazingly well for me, quite a few others have been complaining of significant FPS loss during engagements.

Botanicula is an aesthetic-driven game whose story is told visually through pictures and images. This is similar to Machinarium which is developed by the same team. However, the setting is completely different. You follow a team of magical insects as they try to save their tree.
Optionally, along the way you meet a host of magical insects whose mysteries you are encouraged to unravel and are rewarded with a card for your "Bestiary" collection. The cards are secondary though and merely there to represent that you have explored all the mysteries with that particular insect, and you can move on.
The mysteries themselves are hypothesis-oriented. You attempt various different experiments on that screen until eventually, you figure out how the magical insect operates. Unlike Machinarium, Botanicula has barely any item-collection oriented puzzles (and those it has are really obvious - as in an insect asking for a specific item), so most of the puzzles can be solved on the screen you are on. This lowers the scope of brute forcing and makes the actual puzzle solving a lot more enjoyable. When you need some extra knowledge or oomph from another screen, it completely becomes obvious that you've run out of actions and there's enough to explore that you can leave and then come back later with some novel insight.
However, while I have not referenced a walkthrough once and find this game charming and satisfying, I have noticed other reviewers saying that the puzzles are frustrating and very difficult. So keep that in mind and perhaps this is one of those games that you should DEMO before committing to, to see whether it's frustrating or fun for you.
All in all, a pleasurable and enjoyable experience from a team that I will be following in their future endeavours.

Only not recommending because Steam doesn't allow for mixed reviews, but I feel that when the game is out of Early Access, all the things that I feel are "off" about the game will be assessed and changed.
If you're a fan of Terraria, you will like this game. I know purist fans will despise me for that statement, but there's no denying that the games have many similarities. The game appeals to creative types, having many different items and blocks to place, and you get to choose from many varied planets to settle on when you want to start building.
My gripe is where the game attempts to appeal to the "adventurer" type player, but I'd like to reiterate that I truly believe this will not be a problem when the game is in a more complete state, but for the sake of the review being about the game in its current condition, I want readers to know that this game is lacking in this aspect. The random dungeons underground yield little to no rewards, which make finding them a bit useless. The weapons spawned have stats comparable to other weapons of the same level, meaning little to no diversity in the power of the weapons. Some people can argue that it's balanced this way, but I think there should be the possibility of receiving an extremely OP weapon to make the game more interesting. The bosses are fun and unique, but the quests that you do to reach each boss feel like mirrors of each other and are monotonous. I feel they're time sinks between boss fights that are completely unnecessary, but I imagine they'll be spiced up before the game is out of Early Access. My BIGGEST gripe is the difficulty being attached to certain biomes. This on top of the lack of a true "end-game" and choppy pacing really puts off a player like me who enjoys the factor of progression.
Overall, the game is coming along well though. If you like building and don't mind the game feeling incomplete, definitely buy it and give it a try. If you're wanting it to feel like Terraria in terms of pacing and progression, hold off for now until the game is finished.

I recommend this game because I enjoyed playing it very much, primarily.  The graphics is what people these days call, "old-school pixel-art," but this was probably about the best possible at time of the game's creation.  It is a point-and-click game with an inventory and a grid in the bottom left-hand corner with the action words, like, "look", "pick-up," "talk," etc., which I have seen in other LucasArts games, such as the ancient, original Indiana Jones games,  The Secret of Monkey Island (again, the original), Maniac Mansion (if memory serves me correctly), and the much more recent "Thimbleweed Park."
The game ran smoothly all the way through, without any bugs that I noticed.  The game incorporated several humorous moments that I really enjoyed.  However, there were some parts that I found tricky, because those puzzles were very unique to any other games I have seen or played. The game got the hardest towards the end, as the story was coming to a climax, and the main character was trying to evade capture, so it made sense that you had to make quick reactions, when the accompanying music added to the tension.  I died a few times in a row trying to figure out what the heck I was supposed to do, as in not knowing how to use the controls. During a chase scene, when the main character was running for his life in an underground cave system with many routes to choose from, there appeared on-screen the image of a mouse, with a red dot appearing and disappearing a few times per second on the left and right mouse-click buttons, as the image of the mouse moved across the screen either forwards, or forwards and to the right and to the left of the screen (making a 90% turn midway up the screen).  I died just watching this image to see what it was showing, but after dying, I was given the option to continue or load a game save. I didn't know whether I was supposed to repeatedly click, click and hold while moving the mouse in sync with the mouse image,  or what.  I was stumped for a moment, but pretty quiclkly, after a little trial-and-error, I figured it out.  Once I had figured it out, it was no longer difficult to me, as the difficulty wasn't in the actions taken, but in figuring out what the game wanted me to do control-wise.  There was another scene in which my character was in a hotel room with several doors, all of them locked. You wake up in the morning with someone pounding on the door, knowing they meant you great harm.  So what to do when you cannot unlock any of the doors to escape, and you have clicked on every single item in the room, and so have nothing to work with. (Or so I momentarily thought).  If you check the room carefully, you find out that the wardrobe is made of very heavy, hard wood, and the table is very fragile.  That is a clue in itself.  Even after solving that, you will probably die because you didn't yet know you had to do something before going to bed. I will not say any more, because I do not wish to spoil anything for another player.  It all made sense, but took some tries, because there were several things you had to do in order to escape the hotel unharmed, and you couldn't possibly know in advance what to do, because you go to locations previously unaccessible to you, and none of it has to do with what is in your inventory.  Additionally, it is all timed, and if you are not quick enough, you will be killed.  There is no way to know in advance which door to bust down, when there are 3 and a window, and there is no time to inspect or try the wrong thing before getting killed.  I was slightly frustrated, because I just wanted to reach a save point so I could go to sleep, yet I really enjoyed to humor of it, and doing these not seen in any other game, and figuring out what to do.
Even though this game doesn't have a hint system, and there are not any walkthrough guides aside for achievements, the game does offer a long, long list of pre-saves for the entire game, so if you cannot figure something out, you have the option to load a point past the point of difficulty.  There are so many, chances are you will not miss more than several seconds of the game by doing this.
This game is based on H.P.Lovecraft's book by the same title, which is a novel, written as of it were a person's true account of his journey to Arkham that got detoured to Innsmouth, as he wanted to check out all the weird rumors he heard about Innsmouth and its residents.  The book references another book called the "Necromonicon," which droves of people believe was a real book that he referenced, something like a grimoire. There are a few fairly ancient books that bear this title, that many believe was the one he was referencing.  In the story, Innsmouth does not appear on any map, and the townspeople there keep to themselves, and do not at all welcome outsiders.  There is a church their, while appearing to be a Christian church on the outside, is anything but Christian, and trying to snoop around it could be a fatal mistake. The local townspeople look very odd, some rumor to be from inbreeding. There are not any elderly there. It is a fishing town, which was once very poor, until some man came returned from a long voyage with a boatload of gold and fish.  But the bounty came with a very, very hefty price to the townsfolk.  I cannot tell more about the story without risking spoiling anything for anyone.
I found the game entertaining, and enjoyed the humor.  Once of my favorite parts was in the library, reading the titles to the many books there.  It reminded me of a similar scene in, I think it was, "Quest for Infamy."  The game is rather short, if played straight-though without any rushing, but checking every little nook and cranny out, would probably take 2-4 hours, I estimate. It certainly wasn't the best game I have ever played, but it was also far from being bad. Nothing spectacular.  If you like old-school point-and-click games, you probably will enjoy the game, and it is worth up to $5.00, but not a bit more, in relation to current prices for other games. It wasn't nearly as humorous as Maniac Mansion, The Secret to Monkey Island, King's Quest games, or The Quest for Infamy, but it still is enjoyable and entertaining, so I do recommend it, if this sounds in your taste.

As a hardcore Master of Orion I & II fan, I was highly anticipating this modern version. That being said, having experienced the disappointment of Master of Orion III (and I know the game has its fans, I'm not one of them), and having experienced many disappointments of poorly redone classics, I was also majorly cautious. I decided to get the "Early Access" version after trying it out so that I could follow its development. The Early Access versions were certainly fun, but their flaws were also apparent, which made me concerned about the actual release.
Now that I've played the release version, I can say that they've managed to quell my concerns. Once I learned some of the mechanics of this version of MOO (mostly deciding how to prioritize using the colonists to properly research/farm/build), I found a much greater appreciation of the game. I'm in the process of figuring out what weapons work best on my ships, as well as how to deal with being bullied by the Silicoids. After doing some reloading, I blew up their fleet that was surrounding one of my planets. Very rewarding, while I also learned the tactics so that I won't have to reload in future playthroughs.
My biggest complaint is the lack of turn-based space combat. I *loved* that mechanic in the original Master of Orion, so I greatly miss it. I also feel like they needed to be clearer about some of the effects within the game. For instance, they don't fully give the details behind the properties of the different biomes (for instance, the food production per cell or the different cell availability. It was much more readable to look it up on the MOO Wiki). So there are other concerns that have popped up, and I'm curious to see how the AI will stand up to the test of time.
Overall, I'm enjoying the game in the same way I did with MOO I & II. This is not to say that I think the game has lived up to those versions yet. I do need more time with the game before fully comparing it. However, I can say that I'm really enjoying the process of learning & growing.

To put my overall score into context, understand that on a scale of 1 to 10, I would rate MOO1 at 9.0, MOO2 at 9.5, and MOO3 somewhere around 4.0.  To summarize my impression of this latest incarnation (wish I could just call it MOO4), I'd say 7.0.
There are many aspects that are great ... I find the voicework by various well-known sci-fi actors keen and enjoyable including Michael Dorn (Worf from Star Trek: TNG), Mark Hamill (Luke Skywalker from Star Wars) and Alan Tudyk (Wash from Firefly and Serenity).  An amazing amount of features and tidbits are carried forward into this incarnation from MOO1 and MOO2 including elements of the technology tree, race customization screen (though bizarrely -- and really frustratingly, one of many unexpectedly lacking features that reduce my rating of the game -- not able to retain a customized race between games so you have to re-create it each time from scratch, particularly frustrating in multiplayer) and all but one of the races (the Terrans, not to be confused with the Humans -- the Terrans are basically evil humans) are carryovers from the first two games though some MOO2 races are notably absent -- the Gnolams (gnomish folk) and the Elerians (dominatrixes).
Unfortunately, the interface has not been improved -- in some aspects its taken a step backward from all predecessors -- and can be cumbersome in terms of how many buttons you have to click through to get to things you want; using the technology tree as opposed to a one-deep technology, for instance, requires clicking on the science screen from icons at the top right, then a 'View Technology Tree' button at the bottom right, then scrolling sideways through the tree to find the tech path you want before finally clicking on teh tech itself.  You have to do this every time you finish researching the 'tech path' you previously chose -- you can only click on one tech to pursue; it will automatically select the requisite techs to get there if you haven't researched them yet, but you can't shift+click another tech to queue afterward and you will have to start this process again after finishing the one particular tech and its requisites -- including, yes, re-opening the technology tree and the tree always opens all the way to the starting techs at the left; the tech tree is several screenwidths across so you will have to scroll more and more as the game goes on before you can pick a tech you want.
While its okay in single player, this really consumes time in multiplayer.   So do animations like colonizing planets -- there's no option so far as I have found to prevent those and if you go through heavy expansion, you may find yourself unable to colonize planets when your colony ships reach them because of everything you need to set up on a new colony (and no, there's no copy-and-paste-able build queue ... and the build queue is only 5 buildings/ships long -- I recall it being much larger in MOO2 -- which means you have to fiddle with your build queues much more frequently and it gets too cumbersome to manage in multiplayer much past 20 or so colonies).
There are also frequent crashes and bugs ... I find, sporadically, one particularly building for some reason cannot be built after researching the tech even though it should be; this bug persists between saves.  On one game, I was unable to build terraforming -- so I could not terraform my planets; on another, I was unable to build Robo-Miner.
One frustrating missing feature of multiplayer is locking players to the civ they start in the event (more like eventuality) the game has to be continued from a save -- so when a host reloads a multiplayer game due to a crash or folk just having retired from a long game to continue another night, random players connecting in will be assigned the civs that previous players had been playing and block the original players from being able to play them ... seems silly they wouldn't code in a 'lock' of some sort so only either the original player can play the civ, an AI or if the host decides to open up that civ for other players, but as it stands you can't really stop this from happening except to ask the new player to change to a different previously-AI-controlled race or leave the game.
Overall, I like the game, and I do recommend it to fans of the series.  Its nowhere near as bad as MOO3 ... but don't expect it to quite be at the level of MOO1 or MOO2; it has some shortfalls and some bugs.  If you find it on a good Steam Sale, and you are a fan of the series or at least the genre, I definitely recommend a grab.

On launch, the game was lackluster at best.
The world felt empty and dull, with lackluster, uninspired combat. The settlement base building works about as well as would be expected from a Bethesda game, and gets boring very quickly. It's honestly terrible. And a good chunk of their dlc went towards padding out that "feature".
The story was bland at best, with uninteresting characters awkwardly standing about everywhere. The main playable character is just as dull. The entire conversation system is essentially a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ version of Bioware's conversation system, full of dead eyed npcs and awkward jerking movements. In conversations, the player is given options ranging from desperately trying to do whatever the npc ask, to making a sarcastic quip towards the npc, before desperately trying to please them by doing what they ask.
The game was, and most probably still is, filled with bugs, as all Bethesda games are. A lot of them are minor, a few of them are game breaking. My favourite was instantly being killed when touching the bumper of some of the cars scattered on the map. Bethesda is known for releasing games full of bugs, that the modding community would fix for them.
The sad fact about Bethesda is that their games are only worth playing if you've installed a couple of the mods available for their games. Sites like the Nexus have had a wide variety of mods available, from simple bug fixes to complete graphical or combat and crafting overhauls.
Bethesda has made a big mistake here. They've taken the good will of the modding community out back and shot it in the head. Their Creation Club is taking already existing mods and rereleasing them as paid mods, claiming that they are "mini dlcs". Their justification to this is that the mods in the Creation Club go through their own quality control tests to make sure it works in the game without any problems. Therein lies the first problem: Bethesda, a company known for being rather incompetent when it comes to pushing out a properly functional product, is claiming that it is worth paying for these mods, because they are testing them to make sure it works. The second problem is that the mods currently on the Creation Club already exist for free on websites such as the Nexus, and are much better in terms of quality - models and textures look much better, and so forth. The third problem is that everything on the Creation Club is downloaded in its entirety, even if you have not purchased the mod. As they add things to the Creation Club, they bloat your harddrive with inferior versions of free mods.
As it stands, the Creation Club is a steaming pile of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that is nothing more than a blatant cash grab on Bethesda's part. They are very quickly going to kill off the modding community and player base of their current and future games if this behaviour of theirs keeps up.

This game is a pixel-art-rogue-like-bullet-hell-grinder where you strive to gear up and max the stats of your character via "stat potions" that are obtained by slaying gods. In other words, you dodge a lot of attacks while injecting yourself with steroids looted from the dead bodies of gods, and when you die, your character is lost permanently. (You start out with 8 storage spaces to keep extra loot, though.)
Overall, it's a fun game for solo play AND group play with the inclusion of guilds. It's easy to set short term and long term goals alike with various play styles to experiment with. If you decide to support the game, recommending it to friends and creating RotMG related content such as YouTube videos can go a long way in helping the community expand, which the game sorely needs right now. The only major downsides to this game are that you can get easily frustrated with deaths if you don't stock up on spare items in your vault chest(s), and lag will be an issue depending on your connection and whether you play on steam, a web browser, or adobe projector.
(Contrary to what people might say, this game is not pay-to-win. You cannot pay for potions that will max the stats of your character, the highest quality gear is only available from dungeons, and the gear you -can- buy will still be lost quick if you're unskilled and die often. About the game: it's a 30-minute walking horror game a la Amnesia, but nowhere close in terms of quality. It's not extremely bad (at least it's playable and does not have bugs or glitches), and you'll get a couple of jump-scares in the meantime. Mechanically it's as simple as games come; you press E to pick up items, you press B to put a new battery in your flashlight, you press Shift to run (there's a blue stamina bar on the lower part of the screen) and you solve some puzzles. The game does not do a good job of telling you what to do (the translation is half-done) and you may end up using all of your available batteries before figuring out what to do next which means you'll have to restart.
I liked it, and I knew what I was getting into. A short indie horror game for less than 10p (cheapest game I've bought on Steam).

Author's note: Don't judge this review solely on the amount of time it says I've played on Steam. I got the XBox version back when it came out and I've played the game twice (Once was just one month ago). I may not be able to discuss the bugs that might come up in the PC version, but I can tell you about what I think about this game.
The Assassin's Creed series has been around since 2007, with numerous installments since then. AC Unity is the very first "next gen" Assassin's Creed, and they definitely put more time and effort into making this one perfect than they did with Rogue (which had the same release date).
Unity's story takes place during the French Revolution and sets up the main character from the very beginning with its tie-in with Rogue. Before we get any further, make sure you play Assassin's Creed Rogue before playing this. Now, the story is pretty decent, even if it is one we've seen over and over. Arno is out for redemption and vengeance as he gets dragged into the Templar/Assassin war. The game is fairly long (takes about 17ish hours to defeat the main campaign) and the levels are pretty unique. I got a Hitman vibe with the assassination targets, which was a nice change. (You can't disguise yourself though, lol).
Before we jump into the gameplay mechanics, let's talk about the characters. Arno, the main character, is a decent character, but he's far from the best main character we've gotten in the series. He can come off as Ubisoft trying to create another Ezio, but he's not a terrible character. The love interest, Elise, is a character you might not like. She's very focused on her goals and leaves little time for personal matters. The rest of the characters, with the exception of the historical characters like Napoleon, are pretty forgettable. The voice acting is fantastic though, but one thing might bother you in your play through...EVERY ONE has BRITISH accents in FRANCE. Makes sense, right?
In terms of gameplay, they've tried to spice things up here, but they don't go too far away from the previous games, just to make sure things are still familiar. The combat system is pretty good, and has been upgraded here and there. They've added a leveling system, as well as a level system for the soldiers. This way, fights can be a little more difficult (which is something AC has needed for a long time) and it's harder to be OP unless you grind (Which can be a good or bad thing, depending on who you are). The higher level you are, the better weapons you can use (max level is 5). This system is pretty good, and it gets better in Syndicate.
Now, here's the real question...are the enemies stupid? Well, there have been some improvements, but there are still really easy ways of taking all of them out. You'll fight a variety of soldiers, such as standard footmen, snipers, grenadiers, and some ax bois. Fighting a large group isn't as easy as it was in the older games, which is a nice change. In AC 1, if you were good enough, you could literally take on a crowd of 20 men at a time.
To stab these guys, you'll need some weapons. Weapons can now be bought in the 'customization menu'. There are swords, spears, pistols, rifles, and heavy weapons. Each one has different stats and are good for certain situations. There are tons of weapons to try out! Speaking of 'customization', in the menu, you can customize how Arno looks, give him better armor, and unlock skills by using skill points. Money, skill points, and items can be unlocked by completing levels. This system is pretty great and it looks like it'll be around for a little bit.
Something very noticeable is integration of a new stealth system. For the first time in an AC game, you can actually crouch and hide behind walls (I know right? It took THIS long for them to figure this out?). The cover system is pretty great, but can be used to easily kill upwards of 5 people. The game finally has more of a stealth side to it, and it helps when the enemies are higher levels than you. You can even cover-stab people, which works well. This game also sees the inclusion of a new lock picking mechanic, and it's actually good! It's similar to BioShock where you have a bar that moves up and down and you have to hit it at the right spot to unlock it. MUCH better than AC III's poor attempt at lock picking.
Another thing to note is the open world stuff. There are side missions, chests, and even murder mysteries (which are the best!) to explore and find. Your map gets so crowded with things to do and find! I'll leave you to explore ;)
In all, this isn't exactly the best AC game, but these new mechanics get improved upon in Syndicate. If you're a fan of the franchise, definitely check this out, just note that it probably won't be your favorite AC game. (But play the other games first, they are WAY better (Especially AC 2, Black Flag, and Rogue).

If you had a PlayStation 3 during the time PlayStation Home was available, and enjoyed playing it, you’ll love Tower Unite.
The game is in early access, and there are glitches and bugs here and there, but to be honest if you consider all of the work that has been put into the game, and all the future work the developer is intending to do, you’ll give it plenty of grace. The game’s trailer is true to its word, there are NO MICROTRANSACTIONS. This does mean you have to grind for money, but I’d much rather spend time earning the in game money than paying for it out of pocket.
The customization for your condo is pretty detailed right now, with avatar customization currently lacking. This isn’t really a con though, you can tell the developer has tons planned for character customization in the future.
The mini-games are pretty fun despite what some people are saying. Planet Panic needs some work, but the developer is aware of that, and is working on it (as well as a handful of other games to add into the mix).
The casino is probably my favorite place in the game. The machines pay out well, and when you’re playing slots, you’ll keep trying to convince yourself you should take “just one more spin”. Some reviews state that making money takes too long, but I think the rate that you earn the in game currency is fair.
Overall I think Tower Unite is definitely worth the price (even better if you get it on sale). The content currently in the game is enough to keep you interested for quite a long time, and the fact that the developer updates and patches the game regularly makes the future of Tower Unite look promising.

It comes down to the classic question of "What do you want for nothing?"  When the description said this game was short, it wasn't kidding.  The "massive collaborative effort between dozens of fans and designers of adventure games" comes to roughly 40 minutes of content, if that.
That said, it -is- very nicely done.  The narrator's voice starts getting annoying, but the developments quickly make you forget that and start drawing you in.  The soundtrack is lovely, the atmosphere is one that bulds up nicely.  There are wonderful references and in-jokes involving all those famous names and the projects they worked on, such as referenced in the  titles on the bookshelf.  In all truth the length is the only fault I can find with it, and that fact that it's resolved not to satisfaction, but with one of those endings that leaves you staring at the screen wondering "Wait, that's IT??"
It leaves me wondering just what about this game needed 40+ contributers, when these days you could point-and-click flash adventures with similar content that could be done with as many as five people and as few as one.  But again we come back to the fact that it is, in fact, free, whcih eases the sting somewhat.
Play it once, grouse, put it away, and safely forget about it.

Botanicula is by far one of the most charming games I've ever played. Everything about it takes me back to simpler times when I was so easily entertained. If you have any appreciation for a light-hearted point-and-click adventure, then you will greatly enjoy Botanicula.
The gameplay is entirely point-and-click. You will have to solve puzzles and complete fetch quests to progress through the story. Botanicula does a wonderful job of staying fresh through its visual and sound design--i never got tired of doing practically the same thing repeatedly. It also helps that Botanicula will probably only last you a few hours at most. It could have gotten tedious had it lasted much longer. The puzzles are never too difficult either. I had to look up solutions to a couple of parts but ended up kicking myself for not having the patience of figuring it out. The story is light, and is driven by the characters' actions. There is no dialogue whatsoever, rather any information regarding the story is told through pictures and short cutscenes. It's a cute element that suits the game.
One of Botanicula's greatest strengths is its visual design. The color palette really pops off the screen, and it adds to the effect when purposeful colorless segments come into play. The bright and joyful colors are complimented by jovial little characters that you control. Each of the characters in your group eventually play a significant role in puzzles throughout the game. While one of them is much more important than the others when it comes to the story, each character has a part to play. Besides the protagonists you control you'll come across several other botanical creatures you can interact with. Playing their little games or simply interacting with them earns you a card with said creature on it that you can collect. If you find them all you get a little bonus after the credits role! All these tiny creatures are diverse in design and range from adorable to mildly frightening. I had fun finding the rascals and discovering their quirks.
The overall sound design goes hand in hand with the cute aesthetics. I found myself laughing out loud as I heard the silly sounds some of the creatures made. From speech to the sound of movement, everything was spot on to me. Even the darker, scary enemies were well done and felt intimidating in a game where I knew very well that I couldn't be harmed. The music isn't particularly memorable, but I never thought it was bad at any points either. I suppose it just gets the job done.
I loved Botanicula. It's fun, adorable, heartwarming and if I ever have kids someday, I would love to play this with them. This is definitely worth your time.

I look at the reviews for X-Blades on the page and I honestly find myself baffled. Review after review recommending this game that I honestly wish I had never bought. In the interest of honesty, I will disclose that I only bought X-Blades at the request of a friend, with the promise of lunch at a hibachi steakhouse if I got the good ending. And as good as the steak and shrimp was, I'm not completely sure if it was worth it. I'll start with the story. What little story there is is so incredibly generic one could get the main gist with a few key words. Blah blah blah treasure. Blah blah blah Darkness. Blah blah blah ancient power. blah blah blah. This doesn't stop the main characters, though. I suppose just having a story is a major accomplishment for an entity as relatable as the half-eaten bag of crackers in my trash can. This is only half due to the inherent flatness of the characters though. The other half is because of the incompetence of the voice actors. Each and every line is delivered like the person standing behind the microphone has a gun to their head. The incredibly threatening recording sessions obviously having taken place weeks apart and in different locations. Then they just stitched the recordings together like someone trying to make a car by sewing construction paper together with string. The visual design is actually alright, feels like it's a bit behind the times. It would look fantastic on a PS2, but it falls short on modern consoles. The sound design is back and forth, as the music is good, but each individual sound effect feels like a tiny murder every time it plays. And finally, we come to gameplay, arguably the make-or-break point of game design. It's repetitive. It's incredibly repetitive. I honestly can't imagine why anybody outside of an insane asylum would play this game the entire way through without the promise of chicken and shrimp. If you aren't using the weightless melee attack, you're using a small pool of spells that you've picked out until the game decides that the enemy you're facing needs this specific type of spell. One particular boss requires you to use quite a few different spells, and you can only have so many equipped at once, so more than a few times during the fight, your main enemy will be the menu. In conclusion, Don't bother with X-Blades. if you absolutely can't help yourself, go find the soundtrack or something, but the game is absolutely not worth the time it takes to buy it.

50th. review :) This one deserves it. Assasins creed unity is one of the most unjustly critised games ever.
Short review:
Not that good of a story with a bit clunky controls, but the attention to detail and depth is unmatched. Not exactly like old assasins creed games but definitely a historicaly fresh and original look. I bought on a sale and i would say the best assasins creed ever. There is no animus drama in this game. Story takes 25 hours and the map is huge enough. Do not miss it on sale.
Long review:
Assasins creed unity brings yet another new character on to the stage, Arno, who is a child of an assasin leader during the pre revolutionary times of France (Around 1790). This amazing game has tons of pros that will wipe out the cons so lets begin with cons:
- Controls are a bit weird. You may find yourself running circiles on the edge of a balcony or fountain, or hanging on the doorstep while trying go get in the room :D
- The optimization is not that good. You may need a graphic card as good as gtx1060 ti or rx480.
- The sync points (which are used to upgrade the character) are limited in single player. So you have to complete some online missions in order to fully upgrade.
- Enemies have eyes and ears like superman. Do not even try to complete missions in stealth. Just create a chaos with some bombs, divert the enmies and assassinate the target and run away like hell. Snipers are legendary.
- The story has lots of cliche ideas like your childhood crush turning out to be a templar and an a traior in the assasins council.
- Game has som bugs but not that much.
Even with these cons, this game is stil amazing. There are side missions to spend time, nostradamus enigmas to find, murderers to solve and extremists to assasinate. The story takes 25 hours and leaves plenty of other activities to spend time. You can collect cocades and amulets and open chests. These will always reward you with something.
You can reveal the whole map by climbing the historical towers and syncing in first 5 hours of the game. You should take time to upgrade yourself and your weapons because missions will get harder pretty soon. You can realy enjoy coop missions with your close friends. Some missions are going up to 4 players.
The paris is a huge city and there is a connection to versailies. The teritories are divided according to difficulty of the rank of the gangsters and offical officers. But you can still free roam around the city as mush as you want. Just keep away from those nuisances.
You will have an income in this game, so you can just walk around and make money to buy new weapons. You have your own room in the game. It does not mean much since you can customize your character whenever you want, but i saw Arno placing his arms on the fence of the balcony and gazing his eyes around when i stood near by the edge, and it felt like home. Details ;)
There are swords, long weapons, pistols, snipers and big guns. All these types have at least 20 different kinds with unique abilities. You also have money pouch to distract people, smoke grenades to make smoke obviously, stun grenade to stun enemies nearby, poison gas for obvious reasons, phantom blade for remote kills, cherry bomb for taking attention, medicine to heal, and my favorite, the berserk blade to drive them crazy and attack to their own friends. If you want wepons variety and strategies, this game is rocking it.
Missions have side opportunities like creating a diversion by freeing captives. I do not recommend risking the whole mission for these side activities because as i said before, you will probably fail to stay stealth.
Pros:
- This game has lots of development effort that most of the player do not realize. There are newspapers to read around the city to inform you about what is happening. There is information available about every plave and people in the game. There are cafes to buy for income and people will start singing in those lively places. The paris is going to get through a revolution and you can feel and see the clues around the city. Every street is another scene. You can and will literaly go through buildings or get a mission from one of them.
- Visual quality and historical environment is amazing. You can literaly feel like you are living in Paris. There are tons of details that has created a vivid sensation. The historical ambient and decoration looks skillfuly placed in every corner.
- Environment is lively. You do not feel like a ghost and nobody cares what you do. Because every action you do gets a feedback from nearby crowd. And the crowd... That crowd is the best populated scene in a game ever. Some areas like in front of the justice hall, are incredibly dense and the still manages to render the scene, even though some glitches are present. The streets are full of people who are NOT just copy paste animations. I have seen men and women making out, people sweeping the streets, carpenters working, fighting, dancing and singing... And lot others. This is serious effort that most of the gamers just do not understand to appreciate. There are dogs wandering around :D Some extremists will tempt or provoke you while you are just walking by.
- Character customization is off the charts. You can literaly get together a clothing piece by piece. Your hood, chest, hands, pants, boots and belts can be customized. All these pieces have their own specialities for health, stealth, ranged weapons and one more thing that i forgot. So if you chose your clothing according to your favorite skills, you might end up looking like a freak. And this is where preset clothes kick in. You can wear other games assasins clothes and the upgrades would apply without modifying the clothes. I wore Ezios master outfit.
- There are multiple numbers of weapon types. I have never used anything other than a sword and a hidden blade. You will need money to buy new weapons. But don't worry, you will have cafes around the town which will bring you a genorous income after renovated.
- There are historical characters in the game, like Napoleon Bonaparte and Marque de Sade.
- There is a last seen mechanism in the fights. If an enemy spots you somwhere, they will start converging on your last seen location, which is a ghost of you placed by the game. So you can predict where the idiot officers are going and go around them.
- You will be figthing with your crush side by side, even though she is a templar. Cute =)
- Some sequences of the game takes place in World War 2. Or 1. Tha game manages to capture a 1900 years paris and lets you climb eiffel tower and shoot down airplanes and run away from subways. This is called variety.
- The game has a descend button to help you descend from whereever you are. Thus you do not have to find a proper way to get down from heights. Just press a button and Arno will handle the rest.

After playing this Title for over 40 hours i feel i need to re wright my review.  In all my years of playing Anything X-Com.. from the original in 1994, to Terror From The Deep, Apocalypse and even Interceptor.... i have not played an X-Com game that has rubbed me the wrong way as Xcom2 has.  It started with my inability to develop the Plated armor, the Tech 2 armor because for some reason it required advent trooper corpses to produce.  To outfit the entire squad you need 6 but throughout much of the game up to that point.... Troopers rarely spawned on missions that gave me the ability to recover them. So little did i encounter them that making the mistake of selling 2-4 corpses left me 2 short from producing the armor, thats how rare my advent trooper recovery was.  I would of happily acquired more examples but as i've said the game simply did not provide.  So rare was tis that over a 6-10 mission spawn, i was left being one corpse short of advancing my armor, and this became increasingly problematic as enemies were starting to one shot me and this was not remedied until i skipped plated armor entirely and went to power armor. The fact that power armor strangely... did not require corpses meant that i had the material to produce powered armor for a significant portion of my play time already and made me wonder why plated armor require corpses in the first place.....
After this the game improved a fair amount but something still nagged at me.. the timed missions... which their are too many of them. In fact you will be seeing a count down timer to mission fail fairly often as these mission counters are the bread and butter of the game.  I did not realize just how much i disliked these timers until the avenger was shot down and i entered my first base defense mission.  Remarkably... the timer was absent... not to be seen! Instead you were faced with constant alien re enforcements in its place. this proved to be very enjoyable as it puts pressure onto you without binding you with an arbitrary number.  I have nothing bad to say about the base defense mission as really it was my high point of the game. Unfortunately... the mission that followed was one of my least favorites.
Tasked with hacking a data terminal before it explodes, i rushed to the objective and approached the target undetected. However when securing the data... every target in the map went onto alert and in a single turn... i ended up facing 12 targets on all sides.. a force that included an Andromen, a heavy mech and a Sectopod, all targets that require intense concentrated fire to take down.  In a situation like this you'd think you've cleared the objective its best to call the insertion craft and leave a victorious gorilla fighter right? no... despite achieving the primary goal of the mission and preventing the aliens from achievinh a dark event. the mission is counted as a failure.... such a thing when the game makes you to be a resistance fighter was just too much of a stretch after throwing me into a situation i couldn't win.
I don't mind difficult unforgiving games but Xcom2 takes it a little far and creeps into the realms of maliciousness and personally i do not feel that it really respects the player.  Because of this i cant enjoy this game and I'm unable to recommend it.

This game is without question weird. And that’s definitely to its favor.
is a point-and-click adventure game about the faunal flora residents of a fantastical tree trying to stop a dark, arachnid-like entity from destroying everything they know. If it sounds strange already, then trust me when I say you don’t know the half of it.
To begin, gameplay is standard to the genre; as the player, your job is to explore the grand extent of the tree from the dramatically miniscule perspective of your band of five oddball characters. In your adventuring, you are provided the opportunity to interact with nearly every aspect of your environment, collecting items, receiving and completing small quests and challenges, solving puzzles, and unraveling the simple and yet still fascinating narrative before you, often making use of the individual assets of your tiny arboreal team to do so, and all without the game ever uttering more than a few words of human speech in the process.
Using that as a steppingstone, I transition into aesthetics. The artwork is absolutely beautiful, reminiscent of the animated fair of Tim Burton. Yet, even as there is a bizarre and almost twisted nature to the visuals, the presentation remains almost perpetually lighthearted (most of the time). Nearly every aspect of the tree that the small band of main characters inhabits has a life of its own and each is immensely unique from one to the next (so much so, there’s even a card-collecting mechanic within the game that showcases a solid plethora of these many faces whenever the player takes interest in looking back). Meanwhile, the main team itself is an odd collective of friends who, while not given heavy character development, are filled with heart and personality. Matching up with the strange visuals and dreamlike presentation is an almost unearthly soundtrack from Czech musical group DVA, who also aided in other aspects of the final product.
As I stated earlier, there is almost no true verbal dialogue outside of the intentionally indecipherable mumbles of its characters, and next to no text of any kind; the entirety of the story is recalled and played out on screen as if on a stage. Nevertheless, it is an engaging narrative, even as it is a simple one. In the end, the game isn’t especially lengthy, nor is it predominantly difficult (I, considering myself a less impressive gamer, was able to complete it in right around 5 hours); additionally, like most games in its subset genre, it tends to be a casual experience without an exceptional abundance of high-velocity or high-intensity moments during play. Do any of these facts diminish the value of this game? My answer is an emphatic no. When approaching almost any artistic product—be it a game, a song, a movie, or anything else—it’s important to remember that rarely, if ever, will a piece of art appeal to everyone; even the most popular or widely received products will have people who simply don’t enjoy it the way others do, and this one is certainly not exempt by any means.
is definitely a strange piece of work. It’s a wild adventure that takes place almost entirely in a tree; it’s a bizarre introduction to a lovable cast and a beautiful world; it’s a story without many words, yet it is filled with all sorts of heart and humor
; it’s a relatively calm, somewhat brief, light-hearted game that had me entranced, entertained, and engaged all the way through.
To sum it up shortly: it was pretty weird, and it was pretty awesome.

Personal Rating: 8.5/10
Pros:
1. This game allows some good role-playing elements and creative character builds.
2. The perk system is easy to follow and encourages you to make choices between great perks.
3. There is an incredibly awesome and active mod community on Nexus Mods which enhances the game greatly.
4. The dead space that was in Fallout 3 and New Vegas is fixed in this game with the Commonwealth. I loved those two games, but if I did a review on those two that would be one of my only cons. It makes sense why the dead space was there, but makes for a kind of boring area of the map. Fallout 4 doesn't have that problem at all. Especially with great mods.
5. The first DLC, Far Harbor, was a fun DLC with lovable and hateable people/factions.
6. You'll see that I will hate on the faction system in the game a little when it comes up against the story, but one redeeming quality is that there (SPOILERS?) isn't necessarily a bad guy when you think about it. Everyone has a reason for doing what they're doing but it just seems to clash with other peoples' desires/objectives. Makes choices hard in the first play through.
7. It's not like completing the game once is good enough. The game has GREAT replay value.
8. Despite the story being kind of sorta okay, everything else with side quests, settlements, NPC interactions, etc. is very fun and worth constant playthroughs.
9. Settlement building gives you the creative/creation element to the game and it feels great. Mods from Nexus Mods really amplify this in a huge way.
Cons:
1. BUGSSSSSSSSS. Sooooo many bugs. Some can be game breaking. There are mods that fix this, but something like that shouldn't be necessary.
2. The story... just isn't all that captivating for me. I didn't really have a desire to go find my son after the first play through. Same thought with Fallout 3. New Vegas did captivating story telling SOOO well. Wish Bethesda would have picked up on it.
3. The base game factions are okay... but fail in comparison to Fallout New Vegas. (may not be fair to compare games like this, but when a small developer does your game better than you it's necessary lol)
4. I don't really feel like I have a choice in the story. I get "choices," but they are a little lackluster in comparison to Fallout New Vegas. The only difference is who I choose to progress the story with. It's basically the same no matter who you walk with when you get to the bare bones of it.
5. Optimization with an average/below average graphics card and computer build makes playing this game difficult. Framerate drops, texture quality loss, etc. It's totally made to be played on a good quality computer.
6. After Far Harbor, I could take or leave DLCs. It's content you pay for that you probably could get in mods and it would work better.

This is a great game. I'm glad I bought it late considering they fixed most glitches and crashes. I only got stuck in a wall once and you can just fast travel. Really not a big deal. The main bug that really is annoying is when your supposed to kill someone and they are invincible. So I had to fail the mission and restart it to beat it. But only happened twice so also not a game breaker. Besides those two minor inconviences, This is the best AC I have played yet. (I own it but havent played sydicate yet.)
To start the Fighting is awesome. You are no longer this rare talent that can kill 100's of enemies without a scratch. You have to be careful fighting and is the only AC I have played where dodge has to be used. Enemies will strike you at almost the same time. Its no longer one fights you while the rest sit back like untrained soldiers who have never held a weapon. The guards will shoot in the back while 4 or 5 of them swing at you relentlessly. Sometimes you have no time to strike back, just parry all of them over and over. Your best friends are stun grenades, smoke bombs, and running the hell away. I love it all.
Another lovely change is the parkour moves. You have to either push a button to go down or another to go up. You have so much more control than any of the previous AC games. It takes a minute to get used to. But considering how much more control you have, I wish all of them used this method for movement. Running on rooftops you can push a button to go further or just the run button to sprint across.
The story isn't that bad. I mean it's not a blockbuster but I still enjoyed it. The Coop is fun even with other people. I played a couple and honestly it was kinda fun seeing how other people played the game. Double sync assassinations and sitting on the roof throwing smoke bombs while the rest sneak in and murder everyone before it clears. It was a unique way to make a multiplayer game.
All and all this is a good game. I don't see why it has such negative reviews on recent ones. The game played fine for me in the 60 hours I have played it. I would say a diamond in the rough. The few things they changed made the game even better. After playing I am glad I ignored the negative reviews and tried it anyways. Made me remember why I love this franchise. I would rate it a 8/10. Its not the greatest game ever, but it is defiantly worth the money on sale.

This game is mind-blowing.
I've played Harvest Moon games since Harvest Moon GBC and was amazed that there was finally a farming game on the PC. I've done three runs of this game since I got it and each run is unique. I love the diversity in the characters and the fact that you aren't glued into a linear gameplay. You can choose what you want to do, marry who you want to marry, and design your farm the way you want to. I love the unlimited creativity the game has to offer. I've compared this game to each and every HM/SoS game I've played and it got to the point where I couldn't anymore because this game was a powerhouse in itself. Nothing is like Stardew Valley. It's well worth the money, it's worth the hours of the day, this game is a jewel and I am thankful to the creator for taking what many fans of HM wanted in a game and creating this masterpiece.
The music is lovely. My favorite soundtrack in the game (though, sadly it's not included on the music CD) is the library sound. If I need to do something away from the computer or look up something, I pause the game in the library just so I can listen to the song. I love the quirky, banjo in each of the soundtracks and it really fits well with the game.
I also adore the fact that ConcernedApe has made the game quite moldable. It's very easy to mod and coming from a person who plays Minecraft modded, I greatly appreciate how simple it is to mod the game. Even without mods, the game is awesome. I played through it twice without mods and I have no complaints whatsoever.
The controls are very loose, nothing like I've encountered in any other game besides Minecraft and at first, it drove me nuts. Eventually I grew to admiring the fluidity of the controls and thought of it as another way to build my video gaming skill. The art style is cartoony and bright and it makes me kind of cheery when I play the game.
Overall, Stardew Valley is one of a kind. It took my love for Harvest Moon, Minecraft, Sims, any rpg/sim game ever and make it into a love on it's on. 10/10 across the board with this one. I highly recommend this game to anyone who's ever played the games I've listed because this game will definitely be to their liking.

I am a huge fan of the 4X genre. MoO2 is one of my favorite games of all time. MoO4 has done the series and the genre justice. If you liked MoO2, there is no reason you will not like this game. My only disappointments are the fact that the trillarians and elerians are not in the game, and that there are star lanes. However, the presence of star lanes is tolerable, and actually works quite well for the game the way it was designed. Without them, outposts and scanners would serve no purpose, so in that regard I think it was a resonable adjustment to give the game some distinction.
Everything else is excellent. Diplomacy is good. Espionage is good (seriously, they did a great job with it, it is better than any other MoO game in terms of espionage). The combat is good. I, for one, enjoy real time combat over turn based. Turn based combat worked for MoO2 back in the day because of the power of computers. In this day and age, real time does better and offers more interactivity.
Most of the core aspects of the game are still the same as MoO2 with only some minor adjustments, fresh technologies, and modernization. I love the technology tree, it has very sensible choices, and still retains the aspect of MoO2 where you had to make choices between technologies while bringing the technology tree of MoO2 more into the 21st century.
All in all, it is worth your money. Support the developer, they did a good job. I paid for this to be a reboot of MoO2, and it is exactly that, with all the flavor you'd expect.
Side Note: Add Trillarians and Elerians as DLC, and it would probably be worth a 10/10 for the effort of rebooting a legendary franchise and not making the reboot suck.

I have to admit, this was really well done.  It was short, but a lot of detail and emotion is packed into the short time.  The voice acting is pretty good, if a bit flat at times.  The atmosphere of the game is suitably ominous and oppressive.  Several times I thought I knew where the plot was going, but the surprises at the end caught me completely off-guard. For experienced 4X players this game may feel dumbed down or lacking, especially in terms of micromanagement.  If you are looking for the next Distant Worlds, a graphical version of Aurora 4X, or something more like Europa Universalis or Hearts of Iron in space this ain't it -- and I don't think it was ever supposed to be.
For new players, who may be concerned with the (perceived) depth and micro management of the 4X genre, casual players, or players who want to complete a game in a few hours instead of a few weeks, MOO:CTS is a great game and a great entry point into the wonderful universe of 4X space games.

The new 'Timeline' system enables you to review your progress and reload previous turns to change strategy and rectify missteps. For the most part, the interface on every menu screen is sharp, clean, and efficient, giving you all the info you need with no clutter. Diplomacy is clear and intuitive, providing clear, real-time feedback on how each response affects your relationships. The designs for each race have been updated perfectly, while mirroring the original Master of Orion aesthetics, and each has a distinct and engaging personality, enhanced by top-notch voice acting. Espionage mirrors the classic Master of Orion setup, giving you complete control over how to use your agents. Revenge of Antares switches agent recruitment from auto to manual, adding hiring and maintenance costs for each spy. The expansion adds the three races added in Master of Orion II - Elerians, Trilarians, and Gnolams, all of which have been well-updated to match the quality of the rest of the species in the game. Ship design and real-time combat work well, though there are still only a few options for modifying your ships' appearance.
The game still suffers from the same clunky economic model, expensive short-term trade treaties, impossibly expensive research treaties, lack of freighters, and high facility maintenance costs. Random events are more often annoying than helpful, and the game's exploration still suffers from lack of range limitations and sparseness of anomalies. Pollution can no longer be removed manually, instead decreasing gradually over time based on each planet's threshold, which can be raised by building pollution control facilities.
Leaders have made a return appearance, though they're generated in specific quanities according to each race present in the game. Gone are the colorful characters of MOO2, instead replaced by a fixed roster of generic, fairly forgettable race-specific commanders and administrators. Most are often lacking more than a single ability, giving them less bang for the BC despite their fairly low hiring cost. This is the one addition where the interface is not quite up to par, as the system seems tacked-on and clunky compared to the rest of the game's menus. Still, having them is a bonus, though it could stand some improvement.
The inclusion of the Antarans is the most significant change to the game. Their periodic appearances are much less randomized than they were in Master of Orion II; they seem to fixate on the same handful of systems, refusing to attack alternate planets until the first target is obliterated. Their fleet strength seems to skyrocket on a very steep curve as well, making it nearly impossible to fight them off ship to ship, even in the late game. Overall it feels like their mechanics could use some fine-tuning.
Master of Orion, with or without the Revenge of Antares expansion, is a very well-designed, well-balanced, challenging strategy game; though not without its flaws, I don't feel that any of them are so glaring as to affect the overall quality of the experience. The changes made by the expansion are all welcome additions, albeit imperfectly-implemented ones. The game is still being updated according to player feedback, and thanks to the community, there are a variety of mods available to fine-tune things.

After playing this Title for over 40 hours i feel i need to re wright my review.  In all my years of playing Anything X-Com.. from the original in 1994, to Terror From The Deep, Apocalypse and even Interceptor.... i have not played an X-Com game that has rubbed me the wrong way as Xcom2 has.  It started with my inability to develop the Plated armor, the Tech 2 armor because for some reason it required advent trooper corpses to produce.  To outfit the entire squad you need 6 but throughout much of the game up to that point.... Troopers rarely spawned on missions that gave me the ability to recover them. So little did i encounter them that making the mistake of selling 2-4 corpses left me 2 short from producing the armor, thats how rare my advent trooper recovery was.  I would of happily acquired more examples but as i've said the game simply did not provide.  So rare was tis that over a 6-10 mission spawn, i was left being one corpse short of advancing my armor, and this became increasingly problematic as enemies were starting to one shot me and this was not remedied until i skipped plated armor entirely and went to power armor. The fact that power armor strangely... did not require corpses meant that i had the material to produce powered armor for a significant portion of my play time already and made me wonder why plated armor require corpses in the first place.....
After this the game improved a fair amount but something still nagged at me.. the timed missions... which their are too many of them. In fact you will be seeing a count down timer to mission fail fairly often as these mission counters are the bread and butter of the game.  I did not realize just how much i disliked these timers until the avenger was shot down and i entered my first base defense mission.  Remarkably... the timer was absent... not to be seen! Instead you were faced with constant alien re enforcements in its place. this proved to be very enjoyable as it puts pressure onto you without binding you with an arbitrary number.  I have nothing bad to say about the base defense mission as really it was my high point of the game. Unfortunately... the mission that followed was one of my least favorites.
Tasked with hacking a data terminal before it explodes, i rushed to the objective and approached the target undetected. However when securing the data... every target in the map went onto alert and in a single turn... i ended up facing 12 targets on all sides.. a force that included an Andromen, a heavy mech and a Sectopod, all targets that require intense concentrated fire to take down.  In a situation like this you'd think you've cleared the objective its best to call the insertion craft and leave a victorious gorilla fighter right? no... despite achieving the primary goal of the mission and preventing the aliens from achievinh a dark event. the mission is counted as a failure.... such a thing when the game makes you to be a resistance fighter was just too much of a stretch after throwing me into a situation i couldn't win.
I don't mind difficult unforgiving games but Xcom2 takes it a little far and creeps into the realms of maliciousness and personally i do not feel that it really respects the player.  Because of this i cant enjoy this game and I'm unable to recommend it.

If you're reading this review, you more than likely already know about Fallout 4 and the controversy surrounding Bethesda's decisions regarding mods, the creation club, all that stuff. As someone who is not a member of the modding community and uses mods sparingly, I can't say I can adequately weigh in on the discourse, but I will say it seems like a dickish move from a developer now known more for its dickery than for making solid games.
Fallout 4 is a game I have not finished, intend to finish someday, but possibly won't. Like Skyrim before it, Fallout 4 has a ton of grand ideas that are presented with a fair amount of polish, but not enough to compensate for its lacking in atmosphere and ability to engage the player. Once every couple of months, I'll come back to F4, finish a few quests, shoot a bunch of guys, maybe toy around with the settlement system a bit, then quit after about 2 hours from boredom. The game doesn't present itself in a way that makes me care at all about the story, characters, or world. What's the point?
There are a few things I can compliment the game for. The combat system, which is more like an FPS than Fallout 3 or New Vegas, feels more dependent on skill and aiming than perks and the S.P.E.C.I.A.L. system, though it can make it too easy and lead to an unbalanced and unsatisfying feeling later on. The crafting system is good and makes use of all the clutter and scraps you come across, which served little to no purpose in Fallout 3.
Even if the mods controversy had never come up, even if Bethesda cancels the Creation Club altogether and makes mods free forever, I would still not recommend Fallout 4. You could fine tune any number of gameplay elements with any number of mods, but you're still left with a boring story and boring characters in an empty, soulless, boring world.

So let’s review Master of Orion, the rebooted offering from NGD studios. I have a love hate relationship with 4x games and often get the feeling that they all offer the same gaming experience. You get tech trees, alien species, anomaly bonus crates and a thin veneer of a story which is fluffed out by how you go about your galactic business. Weather it’s uniting factions with your diplomatic hippy powers or crushing your enemy’s with fleets of alien♥♥♥♥♥♥kicker ships. You can pretty much do as you will.
Master of Orion or Moo as it’s funny acronymic title is okay for a 4x title. I see it as more of an entry level 4x game. It has nice cut scenes, fairly in-depth tactical space battles and a Klingon traitor doing the voice overs. The problem I had with the game is I just couldn’t get in to it. After the first opening moves (or turns) everything just seemed to slot into generic 4x. The thing is I’ve played Distant Worlds which is a huge real time 4x game. Okay DW has graphics that would make a C64 blush but it has enormous depth and customisation. I’m not bashing Moo but just warning seasoned veterans of the genre that Moo in my opinion won’t satiate that galactic empiric feel you get from other 4x titles.
So on to the obligatory pros and cons:
PROS:
Michael Dorn
Nice art assets and animations
The races are pretty well thought out but limited
A solid entry level 4x game
CONS:
Generic 4x gameplay
Pretty limited tech tree
Not enough ship and general customisation

I'm all for supporting Indie horror games, even if they do suck a little. But there are so many things off about Despair that I'd honestly recommend avoiding it, unless of course the devs give it some much needed love and polishing. I don't expect a luxury big name game experience for two euros, but even that price seems a little too much for Despair, at least in it's current state.
- The graphics are quite an eyesore. Granted there's only so much that can be done with the engine, but still. A luminance slider bar would have done wonders here; in most parts, the umbra doesn't blend well with the atmosphere and creates a really wonky silhouette/cartoon effect. The highlighted puzzle/progress elements feels cheap.
- The translations feel sloppy and incomplete. There are some words that are not translated at all, and the general wording & expression could use a polish up. There are a lot of people out there willing to help with this! This also applies to the blurb on the Store Page. Please don't hesitate to ask for help!
- The Store Page for Despair doesn't mention that it's early access. Yet the game seems to have no proper ending and cuts off abruptly. It leaves us as the players hanging; what does this mean exactly? Will you polish it up in the future? Do you plan to expand the game? There is little to no story in the game save for the generic, cryptic notes. They don't tell us much. :/ Will we have to pay for the continuation? Or will this game simply be expanded and updated?
- An inventory or at least a general notepad/diary etc. would be nice so we could go back and read the notes we've picked up and view the items we've picked up, too. This if course isn't super necessary but allows a player to keep track of picked up items easier.
- An auxiliary light source. The batteries last decently but only if the player knows exactly what to do - those who do not immediately spot the solution / way to progress forward are left fumbling in the dark without any light source. A tiny light source to keep us going until we find more batteries would be wonderful.
- Just in general, this game feels like the devs were in a serious rush to release it. It feels incredibly incomplete and painfully short. Which would be fine, but the Store page neglects to mention early access. What's the deal with this? Will we see more? Or is this a prequel to something? If so, once again, it would be nice if this was mentioned. We as the players are left hanging at the end of the game, nothing is explained.
- I forgot who it was exactly, but some person on the forums stated that "darkness and noises do not a scary game make". I'm inclined to agree, at least concerning the horror elements in the game. The darkness was frightening only for a little bit, after which it came merely annoying. The "generic, dark haired horror element lady" could be made into something a lot more intimidating. Monster / enemy designs don't always have to be super original, but they do need that oomph in order to scare us, at least a little bit.
- All appendages crossed in hope that the devs will better this game. Albeit it's nothing short of a hot mess at the moment, it technically does have potential!
