Alright.
When I started writing more reviews, I told myself that I should do so after finishing the game. But this here. This game. I... can't wait until I've finished this mess before I write down what exactly I think of X-Blades.
You see, the game suffers from three big R's. Repetition, Recycling, and Redundancy. How so?
For a start, you'll be spammed - SPAMMED, I tell you - with the same enemy type in one of the mind-numbingly short levels for minutes. You better have a durable thumb (or forefinger, depending on wether you play this with a controller or keyboard and mouse), because you'll have to spam back attacks to control those monster hordes. And it's not really entertaining at all. This will go on for every single level. Even the boss battles. You'll be swarmed by mobs.
It's not bad enough that the level design is already redundant with the endless monster hordes. Oh no, it gets worse. Because every single level will be the same. Bit of running around, bit of smashing things, button mashing, next level. Rinse and repeat. Rinse and repeat. I last for about 2 or so levels per sitting. I just can't do much more because it's so incredibly badly made.
Oh dear. They did not. - Hell yes, they did.
See, it's not bad to use a level again at a later point in time, in maybe slightly altered form, to give the game a nice little looping back. But X-Blades takes it to a sadly very, very lazy extreme. See... you go through the whole dungeon twice. At day and at night. The exact. Same. Rooms. And you do the exact. Same. Thing. Again.
For a game which claims to be of the Hack and Slash genre, X-Blades does a terrible job at introducing something which makes it stand out in the genre. The claims of the reviews that X-Blades is anywhere near as good as DMC is preposterous, even ridiculous. You better check out Metacritic first, and maybe a gameplay video on Youtube. Also, you should probably search for something superior to this.
Even if the game is a bit over 5 years old, this is no excuse at being so utterly terrible. 2009 brought us Overlord II, Dragon Age Origins, and Batman Arkham Asylum.
Think about this.
THINK ABOUT IT.
And keep your hands away from X-Blades.
Oh, in a slightly belated addition: I didn't talk about the gameplay, story, and any of that, did I now? Well. If any of it had been good, I miiiight have forgiven the triple-R offense of the game. But sadly, nothing noteworthy of a story to be found here.
The gameplay and controls feel stiff and rather ininspired. I played with an X-Box 360 Controller for Windows, and, bad as that is, I sometimes didn't notice the controller had lost power and disconnected from the receiver. It took me several seconds to even bother to check the controller at times, since X-Blades's controls have the tendency to feel a little sticky, at least to me.
Next, I'd like to talk about the music briefly. Sadly, the tracks are repetitive, and the in-game music was much too loud for my taste. I had to reduce it to near silence to be able to enjoy the music even remotely. That being said, it was most of the times highly unfitting for the current mood of the game, or at least what I perceived to actually be the intended mood. A tense moment was completely shot to pieces by much too heavy and fast-paced rock music (double offense for the track being the bad, generic kind), and the rest of the time, the music wasn't really adding anything for me. In fact, it felt more like background noise of the obnoxious kind.
Tiny little excourse to the voice-acting - there actually is some in the game! For some reason, even though I selected English as language, the voice-acting was in German... and... meh. MEH. Sorry, but it really, really destroyed the game even more. The voices didn't fit, they sounded uninspired, and the bickering back and forth between Ayumi and the dark wolf boss thingy was painfully childish and immature. Unnecessary, in other words.
Oh, right, the story. To be honest, since I don't plan on finishing the game (yeah... there's only so much mind-numbing stupidity I can deal with), I have nooo idea what the story is about. And even as I read up on it, it seems like it is all over the place. Something of an artifact, someone being possessed, getting repossessed, un-possessed... whatever. I have no idea. I really don't.
Maybe I should also add something about the character design. Good? Good. Or rather, bad. See, there are sexy heroines in tight, short outfits, and then there's Ayumi. I actually felt horribly uncomfortable with her. She looks much too young to wear little more than straps passing as an excuse for clothes. I don't view her as sexy. She has some adorable about her, and that makes things really awkward really fast. Add to that the uninspired childish bickering mentioned in the voice-acting paragraph of the review, and it gets really, really, REALLY awkward and weird.
So, with that added to the already terribly done R's... nope. Not looking any good here, X-Blades. I'm going to play Alice: Madness Returns next, to have some really good Hack and Slash.

Editting Review due to latest patch:
Original:
While I love this game, and want to recommend it, I won’t recommend it due to the decision they’ve made on how to implement the Creation Club. While claiming its providing options, it’s blatantly about forcing micro-transactions into the game. If it was truly about options the Creation Club would be an optional download just like the other DLC content. They didn’t do that though as no one would bother with it. If, hopefully when, Creation Club becomes an optional download I will edit this review to give it a recommendation.
Updated for 1.10.40:
With the latest patch Creation Club no longer forcibly downloads their overpriced paid mods onto your SSD/HDD, and then attempts to charge you for access. While it's not removed the tumour, it's at least contained it. They'll no longer update the .exe simply to install the latest batch of paid-mods, so safer to mod your game. Less frivious updates means less chance of an update breaking your modded game.
Moving on from the bugbear of the moment and reviewing the game.
First up, we finally we have a voiced protagonist! Actually hearing my character talk has been on my wish-list since FO3/Oblivion. The general changes have tightened up combat massively, specifically the changes VATS. It’s no longer a magical pause enemy button.  In previous games I wandered the wasteland solo as followers just got in the way or got me killed. While it still happens, it was a rare occurrence compared to the suicide cultists of New Vegas and Skyrim, who seemed determined to absorb every bullet, arrow, melee blow, and spell you shoot/cast/swing etc. The perks for companions actually help a lot, Dogmeat as an example became a guided missile to tear out a targets throat as well as great for carrying spare stuff. The companions also have some interesting quests tied to them such as Curie’s and Nicks.
The main storyline is at best functional for driving the plot, but lacks any major twists or turns. I think most people will pick up on the plots “twist” well before the reveal. A lot of the new features are great ideas with bad implementation. I enjoy the survival mode, but it needs changes to make it somewhat more accessible. Bethesda games aren’t renowned for stability after all. A transition-save is less intrusive and to some extent more immersive than having to take an hours nap every twenty minutes. A more realistic metabolism would be nice as well, you have a metabolism that makes a hummingbird look like it has issues. Thankfully mods (free) can solve both of these issues.
I’m somewhat indifferent on settlements. I’ve seen a lot of hate for them, but for me it was the implementation. There’s too many, when five or six across the entire map would have been enough. Each settlement should then have had something unique about each one. In my mind Sanctuary, Abernathy Farm, the power station, Vault 81, General Atomics Galleria, and the Minutemen Fort would be about right. Each of these would then have a quest to free up each settlement, and in turn this has an effect on the Commonwealth. This point leads sneakily on to what I didn’t like.
The major complaint I have is that FO4 is overly simplified. There is a distinct lack of consequence, and worse there is often one way to resolve the entire quest lines. The example I’ll use containers some spoilers about one companion’s quest.  So one companion wants to cure to an addiction, and repair the damage they’ve suffered. In previous games you would likely have been able to help them, just refuse, or share some chems while you destroy the cure. In FO4 you can just help them or not do the quest. Sadly that is the typical type of resolution to every quest. Far Harbour, and to a lesser extent Nuka World, makes some improvements on that front but in the main game everything is resolved in one way: go to a place and shoot whatever needs killing according to your employer.
The Sole Survivor isn’t free from this shallow depth. Nora is a lawyer but seemed to have settled into a housewife routine in the faux-1950s of pre-war Fallout. The husband meanwhile has combat experience and likely extensive survival training from his military service. These are quite distinct backgrounds but gameplay is completely unaffected by that choice. I’m left feeling this was a missed opportunity to add little bits of depth. A simple option would be each one has a couple of free perks reflecting their skills. While there’s a mod available for this, it would’ve been nice to see some direct in-game affect. A simple example being when/if the sole survivor joins the Brotherhood of Steel. Due to his combat experience Nate discusses with the knights pre-war combat strategy and tactics. Nora meanwhile as someone with a college/university level of education gains a few bonus interactions with the scribes.
There’s a couple of niggling issue such as the change to the HUD during conversations. I get that they wanted something concise for consoles but the old scrolling was better and allowed for more options. Again free mods sort this out. Weird observation but am I alone in finding it weird that in Fallout the character can drink a litre of vodka, chase it with some beers, huff some Jet, take some psycho (PCP) and pound some Med-X (Morphine), into their eyes on a regular basis; but cigarettes? Very high learning curve, fairly faithful adaptation of the board game.
It is unfortunately not "Full featured" as some of the star players are missing and some skills don't work quite right, but it's pretty close, and a good substitute for spending a couple hundred dollars on minatures and spending a weekend with a bunch of sweaty geeks.
If you get frustrated easily, this game will not be for you.  The amount of times you seem to fail die rolls while the computer doesn't will aggravate you to no end until you understand all of the rules of the game, at which point the AI will be a pathetic competitor, providing no challenge at all.  Given all that, you can still get many hundreds of hours out of it, fine tuning your strategy in single player, playing many different races in many different manners.
The online league interface is unfortunately a little haphazard.  League management controls are somewhat limited and not as fleshed out as I'd like them to be, but it's entirely serviceable.  Random online matchmaking does exist, but you'll notice that the matching system isn't based upon skill as much as it is based upon cheesing the system, by using teams at their specific overpowered points in the rankings.  Really where the game shines is in a league setting with 16 or more like minded individuals in a structured season/playoff format.  I ran an online league for several seasons, and most of the guys would agree it was an incredible amount of fun, even when their team was getting destroyed.
It is a pretty niche game, but if you fit that niche, you will enjoy it to no end.  Or complain about the RNG and never play it again.  One or the other.

If I had to describe the game in one word, it would be an unflattering "Competent". The game brings nothing new to the table, nothing innovative, nothing exciting and different. It's formulaic and is merely competent at the formula. The main attraction seems to be the near nudity of the main character, the clothes go to a level of lunacy most games of this visual style don't, and the weapons are simplistic and uninspired. You get a pair of gunblades and you either slash your way through wave after wave of enemies, or shoot them, or mix it up and do both. You will learn some new abilities by finding artifact pieces which add new skills for shooting things and hitting them with swords. The artifacts are arguably essential, as they unlock combos and more combos are useful, so you'll have to hunt these things down to have an alternative to clicking one of the two mouse buttons repeatedly. As long as you can crank the resolution up on your display, the controls are fine, if amazingly uninspired. If you have to use a lower resolution for performance the mouse becomes unplayably twitchy and fast. My one complaint would be that the entire game is one formula. You enter an area and fight off some sort of boss monster. You fight either a boss, waves of smaller enemies, atatck stationary things until the bar is depleted and things stop spawning; then you kill the remaining ones and get to move onto the next area where you repeat the process. Sometimes you'll have it easier and have to run through an area avoiding arguably simple obstacles with dodge, or running through a puzzle of blades. Those would be a lot easier if the game explained the controls well, but following the game exactly results in dodge and other moves being wildly inconsistent to do. There is nothing inspired or amazing about this game, but it's a hack and slash. If you like just hitting things with swords, it does it just well enough that i can't say I recommend avoiding the game. It's not terribly good, but it can be enjoyable enough if very repetitive. I would not play the game again after completion unless achievements were added or some other incentive, as it is the game is acceptable enough to get a playthrough and then be left alone.

As a bit of background before the actual review. I started with this series back in '96, sitting on my father's lap as he played on our old Aptiva. Master of Orion 2 was one of the first games I owned myself and I got hundreds of hours on that in my childhood. So I am a bit biased towards the series.
However in regards to this product I can say that I am quite happy with how it feels. It has much of the same feel as the older members of the series, with exploration and fleet development being a major part of it's overall appeal. The graphics are lovely and so far I've had no framerate issues to note. The game runs very well and crashes have been non-existant, even though I've only had it around a day. The characters all feel nicely animated and as though they have a personality profile that helps to flesh them out. The voice acting probably helps a great deal with that (John De Lancie, Mark Hamil, Michael Dorne and other big names) to the point where when the humans deciede they don't like my expansion and roflstomp me I find myself yelling a definitive "Damnit Q!".
Now for the cons of this piece.
One of the commonly noted issues with this instalment is the lack of certain features that the previous games had. I can understand that, Heros were a useful feature that I do miss somewhat. As well as missing a few races if memory serves me. However in both cases I am willing to overlook them due to one simple fact. This is a reboot, it isn't Master of Orion 4. So when looking over everything one must keep that in mind. Things tend to be a little different in a reboot if a series.
In all I can safely say I've enjoyed my purchase and happily recommend this title to those who are both returning fans as well as new buyers. Now if anyone needs me, I'll be dropping mad production with my sphess-bugs, Peace.

TL;DR: Rough-around-the-edges social minigame lobby with a lot of promise
EDIT: Since I posted this - or perhaps a bit earlier and I hadn't noticed - the "Laser Tag" gamemode was added. Updated to reflect this.
I just bought this in the Steam summer sale and never played GMOD Tower, so hopefully I can provide a more up to date review for completely new players like me.
This game is essentially a minigame lobby with a social shell surrounding. You can walk around the plaza to see some sights (and ride a ferris wheel), as well as meet other players. There are also the user condos that you can visit if they are open, as well as design your own. Most of your gameplay, unless you're truly dedicated to condo building, will be in the minigames however. The core gameplay loop is described as Play Games -> Get Units -> Spend Units on Stuff (like condo decor).
Reviews of the minigames:
MINIGOLF - Minigolf is bizzarely robust, boasting a good amount of well-designed, entertaining 18 hole courses and satisfying physics. If this game took out all its other trappings, it could be sold as Minigolf without people thinking it felt like only 10% of a full game.
BALL RACE - My main complaint with this mode is that it looks really goofy and cheap, visually. The gameplay however is satisfying. It's basically Super Monkey Ball. Pretty difficult.
LITTLE CRUSADERS - A great idea for a minigame (1 dragon v. tiny, weak knights. Knights must press a button on the dragon's back) that suffers from unsatisfying controls. Your actions don't feel like they have the right "weight" to them - a very "floaty" sort of feel. Hard to describe exactly why this is disappointing, but it was just too imprecise for me.
VIRUS - My second favorite of the four core game modes that exist right now. Players get a small amount of time to set up, then one player randomly becomes infected. They are a fast moving zombie with no weapons that must touch other players to infect them; the other players have guns and dynamite. If everyone is infected, infected win. Otherwise, survivors win. The mechanics in this game feel right, other than the lack of reticle on some guns being annoying (but it seems like an intentional balance thing). Biggest complaint again here is that the visuals of the infected are kind of cheap looking.
PLANET PANIC - This is in early alpha and has some major updates planned. Good, because it's garbage and I had to go back and remember to add this part here after writing signficantly more of this.
LAZER TAG - Occupies a space in between plaza activities and gamemodes in that you MUST access it from the plaza, but it does send you into an instance. This is a decently fun take on an FPS minigame. Make sure you have a reasonable framerate to have any chance. When you're hit you must run to a "Charging Station" as a sort of respawn point, which is an interesting mechanic.
The plaza/lobby itself also boasts a number of minigames. These are some of my favorite features because they help you feel more like you're walking around in a living world with activities available, rather than queuing up for faceless games. A review of some of these:
TYPING DERBY - It's like those games where you must shoot water at a thing to make a horse move, but the typing replaces shooting water. I personally find this one very fun but its one of the less popular activities with the player base so finding matches can be difficult.
BOWLING - A fine concept, if a bit easy to figure out. However it seems to currently be glitched to hell and back and isn't a fun experience as it is right now.
TRIVIA - A well done, simple trivia game. If you've ever played "Kahoot!" in a classroom, it's basically that. The questions suffer from some large swinginess in difficulty due to them being user generated, but everyone is playing the same ones so it doesn't imbalance any given play.
CASINO - Somewhat disappointingly, this is where most players are haning out. It features a number of different slot games and video poker/blackjack. I prefer a bit more agency over the games I play other than pure randomness, so these are only a bit of token entertainment. "Double or Nothing" (exactly what it says) at least has the push your luck aspect. "Spin to Win" gives item prizes, and is amusing for how eclectic they are. Texas Hold 'Em is well done, but you have to rejoin the table every hand and it's hard to get people to stay for more than one. Apparently continuous play for it is in the works, which would make it immensely better. Bizarrely, the Casino is the fastest way to earn money - there isn't a house edge.
As far as the plaza activities go, an arcade is in the works. This looks like it will more than double the number of plaza activities available, especially single-player ones, and they won't be completely random/no control ones like you find in the casino. I'm very excited for that.
The plaza itself... is rough. This is mainly due to the presence of an EXTREMELY annoying stutter/flash thing that happens intermittently when you move the camera. My main other complaint is the NPCs are rock. solid. stone. It's just sort of creepy. In many cases they could simply be removed - for example, the Poker tables have a perfectly serviceable queuing UI floating above them and the presence of the same unmoving woman at all four tables takes away more than it adds. These two problems - especially the shuttering - would be unacceptable in a completed game, but the devs are very active and I am assuming they will be addressed before any full release.
The condo creator is surprisingly robust. I have not earned enough Units to do all that much with it yet, but visiting the condos of the randoms who have left theirs open to the public is an entertaining activity in its own right and has let me see the diversity of what can be accomplished. They are all of course decorated home interiors, but I saw for example one that was dedicated to placing a ton of easter eggs/secrets to find in it. Seemed like everywhere you walk there was a new pathway opening up or something new to interact with. Others are more typical house designs but well done in their own right. Overall this is a satisfying and worthy piece of content for the game. "Community Condos" that allow multiple builders are an exciting planned feature.
Overall, this is a ROUGH around the edges, glitchy game. It would be an absolutely unacceptable full release, and if this were the full release I couldn't recommend people buy it in good conscience. HOWEVER, this game has a Trello page where the devs track their progress and planned progress, they stream development on Twitch regularly, and truly listen to the community forum. It is some of the most transparent developing I have ever seen and has given me a lot of faith in what this game will become. That in mind, for myself, I can recommend this product as long as you come into it with it in mind that you are playing an Alpha. It is entertaining in its current state, but almost entirely unpolished.

My impression of this game is, overall, good. Not great, not bad, just good. If you like Space 4X games and enjoy keeping things simple, this is a respectable game to get, and 30 bucks is exactly the price it should be at.
The game has a good deal of polish, and it looks and sounds absolutely great. The gameplay is stuff you've already seen before, nothing really stands out about it, standard 4X fare. However, I will say that my major complaint against the game is how simple it is, AND the complete lack of any strategy in regards to planetary building.
When I say simple I mean simple. The tech tree is simple, your "choices" are pretty easy to make, economy is really easy to get going, things like that. What bothers me the most, though, is that there is no planet space you need to worry about as far as building things, so there is no strategy involved. Usually in games like Stellaris and Endless Space and the like, the planets you colonize have spaces to build improvements on, many times with a certain property to them, that forces you to make choices on what to build, when, and where to put them. The planets in this game have infinite space, and thus the determination of whether to build them comes directly down to 1) whether you really need/want that building on that planet and 2) whether you want to take the hit to your upkeep (don't worry you get tons of money anyway). There is no restriction to any of the buildings except having a few that need certain planetary properties (you can't build X unless the planet is mineral poor, for example).
Finally there is a good bit of the combat that needs to be adjusted (why can enemy scouts just ignore my blockades? why are space amoebas so freaking ridiculous in combat? why can't i see my ship health in battles anymore? WHY ARE MY BLUEPRINTS LIMITED TO 5? Blueprints should have no number restriction), but as I said, overall it's a respectable game. If you enjoy 4X games that aren't terribly deep, this is a good one to get for 30 bucks.

After 74.5 hours of playing (also hours more during the early access stage) I can say that MoO is a mediocre 4x game. It mimics most of the features of its legendary ancestor (MoO 2)
I am sad to give a negative review for this game. It is certainly playable and you'll have fun with it. But for a 2016 game, I honestly expected much more... Here is a list of pros/cons.
Pros:
1. Excellent cinematics and voice acting.
2. Good language support.
3. Graphically well designed races, race animations, in game research assistants.
4. Fluent game play.
Cons:
1. Repetitive technology tree. Too few creative weapons or technologies. Most of higher tech nodes in the tech tree just replicate the early nodes by just improving parameters. +1 production buildings become +2, x damage weapons become 2x damage weapons and so so. In some tech tree nodes you can decide from 2-3 different technologies but the better tech is in most cases obvious.
2. Although the races are parametrically different (some get bonus to diplomacy, some have better spy mission success chances, some have better ground troops etc.). They all share the same technology tree without a single variation. This makes the game very dull and uninteresting.
3. The game is very uneventful. Unless you provoke the AI (by colonizing near their systems) you can be in good terms with all AI races for the entire game. The AI does not challenge you. No random events that may cause a political crisis between your race and some other AI race occur.
4. The AI is not smart. They do not colonize the choke points systems to protect their borders. They do not make clever attacks or defense. They just throw whatever they have towards you (2-3 fleets at most) and once you deal with em they are left completely defenseless and broken.
5. As with almost all 4x games, harder AI does not mean smarter AI but rather cheating AI.
6. There are no strategically important bread and butter resources in the game. The game needs resources that would end alliances. Resources that will cause every race in the galaxy hunger for them and eventually cause galaxy wide wars. Resources which will enable you to unlock technologies, build buildings and new ship hulls etc.
7. Governing complexity is not scalable. After you acquire 10 or more planets you'll quickly realize this. There is no abstraction method in MoO (such as Stellarsis' sector governing) which will enable you to govern huge empires.
8. I do not understand why the number of different ship classes you can design is limitted. I might be ok with a limit (like 20-30) but 5-6 designs? Seriously? Why?
9. Some annoying bugs which should have been solved in early access at least a year ago. For instance you cannot save your keyboard mapping if you change it. Everytime you enter the game you have to change key mappings again and again. Also the game may lock up or crash after long lasting space battles.

I have a strange nostalgia for these sort of "internet party" games. There's something about a collection of mini-games and earning tokens/tickets for playing them that makes me feel like I've jumped back into a 2002 arcade (obviously I'm looking forward to the arcade update, which appears to be exactly that). Like an arcade, very few of the games are absolutely amazing (although I was surprised by how much fun I had with Ball Run), but together, they create a really fun, silly environment.
The best thing about Tower Unite is actually my biggest concern about it: there's no microtransactions after you buy the game. On the one hand, this instantly makes it the best game of this sort ever made, when you consider soemthing like Playstation Home, which would charge you $5 to put a virtual couch in your virtual apartment and another $3 for a virtual hat for your virtual head. In TU, you can earn those things just by playing some mini golf. Even if you wanted to, there's nothing to spend money on. The concern is that I have no idea how they're going to be able to keep that up. The game is surprisingly high quality and content rich for a $15 game, and without any income past that, I'd worry about how much they're going to be able to support and improve the game in the future, unless it becomes popular enough for a giant wave of purchases (which hasn't happened yet, and in that regard, the initial cost may be driving people away). Granted, that's all speculation, and as of the time of writing, they seem to be releasing updates regularly. I'd be perfectly fine if they eventually went the route of something like Guild Wars 2, where the meat of the game is purchased up front, and there's a few extra premium bits that can be bought with money in addition to being earned in game.
The game itself has a few early access flaws, such as glitchy graphics and the occasional bug. Lag was the largest issue I ran into, as some mini games like mini golf are synced to the host player, which occasionally made it a stuttery mess. It also seemed to have occasional issues with either memory or the game engine when a lot of stuff was on screen (high FPS, but occasional hitching and freezing). Lastly, it is a game that focuses a lot on bringing people on the internet into one place... needless to say, there's a lot of super-offensive language being thrown around, and to my knowledge, the community isn't policed much beyond a very basic profanity filter. This is, of course, easier to deal with outside of public lobbies.
Overall, though, I had a blast exploring TU in its current form. I'm looking forward to future updates and I really hope it gets enough attention to keep it going - it could be something really spectacular one day.

+Great production values (great leader voicing and event narration, design, animations, art style and music)
+Runs smoother (and gets through AI turns faster) than any other contemporary 4x
+Has that Master of Orion je ne sais quoi
+Core mechanics are well-balanced and solidly built
-Some mechanics are obtuse ("+6 damage reduction"? "+4 city tiles"?), and there's no in-game encylopedia or help system
-The advisors are all great at first, but they mostly recite the exact same two lines every time you unlock a new tech (and those same two lines will be ~90% of all the spoken dialogue you'll hear in a given game)
-AI is terrible, especially around diplomatic deal weighting and colony capturing (I've yet to even see one build a troop transport - they always just bomb colonies to death), and indistinguishable between civs
-Manual battle mechanics are kludgy and unresponsive at best
-General severe lack of variety in the experience (galaxies mostly look the same, AI races mostly behave the same, everyone says the same 2-3 lines dozens of times, colony micromanagement gets more and more repetive the later you get in the game, etc.)
Overall it's a solid-to-good successor to the previous MoOs, it's beautifully polished on the design level, and the framework is all in place... but it's also a highly repetitive experience without a lot of extra muscle on that framework. Providing mod support and better customization options (especially colony renaming and starting condition options) would resolve most of the issues I have, though, and move this up from a hesitant recommendation to an enthusiastic one.

Game was crashing every 15 minutes, regardless of whatever was happening in the game. After discussion with a Ubisoft rep, we've finally managed to find the source of the problem: the XAudio2_7.dll file in the drive\Windows\System32 folder was causing the crash every time. Renaming the file fixed the constant crashing. However, it now causes the Ubisoft logo sounds to stop playing but otherwise the game works fine. Sometimes the game re-creates this file so I have to re-do the process again.

Oh, you managed to have a solid, well though plan which worked well and you even assissinated the target but then you died?
Oh, don't worry! We'll just throw you back before you even infiltrated the place! (Really really bad checkpoints)
Remember the features introduced in other games such as double assissination, whistling while covered and such?
Oh boy, those? They're locked of course!
Game-lengtheners? Definitely, remember Assassin's creed II where you had to look for these emblem rock thingies to unlock the Altair armor? It's okay! we'll throw in some emblems you don't even know how to decypher just so you can unlock the same old boring armor from the other previous games!
Stealth? What's that? Your stealth abilities are based on your armor or boosts/skills, amazing, a chest armor with FLOWERS all over them are stealthier than a regular vest, coloring your armor does nothing btw, even though camouflage is a real thing used by soldiers to be more stealthy.
Good clothing/amor/weapons? Well, yes! This AC title has one of the best customization features, it allows you to have different parts of armor, chest, trousers, boots, gauntlets.
This AC title also features a variety of weapons you didn't see on other titles like heavy and long weapons.
The map design is a bit mediocre, sure, it's meant to look like France but it really has nothing to benefit stealth.
The climbing is obnoxious and hard, you can't move to where you go and if you press to go left it will have a delay, go to the other direction and return to the directed you pressed before.
Covering is annoying, you want to cover and there's an enemy in front of the object you're covered on, the game will not allow you to assassinate at first, you'll have to glance in and then MAYBE you can.
Want to get over the cover? Oh, boy. Let's get you on TOP of it instead, exposing yourself to everyone!
Again, I get that they tried to make the map as best as possible but it doesn't have anything to benefit your climbing, again.
Wanna look badass like Ezio when fighting? Too bad.
Low health and want to win a fight badass looking anyways? Too bad, guards one hit kill you when you're low and out of medicine.
Surely, you can parry really easily just like other games and still look awesome right? Nope.
Enemies get really hard to fight at points, I just try to avoid any confrontations at all.
They are way too fast or too many for you to parry sometimes, damage is also increased if you're looking to have a stealthy armor, knocked down to the ground? RIP, stabby stab on ya!
The plot is nice but it really doesn't make you feel like you're gonna get rewarded for anything you do.
That's all, I rate this game 7/10.
Buy it if you're into Assassin's Creed, into the plot or just like the way it feels.
This game isn't recommended for people who have not played any other AC game though.

Assassin's Creed Unity is by far the most underrated game in the series. The amount of hate and negativity this game gets is very undeserved for the clear amount of work that went into making it. I would go as far as to say, beyond the somewhat questionable performance and glitches here and there. Assassin's Creed Unity is the most detailed and fully realized AC game in the franchise.
There's a lot of things I really like about the game just from the get go. The French Revolution setting is an A+ already in my book, it's one of the most under represented settings in video games. They went above and beyond with trying to capture Paris during this era. They spent 2 years just building Notre-Dame cathedral. Beyond the gorgeous architecture you see things like peasants revolting in the streets and mass executions regularly throughout the map. It makes the world feel extremely alive and allows for lots of opportunities for very natural stealth during missions.
But that's not all. The developers also enhanced the gameplay of the Assassin's Creed formula to an extent I didn't think was possible. The player can now customize almost every part of their outfit. Not only that but different outfit parts also change the player's stats. The game now includes fairly broad RPG elements ranging from skills to stats of the player's health and attack power. This makes the open world side of the game feel much more motivating to do because it's directly tied to making you feel stronger and look cooler. The game also has coop missions and thankfully allows you to do them solo if you want.
But by far the best aspect of the game I've seen is the enhancements done to combat. Unity is by far the hardest game in the series. Part of this is due to many changes done to the enemies and overall gameplay. Enemies in AC Unity now can do multiple attacks. And depending on which attacks they use the player must either counter or dodge them. They also modified enemy AI so that when you are fighting multiple targets they will often pull a gun out and shoot the player while you are distracted. This makes combat feel much more tense and requires you to actually pay attention to what is going on since you can lose health very quickly. Many of the missions are very open ended in this regard allowing you to either engage in combat or more safely engage in stealth. SInce your health doesn't regenerate it makes it so you are very fragile and actually encourages sneaking around much more. It's somewhat shocking it took this long to make a competant combat system.
While the performance and frequent pop in leaves something to be desired, the actual minute to minute gameplay is nothing short of steller. It's somewhat depressing that this game didn't do very well critically because later Assassin's Creed games ignored many of the improvements this game offered. It's a rare example of a sequel that improves on everything and yet doesn't get the attention it deserves.

Completely rewriting my review after playing the game more, and changing my rating.
I've played the first game and enjoyed it, and I still play this game and enjoy it, but overall I regret buying it and have decided not to buy any future installments of the series unless there are changes. The gameplay brings a lot of enjoyment, but there are way too many frustrating elements.  I feel like instead of improving on it's predecssor, it just tweaks certain gameplay elements and advances the "plot" of the series (which I never really cared for....it's a pretty run of the mill post-apocalyptic alien take over type plot). I'm only going to focus on the problems with the game in this review:
It's become more and more clear to me that the flanking/cover system is buggy, which means it's not really possible to predict your chances of hitting the enemy or the enemy's chances of hitting you, making battles way more luck-dependent than strategy dependent.
Random bug I've found:  Enemies can explode vehicles with melee attacks and perform melee attacks through walls without destroying aforementioned wall.
The game can be enjoyable when it works, but it doesn't alot of the time, and it just snaps you out of the game.
The gameplay really needs an ovehall with consistent cover/flanking bonus system.  Also the ability to tell how much health/ammo your units have without selecting them (since it doesn't allow you to select them at certain points).
It's a tactics game like final fantasy tactics that takes everything that made FFT's gameplay incredible and throws it in the garbage to make it "challenging."  Lowering the games difficulty setting, as far as I can tell, doesn't really change the "difficulty."   Changing it from moderate to easy just changes the number of enemies you typically face in a battle and I think makes them slightly weaker.  I've played the game on both easy and moderate and will typically have 5-10 successful missions without losing a man and then have one or two where I'm completely butchered, either becuase of a string of bad luck shots at key moments in the battle or the game spikes it's diffculty out of nowhere with higher level badies that I'm not prepared for.
I think if I pushed through the string of bad lucks I could probably beat the game, but I tend to just quit and restart in annoyance. I hate that units I spend hours leveling up die, and often with an embarrassing amount of ease.  I mean, I understand that you're expected to lose a man every now and then, but there's an inconsistency between the fact you can literally write a backstory for all of your characters, they get nicknames, and yet they can get one hit killed at almost any time.  More often than not, if the enemy scores a single crit hit on even a full health unit, regardless of it's level,  you can pretty much kiss that character goodbye.

Editting Review due to latest patch:
Original:
While I love this game, and want to recommend it, I won’t recommend it due to the decision they’ve made on how to implement the Creation Club. While claiming its providing options, it’s blatantly about forcing micro-transactions into the game. If it was truly about options the Creation Club would be an optional download just like the other DLC content. They didn’t do that though as no one would bother with it. If, hopefully when, Creation Club becomes an optional download I will edit this review to give it a recommendation.
Updated for 1.10.40:
With the latest patch Creation Club no longer forcibly downloads their overpriced paid mods onto your SSD/HDD, and then attempts to charge you for access. While it's not removed the tumour, it's at least contained it. They'll no longer update the .exe simply to install the latest batch of paid-mods, so safer to mod your game. Less frivious updates means less chance of an update breaking your modded game.
Moving on from the bugbear of the moment and reviewing the game.
First up, we finally we have a voiced protagonist! Actually hearing my character talk has been on my wish-list since FO3/Oblivion. The general changes have tightened up combat massively, specifically the changes VATS. It’s no longer a magical pause enemy button.  In previous games I wandered the wasteland solo as followers just got in the way or got me killed. While it still happens, it was a rare occurrence compared to the suicide cultists of New Vegas and Skyrim, who seemed determined to absorb every bullet, arrow, melee blow, and spell you shoot/cast/swing etc. The perks for companions actually help a lot, Dogmeat as an example became a guided missile to tear out a targets throat as well as great for carrying spare stuff. The companions also have some interesting quests tied to them such as Curie’s and Nicks.
The main storyline is at best functional for driving the plot, but lacks any major twists or turns. I think most people will pick up on the plots “twist” well before the reveal. A lot of the new features are great ideas with bad implementation. I enjoy the survival mode, but it needs changes to make it somewhat more accessible. Bethesda games aren’t renowned for stability after all. A transition-save is less intrusive and to some extent more immersive than having to take an hours nap every twenty minutes. A more realistic metabolism would be nice as well, you have a metabolism that makes a hummingbird look like it has issues. Thankfully mods (free) can solve both of these issues.
I’m somewhat indifferent on settlements. I’ve seen a lot of hate for them, but for me it was the implementation. There’s too many, when five or six across the entire map would have been enough. Each settlement should then have had something unique about each one. In my mind Sanctuary, Abernathy Farm, the power station, Vault 81, General Atomics Galleria, and the Minutemen Fort would be about right. Each of these would then have a quest to free up each settlement, and in turn this has an effect on the Commonwealth. This point leads sneakily on to what I didn’t like.
The major complaint I have is that FO4 is overly simplified. There is a distinct lack of consequence, and worse there is often one way to resolve the entire quest lines. The example I’ll use containers some spoilers about one companion’s quest.  So one companion wants to cure to an addiction, and repair the damage they’ve suffered. In previous games you would likely have been able to help them, just refuse, or share some chems while you destroy the cure. In FO4 you can just help them or not do the quest. Sadly that is the typical type of resolution to every quest. Far Harbour, and to a lesser extent Nuka World, makes some improvements on that front but in the main game everything is resolved in one way: go to a place and shoot whatever needs killing according to your employer.
The Sole Survivor isn’t free from this shallow depth. Nora is a lawyer but seemed to have settled into a housewife routine in the faux-1950s of pre-war Fallout. The husband meanwhile has combat experience and likely extensive survival training from his military service. These are quite distinct backgrounds but gameplay is completely unaffected by that choice. I’m left feeling this was a missed opportunity to add little bits of depth. A simple option would be each one has a couple of free perks reflecting their skills. While there’s a mod available for this, it would’ve been nice to see some direct in-game affect. A simple example being when/if the sole survivor joins the Brotherhood of Steel. Due to his combat experience Nate discusses with the knights pre-war combat strategy and tactics. Nora meanwhile as someone with a college/university level of education gains a few bonus interactions with the scribes.
There’s a couple of niggling issue such as the change to the HUD during conversations. I get that they wanted something concise for consoles but the old scrolling was better and allowed for more options. Again free mods sort this out. Weird observation but am I alone in finding it weird that in Fallout the character can drink a litre of vodka, chase it with some beers, huff some Jet, take some psycho (PCP) and pound some Med-X (Morphine), into their eyes on a regular basis; but cigarettes? That♥♥♥♥♥♥ll kill you! :D

In summary it’s not a great game as it lacking the depth of its predecessors, but it is a solid game, and if Creation Club is excised I would recommend whole-hearted..

My first experience with XCOM was XCOM: Enemy Unknown. I never finished it, but moved onto XCOM: Enemy Within,  which I heavily enjoyed, both the story, the gameplay, the balance of challenges. Deciding whether or not securing MELD was worth a rookie's life, deciding to invest in robots, psi troops, the next weapon/armor type, or genetic enhancements, or best of all mixing and matching, if you had the recources.
XCOM 2 does not, in my opinion, present similar choice-making importance. A maxed out healing specialist will hit just as hard as a maxed out grenadier, in most situations. Enemies also feel like they have less impact. In Within, Crysallids were terrifying foes, only to be engaged with when I was sure that I knew where every single one was, to avoid nasty suprises. While it may just be a result of more experience, I do not feel that the Crysallids command that same caution.
Not to say the 2 is inferior, I very much enjoy the Armor, Hacking, and Stealth mechanics the game offers, as well as the feeling of time mattering with the AVATAR PROJECT progress meter at the top of the screen in red. I just feel that the game it self was a little short, being basically over once the Shadow Chamber was constructed. Story also advanced a little too quickly, hardly stopping to introduce new enemies. I remember the Whaling Town mission that revealed Crysallids to me for the first time, it was very effective in demonstrating the new aliens and their potential.
Overrall I enjoyed the game, I hope that after picking up some of the DLC I will further improve my experience with the XCOM series.

I'm somewhat new to the 4X genre, I don't play alot of these games and never played the previous Master of Orion games.  If you're looking for a polished and accessible 4X space strategy, this one fits the bill although the content of this game is somewhat limited for $30, it's more like a $20 game.  There's no campaign and no ship designer.  I will go ahead and recommend it because as I said it's polished and is accessible someone like me. This is probably a good one to start with before moving onto more complex 4x space strategy games.

Pros
*Great visual design and animation. Great music and the atmosphere and non-verbal story-telling is really cool, similar to Machinarium (same devs) as far as characters speaking through picture speech bubbles. I like the contrast of the very vibrant, colorful, livid, lively, green environment and some parts where it's dying and a part close to the end when things get a bit dark, but no very heavy.
*Would probably be great for children
*Can run on very low-end computers
Cons
*There are only a couple things that were really puzzles. Mostly I was just clicking a bunch of stuff watching all kinds of weird (yet entertaining) things happen before it gave me whatever item I needed to proceed at the time.
*It's very abstract (which I like) and not really as much of a little world that Machinarium was, having really randomness to the different places and organisms you meet. Which I think Machinarium is a better game overall, telling a more cohesive narrative versus this game's sort of child drawing story (that could be taken as a negative or a positive).
*The game was really short. I have 2.7 hours on this game and that was with clicking on everything I could find, though I didn't quite 100% it but I wasn't far off. I had little to no problem with the "puzzles" so I went through it pretty fast but even someone getting stuck a lot, if that's even possible, would still beat it fairly quickly. I think $10 is a bit pricey for a game that has little replay value and is so short.
In summary, this was an enjoyable experience especially at first glance at how wildly out there it was. It's a very sort kid's dream and occasionally nightmare with how abstract it is. But it was very short. I liked Machinarium more.

A follow-up to the excellent Nation Red is a tricky thing. Sometimes a bowl of deliciously simple ice cream isn't improved upon by adding a pile of whipped cream, sprinkles and other toppings.  And Versus Squad doesn't quite find the right balance but you still wind up with a pretty good dessert.
The premise is simple: A twin-stick shooter where you mow down waves of zombies in a never-ending endurance fight.  Weapons and power-ups abound and you gain selectable perks as you progress.  Versus Squad adds a defense element by allowing the player to purchase and place walls, fences, sentry turrets, explosives and other items to protect themselves and funnel the zombie hordes.  Unfortunately, the defense part didn't always seem to make the game better.  In my first game, it bugged out and locked up the game (that hasn't happened since).  In other games, no one had enough coins to do much between waves. The UI is clunky which just adds to disrupting the flow of the game.  There's also a survival mode where you place items once and then fight continuously without wave breaks.
Although I didn't think the defense aspects were entirely ready for prime time, the game itself remains solid and the other improvements are nice: you can earn points to buy permanent perks, the graphics are much improved and the game still feels solid.  It's not a bad game by any stretch; it's a pretty good one.  But the new elements need some more tweaking to match the simple beauty of Nation Red.  Fortunately the developers remain involved in updating the game and I expect good things for it.

From the creators of one of my favorite topdown shooters, Nation Red, comes Versus Squad. This game is an improvement on Nation Red in many ways. The new enemies are epic, the guns are great, and the maps are well made. The perk system is well made much like the first game, with Perk Modes dictating how you recieve them in-game. New to the series is the ability to gain "Perk Credits" by leveling up your character. Perks bought with these stay with you in-between games unlike normal perks, which reset after every attempt. The most important new feature is the ability to build. You and your squad can build barricades and turrets, among other defensive items, on the map either before playing or in-between waves depending on the game mode you choose. These things along with the constant updates and very responsive dev makes Versus Squad a must have for people who love topdown shooters. Be warned though, while fun in single-player the game is intended for (and thus 100x more fun with) other people. So if you can grab some friends that are willing to buy this game and play it. And while you are at it get Nation Red. It is an older game, lacking some of the features of Versus Squad, but it is still very fun and includes a little mini-storymode of single-player levels. Nation Red also have and amazing multi-player so you can pick and choose, or do what I did and buy both.

I bought Versus Squad during the summer sale with the notion that it would be a “fun 4 dollar game”, but it turned out to be a lot more than that.
Versus Squad is one of those games that can easily become an addiction. From the outside looking in the game might seem repetitively simple. “Build Here. Kill Here. Die Here.”, is how games like this normally are and once you establish that the game can become stagnant fast. Versus Squad isn't like that. While this game isn't overly complex it does have enough complexity to keep you playing.
If you're interested in the array of things that make this game what it is then I will point you in another direction.
If you're interested in the positives and negatives of those things then continue on in this review.
• The Perk System plays a large part in how the game will progress for the player. As the game progresses you're able to choose Perks to help you fight off the attackers. In the end
you might be able to get most of the Perks in game. Choosing the right Perks in the right order that fits your play style is what will help get you there.
• Defenses are a very large part of the game and the main reason I keep coming back. The map is a Sandbox and how you set your defense up will directly impact how long you last. There is always room to improve upon your failed attempts.
• The game plays smoothly. The rolling. The shooting. The running. The surviving. All of these things match together perfectly and brings an overall enjoyable feel to the game.
• It's a great COOP game. Playing this game with 3 other people is a hoot. I don't know how to praise it enough. If you like playing with friends then you will like this game.
• Achievements can keep the game interesting. If you're interested in Achievements like me then you will be happy to know this game has some fun ones. Take a gander through the Achievement list to see for yourself.
• The Dev actually interacts with the community. They actually listen, communicate, and try to fix the problems that the community faces. I think this says a lot for a game.  Take a scroll on over to the Steam Forums for this game to see what I mean.
•
In the 25 hours I've played I've yet to run into anything game breaking. There are bugs that range from a minor inconvenience to flat out annoying.
If bugs completly ruin a game for you then they might ruin this one.
• The game is dead. There is no good way to put this. I can make a few public matches over the course of a few hours and wont have a single person join. Than other times it will fill all the way up by wave 2. Sometimes there wont be a game up for seemingly hours, but other times there will be a few. If the main reason you're buying this is for the COOP then I highly recommend you convince a friend to get it or are at least willing to actively look for people to play with.
• It can get repetitive. I wont lie and say this game will keep you entertained for months on end. That is just the nature of games like this. The only difference is that this game lasts longer than most.
• The menu controls are clunky. Navigating through the menus isn't the best experience around. It can be confusing at times and a little frustrating at others.
• The connection type is Peer 2 Peer. I don't see this so much as a negative, but something that is just worth mentioning. If you've played any other game that is Peer 2 Peer you will know what it's like to play this.
Simply put this game is fun and is well worth the money. If you can pick it up on sale even better. If you can convince friends to get it then hot damn you're golden. While getting into a match
can sometimes be a burden once you get into the match be ready for 30+ minutes to just sail on by. I mean I've put more time into this little game than most AAA titles I buy during sales. I would recommend it to anyone who is looking for a Sandbox Twin Stick Shooter. Heck even people who like Tower Defense would like this game.

So... Blood Bowl. This is gonna be a weird review for me - since I'm on one hand going to praise it to heaven, and on the other, slam the developer for being bad.
About the game: Blood bowl is a turn-based mix between chess, american football and warhammer fantasy. You get over 20 races to pick from, with different players, each with their own stats and starting abilities. A lot of the game is based on dice-rolls, with modifiers, so that you can 'control' the risks you take with each dice roll. And it is a risk each time. Because failing the roll can often end your turn.
So, the good part: The game feels awesome, the wealth of different races, abilities, etc. are great, the rules are well-fleshed out, and some of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that can happen, if you are lucky enough, is amazing (If a bit infuriating for the one losing because of it). What I'm saying is, basically: The boardgame is AMAZING, and the idea of having a digital version, that does all the dice-rolls and remembers all the rules about dodging, throwing, catching, blocking, etc. for you, is nice.
Now for the bad part: Cyanide, the developer.
Basically, this game is just not well made. You'll constantly ask yourself what the hell went through the developers mind when they made it like this. All the parts that is the game itself is brilliant, since it's a straight copy of the boardgame, but stuff like the interface, the online lobby system, the terrible path-finding, the few bugs, graphical choices, there's so many times when you just don't understand why they made it like they did.
Conclusion: I still love this game to death. Cyanide didn't ♥♥♥♥ up enough that I don't love it. There's luckily not that many bugs left, and the game itself functions well enough. You'll just have to get past the stupid design decisions first.
TL:DR This game is awesome, if you love Turn Based Strategy, Warhammer, and violent sports. Developer is a Piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥

Important Notice:
In order to play DayZ Mod it is essential to use a free launcher utility which will download and update custom mods, maps, and weapons required to play on most servers. Launchers will also allow you to search for the type of server you want to play on as many different play styles and maps are available. Just launching this basic DayZ Mod download here on Steam will not be enough to connect to the vast majority of servers. So the first thing you should do after installing Arma 2 is download a launcher. Some of the most popular DayZ launchers are:

(also supports hundreds of other mods for ARMA 2)
I've been playing PC games since the PC was invented, and DayZ Mod is one of the most interesting, exciting and immersive games I've ever played. It's basically a multiplayer apocalyptic virtual world or sandbox without any quests or storyline unless created by the players themselves. You go where you want and do as you want. You determine everything that happens except for the response from other players. You can be a bandit or hero engaging in constant gun battles in the busier towns or you can run off into the wilderness and build yourself a cabin in the middle of nowhere and hunt to survive. There are very few limits on what you can do.
I recommend DayZ Mod over DayZ Standalone for several reasons. One of the coolest things about the Mod is that because it is not centrally controlled and developed by a single team it offers many different types of games, maps, and improvements for free from hundreds of different players and community developers and continues to evolve in many alternative directions. There are Hunger Games type mods to play like Battle Royal where it's everyone for themselves and you fight to be the last one standing, militarized mods like Overwatch full of heavy military weapons, aircraft and tanks, crafting and base building type mods like Epoch and Origins that allow you to more permanently carve out your own piece of the world and make it your home, survival type mods like vanilla DayZ, and even alien type mods like Invasion. With the Mod there are so many different options and environments available for play that you're bound to find a server that suits you and if you don't you can even set up your own server and customize it just the way you like. That will never happen with the Standalone.
The Mod is also much cheaper as Arma 2 Combined Operations and Arma X Anniversary keys can be bought for about $5 and $8 each, just search Google. Not only do you pay less and get dozens of different games and options for play, but you also get the original Arma 2 combat simulator games too, which are not too bad themselves.
Overall, DayZ Mod is a must have if you enjoy PC gaming. Many games are trying to imitate it now, but nothing really compares so far, and it will probably remain that way simply because free DayZ mods are community developed by those purely passionate about making cool mods and games while everything else is being developed primarily for profit

MASTER OF ORION a return to form in the classic addictive style of the earlier games. Once again i find myself immersed in the world of MOO with its haunting lonely vast expanses of space where home is onboard a huge colony ship or other space faring vessel. Exploration and discovery abound in joyful moments of finding a planet that can be colonised in all its mysterious beauty waiting to reveal its naked reality to you. Then there are asteroid fields which can be mined as well as strange signals in distant places where advanced technology or some anamoly which may or may not be a threat could be waiting to be discovered.
You will encounter other races alien and inhuman looking who may or may not become your ally depending on ones skill at universal politics. Of course there could be some who because of their tempermental and competitive nature will turn on an ally just for the fun of battle such as the flirtatious and easily offended Mrrshan ruled by the feline Empress Marupa.
Then there are the space pirates who are a constant threat but with a bit of exploration and bomb capable space ships you can discover their bases of operation and blast them to stinking fragmented bits of charred flesh.
Taxing your empire for much needed coin to run it is a necessity to be able to afford the research and development to create the habitats, weapons, ships, electronics, population motivating items etc etc needed to grow and florish across the universe as well as be more attractive to other races as an ally when making many types of agreements, trading tech, paying tribute, giving gifts etc. Just make sure not to tax your people too much at the wrong time or you may find them rebelling as they unleash their displeasure until you act one way or the other.
Graphics bring the infinity of space along with the bliss and horror of new worlds. Alien races are a sight to behold capturing a 1990s science fiction quality as if from an episode of BABYLON 5 and STAR TREK. Battles are violent and catastrophic as scenes of ships charging full speed ahead with ballistic and energy weapons blazing across monitor screens create exciting encounters which are played depending on whether you auto resolve, give partial control to the ai or take complete command of the battle controlling your ships in battle which is wonderfully executed.
Music captures a mix of classical and 1990s science fiction ambience relaxing yet full of suspense and the wonder of discovering a universe. Hearing the insane amounts of voice acting by an all star cast who create characters who are very diverse, full of depth and unique is an incredible experience to go through which motivates me to keep diplomatic contact with them.
MASTER OF ORION a true successor and success of a time past which has risen to claim its place once more in the annals of gaming history.
MASTER OF ORION, BUY IT! PLAY IT! and become SUPREME RULER OF THE UNIVERSE!!!

Keep in mind I have never written a review, nor played any of the previous XCOM Franchise, however for this game I felt the need to convey my experience for this game.
I have only ever played a turn-based tactics game once prior to playing XCOM 2, which was an old game on DS called
Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon: Shadow Wars, which I enjoyed quite a lot as a child. Ever since then, I had wanted to find a game similar to it.
As you progress in XCOM 2, you expand your monthly supply income by reaching new regions, as well as gaining Intel to fly to new regions. Every mission you begin has an objective. How you complete it is up to how you decide, and every move can have a consequence. I was extremely new to this style of a strategy game, so starting on the medium difficulty, I was clumsily rushing into missions getting my soldiers killed, so I had to restart with a new approach and carefully approach new scenarios and objectives.
As I progressed with this new mindset missions became easier as I was able to gain an understanding of the game, and upgrade my soldier’s abilities, skills and weapons. Throughout these missions I started customising the names, colours, back stories and camouflages of my soldiers, and I built a connection with each of my soldiers.
Every time I launched this game, I couldn't stop playing for 6 hours losing track of time into this amazing game,
HOWEVER
I bought this game on sale at around $30.00, so for me this game was worth every dollar I spent on it. If I bought this game at full price I would have expected a little longer storyline with some more mission scenarios other than Saving Civilians, Destroying a beacon, Killing all enemies, Planting X4 charges, Kill/Capture VIP, UFO Crash Sites, Your own ship crashing potentially and a few others I may have missed. They are a few; however a lot of them feel quite similar. I did pay too much attention, but each mission’s terrain seemed randomly generated, which was a nice feel too.
I Rate 9/10, buying at $30.00

I wanted to like this game so that I could play it with a friend of mine, but alas, the few hours I played it proved that that was not going to happen.
After spending a great deal of time trying to get past the splash screen, I found out that the game isn't very fond of running from any other location than the C: Drive. Apparently this is a common problem with Ubisoft games, which can be problematic when a single game occupies one third of my SSD. Nevertheless, I managed to make room for it, and set out to try it.
In the few hours I played this thing, I encountered way too many bugs for my liking, such as invisible enemies, not being able to attack or press the E button, my friend becoming stuck in nothing, NPCs glitching through the floor and taking damage from nothing. (Though I wouldn't insist that the latter wasn't due to me not paying attention.)
With this many bugs only a few hours into the game, I simply cannot recommend it, regardless of how pretty it might look, how good the story might be, or how swell the gameplay might be. I might add that the story felt a bit rushed, and that the gameplay seemed very much like the other AC games, but I do not feel I got a very good insight in those parts.
As a last note, I'll say that I was rather disappointed with the co-op. There isn't really much to do in co-op, apart from running around doing mindless combat. Both/all players will have to open the same chest and take the same collectible to get it, so you might as well do that in singleplayer. There will be a lot of waiting around otherwise. Most missions are singleplayer, meaning you'll have to play the game alone to progress. The missions that aren't singleplayer are repeatable quests you do to grind money. And whenever your buddies leave your game, the game will desynchronize. So if you are looking for a co-op game to play with a friend, I suggest you look elsewhere.

A casual-looking, resource-gathering, timing game that actually has some depth.
--------------------
Gameplay consists of gathering resources and spending them on removing obstacles or building resource generators.  There are 3 resources: food, wood, and gold.  Each level is timed, and the time determines the whether a gold, silver, or bronze is awarded.
In each level, each supply gathered gives a finite amount of resources, which in later levels can be increased through building stores.  Each obstacle requires a certain amount of resources, and sometimes gives a certain amount back.  In later levels, there are resource-generating/increasing buildings that can be built at the cost of wood.  These give resources after a set amount of time, increase the amount that is collected, or in the case of gold, gives gold in exchange for food.  There are also pads that respawn resources.
The fun lies in balancing out how much to spend, how much to gather, and where to go.  Each level consists of paths laden with supplies and obstacles.  Some paths lead to resources that might not help in the moment, other paths lead to objectives which are best saved til last, and other ones lead to resource generators.  The fun is in planning out where to go so that I do not get myself stranded and end up having to wait on resources to respawn.  Luckily, the levels are well made that it is hard to miss the gold award, unless the difficulty is set to expert.
The voice actor has a good voice but is obviously reading from a script and does not know how to correctly pronounce some words.  Cerberus was pronounced awkwardly multiple times.
The boss mini-games consisted of only tapping on incoming enemies, or only tapping on things once they are activated, with resources excluded.  For example, I would tap on incoming harpies or tap on path obstructions when I am allowed, repeating these until I reach the end.  I see that the game tries to give breaks and throws in something that is different from time to time, but the gameplay is overly simplistic.  They detract from the enjoyment and cheapen the feel of the game.
Story?  It barely exists and is told mainly through gameplay.  Hercules' wife gets kidnapped, and Hercules travels to rescue his wife.  He and his servants clear roads and gather allies to assist him in his travels.
It's a mobile game, what did you expect?
--------------------
Do not be fooled by the casual- and mobile-looking nature of this game.  There are some elements of that, but the core gameplay relies on mildly sophisticated route planning and resource balancing.

Even at the low low price of 99 cents it is impossible to recommend this game. With graphics befitting a 2008 Unity game that even thongs and jiggle physics can't save, and controls worse than a fever dream, X-blades is an entirely unrewarding experience.
Your adversaries are either ripped apart like the tissue paper in a sports bar urinal or take an unneccesary number of swings to kill. Jumping is clunky and aerial combat is near impossible. When faced with numerous mobs, they suffer little to no knockback, meaning that if in your bored tyrade of 'click repeatedly to use sword on mans' you start to take damage, you stagger and your health can be depleted fairly rapidly. There is an illusion of variety in combat, but it ultimately boils down to clicking on everything repeatedly until it stops moving,  and if your blades don't kill it, shoot it or throw fireballs at it until it dies.
X-Blades also opens with cinematics - albeit in an entirely different art style - but then ends abruptly when you are transitioned from stage to stage with no advancing in the "storyline" or any idea what your purpose is for being there.
Although not as polished as similar titles like God of War or Devil May Cry, this games spiritual successor "Blades of Time" is all around a better experience.
