As a longtime fan of Nation Red, there wasn't any hesitation whether I should buy this game or not.
The developer has a wonderful connection to the community and Nation Red received frequent updates, adding more content and improving things, directly based on player feedback from the steam forums.
I have no doubt things will be the same with Versus.
That being said, this game is a bit different from Nation Red.
Some things I like, other things, not as much.
The glorious mayhem and destruction from Nation Red is the same.
There are perks, powerups, weapons, boss zombies, etc.
The graphics now have this smudged painted look, along with outlines.
I like how rough and grimy it is, but the levels suffer a bit from things blending together. I like night time the most because zombies stand out very clearly towards the background.
The visual effects can get a bit overwhelming though, as it gets harder to figure out what is going on.
The powerup effects and such can easily get drowned in the flood of various effects, this applies to the sound effects as well. The level up effect which is quite important is also easy to miss in the ensuing chaos.
A really cool and unexpected feature was how you can customize your character visually.
Right now there's only toggling on and off various clothing and accessories, but I'm hoping to see additional gear in the future.
I really like the building mechanics, but I wish the maps had more inherent and larger obstacles to take advantage of.
The controls in the build mode confused me at first as I tried to swap between using a mouse and the controller.
Once I got the hang of it, using only the controller, the only issue was the sensitivity of the analogue stick when placing things.
The thing I like the least has to be ammunition.
I like the idea, but in practice it's frustrating. When you run out it usually means you lose.
And there's various kinds of ammunition making it even more confusing.
When you play, you just want to mow down hordes of zombies, the quick paced action doesn't go well with the idea of conserving and keeping track of your ammo.
I've always thought the best thing about Nation Red was the perks and especially Random Perk mode.
Each time you level up you'd get to select from a handful of random perks, because it's random you'd usually go with a different build each time, which added great replayability and you'd change your style of play depending on the perks.
This hasn't changed in Versus.
But Auto-perk mode is the default one and I'm sure new players won't bother to change it, which I think is bad as a new player won't even know how it works or what perks are.
I guess I have to write something at the end here, huh..
If you like building barricades and mowing down hordes of zombies. Get this game!

is a casual time/resource management game, mostly suited to younger audiences. The cartoony styled animations are pleasing to the eye and the level of difficulty is toned down to make it easy enough to unlock all achievements with moderate effort, even on expert level. The game is part of a genre most suited for mobile/tablet touch-screen gameplay, with the PC port still being fun in small doses.
12 Labours of Hercules does not take itself too serious (not much to do with the actual labours of Hercules), a fact conveyed by a lazy Hercules rocking in his hammock most of the time, the colourful map designs, the fun mini-games and the comic narration of the story videos at the end of each chapter.
All in all a relaxing and fun little game, ideal as a filler when you need a break from your normal gaming habits.
-----
Pros:
+ Tight time/resource management gameplay (expert mode)
+ Well designed maps providing diversity and challenge
+ Colourful art style
+ Steam achievements and trading cards
+ Well liked by younger audiences
Cons:
- Too sort at ~5hrs to complete
- It becomes repetitive after a while
- Not much replayability

Whilst you should certaily try this (it's free)  and I have given it a positive review, the game is not some artistic masterpiece others make it out to be.
A lot of the dialogue and writing is bubbling with cliche, although some of that is intentional (can't give away too much). There is enough subtlety in clues and visual information to pique your interest - the only time I became stuck was due to my own fault for not picking up on a clue. The game also exudes an unsettling tone very well, causing me to 'feel' the game for a good while after I completed it.
So don't let your expectations be set too high by glowing reviews, play it as an interesting treat to keep you occupied for 40-50 minutes or so.

In a world of so few friends, I begin to realize that we dont get to choose our friends, we dont get to decide how they act, and worse of all how that comradre is severed. just 15 or so hours earlier, we had been a tightly knit unit. laughing, argueing, and generally enjoying ourselves. But one certain problem began to crop up in the group, with a specific person. There was a systematic failure to communicate. As gear began to dissapear, it was obvious, very obvious, who was stealing it. Finally when a ghillie suit disappeared, and this individual claimed to have found it in a barn, the level of distrust was pushed over the line by the lies. lies told well are one thing, but lies as transparent as this spoke to how little he thought of our intelligence.
We discussed what we should do in a seperate message on steam.
......................................................................................................................................
I didn't pull the trigger my self, in fact, i didnt even hear the shots go off. But as i fortified my base, i also saw him leave, i hadn't even been sure when it would happen. Just as i finished making my base sealed off, i saw the words.
Wolfy was killed
Eerie as ♥♥♥♥ for a brief second
followed by the exasperated sounding words "Dude.....What the ♥♥♥♥?"
The conversation that ensued was that reminiscient of an ugly Divorce. I didn't speak much during this, But he was presented with the facts. He denied these vehemently, trying to blame others. He claimed he had no choice but to kill us, now. After awhile of this i spoke up and agreed with the triggerman, he had crossed a line. the conversation degraded into denials and insults. There was nothing else to do but hang up and delete him from steam.
As our reality begun to settle around us, the impact of what we had done hit us full force. the person we had spent almost 20 consecutive hours with, looting, shooting the♥♥♥♥♥♥ and even executed several well coordinated operations with, was dead. not the kind of dead where, when he respawns he'll just meet us at base. no, this felt real. it felt real because we knew him. we knew him on a personal level. the diffrence between killing someone with whom ive never had extended interaction with, and killing wolfy was monumental. It felt real. As we discussed it and dissected what it was,and how wierd we felt, we came back to one amazing fact. An amazing fact that we have always known, one that sharply blew our minds. it was so obvious.
This is a video game.
How? Just How? we began to discuss that too. After having disscussed at depth for about an hour, we slowly went back to our normal habits. hunting and gathering supplies. wolfy was out of our minds soon after. However he is still in the back of our minds, and this morning after three hours of sleep i feel heart broken. I Very much expect that wolfy is equally heartbroken, but that this will be masked with rage and un-adult rated vengence. we have to relocate now, and despite this base being a dream come true. i know i cannot fight him off 24/7. i know we cannot undo what we did. words have been exchanged, actions have been taken. Heavy Fire: Afghanistan is one of those "budget titles" that is easy to play, but left you rather empty. It is a rail shooter similar to old arcade game Time Crisis (yes, the one with the light gun) where you need to shoot enemies while popping in and out of cover. It plays fast, its graphics looks quite decent, but it is buggy and at certain stages, near to impossible to pass. Even at the price of only a few dollars, it is still hard to recommend.
A rail shooter basically moves for you, stops at certain locations with cover. Duck behind the cover to reload, pop out to shoot (when enemy stops shooting). In this game, if the enemy has the red exclamation mark he's about to hit you, and your health bar only goes so far. The problem is when there are like 6 to 7 bad guys on the screen, 2-3 are shooting at the same time. There is no correct time to shoot (or is there?) As you clear area after area, with enemies poping out from close to far, you have to ration your shots carefully (one shot will kill the enemies) lest you fall back to your pistol. Yes, you do shoot pistols too. Occasionally you get to play with vehicle mounted weapons, same idea.
The levels are quite decent, actually, look "reasonable" for the area they're depicting, villages, caves, mountain paths, city ruins, you get the idea. But enemies just... pop up, pretty much.
The only powerups you get are ammo, health, and grenade (only ONE) which blows up enemies on one side of the screen.
The game is buggy in that exiting the game can sometimes result in the game not starting the next time. The game's "launcher" will start, but as you click "play" both crashed to desktop, no error message. Sometimes change the video options and reinstall Direct X may cure it... until it happens again. There's seemingly no pattern to the crashes.
All in all, there are better "rail shooters" around than this "topical" shooter rushed out to fit the news cycles.

I really really Tried to like it. I loved the first game, what a fresh breeze of air. This one however ( and i will get alot of flak from fanboys for this) is not good. The Presentation is breathtaking. Super epic Music intros and all manner of awesomeness. Great Voiceacting and so on.
However you deserve to know why you may not like this one. Xcom is a Tactics game. It lives and breathes from being 70% Tactics, 20% Strategy and 10% luck. Xcom2 is 70% luck as far as i experienced it. Because of a few mechanics, most missions have a pretty brutal Timelimit. You either need to cross the whole map to reach a certain point, or rescue somebody, or rescue alot of people. You have around 3-8 turns time for this. That means the game forces you to rush. I personally hate this in tactics game. You cant set up a propper ambush. And more often then not you end up with your pants down running in a group of Aliens. Ok RELOAD.
Now you know where the aliens are, advance until then. Take them out. Oh Soldier 1 Missed. Soldier 2...he missed aswell. Soldier 3... 2 Damage! Enemy proceeds killing the Squads. RELOAD!
Ok this time Soldier 1 Hits. Yay, enemy dead. Soldier 2...missed. Soldier 3...missed again. Enemy kills soldier 3, Soldier 1 is panicked. RELOAD (spoiler...next turn everybody is dead)
When you finally get to the terminal (after MANY reloads), Oh reinforcments are coming and dropping in the flank of my squad. Sucks to be me i guess. Squad dead. RELOAD
Now i know that reinforcements are coming, Get to the terminal, Have everybody in position. Reinforcments now arrive at a different place. (again flanked) Squad Dead. RELOAD
After countless reloads the mission is completed.
Im sorry but this is NOT fun. Its bl00dy frustrating.
Another big problem is that enemies can more often then not shoot through walls. Also once you are spotted the enemy ALWAYS knows your position even if you are not in its line of sight. So outflanking an enemy, or trying to be sneaky doesnt work. Why the timelimit on the missions? I dont get it. Anyway if you look for a good Tactics game and you liked the First Xcom, get yourself Jagged Alliance 2 it is still today unsurpassed in quality. If thats a bit too old, try Silent Storm. Also a Brilliant Tactics game.
However if the afromentioned scenario and type of gameplay doesnt bother you, go for it.

Specific complaints:
- The AI is terrible.
- The tech tree is poorly thought out, lacks differentiation on many techs, and the choices on some techs are a joke: there's one clearly optimal tech (i.e. Microbiotics vs Cloning Center) and one trap tech.
- Pointless micromanagement of things like pollution and spies.  Adds nothing to the game and simply forces the player to waste time micromanaging basic stuff.  Poorly thought out mechanics.

Clocking in at around maybe 30 minutes of game time, Serena is a short explorational point-and-click adventure title from the developer Senscape. Released as a free title, this is effectively a glorified tech demo, created to show off the engine used in their upcoming crowd-funded game, Asylum.
The premise is simple.  “A man sits in a distant getaway cabin waiting for his wife Serena.  How long has it been?  Where is she?  Things in the cabin evoke memories, and the husband comes to a disturbing realization…”
With over 40 contributors providing their wit and talents, and described by the developers as a (twisted) love letter to the adventure gaming community, this is certainly an impressive sounding title.  Unfortunately, the game itself – while not necessarily a bad game per say – failed to live up to the supposed pedigree of the developers, and I walked away feeling unimpressed by the experience.
To be fair, I was originally quite positive about the title despite its faults – if not for the actual game itself, then at the very least for the premise, and for what they have tried to achieve.  However, having had some time to reflect (and me being the skeptical ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that I am), I am sad to report that the game have left me with a rather sour taste in my mouth.  The whole project just felt too much to me like one big collaborative marketing campaign, designed to provide opportunistic self-promotion for a bunch of small unknown and unproven indie companies, fronted by talents with dubious track records.
-
S +
- Attention to details.  A lot of seemingly unrelated little details have been added to the environment, giving the game and its characters an air of mystery.
- Ambiguous ending.  While it did feel to me like lazy pretentious writing on the developer’s part, it does open the game up for interesting player interpretations.  In fact, I can go as far to say I had more fun reading forum discussions than I had playing the actual game itself.
-
S -
- Ambiguous writing.  The predictably vague story I felt gave the game an illusion of depth which perhaps really wasn’t really there.
- Uninspired gameplay and story that seeks to emulate recent titles of the genre, but fails to the strike the same emotional impact.
- Does not live up to the promise of “an extremely depressive haunting story that will challenge the players’ intellect (and temerity)”.  This game provided zero challenge – a completely linear title with the only gameplay consisted of literally clicking on every single clickable item multiple times.

I kinda wanted to write "yeah its ok" and have my hours just sitting up there to laugh at but man Starbound deserves better than jokes.
Starbound is just a really well made game in general. It's still in early access mode, and already it has loads of interesting lore, fun mechanics, and it just looks good. Super pretty. The crafting is fun and there's lots of straight up j u n k that looks awesome in the cool structures you can build. You won't care HOW many itty bitty flags and thatch roofing you have, you need more, for your space ship, or your beach house, or your crafting village. With the new updates there are even quests, which, while I started playing and loved it without them, definitely adds to the experience.
It's fun multiplayer, though it can be a little difficult to set up, and prone to crashes. I blame this on early access, as multiplayer fixing doesn't seem to be the focus of the devs right now. The monsters still need adjustment, their hitboxes and their health and power alike. (Getting vague complaints out of the way so I look slightly less biased, though I love it even for its faults)
Personally I'm more here for building. Again, it's already super pretty. There's lots of materials to choose from and collect, and lots of technical stuff you can do (IE: the only thing I've really figured out is making doors automatic. I'm not so great at it myself, but check out starbound's wire system on youtube, it's pretty cool so far!) There's a good mix of useful things like storage and places to craft, and purely decorative things like potted plants and goblets. Everything just looks good, and there's lots of themed items and upgrades to play with.
Then there's more junk like recipes, music and making bands, and other such weird stuff, to be honest the game just has a lot of little things like that to offer. I have been playing for more than a year I'm pretty sure? And I just keep finding new little things, and they bring more little things (along with of course HUGE THINGS) with every update. It's been fun, both the game itself and discovering all the new stuff the devs are giving us.
I'm so biased it's disgusting, but yeah 10/10 will probably keep playing in my free time until long after its full release. Full recommendation, as this is my most played and favorite game on steam.

X-Blades try to be spectacle fighter like Devil May Cry, God of War and so on, but it's far, far away from them. Here you don't have different weapons to choose or set of move. You relay on two swords and guns which are useless (after upgrading the guns they start to become somewhat useful) and a lot of mashing buttons.
After killing an enemy, you collect souls, which are the currency of the game, With them you can buy magic spells. You can equip four at any time. But they are almost the same!!! Lightning on sword, fire on sword, Earthquake or Fire Rage it doesn't matter.
From time to time you see new skill is unlocked, you open the menu to check it and where is it? You have buy some of the available spells and then you see what is unlocked. But what if i don't want to? Well there is no choice. The spells are tight with the bosses, not all but still. For example, there is this werewolf looking boss (which i fought 3 times) For 20 min or more i didn't hurt him once, then out of frustration i open you tube. You have to buy a specific skill named Sparkling Sword to beat him. How can I know that?! There is no indication that you need it. This is the same thing for some of the other bosses. And the fights with them are too long.
For activating spell you need Rage. This is why you use the swords, other than that as i wrote they are useless, so most of the time you count on spell with area of effect, like Fire Rage. Later in the game the skills are quite expensive, so prepare for grinding. The difference between area of effect spells are the animation for each one. They take you out of the action and after that the camera is in weird angle.
Games like this have some sort of move to avoid attacks. Here you can buy one, but it's not that useful and a lot of attacks become hard or impossible to avoid.
Graphics are good, but the cutscenes are bad, they look worse than the in-game graphics. Level design is boring, just ruins and they are basically arenas. To move to the next area you have to kill all enemies on screen.
The music is okay, rock and metal tracks, probably you won't remember it. Same thing can be said about the story. You play as Ayumi, treasure hunter and she touch something and she is cursed. It's completely forgettable.
I mentioned you don't have different set of moves. This isn't quite true. In the game you collect three types of artifacts. When you find enough, you gain more life or some moves for the swords or new skills for the guns (then they become somewhat useful). Let me buy them, I don't want look around just for upgrading my airstrike, which is useless!!!
I can go on and on with the negativity. There is some pleasure in the mindless action, but it won't last long. I didn't expect AAA game, but me some bad design decisions ruin the potential of X-Blades. It's not the worst game i've ever played It's often on sale if you have some interest, but don't even bother.
: nice visuals, okay soundtrack, some mindless action, responsive controls
: boring level design, no debt to the combat, repetitive, some skills/spells are directly tight with the bosses and it's not at least hinted what you need to buy for them, annoying heroine, forgettable story

DayZ Mod is one of the most interesting, exciting and immersive games I've ever played. It's basically a multiplayer apocalyptic virtual world or sandbox without any quests or story-line unless created by the players themselves. You go where you want and do as you want. You determine everything that happens except for the response from other players. You can be a bandit or hero engaging in constant gun battles in the busier towns or you can run off into the wilderness and build yourself a cabin in the middle of nowhere and hunt to survive. There are very few limits on what you can do.
DayZ Epoch (mod) Building & Crafting
I prefer DayZ Mod over DayZ Standalone for several reasons. One of the coolest things about the Mod is that it's essentially a game with hundreds of free expansions and DLCs. Because it's not centrally controlled and developed by a single dev team it offers many different types of games, maps, custom mods, play styles i.e PvP, PvE, RP, and game improvements for free from hundreds of players and community developers and continues to evolve in many alternative directions. Most mods are open source and you can modify them or help develop and improve them yourself. There are Hunger Games type mods to play like Battle Royal where it's everyone for themselves and you fight to be the last one standing, militarized mods like Overwatch full of heavy military weapons, aircraft and tanks, crafting and base building type mods like Epoch and Origins that allow you to more permanently carve out your own piece of the world and make it your home, survival type mods like vanilla DayZ, and even alien mods like Invasion. With the Mod there are so many different options and environments available for play that you're bound to find a server that suits you and if you don't you can even set up your own server and customize it just the way you like. That will likely never happen to the same degree with the Standalone.
800 free mods are available for Arma 2:
The Mod is also much cheaper than Standalone. Arma 2 Combined Operations and Arma X Anniversary keys can be bought for about $5 and $8 each, just search Google for keys or wait for a sale. Not only do you pay less and get dozens of different games and options for play, but you also get the original Arma 2 combat simulator games too, which are award winning games themselves.
Overall, DayZ Mod is a must have if you enjoy PC gaming. Many games are trying to imitate DayZ Mod now, but nothing really compares so far and it will probably remain that way simply because free DayZ mods are community developed by those purely passionate about making cool mods and games while everything else is being developed primarily for profit.

Heavy Fire: Afghanistan is a well polished, if short, rail-shooter with cover mechanics, unlockable weapons and equipment, and quick-time events.
Full of quick-moving, adrenaline pumping firefights that occur in numerous fixed locations keeping you on your toes and forces you to take cover, acquire where targets are located, before shooting or blowing them up!  Limited ammo and explosives mean you are always looking to replinish your ever decreasing resources as the sequence of fights never let up until you complete the mission.
Between missions you can update your equipment and weapons with up to twelve unlocks suchs as better weapons, larger ammo capacity or more grenades.  The enemy A.I. is competant enough to provide a challenge especially on Veteran difficulty.
There isnt much of a learning curve and it doesnt last very long but in the few hours that you begin and end your mission you will get to experience a lot of fast paced and explosive action.   Being a relatively cheap game it punches above its weight..., I mean cost!
It best feature is the way it keep the action moving forwards towards a conclusion just like a good novel.  Together with the excellent graphics, atmospheric sound and easy to use controls you get a great feeling of immersion.  It worst feature... well apart from its shortness.... Has to be the awful voice-overs during the mission de-brief... argh!! :)
Will appeal to fans of the genre, achievement hunters or anyone who likes a cheap game.  If you dont like linear gameplay then avoid.  Personally I loved playing through it twice.
... MORE DETAILS BELOW ...
FPS Military themed, Rail Shooter w/ QTE
Modern Day, Afghanistan War
You play the role of a soldier in a unit of the United States Army.  You are currently based in Afghanistan fighting a fictional skirmishes against insurgents.
Fourteen mission single-player campaign played in two difficulty settings - Rookie and Veteran modes, one after each other.  Play mostly as (grunt) foot soldier, with a very few missions as a gunner in armored vehicle or tank or helicopter.  These do a nice job of shaking up the action somewhat.
Game mechanics couldn't be much simpler.  A series of linear firefights that take place in predetermined locations interspersed by sections of fluid automated movement linking each  location.  At each location enemies appear and try to shoot at you.  You in turn shoot/lob grenades, reload, get into cover.  Rinse and repeat.  Cover sometimes provides two or more options in the direction you choose.  This is something of a tactical decision as part of the screen remains open to enemy shooters so you may find you have to change cover position to remain safe.  Intersperced throughout every mission are a number of Quick-time events, introduced to shaken up the regular rhythm of gameplay specifically to keep you on your toes throughout the firefights.
Visual threats are indicated on screen so you can determine which enemy soldier is the biggest threat at a particular moment in the mission.  While additional audio indicators are used to indicated danger from heavy weapons.  Environmental elements such as smoke and sunlight are used to good effect to blind you from possible enemies lurking at a location.  While also adding an additional element of immersion to gameplay.  In addition the constant moving,  swaying, and ever changing line-of-sight, means you never quite have the time and occasion to take a perfect shot.  While the ever constantly changing camera angle greatly enhances the real threat of friendly fire taking place towards other members of your unit.
Difficultly is implemented though a combination of factors the speed at which enemies appear and shoot, enemy numbers and a reduction inresource replenhishments.  As you progress through each mission there are numerous resource refil icons to replenish ammo, health and grenades.  But you have to be quick.  If you miss them you must do without until the mission is completed.
There is an Armory screen that shows twelve unlockable weapons and equipment upgrades that makes the game easier and more fun to play.
There is a ranking system that promotes you as you progress through the campaign twice; first on novice difficulty, followed by veteran mode.  This makes for a good learning curve as the harder difficult provides a decent challenge.  Completing missions gives points that total up towards a Ranking level.  The greater the combied scores the higher the rank.  The higher the rank the better the player.
Muhjahadeen and insurgents armed with AK-47s and RPGs.  Some heavy machineguns and rocket launchers mounted on pickup trucks, BTR armoured transports, and Hind helicopters.
Short, immersive levels. Uses a terrific range of locations so that you are never bored of the surroundings you find yourself in.  Camera sway and movement adds an extra dimension so you never quite feel in control of the situation.  Otherwise the threats are limited to mainly enemy soldiers and a number of heavy weapons or armored vehicles and helicopters make an appearance like end of level bosses.
Robust if somewhat basic.  Then again this genre really doesnt need anything other than an A.I. that provides enough of a challenge for whoever is playing the game.
Excellent mouse and keyboard functions.  Especially pertinent is the mouse sensitivity options.  You may need this if you're mouse moves like a lead ballon as there is no light-gun for PC... :(  Whats a light-gun?  ^^
Great.  Very colourful and adds to the immersion.
Basic.  A single catchy soundtrack that eggs you forwards.  Some decent weapons sounds, shouts, screams, radio chatter and background explosions add to the immersion.
Not a big fan of the voice-overs in this game.  Felt like the voice actors were sub-par but thankly their use is limited only to the mission debriefs.
A breeze on Novice difficulty.  Actually challenging in places on Veteran difficulty.  The save checkpoints and environmental features add to the difficulty in veteran mode.
No problems were encountered installing, running or playing this game.
A good mix of achievements.  Mostly standard achieve x kills.  Complete mission y, etc... All easily obtainable by plaing through the campaign in Novice and  Veteran difficulty modes.  There are a few combo related achievements that may require a replay of a level or two.
None.
From five to ten hours to play the same campaign twice.
Fans of the genre who dont mind replaying the same campaign can do so to better their score.  If you're an achievement hunter then you will play through the campaign twice and most likely complete all but one achievement during those playthroughs.
If you are fan of this genre or are too lazy to play a bon-a-fide FPS then this could be something you should consider.   Especially if you have a preference for modern day military themes set around the recent wars against religious fundamentalism.
Perfect value for money.  If only it was a little longer.  A steal on sale.  An easy recommendation.

I guess the concept is kind of interesting... many people (myself included) quite enjoy rail shooters in arcades. So... why not take the concept, but allow people to play in the comfort of their own home. Unfortunately, without the virtual gun, and with a not-quite-as-intuitive cover system, this rail shooter falls flat. Whether you play with a gamepad or keyboard and mouse - the controls are slow and sluggish, and the movements and animations just don't feel right. This is exacerbated by the Quick Time Events... probably one of my least favourite mechanics or gimmicks in any game - there is just no need for them, and they don't add anything to the gameplay experience except annoyance.
Additionally, considering this is on PC... the limitations of a rail shooter are woefully exposed when compared to the vast array of FPS games already on the market: you are directed where to go with no freedom at all except to duck in and out of cover and pop off a few shots. Even in FPS games with very linear levels, at least you can look around a room: not so in a rail shooter.
The audio for the game is pretty terrible, the weapons and explosions don't sound good at all. They sound generic, flat, and are of pretty low quality. The voice acting complements the poor soundtrack, with the voice actors not playing their part very well at all. This is compounded by the writing: not only is the overall plot of the game short and poor, but the dialogue is also poorly written, and is completely out of place.
Then there are the visuals, which look... reasonable, I guess. Not great, but not absolutely terrible like everything else about this game. Still, the ability to be completely blinded and be completely unable to see anything at all by sun glare and the excessive muzzle flash are both major weaknesses. Realistic perhaps, but definitely not conducive to a fun game.
For me, the only redeeming factor for the game is the progression, with the ability to pick perks after missions to customise your character.

*WARNING* Possible spoilers ahead'
I have only played this reboot of the "Master of Orion" series for about 4 hours, but already I see the immense detail, time and care put into the game. Firstly, they hired top notch voice actors *cough cough* Mark Hamil *cough cough* . They paid these actors probably hundreds if even thousands of $$$ in order to have this game in top quality standard before release.
Secondly, the actual structure of the game and lack of glitches and bugs are absolutely fantastic. The way that they designed the ship paths around stars and the way that everything was animated really made me feel like I was commanding a galactic empire. Good ol' M.O.O.1, the legendary M.O.O.2 and ESPECIALLY the godawful M.O.O.3 do not live up to this new competitor. And dont get me started on the AAA graphics.
Lastly, the way that they structured the gameplay is fan-f***ing-tastic. The A.I is so well developed that top players from Stellaris, M.O.O.2 and other strategy games lose so often to the A.I. The A.I will do the most seemingly random things sometimes, such as blowing up your space-factory when they are on the verge of defeat in order to distract/annoy you, they might give you technology and befriend you even though they are more advanced and they may even destroy you before you have researched Xeno Relations. They are just that good!
In Conclusion, we can see based on my experience that this new iteration of the "Master of Orion" franchise lives up to the legends of old and then some. I Highly recommend this game to all those that are looking for a fantastic, humorous 4X strategy game.

Re-evaIuating this title after some key gameplay changes and additions as well as some new DLC.
I still recommend this to new fans of the series as well as fans of the classics.  If I had to rank them, 1st place goes to MOO2, 2nd - MOO1, 3rd, MOO (this title) and lastly MOO3.  No shame in coming in 3rd to 2 titles that made PC Gamer's Hall of Fame ages ago.
After a few updates, MOO has heroes, as well as Gnolam, Elerian, and Trilarian (sp?...I've been playing the series for more than 20 years and I can't spell for beans).  It's beginning to remind me of MOO2, which is one of my all time favorite games, period (Where have you gone, Steve Barcia?!  Any chance Agents of Justice will ever get done?)
I played MOO1 back around....94?  And loved MOO2.  This is neither, but, still very fun!
I got this early access, and have played through the present build and liked the character that has been added to the game, but, the repetition wears a little thin.  A little.  There is still something very gratifying about amassing a huge fleet and wiping the Galaxy clean of your enemies.
Ship design was much simpler and intuitive in the original titles, and I think it could use some more polish as the auto-updating gets a little cross-eyed when you get a new tech.  The auto-design doesn't know how to use specials, particular the space-saving ones that can really make for a powerful, albeit slightly longer to produce, ship.
So, you'll want to get in the habit of micromanaging this.
Tactical combat is simple...not bad.  I tend not to interfere with auto-combat too often except when it's an advantage to take out harder hitting/high value targets first.
That being said, graphics are decent, and gameplay is fun.
I think a little more polish with the UI and UX.
Here's what I liked:
-Graphics aren't world-renowned, nor is the voice acting, but....they're good!  There are a finite amount of lines of spoken dialogue so that does kinda wear thin after a while (see 'What I didn't like').
-The races really have a lot of personallity.  I am going to do a bad job describing this, but it's a jes ne se qua.  Every game I play I always seem to step on the toes of a different race, but become very close allies with other races; this has kept it very interesting for me!
-Ship Design (I'll put this one in both categories for different reasons).  It's easy, it's intuitive, it can and probably should be time-consuming and full of micromanagement.  It can make a difference depending on which race, or which space monster, or what *type* of warfare you are conducting (swarms of lots of little ships, massive machines of war, or, my favorite, Interdictor type "Hunter-Killers" geared at chasing my prey like Hounds of Hell throughout the galaxy.)
Here's what I didn't like so much:
-Things do get repetative.  The dialogue from your advisor and AI races.  The gameplay.  The colony micromanagement.  You learn to tune some of it out.  And, I might be deranged, but I actually enjoy micromanaging my colonies, but I'm aware that others probably will not enjoy this.
-Ship Design.  As mentioned above, the simplest solution would be to let the game mechanism add new tech automatically, auto-upgrade your fleet, Upgrade, or Scrap-and-rebuild to newer designs.  That's fine and dandy, but the auto-upgrade skips some very important Special Techs.
That's all I've got.  I hope you enjoy the game as much as I do, and you'll have an opportunity to pick this title up during one of Steams many sales and deals!

After receiving a 22% helpful rating based on my original review I've decided to attempt a proper review;
As you're probably well aware the latest incarnation of Masters of Orion is what is commonly called a 4X game. eXplore, eXpand, eXploit, and eXterminate.
When you start a new game there are a myriad of options when 'creating' a new galaxy within which to play. Be it a large galaxy, small, how many empires inhabitat said galaxy, which species they are, game speed and other options besides. Meaning you can setup an epoch spanning game that could easily lasts days or weeks (it seems) to games that perhaps take a mere afternoon. I'd have to spend some more time with the varying settings to give you more details on this.
As your sweaty little fingers eagerly click your abused mouse button, with it's cursor hovering over the start game tab you'll find yourself transported to your galaxy and a single planet. From here you will manage your population putting them to work in the food industry, manufacturing plants and labs. Managing your output of food, construction of buildings and space ships and research into new technologies.
You'll eventually send scoutships out to discover new systems full of juicy (or not so juicy) planets to explore and perhaps even colonize. When you colonize your new planets you'll have to carefully manage their early years, it helps to buy (automatically receive) automated construction factories, biomes and indoor farming to help your colonists thrive and build newer structures quicker, increasing your population size and therefore food construction and research speed, eventual increase in taxes with government buildings and tradeports and increasing your fleet size with starbases.
Some planets have negative effects, such as high or low gravity, toxicity, barren, gas giant or asteroid. Eventually you will unlock techs to change all of the above into habital planets or at least more appealing to your average space colonist.
Diplomacy seems to work well, in as far as I've experienced it on my singular game I'm still going through. I don't attack the marlocks, (or whatever the hell they are) and we trade technologies and set up trade between us increasing our monies.
What does annoy me though is that when it comes to espionage in order to put an agent on an enemy planet you need to have visited it first whereas my friendly foe has no problems with this, having made sure their ships never entered my space in a couple of rather more violent forms of diplomacy. Yet they still have agents on all of my planets. Perhaps this is a racial perk as their faction is the espionage specialists. But still, it annoys me.
The space battles themselves are a bit... Meh. Still, better than most space battles I've witnessed in other 4X games.
Despite my lack of conversing with all of the races within the game, I rather like the characters I've seen so far and the 'Global News Network' droids that tell you everything you need to know about the galaxy in a fairly amusing manner and occasionally some helpful news too. Such as detailing the top three races in colonization, population, military etc. The most recents news story was several cips about a star about to go supernova. You'll be pleased to know that on the brink of disaster the weird turtle people managed to save themselves and stop the star going supernova.
Overall, probably my favourite 4X game. It's relatively complex and yet VERY streamlined. Fans of the genre should enjoy this.

Mideval sports where killing is legal! That's one of many ways to describe Blood Bowl, a game that has you jumping for joy one minute and crying the next.
Based off the original board game, Blood Bowl is an American Football game mixed with chess-like strategy. You'll position players, throw blocks, and hopefully score touchdowns. Graphically BB doesn't offer much, you have a handful of stadiums and some customizable players, but where Blood Bowl really shines is its diverse character roster. 23 races fill BB stadiums, from the sleek Amazons, to the toughened Orcs, to the completely useless Halfling teams, each race works differently, and it's up to you to find which one fits your play style. For those who love destroying the enemy team, the minotaur teams of Chaos are for you, boasting strong players to help maim as many players as possible. Want to go around them, Skaven will do just fine. Wanna launch a hail mary, High Elf. However, keep in mind that each team has conflicting weakness that you must tailor your strategy to.
BB plays out kind of like chess and American Football wrapped in one. Two teams battle it out over 16 turns to score as many touchdowns as possible. This is where things get interesting. It takes a whle to get used to the rules and understand how everything works, but stick it out and you'll see the beauty. You'll see all kinds of strategies, like the typical punch everything style of Orcs to the outrageous physical game with Skaven, and you have to tailor your plan accordingly. Keep in mind that all the mechanics are dice based, like the original board game, so even though you baited the team and are set to make a perfect hand off, Nuffle (the BB God of the Dice) may say "Nope!" and have him drop the ball, so no strategy is fool proof. When your not beating people/getting beaten sensless, you're buying players, leveling up players, and hiring cheerleaders and coaches. Blood Bowl's skill system is a lttle weird, having you roll dice. If you roll singles, you get to choose from a select few. Singles over a certain amount allow you to boost one of their skills. Doubles lets pick any skill or, if allowed, mutate, which gives you special abilities for certain races AND changes the corresponding character model, so expect to see a few Chaos Beastmen with tentacles, claws, or an extra head or arm.
The Verdict:
+Fun Customization
+Strategies for each race
+23 races
-Dice based combat system
8/10 Great
If you can get past the rules, find the right team, and accept that a few bad rolls are going to happen, then I sincerely recommend buy Blood Bowl.

I don't know how many actual labors Hercules does in this game, but overall, he's pretty lazy. Most of the work is done by normal people, and boy do they have to hustle. The essence of this game is you have to accomplish an overall goal in a set amount of time. To achieve the goal, you have to do smaller tasks. Like to get food, you have to pick it from bushes, or plant gardens. But to do that, you need wood. To get wood, you have to cut trees. And so on and so forth. How you manage these tasks, determines how fast you can beat the level. Special power ups are available to help you. At the end of each level, you have to defeat a mini-game, with each one being different. I enjoyed the mini-game boss fights, as I felt they added some variety to the game. And that's pretty much what 12 Labours of Hercules is about.
The graphics are cartoonish, but they look good. The music is a bit repetitive and nothing special, but it didn't annoy me. The control is fine. And the challenge level, I'd say is easy. I played on the default level, and beat the game with 100 percent achievements in a little over 5 hours. I probably won't play it again, but I had a decently fun time. I got the game on sale for around 50 cents, and for that price, I definitely got my money's worth. If you can get it for around that, and want an easy little time waster of a game, Hercules is a good choice.

I'm going to be honest here. 2 or 1 year ago I wouldn't have recommended this mod. As this mod is brilliant and phenomenal it has been very unstable since it was relased early 2013. The concept sounded cool but back then DayZ had dozens of issues which prevented me playing and enjoying this otherwise so supreme title. Glitching zombies, clumsy and buggy user interference and constant uncertainity of losing everything you had collected caused by server crash were serious problems. However - what could one expect from the free mod for players of ARMA2 and ARMA2: Operation Arrowhead?
Fortunantly DayZ mod has grown these past years. With the help of active community it has gotten various new maps, the UI have been enchanted and is much more easier and safer to use. Third party management programs such as DayZ launcher and DayZ Commander have done indispensable work releasing players of most of the updating burden.
Of course this mod still isn't flawless and some annoying surprices happen every now and then, but considering how well it has gotten upgreaded these last years I say the future looks encouraging. DayZ mod prospers and lives well and dozens of servers have always players to keep the game hectic and interesting where - or when ever you play. DayZ mod is still one of the greatest survival, open world titles in the world and at the moment imo it is DayZ standalone's superior.

I really really Tried to like it. I loved the first game, what a fresh breeze of air. This one however ( and i will get alot of flak from fanboys for this) is not good. The Presentation is breathtaking. Super epic Music intros and all manner of awesomeness. Great Voiceacting and so on.
However you deserve to know why you may not like this one. Xcom is a Tactics game. It lives and breathes from being 70% Tactics, 20% Strategy and 10% luck. Xcom2 is 70% luck as far as i experienced it. Because of a few mechanics, most missions have a pretty brutal Timelimit. You either need to cross the whole map to reach a certain point, or rescue somebody, or rescue alot of people. You have around 3-8 turns time for this. That means the game forces you to rush. I personally hate this in tactics game. You cant set up a propper ambush. And more often then not you end up with your pants down running in a group of Aliens. Ok RELOAD.
Now you know where the aliens are, advance until then. Take them out. Oh Soldier 1 Missed. Soldier 2...he missed aswell. Soldier 3... 2 Damage! Enemy proceeds killing the Squads. RELOAD!
Ok this time Soldier 1 Hits. Yay, enemy dead. Soldier 2...missed. Soldier 3...missed again. Enemy kills soldier 3, Soldier 1 is panicked. RELOAD (spoiler...next turn everybody is dead)
When you finally get to the terminal (after MANY reloads), Oh reinforcments are coming and dropping in the flank of my squad. Sucks to be me i guess. Squad dead. RELOAD
Now i know that reinforcements are coming, Get to the terminal, Have everybody in position. Reinforcments now arrive at a different place. (again flanked) Squad Dead. RELOAD
After countless reloads the mission is completed.
Im sorry but this is NOT fun. Its bl00dy frustrating.
Another big problem is that enemies can more often then not shoot through walls. Also once you are spotted the enemy ALWAYS knows your position even if you are not in its line of sight. So outflanking an enemy, or trying to be sneaky doesnt work. Why the timelimit on the missions? I dont get it. Anyway if you look for a good Tactics game and you liked the First Xcom, get yourself Jagged Alliance 2 it is still today unsurpassed in quality. If thats a bit too old, try Silent Storm. Also a Brilliant Tactics game.
However if the afromentioned scenario and type of gameplay doesnt bother you, go for it.

At first before I get into the review, let me explain the game:
1. No video options. Stuck to monitor's maximum hertz. When I mean no video options, I mean like no graphical options like consoles. No resolution, nothing. Guise of the Wolf (which only had a resolution option) even has an option!
2. You have a score at the bottom of your screen. In my opinion, useless.
3. It's an on-rails shooter by Teyon, the same people who made Rambo: The Video Game. BUT, because this was originally made for the Xbox 360 in 2011, they get a free pass right? WRONG!
4. One of the worst ports to PC I've ever seen.
I thought to myself as I saw a bundle with this game in it. "I've beaten Ride to Hell: Retribution, nearly beaten Rambo: The Video Game, played the Slaughtering Grounds and The Walking Dead: Survival Instinct, how bad can it be?"
OH GOD. So I buy this bundle from
(BTW, great website) for $3.49. I open the game to loud audio and it says, "Controller recommended" so I turn on my wireless Xbox 360 controller for Windows. Ok, three options in the Audio, that's ok. "But I have to use the triggers to change them and press X to accept the options?" From there on, I knew this would be going downhill fast. So I boot up the campaign to see 12 missions and a Veteran mode. I was aparently in the "Rookie" section because I probably would have to beat the game to go into the "Veteran" mode. That's fine. Launching the game, I hear an OK backstory of a soldier and then we arrive on a helicopter to Afghanistan. The first thing I noticed was the sterotype that all Afghans wear either turbans or balacavas. I thought, "Wonderful". The graphics are ok for 2011, so I try to move my standards down a little to that year. When I got into the game though...
The first thing I noticed was the M16 they supplied me with. When you run out of ammo, you have an infinite extra ammo Berreta they switch you over to when you run out of ammo. I'm surprised they added an actually "ammo" feature. When I shoot the gun for the very first time... I said, "The Slaughtering Grounds and Ride to Hell: Retribution have better sound quality than this!" The gun sounded like you tapped a button on your controller. The pistol has a very small sound. Then I noticed that I was invincible. I couldn't die, like I was a god. My health wouldn't go down (speaking of which there is no difficulty option) and then I got worried. After I beat the first level, I'd rather "masturbate with sandpaper".
DO NOT BUY THIS GAME! $3.00 isn't worth it, heck, it's worth $0.05 for maybe a giggle with your friends.

0.3/10

P.S: RAMBO: THE VIDEOGAME IS BETTER BY INFINITE AMOUNTS COMPARED TO THIS!

Botanicula is amazing. Amanita really outdid themselves with this one. The game is beautiful and detailed, and at the same time elegant and simple. It's cute, it's funny, but it's also quite pretty. And they manage to tell an interesting and entertaining story without a single line of dialog (spoken or written).
Yes, the puzzles are noticeably easier than they were in Machinarium, but I feel like the puzzles aren't the point of the game. Rather, your goal is to explore this wonderful and whimsical world of cute little plant and bug creatures, all while trying to save their home from an encroaching monster.
To really get the most out of Botanicula, I strongly encourage you to scour every nook and cranny of the world, because there is always something special to be found. I'd recommend this game to anyone who likes simple, yet gorgeously-rendered puzzle games and point-and-click adventures.

Materially, this is just a simple point-and-click adventure. It does not open up any new frontiers and it will not burn your brain attempting to solve the puzzles. If you are looking for a deep gameplay experience, look elsewhere.
This game will appeal to people who appreciate the idea of video games as personal art. Not necessarily thoughtful commentaries that "have something to say" about social issues, but rather just as works of reflection, crafted by a creator who actually cares about the work he is producing.
This game is ugly and beautiful at the same time, and strangely compelling in its own way. I felt rewarded when I had completed it. Not really for the sake of the game's story (rudimentary and nebulous at best), but for the sake of having experienced something that other human beings shaped and created for their personal satisfaction, hoping that I, a stranger, might like it too. Sometimes I did, sometimes I didn't. That is art to me.
If the thing I've described above is what you want to see more of in "indie" game design, then spend a couple bucks on this and I think you will be happy.

Stardew Valley is a relaxing, cute, farming game set in a small town filled with a range of colourful characters. The basic premise is similar to that of Harvest Moon, so if you've played that you would no doubt be familiar with the game mechanics. This essentially consists of growing crops, harvesting them and selling them for money which you can then use to buy more seeds, buy animals or upgrade your farm. That's not the only options to make money though, mining, fishing, crafting artisan goods and foraging also provide additional ways of making money. All the while, you are tasked with making friends with the town's citizens, including finding love and getting married, and rebuilding the neglected community centre and in doing so revitilise the town.
One of the good things about Stardew Valley is the sheer range of content and things to do. You can easily spend a day or several days focusing on one particular activity, then if you get a bit bored with that activity, you can focus on something else.  For example, you might want to focus on mining for a bit so you can get some metals to upgrade your tools, then focus on fishing for a bit. There's a lot to do, as such I'm well into year 3 and I'm still not very far into the story.
The game's setting, as you would expect from a Harvest Moon-style game, is quite relaxing. There's a bit of combat in the mines but generally it's a peaceful, stressless game, perfect for unwinding after a long day at work. The relaxing simplicity of growing, harvesting and selling crops is something you can come back to.
One of the less strong points about this game, however, is its soundtrack. The music itself isn't bad, but there's just not much of it. You'll wake up and there's a bit of music, but by lunchtime there will often be no music. That's just a minor point, but it may affect the atmosphere of the game for some people. Some people may not appreciate the 8-bit graphical style, however it does seem to work pretty well with the setting of the game.
As you become friends with the NPCs by giving them gifts and doing chores for them (mostly retrieval quests), you'll gain hearts and can romance a character. However, in my experience romancing or even becoming friends with them doesn't change what they say when you speak to them that much. Occasionally they'll say a few different things, but a lot of what they will say will be the same or similar to what they would say when you're not friends with them. Except a couple of characters. I mean, with the character whom I've romanced there has not been a huge difference in what they say to me, despite being in a relationship with them.   In fairness, I have not made friends with the entire town yet.
Also, you cannot save manually and it saves automatically at the beginning of a day. This has a way of encouraging you to kee playing the next day (think 'one more turn' with games like Civilization) so you can sell your now ripe crops, but can be slightly annoying if you have to leave suddenly.
Despite the few relatively minor criticisms, I very much recommend this game for anyone who's seeking a relaxing, stressfree farming/small town simulator.
TLDR;
+ Relaxing, peaceful setting, perfect for unwinding after a stressful/long day IRL
+ A wide range of content and options for making money
+ Good value of money with the potential for many hours of gameplay
- No manual saving
- Not the best soundtrack

Update:
I still enjoy playing this game, for what it is, a streamlined, rapid-fire galactic chess game rather than a fully-developed 4X title. The AI could still benefit from improvement; added depth would make this title a little more replayable. However, after purchasing and playing Stellaris, I have to say Stellaris is the superior 4X game by a light year, particularly with the new Utopia expansion features. The interface and graphics of MoO:CtS are more polished, but for pure galactic game-play joy, I recommend Stellaris.
Original Review:
As another big fan of the original MOO games, 1&2, I've been struggling whether to recommend this remake. It was in pretty rough shape when the first Early Access edition was released (realeased too soon, if you ask me.)  However, since then the developers have really listened to the playerss feedback, and they have dramatically improved the game experience. Overall, I am very happy with the game. It perfectly captures the Master of Orion experience. The graphics, sound design, and control architecture are flawless. The most important feature - the AI has significantly improved. Diplomacy has significantly improved. Ultimately, I find the game to be just as addictive as the original title.
I do have a few caveats. I'm not a fan of the mostly linear tech tree. I wish combat were a little more interactive. (I don't mind that it's not turn-based.)  I wish the game had a little more depth, with more developed trade, economy, governors, heros, land assults, greater depth with Orion technology and the missing Antarans. However, minor races will eventually be added, and the developers are planning to open the game for mods. Yay!!!
Ultimately, I have to say the game is exactly what I wanted it to be - an addictive, streamlined, intergalactic MOO chess game with a modern face-lift. Cheers to the developers for resurrecting one of my all-time favorite games!

This is basically a resource + time management simulator. The first game of the kind that I've played, and if you're as unfamiliar with them as I was, the next paragraph should help you:
Hercules (or rather, his servants, who do most of the work) is stuck in succession of maze-like levels in which resources and obstacles are interspersed. He’s supposed to reach the exit (fulfilling a few conditions unique to each level along the way) within a specific timeframe. Each obstacle cleared takes some time (as the servants run to the obstacle and work) and resources (typically, food). So you have to both calculate the optimal route to get all the resources you need in the bag to continually overcome obstacles, frantically click to keep sending your servants about their tasks, and juggle temporary bonuses (speed boosts, extra resources) and resource management (do I want to use my wood supply to build a farm that will spawn more food, or to build a bridge into an area with extra resources).
The final result is an incredibly addictive mix of frantic clicking and on-the-run thinking. It helps that the game plays and sounds nice. The graphics aren’t amazing by any means, but they are pleasantly smooth – the characters scurrying around are always fun to behold. The music is catchy, and while repetitive, also calculated to be inoffensive. The game (and each of its sequels, that I’ve also played) regularly goes on sale for 0.5$, though it’s probably worth it even at its modest full price.

Quick review.
So far, the game, for its current state, is actually a lot of fun. It's obviously a very co-op based game and encourages a tremendous amount of team play. Not only with your crews communications to your captain and vice-versa, but your captains to the rest of your fleet (If playing more then a ship 1v1).
The concept is nothing new, but actually refreshingly different. Shades of Guns of Icarus are prevalent, however you can literally board a ship and take out an entire crew. Obviously, being based in the correct era also helps.
Seeing people work together, via both VOIP and p2p is actually something refreshing to see. So often am I used to playing a game where there are many trolls, Blackwake is simple enough that the trolls seem to be kept at distance (FF is off thankfully) and the primary function is to work together and you are rewarded. Points are both individual and team based, which encourages team work for all actions (shooting/killing/repairing etc).
There are currently two different ships which players can occupy. A 13 manned crew and a 7 manned crew. Both offering vary different experiences. The larger gallaeon ship truely does give you a grander experience and you feel the weight of the ship when moving about. Whilst at the same time, occupying the smaller vessel means that you must ensure you are all working effectively and smartly.
PvP needs to be worked on some what, (Melee mostly) however I have been surprised at how well the hit registry when using rifle ranged shots is. It appears it is actually, for the most part, fairly reliable.
The most satisfying part of the game has been when our captain ordered us to grapple hook another ship. This means that the ship being boarded has a 2 minute penalty to spawning and the aim is to kill all the crew, which defeats the pirate ship. Our gallaeon was actually on the verge of defeat until we managed to board their ship and defeat them, much to the roars and cheers of the fellow crew when we were victorious.
Graphics wise the game is a little outdated. Hopefully this will be worked on, more so the characters are lacking somewhat in definition. There are also limited unlocks for crew progression atm (which are all cosemetic based, not skill based).
The main negative I have is the constant FPS drop that myself, and many other people are experiencing. Often it occurs in crucial PvP moments, leaving you stuttering whilst all the action goes on around you, and you are waiting 3-4 seconds for it to clear up. The devs have made it quite clear that this is a priority to be fixed.
A pleasant surprise has been the amount of Australian Official servers on release. Unlike many other Early Access titles, Oceania has been forgotten.
Definitely worth the investment at the moment and something to continue to play as the game further develops.

A bland game chock-full of uninteresting choices and frustrating limitations. Despite months of EA, and lots of great feedback from players, the devs made only minor changes to the game, and have now released the full game with most of its original flaws intact. I have played a number of partial games, throughout the EA process, but haven't yet had the heart to finish one.
A few of the many unnecessary flaws and limits:
- Why can't I put multiple layers of armor on a ship? Multiple shield generators? Multiple engines? Where Stardrive 2, Star Ruler 2, and Endless Space give you real freedom in ship design, MoO seems determined to limit my imagination.
- Why can I design combat ships, but not stations or civilian ships? Again, where Star Ruler 2 allows wonderful freedom in design, MoO creates unnecessary limits.
- Tactical battles just aren't real tactical. This is a deep and complex problem, too complex to outline here, but there are many deep and thoughtful discussions of this topic in the forums.
- The tech tree is bland, full of lots of incremental improvements, but rarely anything that feels interesting or meaningful. The game plays (almost) the same from start to finish.
- Planetary special resources are piddly, giving a simple +1 or +2 to research/money/production. This means that, except in the very beginning of the game, there's no reason to choose a planet with a special resource over one without. This is a huge missed opportunity.
For sure, there's some fun to be found in this game, but with such a bland design, there's little replay value. And in this age of gaming, with so many better choices around, why waste your time with something so bland?
If you really want a space-based 4x game, go for Stardrive 2 or Star Ruler 2. Both are a bit buggy, products of small teams stretched to their limits, but both are also full of genius and innovation - and that genius makes both these games far more fun and interesting than MoO.

In this game, you play as a group of protagonists – Mr. Lantern, Mrs. Mushroom, Mr. Poppyhead, Mr. Twig, and Mr. Feather – who are trying to save their home from the spider attacks that plague it. To save your home, you must solve puzzle after puzzle, most of which are easy. I did get stuck once, though that may have been because it was getting late and I’d already been playing for a while. I picked it up the next morning and instantly figured it out.
Pros:
- This game is truly beautiful. The art style is unique, the soundtrack is incredible, and the five playable characters have so much personality without actually saying a word.
- I love how interactive this game is. Random bugs, plants, etc. can be clicked on and most give you achievements.
- The storyline is well developed, as are the minor characters. This game is filled with little whimsical moments involving the littlest things – a spider hiding behind a leaf, eggs hatching.
- Pretty sure I sat at my desk with this amazed expression on my face the whole time (the soundtrack gets to you, man!).
Cons:
- While I played through this twice (once for story, once for achievements – I’m not posting a review of anything until I 100% it), there is very little in the replay value aspect. Keep in mind if you play this that you should really pay attention and experience the story the first playthrough, because it won’t be the same the next time.
- The puzzles are very easy, which would make this a great game for younger children, but might become a bit boring for those who like a challenge.

This new Master of Orion is a pretty good game with a few disappointments. It ultimately delivers a game I'll play again and again - as such, it has succeeded.
WARNING! A lot of reviews will hate this game. In the end of my review, I'll explain why I think that is actually a mark of quality.
This review covers "the good", "the bad" and "the hate".
The Good
- Has that MoO feel. Congratulations! Not an easy feat. I thought it'd be lost with stuff like space-lanes, but no, they pulled it off IMO.
- A looong EA (true EA, not the "lol test our servers" kind of EA) has made the game pretty polished.
- The combat. It isn't turn-based and that is fine by me. I loved MoO2 back then, but now... It would have felt really weird. Instead, new mechanics emerge where small ships have advantages over big ships - it becomes a risk vs reward situation and I like it. Also, creating that one, big ship that can beat _everything_ is actually quite difficult. Have fun!
- What seems like a dedicated company set on making this a solid product. And with simple mechanics, stupid flaws are less likely and more stuff can be build onto it. Sooo many races and mechanics can easily be added in the future and I'm hoping for it.
The Bad
- Released a bit early, more things aught to have been implemented before release instead of coming later.
- No multiplayer tactical combat. For me, this is the simgle biggest disappointment. But ultimately, I still play this game and mainly as a single player game, so I have to be honest with myself and say "I still enjoy the game". But man... really?
- The lack of heroes and ship-experience takes some emotional heft out of the game. We'll all miss something, this is what I'll miss.
- All the advisors annoy me :( Luckily, they can be turned off :)
The Hate
There's a lot of fans of this old, beloved franchise. They all love the original 2 MoO-games for different reasons and have fond memories. I even got this game as a gift from an old friend I played MoO2 with "back then".
But the developers have made quite a few "tough choices" on cutting out content and mechanics, simplifying the game. You can call it "dumbing down", but the opposite can be called a boring clusterf**k with MoO3 as the sad pinacle.
I'll miss some of the mechanics, but overall I like the result. People who find that the devs have cut content from which they had fond memories will often hate on the game. A lot simply wanted a MoO2 redux - it was a good game.
But ultimately, changes had to be made, choices were made. You can't keep everything from the old games and add new stuff without ending up with a bloated game. I prefer heartbreaking choices over a game-mechanically bloated game with no focus and more nuances than could be balanced.
The Hate is a result of choices on the devs part, if that is what keeps a repeated MoO3 failure at bay, it is a quality mark in my opinion.

Master of Orion 4 is not a remake of Master of Orion 1 or 2.
It's pretty much the game we needed instead of Master of Orion 3.
You see, back when MoO3 was announced I was very interested in it.
MoO2 was one of the games that kickstarted my love for videogames and boosted
my switch from consoles to pc.
The horrendous ui, bad ai and terrible gameplay mechanics in MoO3 killed my dream of a more modern and refreshing MoO experience and as such left me with replaying MoO2 countless times.
Which by no means should be interpreted as bad, because to this day I still love booting up MoO2 and the original CD-ROM plus euro box are on display on my shelf.
However as much as I love MoO2, it has flaws and with these flaws it would never survive a simple remake in today's gaming world.
Game franchises of the older days like Civilization, Total War and X-COM have shown that slow paced 4X games aren't dead, but at the same time require careful updates to keep up with today's audience.
And all of these changes are usually either dumbing down game mechanics (Hi, Total War post Medieval II) or changing the franchise itself to a certain degree, making it far more accessable for newcomers (X-COM 2).
I have to admit it's not the worst approach, it's actually not even a bad one when done well.
X-COM 2 and Civilization V have shown perfectly how we can get very fun and deep 4X games that proceed to build the bridge between "casual" 4X and the "number crunching" ones.
Master of Orion 4 is such a game.
Hate it or love it, it's the Master of Orion I would play in multiplayer with people younger than me or those who had no previous interest in 4X games.
MoO2 would just make the average joe turn away from the genre with it's focus being more on the number crunching and in-depth game mechanics rather than the steamlined approach of MoO4.
Now of course it's great that the game caters to a wider audience by including those that have no previous experience with the genre, but what of the "veterans", those who have played 4X games since their earliest incarnations?
It's pretty simple, either you can appreciate what the game does in it's own way, or you'll never like this game.
I wrote in the very beginning that MoO4 isn't a remake of former games of the franchise.
It's a new game in the franchise, taking new approaches and changes to not only simplify existing game mechanics, but also adding new ones.
Take the change from tactical to real time combat for example.
I like that change, I also liked the real time combat in games like Imperium Galactica II, I loved the newer Sins of a Solar Empire for it's great real time 4X approach.
It's not only more graphically pleasing, but also interesting in it's own way.
Turn-based combat leaves a lot of it's representation to the player's imagination, which is enjoyable, however also confines it into a corner of the room.
To put it simple, turn based combat is methodical, more like a puzzle, while real time combat also relies on player instinct and ability to adapt to situations quickly.
They're too different to each other, but interesting for exactly that reason.
Turn based combat in any game makes me want to min-max my troops performance as much as possible, granting me perhaps the chance to turn a devastating loss into a victory by making the puzzle pieces fall into the places I want them to be.
Real Time combat fills that itch of mine to do my best possible within the time granted.
It's decision making on the fly, identify the outcome, proceed or change the tactic used and work
with the results to prepare for the next step.
And that describes MoO4 perfectly, too.
It's not MoO2, it didn't try to be to begin with.
It's a game on it's own.
Does it have flaws?
Oh yes it does, some of which prolly won't be fixed until later and some of which are flaws of the genre itself and are unlikely to be ever "fixed".
MoO2 had flaws, too.
Different ones, from a different genre subtype.
Did these flaws make it a bad game? By no means.
Do the flaws in MoO4 make it a bad game? By no means.
As such I recommend to buy MoO4 to anyone who likes the 4X genre in itself and not just certain subtypes of it.
It certainly isn't a game for someone who only appreciates the number crunching Paradox-esque 4X games of this world, but for people like me who enjoy all the subgenres it'll be a good gaming experience.

You're alone in your cabin, you remember your love, Serena... But for some reason that's all you can remember. Her name. Where is she? What does she look like? How long have you been like this? What happened? The anwsers will come to you by searching through the cabin.

These devs have released a lot of new editions with very minor differences in the 4-5 years leading up to Chaos Edition and got on my nerves, but I'm willing to forgive them for it because Blood Bowl is a great game. If you like American football with slightly less violence, this game is a lot of fun. Strategy reigns supreme, you need to learn the strengths and weaknesses of the various teams and take advantage of them. For example, the Elve teams tend to be great at running and throwing the ball, able to easily and quickly score touchdowns if allowed to remain on their feet, while races like the Dwarves take the slow and steady approach to (literally) steamrolling enemy teams as they make a group push towards the end zone. Killing the enemy team outright is a viable option and some races such as Chaos and the Orcs depend on incapacitating the enemy team to make up for a lack of a strong passing or high defenses like the Dwarves.
The dice gods, as always in Games Workshop properties, ultimately reign supreme in Blood Bowl. The best laid plans can still go all wrong, and that is part of the fun because it will happen to your opponents as often as it happens to you. There ARE steps you can take to minimize the impact of the random number generator though, in the form of bribes to the referees, wizards in the audience, etc... In terms of game modes you have a full season Campaign, in which the goal is to win enough regulation games to take part in large tournaments. Over the course of this mode you will draft new players and watch existing ones become better at the game, managing team finances and the players in a meta-game in between actual matches. Also ready for your enjoyment are one-shot tournaments organized by yourself in Competition mode, one-shot games called Exhibition Matches, a Tutorial for new players, and a Story Mode which has you playing with various famous teams over the course of a career as a coach. Lots to do, for sure, and if you like multiplayer there are still many active players online in the matchmaking service. Even if there wasn't though, you could still play over LAN using Hamachi or local hotseat.
Overall I do recommend the game, and I hope when
comes out they attempt to keep it contained to fewer iterations. I doubt they will though based on the last run... The good news is that Chaos Edition is the final version of this run, so if you see it on sale and you like turn based strategy games with a lot of over-the-top sports humor thrown in, you can't go wrong with Chaos Edition. It feature local hot seat play, so even if people stop playing it online you can still play it with your friends in your own home a lot cheaper than you could by buying the actual board game.

The Good:  -  This game is not a bad ~concept~.   Cel shaded female anime character wielding two gun swords, who can shoot, slash, and cast spells you unlock with souls.  Character moves quickly like sonic the hedgehog, so think a quick moving sonic the hedgehog hack and slash that collects souls instead of rings... except the souls look like rings? The Bad:     -  The graphics are not there.  This can be understandable in low budget first game. They are not downright terrible by any stretch of the imagination but with the high speed it makes me almost nauseus.  Feels like spawn rate is just too high / quick on monsters.
-  The cut scenes keep going choppy on my computer.
The Ugly:    - The way you assign the spells and buy the spells to the menu, the system is just kind of clunky and not easy on the eyes.   I think some improvements here with color scheme, easy UI, would really really help this game.
-  Why the music does this horrible garbled thing on my end I still fail to understand.  The music is generally fuzzy but it ups the level to a car radio in a tunnel during battles.

Ctrl-Alt-Delete caused it to just become angry and make it's static loopy metal track go insane on my computer. Do yourself a favor and don't try to kill this program it's one of those that can't be killed and just gets more angry.
