Early Access Watcher Reviews Prominence Poker
Update Version: 14.320.006
Disclosure: This is a free to play game with micro-transactions, so I didn't pay for anything.
Usually when you wish to find yourself at the gambling table, real money is required to buy in. Prominence Poker on the other hand provides a quick and free option to sate your poker fever. With up to six players and a booming online community, it is just a manner of downloading and jumping into a game. Unfortunately, it is never that easy when it comes to gambling simulators and the chips start to fall as soon as they are won.
Prominence already wins several favor points for creating a stylized environment. Everything from the character models to the local have a solid look. Card motions such as dealing and folding are fluid while small touches such as drinking and provocation help embrace the tense mood. Background ambiance is always moving with customers walking in, interacting with items and conversing in the corner of your eye. Sound plays a similar roll with some alright music to complement the scenery. It does the required job of adding to the experience,which keeps the environment interesting enough while waiting for the AI to make their move.
Poker is the name of the game and makes up the entire gameplay. There are plenty of challenges that you can complete during normal play, though I never seemed to make the challenge objectives increase no matter how many times I qualified. There is an excellent tutorial used to explain the controls. Multiplayer only supports casual games right now while single player has a practice and underground mode used sort of like a story mode. Rules are followed faithfully (from what I have seen so far), but the actual gameplay is hindered by some grim issues.
It is difficult to enjoy this high stakes game when the highly annoying bugs start to set in. One such error can be extremely devastating to your progress and occurs right after a hand has been finished. The characters would simply stand or sit in a repeating loop animation while you wait for the game to reset the last hand to continue with the match. I was forced to quit the match and forfeit any chips in order to break the stale, even having to go as far as closing the client on one or two occasions. Commands can also suffer from an identity crisis as the input delay can mistake a check or raise for a fold or a call. It might have to do with the user's internet connection, but it presents a possibly dangerous issue when dealing with a fatal hand.
Optimization is severely needed at a basic level to address some of the performance issues. I understand this is early access, but when it takes as much luck to draw a pair as it does to hope the game will launch without freezing, then you have a problem. Settings do not offer much in the way of customization except for a generic low to ultra graphics bar. Loading times are inherently long from starting the game to waiting for matches to load. Micro-transactions are alive and well too with their main focus revolving around cosmetics and table items that provide experience boosts. These items are bought using in-game currency, but with the inability to finish matches it becomes unlikely for one to gain them naturally.
I have always been a fan of Poker and Blackjack, which is why I was so disappointed to see the issues slowing down the cards. It is very pleasing to watch with some absolutely fitting backgrounds and character models. The small details from the pedestrians playing pool to the motorcycle and laundry machine noises adding some simple ambience. Unfortunately, the cards seem to suffer from bent edges as games can suddenly lock up after hands are completed, leaving the player forced to exit the game and forfeit the chip reward. While it may not seem game breaking, the chips are crucial for online play and the attire found in the micro-transaction shop. It is with a heavy heart I give this one a pass and hope that when I review it in the future the issues are resolved.
Pros
- Stylized visual aesthetic
- Music and sound effects breath immersion
- It is Poker. Card play rules are followed strictly
Cons
- Micro-transactions
- Game breaking issues with completed hands freezing mid game
- Internet connectivity issues greatly halt game flow

A long, long time ago I stumbled across a farm simulator that kinda went under the radar known as Harvest Moon 64. It had the simplified objectives of growing crops and raising barn animals then following with shipping out the products you've attained from doing both. But it's not just the same old, same old, you could participate in town events and even date one of the charming ladies in the area.
Stardew Valley takes all of that and increases every aspect of that game tenfold making it even better.
You're not just some average farmer living off the land, as you make money from the ground up in a similar way, you can also request to have a handful of barns and coops, gather and craft natural objects to build farming tools, invest in a bigger house, go dungeon crawling in a mine for minerals and even gather some neat rewards for increasing levels in friendship from the citizens in your town, and yes you can even marry regardless of gender. Strongly recommend this game to players who like X4, general strategy games or building games and have some patience to see its empire grow.
First of all, the actual game cannot be compared to the Early Access. Much has been improved.
+ Taking care of the development of your planets is a very rewarding experience. There are tons of structures that will definitely affect its growth and specialization.
+ Can play at ultra-high settings with an old video card (GTX 670)
+ An excellent tactical and diplomacy IA. It will squeeze with efficiency every available action.
+ There are so many ways to play the game like industrial producer, warchief, technocratist, expansionist, diplomatic negotiator, and much more.
+ A complete espionage system with many possible actions that also affect diplomacy.
+ Every race takes decisions respecting their natural traits. Even when they should betray you or not.
+ Artistically beautiful and diverse.
+ The game works flawlessly. Never crashed.
+ The game, as it is now, has solid potential for expansion.
+ Every time I want to exit the game it might take me another 10 turns, it keeps you going for some more managing.
+ Some tech researchs will require you to choose one and loose the other, but then you can trade the missing tech with other races via diplomatics.
- The game is complex and could be hard to learn for non fans of the genre. But it's worth to pass the initial complexity.
- Micromanagement can make a difference so this could sometimes make the game longer if you wish to get the most of every turn.
- I miss the possibility to stack several actions for the space factory and scouts.
- When you have to choose between two technologies sometimes is not very clear which one is better on the advanced tree levels (Just a few descriptions that might be improved).
- I didn't get to use often the land troops.
The first time I played the game I was fully focused to win it by warfare, but then my second playthrough was like a tycoon industrial producer, almost zero confrontation and some diplomatics. Then my last one was as technology victory with spies and full diplomacy.
I think this is remarkable. To be able to play the game as you prefer and win it in it's different paths. It has a good internal balance.
I give the game 9.5 as fan of the genre and 8.9 as general gamer.

Okay, first things first, this is what is called an ON-RAILS-SHOOTER.  If you're unsure as to what this means, it's a bit like those "House of the Dead" arcade machines (or "Time Crisis"), where you don't really control where your character - the only movement you have is to duck into cover.  If you're expecting Call of Duty or Battlefield, you'll be disappointed.
It's actually not too bad a game.  The animation and graphics are pretty good (even if the effects for explosions are crap) and the makers have made a decent effort in this area.  Voice acting is fair too.
The cover system in the game is pretty reasonable - not all cover provides total protection from the bad guys.  You may be hidden from most of the enemies, but there may still be one or two that can hit you.
It's not an awful game.  But it could be better.
As I said before, the explosions are rather disappointing - they don't look realistic at all (and no I'm not expecting huge fireballs from grenades).  A little more effort here would make the game a bit more realistic.
You do tend to rely on shooting first-aid kits (for health) and ammo crates (for ammunition) but these are sometime rather difficult to see when half a dozen enemies are shooting at you.  (Ctd...)
There are a few parts of the game where you reach a checkpoint with low health, and then get killed shortly afterwards.  You have the option to re-start from the checkpoint, but this is with the same level of low health, which then makes it tough to progress from there onwards.  In that respect there are bits of the game where you end up re-starting the entire level, and it gets frustrating.
There are also a number of quick-time events (where a key will flash up on the screen and you have to press it quickly) that initiate a particular movement (dodging falling rubble for example).  However, I didn't really feel that they added that much to the game, or even that they were very important.
When balancing all this though, you have to remember - it's only £3.99 at its regular price.  You could put that much into an arcade game and get about ten minutes of fun.  So for less than £4 you're getting a decent full game, but bear in mind that it's not a big-budget title, and adjust your expectations accordingly.
Incidentally, some reviews and discussions mention problems with getting the game to run and/or stability (ie crashes) but I had no problems at all in this respect.
I'd give it six or seven out of ten.

One can fix the bugs, glitches and even contents with enough patches. However, one cannot fix bad gameplay design decisions no matter how much one can pour its money and time. The new Moo is the prime example of the latter.
I had been maintaining weapon mod list thread in the official Moo forum until I gave up on the game.
This game massively suffers in three areas: combat, content, and game design which is terrible.
I am not even going to talk about the tactical battle being real-time instead of turn-based, or staranes instead of free movements, because those issues are actually trivial issues compared to what I am going to discuss here.
No, there is no tl:dr version. You can always choose to not read this.
The fact is that you will probably feel have even less control of the units in the battle than the games like Stellaris and Endless Space. Only game that provides even less interesting and uncontrollable battle is Gal Civ 3, and Gal Civ series was already infamous for such lackluster battle.
You will notice that you really do not have much control on the ship movements in "AI assisted" mode. You could try second option which gives you "total control" of the ships, which is nothing more than making ships basically immobile shooting turrets unless you order it to move. It's really badly implemented.
A good ship movements example would be games like Homeworld, where the capital ships properly make formations (this game's formations are hardly formations except 'bonus' stuffs) while smaller fighters/bombers and smaller ships move around to flank the enemy in fluent way. Despite 2016 game, New Master of Orion provides worse battle than a game that came out in 1999.
Also you will realize that you have no clue just how effective weapons or have no indication whether the weapons mods or special modules are actually working due to lack of the information. Even Stellaris provides a nice during-battle statistics such as damage, accuracy, and other useful stuffs. For Moo, this is very hard to tell due to fast nature of the tactical combat. One of the reasons why my thread was popular was that people have no clue whether the mod is working or not, and had to be manually tested each in optimal conditions.
This is already a fatal flaw, since the Moo is not really famous for 4X elements, but rather robust tactical battles. By throwing away having good tactical battles, the game is already in mediocre category.
Unfortunately, the combat is the least problematic of the three I mentioned.
The game basically lacks contents. Even if NGO and Wargaming implement minor civs back in a good manner, the game still lacks a lot of stuffs missing. There is no governors, no interesting random events, pirates are half-baked, and the research tree feels shorts even if one can consider they have changed it to Civ style from binary choice method.
The main cause of the problem is... well, starlanes. So what happened? Since NGO has chosen to go from free movement to starlane movement, suddenly there was no need for implementing techs like fuel and reactors. The problem is that those fuel and reactors took a large portion of Moo techs. Because NGO has not sufficiently added additional content to fill this void, the overall tech tree feels short and feel something is missing.
Lack of governors and/or general are really missed features and most likely won't be ever implemented since it was NGO's decision to not implement in the first place.
However, even this content issue is not the most damaging issue for this game. Again, people can change their minds and spend money/time to implement said features, or you can just suck it up since the game is a bit cheap, however....
....One just cannot fix design issues. You cannot fix it with time and money when you have a wrong idea. Try make gold from dirt, no matter how hard you try for next thirty years, you cannot transform dirt to gold.
This issue also unfortunately includes UI issues too. Here is copy-paste from my "My verdict on new Moo." thread regarding UI and micro-management issues caused by bad game design.
(Reminder: this article was written in May. For more than 3 months these issues were never addressed.)
Sadly, it turned out that most of these issues were actually intentional(!!) When someone actually asked why there are only 9 ship design slots available, the dev said it's intentional. Just like terrible pollution mechanics, such arbitary restrictions that cause massive increase of micro-management are all intentional (a.k.a "features".)
This is actually a huge step back from the original Moo and Moo2. Even Moo2 had MORE building queue slots than this modern Moo. Yes, Moo2 had 7 queue slots instead of 5. Sad but true.
So, are there any positives? Sure yes, the game itself is very polished (tho Endless Space is about as polished as this game), and super expensive AAA voice acting, and surprisngly competent AI (then again, the game itself is not that complex to begin with) but none of these can overcome such fatal flaws this game has, particually game design issues.
Only saving grace is cheap price. At least Wargaming did not have balls to charge people AAA price for this game. It's only 30 bucks. If you can tolerate it, all power to you. But I'd recommend to spend money elsewhere.

*** FIRST IMPRESSION ***
Crash to desktop simulator. Absolutely disgraceful. "ACU.exe has stopped working" 3 times in an hour.
Was looking forward to playing this one, having played all the previous ACs. Very disappointed.
*** UPDATE ***
Okay, the community has found a workaround that will actually let me play the game I paid for. Disabling the Windows 10 service TabletInputService stops the crashes. Glad it works, but I shouldn't need a community fix to run a game that Ubi is still happy to sell.
On to the review.
AC Unity is the first of the next gen of ACs after the "New World" trilogy (quadrilogy if you count Liberation). It shows. The game is a big step up in terms of graphics. It looks absolutely great, even though it is noticeably more taxing on my machine.
It's not just the graphics though. The immersion is also much better. Revolution era Paris is filled with sounds and people. Crowds sing and jeer. Fights break out. Thieves run from their victims. The first time I was in an angry crowd, it really felt as though I was in rioting city. Wow!
And I must say, though I enjoyed the New World ACs, it's great to be back in a beautiful, massive Old World city. It makes me want to go back to real life Paris or Rome.
Speaking of Rome, the game is in many ways a return to the Ezio run of ACs. Beautiful European city; charming young protagonist; a story about loss and family; a Brotherhood that feels old, entrenched, and mysterious. Wonderful!
Also like in the Ezio ACs... no ship. Now, I loved the ship in 3 and 4, but by the time of Rogue the novelty had worn off for me, so I don't consider this to be a big loss. Your mileage may vary.
Where in 4 and Rogue the ship was your base, in Unity you get the Cafe Theatre. I have to say I found it underwhelming. It looks nice and all, but it never feels alive, or like "home". Apart from a short quest line there is also nothing to do. It doesn't come anywhere near to AC 3's wonderful homestead.
Paris itself is absolutely full of quests though. Many of them are simple assassinations or ally defenses, but there are also a fair number of murder mysteries, and riddles. And of course there are tons of chests (some guarded with a lock picking minigame) and inane collectables. The murder mysteries are a welcome addition, but the rest I found to be mostly rather boring. There are exceptions though, particularly the many coop missions. Those are generally interesting, though I really don't like that the game tries to force multiplayer on me. I like my AC single player, thank you very much!
The story missions are quite good. I especially like that a fair number of them are now elaborate assassinations, complete with secondary objectives for creating distractions, etc. For a game called Assassin's Creed, previous installments focussed remarkably little on assassination.
Surprisingly, Unity finally keeps the Abstergo segments to a minimum, and actually uses them to good effect, namely by letting you experience Paris in a few different time periods. This is a most welcome development. I hope future ACs will do the same.
On to the mechanics.
Free running has been changed a little. You can now indicate whether you want to go up, down, or stay at the same level. It takes a little getting used to, but it makes a lot of difference, especially when traveling down. Mind you, the free running can still make unwanted decisions at times, but I found it to be much improved.
Combat has been changed quite a bit. In Black Flag and Rogue I rarely bothered with stealth, as it was child's play to cut through any number of opponents. In Unity this is no longer the case. In large part this is due to everyone having guns. If you get in a fight with a bunch of opponents, some of them will grab their guns, and things will get ugly quickly.
It also feels as though your combat moves are intentionally a bit slower, which makes it harder to just mindlessly tear through your opponents. (You're still plenty deadly though.)
One thing that I noticed both in combat and while free running, is that the game really wants to complete its animations. Free running starts going up a wall while that's not what you wanted? Well, mash the "down" button all you want. You're not going anywhere until the animation completes. Want to take cover from that guy who just pulled his gun? Well, too bad, you're already doing a finisher on that other guy. It's not an enormous problem, but you'd certainly feel much more like an agile assassin if the game would just let you do moves when you tell it to do those moves.
Abilties have been changed. This time around, you have to buy them through "sync points" that you acquire via story missions, and multiplayer missions. (Non-story singleplayer missions never award them. Again, the game tries to force multiplayer on you.) Many of these cannot be bought until you advance sufficiently in the storyline. Some are specifically for the multiplayer component. After completing the main storyline, I still hadn't unlocked all skills. Not even all the single-player skills.
Apart from the sync points, there are also "creed points" that you get by doing assassin-y things. These give you an assassin rank (which may or may not have some purpose in multiplayer; I honestly don't know) and can be spent to upgrade equipment. Accumulating these points can take a while, and Ubisoft helpfully offers "helix points" that you can buy for real money to circumvent this proces. Yes, this AC has microtransactions... :-(
Gear of course also costs in-game money, and there is a lot of it, some of which is quite pricey. I didn't check, but I'm sure Ubi will let you spend real money to get a bunch of in-game money.
The final currency is "nomad points". These are tied to the companion app for mobile devices. Thankfully, most of the ties to that app have been patched out, but originally, some things in the game would be visible, but unusable unless you used the app. Again, Ubi wants to force you to do things that you probably don't want to. What were they thinking?!
Lastly, I should say something about the bugs. When this game was first launched, it was infamous for them. So much so that Ubisoft gave the first DLC away as an apology. With that sort of history you'd expect them to make sure that the game is now solid a rock. Clearly, with the crashes to desktop that I ran into, they haven't. :-( The in-game bugs have been mostly ironed out, though I did still run into some. (For instance, in one mission I had an optional objective to set a tower on fire. When I entered the tower without lighting the fire, I still burned to death.)
In conclusion, I think Unity is actually one of the better ACs. The main storyline is good, the setting is great, the presentation is impressive, and the mechanics are overall improved. However, Ubisoft really shows disrespect towards their customers.

Best game $0 can buy.  It's hard to describe this game's effect on the mind.   It is a point-and click adventure, but there are certain "triggers" that allow you to progress.   Controls are like old "Myst", and this is definitely a game that makes you feel.  If anyone is familiar with the old NewGrounds video "Lilium", then that's very much the flavor we have here, but with less red.
Serena starts with you, as an unsuccessful author in a cabin you once shared with your lover as a getaway (surprise, her name is Serena), wondering where she's gone.  He can't even remember how she looks at first, and has no idea how much time has passed.  The game progresses by finding "triggers" that serve as reminders.   "Triggers" fire off an ominous sound like a chiming clock, whispered voices, etc.  at which point you can do something you couldn't do before, or see something that has changed.   You find yourself looking at objects you looked at before, or opening drawers and cabinets you couldn't open before, trying to find those memory triggers.
Memories, as they do, push the player character into new moods, and you get a real sense of anxiety and a little fear.  There's one moment of sudden knowing, no matter what you've suspected up to that point, which shoots a chill down your spine...and the game isn't over.  There's more to learn.   When it does end, you'll find you either want to uninstall it and forget it, or you can't help but look once more.
Beautifully tragic storytelling game.  Highly recommended.

Tower Unite is a Lobby Based Minigame/Lobby simulation that resembles much of what my years from 2008-2012 looked like. A lot of Playstation Home. It is also based of the very popular Garry's Mod Tower (Mod) that was produced around sometime in 2015 (I'v never actually gotten to play GMT but i disgress)
Tower Unite offers a few things.
1. Lobby Based Games and Hubs (Houses and the actual main area to my surprise)
2. A sort of.... Oh whats the word... Atmospheric feel to it.
3. Golf with friends except it's actually fun
4. An opertuinity to grow with the community (Or if your like me devlope a gambiling addiction from the In-game casino and lose 30K on the wheel of fortune trying to get a damn pet)
5. A really fun time killer
---
In short Tower United is an amazing little project for the time being, as where it stands as a community game was already enough to make me spend the $15 the second i saw this game on my steam reccomended.
-------
The Good and the Bad about this game
-----
Good
--
- Atmosphericc enviroment
- Well optimised
- Fun to kill time with
- Great to♥♥♥♥♥♥around with friends.
- A very vocal community and developers
- Community help! (This came as a bit of a shocker to me but you can actually assist them with the creation of this game using their thingy page (forgot the name))
- An experience that can let you forget about our War ravaged world for a while (Rest in peace those who lost their lived in London and Manchester)
----
Downsides
SideNote: I will not be going lightly on this seeing as the game has existed for over a year. I still love it though but these are my personal quarrels.
---
- Loading into a Main City (Hub) Takes atleast 1+ minute (With a goood internet connection AND Harddrive)
- The Bowling minigame has a hard time registering Pin hits (YES IM UNHAPPY ABOUT THIS CUZ BOWLING IS FUN!)
- Lack of customization in the way of clothes (I'm sure this complaing will be obselete in due time)
- Awkwardly enough that amount of mic screaming and racist kids (Then again i dont expect a once G mod gamemode to  NOT have this but jesus)
- Some of the game modes are just not attracting or are just dull (Looking at you virus)
- The object placement. please do not get me started on this. I  spent a good 20 minutes trying to place a fridge the right way and had to actually give up
- Object Rendering seems to be slow at times.
- Lack of general Gameplay customization
- Some of the character Models bug out (Looking at you milk carton)
- This isnt a con but more a complaint. The lack of explorable area. I mean if your not counting the tower the Main area is actually pretty small.
------

Is it good? Yes, yes it is. Do i love it? No, no i don't. Do i like it? Yes, yes i do! Do i regret spending the $15 the second i saw this game? No and hopefully i never will.

Overall this was an amazing game & I can't wait to see what this company does next.

+ Immensely charming
+ Beautiful art style and music
+ A few puzzles make you scratch your head
- Fairly short (~3 hours for a complete run)
Amanita Design bring us yet another point & click/puzzle game in the form of Botanicula, a very cute and charming story of 5 friends trying save the tree on which they live from a menacing corruption. Along the ride one must solve puzzles using the different abilities of the 5 characters.
The main strength of the game is how beautiful the art is. Everything seems hand-drawn and the animations reflect that, sometimes making movements very cut-out-ish. The music and the sound effects both complement that with very natural sounding tunes (as in involving individual sounds and hums rather than just musical instruments) and cute sounds from the environment (for example, when many different-sized bugs start humming a specific sound, the largest ones obviously humming in deep basses).
The puzzles are relatively simple on average, yet some of the later ones prove to be more complicated than you might imagine for what may strike one as a kid's game. What is unique about Botanicula's puzzles is that it is fun to see what will happen if you click on the wrong character. One problem that I have with the characters though, is that they seem like one entity, meaning it is hard to differentiate them based on their personalities.
This brings me on to how short the game is. It arguably contains 5 areas, each one longer than the one before it (which makes sense because you are moving your way down the tree, where the branches are progressively longer). The objective is to pass an obstacle blocking your passage to the next area by solving puzzles in the current area. There are many optional puzzles and things to click on which add to the completion rate on a playthrough, which does give access to additional content near the end based on how high it is. Even with that the game feels like one that should be completed in one playthrough, and, just like most point & clicks, there is no replay value in the game unless one did not achieve 100% completion.
All in all, Botanicula offers a short, but very charming and beautifully simple experience. Its simplicity can be both an upside and, at times, a downside.

Better than the first one, there's 90% chance you´ll like XCOM2 if you are lucky and if you like turn based strategy games. Now if you are boring and think 90% is a pretty high probability chance of something happening, you might be disappointed. XCOM2 defies mathematics as never before, and it'll take your whole notion and understanding of probability to another level. There are 2 circumstances of probabilities here:
1: When you have under 50% chance to accomplish something, the game hides from you that it's not 50% of 100%, it's 50% on top of a hidden probability between 1%-50% you can't see. This number is chosen based on how angry you are. As you get angrier, your chances get lower and lower and more losses you're going to take in the most humiliating ways until you become angry enough and stop playing and maybe destroy your computer in the process. You might decide to play it thinking: "Oh great i'll play this game and have so much fun". That's where you are being naive. XCOM2 plays you aswell, in a very sadistic way.
2: The second circumstance is when you think you're > 50%. Again, the game hides from you some information. There's actually a 50% cap, that's the highest chance for you to succeed ever. But in order to try to not make you not so much angry, the game lies to you showing sometimes that you've like 95%-99% of hitting an enemy, but it's all a big lie. When you realize and it's too late, you're stuck in a samsara like sadistic wheel being played by the game, becoming angrier by every stupid play you do - and you'll do a lot - while making this sadistic algorithm happier seeing your frustrations.
So yeah I recommend this game for a change of pace. You can never win in XCOM, not even when you finish  the game (check the story behind what happened between the first XCOM and this one). It's nice to have this feeling to throw my monitor out of the window often in a while.

Had I been reviewing Altitude four years ago when it first came out (or even in the year or two after its release), I would give it my highest recommendation. Now, however, I can only barely recommend this game.
The game itself is fantastic. It's a 2D, side-view, multiplayer dogfighting game. The controls are tight, the gameplay intense, and the game plays so quickly (rounds last only a few minutes) that it induces "just one more game" syndrome. To keep things from getting too repetitive, there are variety of plane types and boosts that can be earned through an XP system. There are also a number of game types - of particular note is the "ball" game type where players attempt to carry and shoot a ball into the opposing team's goal without being shot down in the process. Scoring the goal is just as exciting as it is in any sports game.
So why can I no longer wholehearted recommend the game? Well, it has encountered the fate that any multiplayer-focused game that isn't as popular as, say Counterstrike, has met: lack of players. There are very few people playing the game now and the few active players left are INSANELY good. Even someone like myself who was half-way decent as a ball runner finds respawning to happen way too frequently.
That leaves two options for enjoying the game: either skirmish against the bots or round up some friends. As with most games of this ilk, playing with and against bots is okay but not a perfect substitute for live players. Perhaps the best way to enjoy the game at this point is to round up a few friends who also own it and host a private game.
Altitude is a great game whose lifespan has run its course. I recommend it for a group of friends or if it goes on Steam sale again (not extremely likely given its age) and creates an influx of new players. Otherwise, I regrettably recommend passing on a game that not enough people enjoyed.

As someone who runs a private server for a few friends every once in a while (when we feel like playing), Altitude is an easy-to-play, easy-to-setup game that we can jump in and out of very quickly. It's very fun for brief stretches of time, and the server options are customizable to favor both the experienced and the new.
In a sense, Altitude's multiplayer reminds me of the feeling of old-school FPSes with the openness of maps and hectic gameplay. The flight and speed of the varying ships have a bit of a learning curve, but once you find that ship that's "just right" for you, you'll either feel like a aerial master or a bomber of death.
The levelling system with perks do lock away some interesting abilities, but for the most part, we haven't seen an issue where the perks themselves overpower players. Thankfully, the only real determining factor is a person's piloting skill. Learn to fly, and you can get into this game without a problem.
Keep gameplay short, as playing it for long stretches of time will wear you down.

Unlike most free-to-play games, Serena is absolutely, totally free. All of the game's features are available for free. No microtransactions, no unaccessible game content. The game is a nice, short, and sweet experiment -- a good concept for something bigger and better. Unfortunately, one is left with wanting more of everything and feeling dissatisfied with what was given. The plot is short and experienced almost exclusively through the main character's own voice. I was hoping for a more dynamic story, or at least a more meaningful conclusion. A better and bigger game of the same type would need a very deep and dynamic story to keep players interested considering the great lack of depth in the setting.
The graphics are very basic -- good enough for a small laptop, but feel lacking on a larger screen. It has a quality that is reminiscent of Myst, or some of the other mid-90's point-and-click adventure games. Unsurprisingly, one is left wanting better graphics. In addition, the world is very small and that also leaves me wanting more to explore. The audio is unsurprisingly no different than the other game features. It's not good, not terrible, just plain ol' sound -- no high points, no demerits.
At the present, the replay value is essentially zero. But considering that it's totally free, one cannot complain too much about that. I wouldn't even pay 50 cents to play the game, but for free? It's a neat little ride and could be a decent litmus test for a similar, but better developed game in the future.

Another day, another arcade-style game.
This time it's a rail shooter, closest comparison is definitely the Namco series Time Crisis. That's a good model to crib from, as most of the games in that series are great. Unfortunately, Heavy Fire: Afghanistan misses the mark.
This is going to come off as a really unfair comparison review. I don't care for writing these, since all too often they boil down to: "Why play this? When you can play this instead?" Also, what's the alternative? The PS2 has quite a few of the Time Crisis games, but you need the console, the games, the Guncon controllers, and a suitable TV. There's also the PS3 compilation pack that includes a couple Crisis games, but you still need the system, the games, a couple of Move controllers, etc etc. HF:A is a game you probably already own via a bundle, so let's try and make the most of it.
The biggest issue I have with the game is the length. It's about 2 hours long. Content is king but when it comes to arcade games, brevity is the soul of excellence(???). The 2 hour play-time involves a lot of padding. Each of the 12 stages is more of what you'd expect from a rail shooter. Go to an area, shoot all of the enemy soldiers, move onto the next one. This repeats over and over again with hardly any variation. The bad-guys are in different locations, but little else changes. Arcade rail-shooters generally take around 15-25 minutes to complete, and yet they still do a lot more in that shorter span of time. There are different types of enemies, some are on a variety of vehicles, others attack from all sorts of angles. Boiled down to the basics, rail-shooters hinge on the shooting gallery aspect, where your accuracy and reflexes are what keep you alive. It's how you dress everything up that keeps them interesting. HF:A doesn't do this often enough, despite how long it takes to complete.
That's not to say HF:A is nothing but soldiers firing away. Every now and then there's a guy with a knife, a heavy-gunner on a pick-up, a couple BTRs, and a Hind. Unfortunately the biggest different between the latter three adversaries is the number of bullets they take to destroy. All you have to do is make sure to get behind cover when you hear the machinegun rev up. Part of the problem I suppose is that this game is very loosely based on reality. I can't go into it expecting things like cyborgs, a final boss that's actually a brain in a jar surrounded by laser cannons, a plot to destroy America with a satellite, etc. Still, there seems like there could be a lot more variety. Give some of those soldiers different guns and have them employ different tactics. Most of the time all the enemies do is run to a particular spot and start firing away, only occasionally ducking behind cover. Something as simple as having some enemies running while shooting at you would have added a lot to the game.
Another problem with HF:A is that it isn't quite sure what it wants to be. The guns you unlock come with larger clips and by the end you've got an LMG and going Rambo on the soldiers. Rail-shooters usually fall into two camps by this point. You've got titles like Virtua Cop and Time Crisis where you're given pistols that require constant reloading, and then on the opposite end of the spectrum there are games such as L.A. & N.Y. Machineguns, Space Gun, and Rambo (the somewhat recent Sega arcade release). HF:A tries to do both (sorta like Time Crisis 3 & 4) but it never really works. For most of the game you just end up feeling like you're over-equipped, so there's no strategy. It's unfortunate that making the player-character into a 1-4 man army would have stretched the narrative far too thin. A game where you walk into an enemy base and destroy everything in minutes would have been far more exciting. Soldiers are pouring in so you gotta shoot them all, then the tanks roll in, maybe shoot some jets out of the sky. Basically this game would be turned into a next-gen Operation Wolf.
So this definitely turned out to be a comparison review. It feels like all I did was mention a bunch of games you'd be better off spending your time with. You could probably play through at least four of them in the time it would take to get through Heavy Fire: Afghanistan, and they'd all be more entertaining.

TLDR: 6/10 - controls are a nightmare, looks beautiful, storyline is AC staple with fun RPG elements.
I bought Unity some time ago but unfortunately gave up on it due to poor optimisation - I found it incredibly unsatisfactory to play. However, I came back with a new GFX card and Unity has been patched beyond. So would I recommend it?
If you're a fan of the series and relatively familiar with the mechanics, then yes.
Just jumping in to AC? This will frustrate the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you.
I only stuck with it all the way through because I enjoy the franchise. The controls in Unity are frankly abysmal - both in their construction and their response. I found myself fighting more with the button combinations than I was the AI. I'd get stuck in cover, furiously trying to free myself as I was spotted. I'd spend way more time than I was planning scaling the wall/foliage/fencing around windows, because the transition from wallclimbing to window-entering is eye-ball bleedingly bad.
You die. Alot. Even for an AC game. But it's mostly because of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mechanics. The AI in Unity is vastly superior to previous incarnations of AC and the combat system has been tweaked so it's more challenging - and that I'm not going to complain about. After turning into Murder McPirateface in Blackflag (Which I loved because it's the best Pirate Sim ever) it was more captivating feeling like I was about to get one-shotted by a sword impale or peppered with gunshot.
While I'm on gunshot - the game gives you zero (ZERO) prep on how to deal with enemies with guns. Which is pretty much every enemy. You will learn through pain of...everything...to pay attention to the heads up display and the small aiming reticles that pop up around your body.
So what's good about Unity? For one, since the patch, Paris feels ALIVE. Like, realy alive. Hundreds of character models ons creen at a time, waving flags and singing songs. Ubisoft have made one hell of an effort to make you feel like you're participating in the French Revolution. It *will* murder the hell outta your rig if you haven't invested in hardware. But it does look and feel amazing.
Another massive plus for me was the gearing up process. I was really disappointed that they didnt keep the same gearing detail and quality for Syndicate because it added a refreshing RPG element to the AC franchise. Yes, there are microtransactions, and unless you wanna grind like hell for the Legendary gear, you may find yourself tempted.
And grinding in AC: Unity is no longer a simple process - in the past, it appears the best source of income (apart from being a limited property magnate) was doing co-op rifts. Except the online community is virtually non-existent in Unity now. Only once did I get paired with another assassin.  Which is really disappointing because although you CAN manage most of the rifts intended for more players on your own with a bit of patience, there are some rifts you just straight up cant practically do as a lone player.
As mentioned before, the scenery is beautiful and the characters are well rendered (personalities not so much). The storyline is your standard AC conspiracies with a bit of back-and-forth with the Templars and Assassins with some shades of grey thrown in for good measure. You do get some interesting mini-levels that throw you into various other time periods including turn of the 20th century Paris, WW2 and Medieval times - but they're far and few between, revisited only as a grindy mini-game.
Would I recommend this? Definitely, as a playthrough in the AC saga.
Will it frustrate the ever living sh*t out of you? Yes. Yes it will.

First, I'd have left a negative review regardless of bethesda's recent moves..
Fallout 4 is the literal definition of an ocean of content with the depth of a puddle..
It looks big and complex on the cover, thanks to the good level/environment design and gimmicks, but really everything feels lackluster and underwhelming in this game. It also provide essentially no new additions over earlier entries in the franchise beyond gimmicks (settlement building, "heavily" customizable weapons) which matter very little in the end.
The plot is literally and frustratingly so, a rehash of fallout 3's plot, without the enclave, and the fun stuff. and its absolutely terrible.. The characters, locations, enemies, and even most weapons are dull for the most part. And I found characters getting duller and duller the more I knew about them.. Story missions(well sidequests too..) feel like chores/filler and mostly consists of really dull shooting galleries for the most part..
I can't really pinpoint what differs from FNV and Fallout 3, but it seems combat got a whole lot more boring. (Gunplay has improved significantly though! Feels a lot better than in vanilla FNV and Fallout 3.)
The player dialogue is braindead, generic and boring. The delivery of the voice actors does nothing to improve on that. It actually may make things worst more often than not.. It often attempts to be funny and fails very hard at it..
The dialog options are poorly labeled, and miseleading, and even though there are "choices" all dialog paths seems to lead to the same replies/results in many cases.. Its as if, they gave player dialogue choices just for the sake of it.
As for the core gameplay, its very similar to Fallout 3's, with a lot of things that FNV improved on left out, except RPG mechanics have been severly gutted/crippled.
Levelling up doesn't feel good at all.. You don't feel like you're progressing. The perk system is essentially not fun.. A huge portion of the perks are somewhat useless. So you'll often end up investing all your perk points into a few select perks throughout all your playthroughs..
Crafting is a grind. And you literally have to haul all the junk you stumble on to craft anything wothwhile. It wouldn't have been such an issue if the inventory system wasn't as bad as it is right now.. Customizing firearms and energy weapons is literally a gimmick.. You can essentially make tweaks to weapons, so they can be used in other niches.. But in practice, if you say make a pipe rifle sniper rifle, you'll find its a waste of ammo, because the actual hunting rifle is better for the job anyways. Same with say the assault rifle or the combat rifle, the most useful mod for a given weapon is the one that just improve on the base weapon, not those that attempt to change its role.. For instance, a slow firing, higher damage per bullet, long range assault rifle is pointless and wastes ammo.. While if you go all-in on firing speed and damage(you can actually have both..) you get something a lot better. But this has for effect of essentially making a lot of modifications useless..
AKA, a lot of the weapon mods that can be made are just not worth it at all..
Also, you're forced to do base building at least once in every playthrough for a really dumb plot device..
Base building is very bad for the most part.. It doesn't even matter how well you build your settlements, they'll always get attacked and can't defend themselves even if you'd setup an array of 60 rocket launcher turrets.. Plus, often the enemies will spawn inside the settlement's walls.. which means defended choke points and walls were kinda useless in the first place.. Also npcs settlers just don't want to cooperate.. They often bug out and don't do their assigned job..
Considering the price was lowered to something less obscene than the original $80 CAD they were asking at launch, I'd recommend to buy this only on sale, and only if you intend to use mods to improve the experience and plot isn't a big thing for you. Otherwise, you might want to avoid it.

I'll try to be as thorough as I can, because I was as confused as many of you might be: I purchased this game off steam, and with the full campaign behind me, along with 67 hours of gametime, I have experienced 0 bugs or glitches, as reported by many of the reviewers here.
Now, to clarify, many of the bugs that originally made the game "unplayable" have probably been patched by now. And it could be due to the fact that I'm running the game on an Nvidia GTX 1080 Ti, along with 30GB of RAM, and an i7 (7700K) Processor. or I could have just lucked out and got a bugless copy.
That being said, however, the game itself is stunning for a multitude of reasons:
1) It is perhaps the most visually stunning Assassin's Creed game, along with Black Flag, and I found myself often times simply watching my character move and marvelling at the fluidity. I've been running the game at Max settings with a locked frame rate of 162.
2) The story is genuinely engaging, and nails all elements of comedy, intrigue, adrenaline, and continuation of the Assassin's Creed storyline. Anyone who's been following game-to-game will enjoy the story.
3) It introduces new mechanics that expand the playability and challenge veteran players. The combat, and stealth, this time around, seemed more challenging (requiring more focus)
There's more, but honestly, it just feels great to play. That being said, all other reviewers have valid points, so to anyone considering buying this game, I would say it's a 50/50 shot and you should hope you're lucky like I was.

Hard to recommend a game in which none of the major problems of the first iteration are fixed.  And I'm saying this as a huge fan of the original original XCOM (1994).
The game is theoretically two games: 1)  Managing XCOM as an organization and 2)  Fighting squad based tactical missions to further your organzation and to degrade and ultimately destroy the alien threat.
The major problem is that the meta game (the stuff between the squad based combat missions) is the only aspect of the game that you can truly lose but it can't be lost by mismanaging the organization, it can only really be lost by losing the combat portion of the game.  If that sounds paradoxical, well, yes you're on to what I'm saying.  To clarify: you theoretically can put 20 hours into this game only to be sent back to the starting screen and told to start over.  But that never happens because the only way for that to happen is to lose a squad of your best troops and since that is so avoidable by loading your game continuously that's what the game becomes: a load-my-game-festival.  It's totally normal to load a mission 10 or 20 or more times in order to complete it with minimal losses; minimal losses that are effectively required due to the nature of the game.
The range of your solders ranges from rookies (I can't even throw a grenade across a street to save my life) to super solder extreme of blasting off multiple headshots across the map with over 100% accuracy.  The game scales in difficulty to require you to continue to upgrade your solders and have them keep pace by leveling up making the entire game hinge on the squad combat and the fact that there is only one way to win it: by having super-solder max level characters that you can't afford to lose.
And calling it squad based combat is a bit generous.  That would require the enemy to think on some degree of par with the player but that isn't what the game is about.  There isn't any overall strategy to what the enemy employs, you proceed in a map triggering various points that alerts squads to your presence, but they are not, in their entirity, acting as a united force trying to stop you.  Also the shot calculator is HORRIBLE, that is the RNG effects are truly horrid.  How % are determined is almost as bad with things like flanking and firing from multiple positions not having the effects that they should toward chance-to-hit numbers.
They could do a lot to fix the next iteration of this game by removing the load/save feature making all deaths permenant, but then counter balancing that with removing the total loss position of the metagame.  Meaning that a very bad mission result would push you back in progress but not expect you to start over clamoring for the load button.  Rookie recruits are near trash in this game so next bring the bottom level ranked troops up in quality and the upper ranks down to create a more realistic and useful range of what human beings are capable of.  Next change the squad based combat to actually allow for multiple strategies.  If I want to throw a bunch of meat against a mission and sustain heavy casualities then the penality shouldn't be losing the entire game but rather some other type of penalty to morale, funding, etc..  Fixing this would do a tremendous amount to fixing the core problem of this game that prevents most people that have no nostaliga factor for this game to get on board.
Also the dialogue is the most expository garbage I've heard in a long time.  The entire writing team should be fired and blacklisted from working on any other games.  It was Transformers 5 level awful.

Some time ago I wrote a very negative review during the early alpha of this game. But many things have changed since then, and it is fair that I write a new one now.
The interface in this new MOO is really similar to its predecessors. It has, however, some new tabs that are a delight for the macromanegement fans. The Empire Tab, that permits you to change your taxes, check all your colonies' production, research and food generation, as well as checking in a glimpse what each one is producing. The diplomatic menu is simple and intuitive, as well as the ship production one (but I'll go in detail about this one later). However I find that the fleet menu is useless -I literally could not find an space factory using it!
Graphics are beautiful and work very well in the MOO game style. While they are not excellent, they are pretty enough to make your MOO experience appealing. The planet zoom looks gorgeous, with the colony lights, aerospace traffic, etc.
The soundtrack follows the same path: It's not a OST that I would listen normally, but it works fairly well with the game itself.
The ship design is here this time, and it works fairly well. However I noticed that it has some problems; more particularly, your own designs may not work at all if you auto resolve the battles. In one example, if you design a missile specialist ship to stay behind the main combat line, you may find in auto resolve that your ship will be the first to die -as its defense values will be very low-.
This may force you to control your own ships directly.
On the other hand, while the ship designer is quite easy to use, it REALLY needs a filter system for the weapons and systems.
All right, now I can say this:
. Previously all diplomatic stuff would go like "give me that or I get grumpy". This time I found more interesting things: alliance requests, allies driving you to war against another ally, requests to stop colonizing, and many ways to influence your relationship with the AI. Not a really complex mechanic, but yet complex enough to make you consider the diplomatic impact of your actions. "If I ally the terran, would the humans get angry at me?".
The spy system is very nice, indeed. You get your spies, infiltrate them in an enemy planet, and start performing your operations. The problems I see: First, it is absurdly difficult to accomplish a "3rd level" operation. Even with the darlok and specialized in spying, I manage to accomplish maybe 3 out of 200 failures.
I also see that the AI will never kill one of your spies if they catch it. No matter if you are at full war, they will always deport the spy back. Thank you, AI!
The diplomatic consequences of spying are really something to keep in mind. It could literally change a relation from "friendly" to "Cautious" in just one turn.
And FINALLY they work properly!
Basically, you can either full control the ships yourself or let the AI assist you. And the AI this time is smart enough! Ok, it uses pretty pre-programmed movements -battleships and bigger ships to the front, while frigates and destroyers try to flank the enemy-. But the important bit is that it really works, creating space battles that are realistic enough to enjoy.
Still, the cinematic camera is very bad.
Previously I said that this game was not worth being part of the MOO saga. Proudly I retract my words: After the last changes, Master of Orion is a very good relaunch for this franchise, and I recommend it to any 4x fan.

I've always thought on-rails shooters were kind of fun, but this game made me question whether they'll ever have a place on PC. It isn't a bad game, but at the same time, it's hard to come up with compliments. If you go into this game expecting a really simple point and click Muslim killing simulator that will last you a couple of hours, I doubt you'll be disappointed.

This is a kind of late review as I've stopped playing the game awhile ago. Trove was a game I really ended up loving. I gave it a chance even after I swore I wouldn't play another Trion game due to what happened to Archeage. I tried to get a better understanding of things by having a conversations with people as to what actually happened behind the scenes, and that is what led to me giving Trove a chance. I've put over 300+ hours into Trove. I think the gameplay is very casual and a lot of fun. I really enjoyed collecting pets and items as well as other features the game had to offer. One of the best things about Trove is it had a really solid free to play business model for the longest time. Unfortunately that changed during at the beginning of 2016 where things really started to get pushed away from the model many people loved and now it really feels like you need a premium subscription to do things you once enjoyed without it.
I understand that Trion needs to make money as it crucial to the continued development of the game but I feel that some of their changes weren't good ones that pushed the game pretty far away what the original business model that made it such a great success on steam.
Playing the game so long with the original business model and then adding such a major change hurt my view of the game as I think it did with many players.
I may come back to Trove later on just to say hello to old friends and possibly give it another go because it is a fun game.. if my view changes if I do, I will definitely give it a new review.

12 Labours of Hercules is a time management game where Hercules is tasked to complete a set of goals to proceed to the next level in order to save Megara, his wife. To do this, he has workers and mythical creatures at his disposal.
There are 40 levels in total, of which 4 are boss levels. The normal levels consist of lanes, filled and lined with resources to collect. Collected resources are used for the goals or to construct buildings such as farms, workshops and shops. Each of these buildings grants a bonus (for instance, a resource every few seconds) and can also be upgraded to increase said bonus. In later levels, players can also activate temporary perks such as more movement speed for the workers or increased resource gathering.
This game is played against the clock; in order to complete the levels with the maximum three stars strategy and prioritization are involved, especially on the later levels, as there are usually multiple ways to complete the goals.
In between regular gameplay there are also the aforementioned boss levels where Hercules fights mythical creatures with his sling shot.
Personally, I like the art style and level design of the game but cared little for the “story” and even less for the looping music to the point where I played with the sound disabled.
All in all, I recommend this game as the core gameplay is well put together and provides enough challenge for those who want to ace all levels.

So for starters, if you were looking for an RPG, look elsewhere, because Fallout 4 is a terrible RPG. It would be more accurrate to call it a First Person Shooter with RPG and base-building elements. If you want an actual RPG, then you'd be better off getting Fallout: New Vegas, a quite frankly better written and in some aspects, better designed game than this one. In fact, I'm going to be making constant comparisons between FO4 and FO:NV during this entire review.
Writing wise, FO4 is WEAK. Rather than give you a (mostly) blank slate of a character so you can play them however you wish like in FO:NV, you are forced into a singular role depending on which character you choose during character creation. You are either a veteran soldier or a law student, but either way, you are married, you have a son, FEEL INVESTED.
Speaking of which, Bethesda needs to stop with this forced tutorial malarkey. In fact, forced tutorials in general need to
. Yeah, the character creation process is kind of fun the first one or two times, but it wears off so very quickly, and eventually you just wish you could just skip the whole thing, especially when it forces you through babby's first dungeon for dumb ugly babbys. Contrast with FO:NV, where right after you finish creating your character you are free to do whatever within five minutes or so.
And then there's the dialogue system which just flat out feels dumbed down for consoles, with many of the great options from FO:NV, and even FO3 are just gone, with speech checks depending only on your character's charisma, rather than relevant stats and skills.
The MC being voiced  can kind of detract from the Role Playing experience. I do honestly wish there were options for different voices for each sex, maybe with different accents like in the Saint's Row series.
Character progression is... weird. The new perks system keeps higher levels of the same perk locked behind arbitrarily high level restrictions and stat requirements, with each stat having ten associated perks. Sadly, gone are the days of speccing a character for pure stealth and glibness in just a couple of levels, or massive numbers of quirky perks that can synnergize together to make certain weapon types even more powerful. Coupled with no actualy level cap, and you will likely eventually end up grabbing most if not all perks, and leveling all stats to maximum. If you can survive the enemy types that level up with you, becoming nigh-unstoppable bullet sponges that deal insane amounts of damage with each hit.
Oh, and then there are the Settlements. The controls are crap, building things is extremely finnicky as where you can and cannot place items is arbitrary at best and ridiculous at worst, not to mention the lack of snappping on certain items, and Preston's constant radiant quests are so mind bogglingly annoying that I wish that there was an option to just sent a team of other minutemen to solve some of these.
...seriously, it just comes across as tedious babysitting. We need the option to get someone else to deal with these settlements in constant need of help. Or maybe even with sufficient defense, they never need help again.
The DLCs were largely disappointing, mainly being additions to the already very flawed settlements system. Again, compare with FO:NV, which had four amazing packs which actually added to the story and gave new areas to explore.
Now granted, a number of these issues can be resolved with mods, but that brings me to the big issue here.
Yeah, you probably knew this was coming since nearly every single review written for this game for the last several weeks, but that is just how badly put together this abomination of business practice is. Now before I begin, it's not the paid mods (and no, Mr. Hines. They are NOT mini-dlcs, no matter how ofter you try to push that term) I have a problem with exactly. The issues I have with this system are as follows:
-

Now considering that 750CC is about 10CAD, leaving each credit at about 1 1/3 cents, each pipboy skin is 66 cents, power armor paint jobs are 132 cents, and each new weapon or armour is around 4 dollars.
Meanwhile, F0:NV's Gun Runner's Arsenal, an actual DLC pack with well over twenty new weapons cost around five dollars when it originally came out. And you are trying to pass these off as "mini-dlc" when they are this ludicrously expensive? Really?
-
Generic skins, single weapons and single sets of equipment and a furniture set. Nothing big enough to be even remotely considered "mini-dlc", and again, painfully overpriced.

Fallout 4 is a terrible RPG game, pure and simple.
Character customisation is reserved only to your body and face, your backstory is already decided and your stat decisions make no impact on the game in the long term. Gone are the skill points that have been familiar in Fallout since its inception, and gone are any meaningful character choices. The only choices the players gets which hold any meaning is when you are pigeonholed at the end of the game into deciding which faction to support. Except they're all garbage.
Speech challenges are reduced to very uncommon one-liners which almost always serve just to net you bonus caps (in a game where you never need to spend a single cap) and which do nothing to help advance the plot of the game.
The gameplay is improved if you like FPS but it is only a surface-level change; the engine is outdated and has been jury-rigged to run the game on better graphics than was ever intended, resulting in a game full of bugs, tearing and terrible optimisation. The level of freedom of gameplay in Fallout 4 is lacking also with a true melee build being impossible due to flying enemies or turrets that live on rooftops. By the end of the game (due to the infinite leveling system) every character build turns out the exact same and the combat runs the same way in every encounter.
The plot is lame, cliched and terribly paced. How is one supposed to care about their missing son if the search is constantly interrupted by settlements needing help and stints of weapon crafting? No character holds significant depth, and if they do they are never given enough time to actually explore it fully. Countless lore is destroyed by Fallout 4 in Bethesda's mad race to pump out a "Skyrim with Guns!" rather than a true Fallout sequel.
I'm certain I've left out a dozen more reasons why Fallout 4 is the worst non-spinoff Fallout game but the other reviews should speak for itself. The one saving grace that I always held in my mind about Fallout 4 was that the incredible modding community was sure to find a way to salvage this trash-heap of a game.
But then Bethesda introduced mods for console, which were often plagiarised from PC mods. And stopped even attempting to care about the community by ignoring their copyright claims. And then introduced paid mods where you pay $5 for an armoured crab. And then stole ideas from the modding community to fuel their DLCs.
Bethesda is a money-grubbing studio as almost all studios are these days. But Bethesda didn't even try to hide it. GJ Todd Howard, I'll be sure to buy the new Dwemer Crab Armour on my Switch!

What can I say about Xcom 2...
Firstly, a question to the reader: Have you played Xcom: Enemy Unknown?
If you have, this game plays similarly, but different in a way.
How might you ask?
Firstly, the AI is more stepped up thank xcom:EU. They will go to flank you, use explosives more if you bunch up.
Secondly, your on a race against the clock. The aliens work on a project to wiperform you out, and advance their tech.
Thirdly, you have different skills, abilities for the most part compared to enemy unknown. For instance, your 4 basic classes are a gunslinger, a class that can focua more on pistols or sniper depending how you  want then to play,
Your specialist, who is a hybrid between a hacker and your healer with long range healing and hacking abilities,
The Ranger,  who focuses on close quarters with both a sword and shotgun, and finally grenadier, which instead  of in EU, you had a rocket launcher, you now have a gremade launcher, with a heavy machine gun.
There are other classes such as the psy operative, and one from a DLC which is OP, but besides that, those are your base classes.
Gameplay wuse this game can be derpy. I've had soldiers on many occasions go to shoot an enemy, veer their riflexible to the right like their aiming into oblivion, then snap back to the target when they shoot a round. The ragdolls are really goofy in this game as well, as sometimes they'll get stuck in a wall or go flying offscreen into nowhere to a simple frag nade. And there's the ocasional "oh there's an enemy walking past this wall that I can't see through, let's shoot him through the wall."
Besides that, the game allows you to tailor the looks and way your soldier's play to the way you wishould. Full mod support through the steam workshop allows you to add custom classes, looks, enemies, etc to your game.
As well, if you plan on getting this game, if I may recommend a few things:
1. Wait till  august 29th 2017, the new dlc with all new 2-3 badass new classes comes out, and you are going to want them.
2. Buy the DLC when you buy the game, but for the love of christ don't buy the anarchy dlc it's garbage.
3. Once you install the game with the alien huntees DLC,  avoid the 3 skull on sticks investigation mission till late game else you will regret it.
4. In missions, scout nearby enemies before you launch ambushes. Knowing what your up against will help late game and getting used to it now will help.
In overall rating. For overall I give xcom 2 after dlc a 7/10. There are bugs that could be pathe but the game is enjoyable no doubt.

A unique masterpiece just like Machinarium in the sense that it has the distinct Amanita touch and overall similar gameplay elements. The hint system is gone, but a flawlessly executed minimap is here as a welcome addition. The atmosphere is quite different but just as captivating, and exploration is even more rewarding, since this time there are little in-game collectible cards (not Steam trading cards though) which are obtainable through interacting with the curious creatures inhabiting the game world. The puzzles are a bit more local this time as the game is broken into different sections, which has its up and downsides, since there are no items you need to have from the previous sections, but you also cannot wander back freely.
Overall, I think the game is a bit easier than Machinarium, but completionists still face quite a challenge since some achievements-getting opportunities are easily overlooked, and casual players won't get stuck in complex puzzles leaving them free to explore the very alive world of Botanicula.

Summary: Don't let the low price fool you, this game is ok; I'd give it a B-. If you ever want a break from the usual modern FPS format, this is an option that's just as entertaining, but in its own way. This game challenges the player; not always fairly, but usually so. The health meter is a welcome change from being able to recharge health by waiting under cover. Your weapons will sound a bit silly, but they get the job done. This is a game with a realistic setting, non-stop action (except for the shooting ranges) and despite its low price, it's visuals are as breathtaking as any modern game.
First, let's talk about the choice of genre: the rail shooter. It's an older style, but age in itself doesn't determine quality. We live in a time where first person shooters are legion, and most operate very similarly. If you ever want a break from that, one option is to try an older style. Would it be more exciting in an arcade cabinet? Yes, and if you tried playing this with an Xbox controller you would have a horrible experience. But as you get past the middle of the game, it gets tough, and if you want to beat the game, you couldn't do it in an arcade cabinet. A mouse and keyboard are the best way to go for this. If you spray and pray in this game, you will get hit even if you kill the enemy. But if you take advantage of the precision a mouse provides, you can get out from cover and have a fair chance of killing him without taking a hit. The difficulty may shock and tick you off if you're used to games where you can press a button to stick to cover and shoot at your enemy without exposing yourself, which is no challenge at all. In my opinion, a quality shooter of any kind is one where you have to make your own cover and get out from behind it to engage an enemy, and this game fills that requirement.
And yes, I said difficulty. Some reviewers claim that this game is as easy as Whack-A-Mole. Maybe they're the god-like, all-day snipers of Counter-Strike and Day of Defeat who cause normal mortals like me to stop playing those games out of having no chance of scoring a point. Maybe they only played the console version. Or maybe they only played the first level on normal mode, because the further I get through this game, the more that claim confuses me. The enemy can shoot back, and sometimes there will be little to no pause between the shots of one enemy and the next, making it almost impossible to break cover and shoot back without getting hit. It makes the grenades like precious gems, because they're the best way to clear enemies that won't hardly let you stick your head up. This game does challenge the player; not always fairly, but usually so. Then there are levels where you get in an Abrams tank or an Apache attack helicopter, where the enemy can't do an opium-picking thing to you, and the main challenge then is hitting everything and doing it fast, because you're always on the move.
Then there's the realism factor. Criticisms are: shoot an enemy anywhere and he dies, we're back to health meters and health packs, and the guns are just plain silly. To be fair, the rifles and pistol certainly are silly, and there's no good reason to spend an upgrade point on a new rifle, because nothing changes. Save it for extra ammo, health, grenades and faster reload time. The guns look highly detailed, but the player's small arms sound like Robotron fighting Megaman in the middle of a disco. The guns of your allies and enemies sound much better, and so do weapons mounted on vehicles. As for health meters and single shot kills, a health meter and health packs are much more realistic than many shooters where you just have to crawl under a rock and wait five seconds for all your wounds to heal, and single hit kills are more realistic than needing to put two rounds into a target's head or five into his chest. Think of the ArmA games: no mercy from bullets. I welcome the health meter back with open arms.
Now for the story. The problems that you can't escape from are the sloppy syntax and prose in this game, mainly in the journal entries before the missions. If you're thinking "This doesn't sound anything like a Marine, or any English speaker", then that's because this game was made by Teyon, a Polish video game developer. This is not the first game to have translation problems, but they could have done better on the journal entries (although the radio chatter in mid-battle sounds authentic). There are some other inaccuracies: the uniforms are Army uniforms and not Marine uniforms, and the Marines do not use the Black Hawk or the Chinook. As for the content, it doesn't deserve the hate that it gets from the politically correct about being a game in a real setting like Operation Enduring Freedom. Nobody has a problem with all the games set in the Second World War, where just about every side can be played as. Spec Ops: The Line, where your main enemies are American soldiers, has gotten a pass, so there's no ground to stand on when ridiculing this game for being from a modern American soldier's point of view. If you ask me, gamers could do with a healthy, even if unpleasant, dose of reality in their lives. Instead of trying to make some idiotic moral equivalence between the US and its foes, this game is based on authentic characters. The Marines are experts and professionals, who pull out all the stops to complete their mission with as few casualties as possible. The game punishes the player for friendly fire and civilian casualties, as it should if it wants to be taken seriously. The game doesn't name the enemy, it calls them “rebels”, but if you don't know who they really are, you must be living under a rock. They are portrayed accurately as well: they wear civilian clothes, take civilians hostage and hide behind them, and know no limits as to where they will fight from. Although the places and times of the battles aren't exact representations of real life, the concepts are real enough: combined arms battles in environments like mountains, small villages, big cities, and military bases. If you want something more varied and fantastic, then play Mass Effect or something.
Finally, I believe the game's greatest strength is in its visuals. They stand with the best of modern games. You could only get a better picture of the Afghan combat environment from a TV camera or actually visiting it. Every pocket of a uniform, every feature of a vehicle or weapon, and every contour of a building is superb. You have to deal with the very real problem of natural and artificial light in a battle, meaning it gets in your eyes. In an age where graphics are as advanced as they are, it might not seem like such a big deal that the game has excellent visuals, but how about when it has them and is selling for $5 on Steam? Now that's a cut apart, isn't it?
In the end, while it may not be my favorite game of all time, it was still a worthwhile purchase that I recommend.

This is a hard game to recommend to anyone.  Every time I start describing the experience of carefully selecting a team, training them, picking a sponsor and selecting your per-game bribes people get excited.  Then people hear that in every match there's a chance that your entire team will be injured or killed after gaining valuable experience points.  People's eyes tend to glaze over at this point.
It's the violence and death that make the multiplayer and campaign so good.  You know that every match will be brutal and chance as much as skill will turn the tide of victory.  Seeing the crowd turn on your opponent to tear them to shreds on a bad play or watching your own blocker critically fail a roll and bounce off the other teams ball carrier like the dude is made of force fields are just flipsides of the same coin.
You can be good at this game or bad.  Awesome or terrible.  In the end this game is like all true Games Workshop titles.  Skill is irrelevant.  The fun is in the stories you get to tell later about the crazy stuff that happened on the dice rolls and how they played out.  Play it with friends or enemies or the exceptionally active Blood Bowl community on Steam if you like, but understand that winning and losing aren't super important.  It's all about how the game plays you.
