If I could give you a computer with Bastion installed, start the game up, and tell you to sit there and play it, I would have a much easier time explaining why this game is truly amazing.
Gameplay: 9/10
The gameplay is truly great, especially as far as an indie game goes. With fluid movement and skill based fights, the simple block, roll and hit gameplay is perfectly done.
Level Design: 10/10
Every single pixel of each level is truly a sight to behold, with the world around you forming as you walk along it, the colour and general feel of the levels sets the scene for the game flawlessly. Each part of the world has its own gimick, making each step you take an adventure in itself. I was simply entranced by this beautiful world.
Music: 10/10
If I could put a rating above 10/10 for this, I would in a heartbeat. Bastion uses it's music in a masterful way, where the placement and soundtrack itself if phenomenal. A simple song in the right place at the right time adds a powerful amount of emotion and feeling to parts of the baron world.
Story: 10/10
This is the part that makes Bastion truly magnificent. The story itself is not the real winner, but the way the story is unraveled. As the first words are spoken "Proper story's supposed to start at the beginning, ain't so simple with this one." The story is told by one man, the narrator. The main character's name is unknown, and you are playing as him as you follow the narrators story. The narrator slowly reveals everything that needs to be revealed, as if he is reading a book of a time that has already passed.
Characters: 9/10
The characters are never heard, but just talked about by the narrator. The characters personalities are not extremely apparent, but each one becomes special to you over time, as they are the only ones you have to share Bastion's shaken world with.
Overview:
Bastion is special. The soundtrack is phenomenal, the world is breathtaking, and the narration is a brilliant new idea for gaming. Finding a new enemy in a normal hack-and-slash is an uneventful affair – you kill it and move on. But in Bastion, the entire battle with Sir Lunky – a giant, colorful frog with a stone-covered head– is narrated and given soul. By the time he’s dead you know more about him than most game characters, connecting you to the world. Nearly every moment of the game is like this, continuously reinforcing your attachment to the game. You’ll be cheating yourself if you skip Bastion

Despite the minor technical issues and the lack of replay value, this is still my favourite AC thus far. The drawbacks are not as noticeable as the game itself is actually quite amazing. The graphics is amazing, the narrative is relatively engaging and interesting, the parkour and free running system is probably the more fluid next gen game (VS Syndicate's horrible system). In this game, parkour has been made significantly easier with the newly implemented parkour up/down system, which allows you  to scale buildings with more ease. The ability to gain access to virtually every single legacy outfit is a huge plus as well. I strongly believe that this "tradition" is one of the more important elements of the game, and it's a huge pity that Syndicate decided to only introduce 2 of the many possible legacy outfits.
This game attempts to bring back the "old-school" combat that was seen in the first AC game, and I really like it. I'm also a huge fan of the wide variety of customization items available. However, it's a real pity that this game had so much potential yet Ubisoft decided to just downgrade it as usual. Even the mission we saw in a trailer/walkthrough at some gaming convention was designed specifically for showcasing the game. It wasn't even in the final game. Nor were the other 3 assassins that worked alongside Arno. It's a disappointment that this game could've been so much better, with the newly reworked parkour system, new graphical engine, the vast open world, and the co-op missions.

Hard to recommend a game in which none of the major problems of the first iteration are fixed.  And I'm saying this as a huge fan of the original original XCOM (1994).
The game is theoretically two games: 1)  Managing XCOM as an organization and 2)  Fighting squad based tactical missions to further your organzation and to degrade and ultimately destroy the alien threat.
The major problem is that the meta game (the stuff between the squad based combat missions) is the only aspect of the game that you can truly lose but it can't be lost by mismanaging the organization, it can only really be lost by losing the combat portion of the game.  If that sounds paradoxical, well, yes you're on to what I'm saying.  To clarify: you theoretically can put 20 hours into this game only to be sent back to the starting screen and told to start over.  But that never happens because the only way for that to happen is to lose a squad of your best troops and since that is so avoidable by loading your game continuously that's what the game becomes: a load-my-game-festival.  It's totally normal to load a mission 10 or 20 or more times in order to complete it with minimal losses; minimal losses that are effectively required due to the nature of the game.
The range of your solders ranges from rookies (I can't even throw a grenade across a street to save my life) to super solder extreme of blasting off multiple headshots across the map with over 100% accuracy.  The game scales in difficulty to require you to continue to upgrade your solders and have them keep pace by leveling up making the entire game hinge on the squad combat and the fact that there is only one way to win it: by having super-solder max level characters that you can't afford to lose.
And calling it squad based combat is a bit generous.  That would require the enemy to think on some degree of par with the player but that isn't what the game is about.  There isn't any overall strategy to what the enemy employs, you proceed in a map triggering various points that alerts squads to your presence, but they are not, in their entirity, acting as a united force trying to stop you.  Also the shot calculator is HORRIBLE, that is the RNG effects are truly horrid.  How % are determined is almost as bad with things like flanking and firing from multiple positions not having the effects that they should toward chance-to-hit numbers.
They could do a lot to fix the next iteration of this game by removing the load/save feature making all deaths permenant, but then counter balancing that with removing the total loss position of the metagame.  Meaning that a very bad mission result would push you back in progress but not expect you to start over clamoring for the load button.  Rookie recruits are near trash in this game so next bring the bottom level ranked troops up in quality and the upper ranks down to create a more realistic and useful range of what human beings are capable of.  Next change the squad based combat to actually allow for multiple strategies.  If I want to throw a bunch of meat against a mission and sustain heavy casualities then the penality shouldn't be losing the entire game but rather some other type of penalty to morale, funding, etc..  Fixing this would do a tremendous amount to fixing the core problem of this game that prevents most people that have no nostaliga factor for this game to get on board.
Also the dialogue is the most expository garbage I've heard in a long time.  The entire writing team should be fired and blacklisted from working on any other games.  It was Transformers 5 level awful.

Review Time :
--------------
There are many good aspects in this game, such as Perma-Death, Constant Updates, a trading server, easy-to-make friends, and a giant variety of items.
Not to mention if you ever get bored you can also play on private servers.
To be honest, there is no such thing as "Pay to Win" reason being because you can gain everything legit without spending a penny, and even if you decide to spend money there are plenty of sales and a 'Beginner pack' Which is very recommended.
Event Updates - As the year comes and goes there are many things added, and what is also included is events for Christmas, April Fools, etc. For example, last christmas they added the event called the 'Ice Cave'  which was a secondary source for Mana and a permanent added dungeon. And for this years April Fools they re-added the chicken for aprox. a week which gave custom items.
Grinding - Grinding takes a lot of time, but can become easier if you have friends. There are currently 8 stats to max, Life, Mana, Attack, Defense, Speed, Wisdom, Vitality, and dexterity. These stat potions can be earned in many different ways, through the Godlands, Dungeons, Realm Events, Oryx, trading etc.
Drops - There are many types of bags, but the most important are -
Blue Bags - Drops a stat potion.
Cyan Bags - Drops a high tier item ranging from 10 +
White Bags - Rare items that have a unique ability to them.
Guilds - Create or join a Guild and talk, cooperate, and host dungeons for your guildies!
There are a lot more positive things to say about this game that it's too much to list.
Overall Rating - 9.6/10

The game is very pretty. It is polished visually, but that is about all it does better than previous games.
Early game is fun when turns are short. Turn time increases at an alarming rate as you grow, if you want to keep your empire as productive as possible. It's similar to MoO2 in that respect, but MoO CTS is even worse in this area. A few examples:
Diplomacy and Espionage are arguably not as important as in previous MoOs; largly because of the changed research system.
Research is linear much like in Civ 5 with a few techs where you must choose between 2-3 different options ('choice techs').
The only techs that can change hands (via diplomacy or espionage) are the 'choice techs'. This means you can never advance your research by spying, and you can also never catch up in research by trading.
The reason for this review is that it's becoming more and more apparent, that they are creating the game for those that like the game as is; pointing to steam reviews being mostly positive, so everything is fine in their eyes. The problems listed above are non-issues to them.
Only buy this game if you like it for what it is now. Don't expect it to change.

Now,
has little to do with flight control. Surely, there are planes, helicopters and airports and surely, you don't want aviational vehicles to collide with each other. Other than that, it's just fun and casual management of emerging chaos in pastel colours.
You do get to control colourful planes. They randomly appear from the edge of the screen (with a convenient warning). If you wish, a handy tutorial will show you the ropes, but controls are fun and easy: just drag a path for the plane with mouse. Ideally, the path would end up in an airport, because points are scored for landing planes successfully. Each plane has a specific airport to land coincident by their colour.
You lose if two aircraft collide with each other. Since the game is in 2D this is hard to prevent for long.
While waiting for the inevitable, you can speed up the game. Conveniently enough, if two aircraft are on a collision course the game slows down to normal pace and highlights the two aircraft.
Even though this is nice, the highlighting backfires when there are many aircraft on collision course at once. It becomes difficult to see where the most urgent flying machine is. So you lose. And try again.
Initially I tried to do nice and pleasant-looking arcs and long-winded landings with the planes but I quickly noted that the planes can actually do 180 degree turns, which dissolved the simulation aspect.
Still, with a large enough number of planes to control, it does become difficult to manage. Different planes travel at different, albeit constant, speed with many having the same airport to land in adding to the complexity. A single game lasts just a few minutes at a time.
There are 9 different levels with varying difficulty (size, variety of planes) and even a couple with special features, e.g. wind that closes up certain airports. Special features are nice but they are only in place in few levels. There's a minor random element in most levels of slightly changing positions of the airports, of course coupled with a randomized appearance of planes.
A word on music: there's the same jolly, easy-going tune in most levels. Just a couple of levels have a special tune to fit their special theme. While the song is fine, it curiously stops after a while and doesn't resume for some time leaving you alone with the minor sound effects of collision alert and successful landing celebrations. Which are fine. It just weirds me out that the music is off for so long.
Even the nine levels do not last forever. There's content for a few hours of fun. For myself, 3 hours were spent on achievements, which were actually very well thought and enabled additional meaningful challenges. Then I spent an hour or so trying to beat my friends' highscores, regrettably without success. Consequently, leaderboards may or may not generate a few more hours of gameplay for you if you are so inclined.
The price is pretty good but since it is already an older game (almost 6 years old as of writing this), I'd recommend getting it on sale.

This review is not just for this game but for all the other 12 labours of Hercules games, which I think stands at around 5 so far.  Calling this a time management game just doesn't do it justice. Each game teaches you the game mechanics, then gives you progressively challenging levels until you encounter those levels that will require you to carefully problem solve and time manage to complete the level.  Each level takes around four to six minutes to complete.  Its a game where you can find you have a few spare minutes, play a satisfying challenge, then go and do something else.  I think this is one of the strongest features of the game!  You don't have to invest a lot of time to get enjoyment.  And if you do invest time, you will get a lot of enjoyment from it.  I think each game is worth owning.  I can't praise this series highly enough and I can't think of one feature of the game I would want to change.

This game has a bleak and depressing tone and that could be impressive if it was also technically well presented. As it is there is no options menu, pressing escape simply shuts down the game entirely. This is frustrating since the narative is slowly paced and there is a complete lack of a progression save system. However that can be forgiven in a game that takes 30 minutes to an hour to complete. The mouse sensitivity was a bit high so I tried for a menu and accidently quit. My dog started barking so I hit escape to pause and it quit. In a game entirely about narative, losing your place can pull you out of the story completely, a simple "Do you want to quit" menu would have sufficed.
My biggest complaint is that the narrative flow is abhorrent. Your character is simply too lazy to open many pieces of furniture for clues until he randomly decides that he should. There was a chest with a keyhole so I went in search of a keyring and I found it, only to discover that I didn't WANT to pick it up and that "Looking at the chest just made me feel tired." The scenery changes slightly as you progress but there is no indication of what changed and what you're willing to do  so that it is simply frustrating to continue. There is no feeling of agency and the flow could have been fixed with dialogue to the effect of "I should go look at that chest now" or "I think I heard something over there." As it is you are essentially clicking random stuff, often the same things over and over, until progress is achieved. If you don't do this you could fail to progress for a VERY long time.
The story, which I understand is the crux of the entire entity, is competent. Though you would do well to avoid it if you prefer to maintain faith in humanity. Existential fiction can be quite powerful and thought-provoking if wielded effectively but this is less intriguing and more depressing and neurotic.
Also I have to deduct points for the character having amnesia and

Overall the game needed a few extra layers of polish, which from a stable of 40 developers, no budget expectations or hard release date shouldn't have been a problem. This was obviously a labour of love and should never have been released in anything less than an absolutely finished state. In stark contrast to this game is Miasmata which was made by 2 people and contained not only an intriguing existential story but also intuitive and completely unique controls and gameplay mechanics.
There is something to be said for this as a "games are art" piece but you have to remember that mechanics and narative flow are fundament to the definition of a "game" and without properly good game design an artistic game can be little less than a very clunky movie or a book with improperly numbered pages. I wouldn't call this game "Bad" per se but not of particular merit. It at least had the intelligence to not charge money or hang around for twelve hours like a game by David Cage would.

First impressions review:
I've played only a few matches, but I enjoyed every one of them.
Of course, this game looks and plays as an early access game. There is still a lot of work to be done, but if properly polished and well maintained (as all mp titles should) it can be one of the best mp games.
Pros:
- Interesting concept with a great potential
- Well maintained balance between complexity of mechanics and dynamism (I think CS GO is a paragon in that sense);
Basic moves and actions are fairly simple to understand, but skill is required to be good, especially if you are a captain.
Both mechanical and tactical skills are needed - one should be aware of the situation, communicate and be a good team player and a fighter.
-Nice loudout system. There are no classes of anything like that, you just pick a weapon that would fit your style better ( in general - lighter or a heavier) and then you do what you have to do, or what your captain tells you to do.
- And yes, there are ranged and melee weapons. Currently there are 3 or 4  types of each, if I'm not mistaken. You have your rifle,  your pistol and a melee weapon.
You wouldn’t necessarily have to use them in a match, you can spend the whole time running around shooting and reloading cannons or fixing the sails, but deck fights are also fun when they happen.
How often they happen largely depends on the situation and playstyle.
- Fun character design and voiceover
- You can customize your char. Hopefully we will see more fabulous beard designs)  And yeah, bring in the parrots!
- So far community looks good, captains are smart and supportive of their crew ))
NB: Can’t comment on graphics as my rig is far from optimal and I don’t pay attention to visuals. To me they are ok.
Cons:
- Early access and all that goes with it  - some bugs here and there, some optimization issues.
- Deck fights need some polish first I think, they are fun but little bit hectic and sometimes buggy
- Server history would be nice
Bug report button and social media links are nicely put in the main menu. I personally got the impression that devs are good about community involvement and are interested in making their product better.

This game falls in one of two categories: You will love it immensely, or you will hate it and wish you never played it.
For starters, it has a tremendously high learning curve. I've put my share of time in with both this and the legendary edition and I'm still learning new tactics. Couple that with every single team having their own specific playing style that you need to learn to a certain degree, and you have a death sentence for a new player that isn't patient enough to actually learn the ins and outs of the game.
If you can get passed that, it CAN be a tremendously fun game. There are few things more satisfying then a miracle touchdown play on the last turn of a game. It can also be so incredibly disheartening that you'll rage quit instantly. That is the nature of a game built around rolling dice though. Tragedy is around every corner.
So what is it? A sports game? Sort of. It's most accurately a competitive turn-based strategy game that isn't balanced. Some teams are specifically there for scoring and making exciting plays. Others are there to break those teams and kill as many players as possible. A third type is a gimmick sort of styled team that can be fun if you can work your way around their (potentially broken) achilles' heel.
There are 23 teams in total in this game, providing enough variety that if you feel like you're not enjoying the game, it could just be you're not playing the right team. For example, my favorite team to play is Lizards. They can bash with the best of them, but the skink ball carriers are more than capable of doing some miracle-esque types of plays that make things exciting. However, I can't stand playing with (or against for that matter) slower, more hit-aggressive teams like Orcs or Dwarves, as they don't bring as much of a high octane energy that I enjoy. The enjoyment this game brings you starts and ends with the teams you pick.
I also recommend having a friend play this with you and not just jump into a league (public or private), as that will be good practice. It will also bring less of a feeling of angst when you start, as (hopefully) either they can help you learn OR you'll learn together.
So, all in all, it can be quite fun. I recommend it, but be warned this game is not easy to play, and can be emotionally crushing if you get invested in a team only to have your star players get killed by a blown dice roll.

I've been waiting patiently to write this and I may revise this upon the game being completed, but I doubt it.
When I heard they were remaking this game I was so stoked. Michael Dorn and Mark Hamill are doing voices as well, that's awesome! Bought into the early access and played the game, thought it was good. Beautiful, great sound and all my favorite races were back. The problem is each time I play it I find I'm less and less interested. The game seems to forgo deeper strategy for a glossy polish that simply makes the replayability slip and fall on it's♥♥♥♥♥
The combat is kinda fun, but I found myself simming through battles more and more. The only time I can remember doing that in Moo 2 was near the end and I had a gross number of doom stars and didn't want to watch every stellar converter animation tear my opponent apart. My choices don't feel like they matter in combat, and you know who will win by the difficulty bar before it begins.
The colony managment is a little better, but growth based off food supply doesn't seem to make much sense. Does having an abundance of food make my population sexually agressive? No freighters either so forget about colonizing that terrible radiated world that happens to have gems on it using food farmed somewhere else...
Tech tree seems really streamlined. By that I mean it's pretty boring. Different weapons don't "feel" different. They get a little blastier as you go, a little more green or blue, but nothing substantial enough to make a mark on your memory like some of the weapons in Moo 2.
Maybe that's not fair, this is a good 4x game, but every person who has played Moo 2 will have their opinion colored by their previous experiences with that game. Maybe they shouldn't have called it Master of Orion. The biggest problem with this game is I've already forgotten I own it and likely won't pick it up again. In contrast, if I'm flipping through my old CD book looking at old titles and find my copy of Moo 2. I usually spend that evening ignoring my wife and conquering the galaxy. I just don't see the staying power that title enjoyed.
So congrats, you cashed in on my nostalgia and made a decent game, but I wouldn't expect people to be talking about in... wow has it really been 20 years? God I'm old.

I grew up playing Master of Orion - and my favorite, Master of Orion 2 - and I was excited to see that the game was getting a reboot.
My goal was not to win, which I did, but to take Orion. I accomplished both on my first and only (thus far) play through.
Other than typos in the subtitles and some very basic gameplay bugs relating to things like memory and processing speed, the game was really well put together for not being a polished release. My family is a game industry family, so I have pretty high standards for a game in early access, and Master of Orion did not disappoint.
I would like to suggest, however, that the devs consider a couple of things:
1 - Make it more obvious when something negative is happening or about to happen. It was particularly difficult to keep track of the pollution levels of my dozen-plus colonies, for instance.
2 - More fun random occurences. I only had a handful of interesting things happen (quake, population boom, etc) in nearly 600 turns! Those, plus GNN, were my favorite things about MoO2!
3- PLEASE let there be a way to decline diplomatic messages from other races! They can refuse an audience with me - it's only fair I can choose to do the same!
Overall, the game FEELS right. I enjoyed it, I LOVED the voice casting, and I was impressed by the stability and playability of the game so far.
Questions for the devs:
- Will you bring back some of the other races, like the Elerians? PLEASE. I LOVE THEM.
- Are you going to do an Antares expansion-type thing at any point? That would be fun.
- I assume you guys will be introducing more of the tactical elements (or similar elements) that were in MoO2. Will you be making this version of the game more tactically-oriented, or are you starting off slow so that new players to the franchise don't get caught up in a very steep learning curve? For example, I'd love to see the leader assignments return and more opportunities for diplomatic interaction.
That's all. Thanks, guys! I loved it.

As an ATC (Air Traffic Controller), I really enjoyed this game, even though 2 hours are enough to get all of the achievements, playing a decent amount of times on each level.
The idea beyond this game is pretty simple : manage different runways regulating aircraft, taking into account their type (it means that they have different speeds : the largest, the fastest). You have to match the colour to land on the adequate runway, avoiding collisions. A safety net will trigger to warn you about a short term conflict so that you have enough time to react. Almost each level has a specific feature : wind, water, emergency aircraft (get out of its path !), stunt, ...
Initially, this game has been designed for tablets, but the gameplay is fine on Steam, even with a mouse and a keyboard : drawing trajectories should not be an issue. Having access to leaderboards kind of increase the end game, but, sadly, at the moment, almost nobody is playing this game. At only 3,99€, I strongly recommend it !

In the drought the West is on for a good recent MMO that is not♥♥♥♥♥♥bc of the business model and my hunger for an MMO that hasn't been sufficed in a while that also cannot wait for 2017 and Lost Ark (or Lineage Eternal - MU Legends for that matter) I found Trove really fun to play! And considering is Trion, so far I haven't had anyone tell me is pay-to-win or that you really have to pay for something to enjoy it.
Keep in mind this game is basically "questless" and has no storyline. You free roam doing dungeons and levelling up as well as gathering resources. It's basically like Minecraft but has a more RPG style touch to it, which I thank for.
My PC is not the best (i3 3220 - R9 270x - 8GB RAM) and I'm aware of that, however there have been more demanding games (Swtor, TERA, WoW, Overwatch, etc) that I can play 60+fps without problems even on low settings, however this game for some reason, I do have to play it on low. Medium and beyond doesn't give me 60fps at all. So I don't know if it's because I have an AMD card, or the game needs optimization... just keep that in mind when playing (yes, my drivers are up to date and I'm running latest Windows 10). This is not a deal breaker though.
You basically have a lot of classes you can choose from, which are switchable, each with their own role and skills as well as own "character inventory" (equipped things) that remain safe when you switch classes. Whenever you switch, the different classes have different levels (But mastery level is always the same).
If you're like me and you're tired of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Asian mmo ports with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ business models, and also don't wanna pay up (or can't) big cash for GW2, ESO, WoW or other game, you might like Trove. It has its own style and appeal and while the gameplay is not really overwhelming or surprising, it gets the job done for the meantime. :)
Edit: I forgot to mention that the "building/crafting" aspect of this game is quite complete! You've got gear, furniture, cube-color changing, etc. At first it might seem stupid or dull, but once you realize how deep the system is (for what it is tbh) you'll find yourself gathering resources all the time trying to get that sweet mansion with the ♥♥♥♥ing cool cubes you've always wanted!

Normal is brutal difficulty. Some criticize the timers. I love the timers, it adds an element of purpose and urgency and makes you plan precise moves to what would otherwise by less exciting game play.
You can give a good stab at a mission in under 30 mins so it is possible to play semi-casually. Saving often will soften the difficulty for more casual players.
If you played the xcom before this, you will be familiar with the formula and feel right at home. The story is more fleshed out on this one while not being overdone. There is more mission variety and mission randomization for replayability. There are also more items and unique items almost right off the bat for different playstyles.
If you played Fallout 1 or Fallout 2 and enjoyed the combat mechanics but not so much the exploring and story aspects, you should give this franchise a try.
This is also reminiscent of Syndicate Wars, and other isometric top-down  squad-based games, particularily ones set in dystopian futures.
Although I typically do not favor turn-based game-play XCOM 2 does it right, fast paced, I guarantee you will not get bored waiting for turns. Of the squad based games, including real time and turn based, this is one of the best and most polished, if not the best ever.

Best turn-based tactical game - hands down.
1. I love the time-based missions and want to seee more of that in future encarnations of this game.  I feel this was an excellent way to nudge the player from "gaming" the system - Spending several turns stationary, to recharge cooldown abilities and to reload.  While that strategy was very effective in previous XCOM games, it always felt as though I were cheating. Enemy Within (expansion to the previous XCOM game) was a step in the right direction, with the Meld containers, but I felt they did not quite get it right. The timed missions are a big improvement.
2. I thought the graphics were great for a turn-based strategy game, though I do have the graphics  at maximum setting.
3. Love the action-cam carryover from the pervious XCOM. I find it very emmersive (I suppose that is the point). I am suprised that more turn-based tactical games do not have something simialar.
4. I feel RNG in this game is well balanced. I will occassionally miss a high-percentage shot, but I simply counter that possibility through my tactics. For instance: If a  shot absolutely must land, or you may be flanked next turn, use a grenade or one of several other abilities/items that gaurantee damage. There are ample ways to counter the occassion RNG scorn.
5. Never had a crash and have yet to encuonter any bugs while playing, Very stable.
6. Music is very engaging as well.

Blood Bowl: Chaos Edition is a fantasy football video game with the option for turn based or real time game play. This game is an expansion to Blood Bowl that was developed in 2009 by Cyanide and published Focus Home Interactive and is based on the board game "Blood Bowl" that is produced by Games Workshop.
Blood Bowl: Chaos Edition has a great variety of game modes available for both single player and multiplayer that will keep you entertained for days providing the dice gods don't come down on you too harshly.
It is however recommended that you play using Classic mode and playing using turn based due to the fact that blitz mode is an awful edition to the game since it does not fit in well and functions clumsily.
There are a 23 races to choose from in Blood Bowl chaos edition and helps to add a nice variety to the teams you come up against, some races share similar players but overall there is a lot to choose from and picking what team you want to play as can take quite some time.
Blood Bowl: Chaos Editions graphics are perfectly suitable for what it is trying to achieve and generally looks visually pleasing and adds a fair amount of detail into the surroundings and units, for a game made in 2009 you defiantly can't complain.
On lower difficulty settings the AI make irrational moves that tend to lead to costly mistakes, while the higher levels of AI provide some challenge but you most likely will want to look for opposition using multiplayer.
If you want a faithful recreation of the board game Blood Bowl this is the only video game you should currently choose to try out due to the fact that it is quite high quality and is a quite compelling experience overall.
I highly recommend that you give this game a try if you like a challenging board game-esque strategy game.

BB must be judged in two seperate ways: as a boardgame, and as a pc game.
As a boardgame, it is an extremely interesting, very deep, beautifully balanced strategy boardgame. The variety of races, skills, and the fact that each team's playing style, potential and builds are truly unique and different, make it stand out.
The only fact that may discourage or frustrate players, is that luck may make or break a game of blood bowl. The game is intentionally made so, that anything can fail quite miserably, or succeed quite unexpectedly, if one is lucky enough. To some players this is intense and exciting, to others it is maddening and rage-inducing. Avoid, if you count yourself among the latter.
In general, it is one of the most interesting boardgaming experiences one may have.
As a pc game, it does have some advantages. It is pretty solid, and the multiplayer works excellently - it is relatively easy to find an opponent, and many times, even if one player loses connection momentarily, it succeeds in reconnecting. The community is usually friendly, and bad manners aren't that common.
On the negative side, everything other than the online multiplayer is laughably bad. The game doesn't feature any interactive way to teach you the rules of BB - of which there are many - and you have to learn them by reading the pdf rulebook. The single player campaign's AI is horribly bad; so bad, that playing vs AI has no value whatsoever, as the computer's moves are illogical, and the team builds it uses are unorthodox and usually worthless. Blitz mode is amazingly awful and doesn't deserve looking at.
Concludingly, I would say, BUY THIS GAME.
But only if you are fully aware what you're getting into: a deep, complex, multiplayer strategy boardgame with a steep learning curve. Oh, and visit
, it will make starting up a lot easier. Good luck, have fun.

Imagine yourself as a swashbuckling pirate soaring the seas, drinking, sailing, blundering, killing and hjijacking other players ships in an intense naval ship battle. Limbs blow off, sails break, rum is consumed, live are lost, but most of all, YOU are the captain of a pirate ship who took down 15+ players by ramming into them, boarding them, and trying to reload a musket that takes almost 15-30 second reload time.
As your reloading a cannon ball shatters your skull, your limbs explode in every direction. Your teammate next to you catches fire. He pathetically runs to the stern attempting to refill supply of canon balls not realzing he caught 3 other teammates on fire in the process. I, the captain of the ship, see the stupidy on my own teammates behavior from afar. I jump down, grab a bucket, and smother them with water; only to be hit with a canon ball killing all 4 of us instantly.
A giant hole is in the side of our ship flooding rapidly. My teammates spawn, pump out the water, patch up the holes until we notice the enemy ship only hundrends of feet away. "Oh my god" I cried, "We're going to get rammed" and we sure did. Now we're being boarded by the British (yeah, the people with gaps in their teeth) and being slaughtered one by one. Unable to face my failure, I jump onto the enemy ship, get a double kill with my shotgun musket, pull out my sword, kill 2 other players, take a swig of rum to heal -- my vision blurs from being drunk -- I collapse to my death with rum in hand.

Before recently I would have given the game a thumbs-down. The gameplay was just boring and got old very quickly. But things are different now, and the game is much better. The music is excellent and fits well.
My favorite part about this game is probably the musical instruments. You can find many different instruments in the game and then play your own custom songs through them. Think MIDI music, where the music files are made up of notes and have an instrument made for each of them. The music even transfers in multiplayer, so I could play "The Legend of Zelda Wind Waker - Dragon Roost Island" on a flute and everyone else would be able to hear. You can also play in groups, so one player could be using the violin while another uses the flute.
I will point out that I really like both Terraria and Starbound, but they aren't alike at all besides the fact that they both do the same simple things. Personally I enojoyed Terraria much more on my first playthrough but I believe Starbound has better replayablility.. if you could call it that.

Completely oscillating design changes appear on a patch by patch basis that suggest there is not so much a plan as a "hope this works" mentality.  I've spent many hours on this, and I can honestly say I enjoyed the first version far more than the last.  A half year in, and the game feels less finished and polished than the beta started with.
Maybe they will recover and launch to acclaim and wide-eyed optimism.  I no longer wait for that day.

In a world crowded with games that seem to be repeats and rehashes of the same thing,
may not stand out at first glance. It’s yet another time management game in an already large pool for the casual game market. However, this game has a spark to it that’s hard to explain. I personally ended up playing the entire game to the end and rarely found myself bored with the sometimes repetitive nature this genre can have. I highly recommend this title for fans of time management games.
One thing that stands out about the game is its story. It’s not very complex or in depth, however, I found it cute. As a fan of mythology I was drawn into the world of Hercules and his mythical friends like Pegasus and Medusa. Of course the story isn’t very accurate to the source material, instead taking a more whimsical approach and portraying Hercules as on the lazy side. But the demi-god jumps into action when his love Megara is taken hostage by Hades. The game progresses as Hercules travels to the depths of Tartarus to save his beloved.
As a time management game, the goal is to complete a certain list of tasks in each level to get to the end. Since Hercules is lazy, he has workers who clear the path for him and those workers need to be fed which means managing your food supply for them. Your other resources are wood and stones for building structures, fixing bridges, and filling holes- and then gold which is used to pay your mythical friends for their help. Certain things only Hercules can do, which also requires food, such lifting heavy boulders. The game has two modes, a normal one and a relaxed one. In both modes you are timed, however, the relax mode goes at a slower pace. Every ten levels you’ll have to play a mini game as Hercules, sort of like a boss battle, these are pretty fun and range from destroying boulders to shooting down attacking birds. I found that these levels helped break up what could easily be a very repetitive game.
The graphics are pleasant and colorful, they will grab your attention and keep it. Great for children and adults alike, I enjoyed the simplistic approach. It won’t strain your computer at all to run this game. The audio is alright, a bit generic at times but in no way annoying. The cut scenes also have voiced narratives but there is no other voice acting in this title. The game does have some sound effects so it’s not all background music. The character designs are well done as are the in game animations.
I ended up enjoying this game more than I expected to, it just was very cute and fun. It’s a great casual game for all ages and is the first in a series that follows Hercules on his adventures. The game on Steam has trading cards and achievements, if you play in relaxed mode they’re easier to obtain. I recommend
if you’re looking for a game to kill some time with when you’re bored and don’t mind relaxed paced games. There are no bells and whistles, it’s just a simple time management game that is very well done.

On the other hand, I was sorely disappointed with the overall game experience. Took me just under an hour to get through and at about 10 minutes in, many will have already guessed how the game will generally end. I suppose I was expecting more of a twist and because of that I was left hanging a bit. In addition, I wasn't a fan of the restricted movement around the cabin. Best turn-based tactical game - hands down.
1. I love the time-based missions and want to seee more of that in future encarnations of this game.  I feel this was an excellent way to nudge the player from "gaming" the system - Spending several turns stationary, to recharge cooldown abilities and to reload.  While that strategy was very effective in previous XCOM games, it always felt as though I were cheating. Enemy Within (expansion to the previous XCOM game) was a step in the right direction, with the Meld containers, but I felt they did not quite get it right. The timed missions are a big improvement.
2. I thought the graphics were great for a turn-based strategy game, though I do have the graphics  at maximum setting.
3. Love the action-cam carryover from the pervious XCOM. I find it very emmersive (I suppose that is the point). I am suprised that more turn-based tactical games do not have something simialar.
4. I feel RNG in this game is well balanced. I will occassionally miss a high-percentage shot, but I simply counter that possibility through my tactics. For instance: If a  shot absolutely must land, or you may be flanked next turn, use a grenade or one of several other abilities/items that gaurantee damage. There are ample ways to counter the occassion RNG scorn.
5. Never had a crash and have yet to encuonter any bugs while playing, Very stable.
6. Music is very engaging as well.

A white-haired, pensive kid hammers his way through a mystical landscape to restore his broken home from The Calamity, an event that wiped away all that is dear. Along the way, he conjures amicable friendships which are a part of what later seems like an ensemble of ghosts swaying to sweet-sounding tunes of the soundtrack. Amidst the dreamy action concerto running parallel to a jazzy voice-over, you might come to understand this is a story not just about the kid but of the world he is in and how its finely attuned harmony mirrors absolute chaos. Engraved with a melodic nature, the kid's journey seamlessly corners him into a cathartic finale. Its perfect pace is accompanied by challenges that require you to use the culmination of your skill and knowledge and leaves replay value based on how skillful you think you can get rather than an empty grind on achievements, Bastion is an unforgettable example of artistic achievement in video games.

Finally decided to get Xcom 2 on sale as I was unsure about the new mechanic, that is many missions have turn limits.
Also let me say first that I really loved Xcom EU/EW and have over 360h played. But the one mission I hated above all else was the bomb disposal mission. So honestly I expected Xcom 2 to be horrible.
I was so mistaken.
If Xcom EU/EW has just one flaw, it’s knowing you as a gamer you can only take a few steps forward with you soldiers and put them on overwatch, repeat this every turn till you encounter and alien force and you beat the game easily.
Now you can no longer do that in most missions and have to really pace yourself in a mission. Also with the way the world is under alien domination it all makes perfect sense, of course if you spend to much time on a map the aliens would box you in they control the country in question never mind the entire world. So it makes sense in a practical way.
Honestly Xcom 2 gives me everything I loved about the first and prevents me from cheating on my Ironman runs. So thank you so much firaxis.
Lastly a word on the DLC Alien Hunters and Shed’s Last Gift. I actually find the both to be good but Alien Hunters the better.
Lots of people complain about Alien Hunters, just remember this, you don’t have to activate the mission right away yet you can still get the weapons. So it is possible to use the weapons throughout your campaign wait till you have the best of everything the game has to offer and then do the mission. I did and sadly killed the viper king the first time he was spotted without him getting a single action.
All in all Xcom 2 in my opinion is the equal if not better than Xcom EU/EW.

I've played this for 5 years. While this is a port of an iOS game, the port is fine, there's no cash shop, and it's built up around actual game mechanics that have some actual depth behind them. The graphics are flash, so they're simple but scale infinitely without quality loss, regardless of the player's resolution. If you have multiple monitors like me there's some weirdness with the game pausing if I do something on a different monitor, but that ended up feeling like a feature instead of a bug most of the time.
The basic gameplay is managing different kinds of aircrafft that are coming in for landing at an airport. The craft can't land just anywhere and are color coded to match the correct runway. They're smart as bricks but always follow orders perfectly, even at their own peril. The player directs them by clicking and dragging their desired path, similar to how a graphic artist uses a vector pen tool. Different levels = different airports, with their own sets of obstacles and challenges. There are 9 levels and speed up button (hotkey F), but the game autodrops speed back to normal if it decides two planes are too close.
The main gameplay challenge to the player comes from the random nature of when and where planes appear, the game ratcheting up the number of incoming planes over time, and that the planes come in at different speeds. If two vehicles ever crash, the level is over.
So what kind of player is Flight Control HD for? The main appeals are:
(1) Stress relief/relaxation/a diversion. Somewhat like the effect last hitting and denying in DOTA produces for some people, Flight Control creates a zen sort of state where I can turn my higher brain off, wind down, and just enjoy directing planes around for a bit, then get back to whatever I was doing. For me the perfect time to do this is when I'm trying to solve a completely different problem. The casual pick-up-and set-down-whenever-you-want nature of the game also lends itself to this. The soundtrack has only one song. While it won't win any awards, it does fit the mellow mood the game is going for quite well.
(2) Score attack, and RTS micro practice, although this can conflict with using the game to relax. There are online leaderboards, which still work fine 5 years after the game was released. As far as I can tell, the leaderboards also seem to be free of cheating unlike, say, certain indie platformers or the latest Call of Duty titles, so props to the developer for that. Levels start easy but ramp up to quite hard if you're going for a top score. In other words, the game scales with what you put into it. As a result you'll probably get out exactly the level of challenge that you want. Be warned that having 50+ planes on the screen gets stressful, especially on maps with a lot of plane types. My brain just doesn't like that, and I've ragequit a few times.
Probably not worth full price, but for me this game has been surprisingly good.

I went into this game apprehensive. I loved the SNES Harvest Moon and none of the future installments of the series ever really "clicked" as well as that one, though a few came close (mainly Back to Nature). So for me, farming simulation games are held to the high standard of SNES Harvest Moon.
Boy, was I surprised. This game exceeded any expectations I could imagine. How do I sum up a game as great as Stardew? It's an escape from reality, that draws you in with charm and simplicity.
First, the farming aspect. This is handled wonderfully. There's a wide variety of crops (including mods that add even more, but more on that later). There's even something Harvest Moon didn't have, in automated sprinklers. This makes tending to large amounts of crops at once so much easier, and they aren't gated behind large walls, they're realistically obtainable with little trouble. There's even a crow system implemented, requiring you to place scarecrows within 8 spaces of a crop, or it risks being eaten. The scarecrow has a large enough range that it doesn't get over-saturated in the field, but helps improved realism in that birds will eat crops if there isn't something adequate like a scarecrow to scare them off.
Animals are handled wonderfully in the game, and come in multiple varieties. There's 4 types of chickens, 2 types of cows, the expected pig and goat and even other species to mix it up for a farming game, like Rabbits and Ducks. There's even hints of Slime Rancher, as you're able to breed and raise Slimes of your own, from eggs you obtain from killing slimes in the mines, or from making them out of slime balls with a specific machine. There's one other animal but I don't want to ruin the surprise. It's probably the most imaginative of the animals and although it detracts a little from the immersion, it's worth it.
Second, relationships. Everything you do for someone, be it giving them a gift (twice a week max), or even just talking to them gives you friendship points. Giving them a gift on their birthday multiplies the amount exponentially. (CA was smart and made it so you can still give a birthday gift if you'd reached the 2 a week limit already) As you talk and befriend these NPCs, their attitude towards you changes. You'll see a ton of cutscenes where you learn more about these NPCs, usually 2 each, though bachelors and bachelorettes have 5-6 each. Some characters have complete personality changes while you gain friendship with them. This is one of the best parts of the game, as it helps really immerse you in the game.
My ONE gripe with this game however, is that each day you don't talk to someone or give them a gift, you lose some friendship points with them. It isn't much, you only need to talk to them like once a week to negate an entire week of neglect, but it sometimes can be arduous tracking down all 33 villagers each week. However, if you manage to reach 10 hearts with someone, their friendship will cease to decay. (or 8 hearts for bachelors/bachelorettes you haven't started dating yet)
One thing that makes this game stand out from Harvest Moon and Rune Factory to me is that you are free to marry whoever you want (Well, if they're a bachelor/bachelorette). There's no gender limitations. If you marry someone of the same gender as you, you simply adopt children, rather than one of you getting pregnant. For me, this was a big selling point of the game.
And although not a part of the main game, there is a very active modding community that does things from adding new crops, adding entire new areas, adding new villagers, adding new animals, etc. If you can think of it, it's been done. You want the bachelors to be bachelorettes? There's a mod for that. You want the portraits to be anime-style? There's a mod for that. Wish you could access your chests anywhere? There's a mod for that. The modding community for this game is amazing and just adds to the longevity of this game.
There's so much more I could go over, but Stardew at its core is about farming and the friendships with the townspeople, so to keep the review short, I'll stop with that. Don't think that's all there is in Stardew though! There's fishing, mining, questlines, and an epic quest to restore the beaten down community center, should you choose to take on the challenge.
I will however say one last thing: Nothing in Stardew Valley is timed, and the one thing that is can be repeated at any time, so you never ever have to feel rushed. Completing something in Year 6 would be the same as completing it Year 1. You're completely and utterly free to relax and do things at your own pace, and be 100% confident that you won't miss out on anything.
Long Story short: After Stardew Valley, Harvest Moon SNES is no longer the standard for these types of games for me. Stardew Valley is. Be careful while playing it, you'll find yourself telling yourself "I'll go to sleep after this day." and then it will suddenly be 5 hours later. You really get lost in this game, and time passes very fast.

A great game given new life. A couple of hints to improve gameplay. The game only runs slow because the CPU cycles in dosboox are set too low by default. To change this hit alt-enter while in game. This makes the window smaller so you can see the CPU count on the top left, it should read  3000. Hit Ctrl-F12 many times till it reaches a smooth frame rate, this is around 52301 for me. Hit alt-enter to return to full screen.
Alt-S  turns sound on and off in game.
F10 allows the detail levels to be set higher.
In campaign mode your supply and bombard task forces will change speed as they approach Henderson field without you ordering it. This is not a bug, this is done automatically by the computer to allow your ships to reach Guadalcanal at nighttime to avoid air attack.
There is a new patch update to the game which fixes some waypoint issues and comes with the manual.
Many times in battle, ships or columns under your control will not do what you want. Usually this happens when ships in formation take damage lose speed, jam their rudders or swerve to avoid damaged ships. It is frustrating but realistically frustrating!  The enjoyable part of this game for me is trying to keep the task force in organized-order throughout the battle. This rarely happens. It is easier to do this in later battles as the Americans as they have radar and can detect and fire upon the Japanese out of visual range.
If Japanese destroyers see you and illuminate you with flares, you will have torpedoes hitting you within a couple of minutes. Then you will die.
The ships and shells are really 3d not sprites. This means ships are damaged where they are hit and shells are tracked individually on their trajectory as they leave the guns all the way hit or miss.
If you were frustrated or appalled the first time you saw this game  read the manual play the tutorial and work yourself into it.

An initially disappointing re-release of an old relic.  Oversights included a missing manual, an unapplied patch, unoptimized DOSBox settings, broken DRM and some "extra" files.
This issues have thankfully been corrected, so I can recommend this game now... with caveats.
This is a direct-to-DOSBox dump of the 1992 game.  If you were expecting any modern updates or conveniences, you won't get them.
TF: 1942 decent attempt at a WW2 3D naval simulator covering the crucial conflicts around Guadacanal.  These were brutal and often-confused (at least from the American side!) slugging matches between generally equal forces.  Historically, the USN took quite a few to the chin before they got their act together.  You can play either side, and can man various stations on the ships involved, and/or control things from a more strategic perspective.  There's lots of ships to play with, but unfortunately air power is not taken in to account -- the focus is strictly on the surface action.  As for that action, you get fixed scenarios, campaigns (that can be a little wonky), and a scenario builder so that you can match the USS South Dakato vs. a bunch of Japanese transports, or whatever.
Graphics and sound are straight outta 1992.  The ships were remarkably detailed (in clean, untextured polygons) for the day, however.  Controls also harken back to the dark days for pre-professional UI design, so be prepared to read the manual to figure out what's going on.
So, look -- this game is OK.  A dinosaur, but some of us have fond memories of our dinosaurs and want to spend time with them again.  Younger gamers -- even those grognards and history buffs amongst that set -- will likely sniff over this as move on.

The main reason to play this game is for the story, most particularly the interesting way that story is presented.  Everything is narrated, and the narration serves both to guide the player through various parts of the game, it's also informed and appropriately altered by the player's actions.
The gameplay is very solid in most aspects, and works very well in its isometric framework.  The graphics are excellent, and it's endlessly fascinating to watch the stages gradually take form as you move around, and just as fascinating to run around destroying as much of it as you can.  The real star of the background is the music, however, which is just chock full of beautiful and catchy sounds.  Shelling out $9.99 for the soundtrack is a bargain as far as I'm concerned.
The mechanics of the game have surprisingly little variation given how many different weapons, abilities, and the like that are available.  Many of the enemies can be taken out in a lot different ways, meaning there's very little reason to bother switching away from whatever weapon you've picked as your favorite since odds are it'll still do the trick.  I do like the combat, but I also think it could have benefited a great deal from just a little more depth.
A very fun game with a damn fine soundtrack and a good, thought-provoking story presented in a unique way.  I would definitely recommend giving it a try, and I personally look forward to seeing and playing SuperGiant Games' future endeavors.

I'm unsure whether I recommend this game or not. Features I loved in previous titles didn't make an appearance in this one. However, this isn't a terrible game even though it has more cons than pros. The main reason I still play this game is because it takes place during the French Revolution, my favorite part of history.
-The environment feels alive. The streets are absolutely packed with people. You can hear different conversations (in French, of course). There are entertainers. There are random guillotine executions. Criminals killing civilians. Thieves stealing. People getting bullied. It makes me feel comfortable.
-This game picks up where the story was left off in Rogue.
-You can enter buildings. Some NPC's will be confused to why you're there, as it can be their home.
-The city is large.
-Beautiful sights for taking screenshots.
-The guards are actually a challenge. They fight back and use their items such as stun grenades.
-Character customization. Sadly, the color choices are awful.
-You and your enemies have wounds appear when hit. Blood even splashes on walls.
-The map is in 3D.
-I haven't encountered a single bug and I've been running 60fps with ultra high quality graphics.
-Your character Arno is an idiot. He kills important people before the assassins could look into the situation. This makes the story lacking and boring.
-The only way to kill a Templar is by using your hidden blade. Sure, you can kill them with your sword and all, but you have to go back and stab them with your hidden blade in order to continue.
-You cannot jump off of buildings as you please. You can jump from building to building or climb down, but you cannot jump off onto the ground quickly.
-There's horse crap everywhere. Literally, you can go onto any street and you can find 3-5 piles of horse crap. There's about 3 horse carriages and that's it. I'm guessing it represents the storyline.
-Animations are slow and they're too smooth. Arno literally just floats from building to building. He doesn't even lose health when jumping from 20ft in the air.
-The guard fights are slow and they shoot you if you attempt to flee.
-The game's controls ignore the direction you want to climb.
-All of the characters suck. I usually like characters immediately when introduced, but Ubisoft just did a terrible job.
-Most of the missions are difficult and frustrating. Purchasing upgrades is almost useless because there is hardly any change in skill and strength.
-There are no checkpoints during one mission. If you die, you start everything all over again; such as infiltrating the building, locating your target, assassinating them, and escaping the area. I've been stuck on one mission for the longest time which prevents me from playing this game.
-The characters don't have French accents. Ezio at least had a strong (and fake) Italian accent, while this game has British accents.
-The story doesn't even mention the French Revolution. It completely ignores all the dangers that
happened to the characters.

Having played the beta of the original Blood Bowl when it first came out, I wasn't massively impressed with it, and left it a long time before considering again. When the Chaos edition went on sale for £5, I spent a while trying to decide whether it was worth the gamble, and it turns out it was.
First things first, it's important to note that this is a dice-based game, so there are going to be stretches where you get a run of bad rolls and lose to teams you should beat, players die from tripping over their own feet and falling over, and you can't pass the ball three yards under no pressure whatsoever.
Once you're past the luck-based side of things, this is a pretty faithful rendition of the Blood Bowl boardgame, albeit without the need for a mountain of paper and three hours to finish a match.
Each side has their own strengths and weaknesses (although team balance is a little screwy - there's not much reason to choose outside of 5 or so teams of the 20+ available, that's Games Workshop's error, not Cyanide who developed the videogame version), and there should be a side to suit most playstyles, from 'pass it around' to 'kill the other guys, we'll worry about the ball later'.
Overall, it's not going to blow anyone away, but if you're looking for a nice sports game with a twist, or you like the concept of Blood Bowl but don't have/want to spend all afternoon shuffling bits of paper, this could be a good buy.

XCOM2 is not flawless. It has bugs, including very unfortunate ones (isn't it fun to find out that your beloved colonel Ranger, who has recently become Death, the Destroyer of Mobs, and was knocked unconscious, can't be picked up and will have to go MIA?). The core gamplay of XCOM has long become legendary, and it's as slick and fun as ever, with clear distinctive visuals, great level design, and the ever-beloved option to design your whole extended family into not-quite-space marines and watch them die excruciating deaths due to missing three 90%-chance shots in a row.

Would recommend for: Harvest Moon fans, Animal Crossing fans, first time gamers, Minecraft fans, and rpg fans.
The controls and concept of the game itself is fairly easy to grasp. Stardew Valley has enough challenge in finding and catching the various gems/ores/fish/etc and building your farm all while keeping up your relationships with the townsfolk.  This will keep you busy for a while and remain interesting. There is a crafting system and a building system to set up your farm, and over farm design can become critical. It is all customizable, so you can easily make choices on what you want your farm to focus on. There is a social system that requires you to maintain relationships regularly. No slacking off in that department or you may fall behind everyone socially and wind up a bachelor/bachelorette. For  gamers that have played the Harvest Moon franchise this is a better version or at least equally as good as any of those games. I, personally like it better for the crafting system and ability to design my own farm. It has plenty of story for rpg fans, and is heavily goal oriented. The goals are very clear in the form of a journal and level system that allows you to prioritize which tasks you wish to focus on early game vs. mid and late game. Ultimatly, it makes for a very satisfying, relaxing experience. Great game to come home to and play after work for a few hours, with a high replay likelihood.

Before recently I would have given the game a thumbs-down. The gameplay was just boring and got old very quickly. But things are different now, and the game is much better. The music is excellent and fits well.
My favorite part about this game is probably the musical instruments. You can find many different instruments in the game and then play your own custom songs through them. Think MIDI music, where the music files are made up of notes and have an instrument made for each of them. The music even transfers in multiplayer, so I could play "The Legend of Zelda Wind Waker - Dragon Roost Island" on a flute and everyone else would be able to hear. You can also play in groups, so one player could be using the violin while another uses the flute.
I will point out that I really like both Terraria and Starbound, but they aren't alike at all besides the fact that they both do the same simple things. Personally I enojoyed Terraria much more on my first playthrough but I believe Starbound has better replayablility.. if you could call it that.

Just played my first 15 minutes of it, and I was surprised at how fun it was!  So, I'm writing an initial review immediately and I'll update it later.
At first I thought it might be too simple to suit me, but it got challenging VERY fast.  Plus, you can redirect flights as often as you need to avoid collisions.  In some ways this reminds me of some of those old Atari games but with a fluffy modern twist.

Update:  I've played enough now to say....this thing gets massively hard, FAST!  hehe  Nobody will ever accuse this game of lacking challenge.  This game will _break you_!  lol  It has leaderboards for each map too.
Even the first map gets very challenging after 50 planes, and is rough getting over 100.  My high score is 150 and I'm amazed that I managed that.  I usually lose between 70-100.  I just finished trying the 3rd map, a 5 star map.  It started off slow and easy, and then it opened the mother load on me after about 10-15 planes.  Wow!  Talk about massive mega challenge.
The only thing I would suggest to the Dev, is to add a 3rd speed which is 50% slower than the slow speed is now, that way we can really try and get strategic and micromanage our way through really heavy jams, rather than just saying, "I always lose about here".  That would be great, because as it is, you really can't get too far, unless you're an absolute pro at this sort of thing.
Imagine playing Tetris and going from level 1, to 'Insta-Drop' in less than 5 minutes.  That's how hard this gets that fast.  Again, I still highly recommend this.  Very fun!

So far, TU is looking like a good, faithful port of GMod Tower to the UE4 engine. It already has many beloved minigames from GMT (Chimera Hunt, Virus, Ball Race, etc). Most of the minigames are fully functioning, but many are still WIP (Virus, Planet Panic). The only thing that bothers me about TU is that they didn't keep the original GMod Tower servers up while Tower Unite is still in development, personally they should have kept them up at least until TU got out of Early Access. The developers have an actual roadmap, listen to the community, and from what I've seen they're working tirelessly to get this game out of Early Access by 2018.
Here comes the big question: Should you buy Tower Unite? If you're a fan of GMod Tower or you simply want to support the devs in this endeavor, yes. If you weren't a previous GMod Tower player or you're skeptical about Early Access games, I wouldn't buy it however. The game is still in a pretty early state, so a lot of content isn't there. However, it is fun to mess around in for a while.
Narrative and the story are great. It won't take long, maybe 30-60mins, so don't miss it if you like interactive storytelling. Moreover - it's free!

Serena is what I would call an unorthodox treat. While taking it's cues from a traditional point&click adventures, it doesn't offer a traditional gameplay experience. There are no puzzles or sprawling environments to explore. Instead, the gameplay elements serve fully and solely to deliver an immersive narrative. It would certainly not be uncalled for to consider it more of an interactive short story. And as such, it delivers.
Without spoiling too much: The way the progression of narrative is set up serves perfectly in drawing the player into the mental state of the protagonist, planting subtle seeds of self-doubt and confusion. The visual presentation, while limited, is spot-on, and the voice performances are strong and charismatic. All of this adds up to an experience that evokes multi-layered horror where the implicit is more disturbing than the explicit.
Highly recommended for any fan of horror and/or challenging narratives with a good hour to spare!

XCOM2 is not flawless. It has bugs, including very unfortunate ones (isn't it fun to find out that your beloved colonel Ranger, who has recently become Death, the Destroyer of Mobs, and was knocked unconscious, can't be picked up and will have to go MIA?). It has way too much unskippable animation—even in the faster mode you'll still see "cinematic" overwatch triggers, and managing the base can get a bit tedious due to, once again, animations. Sometimes you can fight the cursor for a minute while trying to make your Ranger attack the enemy from the right side.
But these are all extremely minor gripes, of course. The core gamplay of XCOM has long become legendary, and it's as slick and fun as ever, with clear distinctive visuals, great level design, and the ever-beloved option to design your whole extended family into not-quite-space marines and watch them die excruciating deaths due to missing three 90%-chance shots in a row.
The price tag is intimidating, but if turn-based tactical games appeal to you in the slightest, you definitely should buy this.

Do I look forward to playing this game?  Yes.  Do the kids look forward to playing this game?  Yes.  Do we all look forward to exploring the game with each new early access incarnation?  Definitely yes.  I have had this game since early access 1 (EA1).  It has been and continues to be a fun ride seeing the large and small changes the developers make along the way.  As of the time of writing this review, the game is in EA5.
The game is not yet perfect, but you can sort of feel the trajectory the developers are taking with changes to certain areas of the game.  Feeling nostalgic, I played through a couple MOO2 games recently for comparison.  I now feel colony management on this game is much improved over the original.  This has been something the developers have been making steady changes to with each EA incarnation.  I feel that ship design in the original is still a bit better because one really gets a sense that the way the ships are designed, what systems are installed, really affects their viability.  I was surprised to find that the turn-based combat I used to love in the original game became a bit tedious and I was actually looking forward to the real time combat we have here in this new Master of Orion game.  However, the addition of some turn-based elements to the combat system with the addition of hotkeys to activate various ship systems real time shows to me that the developers are addressing my concerns about ship design but doing it in a real time combat world.  Kudos.  Lastly, with the EA5 update they even brought back the beloved creative/uncreative options as well as added some other novel bundled “Special Abilities” picks to the race creation scheme.
Come, join this journey with us.  Provide constructive criticism of what you do not like.  Provide feedback on what is working well.  Make this game into something worthy of bearing the name of Master of Orion.

Because of the fixed and predictable tech tree each game tends to unfolds the same way.
Your opponets don't have any unique and destinctive tech, they have what you have, or will have or use to have. Hardly makes it woth spying on them.
Combat is dull:
You start over here, they start over there and you charge one another. As there is very little input from the player you end up being a spectator in your own game. yay
You don't decide what to shoot or who to shoot at, the AI does that for you.
You select a squad and the AI makes the fire decisions, usually badly.
eg A cruiser shooting at a group of frigates, it will shoot up one, take a bit off it shields then switch targets to an undamaged frigate. Nothing ever gets killed, meanwhile the frigates eventually wear you down. You will find yourself muttering "Just pick one and KILL IT"

Laser Dmg 5, Rng 50
Neutron Blaster Dmg 9, Rng 50
Gravaton Cannons Dmg 25, Rng 50

Planetary growth

The AI offers you 62 credits for your star maps and gets progressivly hostile if you refuse them.

Your ally will progressivly become less happy with you each time you refuse to accept a tech exchange with them.

There are worlds out there with different biomes, desert, volcanic, swamp, toxic, radioactive, etc

Wonderful! Love the in-depth character modelisation, the graphics, the gameplay, and the touch of realism that exists in every interaction. The passionate modding community also makes playing non-vanilla  a treat, although the vanilla game itself is extremely well done and enjoyable alone.
Some comments: the bachelors and bachelorettes are of difficulty-interpretable ages. Some look like middle-aged men, others look like they are in their twenties, and most of the bachelerottes look like pre-teens or late teens. It's a bit creepy. Mods can fix this somewhat.

ConcernedApe is also very involved in fixing these things, and I am excited to play the new DLC available in 2018 + multiplayer.
Negatives: Default dialogue can be repetitive and uninteresting after a few years of play. The fact the game never technically ends can be both a good and a bad point: I'd like to feel some level of accomplishment beyond grandpa's rating on Spring 1 Year 3. The Xbox Windows controller is not 100% intuitive. French is not yet available, despite being spoken as a first language by over 280 million people worldwide.
Overall, for fans of Animal Crossing, Harvest Moon, Story of Seasons, and Terraria, Stardew Valley comes highly recommended!

[Disclaimer - I've played this game through many times, just not on Steam so my play stats aren't accurate]
Simply beautiful.
What? You want more? Okay. On the surface of it, Botanicula resembles a highly polished version of those online "click all around the screen and interesting things happen" Flash games. And I suppose that's exactly what it is. Unlike Machinarium, Amanita's previous big success, the focus here is less on solving minigames and more on encouraging interaction and exploration. With that in mind, this game is probably more suitable for younger players (although it does get quite dark towards the end) or casual gamers.
Thoroughly charming, with a beautiful setting, fantastic incidental music, memorable characters (who again, tell the entire story without a single line of dialogue) and wonderfully inventive set pieces make this a game well worth your time and effort.
Be warned though, it does run on Adobe AIR so if you have problems with that particular application you may want to try the demo first.

Gave it a negative review on account of having game breaking bugs still lingering years after its release. Decided to change my review because it's actually quite an enjoyable game and it's got a ton of content, mind a heavy lack of RPG elements. The bugs do have solutions in the end, and I only encountered one that messed up things. It only happened once though.
So, the good:
- Astonishing environments. The game hasn't aged a bit in this regard. And actually, in any regard.
- Charismatic protagonist. Haven't seen one since Ezio.
- Lots of customizing options for the character.
- Lots of content, more diverse and better built than in previous franchise installments.
- Interesting enough story. More personal, therefore more immersive. It was refreshing seeing the protagonist not giving much of a crap about the assassins vs templars mumbo-jumbo, being passed by an ancient artifact on the fly and not knowing or caring much what a sage was. Also, there are very little "present day" interruptions. Always found them annoying.
- Great dlc. Its atmosphere is even more immersive that the main game's, and it's also got a lot of content.
The not so good:
- Heavy lack of RPG elements. As in cutscenes that would've brought us much closer to the protagonist and would've made the experience much more immersive. The story is better than in the previous latest installments, but you end up not caring much about it. It's still there just to justify the sandbox.
- Movement bugs. While the parkour is more realistic and spectacular, the character's response to commands it's awkward and he gets stuck in many places.
- Not really a fan of the new combat system. It's still good enough though. Still spectacular.
The really bad:
- The "corrupt save" bug is still there.
